For those dying to have another experience like Dark Souls, this game will do the trick. If you haven't played that game but are looking at this review instead, do yourself a favor a play that one first.
Lords of the Fallen features the similar weighty and meaty combat the series is known for. Weapons have a satisfying heft to them.  You've also got tough boss enemies, and ability/magic system, and dying in the game has the consequence of placing all of your experience points in jeopardy.  In short, it's an acceptable emulation of the Dark Souls system that believes that each enemy and each player life should be important.  The difficulty is tough, but compelling.
Downsides: the game was not optimized well, and I had frequent problems on a 560 Ti, although patches have made things a little better.
The level design, while pretty, isn't nearly as intricate or intriguing.  The Souls series have always had amazing level design as a major highlight, and this is lacking here. The visual design for weapons and armor is way too busy, almost cartoonish.
The story is much more direct, disregarding the subtle environmental storytelling of the series.  Unfortunately, what's left is pretty much forgettable.
All things considered, Lords of the Fallen was an enjoyable game, provided one takes it's efforts to emulate Dark Souls as a sincere compliment and is not too disappointed that the game doesn't quite measure up.

So I played this game for a few hours, this was mainly on the first few days of it being released, a friend got it for me actually, a very kind man and I am thankful he did. I played 80 hours but I couldn't find anything redeeming about it, in fact, I played for 30 hours and found that. I continued on for another 50 hours because I had a lot of map to explore and I didn't want my friend's money to go to waste.
This game is not an RPG like the Fallout games I know and love, it wants to be, but it isn't. It's not even like Skyrim where it can pretend to be an RPG and give you stats, it just has perks and given that I heard the levelling cap is removed, all characters end up the exact same. I spent my time as a wanderer who wished to scavenge in the ruins of Boston, taking what parts he could to modify guns and sell them on to make a living for himself, eventually setting up a base in a garage to keep himself safe from the raiding parties and the harsh wasteland. Except I wasn't a scavenging wanderer trying to exist peacefully, I was Nate. A war veteran who had a child and a wife and was frozen for 400 years and woke up to find his son gone and had to look for him. Good for Nate, I might have liked Nate too if the game wasn't called Fallout.
Really the game is not awful, the shooting is decent, I like the fact there's a cover system and emenies use it, the gun customisation is alright even though it doesn't lead to anything too dramatically amazing, I like the idea of legendary enemies that drop randomised rare loot that give bonuses. I have a nice collection of them, though most of them are Leather Left Legs for some reason, that's how the cookie crumbles. I heard the DLC is middle of the road, really I never had much interest in going back since I was never invested in the plot and I don't feel like I'm progressing, every quest is go somewhere, find a thing, go back. I am thankful that there are no Draugr in every location but it's very similar to that idea, a nice pretty shooting gallery with little options.
I'm not going to say anything else about the game, other people have said far more than I have and in better words, youtube is your friend for 2-3 hour analysis videos or the like. I actually wasn't going to leave a review but I got an update which added a bunch of unnecessary files when I wanted to give the game another shot, files like "PipBoy(Black) - Main.ba2" and other such names. I found out that they were a part of the Creation Club, another shot at the paid mods that Bethesda tried and failed with Skyrim and that Bethesda more than likely want me to pay for the .esm file so that I can turn my Pipboy Black, I would have been thankful for them perhaps also giving me the .ba2 if I ever made such a purchase too and not just force it onto me, but that's too much to ask.
I don't want unneeded crap on my hard drive, I don't want a game trying to masquerade as a series with so much choice and diversity in what you can do and I sure as hell don't want to pay for my mods in a game that £40 was spent on, I wanted to play Fallout and I think I will go do that but this isn't a Fallout game. I wont buy your paid mods Bethesda, I wish you respected me enough as a consumer to not put them on my computer anyway.

Played for a few hours now. Likely won't be bothering to finish it.
Good things about it: with proper hardware, have not experienced any crashes at all. No apparent glitches (things that aren't supposed to happen).
Things I'm not thrilled with:
- chromatics? wearies the eyes
- checkpoints? well, you can get used to them, but being forced to replay a hard-won fight just doesn't cut it for me
- overly complex attribute system, at least for me. Some might enjoy this sort of thing. Boosting my attributes did not really seem to matter as I progressed in the game, causing me to feel I wasted my time on those screens.
- weak dialogue. If you're going to add interaction, then add it, don't just make a stab at it.
Things that put me off this game:
- KEEP THE DAMN CAMERA FOCUSED!!!! I cannot hit an enemy if I cannot see him because the camera goes from a horizontal view to a vertical view. Have it back away so you can see the field AND your opponent.
- my character moves (during fights only) like he's drunk. Reaction time sucks (and that is with weight being 1/4 of maximum capacity).
- weapon's reach is too short (I've got a LONGsword, why doesn't it hit my opponent unless I'm standing on his toes???!!).
- too many keys for different moves. A light attack key and a heavy attack key? Why not just hold the attack key down a bit longer to initiate a heavy attack? I'm killing a monster; hit it hard, kill it fast. These aren't duels, I don't get points for style, only survival.
- being able to see would be nice. In the area of the monastery, I really do appreciate how accurately the environment of a destroyed, deserted monastery was recreated. BUT, I only detected some of the infected because their health bars appeared. Torches, lanterns, something would have been useful to see where things were. I played in a very dark room and still could not see half of what was around me. Hard to explore when you don't know what's nearby.
My hardware consists of a 4-core CPU running at 4.3GHz, 24GB of memory, and an nVidia GTX970 w/4GB DDR5. I use only a keyboard and mouse.
Remember these are just my opinions after some hours of playing this game. Check out the gameplay videos on YouTube, and decide for yourself if you want to give it a try. Personally I think there are more rewarding games out there.

The game has already been released back in 2006 and recieved a new makeup on Steam as well as on PS4 and XBox One.
I bought and played the Xbox 360 version a few months back and I enjoyed the game. On the Xbox 360 the game sometimes simply froze and I lost 30-60 minutes of gametime which made playing this game very frustrating sometimes.
For fans of Koei games I can be very Brief: This game is a mix between Dynasty Warriors and Kessen. It has more strategic elements than Dynasty Warriors because you decide which troups you command or if you go all out by yourself (usually not recommended). There are certain strategic points you should follow but also can achieve a victory by your own strategy. Some quests however demand to follow a certain order to siege on enemy camps.
There is also more action than in the previous Kessen games though the game is less story driven. You have more command not only over your own charakter but also over your troups which you can switch during battle. The difference to Kessen is that your ally npc generals will always be played by the computer and you cannot controll those.
There are a lot cutscenes telling the main story of the hundred years war and its interesting to fight either side of the French or British Kingdom. The skills you can use depend on which troops you command and there are so many different troops you can unlock during the game. Same goes for armor and weapon.
The graphics look far better than the ones of Dynasty Warriors Empire or Xtreme Legends.
You will probably start the game on Japanese settings but it has in fact a good English translation for both voices and menu/subtitles if you start the game with the English -exe in the Steamapp folder. I personaly enjoy the new Nightmare mode a lot since it gives the game not only a good makeover but also a new story element similiar to the Orochi series.
________________________________________________________________
For people who arent familiar with Tecmo Koei games (do they even exist? lol kidding):
This game is a mix between an action and a strategy rpg set during the Hundred years war in France.
You can create your own officer and have already plenty of options to chose from gender, voices, hairstyle, bodyshape etc.
Once you finally created a char which might take you quite a while you start as a mercenary for either the French or British Kingdom and the first battle serves as a tutorial which explaines you the games mechanics. Mainly you have to take controll over a huge range of troops such as spearsmen, swordsmen, archers, lancers and many more. You cannot controll all of the different troops at once but have to first get a command book unlocking that ability.
You also can buy weapons, armor and other upgrades or level up your or your troops skills at the local tavern after you return from a battle. Before, during or after a battle some cutscenes tell the story. Some battles will only serve as a way to get more experience and gold while others will let you progress with the story. The difficulty also sometimes can be chosen depending on the battle you join.
I suggest you use a compatible controller because gameplay might be a bit smoother but that is up to you. I will not review the performance of the game since I do not have a high end gaming pc. Some ppl say they can run a decent 60 fps while other struggle to get 30 and say its badly optimized. You better ask in the forum, let ppl know your pc specs and wait for some feedback before buying the game if you worry about performance.
The game in my opinion is a lot of fun and you can have a lot of hours playing through the story mode. There is another fantasy like mode called nightmare mode including midevil fantasy creatures such as goblins and dragons which give you again a huge amount of gaming time. The graphics arent the most advanced but they are solid and good to look at. I can recommend this game and if you enjoy a game with an action, rpg, strategy mix made by Japanese devs, you wont be wrong with this title. If you cannot make up your mind by watching the screenshots and some trailers/youtube videos I simply suggest you try out a sale. I got this game for about 60% off (23,99 Euros). I didnt regret the purchase.

One of my all-time favourite games, if you love strategy games with plenty to manage and keep in mind, I couldn't recommend it enough. Currently having great fun discovering the amazing amount of extra content in the DLC, Crimson Court.
+Great artstyle.
+Great character/enemy concepts (DLC adds vampires based on mosquitoes, for example).
+Fantastic dynamic soundtrack that gets more intense as light levels drop, really adds to the atmosphere.
+Narrator Wayne June provides a jaw-droppingly satisfying performance.
+Tight inventory management, stress management, resource management, party management etc. Forces you to make tough but satisfying prioritisation decisions based on your situation.
+Game is IMO perfectly balanced so that you can make almost any situation work with enough skill and a maybe a lil luck. You can put your healer at the front of the group if you gear your party for that. If you think a class is bad, it's because you haven't used them enough.
While, yes, each area has maybe 20-30 distinct encounters that you will see time and again, each encounter is tailored to provide its own challenge in prioritisation based on who you're using, what attacks they have, which enemies are in what position, who ends up going before who, and what state your heroes are in at the time, among other subtle factors (phobias, buffs, debuffs, trinkets, etc etc). Having a team that can move the enemies out of position gives you much different options for strategy comparted to having a team that stuns well, for example.
I would definitely recommend skimming through a couple videos seeing how people prepare for different areas, and how well it goes. You can find detailed spreadsheets giving outlines for what to bring where. Youtuber Baertaffy has played this game so much, and at the start of his videos he explains who and what he's bringing where and why. Maybe watch the first few minutes of a handful of his DD videos to get an idea of how to prepare. If you're unsure on what to bring, overpreparation is a safe bet. Bring lots of food and shovels.

Metal Slug X (MSX) is a 2-D side-scrolling platformer game developed by the company DotEmu with emphasis on action-oriented run & gun gameplay.
+ Remastered version from the year 1999 resolving some technical faults of the original.
+ Each stage has its own atmosphere and iconic art style of the MS series.
+ Two player cooperation contributes to the fun and appeal of the game.
o Solid sound effects.
- Very short game that can be finished in less than an hour.
- Irregular slowdowns in single- and multiplayer.
+ The run & gun gameplay is identical to the other parts in the series.
+ Easy to learn but hard to master combat mechanics.
+ Different weapons and power ups with their own advantages and disadvantages.
+ In comparison with its predecessor Metal Slug from 1996 the overall level of difficulty is higher.
+ Challenging boss battles with extensive attack patterns.
+ Various enemy types with well crafted animations.
o Level of difficulty and number of continues are adjustable.
- Four characters that only differ from each other in appearance.
- Lack of coherent story telling.
- No voice acting.
MSX is an evolution in many aspects from the original Metal Slug of the series. This 2-D run & gun rampage offers more than enough action for a few hours.
Nothing beats the Metal Slug series on old arcade machines, were you had to pay for every time you died.
Estimated time for 100 % completion: +10 hours
Singleplayer achievements: 13
Multiplayer achievements: 2

OMSI 2 is a great bus driving simulator.  If you enjoy simulators or busses, this one is for you. It is difficult to learn in the beginning and given that many things are written in German, it can be off putting. However, once you get the hang of it, it is a load of fun. It is the closest thing to becoming a bus driver yourself.
Positives and Negatives:
+: A true simulator.
+: The busses are well made, most of the buttons, dials and switches have function and even the driver-side window has a beautifully annoying squeaky noise.
+: Gameplay options – You can choose the level realism you would like. You can opt out of ticket selling, you can opt out of collisions and choose if your bus will encounter technical difficulties making the game easier when just starting out.
+: Active – While I enjoyed Euro Truck Simulator 2, the long stretches of road tended to put me to sleep. In OMSI 2, you mostly travel through cities, must pay attention to the route and stop every few minutes to let passengers on and off.
+: I had also tried out Bus Simulator 16 the same time as OMSI 2, I found OMSI2 a bit more realistic in the sense that passengers didn’t always get on at every bus stop or off at every bus stop. Just like in real life, there is no need to stop sometimes.
+/-: While focusing on being a bus simulator, the people are rather ugly in the game and look as if they’ve just witnessed a murder. It’s not really that big of a deal but…it’s there.
+/-: While I enjoy the simulator, I might be nice to see a few other “game” aspects added in to make it more rewarding. Taking all the time it takes to go through a route, doing what you need to do, the only thing you get at the end is a timetable which shows you how punctual you were. While that’s all well and good, it doesn’t feel all that rewarding in the end. After that timetable, you can travel the same route but in the other direction.
-: Price – It’s expensive and the DLCs are usually pricy as well. However, with Steam’s refund policy, this isn’t as big of an issue anymore. Buy a DLC, play it a bit and if you like it, keep it or just get a refund to try another one.
-: Loading times can be long and the game can be rather buggy.
-: There are many times I felt the tutorial was unclear and programming the IBIS can be a pain in the neck.
-: There is still plenty of German in the game, which can make things difficult when you can’t remember all the buttons. Also, when programming the IBIS or using the bus modifications in one of the DLCs, the menus are all in German. It would be nice to see the game fully in English.
I personally would love to see the game redone a bit so it functions better, becomes less buggy and is fully in English but I doubt it will ever happen. The graphics could be better but I feel the simulator looks good where it really needs it, making it easy to look the other way.
All in all, if you enjoy simulators or busses, I think this one should be given a shot.

I was a newcomer to the XCOM series, picking up Enemy Within during the summer sale last year. I was quickly engrossed by the game's mechanics, and when I found out a sequel had been announced I knew I'd have to jump on it. With two DLC packs and a cosmetic add-on released now, as well as several patches, I believe it's just about time to take an in-depth look at the latest product of Firaxis Games.
The most apparent improvement in XCOM 2 is the graphics. XCOM: Enemy Unknown had a distinct art style, but it didn't appeal much to me and the game itself also just didn't look that great because of its low level of detail. There are almost no such issues here. Your troops have relatively realistic proportions, their weapons are properly sized, and the models and textures themselves have improved greatly. This extends to your opponents, as well; each of which receive a fantastic face-lift. The animations are relatively fluid, and XCOM 2 also offers a host of new customization options for making every XCOM trooper feel just a little more unique and personal. The environments are also much more detailed than they were before. Utopian cityscapes maintain an eerie sterility, which contrasts with the wilderness of the cold wastelands of Siberia and the unbearable heat of the Sahara. XCOM 2 definitely earns itself some praise here, and really raises the bar in its genre, even if it isn't groundbreaking.
Another big improvement in presentation over Enemy Unknown for XCOM 2, audio design has been greatly enhanced. Each environment features appropriate ambient sounds, adding to the suspense before you engage. Your enemies all have unique responses to whatever situation they're presented with, from the hiss of a Sectoid to the Earth-shattering stomp of a Sectopod. XCOM's own weapons all sound satisfying, and there are a variety of options for your troopers' voices. Voice acting is of similar quality to that found in Enemy Unknown; while I hoped for an improvement it is still perfectly acceptable. Perhaps one of my favorite parts of Enemy Unknown was the soundtrack, and I am once again greatly impressed by XCOM 2. Every track is splendid, from the suspenseful main menu score to the theatrical combat music. Timothy Wynn's work definitely doesn't disappoint, and XCOM 2's soundtrack stands up nicely alongside that of Enemy Unknown.
I'm afraid that this is going to have to be the low point of the review. XCOM 2 still doesn't perform well, even on a PC that exceeds the recommended requirements by a great deal. It's very unfortunate that this game suffers from such lackluster performance, as it drags down an otherwise well-rounded performance from Firaxis Games. The 30 frames per second I maintain is simply unacceptable given my hardware; there's no excuse for it, and there's even less of an excuse for the 10 frames per second I maintain on the Geoscape map. With that said, I haven't had many issues with crashing, but there are some bugs and glitches that have yet to be officially fixed. These aren't game-breaking in my experience, but they are very annoying. Fortunately, there are a variety of modifications on the Workshop which address almost all of these issues, but I would expect an official patch by now.
XCOM 2 shares many gameplay elements with its predecessor, Enemy Unknown, as you might expect. It is a turn-based tactics game focusing on the control of multiple troopers, and each of them have their own unique equipment and abilities. The game uses a two-moves-per-turn system; every unit has two available actions, and moving any amount within a radial area consumes one movement point; typically, activating abilities consumes one or two movement points, and firing always ends that unit's turn. This comes together very well, and makes for a game that is in-depth enough to excite while not being overly complex. There is a line-of-sight system which is used to reveal enemies and parts of the map, and a variety of units to choose from. These include ordinary humans, cloned government troopers, XCOM's own version of the krogan, xenomorph-like arachnoids, and massive bipedal robots. With this variety, it will take some time before one becomes bored of the game's cast.
The singleplayer campaign of XCOM 2 places you in the shoes of the illusive Commander, a faceless strategic genius in charge of the XCOM organization. This time around, you eschew the underground command center in favor of a massive VTOL supply spacecraft, the Avenger. This mobile base completely overhauls the strategic world map, known as the Geoscape, forcing you to manage your resources carefully since the nations of the world have capitulated to the alien menace, ADVENT. You'll face these human enemies more often than not, but after you escalate and take the fight to ADVENT's strongholds, you'll encounter aliens more and more. Missions are similar to those of Enemy Unknown, but some enforce a turn limit before the mission fails, which is both challenging and aggravating. There are more ways to customize troops than before, as the classes from Enemy Unknown are replaced by five new ones. New technology and stat-boosting items provide various bonuses to troopers, giving players the edge they need to destroy ADVENT and incite a worldwide uprising. The singleplayer keeps you on your toes and threatens you with destruction, from start to finish. Most players will spend most of their time here, as it is the focus of the game.
XCOM 2 also features multiplayer, which allows for players to assemble a cadre of troops from both ADVENT, alien, and XCOM forces, with similar abilities to those of singleplayer units. There are a handful of map types to choose from, but the big issue with multiplayer is the lack of options. The adversarial gamemode quickly becomes uninteresting, and other ways to play would greatly improve the game. One idea is singleplayer gamemodes being introduced to multiplayer; one player must defend an objective, the other must destroy it; perhaps one player is attempting to defend a stronghold of civilian units against another. No matter how you look at it, more variety is needed for multiplayer, and as a result you probably won't spend a ton of time on it.
XCOM 2 earns fantastic praise here. A full suite of development tools, workshop integration, and bringing the Long War modding team in to work with Firaxis on XCOM 2 modding features shows how dedicated the developers were in their integration of community content support. Take one look at the workshop and you can already see a fantastic variety of modifications: New enemies to give you an even bigger challenge. A total overhaul to how the game is played, making it more like the previous XCOM games. A new weapon tier, or new weapon classes. And a host of new trooper voices and customization options, to scratch whatever science fiction itch you have. This plays a big part in my recommendation of the game.
XCOM 2 is definitely a worthy sequel to the previous reboot, Enemy Unknown. While it takes a few steps back with features compared to the Enemy Within expansion, its community content support takes many more forward. It changes enough to justify its purchase without changing too much from the XCOM formula, and once again sets the gold standard for the turn-based tactics genre. Though they might be put off by the performance issues, fans of strategy and tactics, as well as those who enjoy Sid Meier's Civilization V, are sure to enjoy this title.

Played for a few hours now. Likely won't be bothering to finish it.
Good things about it: with proper hardware, have not experienced any crashes at all. No apparent glitches (things that aren't supposed to happen).
Things I'm not thrilled with:
- chromatics? wearies the eyes
- checkpoints? well, you can get used to them, but being forced to replay a hard-won fight just doesn't cut it for me
- overly complex attribute system, at least for me. Some might enjoy this sort of thing. Boosting my attributes did not really seem to matter as I progressed in the game, causing me to feel I wasted my time on those screens.
- weak dialogue. If you're going to add interaction, then add it, don't just make a stab at it.
Things that put me off this game:
- KEEP THE DAMN CAMERA FOCUSED!!!! I cannot hit an enemy if I cannot see him because the camera goes from a horizontal view to a vertical view. Have it back away so you can see the field AND your opponent.
- my character moves (during fights only) like he's drunk. Reaction time sucks (and that is with weight being 1/4 of maximum capacity).
- weapon's reach is too short (I've got a LONGsword, why doesn't it hit my opponent unless I'm standing on his toes???!!).
- too many keys for different moves. A light attack key and a heavy attack key? Why not just hold the attack key down a bit longer to initiate a heavy attack? I'm killing a monster; hit it hard, kill it fast. These aren't duels, I don't get points for style, only survival.
- being able to see would be nice. In the area of the monastery, I really do appreciate how accurately the environment of a destroyed, deserted monastery was recreated. BUT, I only detected some of the infected because their health bars appeared. Torches, lanterns, something would have been useful to see where things were. I played in a very dark room and still could not see half of what was around me. Hard to explore when you don't know what's nearby.
My hardware consists of a 4-core CPU running at 4.3GHz, 24GB of memory, and an nVidia GTX970 w/4GB DDR5. I use only a keyboard and mouse.
Remember these are just my opinions after some hours of playing this game. Check out the gameplay videos on YouTube, and decide for yourself if you want to give it a try. Personally I think there are more rewarding games out there.

Introduction
This game is constantly seen as a half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥Dark Souls copycat because it takes a lot of similar mechanics from it, but the unfortunate thing is that it is getting a bad rap because they feel the need to express how much they love Dark Souls and how Dark Souls is the greatest game ever played. I love Dark Souls but honestly don't compare these games too hard.
Gameplay
This is where this game shines honestly, for the first time I have actually played a game and felt like wielding different weapons completely effected how I faught. Seriously the move sets for the weapons deeply reflect various styles of play, so instead of grabbing the biggest weapon you see to one shot mobs you actually might have to find a weapon that is right for you.
-for example one person reviewed the game saying the combat was clunky. I think that was the wrong thing to say because weapon styles feel more realistic here, swinging heavy weapons is going to actually feel slow, because they are HEAVY. I would honestly say timing is more important in this game than it is darksouls, except for the fact that monsters do not hit as hard so you dont get punished as much.
The spell system is rather small but adds some nice finesse to the different classes. It is more of an avatar system that a spell system so don't expect a lot of glorious magical spells.
Graphics and Art Style
The visuals for this game are done rather well actually. the game looks beautiful but the voice acting needs to be matched up better with the animations. The armor and weapon designs are beautiful but light armors don't portray a light-armor design. Then again, Harkan doesn't really seem like the light-armor type anyway. The game definitely gives you that fantasy sort of feel.
One issue with the game is the lack of variety in monsters and explorable areas. Although for the setting you are given there are tons of explorable ground, the world is mostly contained in a monestary and a rhogar realm. have fun getting lost beneath the monestary though.
Story
The story is a bit breif, but is rather interesting. i'm not going to spoil a whole lot of it for you but I will say that I think this game has tons of potential for later games.
DLC
The dlc sucks hands-down but the companies that made the game are rather small and most of the dlc was extra incentive to people who pre-ordered the game.
Summary
This is the first game that takes a close look at making people feel like they are wielding different weapons, but with having a rather small group of developers the weapon range excludes bows/ or an advanced magic system. The content is a bit short but is definitely worth a couple plays through and the concepts and ideas show a lot of promise for games to come in this series. I would also like to add that the developers show signs of really wanting to improve on this game so keep a look out for a very promising future.

So I played this game for a few hours, this was mainly on the first few days of it being released, a friend got it for me actually, a very kind man and I am thankful he did. I played 80 hours but I couldn't find anything redeeming about it, in fact, I played for 30 hours and found that. I continued on for another 50 hours because I had a lot of map to explore and I didn't want my friend's money to go to waste.
This game is not an RPG like the Fallout games I know and love, it wants to be, but it isn't. It's not even like Skyrim where it can pretend to be an RPG and give you stats, it just has perks and given that I heard the levelling cap is removed, all characters end up the exact same. I spent my time as a wanderer who wished to scavenge in the ruins of Boston, taking what parts he could to modify guns and sell them on to make a living for himself, eventually setting up a base in a garage to keep himself safe from the raiding parties and the harsh wasteland. Except I wasn't a scavenging wanderer trying to exist peacefully, I was Nate. A war veteran who had a child and a wife and was frozen for 400 years and woke up to find his son gone and had to look for him. Good for Nate, I might have liked Nate too if the game wasn't called Fallout.
Really the game is not awful, the shooting is decent, I like the fact there's a cover system and emenies use it, the gun customisation is alright even though it doesn't lead to anything too dramatically amazing, I like the idea of legendary enemies that drop randomised rare loot that give bonuses. I have a nice collection of them, though most of them are Leather Left Legs for some reason, that's how the cookie crumbles. I heard the DLC is middle of the road, really I never had much interest in going back since I was never invested in the plot and I don't feel like I'm progressing, every quest is go somewhere, find a thing, go back. I am thankful that there are no Draugr in every location but it's very similar to that idea, a nice pretty shooting gallery with little options.
I'm not going to say anything else about the game, other people have said far more than I have and in better words, youtube is your friend for 2-3 hour analysis videos or the like. I actually wasn't going to leave a review but I got an update which added a bunch of unnecessary files when I wanted to give the game another shot, files like "PipBoy(Black) - Main.ba2" and other such names. I found out that they were a part of the Creation Club, another shot at the paid mods that Bethesda tried and failed with Skyrim and that Bethesda more than likely want me to pay for the .esm file so that I can turn my Pipboy Black, I would have been thankful for them perhaps also giving me the .ba2 if I ever made such a purchase too and not just force it onto me, but that's too much to ask.
I don't want unneeded crap on my hard drive, I don't want a game trying to masquerade as a series with so much choice and diversity in what you can do and I sure as hell don't want to pay for my mods in a game that £40 was spent on, I wanted to play Fallout and I think I will go do that but this isn't a Fallout game. I wont buy your paid mods Bethesda, I wish you respected me enough as a consumer to not put them on my computer anyway.

It's a good entertaining spectacle fighter wrapped into a loot of poor design decisions. If I could give a sidways thumb, this would certainly be it. I can both recommend this game and tell you to stay away. My opinion also comes from someone that finds the game to have been way overhyped for me.
Pros
- Varied movesets with a good variation of weapons and unlockable techniques
- Lots of helpful items, they're not my thing so I never used them. But you get stuff that heals you after a fatal blow, things that deal a lot of damage, max health boost for 1 chapter, healing items of course, lots of variation.
- Great aesthetics and designs
- That quirky Japanese humor you've come to love or hate in a lot of things, like D4: Dark Dreams Don't Die
- Good voice actors for the Japanese cast, english seemed to be ok from the first cutscene.
- Time slows down upon dodging an attack at the latest possible time (witch time), allowing you to deal a lot of damage in a limited time window.
- Everything is technically dodgeable (but don't expect Dark Souls levels of fairness, I'll explain further in cons)
- The rich gets richer, do well and you'll be allowed to do even better and get a smidge closer to playing like the overpowered daugher of a gun Bayonette is portrayed as in the cinematics.
- Checkpoints for bosses, you won't have to do an entire boss fight from the start, some of them can drag on so thank god for that
Cons
- Terrible checkpoints outside of bosses. You quite often get a checkpoint BEFORE a cinematic, so you have to walk up to a place, trigger a cinematic, then watch it/skip it (if long enough to be worthwile) and then you can try again, waste of time and seriously hurts the gameplay experience.
- Attacked instantly after a cutscene or landing on a platform. Like literally the moment the cutscene ends you have to spam the dodge button to avoid getting hurt the exact moment a  cutscene has played. At one point you land on a platform, no enemies on it, they spawn the moment you land and instantly attack you, you literally have no idea you have any reason to dodge because you never see any enemies or indications of them before you get hit.
- Health drops are a supreme rarity.
The game essentially expects you to waste money or angel attack points on health items or play so well you don't enter a bossfight or hard minion fights with just 10% of your health left. Depending on what kind of player you are, this can be a pro.
- Horrible forced camera angles in "escape scenes", essentially spelling your doom if you don't immediately get what they want you to do or where the entire path goes.
- Quick time events
- Quick time events that even if you know they're gonna happen you can actually fail them because the window of opportunity is really small, or it pops up before you can click it without failing (the kind that has a circle going in to it like a rythm game, you must click it when the circle goes into the button)
- Some deaths are almost unavoidable because of the forced camera angles and quick time events, which will affect your ranking. It's fair that you get a stone or bronze medal for dying in fights a lot, you fought poorly, but for getting caught offguard by a quick time event in a cutscene?
- Whilst there is a tell for enemy attacks, figuring out the timing or understanding when it's move2 instead of move1 isn't that clear. It's no Dark Souls in that respect, spamming the dodge in a lot of situations turned out to be a better strategic move than trying to figure out what they were doing and act accordingly.
- Reused content a lot. It's a visually good looking game with great design, but it seems they put so much work into those designs they only had time to implement a few, so the story works in a way that conveniently allows them to reuse the same creatures in different looks or even just colour, and you'll see the bossess repeated as well.
- Reused environments. For a 10 hour game, seeing the same areaa just in a different state 3 times feels very cheap
- Minigames/change of gameplay that outstays its welcome. I love weird "out of place" minigames in a game, small chunks of gameplay that changes things up. Bayonetta features an arcade shooter at the end of each chapter, a racing section, chase scenes and a bullethell section. They are all good in small portions, but the racing and bullethell part lasted for way too long, the arcade keeps coming back even though it never changes or evolves and is just there for you to get points for items or get gold and the chase scenes could have done with only existing once (preferably not at all because of the camera issues).
- Minions that can only be damaged from dodging and activating witch time, and minions that doesn't trigger witch time from dodging, personally I find this to be a bad way to ramp up the difficulty of enemies, rather than coming up with harder movesets and smarter AI, they just strip away some of your powers which they have taught you to rely upon to do well.
- Combos get you stuck in the animation so you can't dodge. Performing finishing moves and quick time event attacks (like punishing an enemy that is unconcious on the floor) still makes you attackable. For some of you this is also a pro. Personally I despise games that lock you into your button presses, and regardless I can't see any defense for finishing moves not making you invulnerable, they are special attacks targeted at single individuals, why can I be attacked when you give me a special close up camera angle and just want me to basky in the glory and comedy of the moment?

Is it fun? Yes.
Is it worth money? Depends.
The game is an early access version of what will eventually be a free to play game, with a tech tree similar to the likes of War Thunder or World of Tanks. However, it throws away the tiers, and instead balances all ships together into one matchmaking block, similar to Mechwarrior Online. It's enjoyable for a while, but the grind begins to get excessive. The good news is that you're not going to need to worry about repairs or ammo costs, which eliminates a point of stress in the grinding.
The graphics are also absolutely beautiful. Unreal Engine 4 is put to the max, and boy does it look good. The ships also are interestingly designed.
The game has two modes - a TDM style mode, and a capture the base mode. Both are enjoyable, but something like this could really use some more modes to keep its longevity.
And now, onto the negatives. These modes won't keep your attention forever, and you'll quickly want more. The various classes of ships give a huge variety of playstyles, but again - you will be grinding a while to get a ship you may or may not like. UNLESS, of course, you decide to throw money at premium currency, in which case you can push to that ship faster, and this is a bit of a problem... unless you've snagged the game on a free-forever weekend, you've already tossed money at the game, and now they are asking for more money via microtransactions. This however, is only a temporary problem, since the game needn't be bought once it gets released.
There also are major server issues, despite there only being a peak of about 1000 players online IN THE WORLD. Half the matches I'm in, I'll get severe lag stutters that are serverside, not on my end.
Final thoughts - I'd suggest you DEFINITELY get the game on one if its free-forever weekends. It'll definitely net you enough enjoyment to be worth the download. If you want to get the game with money, I'd also say it's probably worth it, especially with the steam refunds should you not like it. Will it be worth the microtransactions? You decide.

The game itself is not very hard, so pretty much anyone should be able to finish it (there are also various options more experienced players can enable if they wish to make the game harder). I can't say enough good things about Bastion - it is practically a clinic in game design. Get it!

A great mix of puzzle, hacking and story. If you're a fast typer, like me, the game probably won't be too challenging.
Hacknet is quite hard to describe. Technically, it's a game where you, err, Hack networks. Essentially, the game hands you a UNIX command line, then gives you a bunch of IPs leading to servers filled with all kinds of side missions and challenges. You take on each job by following a carefully assorted set of IPs which usually lead you down a giant rabbit hole to a hidden server with extreme security that contains the target file that you have to steal, delete or edit.
The underlying atmosphere of Hacknet is perfect. Following long, hidden trails of IPs that lead to corporate secrets feels so right. Hacknet is just a game of "♥♥♥♥ with other people's stuff", but it's so damn satisfying. Altering web servers to change their text, editing online savegames, reading people's emails, finding account credentials and editing medical records has never been so fun (implying I did that kind of stuff before I played Hacknet).
The story isn't really anything special, but it's still there and it's interesting. The game begins, then ignores the story until the end, instead sending you off on an epic quest to deface "Nortron Security's" website. Suddenly you're contacted at the end of the game, which leads you into a the final questline where you find out the secrets of the hacker named "Bit".
The puzzle-type gameplay is on the ball. The game leaves you to your own device and lets you work everything out for yourself. Honestly, I ended up looking up a good bit of it. Your job might be to accquire credentials for a company server, so you then set off, deciding where you're going to look, without the game's support. Will you try to find an employee's email? Or will you search for a company computer, then break into it and search for a text file that might contain a password? Maybe you'll even scan the company's network from there and find a hidden server protected by an unknown type of security?
And that just about sums up my relatively vague review...

XCOM 2 strongly builds on the foundations of XCOM:EU and XCOM:EW. If you've liked the first XCOM I don't think you can dislike the second one. The main risk-taking move from the developpers was to change the campaign, going from a defensive international organisation to an offensive guerilla cell. All the rest stays conceptually very similar to the first XCOM, focusing on lots of small improvements and rebalancing.
Finally, the big advantage of XCOM2 over XCOM is the possibility to have mods. If there's something you don't like, you can change it. You already have quite a few mods in the workshop and it will keep increasing for some time. The Long War team in particular is still working on modding for this new game.
In its vanilla version, I found that the strategical part of the campaign is not challenging enough compared to the fighting part (in particular compared to the last mission). In XCOM1 you knew that losing countries was almost unavoidable, and during early to mid-game you were in a rush to organise your defence. In vanilla XCOM2 I've not felt anything similar, at normal difficulty the progression of the avatar project is always far from being threatening. The campaign is also a bit short (44 hours for me to finish it but I like to take my time, think, reload, temporise, ... ). But with all the mods, I expect this game to have a huge lifetime.

I looked at Hacknet previously, and because of the apparent bugs, I decided to wait a while before I purchased  it. I can no say that I made the right choice.
I've been looking for new games, and nothing has really interested me until I looked at Hacknet again...
The concept of Hacknet is probably the best I've seen in a lot of recent games. The game has a steep learning curve, but when you overcome that, hacking into PCs and server is actually simpler than you think.
The only insight you get when you start up the game is a quick tutorial, teaching you the very bare-bones basics of the hacking. After that, you're on your own. YOU have to teach yourself how to utilize your tools to get the jobs done. You'll get very brief instructions whenever you acquire a new program, but other than that - you learn on the fly.
You accept contracts from various hacker groups (which you have to prove your abilities to enter), leading you all over the cybernet to complete them. There are tons of easter eggs and extra content, one of my favorites being the Shrine of the Polar Star.
The feeling you get when you overcome an especially secure machine is great. It's also fun to come across something you couldn't crack before, but now you realize, "Hey, I can crack this no problem."
Also, the OST is AMAZING. If you can, get the deluxe edition that includes the OST.
I'm not amazing at reviews... but I can wholeheartedly say that Hacknet is one of the best purchases I've ever made.

If you go into this game expecting to get your Dark Souls fix while you wait for the next title, you will only find disappointment with Lords of the Fallen.
I cannot in all good sense recommend this game.
Really, my biggest gripe has to do with the enemies. As a long time Dark Souls player, I've been spoiled by good AI functionality that kept experiences fun and enjoyable, with a sense of Difficulty.
Lords of the Fallen doesn't have that.
What you have instead is AI coded to perform instant functions, from pulling up shields or launching certain attacks that cannot, in all good sense, be countered by a normal human being.
Shields go up on some enemies a quarter of a second after attacking, coupled with the AI's ability to turn and follow you with no delay after every dodge roll you perform and inability to be staggered, you're going to have a bad time.
Archers spin immediately around (granted, if they detect you in the first place), and instantly fire in your direction with no hesitation or aiming, because the AI doesn't need to aim as the player does.
Mobs will spam knockdown abilities to keep you in place to kill you.
But overall, none of that is even remotely as bad as one enemy I found:
A caster enemy I experienced had the ability to ESCAPE A BACKSTAB IN THE MIDDLE OF THE ATTACK AND ATTACK YOU FROM BEHIND. This was legitimately my biggest gripe against enemies. Unstaggerable shield guys who don't actually take damage because their shield is ALWAYS in your face is easily trumped by this one glaring flaw, especially when added to the fact that this enemy has a mid to close range health drain ability that eats away your health within seconds, and is unstaggerable when hit with some of the game's strongest weapons for the area... And it wasn't even a boss.
The bosses, with the exception of one I found so far in a graveyard, which spammed an almost blatantly annoying set of moves, have actually been fun and challenging.
The sole reason I cannot recommend this game is because of the♥♥♥♥♥♥poor enemies and their ridiculously done combat.

Xmas Shooting – Scramble!! answers a question that’s burned throughout the ages; what if, instead of Santa being some tubby guy with a beard, he was an adorable anime girl? One named Aru, who has bunny ears. The answer is Bullet Hell. Because Japan.
Turns out, all the toys have been stolen, so Aru flies off – of course, adorable anime Santa can fly – to reclaim them. Because she can fly on her own power, she has no use for the magical reindeer of lore, so they are reemployed as shooter buddy satellites, and spit out jolly green waves of plasma and death. Then they mow down waves of snow bunnies, Christmas trees and icicle-flinging snowmen who fill the screen with lazily drifting projectiles that are secretly a good thing. Because if you manage to kill whoever fired them at you, they all turn into delicious points, boosting your score and feeding your hyper mode.
Behind all the festive insanity, Xmas Shooting – Scramble!! makes no bones about the fact that it’s a real shooter, and that it’s out to get you. Built on the same engine as previous Orange Juice doujin standout QP Shooting – Dangerous!!, it shares much of what made that game so memorable. They share a goofy cartoonish veneer that hides a hateful, sadistic heart which goes to great lengths to kill you. It’s a shorter game, capped at only three levels, but it still stacks the odds firmly against you by giving you a single credit to work with, and nothing else. You’ll beat the game in one go, or you won’t beat it at all.

This is an excellent addition to the QP Shooting catalog.
It's a bit easier than Dangerous, and the QP mechanics are a little understated here, you don't really need to switch weapons as much. The game is shorter, of course, hence the term "Scramble" referring to a scramble or "caravan" mode, although this is longer than your average caravan by about 3 times. Having 1CCed the game on Easy mode I can say that this is more accessible to your average gamer than Dangerous and that's probably a good thing. I think the price is very fair for the content on offer but in a way I wish they had made it a free game that could serve as kind of a demo for QP:Dangerous and a promotion for Deciga's localizations in general. A free game like this would be great to suggest to friends, where normally I would suggest the excellent Jigoku Kisetsukan, but since Degica have such a strong presence on Steam it would be great to have their own "flagship demo".  This really has nothing to do with the pricing of the game, and you should totally buy it. For new players I would normally suggest to play QP Shooting: Dangerous first, but as I said, this one is easier and more accessible, and Dangerous is, more dangerous, so you can take your pick as to which you fell will be a better intro for your skill level. Of course both QP games on steam have brutal difficulty on the harder modes, so you won't be missing out in that regard either way. All in all, the game is bright, light-hearted and pretty easy, something you might want for a christmas.

Simply put Metal Slug X is one of my favourite games of all time. Originally introduced to the series by Metal Slug 2 (my favourite of the series) I quickly fell in love with the Metal Slug series for many reasons, chiefly it's addictive gameplay but also it's comical sense of humour and the absolutely amazing pixel graphics which I still rank as the greatest pixel art I've ever seen in motion. You take control of one of four soldiers as you battle against the rebel army who naturally have focused their sights on world domination. Taking place across eight levels you'll run and gun across a 2D plain dodging bullets and destroying everything that opposes you. Along the way you'll rescue POWs who will reward you with weapons and items and you'll take control of vehicles such as the titular Metal Slug, an armoured tank that can crush anything in it's path. Metal Slug X is a non stop adrenaline rush that'll have you addicted in no time, the hallmark of any great arcade game, you'd be mad to miss it.
As of the time of writing this review the original Metal Slug and Metal Slug 3 are also available on Steam and are also well worth picking up. It's a shame the west doesn't have arcades the same as it did back in the 80s and 90s, it's something I grew up with and produced some of my favourite games of all time. Hopefully we'll see a resurgance in arcade style games in the near future, it's something the current generation deserve to enjoy.

I bought this game primarily for 2 reasons: The 100% Orange Juice DLC, and the fact that Aru is so cute I dropped my wallet on the "add to cart" button.
I'll begin my review by comparing it directly to my
. In short, many of the things I did not like in QP Shooting - Dangerous are still present in Xmas Shooting - Scramble (pun intended).
In the options menu, there's an option to dim the background to make bullets stand out more, and the bullets in this game seemed to have better borders; overall the game felt slightly less fuzzy and blurry. However, the game fails to distinguish "friendly colors" from "hostile colors" in that there are many bullets that are
as well as colors that like to blend in with the background and just turn the screen into a convoluted mess rather than a proper bullet hell curtain, something present in QP Shooting as well (again, pun intended). The worst offender is the final boss, having to dodge dark-yellow knives against a dark-yellow background. Another thing I'd like to note is that, also in the final level, the enemy shoots missiles at you; if you shoot them, they explode. This explosion does not damage you. If the missile detonates on its own (such as colliding with the edge of the screen), this explosion
damage you; these explosion animations are 100% identical. The amount of effort put into making the game graphical and animated actually deters from its intuitiveness as a bullet hell shooter unlike
Another minor thing that kinda struck me was the lack of music during some conversations, especially towards the end. I'm not accustomed to reading in-game conversations in pure silence, as it feels jarring to me. Whether this is a bug or intentional, I do not know. I just found it noteworthy.
In conclusion, I enjoyed this game a bit more than QP Shooting - Dangerous because it's shorter, and bunny Santa chasing after presents is more entertaining than a dog girl frothing at the mouth over pudding. Ultimately, I stil cannot recommend this game in comparison with other bullet hell shooters due to its egregiously poor color selection and screen clutter of distracting animations to divert your attention from what you're trying to avoid.

Innovative indie game that swung and missed.
Darkest Dungeon doesn't know what it is.  It's not sure if it is a town management game with an extremely brutal dungeon adventure mode or if it's a customizable party based dungeon crawler game with a little town management.  It doesn't do either very well.
You can't play DD without being 100% focused on the money aspect of the game, I'm talking about maximizing the loot per run to the absolute limit.  So for that reason I say this is much more of a town management game.  So forget about naming a single party member with a unique name, he's going to die or become useless and you won't even care because if you were paying attention in the first week - upgrading your town is much more important than any one party member surviving.
If this game had some way of making that human meat grinder viciousness morbidly satisfying I'd say great, here's a thumbs up.  But it completely detaches you from your teams by doing things like not letting a level 3 party into a level 1 dungeon.  Or making hospital visits for your favorite characters much too expensive to afford.  Why?
This game has schizoprenia, it tries to make all these horrible moments your party faces totally demoralizing, but a good player knows when he is pushing too deep and getting too greedy. Instead those demoralizing moments come from RNG ridiculousness where your whole team of veteran warriors who killed 60 monsters in a row without a single issue become panicked from a single mob that none of them can hit.
This game is not like X-Com, it doesn't let you get attached to your characters and it doesn't have the satisfying town building aspect of something like Rimworld.  I will definitely be interested in a Darkest Dungeon 2 but neither the DLC nor Radiant mode fixed any big issues with the game.  In fact the DLC added more brutality with more afflictions and a new DoT stress spell for your teams to deal with.
I hope the devs understand why they have mixed reviews right now, this game is so close to holding the title of undisputed champion of party-based dungeon crawlers. Major flaws are here though.  For now I would recommend just watching on Twitch.

I was a newcomer to the XCOM series, picking up Enemy Within during the summer sale last year. I was quickly engrossed by the game's mechanics, and when I found out a sequel had been announced I knew I'd have to jump on it. With two DLC packs and a cosmetic add-on released now, as well as several patches, I believe it's just about time to take an in-depth look at the latest product of Firaxis Games.
The most apparent improvement in XCOM 2 is the graphics. XCOM: Enemy Unknown had a distinct art style, but it didn't appeal much to me and the game itself also just didn't look that great because of its low level of detail. There are almost no such issues here. Your troops have relatively realistic proportions, their weapons are properly sized, and the models and textures themselves have improved greatly. This extends to your opponents, as well; each of which receive a fantastic face-lift. The animations are relatively fluid, and XCOM 2 also offers a host of new customization options for making every XCOM trooper feel just a little more unique and personal. The environments are also much more detailed than they were before. Utopian cityscapes maintain an eerie sterility, which contrasts with the wilderness of the cold wastelands of Siberia and the unbearable heat of the Sahara. XCOM 2 definitely earns itself some praise here, and really raises the bar in its genre, even if it isn't groundbreaking.
Another big improvement in presentation over Enemy Unknown for XCOM 2, audio design has been greatly enhanced. Each environment features appropriate ambient sounds, adding to the suspense before you engage. Your enemies all have unique responses to whatever situation they're presented with, from the hiss of a Sectoid to the Earth-shattering stomp of a Sectopod. XCOM's own weapons all sound satisfying, and there are a variety of options for your troopers' voices. Voice acting is of similar quality to that found in Enemy Unknown; while I hoped for an improvement it is still perfectly acceptable. Perhaps one of my favorite parts of Enemy Unknown was the soundtrack, and I am once again greatly impressed by XCOM 2. Every track is splendid, from the suspenseful main menu score to the theatrical combat music. Timothy Wynn's work definitely doesn't disappoint, and XCOM 2's soundtrack stands up nicely alongside that of Enemy Unknown.
I'm afraid that this is going to have to be the low point of the review. XCOM 2 still doesn't perform well, even on a PC that exceeds the recommended requirements by a great deal. It's very unfortunate that this game suffers from such lackluster performance, as it drags down an otherwise well-rounded performance from Firaxis Games. The 30 frames per second I maintain is simply unacceptable given my hardware; there's no excuse for it, and there's even less of an excuse for the 10 frames per second I maintain on the Geoscape map. With that said, I haven't had many issues with crashing, but there are some bugs and glitches that have yet to be officially fixed. These aren't game-breaking in my experience, but they are very annoying. Fortunately, there are a variety of modifications on the Workshop which address almost all of these issues, but I would expect an official patch by now.
XCOM 2 shares many gameplay elements with its predecessor, Enemy Unknown, as you might expect. It is a turn-based tactics game focusing on the control of multiple troopers, and each of them have their own unique equipment and abilities. The game uses a two-moves-per-turn system; every unit has two available actions, and moving any amount within a radial area consumes one movement point; typically, activating abilities consumes one or two movement points, and firing always ends that unit's turn. This comes together very well, and makes for a game that is in-depth enough to excite while not being overly complex. There is a line-of-sight system which is used to reveal enemies and parts of the map, and a variety of units to choose from. These include ordinary humans, cloned government troopers, XCOM's own version of the krogan, xenomorph-like arachnoids, and massive bipedal robots. With this variety, it will take some time before one becomes bored of the game's cast.
The singleplayer campaign of XCOM 2 places you in the shoes of the illusive Commander, a faceless strategic genius in charge of the XCOM organization. This time around, you eschew the underground command center in favor of a massive VTOL supply spacecraft, the Avenger. This mobile base completely overhauls the strategic world map, known as the Geoscape, forcing you to manage your resources carefully since the nations of the world have capitulated to the alien menace, ADVENT. You'll face these human enemies more often than not, but after you escalate and take the fight to ADVENT's strongholds, you'll encounter aliens more and more. Missions are similar to those of Enemy Unknown, but some enforce a turn limit before the mission fails, which is both challenging and aggravating. There are more ways to customize troops than before, as the classes from Enemy Unknown are replaced by five new ones. New technology and stat-boosting items provide various bonuses to troopers, giving players the edge they need to destroy ADVENT and incite a worldwide uprising. The singleplayer keeps you on your toes and threatens you with destruction, from start to finish. Most players will spend most of their time here, as it is the focus of the game.
XCOM 2 also features multiplayer, which allows for players to assemble a cadre of troops from both ADVENT, alien, and XCOM forces, with similar abilities to those of singleplayer units. There are a handful of map types to choose from, but the big issue with multiplayer is the lack of options. The adversarial gamemode quickly becomes uninteresting, and other ways to play would greatly improve the game. One idea is singleplayer gamemodes being introduced to multiplayer; one player must defend an objective, the other must destroy it; perhaps one player is attempting to defend a stronghold of civilian units against another. No matter how you look at it, more variety is needed for multiplayer, and as a result you probably won't spend a ton of time on it.
XCOM 2 earns fantastic praise here. A full suite of development tools, workshop integration, and bringing the Long War modding team in to work with Firaxis on XCOM 2 modding features shows how dedicated the developers were in their integration of community content support. Take one look at the workshop and you can already see a fantastic variety of modifications: New enemies to give you an even bigger challenge. A total overhaul to how the game is played, making it more like the previous XCOM games. A new weapon tier, or new weapon classes. And a host of new trooper voices and customization options, to scratch whatever science fiction itch you have. This plays a big part in my recommendation of the game.
XCOM 2 is definitely a worthy sequel to the previous reboot, Enemy Unknown. While it takes a few steps back with features compared to the Enemy Within expansion, its community content support takes many more forward. It changes enough to justify its purchase without changing too much from the XCOM formula, and once again sets the gold standard for the turn-based tactics genre. Though they might be put off by the performance issues, fans of strategy and tactics, as well as those who enjoy Sid Meier's Civilization V, are sure to enjoy this title.

As a player of many simulation games, I can say hands-down that this is the best simulation game I have ever owned. No game have I ever been as engrossed into as this one. So let's take a look at what makes this game such a fantastic experience.
OMSI 2 was developed by two German guys as the sequel to the very-popular OMSI. OMSI 2 is the only game in the series that was released on Steam, and because of that it has become the definitive version over the years.
The driving experience itself is fantastic - it's very hard for simulators to capture the feeling that you're actually controlling a vehicle, but with the sound, weight and turning, OMSI 2 does feel like driving a bus. The most incredible part of this game is the sound, which could not be any better than it already is. Sound is an essential part of a game, especially in a driving simulator. Every sound you can hear is from real life - from the motor noise of each different bus, to the surrounding AI traffic, to simple sound effects - it's all taken from real life and implemented perfectly into OMSI. Each bus is modeled from real life, and everything you can see is clickable and has its own function.
With a game as open-ended as OMSI 2, you'd expect an active modding community, and fortunately there's plenty of it. Aside from the occasional payware DLC on Steam, which ranges from maps to individual vehicles, modders are constantly developing new buses and maps for you to download and play for free.
Every game has its downsides, however, and OMSI 2 is no exception. To put it lightly, the game is quite poorly optimized. When it first launched back in 2013, it was barely playable, with crashes and bugs galore. It has since been patched many times and thankfully runs much better than before, but it is still prone to random freezing and crashing. Some maps, such as Projekt Gladbeck, are much more poorly optimized than other maps, like Berlin X10 or Hamburg.
In addition, this game is incredibly hard to learn. Before you can start driving, you need to figure out the complex UI of OMSI to first load the map, then jump into an existing bus or place your own. That alone could take you ages. Then you have to actually start the bus, which on your first playthrough, will take you forever to figure out. You will randomly click things; you will try combinations of buttons to get something, anything running; you will probably become incredibly frustrated. And none of this is your fault, because the game doesn't tell you how to do things. There are four tutorials available, but they don't help much when you consider there are a couple dozen buses that come with this game (not to mention the hundreds of buses available through DLCs and freeware packs), and each bus is different from the next.
If you expected OMSI to ease you into things gradually, similar to Train Simulator or Farming Simulator, then prepare to be surprised. If you don't concede to the manual, you will most certainly not figure everything out. But here's the thing: once you do figure out how to place a bus, start the engine, and program the route into the IBIS system, this all comes naturally. It may not seem like it the first several times you play, but you will get the hang of OMSI's UI system and how to set up everything so you can start carrying passengers.
In conclusion, OMSI 2 is one of the very best simulators you can get, if you ask me. Don't let the optimization issues prevent you from buying this game. I've barely scratched the surface on what this simulator has to offer, because you just have to play OMSI 2 to really know what the driving experience is like. And with many payware maps available (with more to come, including London) and countless bus & map mods, OMSI 2 will never fail to suck you in.

Insecticide Part 1 Review
Insecticide is hard to recommed as a game worth your time, mainly because it leaves off on a cliffhanger that is never to be finished.  According to online sources the publishers were aquired by SouthPeak Games who then decided to cancel Part 2.  All that said, you might find enjoyment in Insecticide if you are a more casual gamer, or are just curious as to what it is.  Gameplay consists of stages that are split up into action and "detective" parts.
The action ones control like a standard third-person shooter.  You start off with a simple gun and then get stronger guns later in the game.  Unfortunately there are areas where you have to platform, and these controls simply don't work well here, not to mention there are times you can't tell if what you're trying to jump on is actually where you have to go or not, or you might slip off and die.  The enemies use the same model over and over again, occasionally get stuck in walls or do a glitchy bullet-dodging dance within two square feet.  The only source of replay value here is the collectables that are Soda Bombs which are littered throughout the environments.  You can try getting all if you want but be prepared for frustration if you decide to do this as any time you die all the Soda Bombs reset to their original locations, as well as any enemies you killed.  There are also wires you will have to cross which may or may not work.  I died more than once trying to get on the wires only to fall and die because I wasn't in pixel-perfect position.
The detective parts are easily the worst parts of the game.  The only reason I beat these parts is because I had a walkthrough kept open in another tab, and that's honestly how I recommed you play these parts as well.  You essentially have to talk to other characters to get clues, get a few items, use items in specific parts and then move onto the next board.  Maybe I'm just bad at puzzles and such, but the logic didn't quite seem to click with me here.  The game will give vague instuctions but you'll be dozing off from boredom at that point.  Once again there are parts where you have to stand pixel-perfect for certain things to work.  It's kind of a shame that these parts are so story-driven yet the story doesn't get a proper ending.
My last complaints about this game are trivial but I want to mention them anyway.  While the voice acting is decent, you will be hearing a lot of the same lines over and over again.  The lines that you do want to hear will likely be drowned in the sound of other explosions and gunshots going off, or your own character having to say her own line, thereby cutting off the soundclip that you needed to hear.  Also the enemies that hide under the manholes in the final stage can only be killed by hista-mines, not that the game ever tells you (or if it does I didn't notice).  Although I know it's a "Part 1," it's still too short.  The final boss simply didn't feel like a final boss and instuctions were vague on how to kill it (lure the spiderbot to the railroad and shoot it with the ambergun right before the train comes).  And of course, the game has no ending.  I honestly wanted to see where the story led, who the ultimate bad guys were.
I still give Insecticide Part 1 a thumbs up as there is stuff to like here.  It is a very quirky game and self-aware.  There are plenty of bug puns from start to finish both in the dialoge and the environments you play through.  Casual gamers will probably like it more than the hardcore crowd.  There is also a Nintendo DS version of Insecticide but it seems to be pretty much the same game.  I would say if you're curious, then give it a go.  However if you decide to pass it up, you're not missing much.

This game is nauseating to play. Not because the characters are all bugs, mind you, but for reasons that are hard to put your finger on. Well, I think I have it figured out:
1. No AA. That's one thing. The game is full of jaggies. It is AWFUL.
2. Framerate locked to 50 FPS. What is this? Seriously? What the actual f*@k.
3. 1080p? Kind of... but the FOV doesn't change, so really it's just as bad as sloppily stretching 1280x1024 over your whole monitor. Looks like complete balls.
4. Strange mouse movement. This is linked to the resolution thing, I think, but here's the basics: in menus, it's too fast. In gameplay, it's just kind of awkward.
5. Altogether poor controls. Seriously, what is this? The controls for the third person shooter parts are clunky to say the least, and then there are the "Detective Mode" controls. Unlike your traditional point n' click adventure game, this crams those third person shooter controls in with very few changes. In short, it makes no sense.
6. Unrelated to performance, but it takes itself WAY too seriously.
All of these issues combined make it unplayable for me. As I said, I feel slightly ill after playing for five minutes. It kind of sucks, because there are some good qualities:
1. Character designs. They remind me of psychonauts, which is always a good thing.
2. Voice acting. Meh, it isn't awful. Better than early Telltale stuff.
I can't comment on the plot, though, because I can't play this game. And really, I don't think anyone should play it. Watch the cutscenes on Youtube or something. Because this game can be summed up in one word: sloppy. Seriously, don't even buy this for 79 cents on sale like I did.

I would recommend you start with QP Shooting, then buy this as a Expansion Pack/DLC if you enjoyed that game and want more. You can also import all your earned attack formations from that game and continue on easily.

There are so many ways that this game is great.  For starters, it's free, so there is absolutely no risk of buying the game and hating it, then deleting it and watching your money fly away from you.  Another way that this game excels is in the gameplay.  It's essentially an overhead shooter with RPG classes as characters.  When starting this game, you will realize that you only have one class: the wizard.  All other classes can be bought with gold purchased with real money, which I'll touch on later, or by reaching certain levels with other classes.  This unlock by leveling makes the player want to play more, as a death just before reaching a class unlock level is disappointing and will cause the player to want to try again, and causes players to experiment with other classes.  One might find a class they love due to a need to use it to unlock another class.  However, the game does have a few downsides to it.  One is the previously mentioned gold, which can be used to purchase character slots (extras are required to be purchased with gold), equipment, and vault chest, which are used to store items.  The gold is completely optional, but it is nice to have multiple characters or extra chests, as only 8 items may be stored at a time.  Also, a warning to those who hate permadeath, once you die, that character and all of its equipment are gone and you will have to start again as a new character (all unlocked classes, slots, vault chests, etc. will be saved).  This can be aggravating, but at times it will make you want to play more and get everything back.  In conclusion, this is a great game and anyone even considering buying it should do so now.  I highly recommend it.
