I've played this on and off for about a year now and to be honest, this is one of those games I keep coming back to because of the atmosphere and the combat style that it has.
In a nutshell, this is a MOBA with you as a spaceship playing in a completely 3D environment where everything, including hiding in cover behind asteroids, is an essential part of gameplay. There are several types of spaceships available and each of them can be customized using crew cards that add certain bonuses. You can also upgrade weapons and various other modules to make your ship more effective.
Once a ship is selected, you are thrown into a 5v5 battle with 2 lanes and 1 central area that gives bonuses upon capture.
So although this may sound like a typical LoL and DOTA clone so far, it really isn't and is a very unique battle arena game that will definitely make you come back for more.
One of the unique features for example is that strategic team play is exceptionally well executed here. A single ship if planned in advance, can easily get to the enemy base and capture/destroy it while the team mates are distracting the enemy.
On top of that, the game features relatively good graphics, music and sounds effects and has excellent optimization too.
The only real weakness currently is that it does occasionally have low playerbase, but hopefully this will improve with time.
UPDATE: certain concerns that others had from before such as overpowered snipers or people quitting mid game and causing the team to lose have been addressed already and are no longer a concern.

The only couch arena combat game that just works.
You go "Hey, I wish there was a game that was simple but really engaging, with finesse but not a lot of rules that you have to learn."
So you look at Nidhogg and you run into the issue where your one friend just always beats you for some reason because he rolls around like a jerk.
So you look at Towerfall Ascension and you're dealing with upgrades and stuff and you don't wanna deal with that.
So you look at Dive Kick and you and your friend are just randomly hitting Dive and Kick until someone dies.
So you look at Gang Beasts and it's ptretty great but really sloppy and you're tired of it after 30 minutes and your hands hurt.
So you think about a normal fighting game and realize the only PC fighting game is Mortal Kombat Street Fighter and you aren't about to look up special moves.
Samurai Gunn is to these couch combat games like Cards Against Humanity is to card games, you learn the rules in 30 seconds and everyone with half-descent reaction times is having fun at about the same level. It's fast but controllable. It's sternly competative but always fun. It's simple but flexible. It's a game that you'd try to emulate if you were sent back in time 25 years and had to make a living by becoming a time-travelling game developer when you've already pitched Threes, Lumines, and Geometry Wars to 90s game studios and become a millionaire.

A die-hard simulator, that's for sure.
Good things to note:
Really amazing detail on the busses. Everything is clickable and the sounds are fantastic.
Large maps which are open and unlimited to drive on
Full control on what you want do. For example, if you just want to drive across the cities without a schedule, that's totally possible!
Decent physics, and good thermal physics.
Fully customizable weather and time. Play whenever you want on the calendar in whatever you want. The weather is simulated nicely.
Gameplay takes place in real-time.
Not so good things to note:
There is quite a large learning curve for this game. Hopefully you can ask someone who's played the game for help in learning; not many good instructional videos/just instructions online. The in-game tutorial sucks, just don't do it. I got stuck so many times because things just weren't explained that well.
There's not much in the way of goals in this game. Your only goal is to drive and follow your schedule very closely; when you get to the end, there's not much incentive for the driving you just did. I'd like a career aspect to this since being a bus driver is a job.
AI can be dodgy - best to leave collisions between them off.
Performance isn't all that great. The game is not optimized very well and loading in map chunks hangs the game from time to time. I have a really solid PC, recently built, and I get about 45 FPS average on what I presume to be lower settings. This is a good segway into:
Options menu can be confusing. There's no 'normal' sense in the way of graphics settings; no resolution settings or other normal stuff. The controller setup is tricky too.
While the detail on the busses is second to none, other details seem a bit lacking. By this I mean low-res people and scenery and both are very repetetive. Just to clarify, the map doesn't repeat, just scenery objects.
Overall, it's a fun game. Definitely a bona-fide simulator. I can't imagine playing this game without a steering wheel so keep that in mind. Also keep in mind you'll need like an hour or so to learn some stuff and what to do in the game. After the learning curve, it's quite a relaxing game! Put on some of your favorite tunes and you got yourself an evening!
Truly amazing and just a relaxing game to play, although it might be boring in the start or confusing.

About the Game
Realm of the Mad God is the first ever free to play Bullet Hell MMO. Team up with dozens of players and battle through the Realm of the Mad God, Oryx. With a retro 8-bit style, Realm is an evolution of traditional MMO gameplay. A dozen classes and hundreds of items to discover means Realm is easy to play but difficult to master. Players can jump in Realm for 5 minutes or stay online for hours because there is nothing to install or download.
Key Features
Action combat! No turn-based battles here, only skilled running and gunning.
Epic boss battles. Navigate demented waves of bullets from nasty demons.
True cooperative play. All experience is shared and you win by playing together.
Great 8-bit art: Retro styling straight from the 8-bit era.
Over a dozen unique character classes. Play as a powerful wizard, a clever mystic, a brawling warrior.
Loot! Hundreds of weapons, potions, armors, and rings.
PermaDeath. Dying well means something in Realm. Earn fame if you survive for long enough and kill enough monsters.
Sheep. The sheep say 'Baa.'

It seems I have a terrible issue where I can't stop buying every version or re-release of the Metal Slug games. The games are just that darn addictive.
SNK Playmore has blessed PC owners with a port of Metal Slug X, which is basically the director's cut of Metal Slug 2. Now some people prefer the original version of no.2 because of it's less forgiving difficulty (which by Metal Slug standards, isn't say much) while others appreciate the added variety of enemy, power-up and weapon placement seen in X. Personally I enjoy X more than no.2 but hopefully SNK will bring over no.2 to make everyone happen.
The performance of the PC port is good, but suffers from slow down when things become hectic and this is more apparent during the last mission. Granted this rarely happens, so it never becomes a problem and I've seen worst lag in some of the weaker Metal Slug ports, like no.2 on the PS3. Video options include resolution, full-screen, aspect ratio and scanlines. Plus controller support with optional button mapping. Online leaderboards are also here, so you can see how bad you fared against the rest of the world. Sadly this port is just the original arcade machine, so the Combat School or Another Mission from the PS1 port are MIA. Yes the modes recycled assets from the base game, but still offered great challenges that expanded the game's replay value. I'm also disappointed to see the art gallery didn't make the cut and would love to see all the art work in tasty HD clarity (and without enduring long PS1 fetch times).
The important thing is the main game is here and it still rocks. For those who haven't played Metal Slug before, it's a fast paced, frantic 2D shooter with beautiful hand drawn graphics and catchy music. The game is only one hour long, but they still crammed a lot into these six mission. Caramels with mission guns mounted to them, alien space ships, mummies, mutants and trains that want to run over you. Bosses that try to crush you with tanks, food that makes you fat and shoot bigger bullets, Metal Slug's trademark humour is always a breath of fresh air, especially during today's more serious approach to game design.
However this game was originally designed to eat dollar coins at the arcade, so it's brutally difficult with one hit kills happening every 10 seconds for those who don't pay attention. Fortunately the port comes with unlimited continues and adjustable difficulty. The port also retains local co-op and Metal Slug has always been a multi-player favourite with my friends. Sadly SNK just doesn't know how to make a good netcode for their games and renders the online completely useless.
Online issues and missing features withstanding, Metal Slug X's chaotic, humourous action has successfully made the jump to Steam. I recommend it to die hard Metal Slug fans or anyone who enjoys the odd arcade shooter.

Puzzle Quest: Galactrix was the much-anticipated follow-up to Puzzle Quest: Challenge of the Warlords. CotW took your standard match-three fare and combined it brilliantly with an RPG. You crafted items, went on quests, leveled up, and battled, all by utilizing a fun puzzle game to get things done. Galactrix tried to reinvent the gameplay, which is commendable. But it did a really, really bad job. Which is not so commendable.
The first thing you'll notice upon starting, is that there are no classes to choose from. Okay, that's fine. I wasn't expecting this to play exactly the same. Then you notice that all of the characters are kind of ugly. Oh well, it's the gameplay I'm after. Let's roll!
The game starts off with a boring narrative by a boring character talking about how great he is or something. I admit, I didn't really pay a lot of attention, here - it was boring! Soon enough you're on a map, and now you start to worry. This is a little ugly, too, you think. Not hideous. But it is a lot less visually appealing than the original Puzzle Quest.
You do some missions, and the map begins to bug you further. Your ship follows your mouse, and sometimes when you go to a place, a character speaks. And then the menu for the location doesn't come up, because you have to go to the planet again after the brief scene to ACTUALLY go to the planet. You realize this sometime around the point when your ship is on the other side of the map, nuzzling your mouse like it's ready to settle down and start a family. What are you doing over here, you ask. Why are you not at the planet I sent you to? The ship stays silent.
So you hack a gate. Okay, that was kind of alright. Not something I'd want to do a whole lot of, that's for sure. An hour later, you will look back on this moment as the one where your life began to fall apart. If only you could go back and warn your past self. But it's too late, the damage is done. You're now spending most of your time hacking jump gates. And you despise it. It wasn't even all that much fun the first time, and now it feels like an actual job. You feel the hatred boil with every gate. Every screw-up. Every time the game gives you none of a color, and then asks you to match it for every other match. Every time you lose because you only had to match one more color, but the penultimate match caused a 10x cascade that dribbled on at the speed of sorrow. You briefly consider becoming a super villain to exact your delicious, glorious revenge.
Ah, but here we go! A battle! This is what we've been waiting for! And it's fun. And you fight. And you enjoy it! Boy, it seems like the computer's just having things handed to them, though, doesn't it? No matter, it's probably just a fluke. A coincideOh hello, future self. What brings you here?
STOP. YOU MUST STOP, PAST ME. YOU ARE SO YOUNG AND NAIVE AND INNOCENT. STOP NOW. THE COMPUTER CHEATS. HEED MY WARNING.
I wonder what that was about? Oh well. Hey, another battle! Oh no. Oh no, no, no. No, what have I done?
Puzzle Quest never cheated this much. At least not until the late game, when they needed to implement a difficulty curve to keep things interesting and keep you on your toes! How could the game cheat so bad, so
Oh, hang on. The game crashed. Guess I'll reboot it. And I'll just get back to that battle... Okay, here we go.
How could the game cheat so bad, so early on? It isn't fair, I tell you! No, maybe I'm just ill-equipped for battle. I should upgrade. But where?
And that's when you enter the final layer of Hell: lack of guidance. You can hack any gate and go wherever you please, right from almost the beginning. Side quests are available in nearby systems, and send you several systems outside of your hacked network. Soon you have half of the galaxy opened, and you don't know where to hang out. Where do I shop? Which places are best for me at my current level? Why can't I find any plans? Should I be mining things now, or waiting until I need materials? Should I ignore side quests until the story sends me to further parts of the galaxy? Is there an easier way to gain Psi points? What am I doing with my life? WHAT AM I DOING WITH MY LIFE? And you don't stop playing, because maybe. Maybe it gets better around the corner. It doesn't. But maybe. Please?
The gravity mechanic is pretty cool, though.

XCOM 2 is the sequel to 2012's XCOM: Enemy Unknown, developed by Firaxis Games (Civilization) and published by 2K Games. The game is the latest in a long history of infamously unforgiving XCOM games, dating right back to 1994's cult classic, UFO: Enemy Unknown. The premise for the series is that a hyper-intelligent alliance of aliens invade earth, and the player, known in the modern games as "The Commander", must lead a group known as Extraterrestrial Combat (X-COM) to defend the Earth. The series was rebooted in 2012 with Enemy Unknown, bringing the dated series back into the public eye and gaining newfound popularity.
XCOM 2 takes place 15 years after the events of Enemy Unknown, of which the canon ending was that the player failed to defend the Earth from the alien invaders. Firaxis have said that they decided that the canon ending is failure who have now taken root on Earth as a governing body known as ADVENT, parading as something akin to prophets of the benevolent Elders, providing cures to many diseases through gene therapy and bringing a newfound unity to the human race. A sinister new "Avatar Project" has been discovered by the XCOM Initiative, and it's up to you to investigate and combat the threat to humanity, and hopefully liberate Earth from the Elders.
The gameplay of the game is threefold: first, you have the turn-based combat. This makes up the very core of the game, and the vast majority of your time will be spent blowing aliens sky-high. The combat system is deep, and easy to come to grips to, with 5 classes for your soldiers to experiment with (6 with the Shen's Last Gift DLC). Missions vary, but all take place on procedurally generated maps. The objectives differ as well, you control your squad of up to 6 to complete goals such as stealing sensitive data, protecting a resistance camp from an alien counter-attack or recovering a VIP to gain precious intel - an important currency in the game. In addition to the combat side of the gameplay, there is  a large element of base management whereupon you build facilities with different functions, research new tech, develop upgrades for your soldiers' arms and armor, as well as decide what areas of the "Geoscape" to scan. Your base is a flying ship, and the Geoscape presents you with different options to explore to recover currency, new troops or investigate new leads. The third facet of gameplay is managing your emotional wellbeing. I'm still not quite over losing my favorite sharpshooter, Captain Yoko Littner.
XCOM 2 is perhaps one of the best examples in the video game industry of evaluating your risk vs your reward. As a tactical game notorious for its difficulty, literally every decision you make has an impact on the game. Across the roughly 20-hour campaign, decisions you made near the start can come back to haunt you. A misplaced power relay in the base or a poorly chosen skill selection on your soldier can have serious ramifications. Perhaps the best testament to the difficulty of the series is shown in the plot of the game: Enemy Unknown's canon ending is a failure because "everybody fails their first XCOM campaign".
Normally in strategy games, you can afford to make a mistake or two, but XCOM 2 takes no prisoners. Leaving a soldier without adequate cover can have disastrous effects: not only may your soldier be killed, but its death may send the rest of your squad into a panic, causing them to fire off randomly (possibly at your own troops!) or unusable on the next turn. Similarly, if you hold off researching new armor for even a week too long eventually the aliens' tech will begin to vastly outclass the HP bar of your soldiers, and you will find yourself being steamrolled time and time again. The difficulty takes some getting used to, and can be infuriating on your first campaign after failing your sixth mission in a row, but once the learning curve has been surpassed and the various nuances of the games tactical turn-based combat have been mastered, the game becomes a lot fairer. If The Commander makes good choices, your greatest enemy will become luck.
This, however, leads me onto one of my only criticisms of XCOM 2, and generally one of my only criticisms of the entire series. Luck can be your greatest friend in this game, but mostly you will find it to be your enemy. Chance-to-hit percentages feature prominently in the combat of XCOM 2, and there is nothing worse than your soldier missing a crucial 90% chance shot, or scoring the lowest possible damage and being killed by that same enemy with 1hp left. There is a lot of discussion as to whether players simply seem to notice their failures more than their victories, but while playing the game I couldn't seem to shake the feeling that a 90% chance to hit was something closer to 60%. Similarly, ordering your soldier around a corner and activating three separate groups of enemies at once because the game generated the "pods" unfairly close together is equally as rage-inducing.
Outside of that gripe, however, the rest of the game is an absolute gem. Visually, the game is a huge step up from the previous game, with stunning landscapes and wonderful character design. The models for the aliens are brilliant, and the character creation is incredibly pleasing, and all of your changes are realised on the battlefield. That is, until the soldier you spent an hour customising panics and shoots the soldier you spent TWO hours customising in the back of the head. Wonderful stuff.
Coupled with the gorgeous graphics the game comes with a stellar soundtrack (composed by Tim Wynn), which is well worth a listen to on its own. The atmospheric music sets the tension for the game, adding a wealth of depth to any skirmish. A personal favorite of mine is called "Lazarus", which plays while overlooking the world map on the Geoscape. The deep bass with anxiety-inducing strings complete the wonderful package that is XCOM 2, and bring it to an all-new level of awesome.
XCOM 2 also features Steam workshop support, which adds a fantastic array of community-made mods to the game, with everything from complete gameplay overhauls (a favorite of mine is a wave-based Tower Defense take on XCOM), to cosmetic upgrades and even fan-made soldier classes. With mods, the replayability is endless.
In short, XCOM 2 is a fantastic game, and more than lives up to its predecessor's legend. Simply a must-have for any sci-fi or strategy nut, and will surely give them something to enjoy. It improves upon the tried-and-tested XCOM formula in every way, and I can only wait with baited breath for what Firaxis has in store for us.  I just hope they don't decide that the canon ending is my poor squad dying a horrible death and failing to complete their mission.

Lords of the Fallen is a Roleplay Game that is designed with a classic pattern of gameplay.
The first thing that you will probably notice is the surprisingly easy control. I played the whole game only with my keyboard and as a small side note: I am a left handed player which means I played the game with a unintended keybinding and with no controller and still the game was easy to play for me.
So as a small conclusion you could say that the game has a well designed control-handling and a proper key-binding option menu to make the controls as good as possible.
_________________________________________________________
The next point I'd like to mentoin is the usage of beautiful level-design with high quality meshes and animations like you can't even expect from a AAA title. Each single creature has a fluent and well designed animation part, which looks awesome especially at the boss fights. The usage of modern graphics technology makes it even more beautiful by using special lightning effects and improving the rendering of the game itself.
One point that has gave the game more problems than solutions was the usage of obviously unfinished and unstable NVidia technology which caused some players to have issues with the game stability. For a sequel I really wish they gonna splitt off that way and use a own native system that makes the game look 100% equal to AMD graphics users. During my usage of my HD 7970 I encountered one or two crashes in total caused by my bad software setup. During my usage of my new GTX 970 I encountered some common driver crashes caused by NVidias unstable Turbolence technology.
So as a summary you could say that the graphics are amazing. It is a beautiful looking game but this feature had it's price. I really can't blame the game developers for that because the game needed some money-support which was probably the reason why they used the game as NVidias testing platform for the Turbolence system.
As logical result I would wish that they gonna drop this system and implement the effects on their own.
_________________________________________________________
The Content itself will be my next point I gonna review here.
Starting off with a small opening cinematic you are playing the ex-emprisoned warrior Harkynn who was released by Kalso to help him to save the world from the return of a fallen evil God who's attacking the monastry where one of the  Judges last descendant is being located, one of the last persons that can stop the raging mad god and his army of the Rohgar. During your adventures you are encountering several bosses that are leading the Rohgar army and your job is (who would have ever expected that) to strike down the bosses including their army and restore the balance in the world. But to prevent you to get any hard spoiler: things are not always going as they are to be expected.
The story telling itself is designed a bit too unintense which is actually not that bad because the gameplay itself is speaking for itself. Of course some improvements here would make the game better but I think this can be a optional side aspect.
_________________________________________________________
During my playthroughs I encountered several localization and asynch Text - Sound dialogues (sometimes texts are wrong to the sound or contain words and sentences that didnt appear in the speech sound).
As far as I can get the opportunity I would like to contribute as a game-tester to prevent such ugly beauty-mistakes for a possible sequel of the game.
_________________________________________________________
I also played the small downloadable content (DLC) called 'The Ancient Labyrinth' which is granting some more entertainment for roughly 2 - 4 hours by adding a unique designed new dungeon which can be accessed by talking to the blacksmith after passing a specific part of the main story. The dungeon itself is a giant puzzle which contains some hidding armor parts and also the final boss is granting a unique weapon. To make the dlc worth getting cleared multiple times the designers added a hidding room that allows you to switch the three phases of the boss encounter. Depending on which phase you changed the boss is going to drop another weapon which makes a total ammount of 3 strong weapons + the random drops from the creatures and chests in the dungeon.
_________________________________________________________
Overall I would say that Lords of the Fallen is a good first giant title of a small developer studio called Deck 13 Interactive  which is located in Germany in cooperation with CI-Games from Poland. Deck 13 recently earned one of Germaniess biggest prices for German computer games in order to support them to become bigger and get the opportunity to compete global. So I really wish that a sequel is going to happen and that I can become a part of it by supporting the development of such a sequel as good as possible.

More of an interactive movie than a game, this mash-up of quicktime events and conversation trees will take you on quite the wild ride. I was not familiar with the source material (neither comics nor TV show), so I can't speak to its faithfulness, but I found myself drawn in by the setting and quite attached to the characters by the end of the first Episode.
I suggest playing through exactly once. No matter how much you do or don't enjoy that playthrough, another might just spoil the illusion of choice woven carefully through the narrative by the excellent writing. Even researching differences online based on your choices could leave you feeling a little emptier for the experience, as I felt after frantically searching for a way to avoid a major setback partway through the game. Despite deftly avoiding spoilers, I couldn't enjoy the rest of the game as much as I had the first part, less because of the actual setback and more because the illusion had been shattered.
Your choices won't matter. But that they don't matter doesn't matter either. Go on the ride, make your choices, write YOUR story, and don't worry about what other stories might or might not be written. You'll be disappointed any other way.

I feel like I ought to wait through a couple more patches to write an actual review for this instead of a meme-liner, but on the other hand I do want to relate my experience to any prospective buyers.
Overall it's a moba-type (think WoT) control point struggle between two teams of five "capital" ships. If you need a better explaination than that on gameplay go for another review, there are plenty who've described it better than I will.
I'm here to comment on studio behavior and attitude, and provide an opinion on their methods.
Here's what happened--
Last month sometime (mid january) FS went on a ftp event. Very good move on their part, I wouldn't've picked the game up had I not received it for free. After that they went ahead and passed out ownership access to anyone who downloaded during the ftp event. Once again, good move, but I can see how SOME people might see that as dimishing the account worth of anyone who had already bought in. It's not a very large red flag in my book, but I can definitely see that coming off as uncouth to... SOME.
Anyway, I played about six hours and decided to go ahead and put some money into their in-game-shop while the sale was still running. Actual in-game benefits amounted to a permanent exp/credit boost of %5 + access to an unupgradable "prototype" model of a top tier ship. ONCE AGAIN, I CAN SEE HOW THAT COULD COME OFF AS UNCOUTH TO SOME, but stick with me. They seem to be honestly avoiding p2w with supplying those prototype ships. They have drastically reduced customizability and imho primarily serve as diversifiers in early matches where otherwise only three ships are available. STILL, another small red flag.
So that's the schpeal on that end. They're a developing game with a FANTASTIC product that needs to be polished and hashed out a little bit more. I haven't enjoyed moba-esque gameplay in a very long time, and this game makes me WANT to gitgud while still providing honest playability and... oh, what's the word... FUN.
In closing, if you're rightfully wary of an early access moba, let me console you a little bit-
This is not robocraft, and this team seems to have a very solid grasp on their concept. You're going to be alright. Shhh....shh...

"Darkest Dungeon is about making the most of a bad situation."
I feel as if the meaning of this opening statement is lost on everyone who begins, myself included, and does not take true shape until you actually take a moment to try and tackle the labyrinthine, herculean task of conquering the Darkest Dungeon.
At it's core this game is, to use an easy comparison, an XCOM style game.  You hire troops and manage a base, sending a group of units on a mission that will most definitely seek to eviscerate your every chance of success.  It's very similar, and yet suffers for it.
This game is well made, and is more than willing to give fair warning before promptly applying foot to posterior and hopes into a viscous amalgamation of despair and aggravation.  So what is the difference that causes this game to reach lesser heights than it's AAA comparison?
Connection.  Say what you will, but there is something truly engaging when a game feels DIRECTLY in conflict with you, the player, as opposed to the avatar being played.  XCOM achieves deep connection through it's customization options and allowing you to grow attached to all that you have built up.  It lures you in through succubus like whispers and false promises only to sweep the rug from beneath you.  Darkest Dungeon tries to achieve that by trying to ensure you understand the challenge you seek to conquer.  And it ultimately fails as the player has no investment in paying attention to said warnings.
You can blame RNG (Random Number Generation) all you like, but this game is no more and no less guilty of that than XCOM.  The difference is that you have no personal attachment to the characters.  You didn't spend time trying to make every character exactly as you wanted them, only to have them die in the field.  You didn't drum up a story to them as the character in question was used again and again mission after mission.
This game is entertaining, but the big issue is that for it to work properly in it's design there needs to be actual connection to the characters you use.  The threat of loosing the game is not nearly enough of an incentive to become invested.  And while characters can develop 'Traits' as you use them the Traits become more of a reward/punishment than something that actually means something to the player.
Give us a reason to keep certain negative Traits around.  Let characters bond the more they work together.  If the developers could find a way to incorporate narrative into every character, and the groundwork for that is already lain with the Traits and camping, this game could be so much better.
And yes, while the RNG can really hurt, that's kind of the point.  It's 'Can you deal with everything going wrong in the worst way possible' as opposed to 'Can you tackle these extra hardships and still come out on top'?
This game wasn't meant to be win/lose in the way it feels.  It's meant to be 'how much can you stall failure'.  It's meant to be depressing and capture Lovecraftian horror.

Bayonetta is a fast paced combat action game with fluid animations, gameplay and lots of stuff to kill. Similar in a lot of ways to the Devil May Cry series.
You play Bayonetta - a sassy witch that seems to like getting herself into trouble. She is a great main character with witty dialogue, questionable morals and looks that could kill. Along the way you will meet angels, demons and all manner of wacky people and creatures that have some of the boldest (and weirdest) designs I have seen. While there isn't much to the story, it's not a large issue since the rest of the game is just so much fun.
The main focus of the game is mastering the combat system. The system itself is easy to get to grips with but very difficult to master. This is a hard game - you will die a lot. However, once you spend some time with the game and get to know its nuances and enemy types it becomes pure joy to play. The combat is extremely fluid, responsive and fun.
Graphically it looks surprisingly good for a game this old, but the beauty of it sometimes gets lost in the frantic panic of combat. Sound and music is also spot on, along with some nice voice acting and cut-scenes that are very well done. I have had a few issues with stuttering that seem to occur when wind (or rain) effects are on screen. Weirdly, pausing the game and then unpausing fixes it - if only for a short time. This is a great shame as it makes some levels more difficult when you are fighting against the game engine as well as all the enemies. Apprently I am not alone in this regard, but the recent patch they brought out has not solved the issue for me. I should note, however, that generally speaking the game runs silky smooth.
So, to summarise, it's a fast paced combat action game that is unforgiving and difficult at the best of times, but rewarding when you "get into the groove".
Jimbo Rating: 7/10 (would be 8/10 without the stuttering weather bug)

Like many others I picked this up in a sale at 90% off; and I must admit I still regret it.
I am a huge fan of the original Puzzle Quest and could play it all day but in comparison Puzzle Quest: Galactrix just feels lacklustre.
First of all unique character types are gone which could arguably be a good thing as it does mean that a long term player could customise their skill set (which are now ship parts to be purchased) and makes multi-player somewhat more balanced however the pay off is that the available characters portraits are incredibly generic and limited (I believe there is four) meaning you'll most likely spend the game looking at a character you dislike.
Continuing the focus on the games appearance the new puzzle board (if you can call it new) is nothing more than a simple alteration to a hex grid which is unpleasant to look at and difficult to survey quickly (Making the timed sections of the game even more frustrating) this is made worse by the spinning background behind the board which has actually causes a few of my friends who watched me play to suffer motion sickness once they noticed it.
Outside the battles in the solar systems that you spend most of the game exploring this genericness continues with nearly every planet, asteroid and space station using the same textures and scattered in a nonsensical patten across the system making it rather bland. The system does occasionally have other little ships flying around in a loop and their designs are somewhat okay though in the first section three other ships that are identical to your own make it difficult and confusing to understand what is going on.
The games music doesn't have much appeal, I rather liked the fantasy tunes of the original Puzzle Quest but this game it was just there having no impact on my mood or excitement (apart from the menu music which was rather good) I can't remember a single note even though I was playing moments ago.
Finally coming round to the gameplay and again the two words I've used to describe the experience so far continue to apply bland and lacklustre.
The Galactic map itself is admittedly big however manoeuvring around it is a complete chore as to change system you must first succeed in a timed “hacking” mini game which boils down to matching particular colours in order a certain number of times. There is no penalty for matching out of order but no bonuses either, the only way to replenish the time is to match clock tiles with three giving an additional 10 seconds and a match 4 giving a insulting 12 seconds. Don't expect these or even the colours you need to crop up with an frequency and you will often time out even on the easy challenges due to the general lag in the reaction to a tile match and cascading which just takes time in many cases, making it more difficult to hack instead of easier.
These can be bypassed later by spending PSI points but these require to be collected in battles and feels like a rather cheap way of addressing the issue.
With that finally done every system change then requires the game to load and return to the overview map followed by you then having to click the system you wish to travel to, this gets annoying quickly for short journeys. In addition you have to remember where anything is as there’s no information about any of the star systems for either game or fluff purposes which kills any fun in exploration, this makes the huge map feel like its just there to force you to play the stupid hacking game over and over.
Mining is also another mini game which is available and requires you to match a certain amount of tiles together of various goods to gain cargo to sell at space stations (only a few of them mind others won't let you and particular stations prefer different cargo) however the goods get strange pretty quickly with food, technology and contraband been amongst the things you dig up.  Seriously what are we mining on this asteroid? Did I just fire my mining laser into some orbiting spaceship?
In addition it is mostly based on luck and regardless if you succeed in mining the required materials or not the asteroid will be considered mined out and will not be available to try again until you re-enter the system.
The money you make from this is used to buy ship parts which give you access to abilities but the price on these are varied, you can also buy new ships which slightly change your stats and grant more equipment slots but these ships are extremely expensive. In comparison to the skills of the previous games many of the available parts feel rather weak or just useless.
The battles aren't much fun either, the board can consists of different colour gems to represent Gunnery, engineering and science which do nothing but power your abilities, Intel which is experience points, PSI which allows you to skip hacking (I've found no other use yet), shields and mines. With the introduction of shields as well of health and damaging tiles such as mines been extremely rare (except when the AI repeatedly cascades them) it makes the battles drag on, this is made even worse by the fact that the AI cheats regularly even more so than the original as stated in other reviews the computer will make a move and the gems added to the board conveniently creates chain after chain after chain often one hit KO a player at higher levels or fully repairing its shields.
Even when you win there’s very little satisfaction in it with the pitiful experience points or rewards.
Finally the story and side quests are bland with little variation and many of the crew doing nothing than symbolising you've unlocked a new feature in the story and devoid of personality. It could be somewhat forgiven if any of these were improved but the final nail in coffin is that the game suffers from crashes that the developers have acknowledged and decided to not patch.
That's right they have given up patching the game after its first patch!
If you want a puzzle quest game get the original Puzzle Quest, it was generic yes but it had solid mechanics and a AI that only cheated some of the time and was satisfying to crush not this lacklustre cash in on the Puzzle Quest series.

This game has practically sucked out my ability to form cohesive sentences with the overwhelming might of its sheer stupidity, so writing anything about it is hard, but I'll try to list some bullet points as to why, after several hours of playing and DESPERATELY trying to make it worth the $0.99 investment, I must warn you that it's just not possible:
- So let's say there's an enemy with a special power that skips 2-3 of your turns. Fun, huh? No big deal though, there's a power up that gets rid of debuffs. Cool. Except that you need to have a turn to use it, and all other status ailments I've encountered are incredibly petty debuffs like slightly decreasing energy collected every turn, making this power, like many, many others, totally worthless.
- The combat system itself is some of the most anger-inducing, pure luck based BS that's ever had the audacity to call itself a "Puzzle". You can have an enemy at 10 health after a half hour of matching blocks around (if it doesn't take that long for ever fight, it sure FEELS like it does, because the only blocks that cause damage are super rare and only about half of the other blocks are kind of helpful at all for either side) and then when they take their turn, mines slide in in a deluge by pure bad luck and one shot you from practically full health. Yeah, there was a lot you could do to prevent that.
- Speaking of combat, there is next to no penalty for losing, and just some piddly experience for winning, which feels downright insulting with how long and frustrating battles are.
- And the fun doesn't end there. Exploring the universe is incredibly slow, due to the fact that the game pauses to save (really, you have to make me wait in what's basically a pretty menu when most modern action games could save while I'm in the middle of an intense throwdown) ALL THE TIME. And the galaxy is huge, much bigger than it needs to be for all the content there is to "enjoy". Why are there missions where I'm flying through a smattering of planets, scanning them one at a time to find out where my objective ISN'T, until I finally get a lucky guess or there's only one place left to look? WHY DO THEY DO THIS MULTIPLE TIMES!? You will feel like the developers are intentionally trying to waste your time because apparently they think a good game is one that takes the most time to complete.
- Despite being a casual game, a surprising amount goes unexplained. I blew up one ship that I salvaged Contraband from, a high-value cargo. Unfortunately, every ship in the system now magically knew that I was a filthy drug-runner, and attacked me. Would have been nice to know that would happen! What would have been even more useful knowledge would be knowing that by fighting back, I would♥♥♥♥♥♥off a huge swath of the galaxy, so that even after unloading the contraband, I get attacked every freaking system I travel into, causing travel between missions to take HOURS, unless you intentionally lose every single battle that comes your way.
- Speaking of missions, these make Skyrim's fetch quests and Draugr hunts look like the works of Shakespeare. Search random planets for thing. Fight thing. Win. Or mine 20 Dragon Dildoes and 10 Mountain Dew Cases. Or, my personal favorite (and there are a LOT of these); go to X, Y, and Z and come back. Yes, half of the side quests are fetch quests where you're not even fetching something. Just go to place and come back. No fight, no minigame, not even any dialogue.
- The music is bad, and it doesn't even flow together well. I swear, the battle music loops once, and then goes back to the AMAZINGLY dull space exploring music for the other 25 minutes of the fight. Absolutely inexcusable.
In short, this game is bad. I wouldn't pay 99 cents for this piece of digital trash. I wouldn't pay ten cents. I wouldn't let the developers pay me to play it, I'm dead ♥♥♥♥ing serious. I wouldn't give this to a poor ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child if playing it would make his mom finally love him, it wouldn't be worth it for the poor kid. I wouldn't finish one more mission if every girl from Game of Thrones would be standing naked behind me the moment I did. If this game were around in World War 2, Hitler wouldn't allow Jews to play it because it wouldn't feel morally sound. If Puzzle Quest: Galactrix were a perfectly marbled T-Bone steak, dogs that eat their own feces wouldn't even be able to handle its smell without vomiting. This game's release was one of the final signs of the coming of the End of Times, milennia of madness and horror with no end in sight for the tortured remains of humankind. It's an insult to all things fun, a long, brown, smelly skidmark on the underpants of humanity. It sucks, it blows, it's a piece of ♥♥♥♥ing ♥♥♥♥♥♥ garbage from a medical waste dumpster reserved for pus-oozing rotten scrotums and boil-ridden ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, and I for one do not much care for it.

I can't recommend this.
The game has four different types of puzzles to my knowledge. I didn't get too far into it. They all play the same way, you group three, pieces slide around, you group another three until you finish. The first type is the "battle" puzzles where you and an opponent take turns either grouping three or using a weapon but the random nature takes a lot of the fun out of these. I did pretty well with only a couple retrys but when I won, it was completely random. I would group three bombs, the pieces would slide into a combo, more bombs would appear on the board, they would slide into a combo, and I would win. No skill here, just randomness. Oh, and making a wrong move (IE: Moving pieces that don't make a group of three) results in taking ship damage. So you're punished for making mistakes.
Then there are the hacking puzzles. These are extremely tedious and nearly every star system has 2 star gates to hack and it becomes old fast. The hacking puzzles differ by being timed and having to group specific colors in a specific order (yellow, than red, than blue, than yellow again, etc). It is extremely frustrating because what color pieces are moved onto the board everytime you clear any is random and there are times where you spend 15 seconds just grouping random colors to get the ones you need to show up. You can group clocks to get 10 additional seconds but adding a few more seconds doesn't make these any more enjoyable.
The other two types are mining and crafting. Its the same group three. You "mine" for materials by grouping three or more until you have no moves left. No complaints but you don't get to choose what you keep if you mine too much. It'll even what you mine and you'll have to sell to make room.  You can use those minerials to "craft" which is another group three puzzle.
After a little over three hours and about 30 puzzles, I wasn't having fun.  Game also crashed four times during those two hours.

I find myself laughing at the sheer torrent of negative reviews I've found for this game, both here and everywhere else all over the Internet. Most of those can be written off as either "I don't know how to play, so it's a bad game" or "Nothing like the first Puzzle Quest game, so I don't like it". People who write reviews with those sentiments as their core points should not be allowed to write reviews.
The puzzle board is a refreshing change to the standard "match 3+ of a color" formula. Six directions allows for so many possibilities to surprise an enemy with a strange combo.
Combat is well-crafted and challenging, and there is always a way to win if you're willing to look for it, whether through a suddenly-favorable board configuration or a way to exploit the enemy's resources so they can't use their items while maximizing use of your own.
Hacking LeapGates does not deserve the massive level of criticism I've seen it get; it's a straightforward puzzle, with a simple goal. Yes, you have to hack every gate you want to pass through, but since people seem to think this is tedious, there's always an option to use your PSI points to open the gate automatically - and you're never going to run out of those unless you're reckless, or you use them to dodge every battle.
Haggling for discounts is small and motivating; you always want to do well. It's a minor annoyance that you have to do it for each item you want to buy or sell, but it only makes a real difference for the more expensive purchases like ships, so it's not a concern for the smaller items.
Rumor puzzles are well-designed, but serve little purpose other than as collectibles and experience. I do wish they would've played a larger role, because the puzzles are better than what they're used for.
The faction system is expansive and logical. If you make someone hate you, they'll make sure you don't pass through their worlds without a fight. I see little basis for the near-universal criticism of the game's characters, since the situation the universe is in pretty much justifies the near-total pessimism. And the fun part: it's entirely possible to become allies with literally every faction, except for the story's main antagonist - even the pirates.
I'd never heard of the Puzzle Quest series when I found this game. I'm a huge fan of puzzle games overall, and the RPG elements are a very welcome bonus. The negative reviews actually helped convince me to buy it, since it just seemed absurd that people would hate the game for things that have nothing to do with the actual gameplay. I did get it on a 90% sale, but that doesn't change anything. Galactrix is a beautiful, well-designed game.

The Dark Souls series has been one of my favorite series since the very first time I played the original Dark Souls on the Xbox 360. The first Dark Souls featured an amazing atmosphere and amazing gameplay, so much so that it still remains my favorite in the series, however it felt lacking simply due to the fact that it is a slightly older game. Dark Souls II took the amazing atmosphere and lore and altered the game mechanics a little bit. Overall it was a fantastic game, but the changes made the game feel almost annoying, with estus healing slowly and backstabbing always glitching out. Nonetheless, in the grand scheme of things, Dark Souls II was still a very enjoyable game, and certainly comparable to the original. Dark Souls III, in my opinion, is a culmination of everything great from the first two games. Mechanically, it is my favorite of the three, and I would even see that it is the best game of the series, considering how the storyline is similar to the other games and the atmosphere is also consistent, so combine that with enhanced gameplay mechanics and you have the ideal game. If you are not in a rush to buy this game specifically, and you are interested in the series in general, I would highly recommend starting with the first game and working your way up to this one. I promise you it'll be one of the most rewarding gaming experiences of your life.

More of an interactive movie than a game, this mash-up of quicktime events and conversation trees will take you on quite the wild ride. I was not familiar with the source material (neither comics nor TV show), so I can't speak to its faithfulness, but I found myself drawn in by the setting and quite attached to the characters by the end of the first Episode.
I suggest playing through exactly once. No matter how much you do or don't enjoy that playthrough, another might just spoil the illusion of choice woven carefully through the narrative by the excellent writing. Even researching differences online based on your choices could leave you feeling a little emptier for the experience, as I felt after frantically searching for a way to avoid a major setback partway through the game. Despite deftly avoiding spoilers, I couldn't enjoy the rest of the game as much as I had the first part, less because of the actual setback and more because the illusion had been shattered.
Your choices won't matter. But that they don't matter doesn't matter either. Go on the ride, make your choices, write YOUR story, and don't worry about what other stories might or might not be written. You'll be disappointed any other way.

Honestly, XCOM was my childhood game and when I saw couple of years ago its successor, I was totally excited. The game was absolutely amazing. So, when I read the reviews on XCOM 2 I had been waiting and reading reviews for months before the buy. Finally, the game is absolutely amazing again. There is one reason, the game is expected to be hard and to be hard for your strategic and tactical thinking. If you expect fun from killing aliens, go for some stupid FPS. This XCOM, a strategic and tactical game, probably the best you can find around right now.
For example, the claim that time limited missions are too hard and thus not fun. I hate time limitations in games, but this is not time limit, but turn limit. These missions push you forward, so you can't stay behind and play on overwatch. You need to think about time in you tactical decisions and risk appropriately. I was scared at the beginning, but finally found myself mastering new tactics. For instance, thanks to concealment you can go through some of these missions without being uncovered by aliens until the final battle. If you can risk this and do it with precision, your reward is absolutely amazing. You kill VIP, use all of your special abilities in concert and leave the scene unharmed. Taking higher difficulty makes this tactis a need.
Another example, the game is so complex that you simply cannot go through it the same way as previously. The combination of abilities, research preferences or training preferences gives you so significant different gameplay that the game is replayable. Not to mention Ironman feature. Second play is must on ironman. It's not only about difficulty, but it's about the way how you make decisions when you can't take them back and if you know the game, you do only mistakes cause your personal lower patiency. That punish you of course, but that's XCOM!
Guys, don't believe these easy folks who dislike this game, they tend to play easy games and avoid challenge.

Things like upgrading your town fully and preparing a good roster are something of a grind tho, and some monsters and random encounters (i'm looking at you, Collector) are just absolutely savage.
If you've heard of the game thanks to its fame as a punishingly difficult game, i recommend finishing a regular run and unlocking New Game Plus. You WILL cry. It will MAKE. YOU. CRY.

It's honestly hard to recommend Starbound to anyone that doesn't like Minecraft clones, but to be honest, I wouldn't even recommend it to those that even do...or at least, not now.
It's essencially a 3D Minecraft a.k.a. like Terraria but not really, but there's substantially less to actually do. Even after a few updates this game is lacking in what people go play those games for; and that's to have a significant goal that doesn't get old. Basically, there's not much to do in Starbound. Planets are randomly generated, so you can travel to them to find materials or treasures. But you can't really make anything besides weapons with them. No furniture or anything like that, which you have to find and steal from other places. There's a lot of weapons to loot, but why bother when every weapon you can craft is 3 times stronger most of the time? Digging deep doesn't reward you with much besides small amounts of money, which you can't even trade or buy decent weapons with. Not a lot of explenation or exploration, average graphics, boring landscapes, boring combat with not a lot of divercity...It's probably best to wait until Starbound has something a lot more to offer. Until then, stick with Terraria.

If Bethesda were a guy, then he was a guy anyone would want as a friend, the rare kind of person who worked hard five days a week, doing a job that made the world a better place. You’d look forward to hanging out on weekends, and when you did, he never failed to bring beer, munchies and the smokes. He stayed away from the really corporate guys like EA and Ubisoft, because everyone heard that their idea of a good time was mainlining crack cocaine and murdering homeless people for thrills. He wasn’t like that, his talent and his place in the world never got to his head. But then, he changed.
He stopped returning your calls, you never got to see him anymore, and on the rare occasion that you caught a glmipse of him, you could tell that he’d forgot everything that made them unique. These days, he forgets to take off his business suit on the weekends. He goes to winebars, he’s got a flashy car, but you’ve heard the rumours. Nowadays, they say he spends his weekends in his bedrom closet, dressed up like superman while vagrants take turns ploughing his wife. They say he films it from between the slats. You fear his new twisted form, but for all of your willingness to get through to him, in your heart of hearts, you know he is lost to you.
If Betheda were a guy, then he was once the truest of friends. He shall be missed.

When I first heard Metal Slug X was being released I brought got it ASAP and it hasn't disappointed me yet! It is one of the best classics and ports I have played and it has almost everything a Steam Game should have!
Here are my thoughts on it:
Pros:
♦ Great Graphics
♦ Awesome Arcade Port
♦ Enjoyable Music
♦ Multiplayer
♦ Highscores that sync Globally and with Steam Friends
♦ Many Characters and Many different credit modes
♦ Awesome Cards
♦ Gameplay was awesome (Could have added an actual ending cinematic though, but won't complain)
♦ Sidescroll shooter that just works!
♦ Huge incentive to replay the game to beat your highscore, the global highscores or even your friends highscores!
Cons:
♦ Fairly Short (6 Missions - This is only an issue if you are playing in Free Mode as it's easy to run through. However with Credits you have to try not to die which makes the game take a little more skill and time to finish)
♦ Multiplayer Lobby seems empty (I guess multiplayer is only for friends and shouldn't need a global lobby but still)
♦ Multiplayer seems unneeded (To me it seems pointless to why you'd want to play this with two people, but the option is nice)
♦ Single Player Controls are weird (Would be nice to shoot with mouse left click and throw grenades with right click)
♦ Audio seems really loud (You have the option in settings to turn the Audio to 10... I play on 3 and I can hear the game fine)
♦ Could have had more Achievements (Such as Achievements for different difficulties and for playing as other characters etc to make you want to play on different difficulties and as other characters etc. Don't get me wrong 15 is a nice number, it was just way too easy to get them all quickly)
Overall, even though I found a few cons they are really minor compared to the pros. This game has it all, Steam achievements, cards, multiplayer, Global and Friends highscores, great graphics, awesome audio, epic gameplay and to top it all off it's an epic port from the good 'ol nostalgic arcade machines! So if you ever played this on an Arcade Machine or hell even played a game on an Arcade Machine and want to relive the good 'ol Arcade Machine Days... then this game is definitely worth $8!
PS: Make more of these and my wallet will be yours!

What's the first thing that comes to mind, when reviewing a video game? Well, for me, it has to be the visual world that captures the core of our imaginations. And with this little gem called Half-Life, it comes as no exception that this game continues to boggle the mind and leave gamers alike wondering. There is more heart, creativity and scientific ingenuity there is in this one title than there is in most series and is arguably Valve's greatest achievement. With over 50 game awards, it's a strong justification. Half-Life isn't just one of the greatest FPS' games of all time. Half-Life isn't literally one of the best purchases you can ever get on Steam. Half-Life is quite simply, one of the greatest games ever made.
When compared to certain FPS' games in the past and todays time, which both heavily rely on long-winded cutscenes to present the main narrative of the game, Half-Life annihilates this often compulsed aspect, by detailing the plotlines that keeps the player still in control of the first-person viewpoint, leaving the cutscenes rolling while you still have full access to the gameplay and character controllability. For summarization, You will see through the eyes of Gordon Freeman at all times.
The game is a perpetual maze; leaving the player to work at tasks that involve being locked into battle and overall puzzle solving to advance through the many challenges that wait up ahead. Most of the time, the story illuminates the puzzles by the actions to proceed, such as maze scenarios and building boxes to use as staircases. Although Half-Life has short-lived loading screens from time to time after leaving a certain area for a new one, the game has no levels. But, to make up for this traditional concept, the game is split into a number of mind-boggling chapters filled with rich story and easy adaptability.
To start off with this game's story, you're none other than Gordon Freeman. A young man who holds a Ph.D in theoretical physics who starts his daily grind back at the Black Mesa Research Facility; a fictional complex that is stranded in a remote desert located in the suburbs of New Mexico. Arriving late for work yet again, you take the tram system around the Black Mesa Research Facility and at this point, objectives that his game has fulfilled such as breath-taking visuals and movie quality animation begins to blossom. The tram sequence at the beginning of the game can only be summed up in one word; Incredible. It's as if the things that come flying at you from every angle and position, almost reminiscent of watching an action-packed movie, along with the credits of the producer's names proudly fading in and out on the corner of the screen.
As you make your first step in the heavily secured facility, you're constantly reminded that you put on your Hazardous Environmental suit, or the H.E.V suit for short. While all things are hunky-dory, those things soon turn to the worst very soon. After a failed experiment, involving a collision between a rare intergalactic specimen from another dimension with an Anti-Mass Spectrometer, the Black Mesa facility falls in ruins, meaning you are one of the only key survivors of the infamous ''Black Mesa Incident''. And with this, alien life-forms from the dimension of ''Xen'' are pulled from their dimension into ours and are running amok the ruined facility, along with the Army that storm the place after the gone, haywired facility's emergency call has been echoed. This of course doesn't make things any easier and you soon find yourself battling both the aliens and the military.
While there isn't exactly much to complain about, I would admit that guiding the chickened-out scientists and professors around the facility can be quite a pain now and again due to some seldom poor AI programming, as well as the alien life-form, Vortigaunt, from which you would have to wait and be patient for them to wreck down wooden doors in front of you, as you are not capable of doing that yourself. (You do start off with a crowbar, right?) As well as I'm probably not the only one who made the same mistake by killing them through a small opening, before they did in fact begin to tear down the doors. I managed to pick up this game for about €22,- (including DLC's), whereas the steam store price is €49,99 (doesn't include DLC's). This review is based on that pricetag. €50,- is definitely not worth it.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
This game is like War of the roses was compared to mount and blade.
Only now it is Lords of the fallen compared to Dark souls.
Floatier, clunkier and somewhat laggier but still enjoyable in it's own way.
Many people say it gets boring quickly and i honestly can't disagree. After about one and a half hour of progress through the story i've beaten the second boss and am on my way to the third.
(Almost) all enemies are in humanoid form and pretty much every area is a snowy castle (or it's corridors).
This is a true letdown as variation in both these fields would probably have made the game a LOT better, possibly even excellent.
The combat is, as i mentioned, pretty floaty and clunky. By that i mean that the overal experience feels a little disconnected. Enemies will suddenly get dragged towards you as they do a sweeping attack in ways that don't suit the animation they do and dodging is pretty useless unless you take the lightest armor.
Why the lightest armor? Because otherwise you're too slow to stand up from your roll and strike before the enemy gets his guard back up, plus it's riskier than blocking as the hitboxes for dodging don't always seem to work just right (although they mostly do).
As a seasoned Dark souls veteran i went into this game thinking it'd be a dumbed down version of dark souls, also a lot easier. This got me killed quite often early on, however. I'm not entirely certain whether this is because the game itself is challenging or because i fight too agressively (expect slow, waity combat), but it is a nice reminder that i'm still playing something challenging.
It doesn't seem worth taking the light armor class on my first playthrough as this class requires you to time your rolls or parries at the right moment, which is a guessing game when encountering new foes. It's too risky to do this on the go as some enemies will rush towards you in a flurry and it doesn't help that the hitboxes aren't very forgiving.
Overall i'm not a big fan of the monotone setting and enemies or the slow, shield turtly/waity combat, but this definitely isn't a bad game, i just have to get used to the pace as it's
similar to dark souls, but not entirely the same.
-Edit-
Now that i've played it a little more it seems like the game takes it difficulty from a lack of windows of oppurtunity, meaning you just don't have a chance to hit enemies back or that you can't stagger them while doing so, which results in them mauling away at you while you swing your weapon like a crippled granny.
I'm kind of forcing myself to like this but it's just not working. Enemies are pathetically fast compared to your character which is the equivalent of having 200% of your equipment burden, even though you're actually fine.
The game is laggy as hell for no particular reason (medium settings on high end PC at +/- 46 to 60 fps, usually clinging around 50) and even after changing my weapon i've found no way to strike an enemy in time, as they're faster, have somewhat infinite poise (except if you use a heavy attack which takes just as much time as it would to make a sequel) and interrupt your attacks, even with medium armor (haven't tried heavy yet but that makes you unable to roll).
Also while i was writing this edit i've noticed my health regained almost completely since i summoned a prayer spell despite having paused the game (heals you over time but expires fast and heals just as slow as the game's combat).
Bosses are just as linear and uninspired as the general bad guy.
If they wouldn't have distinguishable names they'd be almost impossible to tell apart.
So there, guys.

-TL;DR at the bottom with PC specs-
I have been having a stable experience of AC: Unity and I must say, I was very blown away by how beautiful this game is. I am getting a solid 60fps, sometimes more, sometimes less (it varies often). I'm playing the game at High settings (with some custom settings) because the Very High and Ultra High settings are actually unplayable, so I suppose there needs to be optimization there. Turning up Anti-Aliasing drops me down to 20fps, so unfortunately I have to keep it at 2x MSAA.
I feel that some story aspects are a little bland and a little sudden. It could be seen as a basic story of revenge in a quest to fulfill himself, but I'm not completely concerned with the story. The gameplay is actually harder and they brought back some game mechanic feeling from Revelations and Brotherhood. Health potions were added again which makes me happy, because now I actually feel more vulnerable. In Black Flag and AC3, I felt invincible because the combat was so easy. In Unity, I've died. A lot. I may or may not suck, but the combat in my opinion is genuinely difficult if you're not careful about how you conduct yourself. Stealth is definitely recommended.
Some game mechanics I don't really approve of like skills. Skills are a little strange, and I feel like 'Disguise' is cheating. I don't want to buy into Diguise because you can suddenly change your outfit and walk past guards right in front of their eyes. I think that's a broken mechanic and should be changed.
Some of the running around still hasn't changed in terms of accuracy when scaling buildings. It's a little fidgety and I've gotten angry at Arno for not going where I wanted him to go.
I've played one game of co-op and it was FUN. So much fun. We both kept failing and it was hilarious because we tried so hard to be stealthy, but in the end we kept getting caught. We finally finished and had a crouch-dance victory. It was very fulfilling. Co-op is a blast and I'm very happy that Ubisoft added this.
Now, onto the micro-transactions. Completely dismissable. I think it's stupid that everyone is bringing this up because it doesn't affect anyone directly unless you buy into it. You can obtain the items by playing the game anyway, so just play the game and get them normally. Micro-transactions are just there to cut the time in half. But, why would you want to cut the time in half when you spent the money to play it?
:: TL;DR and PC Specs ::
So far I'd like to give this game a 7/10. Even though I'm having a relatively stable experience, I would like to experience the higher graphics settings without getting 20fps. The story is mildly uninteresting but the co-op and missions are wonderful. Gameplay is harder than AC3 and AC4 and stealth is much advised.

People like to compare this to dark souls, and it does have very strong similarities to it. I have not beaten the game yet, but I can tell you about most things already...
Is this game easier than Dark Souls? In some ways yes, in other ways no.
So far I have not really been lost in the area as there are not as many side ways you can go. There also is a Journal, but there is no minimap and you'll have to figure out by yourself if the way you're going is the best way.
The enemies are also quite different - In Dark Souls, you will often have to fight a broad variety of human and non human enemies in small groups, but often fight without any kind of defense. In Lords of the Fallen, (so far) most of the enemies have been human-like but also fight with a heavy shield. These enemies clearly act smarter and more tactical than their Dark Souls colleagues, but you'll often be able to only fight 1 of them at a time. Fighting two enemies that carry a heavy shield actually turns into a hard challenge. If an enemy has a shield in Dark Souls, you can often just wait for them to attack, then walk to their right and take away their whole health bar. That's rarely possible in Lords of the Fallen, because the enemies don't really lose track of your sight and are quick to put their shield back up. For your own shield - Its strongly advised to take the shield the second boss drops. It is the strongest shield you can find at that point at the game and pretty much the only shield that the current enemies can't just hit away.
The fighting itself is tight and responsive. Your character reacts good and there is no input lag (I'm playing with a controller, mouse and keyboard input is good aswell). Unlike Dark Souls, you can't directly equip anything you want. If you don't have a shield on, your character will just put a copy of the right hand weapon into his left hand so he carries two weapons. In Dark Souls, you can specifically say what weapons you want to equip in each hand, for instance a spear in the left and a sword in the right.
Swords, hammers, axes, staffs, etc. are also the only combat weapons there are. There is a seperate weapon that lets you fire magic bombs and projectiles, but that is the only thing you will get that somehow fires magic attacks. You are also able to use spells, and between the 3 different classes these spells are not too different.
Two of the boss fights so far have been great. The third boss, which I am currently trying to beat I do not like as much. He spawns endless strong minions, and you can't really fight the minions because you need to evade the attacks of the boss. I really don't like it when you make a bossfight more difficult by throwing minions into the fight - especially minions that spawn endlessly and leap long distances and throw you on the ground :/ The second boss fight also had (strong) minions, but they were not as frequent, and the boss would actually time out so you could fight them. These minions were also not the only reason that made that boss fight hard.
Visuals of this game are absolutely stunning. All textures are sharp and look realistic. I think this might be in the top 5 of hyperrealistic looking games. Its really amazing to fight a boss while the bright sun shines behind him (The sunshine in this game actually blocks your view, how amazing is that). The unmodded pc version of Dark Souls on the other hand basically makes you want to throw up...blurry textures, bad distance rendering, etc. Lords of the Fallen also runs smooth as hell. As said, mouse and keyboard are actually usable in this game, unlike Dark Souls.
Not gonna say its bad, but all in all: r.o.n ♥♥♥♥♥ on this game.

The shooting mechanics are nice and upgrading your weapons is fairly interesting, but as Tim Cain (one of the lead designers/programmers behind the original Fallout games) said: "My idea is to explore more of the world and more of the ethics of a post-nuclear world, not to make a better plasma gun". That's the thing Fallout 4 pretty much lacks, among other things like freedom of choice to make meaningful decisions. I won't even elaborate on the Minute man radiant quest situation and the Preston "Another Settlement needs our help" Gravy thing.
You do not have much control over your backround, you're either a male soldier in the U.S military or a female lawyer. It's amusing to pick the lawyer option if you have♥♥♥♥♥♥poor intelligence or charisma. Personally I don't like that you're forced to choose between these two options and it dumbs the game down a lot.
And giving power armor that early in the game was very odd. The new mechanics with power armors are still fantastic and I got to give credit to that (it making you feel like a tank).
I would have been okay-ish with the game as it is but since they release the Creation Club, I felt that I needed to make a negative review to warn all my associates to stay away from the franchise. That's just shameless cash grabbing and charging 5 dollars from a Power armor feels like a rip-off.
So yeah, I recommend that you dont waste your money on this. I haven't bought any DLC and I'm glad I didn't.

Samurai Gunn is a fast paced arena style "Bushido-Brawler." It's extremely easy to pick up and have hours of fun on the couch with your buddies. From the 10 life/kill Death Match to the life or death Shogun Showdown, the battles get intense.
Only having 3 bullets in your chamber makes ranged battle high stakes, but worth calculating. You have the ability to block strikes with your sword, but whoever swings second goes flying in the opposite direction, making battles even more dangerous when traps are activated or when the floors are spiked.
Although the price may seem steep for a local "party-game" this day and age, the single-player survival mode redeems the price. Some may disagree, however the difficulty starts strong and only gets more difficult with each level. It's a challenge not to be over looked.
Overall I'd say Samurai Gunn is an 8/10 and worth a purchase regardless, but it's even more worth a purchase if you have three friends with game pads to decapitate each other. It'd be difficult to implement online capabilities since the controls are heavily based on precise timing, therefore latency would cause issues. This game is exactly where it needs to be, and provides hours of entertainment regardless of couch-buddies.

I have the same problem with this game, as I had with the first one.  Once you figure out your base build order, the game becomes 100% RNG.  Nothing the player does, no strategy or tactic you can employ, has any real meaning in the game.  Fights are absolutely determined by the RNG.  This is made worse in the second installment, because you are always under the effect of a timer pushing you to hurry.  At least in the first game, you could set up a kill zone and try and pull aliens into it, or split them up.  There was at least the pretense of strategy.
Sadly, the game is best played on the easiest setting, as it has the least amount of RNG destroying your party.
I'll give you a perfect example.  One mob left with 3 hit points, my entire party has at least 60% to hit, my sniper has 93% to hit, EVERYONE misses....mob of course one shots one of my soldiers that's in full cover on the next round.  Uninstall.
The real problem is, especially early on in the game, you don't have enough hit points, to offset lousy runs of RNG.  Given that it's *very* easy for your soldiers to be one shot, especially early on, and it's a rage inducing formula if you're playing on any of the higher difficulty levels, or ironman.
At the end of the day, the worst design descision was the timer on every mission.  It strips the game of any kind of tactics, and makes every single thing you do at the mercy of the RNG.  Why this game gets so much praise I'll never understand, to me, it's shallow, and frustrating.

Honestly, XCOM was my childhood game and when I saw couple of years ago its successor, I was totally excited. The game was absolutely amazing. So, when I read the reviews on XCOM 2 I had been waiting and reading reviews for months before the buy. Finally, the game is absolutely amazing again. There is one reason, the game is expected to be hard and to be hard for your strategic and tactical thinking. If you expect fun from killing aliens, go for some stupid FPS. This XCOM, a strategic and tactical game, probably the best you can find around right now.
For example, the claim that time limited missions are too hard and thus not fun. I hate time limitations in games, but this is not time limit, but turn limit. These missions push you forward, so you can't stay behind and play on overwatch. You need to think about time in you tactical decisions and risk appropriately. I was scared at the beginning, but finally found myself mastering new tactics. For instance, thanks to concealment you can go through some of these missions without being uncovered by aliens until the final battle. If you can risk this and do it with precision, your reward is absolutely amazing. You kill VIP, use all of your special abilities in concert and leave the scene unharmed. Taking higher difficulty makes this tactis a need.
Another example, the game is so complex that you simply cannot go through it the same way as previously. The combination of abilities, research preferences or training preferences gives you so significant different gameplay that the game is replayable. Not to mention Ironman feature. Second play is must on ironman. It's not only about difficulty, but it's about the way how you make decisions when you can't take them back and if you know the game, you do only mistakes cause your personal lower patiency. That punish you of course, but that's XCOM!
Guys, don't believe these easy folks who dislike this game, they tend to play easy games and avoid challenge.
