The longer I work in the game industry, the more types of employees I meet, and the less respect I have for the game industry.
Ridge Racer Unbound is like a companion piece to that assessment.  I honestly feel like someone took what was Ridge Racer (A rather good racer) and then said. "What we need is for this game to be more like Burnout, but I don't want you to change anything about our physics engine"  And off the designers and programmers went to try to do it, and ultimately we have Unbounded.
But this game is just damn odd.  The oddest thing about it is the last burnout game was made in 2008, this game came 4 years later.   It's possible this is trying to be like Need for Speed Most Wanted but even then, I don't think that's the goal.
The game is really split between three modes.  First there's the Time attack mode, that's existed in every racing game ever made.   The second is a drift challenge, where the goal is to drift, gain boost and race past enemies.  And finally, the third, Domination mode, where you take down enemies (Called fragging.. ugh) and blow up buildings to get short cuts.
On the surface that last one sounds great.  In reality.... well honestly the entire game is a bit of a mess, it'd be wrong to just call just that one mode a problem, when the game itself really stands out as the biggest issue.
The core issue I have with this game is I really don't know what it's trying to be.   The game seems to revel in the destruction the player does.  Breaking a wall gives you points, killing people gives you points, there's the whole boost/frag system that seems good, and a frag also auto drives your car a bit.  But the real problem is momentum.
You see hitting a wall or driving through it, smashing into cars, and boosting is all great, but the game doesn't "cheat" physics much.  If you're going slow at 60 mph and another car is at the top speed of 200 mph.  You don't accelerate to 150 without a question, instead you slowly start to go faster, and faster and faster.  The acceleration on the cars is shockingly bad.   So mistakes are costly.  Problem is mistakes happen all the time, and getting taken out does as well.  In fact smashing into anything seems to slow you down and for a game build on drifting, the drifting isn't exactly fast.
This coupled with an attempt to be like Burnout where fighting enemies is encouraged really hurts the experience.  That means you're encouraged to do all those things that Burnout made fun, rubbing, smashing, and just being a nuisance.  But the problem is if you slow down (by rubbing against an enemy for instance) you're penalized because you're going slow.  If you get hit into a wall you're taken out of the race, and if you try to get aggressive, you seem penalized.
This is the opposite of how Burnout does it, rubbing is rewarded, you might go smash into the wall, but you got boost to go fast, and you don't need a full bar.  In Ridge Racer one mistake and you can go from first to last, in Burnout that happens and then you can go from last to first quickly.    Ridge Racer isn't Burnout, so the real question is why does it try to be in this game, because it doesn't even try to explain itself other than a VERY short (two line) tutorial about drifting and boosting.
The fact is the game ultimately isn't fun.  It's not just that it's not Burnout, but it's not really anything else.  The game starts out annoying and hard, and ... well I didn't really feel the need to play more than 6 races because as I said they aren't really fun.  The game doesn't welcome you with a tutorial or a couple easy races or anything, instead it's just annoyingly hard from the first race on, and with no difficulty options and no really interesting gameplay, I didn't know why I should have stuck around.
Now I heard complaints about story, or a reason to race, and guys, it's a racing game, it doesn't need a story.  What it DID need is a reason to really exist, because it's not to drift like the rest of the games in the series, and it's not to frag each other.  It doesn't have the style of other games, because even split second was pretty fun for what it was, and it doesn't even have the gameplay that Most wanted had.  Ultimately Ridge Racer is a game with out a reason for existing.
And what's really sad is this is the last game in the Ridge Racer franchise, it's also the only one which didn't have a Japanese release, which is a bit telling in my opinion.   If Ridge Racer had just made Burnout Paradise, or just Burnout semi efficiently, we'd be singing it's praises because Burnout stopped making Burnout games.    Hell, we've seen the Crew, Driveclub, Trackmania and every Need for Speed.  So racing games are still popular.  The problem really is that Ridge Racer didn't stand out at all at a time when it probably would have been relatively easy to stand out.  That's a real shame, but ultimately there's a reason this is the last Ridge Racer.  It shouldn't have been, but it is the end of a great legacy.

Don't let my short play time dissuade you from my review. I've been playing this game for about 2 years on my laptop. I just played a bit to make sure the Steam version works, and it does. This game has lost none of it's charm, or it's difficulty. It plays simply enough. All you have to do is connect 3-or-more like colored tiles to gain the effect desired. During battle you can only move one tile per turn. The game seamlessly enters weapons and other tools you can use during battle as well. For example, you have a laser. This laser requires 5 red tiles to use. During the battle, you make enough red tile combos to get 5, and then you can use the laser. If you don't want to use it right away, that's fine. Every time you get a combo, these colored tiles are added to the ship's "battle inventory", and are stored for later use. There are tools to alter the gravity of the board, destroy specific tiles to gain their bonuses, affect your (or your enemy's) ship in some way, etc. To damage the enemy ship, you make a combo of the mines that are strewn about the board. Each mine has it's own number blinking on it, which is the amount of damage it causes. A combo of 3 level 5 mines will deal 15 damage, for example. You could get a combo of 7 level 10 mines (
hard to do), and deal massive damage in just one turn. Be aware that your enemy also uses these mines, and has their own weapons and tools. Don't worry though, as battles aren't timed. You will have all the time you need to study the board, and make a decision.
You can mine asteroids to gain materials to sell to any of the star bases, then use the profits to buy new ships, weapons, etc. Each asteroid has different materials on them, and each has an amount listed that you need to reach. If you reach these, you'll get a massive bonus to the resources you gain. Don't worry if you don't meet the requirement, you'll still get all the resources you mined. So it's always useful, and sometimes necessary, to mine during the game. Mining sequences are not timed, but have a limited amount of combos you can make, depending on the amount of tiles present on the board.
The most difficult, and
frustrating, point in the game... is the gate hacks. In order to get to different star systems, more asteroids to mine, and missions, you need to hack into an "star gate." This is not optional. In order to progress through the main story, this is required. Even if you don't want to explore. Each gate has a different difficulty. Every gate requires a certain amount of color combos to open it, and you have to do these in the shown sequence... and in the amount of time it gives you. The harder the difficulty of the gate, the more combos you have to make, and in less time available. Since the way the board works (once you get a combo, more tiles enter the board), you could easily get a string of combos and win within a few seconds. Or it'll give you a couple combos, and you can easily get confused as to why you aren't affecting the hack. You may think you need a purple tile, but the auto combos did it for you, but you didn't notice it. So you're entering purple combos to no effect. You can easily waste time this way, and tiles for future use. Unless you're a puzzle master, and love this much of a challenge, you are guaranteed to get frustrated.
This is an amazing game. I have never played a puzzle game quite like it. Everything it does, it does exceptionally well. The dialogue is great, the battles and mining are fun, the quests (though tedious at times) are well written and unique. The galaxy map is quite expansive, with plenty of systems to explore. There are multiple factions, each with their own feelings toward you, and your actions for or against them are reflected during the game. Each star base has different bonuses (positive and negative) for different resources, so if you care about getting the max bonus for each individual resource, you're going to be traveling a lot. I don't really worry about it, though. Most systems have a "shop" where you can buy everything you need. There's also a crafting system. Sometimes when you destroy ships, meet quest requirements, etc., you'll receive "plans." With these you can create new weapons and tools that were previously unavailable to buy, or make expensive items with cheap resources. Later on, you will have access to PSI abilities that allow you to "skip" battles (at the cost of PSI points) with certain ship classes. So if you have a massive battleship, you don't have to fight a lowly raider shuttle, if you don't want to.
As stated earlier, this game may or may not work for you. It has worked just fine for me. But I highly recommend this game to everyone who enjoys a good puzzle board, or space ship battles, or both. This is a
game.

It's games like this that I wish Steam adds a third review option between "thumbs up" and "thumbs down." But, since I experienced more negative than positive gameplay, I must lean towards a thumbs down. First the positives:
+The time period and history. The French Revolution is one of my favorite historical periods and the fact that Ubisoft is a French company gave me confidence that they would put more information and lore about this critical point in their nation's history.
+I love the characters in the game, as well as the moral ambiguity between the Templars and the Assassins. Arno is a great protagonist, and Elise is one of the best female characters I've ever seen in a video game. Some of the historical figures, like the Marquis de Sade, have a charm to them that just makes me laugh and listen. In addition the voice acting is well done, although I've been playing in French in order to give the setting a more accurate feel (Hearing British accents in the English version breaks the immersion for me, even if the voice actors are talented).
Now for the negatives:
-Bugs. BUGS everywhere! Plus, poor optimization has ruined both the graphical quality and gameplay in this supposed "next-gen" game. While the bugs may be hilarious on some moments (I had a hysterical fit after my character fell into a simulation abyss after jumping from a building), for the most part the bugs are more irritating than they're worth. Usually, I play newly released games for many hours nonstop, but I'm struggling to play even an hour in one sitting because the bugs are a gamebreaker for me.
-Frame rate issues. This is a personal preference, but if I'm playing a PC game, I expect 60 fps to be the standard. My PC can handle Titanfall and Metro: Last Light at around 80fps but for AC: Unity, the game plays at 40 fps maximum, and drops to as low as 15 fps on some areas of the game, like the Cafe Theatre, which is the Assassin's HQ. I could have tolerated 30fps if the the frame rate was stable, but the game constantly shifts in frame rate.
-Microtransactions. If I paid $60 for a single-player game, I expect that to be the final payment for the game. Trying to further fleece your customers as well as purposely failing to tell reviewers about the microtransactions is an unethical business maneuver that should be condemned universally. Shame on you Ubisoft!
All in all, I wanted to love this game due to its characters and setting, but the poor optimization and microtransactions prove that Ubisoft needs to rethink their strategy in developing future games as well as issuing an emergency patch for this broken game. A disappointing purchase for a longtime fan of the series.

I feel like ranting about how great this game is before my brain explodes from keeping it all pent up inside.
When I first saw Darkest Dungeon come out on steam, I didn't think much of it. I thought to myself "Hm, another turn based RPG, surely I can put my time elsewhere." What a mistake I made.
I'm not exactly sure what came over me but I decided to pick the game up on a whim, along with the expansion that just came out yesterday, and I do not regret this decision at all. Darkest Dungeon may well be one of the most intense games I've played in a very long time. Turn based dungeon crawling at it's finest for sure.
Most of my enjoyment from this game comes from the art, sound and how -utterly- dire the situation you've been cast into thanks to your ancestor delving far deeper into the realm of dark powers and morbid curiosity than he ought to. Essentially, you recieve a letter from your ancestor (the narrator) explaining that he basically screwed up big time, unleashed all hell on the world and now you've gotta clean it up. "Fine" I thought to myself, "How hard can this possibly be?"
As I play this game, I find myself oddly immersed and connected to the heroes I've sent to explore the surrounding areas. The atmosphere is extremely grim and spooky right from the get go, and the music only adds to that tenfold. Each step your heroes take almost feels forced, and as we progress deeper into the dungeon, and torchlight fades, so too does sanity.
One of my favorite aspects of this game is that as your torchlight goes down, the music gets more and more intense, and the noises and wailing you hear from the surrounding land and creatures grows louder until it's essentially a cacophony of terror. The first time my torch went completely out and I had none left to replenish light, I found myself pausing to listen and simply sitting there going "Sweet lord... What have I done to my team of 4 heroes?"
I'm a massive fan of the resolve/stress system in place for this game, a lot of it having to do with the reasons mentioned above. People get upset about RNG being a huge factor in this game and although true, for some reason, in a game like this I am unbothered by crushing losses. Each time I'm in a bad situation I always find myself sympathizing with my heroes and wondering how I would react in a similar situation. Sorry to say but I'd probably barely make it past the first door.
Eldritch monsters and the Cthulu Mythos that this game is heavily inspired from is a truly terrifying realm and a world I don't want to be a part of. The art team did a stupendous job on capturing all of this. Each enemy you fight has an extremely unnerving look to it. They feel powerful and frightening as well, with each attack they land sometimes making you squirm in your chair (especially if you get crit).
Not all is doom and gloom though, despite the odds being stacked up against you and hope in short supply, your heroes are quite capable and the appropriate amount of planning and a smart approach to combat can yield great results, with killing blows or a crit heal feeling extremely satisfying and relieving stress from both you and your heroes.
After a succesful or crippling expedition, you return to your hamlet where you're able to take a breather, organize your troops and expand on the buildings there which will all help you in your quest. This is the rogue-lite aspect of the game. Each expedition will help bolster your future runs and any heroes you recruit down the road. It's a nice system and again, the art direction and narration makes it seem like a place that only a madman would want to live.
I can't say enough good things about this game. I plan on playing the hell out of it and you should to.

Previously I mentioned the gameplay is simple. Let me expand on that:
-You run
-You jump
-You can jump off walls
-You swing a sword in one of 4 directions (up, down, left, right)
-You shoot your gun (with limited ammo) in 4 directions as well
-You can deflect bullets back in the direction it came at by swinging your sword at it
-Clashing swords with another combatant causes one or both of you to fly backwards and take no damage
-One hit kills
-First to 10 kills in multiplayer
-Killing yourself loses a point
-When you share a similar score with the winner, you may go to a 1v1 showdown
-There is some destructable terrain
-There are spikes of deathy death and squishy death squishes by moving platforms and icicles
-The maps are circular, meaning when you drop from the bottom you will come out the top. From the left edge of the screen to the right.
That's really about it.

One of the most enjoyable games for me in recent memory. As a general fan of space combat games and stratedy games it just made sense to give this a try. I was not dissapointed!
The slower pace of the game at first gives you a false sense of security once the fighting starts. When you first start playing and just about everyone you're against is in the starter ships combat is generally straight-forward with a few abilities and tricks. As players start getting into the later ships your tactics and stratedy needs to begin to change with them due to the different strengths and weaknesses of ships that may not be direct assault but rather hit and run or ambush. Careful positioning of your ship and use of asteroids to avoid incoming damage, make an escape, or ambush enemies are a few tactics you will need to learn and adapt to.
Team play is what makes or breaks your experience in each match. Granted most beginners won't know what to do until they complete the 3 part tutorial of the game and play a few matches but some veteran players can be very frustrating as well. If you like to lone wolf and do your own thing rather than work as a team you may want to reconsider playing this game. Don't ruin it for others by causing a loss because you don't work well with others.
Overall I have recommended this to a few friends already that I figured would enjoy it. So if you ever played a space combat or stratedy game. Or spread sheets in space for those of you who know what I'm talking about, but it left you wanting more with less of a punishment for dying. This game is well worth trying out and seeing as it is still in early development one can only hope to see it improve. Lag is an issue sometimes and occasional ctd have been known to happen but don't let that deter you from enjoying a great game. Thanks for reading and I hope to see you in game!

This is a great hacking game that uses command prompts in order to do things. The game begins with you receiving an email via a Dead Man Switch, which is something that is sent if certain conditions are met(or not), such as not turning on your computer for a week. This email sent to you was from a Hacker named Bit. He didn't log on after 2 weeks, so the email was auto sent to you. It said that 'if you're reading this, I'm already dead'. The game continues into a tutorial where you complete the tasks that Bit set up to be sent to you as you finish them.
This is the premise of the story(no spoilers in that btw). You go through this hacking world trying to find out what happened to bit. You can explore the various computers you come across in your travels, read the various text documents that can contain story related content, whether it be main quest or side quest, or joke texts. There's a site called
in real life, and it archives funny quotes that people submit that the found on various IRC(chat rooms) conversations. Hacknet is filled with many text documents, usually starting with "IRC" then numbers. They're very funny, and you can even collect them if you wish.
Hacknet is a lot like Uplink, but more modern and polished. There's organizations that give you missions/side quests for you to do, and they're all interesting in some way. The side quests are required to a fair degree, as Bits messages wont tell you more until your skill improves by going up in rank on these Organizations. It's not just randomly generated quests like in Uplink, where the differences in quests was basically names and numbers. All of Hacknets Side Quests/Missions have little stories, and as you do these contracts, you may end up finding text documents that hint at what happened to Bit.
For the actual gameplay, it starts out simple, with a few programs to help break through security You'll find more programs to help you get into more complicated systems.
Now for how Hacknet is different from Uplink. For one thing, there's no upgrades. You can find hacking programs, but there's no upgrading, no hacking store to buy hacking upgrades/software. There's no money actually, and no upgrading your computer. Instead of grinding money to get a more powerful PC and just bulldoze your way through security in Uplink, you need to use your programs and computer more strategically.
This DOSE lower replay value compared to Uplink. In Uplink there's plenty of things to buy and upgrade, and unlimited, if not plain, missions to do. Hacknet is more story driven, with it's main story and the little side stories filled with interesting jobs, info, chat logs, and lots of other things.
I'm not sure how far I am exactly, but at the very least, there's about 35+ side quests at the very least. So there's plenty to do in this game, along with Easter eggs and subtle references to entertain you.
While Uplink was more mouse driven in how you hack, Hacknet is almost entirely with keyboard commands, like Spencer's Hacker Evolution games(The first 2, not the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ Duality). There is some mouse controls, such as using the mouse to quickly move through a computers directories.
If you like Uplink, you will definitely like Hacknet. If you're interested in hacking games, but haven't played one before, this COULD be a good start, as the difficulty curve is very fair, but Uplink might be better for a newbie.
Btw, you can use the TAB key to auto complete words/directories/programs names. Useful for when you need to quickly break through many ports.

Half-Life is a very well known FPS by Valve that has solid single-player campaign and fun deathmatch modes, as well as modding abilities, like any self-proud PC FPS should have.
Now, what kind of deal we get there? HL1 had retail release in 1998 and it wasn't for a while before it appeared on Steam, the kind of Steam that we use. Year or so ago it was updated few times in effort to port it to Linux and Mac, like most Valve games now. No matter what, Steam release seemed to not have all tiny bugfixes that retail has. Also, unlike Retail, it doesn't have "mods" category. You would often see official mods there (Ricochet, TFC, CS, Deathmatch Classic) that you could download for free back then on retail, but as of right now you have to pay for those to purchase them serapately on Steam. On good side, this release comes with "HD Models pack" from Blue Shift by default and you can enable it in options. It increases polygonal prettyness and completely changes look of some of the weapons.
Now, as for single-player... You are Gordon Freeman, a scienist with bright future and classy beardie, champion at speed whacking with clowbar, who spends most of his time mastering skills of duct crawling. Working at Black Mesa, the best and most stable research center around, today is the day you will push unknown material into sciency thingy as experiement on whetever you can do it or not. You can. Now it's your objective to reach the surface alive where military will rescue us all from hostile aliens. While you shoot things and throw grenades like a wussy. And commanding friendly Barneys to follow you with no objection.
Now, many fans would happily tell you that game is freaking perfect and legendary. And it was indeed revolutionary. But you gotta know what exactly was and that well, by now it became just another good shooter. Though when compared to modern FPS, it's quite old-school, with levels design that makes you explore and figure out, in other words, will easily make you lost. Yea, and everybody's favourite health kits are there too. And ability to hold onto dozen weapons in same time, maybe even too many, seeing how I didn't feel like using some of them. With 3 kinds of explosive tools, with enemies happily ignoring tripmines.
Oh yes, and they also, unlike many games, don't have music running all time. Just only occasionally playing to set the mood, otherwise it's only sound. Pretty much trademarkish Vavle approach by now. At least in this current version of HL1 the music doesn't stop suddenly before it's finished when you enter new area.
No no no, the plot itself is not what got most of people, nothing to compare with RPG games. Instead, what got most people is that envirmoment was telling plot. A friendly scienist could tell you some news on what is going on when you would find one (and be free to shoot into their face). And you could tell away that you are in realistical envirmoment, exactly what people loved Duke Nukem 3D for, being able to tell that you are in building that launches rocket salletile and even actually launch it, for example. Before that, you either was playing plot-less Quake (Quake 2 came out year before it, everybody was playing it) or was enjoying some overblown RPG-FPS mix. HL let these Quake people enjoy something what made some sense for once. (If we forget about DN3D, yes)
Well, and AI was getting praised a lot too. Sure, human enemies that could avoid your fireshots and properly throw grenades were nice, and they were damn good at making themselves look like they work as team was good...Until some wounded chap decides that it's excellent idea to retreat toward your position, running botherlessly despite being shot into back by chasing player. Friendly AI wasn't something what Quake player usually saw back then either (ignoring NAM game, yes), even if security guards hate doorframes and stairs, making you to babypush them around. BUT still, having AI divided into 3 opposing groups, with only one of them being friendly to you, it was something unusual.
That was what most likely made it hit back then... Today? Solid shooter. Good one. But don't let hype make you to overstamate this game! And it has it's fair share of glitches too.
Oh, and there is Multiplayer, Deathmatch to be precise... Crossfire 24/7!
As of right now, 2014 year, the game is far far away from the days when it was popular, but it's not dead yet. You may still find few servers having players, 1-4, here and there, playing either Crossfire map or some user-made one, which is kind of enough to have fun. Though I had a joy of playing in TDM server with around 12 players, with one team wokring as team (so it's probably not bots... I hope), just recently. But overall, occasional small casual DM still happens.
And with all variety of weapons, there is enough of fun mayhem to have, killing simple players and getting killed all time by that player with Gauss Gun, combination of insta-kill railgun (after seconds of charging) with "RocketJumping" ability, letting such player to change position quickly. Jump Booster also helps to add fun to DM thing. Yes, it's not perfectly balanced, don't think of it as something worthy e-sport. Yet I still have joyful memories of playing LAN parties, with my friend finding creative usage for tripmines. So, nice bonus.

I'm going to recommend this game, but it does come with caveats. If you're the sort of person who cannot handle loss of any kind, who decries their every death in a game as ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, you may find this a little testing. But stick with it, learn to take a hit, and you'll find a pretty nice and cheaply priced game with fantastic aesthetics, tense duels, and a tale behind every hero.
This is a game dripping with atmosphere, the narrator grimly pronouncing the doom your heroes are charging towards, every inch of dungeon tinged with malice, and every treasure you find a possible liability down the line. The art style is fantastic, rolling with a grim aesthetic to support the grim tasks you assign to the men and women who are drawn to your banner.
The biggest issue people have with the gameplay is the RNG, but I would argue that this is misplaced. The larger issue is a lack of player agency. I’m a big fan of XCOM, and it works well as a comparison. When I play XCOM, I am given a huge amount of choices, from where to position, who to move first, which alien to target primarily, which cover to destroy, whether to get in close and shock the enemies into incompetence or to force the enemies to move to me and wear them down in a long-range engagement. In Darkest Dungeon, my options are far more limited. Each character can only have 4 abilities at any time, and it’s a lucky day when all four are available for use. And equally, the path most likely to succeed is rarely difficult to figure out. This isn’t an easy problem to fix; it’s a structural issue with the gameplay. But the limited options make it far easier for people to believe that they were simply screwed over by RNG. With more experience and time spent on a campaign, your options become more based on preparation for a mission, how much money you are willing to spend to upgrade your heroes, and which trinkets you are willing to risk to provide them with an extra edge. Even so, tactically the game degenerates into pure dice-rolling more than most would like.
This level of RNG can be enjoyable in its own way, if you choose to interpret it as individual's heroes performance. There'll always be the one front-line brawler who always crits when it's time to get serious, or a healer who insists on rolling low and sabotaging your run from the inside. There's always going to be the beaten occultist, focused down by every enemy, who finally hits 100 stress but chooses to stand tall in the face of adversity, and inspires the party to drive the beasts back. But still, for those less narratively inclined, the feeling of a run being doomed by simple chance is a hard thing to simply take in stride.
Still, the game doesn’t suffer greatly for that flaw. The game is not about coming home alive every week. The one resource you cannot exhaust is fresh meat to grind against the darkness, so a death is practically part and parcel of scratching your way through the game. In fact, in one campaign that has been remarkably devoid of deaths, I have found it difficult to make room for all the new blood I needed to conquer earlier bosses. Just remember that any losses you take are no more than temporary setbacks, and there will always be more travellers ready to carry the torch further. If you pick up this game, one thing I would suggest is picking up the expanded roster mod at some point. I don’t think the roster has been expanded to handle the new classes that have been added over the game’s life, and a somewhat frustrating feature is that characters will refuse to enter lower-levelled content. It'll technically make the game slightly easier, but I'd say the trade-off is worth it to give you the ability to choose the quest you go on.
Good luck and enjoyment to all those who choose to buy the game. In radiance, may you find victory.

Simple RNG fest with no real tactical depht. Occasionally, cascades of bad RNG happen, showing how little you can actually do to influence the cause of the game. Here's an example:
After camping, a nighttime ambush happens (bad RNG #1)
Two enemys hit a hero critically (2x bad RNG for hitting the same hero and 2x for crit)
One of them causes bleeding (bad RNG #6)
From all those hits he suffers stress and does not resist the affliction depite wearing an item that supports it (Bad RNG #7)
Another hit by the enemy stuns my second healer (Bad RNG #8 for hitting exactly him, #9 for not resisting the stun)
The hero that is at deaths door instantly dies (Bad RNG #10)
I didnt even include that enemy attacks can be dodged, the only thing i could do during this event was sitting there and watch. Its frustrating beyond everything i've ever experienced in videogames.
The combat is very simple. There are a couple of 2- ability combos, but usually those only make sense against bosses. Against normal enemys, the best thing to do is just clubbing them to death, straying in an occasional stun when you know you cant kill them this round. Also, a healer must always be brought everytime to abuse the "deaths door" mechanic that allows your heroes to stay alive for another hit ot two, if healed the process starts again.
I've invested so much time in this game, thinking that i might learn, that there are some tactical possibilities which i might discover and belive me, i tried. I really went through the heroe's abilities, combining bonus damages from marks, stuns and what not over different heroes and ended up frustrated, discovering only what i already knew: Club to death and heal is the way to go. There are probably guides on the web that tell you more efficient ways, but if you like to discover a game for yourself and enjoy the progress from getting better due to your own learning and ideas, this game is not for you.
The great artstyle and narrator become boring, the latter even annoying after you heard his babbling long enough.
As a conclusion, the game is really great at hooking up people for the first few hours where everything is new and atmospheric. When you actually seek gameplay, you best look elsewhere. This, i hesitate to call it game, offers none.

After playing more and getting saome perspective, I feel it wasn't fair to write a negative review, so I'm changing it to positive, although still with some issues.
The game is extremely engaging and addictive. It looks very good, and has really well designed gameplay, both the strategic and tactical level. It also has great replayability due to many random factors that make each campaign unique.
The game still has some stability and performance issues, even on high-end systems. These can be circumvented by modifying some video options, but this should not be necessary when you have a monster rig.
I recommend playing this game in Legend/Ironman mode. This makes the difficulty demanding even in late game. However, many bugs and gameplay issues that affect this game will be that much more annoying in this mode.
First, the game cheats. Your units in concealment are not neutral to the game's AI - the AI will act according to your moves, even if it has not actually detected you. Also, the aliens sometimes get unexpected turns to act.
Second, Firaxis did not learn from the first game to adjust the difficulty curve. The game is still very hard at the beginning and super easy mid to end game. There is a mnior improvement compared to XCOM, but it's far too low. To have anything close to a challenging experience in the mid and endgame, you have to choose Legend/Ironman and suffer to extreme amounts of RNG killing your game while not making any actual tactical or strategic mistakes.
On the other hand, many of the mods and the game's shortcomings can be circumvented by mods, which are numeroous, and very smoothly integrated into the game.
Overall, the game i a lot oif fun, and lasts for a long time, but sometimes the bugs, gameplay issues and plain ole RNG can make you fling your monitor out the window, especially on Ironman!

This is certainly a masterpiece of storytelling. This game won't be for everyone. It is a point and click narrative adventure, but the majority of the game is cutscenes. The point and click sections are pretty basic, involving you walking around an area, inspecting things, talking to people and sometimes solving puzzles. These sections were alright but felt quite slow and tedious. The cutscenes are good, though. The writing isn't groundbreaking but it was above average and enough to make cutscenes filled with raw dialogue entertaining. What really stands out in this game is the character development. Telltale have really done good job developing the personalities of these characters, and you really feel strongly connected to some of them. This is evident when a character dies, and you will be left absolutely shocked. This game has plenty of shocking moments. Unbelieveble events that will have you staring wide-eyed at the screen, with your hand covering your mouth. These plot twists or unexpected character deaths are what really make the game an unforgettable experience. The game also gives you a great amount of choice. Some of these choices are very tough moral decisions that will have you thinking, such choosing to save one person instead of another. Most of the choices are just dialogue options, but I really liked them because they present different ways to approach a conversation; be selfish and rude, rational and smart or sympathetic and kind. These dialogue options really make it seem like you ARE the game's protagonist, even though you're only PLAYING as him.
Summing up: Excellent character developent, dialogue options and moral choices make this an engrossing and unforgettable narrative experience, even though the point and click sections are a bit boring.

It's not the breakthrough that XCom: Enemy Within was, but I realize that EW was a game that had a lot of time to get refined. Also, I somehow missed the XCom series until EW, so now it's not altogether new.
The graphics are excellent, the game play is very intricate and fun, and the customization options should keep people who are really into that busy for a long time. Best of all, the gamemakers warmly embraced the mod community, ensuring that XCom 2 should have a long, long shelf life (some of them are necessary to speed up the game, or see flanking options). The addition of the countdowns - both in the strategy map and in individual missions - adds some wonderful tension, urgency, and chaos to the proceedings.
The problems? Well, Normal difficulty mode takes it too easy on you, and the second hardest difficulty is too unfair *at times*, but then gradually becomes quite manageable. The real hardship is the road to getting enough experience to know what you're doing. The ways that enemies can be laid out on a board - or triggered - vary, and are very confusing. I'd recommend playing 4 or so campaigns with Save Scum available, because you need to be able to start to understand what's causing your team to get wiped out. The unfair slaughter of your team generally distracts you from realizing what mistake you made.
Two final nitpicks - this was created by the same team behind Enemy Unknown/Enemy Within, but you get a lot of the same information at the end of XCom 2 as you did in EU/EW (even worse, it's all vague information). Also, I really wish the missions were more teaming with aliens and not so much the Advent troopers. It's less exciting and happens way, way too often. But for all I know, the creators will totally revamp this game in a future update, just as they did with its predecessor.
UPDATE:
The Shen's Last Gift DLC makes for a pretty decent addition to the game. I haven't tried the Alien Rulers DLC, as I don't like the cost or what it adds to the game enough.

Samurai Gunn is an extremely fast-paced arena combat game in which players use a katana as their main weapon and may fire up to three shots from a gun as a support weapon. The gameplay relies on players' abilities to quickly move around the levels my means of running, jumping and executing their opponents in one lightning-fast strike. Shots from guns may be used to cover long distances in a straight line, but may also be deflected at the shooter by parrying them with one swing of the sword. Additionally, levels often include environmental hazards such as spikes and moving platforms which can squish any character against a wall, floor or ceiling.
An impressive amount of attention to detail is revealed through such things as bullet casings falling to the ground after each shot. What's more, the casings remain there and may be pushed by any character who steps on them. Another example is the water: if someone dies in a pond, the water acquires a red tint which becomes more intense as more blood is spilled, only to be washed away after a few seconds of no blood-spilling on the same spot. To top it all off, standing in water renders your gun useless even when when you get out of the pond, so keep that in mind.
The soundtrack is a perfect match for the action. Based on traditional Japanese instruments, it's reminiscent of soundtracks from chanbara movies and animes with a historical setting. At times, it reminds me of Samurai Spirits, only faster-paced (depending on the track). On that note, the sound effects are hugely satisfying. Most of all, the katanas cutting through the air (or your enemies, ideally). There's something about that loud metallic *schwing!* that makes you want to keep pressing the sword button for more, even if you're not hitting anyone.
Graphically, it's a beautiful game. The sprites are simple but perfectly distinguishable from one another and each is full of personality. There are three characters for each faction and, even within such simplicity, all of them can be told apart at a glance while keeping a common element that identifies them as belonging to the same group. The levels offer a rather wide variety of colours and designs. The intense lime green and clear brown of the bamboo forests, the purple rocks and pale green bushes of the mountain pass with its Buddha statues or the white snow, dark trees and clear water of the winter areas are all pleasant to look at and brimming with detail. Each gives the battle a particular mood or atmospheric feeling. And yet, they managed to do all this with no real distractions for the player, thanks to its retro-style pixellated graphics. Combining an old visual style with modern-day gameplay fluency is a path that numerous indie developres take, and it was yet again the right choice for this title.
All of it is wrapped up into an elegant presentation that fans of chanbara films and samurai pop culture in general will recognise and love. From the moment we see the title screen, we know what type of world we'll be thrown into. A red band with black silhouettes belonging to a bunch of samurais running through a field is an extremely effective introduction to a high-paced game such as this one and it also serves the purpose of creating a classy main menu. In-game, the brief stop produced by a kill, with the blackening of the screen save for the strip which shows killer and victim, is a charmingly abrupt way of making everyone aware of the death. The slow-motion plus zoom that frames the final kill in a fight always provides for an interesting composition and flaunts the game's colourful palette as well as its sprites, still lovely and worth of appreciation with their pixels brought to a bigger size. The menus are simple and use one font, and the signs which recount the kills at the end of a match have a neat parchment feel to them, with easily recognisable icons depicting each death and its cause.
I recommend obtaining this underappreciated gem while it's on sale, since playing it with friends is the best way to exploit its wonders. Survival mode is fun, engaging and addictive, but nothing beats the variety and unpredictability (or lack thereof) of playing against human competitors. As more people get this game, the more fun it will get for all of us who share it.

I'm going to shove my opinion into this game, seeing how I already have about 70 hours into this game, and a good chunk of time into the SDK. I doubt I'll be putting in a mod, as I just use the SDK for my own personal reasons.
But to put it bluntly, I'm recommending the hell out of this game. There are many aspects of the game I like, but if I were to put it simply, it's this. I like the overall atmosphere of the game. It's different from the last game, and I find it enjoyable.
So XCOM 2 is the sequel to XCOM: Enemy Unknown/Enemy Within, made by Firaxis games, and they stick to the original core mechanics they had in EU/EW, and add some more elements to make it streamlined in some aspects, and complex in others.
Specifically, they mess with the base building system so you only make one of each room, and it's what you build isn't so obvious. (No more sattelite arrays, yay!) So now you can pick what you want first, and you BETTER take advantage of your first building. I like it, since now I'm not railroaded to a certain build queue.
They also add more choices in the soldier skills. Without mods, there are 5, one needing the Psi Lab to get. And each of them benefit from certain scenarios. All in all, good variation.
And now we go into the main part of the gameplay: The missions. This is where my opinion may differ from the critics of this game. The timed missions add a bit more difficulty into the game, but it also means they got rid of the really sluggish tactics of the previous game, where the most recommended strategy was to move like a snail and Overwatch like mad to avoid activating alien pods. I personally found that old strategy boring as HELL. So yeah, being forced out of that felt nice. In addition, the concealment system also gets rid of that crawling strategy, as you're now free to move around without worry about activating the pods.
And now for my favorite aspect of the game, and something I don't see a lot of people talking about: The SDK and the mods you can use. I feel that most of the main complaints, especially the timed mechanic, has been resolved from mods. True concealment, for instance, pauses the countdown until you get caught. The SDK also allows to adjust a LOT of the skills, weapon stats, and many other aspects. You can overhaul the game entirely if you wanted. Heck, the Long War team, which balanced the game and a lot of the critics liked about EU/EW, have a few mods in the Workshop already.
Now, if you are arguing that Firaxis should have done this without the modding community, I guess I can see your point. However, it IS there, and it's there for anyone with the game. (Just go to library, then tools. Download the thing) This game CAN be tweaked to your liking in terms of balance, if you really want it.
And as an added note, I tweaked the ini to give my soldiers 20 base HP, I reduced alien aim by 50 percent on all range values, and I used the SDK to create 60 damage weapons. Cheating? YES. Do I still find it fun? Yes. Again, the modding tools allow me to tweak the game to my preference, and many of you can do the same.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.
Eat.

I don't know why I didn't review XCOM 2 when I first finished playing it - I had the game pre-ordered and immediately spent a lot of time cranking through a playthrough on the default difficulty. It's a good game, but I still prefer its predecessor.
The story is pretty much non-existent, but what does exist is very similar to the first: namely, fight off an alien invasion of Earth. This time around things are taking place later, during an occupation, but it hardly matters - everything feels more or less the same.
On top of that, the  micro gameplay is very similar to the first as well. This time around I think it might be a tad easier - mostly because the displayed percentages seem to be a bit more accurate. The class names have changed, but their general roles and abilities haven't.
The missions are almost all randomly generated levels. This was supposed to make each one feel unique, but in reality the level design still feels very repetitive. There's something to be said for a hand-crafted experience, and there's almost none of that in XCOM 2. I wonder how the game would've fared if all the time and energy that went into random generation had gone into creating unique levels instead. It's hard to say.
My biggest complaint is the meta game. It feels much slower and more difficult this time around. I was constantly out of supplies and intel. And I never seemed to get as far ahead in equipment as I wanted to be. The Avatar project mechanic is annoying. I generally hate any forced time mechanic though.
The final level is poorly designed, especially at the end with its infinite waves - that's just something that doesn't belong in a game like XCOM. But otherwise this is a solid strategy game.
Since this is one of the few times when I've played all the DLC before reviewing a new game it's worth a mention: for the most part, it sucks. Compared to Enemy Within (which I thought was utterly brilliant) there just isn't depth here. The added abilities and units don't add much to a fully upgraded vanilla squad. And while each of the story levels is fun, it's too little too late. They should've expanded the story and given each DLC more missions. It would've made more of an impact on me, instead of feeling like a chore to slog through to get all the added achievements.
The ultimate problem is really by comparison. XCOM: Enemy Unknown was groundbreaking for me. It had both a well-designed meta game and fun action within the levels. XCOM 2 repeats a lot of that, but it's lackluster. Pick up this game if you already thoroughly enjoyed and finished the first. Otherwise, spend your time there instead.

Starbound is a very interesting game, with a terrific concept, potential depth, and pleasant aesthetic.  Looking at other Steam reviews and the forums, there seems to be quite a bit of criticism of the game and the developers. For what it is worth, I've found that the majority of criticism is based upon unreal expectations of the game at this point in its life cycle (especially in concern to development). Basically, if you are the type gamer that wants to fully immerse yourself in a finished product, then I would suggest waiting. On the other hand, if you would like to actively take part in beta testing the nightly builds or play around with the stable build (knowing that it is not a final product), then Starbound can be a terrific experience.
All in all, if you are looking for something fun to do and don't take yourself too seriously (i.e. don't think that every patch or dev update is a personal affront to you) then i think you will have no problem with playing the current build of the game and interacting with the community. I've played this game off and on since last December and have enjoyed everything for the most part. The building, crafting, and basic systems are relatively in place and if you are not concerned with "endgame" content, it is extremely easy to spend a few hundred hours shooting around the sectors and exploring.

Omsi 2 is a game that you cannot take seriously.
You can try, you can set up your fancy steering wheel, clip on your TrackIR, have the IBIS app on your mobile phone of choice, even wear a floppy hat, but when you get started, you learn that the AI is just too dumb to play it seriously.
Part of the fun is the mishaps that happen on the way, which there will be many. Under the hood the game is actually pretty darn great, good bus physics, and the sound design is just one of the best in gaming history (and that is no joke). Collision physics suck, mind. Well, they're great if you want to shoot your own bus, or another bus, into the stratosphere.
For the most part the quality of the content is good, very good in fact. Originally a tiny dev team it is clear that this was a labour of love, and that effort shows in the stock content and some of the DLC. SOME, not all. Very much like Dovetail, Aerosoft are willing to put any old map/vehicles on the Steam store to earn them some cash. This makes purchases very hit and miss, and finding reviews in a place other than Steam could be difficult. In general though, pretty good, and Omsi 2 has a great modding scene, some of which equal or even better the quality of official DLCS.
Omsi 2 is oddly engaging, and entertaining, and sort of falls into that realm of Farm Simulator or Eurotruck Simulator where really the game should be boring as hell, and maybe it is, but you still come back for more. There is a odd satisfaction of driving around a sleek, modern hybrid bus, or one of those real diesel smoke spewers of the 80s, you can practically smell the stubbed out cigarettes and that yellow liquid that could either be beer or urine or both.
What this game begs for is optimisation. The game engine of Omsi 2 is pretty much as good as it can get, DLC creators try their best to improve matters, but the core game itself could do with a proper polish up (pokes Aerosoft in the ribs, you listening?). I would love to see this in something like the Unreal Engine or Unity, doubt that would happen though. Any half decent rig should be able to make very few concessions in game settings, but don't expect constant 60s.
If you want to buy a few DLCs to expand on the stock content, the Berlin X10 is a great buy (huge map), as is Hamburg. The forthcoming Omsi 2 Add On London DLC (formerly the mod called The South London Project) is one I'm very much looking forward to, not only to drive some iconic buses, but also to terrorise the streets of my nations capital.

Mostly a yes from me on this one. The game is a great deal of fun at first, what with its Uplink like music and the gradual progression through the hacking tools and so on providing for a lot of varied fun... at first. Nearing the five hour mark here and already I'm starting to see some fray to the edges though, with some rather repetitive mission design and some missions with some gameplay mechanics that are real unclear, its not as good as it started out as.
That being said, for 10 bucks this is still a worthy sucessor to its clear idol Uplink. I didn't think Uplink was a perfect game either by any means, and some of the issues I had with that game are addressed in this one, namely the fact that hacknet has a better UI (important for those missions where you are on a timer) and a focus more on sussing out how to get into a system and manage your resources than trying to beat an arbitrary clock every hack.
Hacknet has I think just enough going for it at 10 bucks to recommend it, and if they decide to release an expansion or a sequel, I think it would be all the better, as this is a wonderful framework for an excellent game if nothing else.

Simple RNG fest with no real tactical depht. Occasionally, cascades of bad RNG happen, showing how little you can actually do to influence the cause of the game. Here's an example:
After camping, a nighttime ambush happens (bad RNG #1)
Two enemys hit a hero critically (2x bad RNG for hitting the same hero and 2x for crit)
One of them causes bleeding (bad RNG #6)
From all those hits he suffers stress and does not resist the affliction depite wearing an item that supports it (Bad RNG #7)
Another hit by the enemy stuns my second healer (Bad RNG #8 for hitting exactly him, #9 for not resisting the stun)
The hero that is at deaths door instantly dies (Bad RNG #10)
I didnt even include that enemy attacks can be dodged, the only thing i could do during this event was sitting there and watch. Its frustrating beyond everything i've ever experienced in videogames.
The combat is very simple. There are a couple of 2- ability combos, but usually those only make sense against bosses. Against normal enemys, the best thing to do is just clubbing them to death, straying in an occasional stun when you know you cant kill them this round. Also, a healer must always be brought everytime to abuse the "deaths door" mechanic that allows your heroes to stay alive for another hit ot two, if healed the process starts again.
I've invested so much time in this game, thinking that i might learn, that there are some tactical possibilities which i might discover and belive me, i tried. I really went through the heroe's abilities, combining bonus damages from marks, stuns and what not over different heroes and ended up frustrated, discovering only what i already knew: Club to death and heal is the way to go. There are probably guides on the web that tell you more efficient ways, but if you like to discover a game for yourself and enjoy the progress from getting better due to your own learning and ideas, this game is not for you.
The great artstyle and narrator become boring, the latter even annoying after you heard his babbling long enough.
As a conclusion, the game is really great at hooking up people for the first few hours where everything is new and atmospheric. When you actually seek gameplay, you best look elsewhere. This, i hesitate to call it game, offers none.

Mostly a yes from me on this one. The game is a great deal of fun at first, what with its Uplink like music and the gradual progression through the hacking tools and so on providing for a lot of varied fun... at first. Nearing the five hour mark here and already I'm starting to see some fray to the edges though, with some rather repetitive mission design and some missions with some gameplay mechanics that are real unclear, its not as good as it started out as.
That being said, for 10 bucks this is still a worthy sucessor to its clear idol Uplink. I didn't think Uplink was a perfect game either by any means, and some of the issues I had with that game are addressed in this one, namely the fact that hacknet has a better UI (important for those missions where you are on a timer) and a focus more on sussing out how to get into a system and manage your resources than trying to beat an arbitrary clock every hack.
Hacknet has I think just enough going for it at 10 bucks to recommend it, and if they decide to release an expansion or a sequel, I think it would be all the better, as this is a wonderful framework for an excellent game if nothing else.

Its presentation is executed so well that every action you take feels like you've been doing them for years, like hacking into networks is just child's play.
It plays very much like a puzzle-adventure game, so if something like that is up your alley, it's really worth checking out.
Also, it's worth playing to see the final hacking sequence alone.

Eleven years after the release of Introversion Software's
, this Zürich-based indie studio has tackled the subject of thermonuclear warfare again. Has it fared well in doing so?
As far as I can tell, the answer's obviously a resounding 'Yes'. Although as you can already see, it's often going to be compared to
for one reason or another, it's fair to say that
surpasses it in many ways.
First of all, the two offer a very different feel to the End of Times. Both generally draw inspiration from that old 1983 movie,
, the former more so:
gave us an underground, bunker-like, depressing atmosphere. The map was a faithful rendering of the Mercator projections shown in the movie, special effects and all.
literally gives us an overground view from space and the atmosphere is, dare I say, merrier. You don't hear a crying woman and the music doesn't slow down as millions die on Samuel Barber's
playing in the background like you do in
. You'll hear the doomsday clock ticking in the background, but the mood is much lighter and the take on the subject is less serious, more cartoonish in its' overall outlook.
What does
have that
lacks? Regions matter more than towns do in the latter, so the clinical realism of the former (in which heavily populated towns, radars, silos were primary targets) does not appear in this game. Your nukes make whole regions uninhabitable, towns getting blown away by the blast registers as collateral damage in that sense.
Second-strike capability with submarines is nowhere to be found, maritime warfare was half the job in
, this game (again, being more focused on space and rockets) compensated this with a sort of "infinite strike" in which you only run out of nukes once the regions producing them are irradiated.
There are no delayed phases leaving you some time to develop combat readiness at the beginning (no countdown from DEFCON 5 to DEFCON 1), enemies can theoretically launch a preemptive strike on you at the start of the game.
Multiplayer is what makes
a popular game to this day, a pity that
hasn't managed to do the same, this game's longevity may take heavy a blow as a result.
So how does it stand out? I admittedly began playing this game in the same way I would have on
, and turned most of the planet into a baked potato. But interestingly this game allows you to end the game through peaceful, or less bellicose, means. The AI responds to the rate at which you are arming and expanding your country.
The game doesn't force you to ignite Armaggedon, but if you open with aggressive moves, then even those countries you're allied to will turn on you in an attempt to calm everything down. Although I will let players discover this by themselves, there are also ways of destroying your enemies without either firing a single nuke or entirely disarming your superpower. It is an intriguing addition, you can always prevent it, whereas
does the opposite and inevitably counts victory by the millions of survivors who haven't been exterminated in an effort to convey the full meaning of Mutually Assured Destruction.
You get to chose and unlock nuclear superpowers or regional powers who are known to have nuclear capabilities. You can expand them in whichever direction you like. This is a major difference from
, which only gave us the possibility to control whole continents.
The special weapons are amazing and not all of them are offensive in nature. A lot of them are very cool (I know, I shouldn't use that word when this game mainly consists in frying your enemies!). If you have bought the bonus content, you'll get access to some interesting factoids about them (some of which I personally knew, some of which I didn't). This team has certainly done its' homework.
In summary...
-A refreshing take on a gloomy subject.
-Multifaceted AI.
-Several possible endings.
-Fun and highly addictive.
-Contemporary powers.
-Original, well-researched WMDs/special weapons.
-Swiss made (Sorry, I just HAD to say this :P).
-Settlements aren't so important, regions/nations are nuclear
.
-No second strike capability: no submarines. Would have added more danger to the gameplay.
-No countdown to Armaggedon, chaos can start at any moment.
-No multiplayer.
Fun and with enough realism to stay in tune with the subject of global annihilation. All good in my book. A much welcome addition to the genre, and I wish Blindflug Studios AG many more successful stories of the kind.

It's a great sequel (or should I say spin-off) to the 2012 XCOM:EU/EW which I'm very fond of. A fresh take on the previous alien invasion plot coming from an XCOM veteran.
One of those games that would require you to rack your brains out on what to do next. A mixture of planning, execution, and reaction to some unexpected circumstances. Learning to control how RNG would play out for you instead of betting all your chances in a single dice roll all the time.
There's a lot of mods out there but be sure to try to finish the game in vanilla once. Just install some QOL mods for your convenience then embark on your journey.
As for bugs, I haven't really encountered anything game-breaking. But the game uses a lot of RAM. I have to upgrade to 16GB just to be able to play it smoothly without the risk of crashing anytime I ran out of memory. Do not crank up the graphics as well. Just set it to manageable levels wherein you could reliably render 60+ FPS most of the time.
And lastly, learn how to read and analyse. Some mods out there may break your game or collide with other mods. Just pick up those who are proven reliable and/or have synergy with your current mods.
And it supports ultrawide 21:9 monitor resolutions. Just do the necessary adjustments in the XCOMEngine.ini and you're set.

I'm going to give my brutally honest first impressions. The amount of customization in this game is enough to make anybody happy. The maps that you play on are a lot more diverse than the first XCOM, but that's the end of the good stuff about it. This game looks slightly better than the first XCOM, but doesn't perform anywhere near as good. I went from a consistent 90 frames per second on ultra settings in the original XCOM, to 30 frames per second if I'm lucky in this. My PC is out of date, so I'm sure it's not a problem for other people, but that's a huge performance decrease for just about the same graphics. This game is also way too hard. I beat the original XCOM on medium difficulty only losing 12 soldiers. I never loaded a previous save when I lost somebody, because I knew that it was my fault, and it seemed fair. Not in this. You run into sectoids with mind control powers right from the start, which is a bit brutal when you don't have any armor or any equipment at all for that matter. About 5 missions in, I ran into an enemy that has a ton of hp for me still running on starter gear. He can teleport anywhere on the map, and shoot afterwards, which does mean that he can (and will) teleport right behind one of your soldiers and kill them, without you being able to do anything at all about it. He can also disable the weapons of your entire team, making you have to reload. I shouldn't even know that enemy exists until 3/4 of the way through the game...not on my fifth mission. Also, every mission I've played so far has a time limit that you need to complete it in. That is NOT ok. There should never be a time limit in a game that is completely controlled by random numbers. It's got that twitchy ridge racer control that takes a little getting used to. But the drifting mechanic took me forever to use properly. it really should be more simple than it is. For the longest time the drift button for me was the "lose compelte control" button. In some cars it still is.
After you get the control down, and start getting some boost combos, it gets really good and challenging. but at a certain point of difficulty, the negatives really start making it damn near impossible to progress. as you get the faster cars, you catch more air, naturally. This is where the physics engine flips out, trys to glue your tires to the ground and get you spun around. Also, you can flip your car over and the game won't register it as a wreck and reset you. It will only register a wreck if you have a head on collision, or a hard hit on the side. luckily there's a handy reset car option in the pause menu(wtf?). which sets you way farther back than a wrecked opponent btw.
That wouldn't be all that bad, but even one mistake will ruin your whole race. You can get 5sec ahead in first(if you're good/lucky), have one bad drift(spinout) or wreck and you'll be lucky to be in the top 3. The CPU players keep in a tight pack and gain boost from drafting which gives it an unfair advantage in terms of constantly getting speed boosts(which can wreck you as well). If you get to the back of the pack after the first lap, forget it, you'll never catch the top 3. Drafting to gain boost and taking out enemies are the best ways to win a race, if you can't stay with the pack, you'll just lag behind.
Ok, now that i've vented some frustration, let me tell you why I've played it as much as I have.
When you get a boost combo, and take down half the racers, and stay in first place, it's a great time. You can blow up petrol trucks and take out other racers. You destroy buildings to make new short cuts; all very cool. There's also a decent variety of race types. This paragraph is much smaller than the one where i crapped on the game, but these parts almost make up for the downsides.

Starbound is a very interesting game, with a terrific concept, potential depth, and pleasant aesthetic.  Looking at other Steam reviews and the forums, there seems to be quite a bit of criticism of the game and the developers. For what it is worth, I've found that the majority of criticism is based upon unreal expectations of the game at this point in its life cycle (especially in concern to development). Basically, if you are the type gamer that wants to fully immerse yourself in a finished product, then I would suggest waiting. On the other hand, if you would like to actively take part in beta testing the nightly builds or play around with the stable build (knowing that it is not a final product), then Starbound can be a terrific experience.
All in all, if you are looking for something fun to do and don't take yourself too seriously (i.e. don't think that every patch or dev update is a personal affront to you) then i think you will have no problem with playing the current build of the game and interacting with the community. I've played this game off and on since last December and have enjoyed everything for the most part. The building, crafting, and basic systems are relatively in place and if you are not concerned with "endgame" content, it is extremely easy to spend a few hundred hours shooting around the sectors and exploring.

These can be opened by spending Real Money to buy bullets. Bullets is a currency in Black Squad to open boxes, and to also buy exclusive boosters, epic player models, and more. There are a ton of different boxes in Black Squad, so you know exactly what you will get when you open a box. Want a legendary AK-47? You can click the box and know exactly what you might get. Usually they contain an "epic item", such as a rare skin, and all the other prizes include gold, medals, BS coins, and sometimes, even lower tier skins. All the boxes, except for one, require you to pay, and everything inside is purely cosmetic. The only box that you can open for free have exclusive knife skins that you can only get by spending gold to open. Some people get lucky, others do not. This is for you to decide.

The friendslist/chat gets in the way of anything on the right side of the screen, you cannot chat in the main menu screen at all, and some items you can double-click to quickly navigate, and other buttons you can't! Yes, this game is early access, but the only way to find "competitive" players is to either get lucky on a clan match selection, or find a team on the official discord. There are clan ranks, but no one takes them seriously right now.
There have been times where I've went against a team of 5 when I was by myself for 3 rounds before other players connected. This has happened when I've went solo, qued with a team, or just randomly jumped around. The game will TRY to match you up based on rank, but after 30 seconds, it will just throw you with whoever is on. Doesn't really happen in the competitive gamemodes, but if you play assassination, it will happen a lot.
Early access, I know, but if someone is being really toxic, or is cheating, the only way you can report right now is by posting a video on the discord. It's better than nothing, and the mods actually do their job!
There are 4 different types of currency in this game:
, which is gained just by playing the game and given as a daily log-in reward. Gold can be used to buy most guns in the shop, and is easy to obtain a huge amount of it.
, which is gained every 7 days as a login reward, and is gained every time you level up. It is used to buy guns/knives/characters from the medal shop. (There are two shops in this game, more on that later)
, which is only gained by opening boxes. They can be used to buy different skins, compared to just winning them from a box. Finally,
, which is the currency that can only be bought using Real Money. You use these to open boxes, or to buy a special model, or EXP/GOLD booster. I spoke about boxes in my Neutral section of this review above.

This game is great to watch, and frustrating to play. The game itself is well written, animated and visually delightful.
Like all telltale games, it is largely story based, giving you options which will determine the outcome of your characters.
The outcomes, however, are set. If you have a choice to save one person and doom another, they will both die. If you have a choice between letting someone die and trying to save them, they will die.
Telltale uses the death of characters in a way which makes your choices in the game almost pointless, and they do so very frequently. I can recommend watching this game, but not playing it.

The very nature of a game like Darkest Dungeon is based on chance and proper preparation. Anyone who has ever played any tabletop RPG, D&D especially, in his/her life will surely know that chance always has its say on any given matter, whether one likes it or not. Darkest Dungeon does not intend to be fair and just with anyone who dares to play it; it rather crush hopes and see if its players are up to the challenge. Do not mistake this, dungeoneering is quite challenging and the faint of heart should not be put to its tests, for even the best prepared dungeoneers are caught off guard from time to time; and, when it happens, these are the times they must show their true colors and rise to the occasion, or maybe flee to fight another day. As Estel once said "Do not show the mercy to them, for nobody will-show you mercy."

Fractured space is basically a MOBA with space ships. I am not going to pad it out any more than that. The main point of my review to warn people of the horrendous lag (I am not the onmly one who gets his - not by a long shot), badly arranged servers (I play on 300 ping during peak hours in the UK and 170 during "US" hours at night and some dubious at best marketing practices (packs and in game microtransactions after having paid for the game - with the premium pack coming with a ship that you dont see used often - I'll leave it at that).
Dont get me wrong - when the game is actually working (it also crashes a lot - which for a game that has matches lasting up to 30 mins, is a pain in the butt), it can be really quite fun. The ships are different enough from each other, as to give a change in playstyle with each one. Good team work being key to winning the game - like any MOBA one would assume. One major selling point is the community - I have seen nothing but freindly comment and helpful advice. Even in game chat does not have the usual toxic remarks you find in multiplayer games.
Unfortuanlty this just isnt enough to justify you spening your probably limited gaming hours on a product that has problems like Fractured Space has . If the above issues are resolved then I will change this review and whole heartedly recommend it as it can be so much fun. Until then its a no. Especially if you live in Europe.

I love the IDEA of this game, but it's pay to win.
Some of the most overpowered ships can ONLY be bought with in-game currency, and the rest of the ships require so much xp that if you DON'T buy xp booster's you'll be stuck in a level 1 ship while everyone else is flying end-game ships.
There are also 3 totally different kinds of xp, used to unlock 3 different sets of ships - meaning that you can't really experiment with different ships at all as you have to spend all your time grinding down one of the 3 paths to get the ship you want, all to try to catch up to the people that are indulging in the pay to win side.  And if, say, the ship you grinded for ends up being hopelessly underpowered because it hasn't been balanced yet, then back to square one.  There is the 'Front Line' gameplay mode where you can experiment with different ships at Random, but in a week of playing I have never once seen it NOT down for maintence.
This also comes with it still taking a few minutes to 'get inventory' after EVERY game, and it often taking 10 plus minutes to join a game after repeated instance of 'found game, game cancelled, found game, game cancelled, found game... game cancelled.'
I know this is early access, but the system currently being built is one geared HEAVILY towards pay-to-win microtransactions AFTER you've already bought the game.  Did I meant the biggest currency pack is $100, which doesn't unlock everything btw, just the ability to grind the 3 xp paths faster.
