I'm a huge fan of the Assassin's Creed series. As a history nerd and a huge stealth genre fanboy, these games are always right up my alley.
Now I'll tell you why Assassin's Creed Unity is, flat out, one of the worst games I've played in years, and why it's absolutely unrecommendable to everybody who owns a gaming PC.
I want to start off by saying that I was absolutely hyped for this game. More hyped than any Assassin's Creed game since Assassin's Creed 2. I had watched a few gameplay videos that sold me due to the fact that the devs seemed to be going for the classic Assassin's Creed experience: An emphasis on stealthy gameplay, an intriguing historical period, and a stripped down approach to weapons and gadgets. It hearkened back to Assassin's Creed II, which is an amazing game and probably the best in the series, closely followed by Assassin's Creed Brotherhood and Black Flag.
The first drawback is the one everybody already knows about: The game is nearly totally broken at this point. Bugs are everywhere, the game hard crashes quite often, and it runs like a dog even on the most beastly of rigs. For me in particular, the most damning graphical drawback was some kind of weird frame stutter that I would experience literally every 4 seconds without fail, even in menus. I'm not sure what's causing this, but the game is nearly unplayable with it unless you're incredibly determined. As you can see, I have managed to bludgeon through several hours of the game, mostly due to its amazing recreation of Revolutionary Paris, which is by far the best aspect of the game. Most of that is wandering about the landscape and gathering collectables, which has been the peak of my enjoyment of the game, because any missions are so difficult to get through thanks to the fact that it's maybe the single most broken game I've played since Obsidian was forced to release Knights of the Old Republic II in it's half-finished state way back in 2004. And that's saying something, because that game was a broken mess.
There's been enough said about the games broken, poorly optimized state. I'd like to talk about why it would be a bad game even if it were to run beautifully. I'm going to talk about the past couple of AC games here, so bear with me.
I hated Assassin's Creed 3. Absolutely despised it. I thought it was terribly designed. It had muddy control and poor line-of-sight mechanics that often resulted in instant game over detections, it had awfully designed stealth sequences that forced you to follow people at ridiculously close lengths, and it had bad checkpoints that compounded both of those issues. A number of the missions (the midnight ride, the Charles Lee chase sequence) were just horribly designed to the point where they were frustrating. To top it off, the writing was utter trash, all of the characters were cardboard cutouts, and nothing was even worth following.
Then came Black Flag, which was a complete redemption for the series. The game was so much fun, it was beautiful to look at, and, most importantly for me, IT FIXED THE SERIES STEALTH AND GAMEPLAY DESIGN PROBLEMS! Control was smooth. Stealth sequences were designed well. Free running and climbing was nearly bug-free, quick, and intuitive. Trying to achieve 100% stealth in the plantation sequences were probably my favorite missions in the game. Playing Black Flag felt like the Assassin's Creed series had truly taken a step forward, like it was ready to get back to being the stellar franchise that Assassin's Creed II had promised it would be.
Enter Assassin's Creed Unity.
The reason I contrasted AC3 and Black Flag is because playing through Unity gave me the distinct feeling that I was playing a game designed by the AC3 team. It has the same exact pitfalls that I just described in AC3. Controls are muddy and you never truly feel totally in control of Arno. He lumbers to and fro in the vague direction you send him. A cover mechanic has been introduced that's way too sticky, way too close to guesswork, and generally hampers stealth so poorly that I completely stopped  using it except in sequences when the game forces you to. And, to top it off, they've redesigned free running and climbing with a system that seems like it should work beautifully, but fails miserably in every aspect of its execution. The days of your jumping off into odd directions, taking the wrong path up a building, and even inexplicably stopping in place and having to recenter the stick, then hit up again to continue moving HAVE ALL RETURNED FROM ASSASSIN'S CREED II. Seriously, bugs from a game that was made back in 2009 and were just solved last year have miraculously reappeared. How do you ♥♥♥♥ up that badly?
Add in that the music, something that was unbelievably atmospheric and really made the experience of Florence in Assassin's Creed II, and lent you sea shanties that stuck in your head for hours in Black Flag (and was utterly forgettable at best and terrible at worst in AC3) is absolutely unnoticeable. In fact, I didn't think about it once until, midway through this review, I remembered how much I loved Jesper Kyd's work in AC2. That's how forgettable it is.
There are also several instances of immersion-breaking content, including chests that are only open via the Unity Companion App, and microtransactions that are so hamfistedly jammed in they pull you right out of the experience. It's a basic example of an immersion murdering mechanic, and it boggles my mind that developers have not learned why you don't do these things in games. Hell, even the publisher and the money people should know why immersion is important for a single player gaming experience. There's no excuse for garbage like this.
You can also consider Ubi's utter failure to maintain some semblance of business ethics by setting their review embargo to 12:00 PM of release day, rather than the day of or the day before as is common practice. Why would they do this, you say? The only obvious reason that comes to mind is that they knew their game was an unfinished, broken piece of garbage, and they decided that their best course of action was to lie to their customers for as long as possible in order to prevent them from canceling their preorders. Despicable.
It really disappoints me to tear this game apart so viciously because I've been such a huge fan of the series. I'd like to believe that this was rushed out the door by Ubi, and that the team would eventually have produced a good game if they were given adequate time to have worked on the things that fail here. But at the end of the day, blame lies with the developer as well as the publisher.
"A delayed game is eventually good, a rushed one is forever bad"
- Shigeru Miyamoto
In conclusion, there is very little redeeming quality in this game. Unless you're an absolute history nerd or a super hardcore Assassin's Creed fan, this game is completely unrecommendable in its current state. Furthermore, even if the game were totally fixed, even if the graphical issues and the bugs were completely ironed out and the game ran beautifully, this still isn't worth a purchase because it's easily the worst Assassin's Creed and just not a great game period. The dev team here has an eternity of failure to look forward to, as people will forever think of this game as an exemplary pillar of Ubisoft's descent into the basement of video game development and business ethics. Hell, at least Watch Dogs had some interesting mechanics and some competent stealth sequences. This game brings absolutely nothing to the table. Just replay Black Flag instead. Or burn $60 in your backyard while punching yourself in the face, because that's a more valuable, entertaining experience than playing this game will ever be.

For those that love turn based combat, permadeath style progression, and truely meaningful choices in their games, this is for you. If you do buy this, don't make the mistake that most do: Don't get attached to anyone.
There are of course many pros and cons to this game, as with all games. First and foremost that everyone will say, is everything comes down to the RNG gods. Though this does not diminish you choice and actions meanings. You can be completely undone by RNG through no fault of your own, but you are also given opportunity to combat this. In a sense, the same things that can destroy you, can also happen to your enemy, and feels all the more rewarding when it does.
Stress is a killer, and your upmost priority in this game. Let it get too high and your character will basically doom your entire party, or the complete reverse can happen. They can become heroic and basically become the most powerful weapon you have, and when that moment happens, the tension and reward is so tangible. Then you roll the dice and get that feeling of victory.
When that happens, you look to your enemies and say "You're all so ♥♥♥♥ed now."
There's also a very interesting feeling while playing the game. When you're in town and get the opportunity to weigh the pros and cons of an upgrade, you often think; I can't wait to use this in the field. Then once in the field you often think (after finding some valuable items and loot) I can't wait to get back to town and use this stuff for upgrades. This creates a cycle of a sense of reward and tension. Theres serious tension while you're in town, if you can afford to do something or if it will doom you, and that same tension carries into combat.

There is, I think, a beauty in Darkest Dungeon that is very hard to get in games based on Lovecraftian mythos. The creators of DD get the impossibility and helplessness factor perfectly; one tiny thing can wreck your party and, as the intro to the game says, this is about making the best out of a difficult situation.
If you are more of a casual player though, Darkest Dungeon has a difficulty level that can be adjusted so you enjoy the story, the classes, the bosses, the art style and everything this game has to offer minus the frustration. Don't believe for a second, though, that this game is ever easy. Even in the easiest dungeons and difficulties, the intricacies of DD will keep you hooked and alert at all times or, if you ever go easy, the game will bring you back to the cruel, maddening reality that it crafts so perfectly.

Like many of the other reviews I've seen I can say that Fallout 4 did not reach the expectations of the Bethesda community. I tried to hold off on reviewing this game at all, but no more.
Fallout 4 is a sad realisation that Bethesda doesn't care about the quality of gameplay anymore.
- Same old game engine that ran Oblivion a decade ago
- Game mechanics and interface are dumbed down, a lot..
- Not an RPG, it's not so much the voice protagonist for me, but the lack of depth of moral choice, meaning, and such,
plus I saw that dialoge would be hard for mod quests. I'm amazed with the Nora companion mod though, so it's not
impossible but tough.
-Graphics, meshes, and textures are bad, I used to defend the game's graphics, but not anymore, we shouldn't need mods
to completely overhaul Bethesda's games anymore, this is just ridiculous and lazy on Bethesda's part.
-Quests are bad, they have accended into memehood. "Fetch" quests, kill that guy there, you get the point.
-A.I. is bad, Dog Meat walks into things that kill you, we've all seen the videos.
- World feels empty, missing something, too little charaters, small settlements.
- The infamous corrupted saves, disabling acheivments with mods, lagging start menu, stuff like that.
I think my biggest let down when I first played on it's release was the size of the major cities. When I saw the reveal trailer panning these places, like "Diamond city", "Good Neighbor", etc. I thought they would be these massive areas you, as the player, could explore, none of them came close to the sizes of Skyrim's cities, you know, five years before Fallout 4..
They are using the same old engine as stated above. I cannot stress the need for a new engine. This is a triple A game, and it is using the same engine as a game that was released is 2006. It's time for a new one, and yes, this is an important aspect to this review as it shows that Bethesda really doesn't want to spend their resources on a much needed thing.
And now paid mods to top it all off, oh I mean Creation Club... Honestly I see what people try to defend, "modders are finally getting paid for their work," fine, you go ahead, but lets really look into it, they are supposedly paid a flat fee, not commissions. "But then they all get paid, not just the ones that sell," ok so why is it that when a modder is much better than others, his pay out isn't reflecting his preformance? Why are they not recieving both? A cut of the profit? Well maybe that's because Betheda is basically outsourcing their work, and under paying others instead of hiring more employees like they should be doing. We are getting penny pinched, look at how many times they resold Skyrim, look at the season pass problems for Fallout 4, and look at the poor quality dlcs it released. Now this creation club, they just couldn't line their pockets enough on these over sold products... They lied to their community, us. They said they won't be adding paid mods, but they did.

Gameplay is hardly worth mentioning, it's super easy and all as mentioned. But the story is one of the finest I ever got to play, creating a real emotional investment that reminded me a little of "To the Moon". There's lots of drama, flavored after the show of course but a lot more tolerable because there's no lame fillers / much smaller fillers than in the show and you get to be able to participate yourself, even if it is barely more than an Illusion of choice. Prologue-The Sims 3, eat your little heart out and move over! This is one EPIC Mega-Game which puts the 'special' in spectacular! To make it even more special, my copy of Bayonetta was given to me as a gift by none other than my loyal, faithful girlfriend, whom I thank for it here. Many adoring fans have been waiting for the much-anticipated PC release of Bayonetta for quite a long time, now. And since it's arrived, at last, let's jump into it!!
Gameplay-Those players who are already familiar with Bayonetta and her super-ultra-mega-HYPER capabilities to kick♥♥♥♥♥are well-done in this port version of the iconic EPIC Mega-Game. You start off hearing a storyteller's voice-over of the tale of Umbra Witches and Lumen Sages during an equally-epic rapid free-fall on a clock tower face. But don't simply stare in awe...START FIGHTING!! Because many angels will be assaulting you and your protege, Jeanne in what I call the first TRUE interactive cut-scene ever shown in any video game. You can't die here, so simply knock out as many foes as you can as the cut-scene progresses. Afterwhich, you'll be ready to begin the game-proper. Plus, all of the keys to control the iconic heroine are fully customizable. And with five different levels of difficulty, there is a comfort zone for everyone here. The gameplay is quite fast-paced as you travel from location to location in style. There are a wide variety of enemies to beat up, torture, punish, and more. But with practice and perseverance, even some of the biggest, baddest foes can be bested, even while playing on the Normal Difficulty. Plus, even if one finishes the game itself, there are still plenty of mysteries to unravel-All in all, it never fails to impress me. Gameplay Score-10 out of 10.
Items-Mostly consisting of sweet candies called lollipops, they can be bought from the Gates of Hell shop or made using a nifty little interface known as the Concocting Compounds. To access this handy interface, just collect as many compounds as you can find and then press Tab to start creating whatever items you may need from scratch. Concocting a go-go, baby! There are also several more items, two of which will permanently raise the cap on Bayonetta's already-massive health and magic bars. Plus, at least one of these items can deal heavy damage to nearby foes. The only drawback to using such items is a lower overall score for every chapter you complete. Items Score-9 out of 10.
Weapons-There are several weapons available for Bayonetta to line her sexy arsenal with. She starts off with basic handguns but rapidly gains access to much more powerful guns, whips, claws, and more. And each of them has their own unique abilities. Every weapon can be unlocked by fulfilling certain prerequisites for free, but can also be bought, enabling most weapons to be equipped on her hands and feet simultaneously! Plus, they never need reloading or ammunition! There are only a few such weapons which are quite challenging to obtain. Weapons Score-9 out of 10.
Ammo-Seeing as how none of the weapons ever need reloading or ammunition, there's really not much else to say here other than...This is EPIC!! Ammo Score-10 out of 10.
Armor-Seriously? Come on! Bayonetta is way to tough to need any sort of armor. She does however, have several handy accessories to make use of. They are small, but HIGHLY powerful things which allow her to nullify and/or dodge incoming attacks, deal more damage, and even gain more Halos-The currency of the game. Higher difficulty levels mean less accessory slots, but once you've mastered Bayonetta's epic martial arts moves, you won't need any. Armor Score-9 out of 10.
Plot-Bayonetta emerges from a lake with a case of amnesia. She cannot remember her past, apart from small fragments here and there. But over time, along her journey, she regains more of her lost memories. Along the way, she also befriends a couple people-One of whose memories are also shared in the form of sepia-tone filmstrip-style cutscenes. Only the starting scene in the cemetery, where they keep talking about...Eghead slightly ruins this aspect of the game. Plot Score-8 out of 10.
Characters-Bayonetta is graced with a colorful cast of characters, most of whom are quite pleasing to see as Bayonetta interacts with each of them. In addition to this, the characters are shown in the form of trophies, ranging from the shameful Stone Trophy of Enzo, to the much-coveted Pure Platinum Bayonetta trophy. Plus, their personalities range from outrageously comedic to deadly serious! As I often say, the characters offer something for everyone. Characters Score-9 out of 10.
Sound-Angelic teleportation, shooting, punches, kicks, feminine grunting and shouting, and many bangs, thuds, and loud explosions will be most of the sounds you'll hear while playing this game. After all, this is an action game. The sounds are certainly pleasing to me, except for in one missile-riding section featuring Dear and Decorations battle. Sound Score-9 out of 10.
Music-Fast or slow, most of the music within Bayonetta is just as pleasing to the ears as the sound is. The best song to hear would be Fly Me To The Moon (Climax). Music Score-9 out of 10.
Graphics-Fully-customizable with a quality I can only describe as 'EPIC' is the only way I can speak of the graphics of Bayonetta. There is plenty to see here, from trees, grass, airplanes, cars, trucks, the skyline of cities, ancient stone ruins, and much more besides. Plus, Bayonetta's uncanny ability to walk along walls and even fly makes it much more awesome. Graphics Score-10 out of 10.
Final Score and Summary-If I haven't made all this clear enough, Bayonetta is one super-ultra-mega-hyper-cool video game just about everyone will wanna play at least once...If this is their kind of thing. Bayonetta's ability to keep herself, calm, cool, and collected in just about every situation will also instill the player with confidence and a will to continue fighting! Final Score-10 out of 10.

1. If you remap the keys when playing with keyboard/mouse then some vehicles do not work properyl or the pop-up suggestions for the interactive cinematics are wrong or do not work. The only way to go through them is to plug in a controller. This is bad because the most widespread control method on pc is keyboard+mouse.
2. The balance of the difficulty levels is ridiculous: on easy everything is automatic and you start with all the health upgrades and moves unlocked, to the point that you just need to click with the mouse to get through all the enemies. The normal level becomes very hard. This gap between difficulty levels should not be there.
3. The performance is bad. Really bad. Considering this is a game from 2009. I have a GTX970 and sometimes the stuttering makes the game almost unplayable.
4. The plot is ok but not excellent.

This game is amazing.  Although hard at times, I enjoyed nearly every bit of this game... all 17 hours of it.  Yup, that's right, it took me 17 hours to complete this game, start to finish, all while heavily relying on a guide.
The thing is, older games tend to be a bit harder; ever heard of the term "Nintendo hard?"  Although the modes are linear (not complaining there), often I would think I have gotten lost because of how big the world is, but I then found out I was going in the right direction the entire time, or I would quickly find the right direction.  So that's a nice effect.
But for the most part, this game was years ahead of it's time, with dynamic shields, AI, and all sorts of enemies.
You would think this is horror, but this is the older generation, based off of arena-based shooters (Quake and Doom), so your movement takes that aspect away (once I was able to jump off a cliff to dodge an electric LoS attack, then airstrafe back onto the cliff to take him out).
All in all, this is a fun, fast-paced shooter that I would recommend to anyone.

Do not play this game for any sort of payoff or conclusion at the end of the campaign, what isn't pure setup for a sequel is just cringeworthy.  Also, can I have a final mission where I don't miss half the talking-at-me bits because the big bads voices are much quieter than the weapons fire?
That out of the way, the gameplay is good.  It manages to convey a nice sense of underdog slowly coming out on top, and one can drag the end game out further than I could be bothered with if you really enjoy beating things up.  A squad of six psi troopers is horrifyingly effective - which did lead to the heartbreaking moment when I realised my sniper who had led the team for the entire game was going to have to drop onto the B-list.
The guerilla style gameplay, operating out of your flying ship, suits the new base-building much better.  Constantly flitting from place to place, especially for timed missions when you only have half a day left on something on the other side of the globe is annoying.  I'd say the time management aspect adds a bit more depth, however, so it's probably kind of the point of it.
The DLC...  Yeah...  Nope.  The cosmetic options are basically GONE by the time you've got the top tier armours - instead of all those options you had with rookie troops, you'll have maybe two or three choices for each armour type.  I had one run-in with the Alien Hunters DLC and had to restart.  Not my cup of tea at all.  I suspect that after a few playthroughs they might be an entertaining challenge, but dropping them into someone's first game is not going to win you any friends.  Shen's gift showed up partway through my playthrough, so I got the mech troops, but missed the storyline mission.  That's a♥♥♥♥♥♥way to do things, have to restart your game everytime new DLC comes out if you want to know what's going on?  Bugger that!
Stability-wise I didn't have any crashes, although I did have to unplug my joystick to avoid increasingly long pauses so it might have crashed eventually if I hadn't.  Even then the audio was desynched with any videos that played, usually by at least a second, often more.
Overall, I'd probably give it a miss.  Even at 40% off I still regret the chunk of change I dropped on this game.  The DLC is lacklustre and definitely not worth what it costs.  Even if you're a big fan of the XCOM series, I'd say go get the Long War mod for Enemy Within and wait for this one to come out for five bucks (or hold out for a humble bundle).

My favourite Metal Slug game. Metal Slug 3 is probably second, but I don't like all the swimming/flying, I prefer the traditional running and gunning, and there's more of that in this one. Also, there's a lot of chances to drive the titular Metal Slug, or SV-001, which is probably my favourite part.
The music is good as always, although slows down sometimes a little in this port but it's not too noticeable for the most part.
Graphically it's a good as any other Metal Slug game (i,e., very) and it sounds like a small thing but I'm glad they bought back the original portraits in the character select screen. Metal Slug has its own unique art style, and the portraits in MS3's Steam port were alright but kinda inconsistent IMO.
I dunno how the controls are for keyboard, but I use a PS3 controller with a driver to wrap it as Xinput (actual X360 controllers are the bane of my life), and it works just fine. I haven't actually tried online multiplayer yet, but I hear it's pretty well done, and it sounds fun.
My only gripe is that in my first playthrough of the game, I got 11 of 15 achievements without even really trying. I'd like a /little/ more challenge at least, although there are less grindy achievements like MS3's "play as X character 100 times" achievements.
Overall, it's a great run 'n' gun game that stands the test of time, and is great value for money.

I want to give my review of my first few hours with XCOM 2 and I might update this later:
The game peformance coming from XCOM: Enemy Unknown is very shaky. This game seems to stutter a lot during drop-ship cutscences. I can run it and all, but it's not very beautiful at medium settings on a 2GB Asus HD 7770.
The global map and "mission control" is different in that it seems to be that something is always going on and you have to decide what to do (you can't do everything). I like this mechanic. You can feel hard-pressed most of the time, but I like the strategy involved in tough decisions.
Timed missions with countdown timers are much more persistant than before and are unavoidable. I think that they come up too often. I get that XCOM (in the story) is the underdog now and you should feel like insurgents, but I don't like feeling rushed. I think the countdowns don't work very well with the mechanics of the combat. The time contraints end up limitng what playstyles you can do to finished missions with.
There really isn't much else of a difference between XCOM 2 and XCOM: Enemy Unkown besides that. XCOM: Enemy Unkown is certainly the superior game in terms of mechanics, but I already finished that and wanted some more of the franchise. Still a good game, but not much of a step forward.

It does get repetitive, as most games do, but that's the only thing I can say bad about it.
Starbound is a game you should have in your library, if you like a good 2D exploration game.

Disclaimer: THIS REVIEW IS BASED ON PATCH 1.4 I did play this game just after release when it was a mess of technical issues but since I'm writing this review on patch 1.4 and I believe that this patch is the fairest representation of the game I'll base the review on this.
First off this game is more like warhammer than dark souls. It has dark souls combat and SORT OF dark souls leveling. The visuals, storyline, characters and theme are all warhammer like though, it is full of grimdark areas and big burly manly heroes with beards and huge shoulder plates.
Pros:
+Looks really good on a modest computer (as of patch 1.4)
+The combat has a really visceral feel as you swing your gigantic greataxe, ignoring the weak pokes of your enemies shortswords on your bulky armour as you splatter them into the pavement. You can feel the weight and strength behind every swing, block and roll.
+The combat mechanics work really well together they are similar to dark souls mechanics but have added nuances such as animation canceling (cancelling an attack to block), timing button presses to minimize stamina usage you can still mash buttons but it costs you more stamina, being able to charge up attacks for more damage and sprinting shield bashes.
+The game rewards you for being a risk taking manly man like Harkyn; the more experience you are carrying (and risking to a random death) the better the item drops and the more experience killing enemies gives you.
+The cape animations and textures are amazing
Cons
-The environments get a little repetitive
-The game is sort of linear, there are lots of sidequests you can do that influence the story a bit but the main game is pretty straightforward
-Your options for magic are limited in this game. On your first playthrough you pick a set of four spells you can level up in and get some weapons that use magic other than that, pure spellcaster builds aren't really catered to.
-There are some balance issues with the weapons and leveling. Its a singleplayer game so this isn't as important as there are no invaders to punish you for using a weaker setup but the game can become easy mode with the right gear.
Overall I'd definetely reccommend this game if you like challenging grimdark RPGs like Warhammer or the Souls Series and are the kind of player who likes melee builds.

While matchmaking is still being worked on, I can honestly say that the connection quality has shown some improvements, and I'm hopeful for the future.
While it lacks the intense customization of games like DotA and LoL, it's current game format heavily resembles the balancing act that is involved with those games. Controlling stations gains you resources which level your team up, the more stations you control on the map, the faster you level, which in turn strengthens your teams ships. However, killing isn't the goal in this game, rather the capture of enemy forward bases to open the way for your team to capture their home base. Capturing stations will net you more resources, but also will signal to the enemy which sectors you're advancing on and where they should divert more ships to counter.
There's a small series of tutorial missions that will enable you to get a sense of the basic mechanics of the game and how to move about, but it's up to you to get an idea of the tactics and strategy. There's currently three factions of ships, each with their own unique classes and abilities, so there's plenty of variety in the different ship classes, and there is also the chance to further tweak your ships through the uses of different crews and weapons.
The game is slated to become Free-to-Play when it exits Early Access (may even be free now, not 100% sure) but, assuming there aren't any significant tweaks to the EXP and Credit rewards, the spectre of 'grind' doesn't seem to loom heavily as I've managed, as a rookie, to get around 1k of experience each game, making new ships availible every dozen games or so depending on my performance. Money will help unlock things faster, but the only things money can exclusively buy amount mostly to new skins for ships.
It also helps that it scratches that capital ship itch. You know the one, the desire to maneuver a massive ship to bring an earth-shattering arsenal to bear on the enemy...

I was really excited for this game, but I realize now that it's not all that great. There are a couple of reasons for that.
1. So little content. For 15$ you want more variety in characters, more diverse game mechanics, a decent options menu and a better single-player experience. Which leads to my next point...
2. Multiplayer with 2+ people is the only fun option. Unless you have a 2-3 controllers and have people who would play with you on the same computer, there is absolutely no point in buying the game. No online play, so forget about that. AI isn't all that challenging \ interesting, so single-player tends to get boring fast.
Don't get me wrong - Samurai Gunn is well polished. It does few things (too few in my opinion), but it does them quite well. The controls are responsive. The game is immersive and atmospheric. The attention to detail is remarkable. There just isn't enough of a game there to justify getting it at this point.
Maybe one day in the future, some bonus content is released and this review won't be relevant anymore. Maybe not.
Right now I'd stick to Megabyte Punch if you're itching for a nice brawler (though not a 1-hit-kill one), or just wait for Towerfall to make its way to the PC in a couple of months.

What to say about Dark Souls 3, well for starters, it's definitely recommended in my books, but you should know what you're in for. If you're a veteran of the series, be prepared for a LOT of pandering, and recycled boss fights from earlier games in the franchise. The difficulty is laughable at best (for series' vets, though I can see someone who's never played a Souls game to be able to handle this game with relative ease.) - the core concept of Souls in general was, if you messed up it was your fault, however there are points in this game where it feels a lot like you as the player could not in any way anticipate the enemy behaving as such. Another major downside is without the DLC there is very little reason to build anything other than a DEX, STR or LUCK build, since spells do far less damage than their melee counterparts and there are far few supporting items to assist.
I digress however, the good points are, this is the final souls game in the trilogy, yay right? I'd recommend anyone who's not currently got their mitts on the product to go for the full package with all the DLC since it simply is more bang for your buck. On the DLC side of things there are more items to support other builds than simply smacking your enemy around.
All in all, if they had taken a bit more time to flesh out the world and make it less like a love letter to fans of the series, I expect I'd have enjoyed it more than I did. A solid 6/10 from me.

Just like the television show and comic book that this game is modeled after, The Walking Dead is a beautiful and horrifying character study that just-so-happens to take place in post-apocalyptic zombie land.

TellTale has finally hit its stride with this one, and right from episode one you know that they’ve knocked it out of the park. This is interactive storytelling in high form, an example that their future adventure games can emulate with success.

The dialogue options made are (more often than not) given with a fast timer, which requires you to make quick, and oftentimes unsettling, decisions based upon your first instinct. To me, this is thrilling. When I play a game with lasting decisions, such as Dragon Age or Mass Effect, I would oftentimes set my controller down and study my options and carefully weigh each pro and con. That luxury is not afforded in The Walking Dead – you may be given just four seconds to access a situation and save a life.

The voice acting is well done, as well as the animations – you feel that these people have seen some terrible things, and will do even worse to survive. Characters will turn heel and face on a dime and you are forced to adapt accordingly. All of your decisions will carry over from one episode to the next, and finishing a playthrough will leave you wondering what could have been – maybe you could have been faster during the last zombie attack? Maybe you were too hard on a friend who was hungry and tired?

I’m very excited to see where the last few episodes will go, and I hope it keeps stabbing me in the gut with ultimatums. Recommended for adventure fans, zombie fans, and Walking Dead fans…and pretty much everyone who loves storytelling in general.

Point and click adventure games are one of a very few genres I haven't ever really gotten into. In my experience, they all had ridiculous, nonsensical puzzles, characters that wore thin with repeated exposure, excessive backtracking and wandering around fairly limited environments. I figured that the resurgence of adventure games was due to nostalgia that I'd missed out on, and hearing about Telltale's games didn't do much to change my opinion. I heard enough praise for The Walking Dead that I put it on my wishlist to get someday, on a massive sale. One day, I woke up to see that I had generously been gifted The Walking Dead. I installed it immediately, and hoped that it would be engaging.
It was engaging, and more. The Walking Dead has singlehandedly changed my perception of adventure games.
The characters are some of the most well-rounded and realistic that I have ever seen in any game. There's enough detail in the environment that I actually want to go around and examine everything. Even the flavor text is reward enough in itself. There's a good variety of dialogue choices, so I can really customize who I felt my character to be. Some dialogue choices are timed; while I also normally dislike QTEs, the time ticking down while I try to find something to say actually adds a good deal of tension. When I'm asked a hard question, I feel like I'm in my character's shoes, sweating and clearing his throat and trying to say the right thing before I look too suspicious. Sometimes I panic, and I say the wrong thing. I can't just write it off, because this game has already made it very clear to me that my words and choices have consequences, some of which I'm nowhere near seeing yet.
I'm still in the middle of the first episode, and I find myself intentionally dragging the game out already. I haven't felt like this about any form of media since I was a teenager staying up all night reading the last Harry Potter book, wishing that I read just a bit slower. The characters and environment are so well realized that I can take little sips of this game and find myself thinking about it in an idle moment, weaving my own narratives in my mind.
The only negative I can find is that the game isn't always true to its roots. I've seen the show intermittently and skimmed a couple of the comics, so I'm not the person to ask about continuity, but I have noticed that a couple characters refer to the walkers as zombies, which was slightly jarring for me. It's possible that if you're really invested in the universe, there are other things i haven't noticed that might spoil your immersion. All in all, though, this is truly an amazing game. I look forward to diving more deeply into Telltale's catalogue.

One of the best of the series!  Metal Slug 2 was the first MS I ever played nearly 10 years ago.  MSX is a remake of MS2.  The game has been tweaked to make it slightly tougher than it once was, and some of the new guns have been added as well!  The game has fast pace and intense action, EXPLOSIONS, co-op, side-scroller/shoot'em up, well balanced combat for an arcade game, EXPLOSIONS, and much more!
Whether playing single player or co-op, this is one of the few side-scroller arcade titles that feels balanced from the beginning to the end.  The difficulty increase is spot on for newcomers and  veterans alike.  The first few levels can be mastered, which gives the player a sense of accomplishment that is seldom found in this kind of game.  Victory is not achieved through numerous continues, but through sheer skill of the game.
The weapon placement in this game is great.  The player is often given the right tool for the job, but the guns wont last forever.  There are a number of different guns that will be used throughout the levels, and each one of them is given to the player appropriately to reach that fine balance that has been spoken of.
The enemies come in many shapes and sizes, and they act differently enough from one game to the next to offer solid re-playability -- especially in co-op.  The boss battles in the game are some of the best.  Difficult without question, but once again, room is given to master each one of them!
This game is a must buy for single-player purpose or co-op.  Note that the online co-op can be a bit lagy if you are not playing with someone reasonably close to you -- geographically speaking that is.

I'd like to start this review by stating that I hate action games, especially slashing games.
That said this is a fantastic game nevertheless.  The main story revolves around Bayonetta, an Umbran Witch charged with protecting an artefact called the left eye.  On the way through the story you fight a host of angels all trying to kill you, and there are a lot of them.
Cons:
There is only on major con, the plot:
You could play the game a dozen times and still not get the plot.  You can get the gist of it, but It is very badly written.
Pros:
A large variety of weapons, such as swords to whips to cannons.
Dozens of various combo atatcks such as  punch,punch, kick, kick, kick.  Which is one that does fantastic damage but has some slow attacks in it.  In additon, one of the characters, Rodin, also sells new techniques you can learn.
Witch time.  A sort of slow motion you enter when you time your dodges just right, making it easier to get your combos in.
Torture Attacks. Dodging and attacking slowly fills your magic meter (but getting hit depletes it).  If you  manage to fill the meter you can perfrom what they call "torture attacks" which if done right can one shot most enemies.
Very interesting combat scenarios.  To name a few, you fight on the outside of an airplane in fight.  Jump on top of cars on a busy highway, fight a monster in the ocean while riding a surfboard, and outrun lava.
To sum it up:
Even if you hate action games, like I do.  This is a game you will really like.  I am now on my second playthrough, and I will probably go for a third, or even a tenth.

First off, most of the reviews complaining about the optimization problems are no longer valid. That being said, there is no excuse for games these days especially non-indie titles, to be released as beta feeling as this game was. Unforunately that seems to be just par for the course these days in the industry and I won't let my personal feelings on that matter apply here.
This game is a third person action RPG that uses a similar control set-up to the dark souls games and leveling system, but that is where the similarities really end. You do gain and lose your experience by killing/dying and must go to where you died to retrieve your exp. This exp does start to disappear overtime though, and you're not likely to retrieve most of your exp if you're very far from a checkpoint.
The game's difficulty is not high, and most of the struggles you'll face are at the beginning, and very end of the game. The mid-game seems unbalanced and you will be mowing through most enemies.
The combat is much faster paced than the Souls games and I'd say it's about a mid-ground between that and Darksiders 2's combat. They did an excellent job of making each weapon type feel differently and I feel the physics here surpass the Souls series by far. The staff weapons were incredibly overpowered during the time I played the game due to it's fast attack speed and good scaling damage. This could always be fixed in balance patches or mods however.
The bosses were fairly underwhelming, but there are a good variety of enemy types which take different tactics in order to combat as opposed to the souls series (lock on and circle) method of killing just about everything which detracts from my enjoyment of that particular franchise. There were multiple ways to defeat a few of the bosses, and this allowed you to receieve special equipment upon killing them which I thought was a rather neat addition. Some of the weaker and early bosses become elite enemies that you will fight throughout the game as well, forcing you to adapt your combat style when fighting them as well as a group of lesser enemies at the same time.
There are many collectibles in the game, and while the lore is pretty generic, it's still interesting enough to warrant collecting all the scrolls and finding the secret equipment (which there is a good number of).
The games length was decent, and it could probably be played through 2-3 times in order to play different styles, and colelct the new game + gear, however, new game+ difficulty does not scale nearly fast enough in order for it to be a challenge.
As a final note, I do recommend the game, and while it's not anywhere near perfect, there are some innovative ideas here, and I'd like to see a sequel one day improve on what worked, and change what didn't. This is definitely the best game this particular studio has made to date, and I think they should be supported for adding some creativity to this genre which is pretty much dominated by a single franchise at this point.

Hacknet is a new title in the otherwise stagnant, indie genre of hacking simulation games.
And a fresh breeze it is.
No doubt there is hardly any competition for this kind of quality.
Graphics are amazing, the hacking system introduced is quite good and consistent, it has gigantic potential for expansion that desperately needs to be used, and hopefully will. In it's current shape there might be little room for multiplayer gameplay, because of the game mechanics, but hopefully as the game gets finalized it will be implemented.
The puzzles you have to face are fun to solve and most of the time at medium or easy difficulty level.
Even though the game description provided on Steam might be a little misleading, as to non-holywood hacking style, or minimal hand-holding, the gameplay can be extremely exciting and satisfying.
The thrill of hacking, taking unauthorised control over websites, other web services, or user machines and mobile devices, identity theft or destruction, and constantly racing the trace clock are all very satisfying and will give you an addictive adrenaline rush.
Music is a very proper and enjoyable background for your virtual crimes, not quite something to remember.
The game has too high hardware requirements in my opinion. All in all it is a console based hacking game, and it is barely playable on i5, 4GB, Intel graphics HD4000 Lenovo laptop (12 fps max with too much typing lag!!!)
Many people look up to Hacknet in comparison to Uplink.
Based on my experiences with both titles If you did truly enjoy Uplink, You will be dazzled by Hacknet's modern design. Graphics are eyecandy.
The gameplay itself however, as compared to Uplink I have found to be short (if that can be said - I was unable to finish the game due to numerous bugs [despite 50+hrs in-game]), shallow and at many times unchallenging.
If you can bear with, well kinda outdated graphics and a little clumsy UI, I'd say Uplink offers far greater immersion, much more complex world to explore, more freedom, less hand holding.
Hardware upgrades covering several computer components to your machine, or even different, more upgradable machines (you can create them yourself or download one of many community created ones!!!!), software upgrades that all can be purchased are something you won't find in Hacknet, since finances have been taken out of the picture in the first place. Money earning, stock market participation and manipulation, and banking are all absent in Hacknet. So are LAN networks that pose a sublevel of gameplay in Uplink. Hacknet at this stage of developement also gives you the feeling of being the only web user out there, since only on rare story related events will you ever find logs left by anyone else on any servers (even the public services). Tracing other hackers or users is nearly non existent since the idea of connection bouncing has also been skipped so far. In my opinion, with similar development times of several years for both games, Uplink is a masterpiece bot technically and story-wise, compared to Hacknet.
Whatever Hacknet is or will be, I'd say Uplink is worth playing, as the only other hacking game out there with some serious gameplay to this date.
If compatibility issues or the kinda-outdated-look are an obstacle for you playing Uplink, Hacknet will still be a very enjoyable and exciting experience, however I would strongly advise to wait with the purchase until numerous major bugs are addressed and more potential gets released from Hacknet, or you might be facing quite a frustrating struggle with what I can only call a beta version (at best) right now. I have also learned there is a free remake of Uplink to be found out there, I will let you find it yourself tho, since I'd stick with the original version by Introversion Software and support it's makers.
Keep track of Hacknet news and discussion on Steam for a stable version somewhen in the (hopefully) near future.

Just like the television show and comic book that this game is modeled after, The Walking Dead is a beautiful and horrifying character study that just-so-happens to take place in post-apocalyptic zombie land.

TellTale has finally hit its stride with this one, and right from episode one you know that they’ve knocked it out of the park. This is interactive storytelling in high form, an example that their future adventure games can emulate with success.

The dialogue options made are (more often than not) given with a fast timer, which requires you to make quick, and oftentimes unsettling, decisions based upon your first instinct. To me, this is thrilling. When I play a game with lasting decisions, such as Dragon Age or Mass Effect, I would oftentimes set my controller down and study my options and carefully weigh each pro and con. That luxury is not afforded in The Walking Dead – you may be given just four seconds to access a situation and save a life.

The voice acting is well done, as well as the animations – you feel that these people have seen some terrible things, and will do even worse to survive. Characters will turn heel and face on a dime and you are forced to adapt accordingly. All of your decisions will carry over from one episode to the next, and finishing a playthrough will leave you wondering what could have been – maybe you could have been faster during the last zombie attack? Maybe you were too hard on a friend who was hungry and tired?

I’m very excited to see where the last few episodes will go, and I hope it keeps stabbing me in the gut with ultimatums. Recommended for adventure fans, zombie fans, and Walking Dead fans…and pretty much everyone who loves storytelling in general.

Point and click adventure games are one of a very few genres I haven't ever really gotten into. In my experience, they all had ridiculous, nonsensical puzzles, characters that wore thin with repeated exposure, excessive backtracking and wandering around fairly limited environments. I figured that the resurgence of adventure games was due to nostalgia that I'd missed out on, and hearing about Telltale's games didn't do much to change my opinion. I heard enough praise for The Walking Dead that I put it on my wishlist to get someday, on a massive sale. One day, I woke up to see that I had generously been gifted The Walking Dead. I installed it immediately, and hoped that it would be engaging.
It was engaging, and more. The Walking Dead has singlehandedly changed my perception of adventure games.
The characters are some of the most well-rounded and realistic that I have ever seen in any game. There's enough detail in the environment that I actually want to go around and examine everything. Even the flavor text is reward enough in itself. There's a good variety of dialogue choices, so I can really customize who I felt my character to be. Some dialogue choices are timed; while I also normally dislike QTEs, the time ticking down while I try to find something to say actually adds a good deal of tension. When I'm asked a hard question, I feel like I'm in my character's shoes, sweating and clearing his throat and trying to say the right thing before I look too suspicious. Sometimes I panic, and I say the wrong thing. I can't just write it off, because this game has already made it very clear to me that my words and choices have consequences, some of which I'm nowhere near seeing yet.
I'm still in the middle of the first episode, and I find myself intentionally dragging the game out already. I haven't felt like this about any form of media since I was a teenager staying up all night reading the last Harry Potter book, wishing that I read just a bit slower. The characters and environment are so well realized that I can take little sips of this game and find myself thinking about it in an idle moment, weaving my own narratives in my mind.
The only negative I can find is that the game isn't always true to its roots. I've seen the show intermittently and skimmed a couple of the comics, so I'm not the person to ask about continuity, but I have noticed that a couple characters refer to the walkers as zombies, which was slightly jarring for me. It's possible that if you're really invested in the universe, there are other things i haven't noticed that might spoil your immersion. All in all, though, this is truly an amazing game. I look forward to diving more deeply into Telltale's catalogue.

If you enjoyed XCOM: Enemy Unknown/Within, you will definitely want to give XCOM 2 a chance. A lot of what was over- or under-powered in the first FIraxis outing has been balanced in this game. The Grenadier is a good, interesting change to the Heavy from XCOM:EW, making it more versatile and removing the annoying 10% chance to miss. The Support has gone from a don't-bother class to an absolutely critical one. Not having a hacker in your squad means you're extremely vulnerable to dangerous robotic enemies.
The procedural level generation makes for better replayability - you're not constantly dealing with the exact same maps; you always have to learn the level.
You can still completely ignore psy abilities, which is kind of a shame and I really need to get a psy-heavy playthrough in at some point. Perhaps I'm just a bit too inflexible in my playstyle.
Overall - if you enjoy turn-based strategy, an interesting story, and great voice acting, you should definitely check out XCOM2. It's pretty much a must for anyone who sunk hours into XCOM:EW.

Village is another important aspect of the game. You have collect things during missions if u want develop village, there are some important choices: Which building should i upgrade first? The main downside of the game is that you have to farm a lot for exp, for gold, for items. It can take a lot of time which is frustrating because you can't finish the game and you are not doing progress in the story. There is new game mode which is shorter but you don't have all items there.

*In Progress Review*
Lords of the Fallen, so far, has provided me with a more accessible version of Dark Soul's famously hard gameplay.  To be fair to each game, I will try to keep comparisons to a minimum, and to judge the game by its own merits and issues.
To be concise I will divide this review into two sections.  Let me begin with things I enjoy about it:
- Lords does do one or two things that, personally, I think they did better than Dark Souls.  The enemy AI is more varied and a bit more defensive.  Their move sets tend to control your character's motions and mechanics, as opposed to just hurting you.
- I like the setting of Lords of the Fallen.  Post-apocalyptic fantasy is one of my favorites, as it's a combination of two genres I really enjoy.
- Lords also is a very pretty game, I really like the design and aesthetics of it.  Mostly since I enjoy gothic stylings in my games, and Lords delivers that much in spades.  From Harkyn's armor, to the enemy designs, to the locales; all of it just drips dark fantasy.
- Lords is challenging without being too challenging, you won't die as much in Lords as you would in a Dark Souls.  If you keep getting killed generally it means you just should not be wherever you are yet.  The game is gated by "Meat Walls" as opposed to obstructions, for instance locked doors.  Though those do occur as well.
- Lords has an incredible inertia to the combat.  The weapons feel hefty, the strikes of the enemies feel powerful.  At times Lords is on-point with the combat, and you feel awesome about the results of an encounter.  The timing-based nature of combat is also a welcome adition.
Now to things I'm not as fond of:
- Lords needs a bit of polish, especially in just fine tuning the combat.  Occasionally you'll have a strike that should have hit, but did not.  This is just a minor sort of thing, and doesn't detract too much from the overall experience.
- The lore in Lords is very flimsy.  Its there, and what's there is good, it just doesn't feel like there is enough of it.  The world is more sketched out than fleshed out.  However; the story is serviceable, and is good compared to a wide berth of games.
- It seems that the Strength build is the most viable one, or at least the most easily accessible.  I'm about halfway through on a Strength run, and I dipped my toes in as a Dexterity build.  It didn't seem to be as effective.  However; I will not say any absolutes on this point, since I plan on going through the game again with a different build to test it out.
Overall I recommend this game if Dark Souls caught your interest, but you can't get past the difficulty.  However; after playing through this, I recommend you give Dark Souls a try as well.

Okay, this game is poorly optimized, the graphics aren't great, the textures are bad, but that's not what OMSI 2 is about. This simulator is for people who don't need high frames (you won't get above 60 fps regardless of your specs) or photorealistic graphics, this is for simulator people.
The base game comes with two maps, one large reconstruction of 1980's Berlin and a smaller, fictional, training map. It includes four different busses, one bendy-bus, one single-decker, and two double-deckers. This isn't a lot of content for upwards of £20, but there is a strong modding community which can add a whole new feel and look to the game, so dont worry about this when you first play.
For people who like to pick up a game and play it without much of a learning curve, OMSI 2 is not for you. I personally spent at least an hour, configuring settings for my Logitech G25 Racing Wheel, and learning all the different buttons on the bus dashboard. Once you know what to do, this game is alot of fun, but until then, I found it quite frustrating. Look at the forums for Input Configuration for different racing wheels and controllers, someone has already configured them and you can just paste those into the directory.
Performance, don't expect much. This is one of the cons of this game, it is very badly optimised. I reach anywhere from 20-60 frames, and experience frequent micro-stutters during gameplay, however I purchased this game knowing this would be the case.
Actually driving the bus feels fantastic, the physics (force feedback adds lots of realism) and feel of the busses is very well executed. I've never driven a real bus, but I think this could be considered close. The sound engine for this game is phenominal, and is really engaging. This is one of the most polished features.
For those who really want to drive a realistic feeling bus, while configuring routes and lines on the IBIS stystem, worrying about temperatures, and sticking to a strict schedule, buy this game. The price is quite high, but if you're one of those people, you will definitely get your money's worth.
If you've played ETS 2, or City Bus Driving, and think "hey I like simulators", be warned, this game is much more complex. You may still enjoy it, however if you're expecting an easy time I wouldn't recommend it.
In Conclusion:
Pros:
> Realistic Physics
> Realistic Sounds
> Plenty of mods
> Feels like you're driving a bus
> Excellent replayability (different lines/routes and maps)
Cons:
> Poor Optimisation
> Poor Graphics
> Rather Expensive
> Complex to configure and learn

The Ultimatest Battle!
A 2D game developed by EdioGames, a small indie french company trying to survive in this rough worlds with a free to play title. You play as a nub, a weird gray potato which grew arms and legs for some reasons and decided to pick up some guns to punch its little friends. The illegitimate child of TF2 and worms who grew up weirdly, for the best though!
With a pretty large arsenal of weapon, you can easily find one that perfectly adapts to your favorite play style, from the no brain left click gameplay to some evasive high apm things. And if you like the game, you can stick a bit longer to personalize your favorite potato type with a flurry of cosmetics (that do not bring any stats!).
But should you play the game?
Well probably, the game is F2P, you won't lose anything but a couple hour if the game is not what you were looking for. But for the most sceptical ones that are really trying to optimize their gaming time (but are still reading this for some reasons) let's list a couple good and bad points of the game. Don't trust my poor hour count for the moment, I've been playing the game for quite a while and will continue since steam made me come back.
Yes, this is a farm heavy game. The first levels will be easy to grind, and you might end up level 40 in a week or two, but if you want to go further you'll need to invest some time. There is no real goal for the moment, so be ready to have repetitive games sometimes. The only rankings will be... farm ladders for the moment. Seasons of 3 months, play like you never did and you might get stuff. The legend says that there are tournaments sometimes, but that's not confirmed.
The game is really noob friendly tho. Install the game, play a couple game and you'll already have all the basics you need so you can focus on a class/a weapon you like. The learning curve is really smooth don't worry if you get stomped at the start. When a game starts to be crowded with 10+ people, it quickly becomes a big mess where anyone can shine. Feel free to be cocky when you kick the butt of those high-level snobs :p
The game is a true F2P! Pretty rare these days no? You can only get cosmetic stuff and StatTrak weapons from the shop, every weapon is accessible in the crafting area, asking you for a couple resources to give you a random new toy to blow up your neighbour. And please ask high-level players for some starting items, we will gladly give you all our duplicates!
This game is meant to be played with others, so don't be a shy one and go talk to the others, find a guild and go kick asses together! I've met quite a lot of cool people here and I hope you'll be one those I still have to meet after a good brawl while we brag about our loots.
So yeah, play the game, preferably bring a friend or two to start so you can laugh at the mess together at the start or just straight up go bother people on discord. Even if you do not stick around because of the kind of boring casual farming you will 96% get a few laughs from it and a memorable evening/afternoon.
I think a few people already said it, but yeah, the game is clearly not perfect but it's definitely worth a try, so get a gun and jump in there!

If you are a fan of the hacking games that have been popping up now and then over the years, well; this may be the one that you have been waiting for. It truly takes all of the best aspects of the myriad hacker games already around. It expands on them and gives them some finesse tweaks. Some of the hacking games out there were too limited, too small, too difficult, too unforgiving and just too FAIL. That is just my take on a lot of the games in this genre. Not to say that they are all bad, but they all have a plethora of plusses and minuses. When these balance out, it does NOT make for a good game. The plusses need to far outweigh the minuses if they want to go all in for the win. Well, HACKNET is the closest competitor as far as I am concerned. I am very glad I bought this game and have thoroughly enjoyed my time so far.
Now if you are looking for some cinewmatic story telling cyberpunk 3d rendered world of the hacker, then keep on looking. Aside from some menu effects and wallpapers on your virtual terminal, you will not be seeing much in the video area. Instead this is a simulation of old school hacking... Just a boy and his terminal... A lot of typing... Although the game has a trick for saving your fingers a bit. Most commands and paramters of the commands (once you know what they are) just need the first letter or two or maybe four. Hit the TAB key and the terminal will finish the command for you. If there are parameters or variables to be entered as well, thenh you can TAB through those as well.
Now, I am an old school computer user from back in the day. I mean, when I went online for thye first time I had to dial a phone number by hand and then listen for a computer to answer (screeching carrier signal) then very quickly unplug the phone line and plug it into my modem, Then jump into a terminal program and start typing AT commands to make it answer the phone HOPEFULLY. ANYWAYS, I am old school I have done my timeshare on a dumb terminal application.
I paid my dues with a few ring-backs, shoes and FCC triangulating vans of doom. Had a lot of fun with some phreaking, blue boxes and endless hours dialing into Telnet without ever knowing back then that we were the first surfers to hit the oncoming waves of an approaching storm called the internet. What is my point? I am familiar with doing everything from a CLI and "trading" apps, docs and other information that could be used to further our online escapades. This game SORT OF brings back memories of a bygone era.

"I enjoyed the heck out of Metal Slug 3 on Steam,
just played Metal Slug X, why does it feel shorter and not as good as MS3?"
Well let's dive into a bit of Metal Slug History.
They were originally arcade games (as you can see in-game with the credits system)
MSX was originally released in 1999 as a modified version of MS2 (released 1998).
MS3 was released in 2000.
TLDR; Metal Slug X IS THE PREQUEL TO METAL SLUG 3.
Compared to MS3, there's no branching paths, less vehicles, less weapons, less non-human enemies,
but hey, its still a rather fun game if 2D side-scrolling platformer shooter games like Megaman and Contra is your kind of thing.

Sleek, polished, and streamlined for the TBS fans, and it delivers immensely.
Which pains me to say that I cannot recommend this fully.
The single player eventually just becomes a slog to go through, and the multiplayer is as barebones as its predecessor.
Passing time for this game is an annoying process, with constant interruptions and interjections by elements of the story and in-game world. To top it off, the in-game "Avatar Project" is a meta-clock that counts down until the game is over, and can be temporarily halted with great time and cost; in an XCOM game, this mechanic just simply doesn't fit, along with the time sensitive parts in many missions that require the player to outright bum rush an objective rather than play the game at their pace.
However, a possible redeeming point of the game may be the modding community, with a large and diverse bank of mods that may enhance gameplay and aesthetics.
The game still has the main course known and loved by fans of the franchise: the RNG element. It is present, it is frustrating, and by god do I love it.
Simply put, with the high bar set by XCOM: Enemy Unknown, XCOM 2 seems like a small step back in the franchise, though it's not to say that it's a bad game. Still, if given the choice between Enemy Unknown and this, Enemy Unknown would be my pick.
Final Verdict: 7/10, monotonous single player, barebones multiplayer, large array of mods, still has that XCOM feeling of "Oh poop" chance based goodness, but doesn't measure up to its predecessor. Recommended for the casual gamer rather than the long-time fan.

Age of Empires 3 is my favorite game. Yes, that places it infront of other video game giants, including Arma, Warband, Civilization, and perhaps more appropriately, Age of Empires 2.
It's not the graphics... it's definately not the graphics. They're not bad per se, in fact they are sometimes beautiful, but compared to the standard rts of today, they probably rank 4 or 5 out of 10.
AoE 3 is my favorite game because it's *fun*. Over the last decade or so, I've loved and then grown tired of dozens of games, Fallout 4 being the most recent victim. Age 3, however, is always fun. AI provides a challenge, the community is still amazingly friendly and going strong, there are tournaments where you can win cash prizes, plenty of mods, and a quite large amount of diverse factions. When you drop yourself into a game, both single and multiplayer, it's an engaging experience every time. Honestly, I can't even find the words to explain why it's always so fun, it just is. Perhaps it's the historical care given to each unit, or maybe the ridiculous cheats and snarky comments of the AI, I don't know. If I said every game was completely unique, I'd be lying; but that's not a problem, because Age 3 does what works.
I usually don't like writing reviews, especially ones over 9 words, but this game deserves at least a little bit of support from me. It's the least I can do for the most captivating game on the steam market.

This is one of those games that the Yes/No binary just doesn't work for. It's a fun game so despite it's flaws, I can't say don't buy it, but at the same time it has a ton of problems that make it hard to recommend.
To start, it's a really fun super arcade-ish experience. A budget Burnout clone that is more Burnout than what we got with Paradise. But that is also a negative, since Ridge Racer was noting like Burnout, making this a very poorly executed Ridge Racer game. For better or worse, it's just not faithful to the license.
The game also suffers from some poor design decisions. The MP servers were shutdown, but each time you launch the game, you have to wait for 2 full mins while the game attempts to connect to those now non-existent servers. This gets really annoying over time as the game also crashes more often than I'd consider reasonable.
But on the flip side, the game has some amazingly well designed tracks and set-pieces that make for some tense and compelling action that really suck you into the chaotic fray.
All in all the game is a mixed bag. Almost a perfect 50 / 50 split between “this is amazing, I want to play this forever” and “this game is so broken it boarders on unplayable and should be pulled from Steam”, it's a bi-polar hodgepodge of awesome and awful.
I guess I'll give it the thumbs up, and say grab it on a deep discount, but just know, it's definitely a roll of the dice and extremely flawed. For every minute of fun, you'll suffer a minute of mysery.

This is the first Souls like game which heavily divided the gamers. First because it is said to be easy compared to the Souls, second because the game crashed a lot for the people.
To me personally the game crashed only 2 times other than that it ran perfectly. I have never played the Souls games but i was interested how they work, only i wanted to try a more casual friendly version, so I purchased lotf on a sale. So how it's this?
Grapichally the game is beautiful, every armor looks different on the player, every weapon has it's own look. The areas have a cliché dark fantasy design but it works somehow, and the art design creates great atmosphere.
The fighting system is well done. Every enemy is approached with a different strategy, and also the weapons are better or worse against certain enemies as we have special weapons which are a lot better than most, but require a certain amount of skill (strength, agility or magic) to use and sometimes they are hidden. There are different size of armors which give you higher defence but worse manouveribiliy or better movement with worse defense. There are magic skills which help you a lot, and a unique ranged weapon as well. There are boss fights which at the beginning require different tactics, and the devs made an interesting feature if you beat them in a certain way, you got an upgraded version of their weapons as a drop.
I think the fight is good in the game, so why it was criticised then? Because the special weapons and higher level magic skills break a little this balance, you can forget the strategy and skill as the magic and good weapons will do the job for you. Also the bosses are completely exploitable with magic and with a cool weapon. I didn't care it however. I was glad that the game became easier as you progress in it, also because I felt the character progression actually working, and because during playing I realized how the punishing souls style is not for me.
The only real negative thing regarding the fighting system is the last boss fight though. Coz you can beat him only with certain weapons which is unfair, but sadly an existing thing in rpgs.
I was glad that there are npc-s and side quests along the way to break monotony. They are not great but surely welcome.
Now start with the negatives (obviously it subjective): the level design. Don't get me wrong, the areas are cleverly designed and connected with each other but from the second part they become extremely labirinth like, you need to find levers and switches and you will feel yourself lost a lot. This game element is similar to old school games like Rune or Legacy of Kain games. If you loved them, you will enjoy this, if not, that's a problem. This element is easier than in the above mentioned games, but it is still a hit and miss for you. There are only 3 areas in the game, which are huge and connected, but not more. It sincerely ruined the epic and rpg feeling as you feel yourself playing more with an action game than an rpg. You enter to a place which is infested by enemies, you fight your way through using checpoints and beating bosses, and save the day. That is how the game works which is more arcade than rpg like.
Then the story: it is not so bad as depicted, the ending is actually quiet nicely written even if it is predictable. The problem is that the game is only about the story. Through the areas you find audiologs (horrible decision for an rpg) which add info to the story, but not really about the world. We don't know who to save: a realm, a kingdom, who are the people who we want to save. Who is the enemy? Ok, we got some info about them but we don't really know how are they. The funny thing is that there are audio logs also in their realm (you go there during the game), but these logs are told by humans!! It would have been more interesting to hear the rhogars there knowing their motivations.
So the world and lore is completely untouched by the developers which I personally felt a let down.
After all I enjoyed the game even if fundamentally it was not for me: I didn't enjoy the souls style as i expected and i don't like excessive dungeons where you can lost easily. The game is about these 2 things though. Still it was an enjoyable journey, a 6.5/10 but if you love soul games it can be a 7.5-8/10 for you easily, just don't see the reason why not. It is a good game, but definitely not interested in sequels.

As an ‘early access game’ you might expect to be provided regular content updates and progress through milestones towards a future full game release. This is not the case; the developers’ website is full of deceit, falsified updates and broken promises of updates and ideas. You have been warned, this game is no longer in development - and don’t go believing the lies about unstable 'nightly' updates. This game has lost focus and the developer has moved on to their new Kick Starter campaigns and new game ideas.
Putting all this aside, the game is average; it lacks much of the character and charm of Terraria - the game it attempts to copy. Rather than a focus on developing and exploring a random world, the game focuses on a repetitive grind consisting of warp to planet, see if anything good, warp to next planet, repeat. There is no sense of achievement, and the tirelessly repeated 'dungeons' can be overcome with simple block placements around enemies. There is no feeling of adventure and there is no reason to 'dig' deep into any planets, the easiest way to get rare ores is to just run over the surface and then move onto the next planet.
If the developer actually puts some effort into this game they might be able to salvage it, but I implore you to take some time to look over the comments, reviews and forums; you'll notice that the developer has taken the money and run. Please don't support this money grabbing developer, wait for games to be fully developed before handing over your hard earned cash – no matter how small the amount - if the industry keeps going down this route it's going to be bad for all of us.

Surprisingly addicting for what it is, and you get a real action experience. It's quickly stealing Dreadnought's thunder as the big space ship game that relays the excitement of taking a Capital ship and throttling it up full flare and releasing everything you got at the right moment.
If Dreadnought doesn't allow an open beta this year, this game here could steal not only it's thunder, but it's pre settled space that was once almost gurantied for Dreadnought. Fractured Space at description might sound lacking at first glance, but when you get in that ship and roar by for that perfect charge, move through the burning wreckage, and overcharge engines to high power turn behind an asteroid so you can safely space fold to safty for repairs, hoping the enemy won't round about fast enough to hit you while shields are down for jump, you gain a hard to forget experience.
In my sea of games owned, this one has been grabing the most time of my gaming since I started on the free weekend. That free weekend was a good move, because as even now I speak with youtubers about Dreadnought, several of them have also begun Fractured Space via the free weekend, and have bought into the Early Access packs.
None of them regret their investment thus far, and their shared stories of Fractured Space is only draining more people away from the long in the tooth alpha that has been three years of waiting for Dreadnought to allow people other than the high and mighty known youtubers and expo goers to play as they seem to continue to trip over a buisness model before they let others play.
Fractured Space's developers are making all the right moves, and they may have just jumped in for the full broadside needed to steal the big ship thunder that's been baited for far to long by another.
Well met, Edge Case Games. You knew the time to execute, you knew how to execute, and though the Alpha level bugs are still present, like warping from base just to wind up at base again, and being stuck in limbo at the begining of a match and then said match starting without a HUD, this very much is still early early on, and already it's well more polished than other games who have been in Alpha for three plus years now.
If they ever decided to add a mission based PVE experience, or even break moba territory by allowing for a universe that really feels like you're out to travel and explore, they just might become bigger than even they were expecting with this one. There's just some kind of magic in the vibe from the play to the sound design of this one. It's already quite the experience. One that feels familiar enough, but one that's all it's own, all while it delivers where another continues to lose it's buzz.
It's worth the price tags to get in with what is offored for each package at this time, get in to lear the different ways to handle various ships and garner your experience now before the next generation of captains gain all that experience without you. Those who come in late however will still find a fun and sureal experience as they find their way as they set out beside us experienced veterans to be.
SHORT VERSION:
