However, in trying to maintain the same simple-ish gameplay that made the mobile version of the game great, it does not play so well on PC. Hacknet is one of the best hacking simulators I have ever seen. not only does it look realistic, but it uses legitamate UNIX commands in the game. anyone familiar with linux will enjoy this, but if you don't, who cares?! let me tell you what this game has to offer.
first of all, it has a reasonably interesting plotline. I won't say much, but lets put it this way. Bit is a deceased hacker, and you have to find out how he REALLY died. through missions, you get closer to finding the truth, and getting the justice he deserves.
Depending on how you play, you end up following different paths. one being the Entropy path, the other being CSEC, and one more that I'll let you figure out on your own ;)
The GUI of the game is simple and beutiful. it lays everything out in an organized manner that puts all the control in your hands. Not only that, but the audio is just as good as the visuals. The music in this game is something that gets you pumped up for what's coming your way. and if you're into techno, great. I mean, what did you expect from a hacking/computer-based game? opera? pop? not a chance.
One thing I will say though, this game can get REALLY frustrating, and I'm not putting that lightly. You will have to use your brain to get through this game. regardless, the mechanics are simplistic and easy to learn, but the missions aren't exactly what I would call "a walk in the park".
Finally, in the words of the game's creator himself, Matt Trobbiani, "I do kind of hope I'm creating the Hackers of the future, and I think that's great."

In this day of ever increasing indie options of one-off great concepts that try and differentiate themselves from the crowd, this game is a real diamond in the rough.  Sure, it doesn't have many of the extras and filler of a larger title, but it is truly such a rare and beautiful thing to find such an uncomplicated, (and uncomprimised), good time these days. The lack of online multiplayer is for this games benefit  as, despite the shortsighted comments that we see from some of the other reviews, this is a game that is an experience best enjoyed with the other players in the same room playing together for a shared experience like no other. The immediate and visceral impact of every button push is shared, (almost by force) as each kill is given attention through screen focuses of the involved parties as they slash each other down as quickly as possible in this first to 10 battle royale. Everyone gets to appreciate the flow of the match through brief pauses for each score. This is one of those games that is immediately accessible while still offering a serious depth of strategy for experienced players, making it fun to play even with mixed levels of experience. If you have the controllers to support four players at once, you will be hard pressed to find a better way to spend a night with friends than this!

Age of Empires 3
Genre: Strategy - Real Time Strategy
Rating: 10/10
Personal playing period: 5+ years
Is it worth a buy: Yes. Even at full price. This is a necessity for any strategy players collection.
Girl vs Game: Unless it's some super model I'd definately rather play the Game.
Personal Comment:
This is an amazing game with endless amounts of game time. The hours on here isnt a fraction of my actual game time online and offline. Been playing this game since the day it was released and still play it and love it today. I even missed a couple of meals as well as toilet breaks playing this believe it or not. I have bladder and bowel control of a ninja thanks to AOE.
Online gaming:
The online gaming community is still very active and people of all skill levels are on it. You will find anywhere between 500 to 2000 people online at any given time. Beware though that even though AOE is helpful and awesome the online community are sometimes a bunch of cocktonsil nimrod supremists who think they're amazing whilst never having seen or felt a girl up close unless in a magazine. But if your skin is thick and you dont give a flying **** about other people you'll be fine.
Short Summary:
This is a real time strategy game that plays off in the medieval times. There are 8 standard civilizations, 3 native indian civilizations and 3 Asian civilizations. Each civ provides a different set of advantages and it takes time to learn how to utilise the various civs to their full capability. Learning each civilisation takes time and it is great fun doing that. There are countless amounts of maps that allow for the use of different strategies. The game also has a story rich single player campaign. I have not played the campaign yet but never felt the need to as the standard game modes offer more than enough fun and game time.
The game also has progressive improvement meaning the more you play the more items get unlocked and the stronger your civilisation becomes. This ensures that you want to play more and more in order to improve the strength of your favourite civilisation.
Learning Curve and Gameplay:
Easy to start but tough to master. The learning curve to start playing and learning the basics is very easy. Learning the various civilisations and their strengths is more challenging and may take a lot of practice and time. The gameplay is very simplistic in it being a basic RTS with click and place. Gathering of basic resources and using those resources are easy and self explanotary. A tutorial can be played to understand the basics but this game is very playable and a new player will get it after playing only for a few hours.

This game is honestly one of the best games I have played. Hacknet is a hacking simulator which may or may not be realistic, I am not a hacker or very good with computers so I would not know but without a doubt it's worth every penny of those $10.00. The game focuses on you as the main character who is suddenly emailed by a enigmatic hacker by the name of bit who teaches you his techniques which launchs off your career as a hacker. As the game goes on you will later be approached by more and more hackers and hacker organizations. One thing I find so enjoyable is the problem solving aspect, sure plenty of the game is just using the tools at your disposal to get into this system or to hack that site but at times your knowledge of the system and the games mechanics will be put to the test. If you have any chance of beating this game you need to be smart, creative, quick to react, and you cannot break under pressure because this game can get pretty intense. Another great aspect of this game it the difficulty. At first it's relatively easy but as time goes on you will begin to notice how this game is unforgiving when you screw up. Not kidding, it's brutal here dude. The game will have multiple instances where a rival hacker is at your throat or when you have a trace running on you and you need to open and hack the ports as fast as possible to become an admin and stop the trace. Sometimes it's going to look bleak but it is soooooo satisfying when you hack the system with seconds to spare and sooooo disapointing when you fail and are wacked over the nose as a result. That does not mean this game is without problems. For one even though the format of the game is its greatest strength it also can be its greatest weakness mainly due to the fact that it is not a very engaging experience and requires you to try your best to stay on top of actually playing the game. The narrative is good without a doubt but it also can get dull at times and even kind of confusing. It's more of a mystery of trying to figure out what happened to Bit but it seems as if they tried to squeez in more and though for the most part the game flows beautifully at times it does get a little cramped. I also have a personal complaint, every time I start the game, even though my profile is still their, it starts me off at the beggining. I don't know if this is supposed to happen or not but I would assume not. I continue trying to find a solution but otherwise I have to beat the game in one consistan run which is kind of erritating but still fun. overally solid 8.5/10, worth buying.

I'm a damn picky gamer, and am an enormous fan of the original XCOM (+100 hours). I was afraid XCOM 2 would suffer from "Call-of-Duty Syndrome", and that the immersion, strategy, gameplay, and most importantly, atmosphere, would be watered down to appeal to a wider demographic. But instead, we've gotten a damn good game which is faithful to the original while still finding room to innovate enormously.
There is a certain charm to XCOM 1. The aesthetics had comicbook-esque style to them that was unique and delightful. The enemies, in retrospect, had a bit of a comical appearance and were quite colourful. Not so in XCOM 2. Expect a game with a much more serious aesthetic. For example, Mutons here look lethal, like they could really kill me, as opposed to the cumbersome green dumb-dumbs in the first game. Everything in XCOM 2 just looks deadlier and more realistic. This new severity permeates both art and gameplay design. It's not bad; just different. The contrast is Anti-Alien Comicbook (XCOM 1) vs Anti-Alien MilSim (XCOM 2).
My only complaint about the XCOM 2 aesthetics is that sometimes it breaks its own style. Aviator glasses, pony tails, dreads... it all feels sort of douchey and out of place. I get it, XCOM is more rag-tag this time arou- get over it. It doesn't work and it looks stupid. This confusion over design really shows through in the Anarchy Children's DLC. Luckily, these design issues are mainly limited to early game soldier customization, and become pretty much a non-issue as new options/armors are unlocked.
I know that many people have complained about mission timers. While I generally don't mind them, perhaps even enjoy the tension they create, there are two caveats I must mention.
1. They were pretty stressful to deal with even on Ironman Normal for me. They would be an even bigger pain on Ironman Classic/Impossible.
2. Once in a while, the turn timer to enemy ratio is just bullcrap, and you just can't seem to kill enemies fast enought to get to your objective. This problen can be overcome through careful use of concealment but... maaah... meh.
But I'm really nit-picking here. These are a few dodgy strands in an otherwise immaculate tapestry of a game. XCOM 2's new complexities in research, engineering, facility construction, new facilities, and the addition of the world "rebel map" create an enormous experience that feels massive and has giant weight and meaning to it. Campaigns are a rollercoaster of frustration and elation. And the capstone is a boss fight, which, for me at least, was one of the best, most tense I have ever seen, and boy, have I seen a lot of boss fights. Take a hike, Dark Souls.
Basically, this game is the fun you had with XCOM 1 a second time around, and it's just had a bit of a make-over.

This game is fantastic, one of the best games I have ever played in my life.
The plot and characters in this game develop very effectively, which leads you to truly caring about your characters and making you truly think about the decisions that you are forced to make.

The decisions are not always easy in this game. The tough decisions can be very hard to deal with and will make you think about them further on in the game, especially when some characters confront you about them.
This game has a very unique feature, there are mutliple ways you can play it. Examples are saving certain characters and letting others die and saying certain things to characters which they will remember and will possibly influence a decision they make in the game. This means that your playthrough could be completely different to somebody else's playthrough, and may inspire you to play the game again to change things around a bit.
The graphic style in this game is very unique and creative, instead of following the usual 'realistic graphics', this game chooses to have a comic-book art style due to the fact that it is based on The Walking Dead comic book, and it leaves its own little shine on the game.
The controls in the game are very smooth and fluid, and the same goes for the combat in the game as well. It's never clunky and always provides you with the best experience.
The music in the game is great, it adds further atmosphere to the game and fits the situations perfectly. Sometimes bringing even more emotions into it!
Overall, I couldn't really say anything bad about this game. It is genuinely one of the best games I have ever played and I enjoyed every moment of it, I cried at the end, and this is the only game to have ever done that to me.
Therefore, I highly recommend that you give this game a go!

text:
Here's a simple review for anybody who is unsure about this game:
Good:
-Fluid gameplay and amazingly well-designed atmosphere.
-Wide variety of items and objects within many, many different enviroments, all freely accessable (see next point).
-Detailed background lore and welcome, yet slightly limiting, difficulty progession system.
-Simple yet effective building mechanics.
-Well-made mining/looting/stealing system (based on what you are taking).
-Populated towns and rogue NPC cultists/temple guards/ECT.
-Realistic depictions of planets (moons without oxygen, acid rain, gravity differences, orbiting background planets, ect).
Bad:
-Random difficulty spikes in certain areas/planets.
-No "easy" way to create a multiplayer server.
-Infrequent updates.
-Occasionally generic items (pickaxes, ect).
On The Fence:
-Occasionally conflicting towns with enviroments (happy, healthy villages in desolate wastelands).
Overall, a VERY good game for those with a creative and curious mind, but tiresome for those looking for a story-driven game. YOU make your own story through your actions, and very little is given to you ("you crashed, good luck"), which could be tiresome and irritating for those who prefer to have a deep, interesting story to follow and be enveloped by.
Also, as an obligatory comparison to Terraria:
-Played Terraria for about one hour, got bored and only kept playing due to streaming.
-Played Starbound for fourty hours, still happy to explore and build even on unmodded singleplayer.
Game is fun but the maps have really bad design and spawn camping is a real problem.

Ridge Racer Type 4 has always been a favorite of mine, if not my favorite game ever. This game, however, does not even deserve the name Ridge Racer in the slightest. It's a cheap, weird clone of Burnout that does everything that makes it's source of "inspiration" fun, wrong. It's slow, clunky, drifting is awful and the (crash) physics are just dreadful.

So, where to start with this?
If you've ever played a Hack n' Slash game like Darksiders, Devil May Cry, or anything of the like and enjoyed it, make sure you get this one.
Combat system is flawless- I don't think I've ever been cheated out of a combo unfairly, and while the game is a tough one at times, it's never more than punishing you for your own faults.
Difficulty is definitely felt, for sure. It's not a hard game (I played Normal and was able to get through each level without much pain) by any measure, but don't expect to glide through running into each fight without some tact.
Graphics are nice, but it's not made necessarily to show off any of that as the game WAS released on a last-gen hardware originally anyways. You won't think the graphics feel that dated when you play, and nothing is visually jarring.
Optimization leaves a little to be desired from my personal opinion, but I was able to run it 1080p on highest with 60, so I cannot complain. If you're looking for higher resolutions, there's definitely a steep requirement versus achieved result from what I found.
Story is the driving force in this game, and you won't really get tired of it as many levels incorporate unique variables into them. (A level where you race on a motorcycle across a highway as it gets demolished? Hell yeah.) In terms of the story's enjoyment, you won't find it turning you off from the game any more than you'd be turned off if you simply didn't enjoy the Hack n' Slash genre.
Overall? I can't really complain with this title. I never played it when it first came out, so this port to PC is surely something I appreciate being a part of my library.

It would be unfair to call this Dark Souls Lite, as some people do, for it is not simply a watered-down version of Souls. It's a smaller and much easier game in comparison, but has enough character and good ideas of its own. However so many little flaws make this game impossible for me to recommend. The movements are often stiff, and in cramped areas the camera sometimes goes crazy, making it irritating in combat. There's no map, which in a Souls game is not a serious problem because of the diversity of environments, but in this game where there isn't much variety and the level designs are often convoluted, the lack of a map is more than annoying. There are only a few side quests and almost none of them works well--because the game doesn't give you a journal, you often don't know what you're supposed to do, where you're supposed to go, or whether or not a quest is completed. The jumping puzzles are absolutely hideous because whenever your character lands he automatically rolls forward, often directly to a falling doom. But the worst part of the game of course is its innumerable glitches. I've encountered a game breaking glitch where I kill a boss and a door is supposed to open but doesn't, and now I'm stuck in limbo and have to start over. This is after 4 patches which supposedly have fixed already a cartload of bugs. This is exacerbated by the fact that you get only one save slot per character. This is really the last nail on the coffin of an otherwise reasonably enjoyable game.

I picked up Fractured Space during the free weekend last week, and these are my thoughts after 3-4 days of playing it.
Fractured Space is a very interesting and promising space combat game that combines A MOBA and World of Warships
with a space age aesthetic. This game is relatively easy to get into, even for someone who generally dislikes MOBA's, such as I.
The objective of each game is to capture the enemy base while vying for control of two lanes and a middle sector. You capture up to three mining stations to gain resources for your team. Resources are used to upgrade your ships, and the upgrade level of your fleet makes a huge difference in combating other players and capturing the enemy base. There is also the middle area, called the Gamma Sector. This is a large station that when captured by a team, gives the whole team a big damage buff, making pushes much easier to accomplish.
Teamwork is a major part of this game, and this is made more obvious when you look at the variety of ships available. It almost reminds me of a class based shooter, like Team Fortress 2. You have your basic front line attack ships, the super massive defensive ships, and the support and healer ships. Any player can find a role and a ship that fits their play style the most. No ship is outright better then the other, which is a huge sigh of relief in a word of pay-2-win F2P games.
Graphics are quite impressive in this game, though there are some minor rough spots here and there. The skyboxes are beautiful, distant planets look amazing, and the ships themselves are loaded with detail. The ships are the highlight of the audio-visual experience for me, looking like something a real company would make. They also sound great, weapons sound punchy and dangerous, and the warp drive really does sound how you'd imagine massive hyperspace engines would sound like. Though graphics can be a bit uneven in places, especially on asteroids. But as you're usually just flying by them, it won't bother you that much. There is also occasionally texture pop-in when warping into different lanes. But overall, graphics are sound are great.
Gaining new ships and weapon in Fractured Space is a process of gaining experience in one of the three ship manufacturers in the game by using their ships, and making credits, which you gain after each round. It took me only a couple matches to unlock the first ship after the starter ship, and one more day to unlock the one after that. You can speed up the process by purchasing a microtransaction only currency and buying the ship with that, but you still need to unlock the ship with actual play time. And as no ship is a direct upgrade over the other, I find this very fair.
Speaking of microtransactions, they are done very well in Fractured Space. The only exclusive things you can buy are ship skins and credit and XP boosters to use after the match, along with being able to purchase weapons and crew members (five stat boosters you can buy to improve your ship even more) faster. You can still buy these with credits, although it will take you longer. I think this system is totally fair and encourages people to invest in the game if they like it.
My only real gripes with the game come from its Alpha, Early Access status. Matchmaking can sometimes not work, lag can playing borderline impossible, warping sometimes doesn't work, and general wonkiness and UI weirdness crops up. But all these things are being worked on by the devs, and the game isn't even in Beta yet. This game has a ton of potential, and I really hope that this game garners a large following in the very near future. Until then, I'll see you in the Gamma Sector while getting shot down by a Brawler.

This game is honestly one of the best games I have played. Hacknet is a hacking simulator which may or may not be realistic, I am not a hacker or very good with computers so I would not know but without a doubt it's worth every penny of those $10.00. The game focuses on you as the main character who is suddenly emailed by a enigmatic hacker by the name of bit who teaches you his techniques which launchs off your career as a hacker. As the game goes on you will later be approached by more and more hackers and hacker organizations. One thing I find so enjoyable is the problem solving aspect, sure plenty of the game is just using the tools at your disposal to get into this system or to hack that site but at times your knowledge of the system and the games mechanics will be put to the test. If you have any chance of beating this game you need to be smart, creative, quick to react, and you cannot break under pressure because this game can get pretty intense. Another great aspect of this game it the difficulty. At first it's relatively easy but as time goes on you will begin to notice how this game is unforgiving when you screw up. Not kidding, it's brutal here dude. The game will have multiple instances where a rival hacker is at your throat or when you have a trace running on you and you need to open and hack the ports as fast as possible to become an admin and stop the trace. Sometimes it's going to look bleak but it is soooooo satisfying when you hack the system with seconds to spare and sooooo disapointing when you fail and are wacked over the nose as a result. That does not mean this game is without problems. For one even though the format of the game is its greatest strength it also can be its greatest weakness mainly due to the fact that it is not a very engaging experience and requires you to try your best to stay on top of actually playing the game. The narrative is good without a doubt but it also can get dull at times and even kind of confusing. It's more of a mystery of trying to figure out what happened to Bit but it seems as if they tried to squeez in more and though for the most part the game flows beautifully at times it does get a little cramped. I also have a personal complaint, every time I start the game, even though my profile is still their, it starts me off at the beggining. I don't know if this is supposed to happen or not but I would assume not. I continue trying to find a solution but otherwise I have to beat the game in one consistan run which is kind of erritating but still fun. overally solid 8.5/10, worth buying.

This is an OK game. I wouldn't go as far as to compare it to either Uplink or the Street Hacker series simply because it feels more like a demo when compared to them. The execution and gameplay is shallow and naive. It's plagued by many basic design issues and most of the missions are just boring, repetitive, and feel more like a chore rather than a challenge.
My biggest gripes are:
-boring, repetitive and easy missions. Only 2 interesting missions stand out, the final Bit one, and the online pacemaker one.
-no sense of urgency or challenge. If you get caught hacking, that's just a reload to last checkpoint. No point in deleting any logs the way Uplink makes sure that you do. Uplink kept you on your toes because getting caught meant absolute game over!
-Badly designed UI. The workstation "map" is a cluttered mess especially as you move closer towards the end. Nodes are being randomly generated and the ones closest to the edge of the screen have their hover information cut off. How that ever went past the testers, I do not know!
-Weird writing, bad grammar, spelling mistakes, juvenile jokes scattered here and there. The ending was incredibly cheesy and anti-climactic.
Not a bad game to get on sale. But this is no Uplink for sure. The tagline shouldn't be "if you liked Uplink, you'll love this!" It's more the other way around because now I definitely feel like going back and replaying Uplink for the zillionth time! :)

Age of Empires III. How can one possibly begin to review a game of such magnitude and prevalence that this game holds on the gaming world? A game that, even though it has been out for over 10 years, has a large active online community? It isn’t possible, but I shall nevertheless try.
This game has a rich story, which is full of interesting historical points. Even though it is fictional, it pleasantly covers the conquests of the new world. In the vanilla version and “The War Chiefs” expansion, the player can endeavour to fight against various European civilisations in order to achieve glory and fame throughout the Americas. In “The Asian Dynasties” expansion, it spans centuries of Asian colonialization by the British as well as the Japanese and the Chinese Dynasties.
The gameplay is a perfect reflection of the RTS genre. You slowly build your settlement to include markets, barracks and a host of other buildings, increasing your population and army before getting ready to attack your enemy or defend your settlement. Getting the fine balance between your food, wood and coin collection can be challenging but rewarding when you get it right. Will you build a good army to begin with, or a good economy, praying that your enemy won’t attack before you’ve had chance to convert your good economy into a powerful army? Each of the units has a strength and a weakness. For example, skirmishers counter musketeers, cavalry counters skirmishers, and musketeers counter cavalry. So it’s important to get the balance right when creating your army. The new eso-community patch has nicely levelled out the civilisations, making the OP civilisations slightly less powerful and the UP civilisations slightly more powerful.
Graphically, the game is simply gorgeous. Even though it’s definitely not a new game, it doesn’t feel outdated in this respect and looks magnificent from a distance (you’ll want to play fully zoomed out to maximise what you can see on the screen at all times). From buildings setting on fire and slowly crumbling as they take damage, to the glorious water reflections, to the breathtaking bloom effects, you’ll be wondering whether it was actually made in 2005, or 2015.
The music is purely divine. I’m listening to it as I type this as it’s one of my favourite game original soundtracks of all time. As your colony grows into a mighty empire the soundtrack seamlessly transitions from slow, peaceful renaissance/discovery era, to the powerful and more rhythmic late game, mimicking the chugging of steam engines and factories as you journey into the industrial age.
Overall, a stunning game. If you haven’t ever played it, buy it and experience it for yourself. You will not be disappointed.

I played XCOM EU and loved it but this game does nothing but punish you. It's not challenging and rewarding, its flat out difficult and infuriating. Even on the easiest setting. It doesn't feel like a struggle, like you're against time and have to save humanity and that every battle is another hope for the human race. It just feels like you're slowling getting beaten down and whithered away. Whithered away not by the alien invaders, but by the ridiculous RNG that this game has.
This game though, when you have an 95% chance to hit, you miss. Every. Single. Time. Even after you reload your save.  The RNG is so terrible, it's cheating you out of shots. It was never this bad in EU. It's like the devs specifically programmed the RNG to give you hope that you might actually hit something just so they can crush your soul. "Oh you have a 90% chance to hit? JK we actually mean 9% but LOL we're not telling you that. Have fun watching your squad member die because our♥♥♥♥♥♥RNG made him miss a point blank shot with a shotgun, ♥♥♥♥♥."
And then there's the avatar project. When I read some of these reviews, I actually thought the avatar project would make the game more intense but instead it made the whole game cluttered and overall unenjoyable.
There's so many facilities that need to be built and so many things that need to be researched or areas to explore that sometimes it's impossible to do because you're put up against the clock. And world exploration events like supply drops are an absolute pain to do because your focusing all your efforts on establishing contacts and attacking bases to stop the avatar project.
When the RNG doesn't cheat you and throw you into the fricken ground, the game is actually fun and feels polished. But the absolute crap RNG doesn't make this game challenging or rewarding. It makes it infuriatingly difficult and punishing. The RNG is so terrible that it's punishing, makes the game irritating to play and makes me want to kill myself.
And that's what makes it a true Xcom game. 10/10.

The game is an example of some of the worst business practices in modern gaming:  micro-transactions, chests that require membership and particular level on "AC Initiates"
), chests that require wasting your time with their mobile "Companion App" ....  On top of that AC Initiates is not fully functional and partially broken at present time.

Paris looks really beautiful and some interiors are amazing but this is pretty much the only "innovation" you'll find in this chapter of the series.
Unless you are a really big AC fan, don't buy this game in its current state.  AC 4 Black Flag was a better game and until they patch Unity and reduce the price, it's not worth your money.

Motifero Motus is a game where you drive a car down an endless, straight highway. The only buttons required are the up and down arrow keys which you use to shift between the three lanes in order to avoid other vehicles and collect items on the road. There is only one mode and 9 levels, each lasting a minute or two.
There is no reason to buy this game, there is no reason to play this game. You start out in an regular car driving down the highway. A randomly generated series of vehicles comes down and you need to avoid them. A bar at the bottom shows you how much further until the stage is finished. There is also money and every once and a while one of two powerups on the track. Each dollar sign you pick up adds 1 point to your total score. Red crosses give you another life. And the fire gives you progress on an 'upgrade' meter.
Collecting these items is really easy and in the case of the money not even worth the effort. The other cars on the road are static and move from the right of the screen to the left at the same speed. The other powerups are nearly pointless. Health adds another life, represented by an image of the starting car, to the top left corner. The symbols will not go past 4 though so every life past 4 will not be visible to the player. The fire builds up a yellow meter that when full changes the appearance of your car. You can do this twice. This has no bearing on gameplay as far as I could tell as I tried the last level with the level 1 and max level cars and experienced no change.
Each time you complete a level you are instantly brought into the next. The only difference between levels is that the speed is increased very slightly and starting at level three cops are added in. The cop cars appear at random and randomly shift lanes. If they hit you you lose 1 life like any other vehicle but because they have no discernible pattern and you have no options but moving up and down it is pure chance if they hit you or not. Even with that issue there's next to no penalty for losing all your lives. You keep all whatever score and car level you had when you lost and just have to start the most recent level from the start. And unless you are trying to get every single dollar on the road its actually  difficult to lose all your lives in a level.
WHen you finish level nine you are told your final score and then dropped back on the main screen. Out of curiosity I played the last level again and still had the same car and score from when I won and beat it again leaving me with a higher score. So even the high score is a sham because theres nothing stopping you from just playing that level forever to get the highest score ever! But why would you bother?
This entire game screams mediocrity. I wouldnt be suprised if it was actually a school project as it has all the things a beginners course in game design would teach you. The art is plain with the road just having random white spots to serve as 'detail'. There is next to no animation save for a single frame where the car turns slightly when switching lanes and a blinking fire effect when upgrading. The music is a single annoying track that can be turned off thankfully. The sound effects are exactly what you would expect. It even freeezes on occasion to load the next random set of cars.
Good game worth the time and its very fun to play with friends :)

Before I start I have to point something out:
UPDATE YOUR NVIDIA GRAPHICS CARD DRIVERS!
The people complaining about the flickering lights and low FPS could fix all of their problems if they had just installed the required updated drivers.
If you're having the problem on AMD cards, I dunno what to tell you.
This game is pretty good. I think a lot of people are disappointed because they allowed themselves to be hyped up enough to be disappointed when the game didn't live up to their expectations.
Yeah, there are frame drops from time to time, but I honestly am amazed how optimized it is with THOUSANDS of NPCs on screen, all interactive as well. As far as I know, no game has been able to achieve this.
The facial animations are the best I've ever seen in a game. LA Noire comes close, but the graphics on the faces kind of killed it in that game. Unfortunately, because of this, cutscenes are SUPER LAGGY for me. 15-20 FPS laggy. Mouths actually look and talk like real mouths. No more wide mouthed S's.
Co-op is... amazing. It's what AC has needed for a long time, and I'm glad it's finally here. Seeing other people actually working together with you to assassinate some bad guys is a really good feeling. Cutzomization is really well-fleshed out and very cool.
I haven't encountered too many bugs. I clipped through a roof once, and then I fell through the world... but that's about it. Fortunately, it is playable and enjoyable even with a bug here and there. It's a game after all. Expecting games to be bugless is like expecting a burger to come without the meat.
There are a few interesting gameplay mechanics they tweaked/took out. The most notable one being no fighting with fists or hidden blades, which isn't that big of a deal. You also cannot switch to the hidden blades, which I find kind of annoying when trying to air assassinate people. Air assassinations are pretty wonky. Sometimes they just don't work although you're right above them, which is very annoying.
The animation quality of everything, even NPCs, is fantastic. They really kicked it up a notch this time animation-wise.
All in all, after 8 hours of playing this game, I'll give it a 8/10.
TL;DR:
The graphics deliver. Performance is okay, but that's expected with so much stuff happening on screen.
Gameplay delivers. Combat and Parkour are much better. Air assassinations are still wonk.

I was very indecisive about which account I should put this game on. I think I made the right choice, putting it in my "meh, I dunno about this" account. It pretty much sums up my opinion of it.
I have absolutely no idea where they are going with this thing. When I bought in, I thought I had a good idea about what I was getting, but with constant changes in development, I really just don't know anymore. Sure, developing a game requires changes here and there, but SB is a game that really has no idea what it wants to be ultimately. It doesn't give the buyer much faith if the Devs keep changing their ideas. I can't possibly believe this game to be a "vision" when the vision changes every week.
When I bought in, I was given this picture. Like all other early access games, you are given a gist of what's to come. When that "gist" is deluded with constant backtracking, and slow development, how can one help but to feel left in the dark?
Here recently, there is a lot of talk about "progression". What is being described with this new content is NOT what I was expecting in this game.
This linear progression stuff that is being talked about is fine in some games, but in a game that uses a procedural generated universe as its foundation, I feel the mechanics will collide.
Resources as they are right now serve a very finite use. Once you've made your favorite top tier armor, found your favorite weapons and other gear, the whole value of resources comes to a halt. I would be okay with this if the mechanics change in the future, but it doesn't look like it's going to with this talk about "armor progression". It seems as if they want you to eventually find your favorite armor, favorite weapon, and that's that. Like I said, that's fine in some games, but in a game meant to be "sandbox", it doesn't fit well.
So my question is: Why go procedural? It seems like a lot of pointless work. If I get armor and other items that don't require iron anymore (for example), why have an infinite, procedurally generated universe full of the stuff? To build with? Okay, sure. But building needs to connect to everything else in the game. I don't want to build just for the sake of building. I want to build to store and maintain my value and power in the universe. Not just build and horde items I'll never use again. What about selling this iron? Okay, sure. But if I already got my fav gear, do tell what I'll be buying with this money I'll be making.
Resources need to have a constant tangible and economical value in a game meant to have no true end. In a game like Minecraft, having a procedurally generated world works because ALL resources need to be maintained. Since all materials need to be maintained, it has a constant value to all players at all times. All the mechanics come full circle because of this. In SB, the linear mechanics collide with the non-linear mechanics because it does have this infinite universe with resources, but they will eventually fill their finite use.
Imagine in Minecraft once you've made a certain pickaxe, it never broke, and it never needed to be maintained. What would happen? You would no longer need to look for that material, and that whole massive world holds no value to you anymore. Now I'm not comparing Minecraft to SB as the same game, I'm only comparing the procedural generation mechanic they both share.
I'm not saying weapon degradation needs to be in SB to make it work. I'm just saying it needs something to make this infinite playing field flow smoothly. Otherwise, we are all going to get our top tier armor, our favorite top tier weapon, and run around killing each other for the sake of killing each other.
I want battles that are about power and resource. It's the key motivation for any pvp. You can't blame me for thinking that SB was going to be this. So much features promised, and so many different things planned, I feel that everyone who bought in found something about it they wanted, and they pictured their own little piece of paradise within it. That right there is what was banked on.
Do I recommend this? How can I recommend something that changes it's tune constantly? It's a moving target right now, so no, I can't possibly recommend it. I don't know who it's trying to please in the long run. All I can say is: If you got the money to blow, and you're curious, go for it. If not, just wait and see what it will be when it's considered "finished". Whatever that means anymore.

A day after release, having had some decent time with it, I can say that AC:U is every bit what most were saying it was going to be: unoptimized, buggy, yet a logical progression in the Assassin's Creed line. The parkour system is absurdly more intuitive than it has been before (about 96% of the time, but thats pretty decent considering the mechanics). The story is compelling, Arno has some decent quips that elicit a chuckle. The progression of Absertgo pushing forth to the public is at least realized from Black Flag, and the overarcing story is at least coherent.
The game's biggest flaws come in the highly unfinished state the publisher released it in. Kudos aside, the publisher released a buggy piece of software that has inherent flaws. I was able to run it, albeit on low settings with a mixture of medium and high settings. Granted, I have an older Radeon HD7850 and an AMD cpu running at 4 gigz (at overclock to boot!). There are FPS drops, and commonly freezing. I fall through the world, resulting in desynchronization and having to restart memories. I get stuck in gargoyles, railings, and even the floor at times. The cloth and hair sim bugs and starts fidgeting, and overall the phsyics like to go wonky.
Now for the pros and cons:
Pros:
- New and improved Parkour system
- Customizable outfit
- Interesting and acceptable voice acting
- Stunning rendition of late 18th century France
Cons:
- Horrid framerate issues
- Steep performance/qaulity ratios
- Buggy phsyics
- Unfinished feel
- Lack of crowd variability
- Lack of enemy types
- Immersion breaks
Overall, not recommendable in this state. Maybe after bugfixes, mods, and patches this game can be recommended. Yet as of this writing, the game is definitely not worth the sixty bucks.
Besides all of this, and bugs aside, its the perfect Assassin's Creed game. It's what the franchise aspired, and has gotten. Yet its probably far too late for the perfect Creed game, considering how many titles the series has pushed out.

Bayonetta is unlike most games I've ever played and there is so much going on in this game that it's difficult to even describe it adequately. The gist of it is that it's a fast-paced fighting-and-platforming-game where you will spend most of the time punching, kicking and shooting bizarre heavenly creatures or running and jumping to the next fight. The story starts off confusingly and keeps twisting and turning in simultaneously convoluted and awesome ways to the point where even after finishing the game I honestly don't feel like I really understand the plot very well, but boy was it ever a fun trip.
This slightly mind-bending quality permeates all aspects of the game. One moment you're running through a fantastical vision of a hyper-religious isolated European city, the next moment the whole city is flooded by lava and you're literally running on walls. Bayonetta does not shy away from mixing up the gameplay one bit, there's rarely a moment where nothing eye-catching is happening; Vehicle-sections, Starfox-style shooter sections, simple puzzle-platforming, you name it, this game's got it all. The lengthy cutscenes tie together the gameplay sections in a rather amusing manner and while they're totally clichéd, the zany, exaggerated B-movie feel fits perfectly into the rest of the game.
Visually, the heaven-and-hell theme runs very strongly throughout the whole game and creates really unique, weird enemies that come in all kinds of shapes and sizes. A special highlight are the gigantic bosses that you fight in ridiculous multi-stage boss fights, each more grandiose than the last. Fights against human bosses on the other hand are much more focused on the core combat experience and lead to really quick fights reminiscent of The Matrix.
For the most part I'm just immensely impressed at how engaging the whole experience is and how unique it is despite combining so many established elements from elsewhere. The setting, the characters, the gameplay, the humorous cutscenes and the confusing but somehow brilliant plot create a very special, highly indulgent and stylish package that just has this certain X-factor that I can't quite put my finger on. It's obvious that the player is not the only one having fun with Bayonetta, the developers were clearly enjoying their time working on it too.

Ok, this game is early access. If you've seen other early access games that stay in this pre-release state for extremely long periods of time like Minecraft or DayZ, you can get an idea of where this game is headed. From what I've seen of the few changelogs that come to Starbound, the developers have no intention to complete this game any time soon. They are stuck in this indefinite time of "Gimme $15 and maybe I'll finish the game someday..."
Due to this incomplete state Starbound is trapped in, there aren't large amounts of things to do, and there are also holes in the gameplay where it seems like a certain function or addition should be available, but it hasn't been implemented. For example, Hylotl villages and dungeons. The Hylotl, a playable race in Starbound, were strangely unique in the fact that there were no villages or dungeons that are Hylotl themed, while every other race has its own form of village or living space. Although these constructions are around now, they were simply hyped for many, many months while the developers consistently and non-officially told us about them. This is simply one example of the shoddy update schedule and unclear idealogy of Starbound as a whole.
Another thing that really peeved me and my friends was the advancement of tiers and the gameplay balance. In Starbound, there are several different "sectors" comprised of a seemingly infinite amount of solar systems with planets in them. You start in the Alpha sector and work your way up, Beta, Gamma, and so on. Each of these sectors has a few different tiers of weapons and armor in an established hierarchy of worst to best made of different materials that you mine up and craft into these tools. It starts of innocently enough, copper, silver, iron and the sort which don't require TOO much of each of them for a full set of armor and a shiny new weapon. However, once you to get to some of the later sectors like Delta and the legendary final "X" sector, the crafting materials are completely unforgiving. You must mine dozens and dozens of one of the new special ores in these late sectors and mine dozens and dozens of ANOTHER ore and combine these both together. Maybe then you'll have a pair of boots. The problem with mining is how agonizingly slow the fastest and best pickaxe in the game, the diamond pickaxe (creativity right there) mines these ores, the ores that are almost crucial you dig up and make into armor so you don't get one-shotted by the average hostile genetic mistakes that inhabit the late-game sectors.
Don't get me wrong, me and my friends had quite a bit of fun for several weeks while playing in the lower sectors, as reflected in my playtime. However, the gameplay balance is almost as broken AND comparable to the endless grinding in many MMOs, which absolutely ruins any fun set by the standards of the lower sectors and turns it into barely scraping by in a corrupted world. According to the blue words above my review, this game is in early access and should be fixed in due time. But the due time could be a couple more years. I'd say Starbound definitely isn't worth the $15 pricetag, $10 is more appropriate, although there are other $10 games that are more worth that money like G-Mod and Terraria. If you're thinking of buying this game, just wait until it goes on sale AND is full release in a few years.

In an attempt to make Ridge Racer more like Need for Speed Underground and the Burnout series Bugbear have created a game devoid of anything remotely interesting, getting neither their strong nor interesting points right. Less than the sum of its parts Ridge Racer Unbounded (aka Ridge Racer in name only) oscillates between a lukewarm 4 and 5 out of 10. It's a perfectly functional game and anything but horrible but I somehow wish it was horrible so it would have a single memorable ingredient.
Everything you'd expect is sort of there; various generic game modes with sports car pastiches. A bit of drifting from NfS Underground, a little bit of Burnout's car combat, a bit of the destructible environments from Split Second, etc. all of it assembled robotically and efficiently without any creativity, passion or talent. Racing-light is the name of the game - less calories, no taste. For a racing game supposedly based on high speed and drifting neither is engaging and fun enough to keep you interested past the ten minute mark, the bland music doesn't help.
Apparently there also used to be an online multiplayer mode that is now non-functioning. Honestly I'd much rather invite my friends to an office meeting than Ridge Racer Unbounded so this point almost works in its favour but you have to admire the audacity of the publishers who really went the extra mile here, I applaud you.
In short, avoid. It's mindboggingly forgettable and generic, so much so my mind already blurs the select few hazy memories I had of playing it with memories of other, better games. A monstrous waste of time.

Yay for Lords of the Fallen. I've mostly bought it because of the art style and the similiarity to Dark Souls. I've first tried DS, but I found it hard to control (on PC, I had no controller then) so even though I like the idea of a harder game, I couldn't play that. And the LoF came and promised similar experiece but more tailored for casuals like me. My review in one sentence: it was totally worth it, so I recommend it to:
- People who like artistic games, good graphics.
- People who always wanted to try DS, but for some reason couldn't play it.
- People who like defeating big monsters in a well crafted fantasy world, be the badass.
Pros:
- Graphics, music, world design, well tailored together This is what I'd call an AAA quality game.
- Every item you find has a an artistic card, story, unique feel, unique look.
- Not as hard as DS, but definitely harder then I've expected.
- Good learning curve and progress, freedom to choose different styles, combine items..
- Very stable, not crashing, runs well on the following config: C2D@3000, 8GB DDR3, Ati HD7770, SSD.
Cons:
- No native support for PS4 controller. This type of game is "written for controller" in my opinion, but when I plugged in my DualShock controler, it was not recognized by the game, nor it had options to choose it. This problem solved with DS4Windows, a freeware program. Now the PS4 controller works superb, the game even translated the vibrations. I've heared XBONE controlers are recognized by default, so this is just a small con.
- Some items are useless. I've never needed a elemental res shard for example. Small runes are also useless, and you cannot do anything with them, they just sit in your pucket.. I'd be happy to see some method to combine them, reuse them or at least have the ability to delete them..
- Small bugs, I've seen like 3-4 environmental bugs, and when you die the 2nd time, your first ghost is lost, you loose the XP from it.
That's it. All in all a good game, and I'm looking forward for the expansions / LoF2. Well done.

Like many of the other reviews I've seen I can say that Fallout 4 did not reach the expectations of the Bethesda community. I tried to hold off on reviewing this game at all, but no more.
Fallout 4 is a sad realisation that Bethesda doesn't care about the quality of gameplay anymore.
- Same old game engine that ran Oblivion a decade ago
- Game mechanics and interface are dumbed down, a lot..
- Not an RPG, it's not so much the voice protagonist for me, but the lack of depth of moral choice, meaning, and such,
plus I saw that dialoge would be hard for mod quests. I'm amazed with the Nora companion mod though, so it's not
impossible but tough.
-Graphics, meshes, and textures are bad, I used to defend the game's graphics, but not anymore, we shouldn't need mods
to completely overhaul Bethesda's games anymore, this is just ridiculous and lazy on Bethesda's part.
-Quests are bad, they have accended into memehood. "Fetch" quests, kill that guy there, you get the point.
-A.I. is bad, Dog Meat walks into things that kill you, we've all seen the videos.
- World feels empty, missing something, too little charaters, small settlements.
- The infamous corrupted saves, disabling acheivments with mods, lagging start menu, stuff like that.
I think my biggest let down when I first played on it's release was the size of the major cities. When I saw the reveal trailer panning these places, like "Diamond city", "Good Neighbor", etc. I thought they would be these massive areas you, as the player, could explore, none of them came close to the sizes of Skyrim's cities, you know, five years before Fallout 4..
They are using the same old engine as stated above. I cannot stress the need for a new engine. This is a triple A game, and it is using the same engine as a game that was released is 2006. It's time for a new one, and yes, this is an important aspect to this review as it shows that Bethesda really doesn't want to spend their resources on a much needed thing.
And now paid mods to top it all off, oh I mean Creation Club... Honestly I see what people try to defend, "modders are finally getting paid for their work," fine, you go ahead, but lets really look into it, they are supposedly paid a flat fee, not commissions. "But then they all get paid, not just the ones that sell," ok so why is it that when a modder is much better than others, his pay out isn't reflecting his preformance? Why are they not recieving both? A cut of the profit? Well maybe that's because Betheda is basically outsourcing their work, and under paying others instead of hiring more employees like they should be doing. We are getting penny pinched, look at how many times they resold Skyrim, look at the season pass problems for Fallout 4, and look at the poor quality dlcs it released. Now this creation club, they just couldn't line their pockets enough on these over sold products... They lied to their community, us. They said they won't be adding paid mods, but they did.

This game is a mixed bag. If you are a pureist and want everything to be perfect it will probably drive you mad. If you don't mind some quirks there is a lot to like here. The detail on the bus models is amazing and the sheer complexity of all the things you can alter and change on the bus is quite overwhelming to begin with. Reading the manual and having a pen and paper handy to make some notes is a must. The attention to detail in the sound is something to behold. After a bit of digging on google I discovered that the destinctive transmission sound was so familiar because the busses that used to transport me to and from school in the UK used the same transmission as the double deckers on OMSI.
Learning the routes takes some time and keeping to the schedule is very hard to do without upsetting the passengers. If you want a real driving challenge this will keep your mind active for a long time. There is just so much to consider all at once. It's very hard not to become flustered at first. Stay with it and you start to become pretty addicted to the challenge of getting that bus there in one piece on time with satisfied passengers. A lot of love has gone into this by the creators who have succeeded and then some IMO of encapsulating a period of history inside a game that brings a great deal of enjoyment to play.

All in all i give the game an 8/10, id like to see more ships added, some more upgrades added for sure and a co-op scenario in the future along with a few balance tweeks.

This is a great game all around. Fun insta-kill action that keeps your palms sweaty. Either use your swift sword or fire you gun at range, but be weary, there is a limit on how fast you can strike with your sword, making it demand precision, and your firearm only has 3 bullets each life which can be deflected with the sword. Absolutely love this game, but let me start some reasons why you might not.
There is a lot of randomness, meaning that if you save then load enough times you can beat anything. Or, if you play Ironman mode, you have to load from the very beginning of the game because of something that happened completely beyond your control. No matter how skilled you are, it's still technically possible for every shot to miss. Unlikely, but bad things do happen. It also means that a perfect playthrough on a level thwarted at the last moment may never even reach that last moment again, because the string of luck that got you that far just never repeats. If this is a deal-breaker for you, don't buy this.
The second thing is the way the continuity works, which for much of my life, I have believed to be just poor game design. It's only as I get older that I've aquired a taste for it. That is, if you play this level well, next level will be easier. If you play this level poorly, next level will be harder. If a game were trying to keep its players engaged and never quit, it should do the opposite, making the game hit that sweet spot between too easy and too hard, but that's not how this works.
This game actively encourages you to quit, but not quit and never play it again, quit and start over. If you keep playing after a number of poorly executed missions, the game will eventually become literally impossible to progress. Though it will never reach literal impossibility, because you'll probably have stopped playing when your chances of winning fall below 1%.
This does mean playing the same levels again, but the amount of randomness the game has means that the levels are never the same way twice. The strategy you used for level 1 the first time may not work, because the enemies aren't standing close enough together for that sweet grenade shot. As far as quitting everything and starting over, I'm on my third play through right now. Some of the DLC missions are very story driven and get a little lame if you play them through a second time, but not much.
Where many games similar to this one fall down, is the ideal strategy of shoot everything that moves, wait an hour, take a step, wait another hour, step again, then something jumps out and kills you because you were advancing too fast. XCOM 2 solves this problem by adding things that will kill you if you advance too slowly, forcing you to decide which middle speed will have you live. Such elements are not there for every level, but they are there for all the good levels.
Another area where games fall down is having lots of variety in weapons, armours, and enemy types, but it being essentailly the same game no matter what, or even worse, a game of memory match, knowing which weapon works against which enemy. EXCOM2's enemies really feel different from each other, as do the classes, and late game armour and weapon choices.
This game has a great modding community, so whatever issue you have with the design of the game, someone has solved it for you. Just ignore the haters who tell you you're messing with game balance and that your victory will be forever tainted when you beat the game. You do you. For me, the essentail mod is "choose my class". That way, when I design myself and my family into the game, I can make them have classes that reflect their personality, instead of having the game tell me that my girlfriend is a specialist computer hacker, because that's how the dice rolled.
Finally, I will say that this is a great game if you have a baby. Not many games allow you to place everything down at a moment's notice then return twenty minutes later. Even if a game does "pause", it doesn't always let you look around and remind yourself what you were in the middle of doing.

Constantly wrestling with the controls removes any enjoyment that could have resulted from strategically deploying varied missile types, invading surrounding neutral regions, and researching new weapon types. The game also suffers from late-game monotony, as previously bombed territory can be reclaimed, resulting in a constantly shifting and annoying game of whack-a-mole. In the end, First Strike: Final Hour does not offer the accessibility to make it an enjoyable strategy game.

I can't even start to tell you what a master piece Half-Life is..... I highly recommend this game for ANYONE! Most modern gamers shy away from Half-Life because of it's 1998 graphics but if you look past that you'll find an amazing experience... You play as Gordon Freeman a scientist working at the Black Mesa facility when an experiment that you're a part of goes terribly wrong and opens up a portal linking Earth and Xen (Zen) from there on, hoardes of alien's invade the place and you're goal is SURVIVING... Game play wise it flows well and I don't have any complaints about the game play EXCEPT their is way to much jumping in this game... This is just a minor complaint I did love the parkour puzzles because they worked in the game flawlessly as you're traveling through the complex.... The parkour PUZZLES were fantastic but navigating through them proved to be a little difficult and taxing at times... But don't overlook this game because of this minor problem because you'll be missing out on an amazing game! I also like Half-Life because it had great interactive story telling... I mean, sure you could just ignore the scientist and fly right through the game but then you would miss out on the extraordinary experience which is really what Half-Life is all about (and be completly lost and confused by the end of it aswell)... Half-Life has a great beginning even though it is a little boring but I loved that first 20 minutes of strolling through the office and talking to you're co-scientist because it gets you involved with the game.... Half-Life has great narrative pacing which you just don't see in games anymore today..... I also loved Half-Life because the enviroments are so detailed... I have played Half-Life three times already and I still keep finding new room's and compartments in Black Mesa that have ammo and health packs in them.... But although the setting and events of the game are entirly fictional, the detail in first person shooter's had never felt so absorbingly real at the time that it was realised..... So we can blame it for every other thing done in the name of "realism" every since.... I'm talking about Call of Duty, Battlefield, and all the other shooter games that now control 80% of the freakin industry today.... Which I don't hate shooters but Half-Life used it for innovation in gaming, shooters today could care less about quality as long as they're stealing your money.... So just to recap Half-Life has an incredible interactive story, fantastic enviroments with impeccable details, and has suprises and jump scares that you won't see coming even if it is you're second or third time playing the game.... Half-Life is only $9.99 on Steam and if you haven't already played it YOU NEED TO! Even if you aren't in to FPS games and especially if you are.

This game is fantastic, one of the best games I have ever played in my life.
The plot and characters in this game develop very effectively, which leads you to truly caring about your characters and making you truly think about the decisions that you are forced to make.

The decisions are not always easy in this game. The tough decisions can be very hard to deal with and will make you think about them further on in the game, especially when some characters confront you about them.
This game has a very unique feature, there are mutliple ways you can play it. Examples are saving certain characters and letting others die and saying certain things to characters which they will remember and will possibly influence a decision they make in the game. This means that your playthrough could be completely different to somebody else's playthrough, and may inspire you to play the game again to change things around a bit.
The graphic style in this game is very unique and creative, instead of following the usual 'realistic graphics', this game chooses to have a comic-book art style due to the fact that it is based on The Walking Dead comic book, and it leaves its own little shine on the game.
The controls in the game are very smooth and fluid, and the same goes for the combat in the game as well. It's never clunky and always provides you with the best experience.
The music in the game is great, it adds further atmosphere to the game and fits the situations perfectly. Sometimes bringing even more emotions into it!
Overall, I couldn't really say anything bad about this game. It is genuinely one of the best games I have ever played and I enjoyed every moment of it, I cried at the end, and this is the only game to have ever done that to me.
Therefore, I highly recommend that you give this game a go!

Here's a simple review for anybody who is unsure about this game:
Good:
-Fluid gameplay and amazingly well-designed atmosphere.
-Wide variety of items and objects within many, many different enviroments, all freely accessable (see next point).
-Detailed background lore and welcome, yet slightly limiting, difficulty progession system.
-Simple yet effective building mechanics.
-Well-made mining/looting/stealing system (based on what you are taking).
-Populated towns and rogue NPC cultists/temple guards/ECT.
-Realistic depictions of planets (moons without oxygen, acid rain, gravity differences, orbiting background planets, ect).
Bad:
-Random difficulty spikes in certain areas/planets.
-No "easy" way to create a multiplayer server.
-Infrequent updates.
-Occasionally generic items (pickaxes, ect).
On The Fence:
-Occasionally conflicting towns with enviroments (happy, healthy villages in desolate wastelands).
Overall, a VERY good game for those with a creative and curious mind, but tiresome for those looking for a story-driven game. YOU make your own story through your actions, and very little is given to you ("you crashed, good luck"), which could be tiresome and irritating for those who prefer to have a deep, interesting story to follow and be enveloped by.
Also, as an obligatory comparison to Terraria:
-Played Terraria for about one hour, got bored and only kept playing due to streaming.
-Played Starbound for fourty hours, still happy to explore and build even on unmodded singleplayer.
Possbily the worst gaming experience I've ever had, looked forward to this for at least a year only to find massive FPS drops and falling thousands of feet through the ground.

I desperately want to like this game. I helped kickstart it, and I was so excited for it all throughout it's development ....right up until the developers went insane. They lost their marbles, like the characters in their game. The game had an overwhelmingly positive response from players during early access, and then the devs decided the game wasn't gruelingly hard and punishing enough, so they made it absolutely insanely difficult at the higher levels. There was a huge player backlash and outpouring of disapproval and disappointment ....and instead of taking that on boardand walking the difficulty back, they argued that this was their vision for the game now. Eventually they enabled the ability to switch off many of the most frustrating, difficult and unnecessary difficulty features but the game is still infuriatingly frustrating at level 5+.
I've seen videos of people smashing their computer after playing this game and I can fully understand why. This is not like Dark Souls where you can master the game eventually, and skill makes all the difference ....no, you are at the complete and utter mercy of the games random number generator, and the numers are all stacked against you steeply. THIS IS NOT FUN.
This is an example of out of control hubris from a developer who won't listen to their fanbase ....they have to have their 'vision' fulfilled ...even if it means sucking all the fun out of the game. This is an enormous shame because the visuals are beautiful, the music is intense and amazing, the atmosphere is perfect ....but the game is just maddening to play at late levels. It's been like this since release and clearly they refuse to change it. I so want to be able to recommend Darkest Dungeon ....but I can't. Not unless you're a total masochist.

I was very indecisive about which account I should put this game on. I think I made the right choice, putting it in my "meh, I dunno about this" account. It pretty much sums up my opinion of it.
I have absolutely no idea where they are going with this thing. When I bought in, I thought I had a good idea about what I was getting, but with constant changes in development, I really just don't know anymore. Sure, developing a game requires changes here and there, but SB is a game that really has no idea what it wants to be ultimately. It doesn't give the buyer much faith if the Devs keep changing their ideas. I can't possibly believe this game to be a "vision" when the vision changes every week.
When I bought in, I was given this picture. Like all other early access games, you are given a gist of what's to come. When that "gist" is deluded with constant backtracking, and slow development, how can one help but to feel left in the dark?
Here recently, there is a lot of talk about "progression". What is being described with this new content is NOT what I was expecting in this game.
This linear progression stuff that is being talked about is fine in some games, but in a game that uses a procedural generated universe as its foundation, I feel the mechanics will collide.
Resources as they are right now serve a very finite use. Once you've made your favorite top tier armor, found your favorite weapons and other gear, the whole value of resources comes to a halt. I would be okay with this if the mechanics change in the future, but it doesn't look like it's going to with this talk about "armor progression". It seems as if they want you to eventually find your favorite armor, favorite weapon, and that's that. Like I said, that's fine in some games, but in a game meant to be "sandbox", it doesn't fit well.
So my question is: Why go procedural? It seems like a lot of pointless work. If I get armor and other items that don't require iron anymore (for example), why have an infinite, procedurally generated universe full of the stuff? To build with? Okay, sure. But building needs to connect to everything else in the game. I don't want to build just for the sake of building. I want to build to store and maintain my value and power in the universe. Not just build and horde items I'll never use again. What about selling this iron? Okay, sure. But if I already got my fav gear, do tell what I'll be buying with this money I'll be making.
Resources need to have a constant tangible and economical value in a game meant to have no true end. In a game like Minecraft, having a procedurally generated world works because ALL resources need to be maintained. Since all materials need to be maintained, it has a constant value to all players at all times. All the mechanics come full circle because of this. In SB, the linear mechanics collide with the non-linear mechanics because it does have this infinite universe with resources, but they will eventually fill their finite use.
Imagine in Minecraft once you've made a certain pickaxe, it never broke, and it never needed to be maintained. What would happen? You would no longer need to look for that material, and that whole massive world holds no value to you anymore. Now I'm not comparing Minecraft to SB as the same game, I'm only comparing the procedural generation mechanic they both share.
I'm not saying weapon degradation needs to be in SB to make it work. I'm just saying it needs something to make this infinite playing field flow smoothly. Otherwise, we are all going to get our top tier armor, our favorite top tier weapon, and run around killing each other for the sake of killing each other.
I want battles that are about power and resource. It's the key motivation for any pvp. You can't blame me for thinking that SB was going to be this. So much features promised, and so many different things planned, I feel that everyone who bought in found something about it they wanted, and they pictured their own little piece of paradise within it. That right there is what was banked on.
Do I recommend this? How can I recommend something that changes it's tune constantly? It's a moving target right now, so no, I can't possibly recommend it. I don't know who it's trying to please in the long run. All I can say is: If you got the money to blow, and you're curious, go for it. If not, just wait and see what it will be when it's considered "finished". Whatever that means anymore.

The game oozes with terrific grimdark lovecraftian atmosphere, with beautiful art, minimalistic yet impactful and vivid animations, great narration.
The people complaining about the randomness in this game don't quite realize how integrally it is designed for both the world building and genre of this style of game, which hasn't been falsely advertising itself as anything else but a roguelite, you get what you bought.
Your role in managing a party with characterbuilding quirks creates quite literally the unique personality of this game, and isn't something you can or should simply "fix", it's purposefully made this way, and if a roguelite with such elements won't suite some then fine, but this game succeeded in making exactly the type of game it was meant to be.
The game's hard and I'll probably never master it, but I still find endless enjoyment and amusement in the chaos and spiralling madness that eventually accumulates to all my poor party members.
All the art, gameplay and general presentation feels extremely well polished, but I have been having some crashing issues  lately that don't seem to be tied to anything specific.

SUMMARY
I'd have a hard time saying that I didn't recommend this game. I think any fans of the Souls games should give it a shot. It's not going to be for those who insist on everything about Dark Souls being the same. This could have easily even been the game that came out before Demon's Souls if FromSoftware had taken a little less time to figure out what they wanted to do - but that's not necessarily a bad thing.
DIFFICULTY
Everyone seems to be complaining about the game being too hard - especially the bosses. I thought this game was a bit easier than the first Dark Souls game. Dark Souls has a couple of hurdles like Capra and Anor Londo... this wasn't too bad. I played as the Cleric class, and ended up shifting into an Agility-based weapon tree. Gargoyle and Hawk was my finishing weapon when I killed the last boss.
LENGTH
For me, this game lasted about as long as I wanted it to. I clocked in around 18-19 hours, counting a little grinding I did towards the end to make sure I was ready for the last boss. For a world like the first Dark Souls with so many different locales, I want to get lost there and live there. This was just a brief trip and that's all it needed to be.
ENVIRONMENT
The environments in this game look great. The problem is that there aren't very many of them. Everything has a bit of a wintery castle vibe, and brick walls tend to look like other brick walls. Nothing is distinct, which makes it a little tricky figuring out where you're going later in the game - at the point where areas begin to connect back to older ones.
AESTHETICS
The music is decent, though the main theme plays throughout the game when there is music, but like Dark Souls, there generally isn't much. The boss and enemy designs are decent, but the same enemies are everywhere - there are maybe 15-20 different types of enemy models total. One could argue that this makes things easier as far as what to expect. Visuals look really good, but sometimes I noticed a weird effect that made parts of the game look as though it was trying to display in 3D. Probably just a weird coloring effect seen at times.
STABILITY
I actually found the game to be fairly stable. I think it had crashed on me once or twice through my entire playthrough. The only thing I know for sure is that the Nvidia Effects setting (or whatever it is) isn't really great for the game (and I'm using a 970). I was usually running at around 60fps, but sometimes it would dip into the 40s in a couple areas. It didn't hinder combat or anything too much though.
COMBAT
Combat is pretty good - my only complaint is that it seemed a lot of the time that I was being knocked over or staggered quite often, even when I was blocking successfully. Maybe it was something that I missed, but I found that to be a bit annoying. The unfortunate thing about combat generally is that it's fairly slow - weapons have varying speeds that they'll swing at - some are 75% attack speed and others are faster. The only difference is that slower weapons are usually heavier and will do more damage, etc. However, using a slow heavy weapon has the potential to leave you wide open to getting hit - and if you're like me (or maybe just not wearing heavy armor, that means you're going to be on the ground quite a bit.)
BOTTOM LINE
I would say to wait for a sale for this game. I picked it up at $25 and I'm content with my purchase, so I'd recommend something like that. I'd love to see a sequel because I'm sure this was a learning experience for the Devs, but we'll see what happens. Don't ignore this game just because others are giving it a bad rap though, it's worth experiencing at least once.
