Those are all horrible nerfs they made, but I could have handled that, though I would have severly disliked it, but making it so you have to use REAL MONEY to progress at all did me in, let me explain in FULL detail why this is so horrible. I speak for the new people and people with a small amunt of classes bought before the update. There will no longer be any diversity in trove, everyone will find the best starter class, and EVERYONE will go with the same class. Not only that, but they only get 2(!) class coins free (Trion says you get 3 free, but you have to BUY something with real money before you get the "free" class). Then you can get Chloromancer free by putting some time into Rift which is annoying that you need another game to get a class... Then referral links, which, as most more exierenced trove players know, isn't a fun task to take up. After that, they have to use real money, or grind for weeks to buy one class coin on the market (for mid to late game player, maybe a week). On top of that, You basically have to PAY for MASTERY being as classes were a main source of mastery levels. Most people won't play trove long enough to get much interest because it is now SO RESTRICTIVE once they get there starter class to level 20 they will get bored. But wait, There is more! With this one time offer of a crappy pay to win game, we give you a gurantee that there will be new classes which you can't touch unless you spend $19.99. With that said, no matter what I do, even if I owned EVERY. SINGLE. CLASS... I would have still used all my class coins, and then couldn't unlock any of the new classes unless I paid money. So not only has this update hindered new players, but also late gamers.
For people looking to get Trove now, this is what this update basically means for you. You no longer have the availability to get other classes, allowing you to try out new classes, so on so forth. You can't make a single mistake with what class you choose, because if you figure out you don't like that one class, you don't get any chance to redeem yourself, in other words, you are screwed, so if you are looking into new classes, wait a while and figure out what each class does before getting it, becuse you only get two free chances now to choose out of 10+ classes that used to be available for free. You are going to have to grind for a MUCH LONGER time than you used to, to get the mastery and things you need to have to do well, you will now have to spend a much longer time grinding and doing nothing else in order to be able to enjoy the game later... and I mean months. So ya, trove is all in all ruined.... It saddens my heart to see such a good game go down the path of "Pay To Win".

This game is... in a word, beautiful. If I'm honest, I'm a little at a loss for words here. The soundtrack is simply perfect, the levels, characters, just the art in general is astounding, the narration is unique and well voiced... hell, even the story is a neat idea.
I walked into this game expecting something decent-to-fun. I eventually managed to walk out with one of - perhaps the - best indie game I have played to date.
It's one player, but my word it's the best one player experience I've had yet and I'm probably not even a third through it.

The slow-mo crashes look cool, especially since just about everything short of entire buildings is destructable. That's where the positive stuff ends.
For one, when you start the game it's immediately obvious that PC wasn't the lead platform. The options that you can change are minimal, so you won't be able to get rid of the disgusting instagram filters and nauseating overused bloom effects that make the entire game look like a trashy CoD killstreak montage video. And that's just one of the game's smaller problems. The physics are horrifying, and I don't say that from the perspective of some elitist sim-only race enthusiast; I LOVE arcade racers, and the games that Bugbear made before this one (Flatout 1 and 2) were both tons of fun. Ridge Racer has always been about speed and control, but something is definitely off with the handling model here. Cars feel like absolute tanks when you're driving in a straight line, but initiate a drift and suddenly your car will feel as weightless as a paper airplane. I know that's kind of how drifts are supposed to feel (in a very VERY simplified, vague sense), but it shouldn't be that exaggerated in ANY game. On top of that, in the time that it takes to get used to the handling model, you'll realize that you've seen just about every game mode that Ridge Racer Unbounded has to offer. It's extremely repetitive. I've re-installed this game on 3 or 4 separate occasions, and I've really tried to give it a second chance more than once. I'm disappointed every time.
Save your money. Bugbear's older games from the Flatout series are fantastic, and their new game Wreckfest (Next Car Game) is a little more on the realistic side but it's more fun than this. I'd skip RR:U if I were you.

So accessing other user's content and the majority of online services are gone. What's left of it is a mediocre racing game having little of the charm of either Flatout or Ridge Racer. Yes, stuff blows up and Yes, there's super exaggerated drifting. A clear connection is drawn to RidgeRacer and Bugbear, but sadly, the drift mechanics feel weak and are poorly implemented compared to other RR games. As for the destruction, it comes off as canned and grows largely unimpressive as believeability escapes with the game choosing what can and cannot be taken apart. That and the cookie cutter maps and environment start running together and weren't that great looking in the first place.
As it is, it should be in an arcade cabinet at Chuckee Cheese. If you're looking for an arcade racer to really stay with, I'd pick up almost anything else. If it's priced at like a dollar and you're only expecting that much out of it, you wont be as disapointed.

I was really looking forward to this game, because I really like the Dark Souls style of games and combat, but rarely you see combat that's like that. So most likely I am biased towards a game like this.
The combat is rather similar to Dark Souls, especially when it comes to melee weapons, but there are still differences. The melee combat felt as satisfying to me as in Dark Souls, so I would say it was pretty good.
A big difference would be that there are no changeable ranged weapons. You only get your gauntlet near the start of the game and that's it. The gauntlet functions as a mix of a ranged weapon and also spell weapon as it drains your mana and isn't just simple projectile shooter weapon like a bow would be. It has 3 different modes, that are quite different from each other, and later on in the game you'll get the ability to further customize and change how the gauntlet works in each of the modes. Meaning that you aren't just changing the stats of the weapon, but rather you are changing what the projectiles do. (e.g. making a projectile attrack enemy attention, drain life, knockback enemies, etc.)
On the other hand there is a lot of melee weapons, but as you soon find out (especially after you get to socket runes into them), many of them are obsolete compared to other weapons. The only redeeming factor for the weapons might be their moveset, which can matter a lot to some people, but to me it wasn't enough of a tradeoff when I could be doing significantly more damage with the other weapon. So in the end I was finding that I had at max 4 viable weapons for myself when I played with a really heavily str focused build.
Another significant difference is that there is no way to be a mage like you could be in other games. There are no spells that do damage on their own, rather they usually support your combat skills or weaken the enemy, etc. The gauntlet might be able to compensate for that, but I'm not sure it would be enough. Especially because when the few times I tried how viable it would be to use it on its own, I found out that the shots consume too much mana and don't deal enough damage. This however might not be such a bad thing, because at least from my experience fighting ranged or with spells in a souls game (in pve at least) makes the game much more easier and less fun because you no longer have to get up close and have to be so careful when you attack near them because they could countera-attack you.
One thing I really missed though is the lack of PvP. Fighting others can be pretty fun in a game like this and it can create a lot of tension if you have a lot of souls on you at the time, but nothing like that can be found in this game. It was probably a conscious choice on the dev's part, but I think it could be more fun with it.
I noticed a really big problem with the armors in this game. Later in the game when I had a decent amount of strength, I could equip the best and heaviest armor without any penalty and it made the game far too easy in my experience. Bosses were still difficult, but normal enemies did between 1/5th and 1/10th of what they did to me before, which was such a big decreese in damage that I stopped caring about getting damaged, because I could do that without being punished (even if I got hit). Not sure if this is a problem with how much points I put into strength or what, but it made the game less enjoyable and too easy in my experience.
The enemies looked interesting at first, but after a while I got bored of the Rhogar all looking the same and being pretty much the only enemies with few exceptions. The enemy variety got better near the end of the game with new enemies being introduced, so I wouldn't say it was that bad overall.
The cast of enemies certainly had some interesting enemies, for example the most fragile enemy can't see, so you can easily avoid them if you want to or ambush them.
I think the bosses were great, much better than in pretty much any game including Dark Souls. Many of them had interesting mechanics tied to them or were somewhat different depending on how much health they had and apart from 1 bossfight you never had to fight multi-boss bossfight. And even that bossfight wasn't that bad because every once in a while one of them removed themselves from the fight, so you had to deal with only one of them at a time most of the time.
Overall most melee enemies had big sweeping attacks that can also easily turn around or hit you when you are behind enemies, so you had to either roll to dodge or block, which I found a bit dissapointing, because I like being able to dodge enemies just with the right positioning and movement, but that wasn't possible.
The story seemed interesting, but I didn't pay that much mind to it and I think I missed important parts of it, so can't give a good opinion on it.
One thing I really didn't like on the story though is how one big important choice was presented in the game. It was rather contrived and felt forced, because how the choice was made, made it look like it's just a choice for how to use something given to you, that doesn't even affect how you will be able to use it after you select one of the choices, and yet it seems that choice chooses which one of the 3 endings you'll get.
The way it was given to you was more direct way than in Dark Souls. There are many cutscenes and conversations with characters, but also part of the story is conveyed through the environment and through scrolls that you pick up.
I found the setting interesting and I wouldn't mind exploring it more. Unfortunately, the game forced you to revisit old areas with new enemies, especially at the end of the game, instead of new areas, which was kinda dissapointing, because I wouldn't mind exploring more areas.
None of the areas came out as cohersive wholes and even though some of them looked rather nice, it often felt like they made a nice area and then randomly placed random minions there. Dark Souls in comparison has areas that have enemies in them that make sense for the areas, for example a lower area of one of the earlier areas you find yourself in is full of old houses that seem abandoned and damaged and the enemies in the area are lightly armored enemies with daggers that try to ambush you and work in groups.
I think the game is really good, especially if you like the way Dark Souls combat works, but note that the game is much shorter than Dark Souls and besides the combat it's not like Dark Souls and if you don't mind that then I would recommend it.

Absolutely love this game, but let me start some reasons why you might not.
There is a lot of randomness, meaning that if you save then load enough times you can beat anything. Or, if you play Ironman mode, you have to load from the very beginning of the game because of something that happened completely beyond your control. No matter how skilled you are, it's still technically possible for every shot to miss. Unlikely, but bad things do happen. It also means that a perfect playthrough on a level thwarted at the last moment may never even reach that last moment again, because the string of luck that got you that far just never repeats. If this is a deal-breaker for you, don't buy this.
The second thing is the way the continuity works, which for much of my life, I have believed to be just poor game design. It's only as I get older that I've aquired a taste for it. That is, if you play this level well, next level will be easier. If you play this level poorly, next level will be harder. If a game were trying to keep its players engaged and never quit, it should do the opposite, making the game hit that sweet spot between too easy and too hard, but that's not how this works.
This game actively encourages you to quit, but not quit and never play it again, quit and start over. If you keep playing after a number of poorly executed missions, the game will eventually become literally impossible to progress. Though it will never reach literal impossibility, because you'll probably have stopped playing when your chances of winning fall below 1%.
This does mean playing the same levels again, but the amount of randomness the game has means that the levels are never the same way twice. The strategy you used for level 1 the first time may not work, because the enemies aren't standing close enough together for that sweet grenade shot. As far as quitting everything and starting over, I'm on my third play through right now. Some of the DLC missions are very story driven and get a little lame if you play them through a second time, but not much.
Where many games similar to this one fall down, is the ideal strategy of shoot everything that moves, wait an hour, take a step, wait another hour, step again, then something jumps out and kills you because you were advancing too fast. XCOM 2 solves this problem by adding things that will kill you if you advance too slowly, forcing you to decide which middle speed will have you live. Such elements are not there for every level, but they are there for all the good levels.
Another area where games fall down is having lots of variety in weapons, armours, and enemy types, but it being essentailly the same game no matter what, or even worse, a game of memory match, knowing which weapon works against which enemy. EXCOM2's enemies really feel different from each other, as do the classes, and late game armour and weapon choices.
This game has a great modding community, so whatever issue you have with the design of the game, someone has solved it for you. Just ignore the haters who tell you you're messing with game balance and that your victory will be forever tainted when you beat the game. You do you. For me, the essentail mod is "choose my class". That way, when I design myself and my family into the game, I can make them have classes that reflect their personality, instead of having the game tell me that my girlfriend is a specialist computer hacker, because that's how the dice rolled.
Finally, I will say that this is a great game if you have a baby. Not many games allow you to place everything down at a moment's notice then return twenty minutes later. Even if a game does "pause", it doesn't always let you look around and remind yourself what you were in the middle of doing.

The Walking Dead A Telltale Games Series
Story
The story is very much the same as the popular TV show on AMC a zombie apocalypse has broken out and you must survive with your group. You play as Lee Everatt a convicted criminal on his way to prison at the beginning of the game but when the police officer driving you there crashes into a walker and crashes his car with you in the back seat you must find help to survive this hell you have just woken up to. This is a game that must be played for the story this truly is a masterpiece of story telling and deserves to be one of the best stories in gaming which I believe it to be so, with twists and turns, deaths and chaos you must protect a little girl called Clementine from this hellish nightmare of a world. There is much more I could talk about but this is a game that must be played for the story so I will not include any spoilers in this review.
Gameplay
The Walking Dead is a point and click Adventure game with many choices and dialog options along the way the game remembers your choices and dialog and the characters will constantly mention the decisions you have made for example if you have an argument or a fight with another character they will mention it at a later stage in the game or in the later episodes. Otherwise this is not really a game this is more like an interactive movie so honestly this is a more chilled out game than anything else but can be intense at some points. There are also puzzle sections where you will use your brain rather than your brawn also nth puzzles aren't too difficult they just take some common sense to complete.
Graphics
The graphics in The Walking Dead are Ok they are something that a gamer with a starter graphics card can run easily I have a starter one and there were no lag spikes or anything just clean perfromance.
Final Verdict
The Walking Dead has one of the best stories in the media and not just gaming is 12 hours long and is a relaxing point and click game to have a calm down for when YOU GET DERANKED FROM SILVER IV TO SILVER III IN CS:GO got damnit anyway if you want a game to actually properly play then this is not the game for you but if you enjoy a heart warming and phenomenal story then you must play this ga... uhh interactive movie.

It does feature some other types of modes where you have to drift and gain points with a time limit ticking, and another where you drive a truck, although both are seldom. The car also functions unintuitively and could get frustrating.

The graphics in
are clean and beautiful, but certain models could glitch, especially the cars when they suffer damage. The interface and the overall design while driving is only slightly reminiscent to previous Ridge Racer games, but mostly inspired by other games.

Ok so after playing Trove for a while I have decided to make a review about why I think this game is no longer a good MMO. First of all, I'd like to say that the game is a good game, for a time at least, and I enjoyed the time that I played it, mostly because I found a very nice club with a good community (Trashbins, cheers to you m8s). However after leaving it I just couldnt find anything that made me want to come back. Here a few pros/cons I found:
PROS:
-COSMETICS. Tons of thems. New community generated cosmetics to gear, weapons, hats are added to the game. This gives you the chance to stand out, even if just a bit.
-CHALLENGES. Probably one of the most controvertial aspects of this game. For me it was one of the best and at the same time one of the worst things. On the pro part of it, it allows tons of players to participate in massive groups to clear dungeons in order to rack up point and win crates, which were filled with either in-game currency or items.
-CORNERSTONES/CLUB WORLDS. This is something that I haven't seen done this well in many games. The ability to create your house that can be easily shown to anyone is amazing. It felt really great to build your floating castle over a pirate ship and have people compliment on it. And club worlds allow you and friends to build freely with a nice variety of blocks and placeable items. Also club worlds where easy to join, access and manage, and was easily what I most enjoyed out of this game.
-ACTIVITIES. Theres a lot to do in this game. Fishing, crafting, leveling, gardening, hunting recipes, recently added pvp, and more.
-FORGING. upgrading gear was done pretty nicely in this game. Getting the stats you wanted on a piece of gear and getting it up to radiant felt rewarding and satisfying.
BIOMES- The world is divided into different levels which required you to be a certain lvl to access them (though this could be easily bypassed with invites, changing to a different class, joining a friend) and has a fairly diverse and unique selection of themed biomes.

CONS:
-REPETITIVE. This game is a grind, theres no way to argue that. You'll spend hours upon hours repeting the same activity with no real rewards other than allowing you to progress a bit so you can grind some more. Almost every activity on this game revolves around doing it over and over again.
-MOUNTS/PETS. While there are many mounts and pets to be collected, most of them offer no help ad the stats or boost they provided are clearly not as usefull as the select few ones who everyone uses. In addition, many of these are just reskinned copies.
-MASTERY. The mastery system rewards you for doing different activities, but punishes you if you do not want to do something, as it reaches a point where if you dont level up every single skill you wont be able to reach higher mastery levels. Its either that or spend money in the cash shop to buy shop exclusive items which grant some mastery points (as does doing mostly anything in this game) Basically the main point of the game is to raise this. For some people this is a good system, for others is not, just a matter of preference.
-CHALLENGES. while very enjoyable, can get very repetitive and ruined if people decide to play hero and clear dungeons next to you alone. You will feel left behind if you don't collect all the Legendary dragons spirits, as these grant pretty big bonuses but required a lot of time to acquire (which in itself is not a bad thing, until they add the next one, which makes obtaining the other ones harder and/or more expensive)
-MOBS. ♥♥♥♥ing punchbots. While there are many biomes, there arent as many diferent mobs. They may look different but essencially attack the same way as their other-biome counterparts. Same goes for bosses.
-DUNGEONS. With the exclusion of the Shadow Tower Bosses, the normal dungeon bosses feel like bigger mobs with more hp and damage. The dungeon layouts are generic and get old really fast, and can be rendered useless due to enviromental destruction.
-CLASSES. Theres a good number of them. Sadly unbalanced and only a few good ones. while theres some capable of playing a "role" (not that it matters much in this game) others are just not viable in almost any situation.
-COMBAT. There may be different classes but combat is pretty much the same, each class with some basic abilities and no skill progression whatsoever. Its fast paced but oversimplified.
-CRAFTING. Theres a lot you can craft but so little of it you will use. Many crafting categories (or skills) are wasted potential, as they could be used to make more relevant crafting materials (that were actually cheaper to make), potions, enhancement, etc. Youll spend your time leveling up skills that you will never use, just so that you can raise your mastery a little. A good part of it is due to RNGsus (all praise be to him) the random number generator that destroys wallets in this game. You can open a 100 crates and get a single good thing from them, specially ring boxes, or you could open 10 and get 2 good items (which is extremely rare).
-CASH SHOP. The cash shop is slowly turning more into a p2w formula, with classes getting locked unless you pay to unlock them (before you could buy them with currency obtainable ingame) and items and cosmetics giving you either a boost in combat or a mastery rank boost makes the game unbalanced.
-CONTENT. Lastly there's no real story to this game aside from some cutscene slapped into the game a few months ago. there are tons of activities that don't really fit together and feel like they were just thrown in there for the sake of quantity. Theres no real goal in the game aside from raising the Mastery level, unless you are into building stuff, which there are better games that offer better ways to do that.
Overall Trove is a fun game that has enough to get your attention, but little to keep you from leaving, sadly the developers are taking the game in a direction that favors those who pay and penalises those who cant play for extended periods of time.

Trove is a quick switch class-based MMORPG. There are 12+ classes. It differs from the classic Healer/Tank/DPS as it is a basic 2x2 split of ranged vs melee, with the option of ranged characters being physical(bows) or magical(magicks). Some classes are tankier, Revenant being the obvious tank(Damage based on HP), but there is no designated healer.
You receive one class when you start, and you unlock 2 more free by simply leveling up. Others can be purchased through the MTX store, or through the auction house form other players.
Gameplay is very well explained in the tutorial that forces you to learn the game. You learn pretty quickly that you will be running a lot of “Dungeons” that are more like quick, open, multi-user, boss fights. There is no party system, so everybody standing in the dungeon when the boss dies receives experience and everyone standing near the chest when it is broken open receives loot.
Combat is very base. 4 attacks tied to M1, M2, 1, and 2. M1 is your basic attack. M2 and 1 are more powerful, have varying effects, and use a varying amount of “Energy”, 2 is your ultimate with varying cooldowns based on class( ~30s to ~75s I believe). Combat itself is very fast paced, but the new balancing changes have helped. Still, normal boss fights take less than 10s with 2 DPS characters. The “Raid” of Trove is the 4 tiered Shadow Tower, raid bosses take up to 2 minutes with a poorly geared 2-man party. The max players you can have in each instance of Shadow Tower is eight players.
All in all, it’s a great game to play with your buddies. Combat is quick, there are plenty of perks for logging in for half an hour or so each day, so it’s a great game to use to take a small break from your other games. Trove is also nice if you don’t have lots of time to grind out raid dungeons/etc.
I highly recommend playing this game.
Edit 2/11/16:
Those worried about the “Heart Attack” update, it was just balancing changes and a slight imposition of the MTX store. You still get 4 classes for free, and can easily get enough Flux (in-game money) to buy the tokens from the auction house. Yes, it’s sad you can’t farm all of the classes now, but you aren't paying for this game. It is FREE. If you enjoy playing it, you can spend a few bucks to unlock all the classes. A LOT of the stuff in the MTX store is purely cosmetic, and the majority of people have purchased things from the MTX store.
No, characters were not “Super nerfed”. I have been playing MMO’s for upwards of 10 years. The characters were balanced. Trove is headed in the right direction with their character/NPC updates. I’m looking forward to the future with Trove. Classes were balanced.
Edit 2/17/16:
Dragon coin update. Hurt my feelings, but it actually isn't a terrible update. Just balanced out the soul getting, and gave us all something more to throw cubits at. I'm pleased, though, pleasantly farming for coins, for hours.

I really like this game.  As many have said, it borrows from Dark Souls, but that's not to say it's merely a copycat.  It also has tinges of Darksiders!  At any rate, it improves upon the Dark Souls model quite a bit, having more frequent checkpointing and slightly more forgiving combat makes it more playable and less punishing, but still a decent challenge.  Graphics with everything turned up are absolutely stunning, but demanding.  Enemy designs and environs are wonderfully dark, brooding and awesome.
This world is alive with weather, fire, debris, flickering lights and billowing banners.  You also will interact with various NPCs that offer a decent amount of interactivity and depth.  It has more than just incidental music (although it's mostly just ambient background sound except during important events)... there are trips to a shadowy netherworld which are really quite atmospheric...  The voice acting is decent and the sound effects are bone-crushingly appropriate, as well as offering audible cues for various events (such as locking onto enemies, magic regeneration, etc.)
Controls are tight, fluid and easy to use (gamepad!).  Occasionally you will have camera issues in tight spaces, but this is pretty standard for games of this type.
The game also constantly rewards you with new equipment and upgrades, which helps keep you interested.  This game offers both stick and carrot, challenge and reward.
Graphics: 5/5
Sound: 5/5
Fun: 5/5
Highly recommended whether you liked Dark Souls or not.  It's a worthy melee-focused action-RPG.

Overall, Lords of the Fallen seems to be a lesser version of Dark Souls with a couple interesting twists, good graphics and could potentially scratch that DS itch; however, there's one major flaw that ruins everything: the shaky/bobbing camera.
Now, having some camera movement while running happens in some 3rd person games, but Lords of the Fallen is like the San Francisco Earthquake of 1906 simulator. There's a significant amount of movement and disorientating bobbing  when doing anything such as walking, running, rolling or attacking. I never get motion sickness, but this effect was immediately nauseating and gave me a headache. Unfortunately, there's no way to disable this, so if this sounds like it would potentially be an issue for you, then avoid. If not...
...I otherwise like the game and would recommend it if you're looking for a Souls-like experience. Sure, Lords of the Fallen has stupid, cliched anti-hero dialog, sports overused audio logs (they're "scrolls" in this game) and the areas (at least initially) are a little claustrophobic for my taste, but there's a lot the game does well. Combat (camera shakiness aside) is very kinetic, heavy and clunky (in a good, realistic way, not a mechanically broken way). Weapons take a bit to swing, each weapon has its own moveset, melee takes a greater importance whereas magic is more supportive, sparks fly when you block with your shield, and everything about it feels very satisfying. Graphics are very crisp and there's a lot of detail in the environments. Bosses have stages to them, so you're constantly adjusting your strategy to new attacks they reveal as their health depletes, keeping the battle fresh and tense. In terms of difficulty, the game is hard with things like ambushes, enemies around corners, etc., but it's not nearly as unforgiving as Dark Souls. An enemy may take 1/8th-1/10th your health per hit instead of potentially killing you in 1 or 2. Lords of the Fallen also introduces an interesting risk/reward system where you have a constantly building XP multiplier as you play. The more hits you land and enemies you kill, the higher this multiplier gets. If you get to a checkpoint, their version of a bonfire, and decide to bank your XP into either magic or stat points, it resets the XP multiplier. At each checkpoint you'll have to make the choice between playing it safe or getting greedy and I quite enjoy this element.
In all, Lords of the Fallen feels like the Go Bots to Dark Souls' Transformers and would be an enjoyable (though obviously lesser) experience if not for that damn shaky camera.
Also of note, it seems like the game is significantly more stable now than it was on release, but during my first NPC encounter I was presented with dialog options to select from, however the game didn't recognize any of my controller inputs, preventing me from making a selection and continuing the game. Restarting my machine fixed this problem and I haven't encountered any issues since, but given the game's historical issues, this wasn't very comforting.

Once you start playing, It'll be hard to get out! It's a very fun and addicting game, allowing you to talk to whoever you want, and farm whatever you want. It has many choices and I definitely recommend playing this game!

Let me start off by saying that Lords of the Fallen is a great game.

Now, there are a couple important points I'd like to make, first regarding the claims of extreme game-breaking bugs and the second to its comparison to the Dark Souls franchise.

Zum Release gibt es auch ein aktuelles Review.
Fractured Space ist keine 0815-Kost. Der Anfang wirkt chaotisch und unfair. Das liegt mehr oder minder daran, dass die meisten Schiffe spezielle Rollen erfüllen. Fast noch spezieller als in jedem anderen MOBA. Beginnt man mit dem Spiel, denkt man anfangs von seiner Brücke aus, später fängt man (wenn man die anderen Schiffe kennenlernt) an im Teamrahmen zu denken. Dann wird es richtig interessant, aber streckenweise auch etwas frustrierend (wenn das eigene Teamplay nicht so wirklich funktionieren will).
Für Solospieler und lonely wolves ist das Spiel nicht geeignet. Für Casualplayer die ihr eigenes Killbedürfnis auch mal hinter Teaminteressen zurückstellen können schon eher.
Spielst du mit Freunden? Umso besser! Da es noch keine Ingamevoice-Möglichkeit gibt, bleibt nur der 90iger-Jahre Chat. Das ist definitv nicht zeitgemäß, aber sofern ich die Devs richtig einschätze - und ich habe das Spiel schon eine ganze Ecke - wird das auch noch kommen. Dann eben Curse, oder TS oder wie sie nicht alle heißen :)
Fractured Space hat eine steile Lernkurve, sofern man denn will. Auch ist es eines von wenigen Spielen heutzutage, bei dem es Sinn macht Guides und Tipps von erfahrenen Spielern zu lesen. Es ist ein kleines Microuniversum. Genauso wie Schach. Nur eben bunter und bombastischer.
Grafik wird durch die aktuelle Unreal Engine auf die Monitore gezaubert. Auch wenn ich kein Fan der UE4 mit ihrem fürchterlichen AntiAliasing bin, so knallt und explodiert es überall ziemlich farbenfroh. Da gibt es kaum etwas zu beanstanden.
Der Sound ist ein eigenes Kaliber. Jede Waffe, jede Fähigkeit, jede Tätigkeit hat ihren eigenen einzigartigen Sound und erhöht deutlich die Athmospähre. Es besteht für mich kein Zweifel, dass (wenn die Spieler so wollen) FS ein ordentliches Zeichen im E-Sport setzen kann.
Thema Pay2Win:
Sofern man Echtgeldkäufe für Schiffe (die nicht besser oder schlechter sind als die Starterships), die man problemlos (4-6 Spiele für die ersten) auch für Ingamewährung kaufen kann als p2w bezeichnen möchte, dann ist es das. Einen Vorteil erhält man dadurch nicht. Fractured Space lebt vor allem von der richtigen Einschätzung der Situation. Wer meint ein teures Schiff kaufen zu können und damit newbs wegzubocken, findet sich schneller auf dem Respawnscreen wieder als einem lieb sein mag.
ES GIBT KEIN P2W in Fractured Space.
TL:DR
Downloaden und ein paar Tage spielen. Nicht von der steilen Lernkurve abschrecken lassen. Es lohnt sich! So etwas gibt es nämlich nicht noch einmal.

Why Do Current Games Have so Much RNG
==============================
Seriously, why does EVERYTHING have to be subject to a ♥♥♥♥ing die roll?
Laziness that's why. Developers are too cheap/lazy to code a decent AI so the only way they hold the player back is by making everything randomized. Setup the perfect ambush? Five squad members, all on overwatch and they all miss one guy coming through a door. That's simply not a rational game, It's not as bad as the arguably-worst-game-of-the-century XCOM, but it's not that much better. This isn't a strategy game it's a slot-machine.
Just reload if the rolls don't go your way.
There's a ton of other stuff wrong with the game, but for me that's the biggie.
(just for completeness here's some other broken stuff)
- % chance to hit is totally inaccurate in any case. Anything less than 50% is a guaranteed miss
- Alien cover bonus is broken in that they always receive their cover bonus even when flanked.
- Lack of options at the strategic level, it may look like you have a choice, but you really don't. This leads to poor replayability because each game follows exactly the same pattern.
- Some start positions are effectively unplayable.
- Timed missions. Especially since each mission counts for so much and soldiers are out for so long when wounded,
- Poor balancing. Game goes easy at the start then right to impossible and then to brain-dead-monkey easy as soon as you get decent upgrades.
- Hidden/opaque game mechanics.
- Cut-scenes. Just why? They add nothing.

I dont understand the criticism about this game, it's been running like butter on my system. Which, granted is a GTX 970 and i74770k which is quite a bit higer end. But regardless of the technical issues people have been claiming about and I have no doubt that they're there. But the game itself is in my opinion great. It alters the traditional formula that ubisoft has been employing for years making it a refreshing new expierience. One example is the combat, it's now at least somewhat difficult. There were a couple times where I died and not due to ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t reasons. This is refreshing for assassin's creed, seeing as for the past numerous games the auto "counter" was essentially the kill button. They altered the way you approach assassinations too, more like a puzzle analyzing your envrioment careful to take out a target, I also like how there's numerous ways to assassinate different targets. The emphasis on the assassination, and this new planning mechanic towards your meaningful assassinations are rewarding. Perching up on a rooftop plotting your entrance, how you'll assassinate the target and planning your escape route, then seeing it all come together is satisfying. XCOM 2 is the best turn-based strategy game of all time, period. It takes everything you enjoyed about XCOM: Enemy Unknown, cranks the tension up to 11, pushes your back against the wall, pits you against an overwhelming and massively advanced enemy force, and says "Good luck, kiddo." * Gorgeous visuals and effects, with significant improvements from Enemy Unknown
* Tense, polished turn based strategy gameplay
* Unbelievably extensive soldier customization
* New mechanics, such as stealth and free reloads
* Interesting, if predictable plot
* Solid voice acting, both by story characters and your soldiers
* New and fun abilities, such as Slash (my personal favorite)
* Significantly harder than Enemy Unknown, but fair
* Some performance issues, especially with anti-aliasing
* Minor but annoying bugs, mostly dealing with the action camera
* Timer mechanics - these usually aren't a big deal and can be dealt with fairly easily, but could have been used less frequently
* Multiplayer feels tacked-on and can be ignored

I don't normally review games, but I couldn't hold my tongue.
I've been following Assassin's Creed since the first game all those years ago, and have enjoyed each and every following installment in their own right. Last year's Black Flag was an unexpected change from rooftop crawling, but it was fantastic. With Unity, there are some strong points: the game looks stunning (when it isn't glitching and stuttering), and the co-op is refreshing (when it isn't glitching and stuttering). I even like what bits of the story I've played so far (which is why I play these games in the first place).
That being said, this review is less for the actual game and more for the company which made it.
I cannot believe in my right mind that Ubisoft didn't know it would release like this. From the "review embargo" to the microtransactions, what they have done with Unity is completely unacceptable. It looks as though they were trying to supress bad reviews of the game in order to make as much money as they could before the obvious performance issues came to light. This was an incomplete game and a game which required much better porting than what we were given. I've never felt like I was playing a simulation while in the Animus before, but now it feels exactly that, and between the stutters and the random framerate dips, it is like playing a laggy MMO when your ping is too high.
Guards glitch in combat. You're at full health and all of a sudden the guard transports across the screen and your dead. Player character falling through holes in the world. Borderless windowed mode does not work. As the other reviews will tell you, the list goes on.
On a bit of the stranger side, my game crashed early on after stuttering and framerate dips and a whole plethora of other problems, only to reboot and have no stutter whatsoever. The game has been fairly stable since then, but I'll be knocking on wood after posting this review. I have literally no idea how or what caused this to happen.
So, would I recommend this game?
Not in its current state. I'm glad to see Ubisoft is taking fire for this, but I'm hoping there will be a patch soon which will fix this issue. I meet the hardware requirements good and well. Like many of the reviews are saying, it has nothing to do with not meeting hardware specs.
It's just a horrendous and lazy port.

I love this game. It's utterly captivating. Each decision you make, at any time during the game, is irreversible. Yet this is what I find oddly relaxing about the game. There is no save-scumming, no reloading, no worrying about whether you could do this one fight better if you replayed it. That decision is out of your hands and this makes the game much more relaxing to play for me than other rogue-likes (or rogue-like-lights?) that allow you to go back and replay a situation a hundred times until you get it "right".
There is no ideal run in Darkest Dungeon, the merciless RNG makes sure of that. Sometimes, you just lose, you have to retreat to save what you can (be it loot or lives). Bad things happen and sometimes you just have to accept them. Learn from your mistakes, adjust your strategy and rejoice as you kick the obstacle that hurt you the first into the dust. The mechanics make for a very satisfying gameplay if you're up to investing some time into learning how the game works.
Sadly, the game doesn't help you a lot in the learning department. If I have one critique of the game it's that the interface could be improved. There could be more, or just more expansive tool tips. A lot of your heroes skills are very badly explained or not at all. For example, mousing over the Arbelest's "Flare" ability doesn't tell you that it benefits your entire party whenever you use, not just a single target. Neither does the game tell you that the Houndmaster's "Howl" can affect your entire party (the game choses 0-4 targets to heal randomly).
Lack of information like this made me not equip and try out a lot of actually very useful skills because I assumed them to be single-target which would have made them too ineffective to waist a slot on. Even a hint somewhere in the tutorial that some abilities can affect the entire party even if it isn't spelled out in the tool-tip might have gotten me to just take some of them on a trial-run.
This is a game design decision I just don't get. It's not like telling players what an ability actually does is going to make the game any easier, but it may prevent players from starting to look up stuff in the wiki right away and thus spoiling some of the fun.
I still wish to recommend this game heartily (unless having control of the game 100% of the time is something that's important to your gaming experience, in which case you should stay away. But if you love fighting a game for that control, or even find merit in surrending that control and accepting that sometimes things don't work out as planned play! this! game!).
It's a treat once you get a hang on some of the more oblique mechanics.

First things first, I would most recommend this to people who loved stuff like Burnout and Split/Second; if you haven't played those, I'd say to go to those first. This game fits the niche of over-the-top aggressive combat racing that sadly seemed to taper off just around the time it hit the track, and if you're craving something new of that ilk, this is a pretty neat combo of that sort of thing!
I will bluntly say that while I consider myself a die-hard fan of racing games, I've yet to play any other Ridge Racer titles. From what I've seen and heard, this doesn't resemble the series it's supposedly part of, like, at all. It's got the insane, incoherent drifting (the number one issue with the game, in my book, is how finicky this is; be prepared to spin out a LOT as you get used to tapping the handbrake and coasting along), the boost meter, and... is published by Namco. Otherwise, it's by Bugbear, who made the original Flatout and, more recently, Wreckfest, and as such, it ends up being a very floaty, hyperexaggerated, sort of arcade racing. It's very Hot Wheels-y. This is the kind of physics you get when playing with toy cars on the floor; reason goes to the curb for cinematic appeal.
The strange thing about the game in motion is the inconsistency of this game's "Frags", which you will likely know better as Takedowns or slamming-your-opponents-real-hard-until-their-vehicle-goes-boom. For the most part, it can only be done by boosting straight into them, unless they are also boosting. Drifting into an opponent at an angle also wrecks their machine, unless they are going faster than you or also boosting. Boosting makes one invincible to frags. It's... it makes sense eventually, but it's not really explained. In short, you can't wreck anyone unless you're boosting, and anyone boosting can't be wrecked.
There is a nice sprinkling of Split/Second here in the form of Targets, which are basically glamorized shortcuts you boost into. It's a lot cooler than it sounds; where Split/Second had you pushing buttons to detonate areas of track, forcing you to memorize them, Unbounded just has you boost into walls, malls, banks, train stations, and trucks full of explosives so hard that you just smash straight through them. It's
satisfactory. I mean, let's be honest, most of why I still play this game is just to ignore the races and try to smash absolutely everything. With the right machines (the one other holdover from other Ridge Racer titles is that they are machines. Not cars.), each of the categories of Domination racing becomes a cakewalk, and if you get as much of a smile on your face from being dubbed a "City Destroyer" and tearing down entire (unpopulated) districts, you'll love this for Rule of Cool alone.
Multiplayer is gone now. The online servers are entirely unaccessible and no substitutes exist, to my knowledge, so if you want to play on any tracks not in the main single-player campaign, you'll have to make them yourself with the Track Editor, which is kinda standard early 2000's PC racer fare. If you just want to drive around solo, the main career is a decent challenge, with Domination Races that let you tear your own shortcuts through the city, Shindo races which are cleaner, more serious affairs in line with past RR titles, Frag Attacks which are Burnout's Road Rage events but kinda sucky due to Boost, Drift events which just suck, and Time Attack events which tend to be bonkers in the best way. There's a good variety of locations, from city outskirts to tunnels to the heart of the city itself. Bonus points for the final area basically being the bombed-out wasteland you've left the whole rest of the game. Bizarrely, the way the game totals points can lead to some grinding; you may have to smash into a bunch of lamp-posts to be able to unlock more actual races, instead of better driving ability.
In short, this feels like a game displaced in time; very 90's in gameplay design, very early 2000's in terms of being hilariously not-really edgy, and very 2010's in visual and audio design. Drifting around corners to build up boost before Skrillex's "Kill Everybody" comes blaring on and then flooring the gas to plow through a high-rise is very much a unique experience, and if you love and miss this kind of game, I'd say it's worth a go.

I honestly cannot praise this game enough. I was lucky enough to not walk into this game like most people unfamiliar with products of this genre probably did. By that I mean I knew about franchises like Harvest Moon, hence I did not think I was purchasing FarmVille like others did.
Great thing about this game though is that it surprised me nonetheless even considering my experiences (I do have to admit though, there wasnt much). Let's just list few aspects that made this game so deservedly popular:
- Great soundtrack that fits the main goal (relaxation) of the game perfectly
- It gives a choice rather than just being a simple farming simulator (meaning you can go for combat, fishing, foraging etc.)
- Its social aspect is amazing and fun and keeps the game from feeling dull even after years of time (in game's time of course)
- It has immense amount of achievements and possibilities to collect which makes it something you can spend hours on without actually running out of things to do. - It just speaks to you on a personal level if you are the gamer like me who plays game to escape certain difficulties. Story of someone giving up urban life in exchange for peace and quiet is a great thing to experience.
Overall, this game is certainly not for everyone, it does not contain any action, explosions, nor is the pinnacle of story telling to be honest, even though this aspect is not lacking either. If you are looking for something to relax with and to lose some hours in - you've just reached a worthy contestant in this category

Throw Tarantino, Hotline Miami, and 47 Ronin in a blender, and you'd get Samurai Gunn
First off, I've only played solo Survival but that's impressive and substantial enough to enjoy.
So you might be thinking that those three elements in the title seem like a weird mix, but that's the kind of vibe I'm getting during my time with Samurai Gunn. Take the samurai films of old, ramp it up to eleven with the Tarantino-style violence and blood, and then imbue that with the lightning-fast white-knuckle pace of Hotline Miami, and that's Samurai Gunn in a nutshell
Choose a samurai, choose an arena, and then fight. One hit kills. Armed with only your blade, your handful of bullets, and your agility, you must survive against increasingly challenging waves of enemies in increasingly complex arenas. Like Hotline Miami, death comes fast and at a moment's notice; a single lapse in timing, in reaction and reflex, and your blood will stain the ground rather than your opponent's.
There are no power-ups to equip, no special swords to unlock, or abilities to use. You and your foes are equally matched; superior skill and reflexes are your only advantages. Each battle is one of hair's-breadth dodges over swinging blades, of smart positioning, perfect timing to strike down an enemy in mid air or deflect his bullet back at him. And that's just against one opponent; it only becomes more intense once you're down to one life and three enemies are out for your blood.
It's not just this frantic dance of death that makes Samurai Gunn so compelling, but the sheer variety of arenas as well. From levels consisting of moving platforms and traps to levels with spike pits and saw blades, to levels made of nothing but easily breakable bamboos so that the layout changes and shrinks as you play, they are numerous and each must be learned and mastered if you wish to succeed.
It's the little details that round out this impressive package. Fall into a pond and your gun won't fire but instead misfire and discharge spurts of water. Your blood and bodies stay behind, monuments and reminders of your past failures. Play dead among the corpses to confuse your enemy. Slash at your foe at the same time he does, and you'll clash swords and fly apart, leaving a dust trail in your wake.
So again, I've only played single player, but I can only imagine that multiplayer is even better thanks to human players instead of AI. You can play co-op against bots or fight against each other in Versus mode. As for Samurai Gunn's future, the developer has said he's "interested in experimenting with different types of enemies, modes, and other things" so there's only more frenetic bloodshed to come.

This game is a masterpiece. I'm pretty sure I'm not the first to say that, but it really feels like one. Many things in this game make it what it is. First, the gameplay in this game is just marvelous, you can't feel closer to the game with its amazing mechanisms, shooting, jumping and everything you can do, it just feels right. It seems like it's really you that controls the game and that the final result, good or bad, is always the product of your moves. With great shooting and movement mechanisms, everything feels right.
Secondly, another thing you can't complain about this game: its story. The story of Half-Life, the one that gave birth to this amazing franchise, is just a beautiful piece of work. It fully accomplishes its mission to take you to another world. With the fact that, Gordon Freeman, the character which you control, is entirely in your possession feels like you are in this story and you have the power to change it. The game doesn't even have cutscenes so everything is seen from your point of view. The story is captivating; it treats the alien subject differently from most stories told on this subject. It contains a government trying to hide the alien-incident, a mysterious G-Man (the man who always watches you) and a chaotic man vs alien battlefield. Maybe after all, they're not what we thought... So many questions will fly around your head and will give you the desire to continue this mysterious story.
Thirdly, I have to talk about the graphics and the level design. Those both, like everything I said before, are just truly great. While the graphics may be considered "ugly" or "old", they are for me still beautiful even if this game is from 1998. The game has great details, textures and colors. Just imagine how it felt back in the days. For the level design, nothing as changed. What I mean by that, is even after more than a decade, the levels are still pure genius and are so well used that you need to think and to familiarize with them so you can use them as your advantage. I have to tell you that this game isn't like most of the games today and is longer, which is really nice, because you'll want this game to never end. There is also a multiplayer mode which can be fun, but, as you guessed it, is mostly dead.
From a negative point of view, I don't have a lot to say. For the people that won't like the graphics, you can always buy the Black Mesa game, which is the same thing, but updated for the new generations (or old time fans). All I can say in the end, is that this game is a must!

So there's a lot of reviews about how horrible this port is and how bad the frame rate is and I'm not sure what the deal is but I don't get that at all.  I'm running an i7 3770 @3.40 GHz, i've got 16 gigs of ram, windows 8.1, and an Nvidia GTX770 with 4 gigs of vram.  It doesn't seem like a better system than some of the ones reviewing and yet I get a constant high frame rate with absolutely no video problems even in huge crowds.  I also never had problems with Watch Dogs and everyone was complaining about that game too.  All that being said this game is SUPER buggy.  I haven't had any crashes, but the NPCs and the parkour are both very buggy.  An even bigger issue though is the one that's not a bug it's a feature, and that's the absolute SH** stealth system.  The cover mechanic is just awful.  He can't get behind everything only somethings, he takes forever to get in and out of cover, the cover toggle button is space and so it's also about a million other things, there is no button to go around corners in cover, and the cover switching mechanic may as well be broken it's pretty much impossible to use.  Also if AC wants to be a stealth game they need one simple mechanic: quick save and load.  Without that it is just simply infuriating to try and play this stealthily, but the combat is tougher now and enemies can one-shot you so you are still forced to play stealth even though it is just absolutly horrible to do.  This is a first attempt in this series at stealth but with a publisher catalouge that includes splinter cell this should have been way better.  My hope is that Ubi will release a patch to fix all of this but I know that that is very unlikely.
Also, this is a pay-to-play, pay-to-win game.  That's right, Ubisoft just charged you 60 dollars for a game that they also want you to buy items in with real money.  Here's the pricing of the weapons in game:
-$250 (I know they aren't dollars but dont tell me to look up that symbol)
-$1000
-$2500
You might be thinking well these all sound managable and they are but here's where the price jumps to a minimum of:
-$125,000
If you ever wanted to think about owning that last weapon (which is super powerful of course) Ubi offers microtransactions of up to $100 USD.  This is unnaceptable and just an awful business practice.
The only reason I would tell you to buy this game now is if you have a very good PC and enjoy the free roaming the most in AC games.  The city is huge and beaitiful and varied, and the parkour system, while buggy and more unrealistic, is fun and fluid for this new city.  If that's all you care about buy this game now, but if you want to play the story and don't really care about exploring than I think maybe your best bet is to wait either for a patch or for Rogue.
Overall I wish they had delayed this game a whole hell of a lot more than 2 weeks.  Another year's polish would have done this game very well but this is Ubisoft we're talking about and that didn't happen and this game probably won't even get patched.
UPDATE: The patch corrupted my save game, deleting about 20 hours of gameplay.  Not sure I can motivate to try again.  Highly recommend backing up your saves.  Screw this game.

Note: I have not completed this game yet, but I have cleared the second floor of the darkest dungeon on medium.
Darkest Dungeon is a RPG where you guessed it, have to explore a bunch of Dark Dungeons. The goal is to bring a party of 4 people through the dungeon and hope that they do not die or go insane from the monsters lurking in the darkness. There are 15 (soon to be 16 with the upcoming dlc) heroes all with different playstyles and abilities to bring to the table, and it is fun to mix and match your party to find hidden synergies.
Although it may seem a little overwhelming at first, the games mechanics are easy to learn and remember, but the most important (and interesting)  is managing stress. Your heroes experience stress in battles, or while exploring the halls of the dungeons. If the stress bar reaches 100, they will either go insane (which is very likely) or become virtuous, giving that unit a buff for the rest of the adventure, and I will tell you there is nothing more satisfying than seeing your highwayman become virtuous after 1 too many stress waves.
My biggest complaint with this game is the difficulty spike once you start running out of Medium difficulty expiditions. This can be a very difficult time if even a few of your units perish, because once you run out of good units, it can be hard to recoup with only level 3-4 heroes.
TL;DR: This game is a lot of fun if you want a game to sink time into, it has a lot of interesting mechanics, and the difficulty spike is a little rough. (you won't need to worry about it until around 25 hours into the game) I HIGHLY reccomend you purchase this game seeing as the DLC is coming soon!

Game feels like the first Dark Souls, but slower overall and with a less reclusive plot, and a little more challenge added to it with how the experience system works.
In Dark Souls, you dropped all of your souls where you last died. Run back to the spot, reclaim them, and carry on.
In Lords of the Fallen, you drop your experience where you died. Run back to reclaim them, or you can leave the bloodstain where it is in exhcange for a healing aura that restores health while you're near it, which is handy. Downside is, the longer your 'ghost' remains unclaimed, the less experience you get back.
Let's say you died with 150 EXP in your pool. If you take the time to return to where your ghost was, there will only be about 75 EXP left. If you hurry, most if not all of it should still be there. It becomes a test to see if you can reclaim them fast enough, or use them to your advantage for a difficult fight.

OMSI 2 is not without it's faults, but overall is a really in-depth and high quality bus simulator. It is a game crafted with love and attention to detail, unlike certain other simulators.. *cough* Train Simulator.
So what's so good about OMSI?
+ The buses are very high quality, and almost every button in the cab works. Every little function in the bus actually works. Even the driver window slides! The bus sounds are top notch, and this game has one of the best sound engines I've ever heard.
+ The game simulates passengers, and it does it very well. The passengers evaluate your bus driving, and will moan at you if the bus is too cold or too warm or you attempt to short change them. They will want to get off your bus if your driving is not up to scratch!
+ The game fully simulates a 24 hour clock, and various types of weathers such as rain, snow, fog, etc. You will notice less cars and passengers at night, and lots more at rush hours.
+ OMSI has a huge modding scene, which means you can download tons of new maps and buses for free. There's always more to do, and you don't have to fork out £24.99 cause you want some different scenery.
+ Timetables are fully simulated, and AI buses follow them just like you. You can even take over an AI bus if you wish.
+ The included Berlin map clearly had a lot of detail put into it. Compare it on Street view or compare images and the similarities become obvious right away.
+ The game is supported with Official DLC's which are of great quality.
+ The game has full steering wheel support which is really great if you have one.
Okay, so what about the negatives?
- The game WILL micro-freeze and suffer from framerate issues. If you are really really sensitive to issues like this, I would not recommend it. If like me you are willing to look past these issues, you will be fine. It doesn't prevent me from enjoying the game.
- There are various bugs here and there such as the AI hitting you sometimes, passengers noclipping through bus stop shelters, etc.
- The graphics are by no means amazing and they could be better, but I do think they do the job.
- The game can be intimidating at first and the tutorials really are quite useless, don't bother with them.
- The settings can be hard to configure, and aren't as simple Low, Medium and High. This can also be seen as a good thing as you can customise them best to your system.

I have only played a few hours of the game (4.7 at the time of typing this review), but what i have played has been very enjoyable. While it does take a while to get into a game, i think it is well worth the wait. The battles are intense and the game is fairly stable even in alpha.

PROS
* Love the ambiance of being a global resistance against evil dominators ;
* When you have rookies with no improved armor, the game is brutal !  Although somewhat stressful, I like a challenge!  Once you have gear and skills, it's easier, but you have so many more options in combat, so it is really fun and feels like payback!
* The visuals for the combattants (even without mods) and the in-ship characters are really cool.  Chief engineer Shen being my favorite of course.
* Some of the missions were epic !  It felt empowering when my team pulled through.
CON :
*  I felt the campaign was not long enough.  I even avoided the last missions to try and do more before...  I would have liked a few twists and turns, surprises (either in storyline and/or combat), before the end mission.  At Veteran difficulty, it took me 95 hours (really taking my time).
* Initially, the game was crashing on me often : I had to triple check the graphics settings in-game, making sure they were coherent with the NVIDIA control panel.  I had to tone down some settings to reduce lag during cut scenes (it seems to me a GTX 960 with 4Gb should be plenty for cutscenes!).
* Saved games are linked to the mods you have active : wtf !  Never seen that before in other games (senseless).  Good news is the current version (June 2016) allows you to load a saved game without the initial mod(s) you had (if any; just with a warning message).
TIPS :
* For begginers, I recommend the difficulty Veteran : it's hard, but can be done once your combattants have gear.  I succeeded almost all missions on the first try with trained teams.  Accept that poorly geared rookies will sometimes die and honor their names.
* Altough it is a tactical game of course, luck/bad luck has a huge impact, so I suggest using Saved games and Autosaves just in case things go too wacky or in case you accidentally click to move.  Not to mention the game can crash.  The luck factor when shooting has its appeal also: it creates some surprises.
* With Windows 10, I have to play in Borderless windowed to avoid crashing, instead of Fullscreen (this issue could be only on my rig).

I think this game is an outstanding improvement over enemy unknown. I'm not terribly great at reviews, so I'll summerize my thoughts on the game in itemized form.
1) Combat is more interesting: I feel like the amount of abilities the enemies possess is much more diverse and so makes for more tactical decisions in deciding how to engage.
2) Soldier classes much more balanced: In enemy unknown, some of the classes just didn't hit the powercurve properly. Support was generally meh, snipers were generally OP past squaddie, etc. etc. Now it seems that there is no single class I groan about my rookies becoming because they all serve incredibly useful purposes (though rangers and grenadiers are preferable in the extremely early game).
3) As in the first one, "perfect play" is rewarded. I can generally get through the first 8 missions or so without the enemy getting off a single shot. As enemy HP increases, this becomes more difficult, but good play will rarely leave your soldiers in mortal danger.
4) The power-curve is very well balanced. Even on a blind playthrough on normal difficulty, I never felt like I was impossibly behind the aliens (but I also had very good play and only needed to recruit one soldier, that probably helped, haha!). This kind of dissappointed me, but I guess I can crank up the difficulty. New species are encountered one a fairly regular basis, each one upping the ante, but until the mid-game/end such sightings will rarely perturb the balance of power.
5) XCOM development is somewhat less linear. Once the proving grounds is built, one may devote resources to new ammo, armors, grenades, etc. I enjoyed being able to choose what new items were being developed and it helps shape playstyle.
The bad:
1) Timed missions CAN be tedious. Some of the new missions are timed, i.e. you have x number of turns to accomplish the objective and evac. This will sometimes prove incredibly difficult to manage. I enjoy the fast past, but ironman players should be aware that many timed missions will force an uncomfortable push forward with the tradeoff typically being massive mission rewards.
2) At higher levels, missions start to come in very quickly. From a gamplay perspective, this is fine as it forces either a large soldier pool or skilled play, but from a human perspective sometimes I burn out from missions and just want to watch XCOM progress their tech a little. This issue is covered more extensively in other reviews, and it is a legitimate concern, but nothing to warrent a negative review in my opinion.
In summary, I think this is a fantastic tactical game. It is not without its flaws, but they are generally minor and have yet to detract from my enjoyment thus far. I had read reviews complaining of how it was unstable, contained glitches, or was unfair, but I have not encountered any of these issues.

A few months ago I was introduced to this game by a friend, during the Thanksgiving events of 2015 to be precise, and every day my sister and I would clock hours into the game. (My hours on record are a split between my sis and myself.)
Really up until now I would've recommended it as one of the best free to play games I ever saw, as at the time the cash shop they had was a reasonable one.
However once they came out with the "Heart Attack" update on Feburary 2016, at first we thought "Oh hey they changed what each day gives bonuses to, oh hey there's this new power rank stuff, oh hey two free class coins."
Then however a friend, the same friend that introduced us to the game saw something in the patch notes we missed.
This made us just let out a flat "What." Before then, you could always and I do mean ALWAYS get a Class with Cubits, it's part of what brought us to the game. It rewarded both being free to play, but being able to buy stuff with real money or "Credits" if you so chose. However now with this new system in play, if you don't have a class, you either have to dump real money in, or hope to whatever deities you may or may not worship that there'll be a cheap "Class Coin" in the market place. Also with their "Mastery" system and their newly introduced "Power Rank" system, both of rely partially ON being a completionist. Leveling classes, collecting items, fishing, crafting, nearly anything.
Now it was one thing when there was powerful items or cosmetic things locked behind the pay-gate, that I understood, it was incentive to support the game if you wanted to. But when you lock basic gameplay features behind it. What's next? Not being allowed to play without paying for all your stats and classes you already own? Or maybe they'll even make you pay for the jump button of all things!
My rambling, snarkiness, and bitterness aside, this move has turned the game from being a fun free to play experience, to something that will not just drive my sister and I from this game-- but any other game this company has or will make.
In short? It used to be a wonderful free to play game, but now the greedy developers ruined it. I'm going to say this however. It's one thing to be pay to play, in fact Final Fantasy XIV is a pay to play MMO my sibling and I both enjoy. Hearing Trove similarlly let you play and level any class is what brought us to it. But really no matter whether a game is free to play or pay to play, the cash shop should not be a place to FORCE players to go to, it should be a choice.
And that's why I'll end this review with saying-- Go play FFXIV instead, it's pay to play, but it's fun and it's cash shop is really just vanity stuff.
If you're looking for another free to play option-- Just... Just play anything but THIS.

There seems to be a lot of criticism surrounding this game, and most of it is for good reason. Ubisoft has yet again released a fairly poor PC port packed with bugs and glitches as far as the eye can see. Though after a few hours of tweaking setting I finally ended up with a playable version. That's not so say it wasn't without it's bugs, but it is a version of the game that I can recommend. Before I go on, I will mention that this game does in fact have micro transactions. Which is greedy and unfortunate, but they aren't required and used as an optional way to unlock things without playing the game.
The art direction is enough to sell this game, it's beautiful and the most realistic open world I have ever seen in a game. People fill up your screen as far as the eye can see which is impressive in itself, but it also adds the mechanic that we saw in the first AC trailer where Altair is picking off people in the crowd. Looks isn't all this one brings to the table though, this game is one of the most innovative ACs in terms of gameplay. This time around you aren't given so many tools, but you're able to specialize in a weapon of your choice. Swinging a rifle around like a bo staff is something I don't think I've seen in a game, and it's pretty ♥♥♥♥ing awesome. Aside from combat though, the free running system has been tweaked with two buttons, one to go up and down, this is such a small change but it gives you so much more freedom.
All and all, technical issues aside, this game is well worth the price of admission for any AC fan in my personal opinion.
*Edit: I suppose I should note that I'm running a 690(Multi-GPU) with one half dedicated to phys-x. Thats what I had to do to stop the stuttering. Textures are set to high, and AA is set to FXAA, everything else is set to very high and it runs at a fairly consistant framerate.

This is the fourth installment of the Age of series (including Age of Mythology), progressing down the evolution of civilization. Historic real-time strategy games tend to stay around the Middle Ages of Ancient Civilizations. It’s nice to see a game in the colonial era of history.
Unlike Age of Empires 2, it feels like this game was crafted entirely with the idea of balance. Every civilization has an answer to any problem thrown at you. Most of the civilizations have a heavy and counter variant of each of the three main military groups (infantry, cavalry, and siege weapons). This game ‘should’ be the best in terms of competitive play, since the game mechanics are well rounded and nothing is too overpowered.
But this is where the positive part of the compliment sandwich ends.
If you were to compare each of the Age of games to days of the week, AoM is the ambitiously positive Friday, AoE2 is the kick♥♥♥♥♥Saturday, and AoE3 is the lazy Sunday. Every time I play this game, I feel like I should be doing something else. “Sure, I could be playing this, but I could also practice bass.” (AoE1 is a non-existent day where Horse Archers rule the streets).
As I mentioned, this game is very well balanced. The problem with this is since every civilization has a well-built set of answers, nearly every civilization feels like they play the same. In the two expansions, the only truly-unique civilizations are the Aztecs (only infantry) and the Chinese (batch-based unit creation). The other two native civilizations feel identical to each other and play like a weaker European civs.  The Indians and Japanese have their gimmicks (villagers cost wood and houses attract animals to trickle in resources, respectively), but don’t feel that unique.
Gathering resources is a complete yawn, especially once you’ve got your farms and plantations organized. It gets even more laughably easy when you’re Japanese with the shrines and rice paddies. Even if there is no wood left or it’s all in hostile territory, you can just order a factory from the home city to make you wood for free. Unlike AoE2, there is little reason to aggressively cultivate resources.
The campaign is decently written (about equal to AoM), but it infuriates me to no end how you can’t change the game speed in the campaign. I’m used to the fast-paced speed of ‘fast’ in Skirmish mode. When I start a campaign mission, it feels like the game just chugged two cartons of molasses and is recuperating from the syrup hangover. They may have slowed it down because the AI can be a bit difficult, but I feel like they did it so people wouldn’t think the campaign is too small.
However, despite all of my issues, I still love the game and would recommend it to anyone who likes RTS’s. I am a big fan of the home city mechanic where you gain experience when you play Skirmishes and can improve the shipments you receive in-game.
However, I wouldn’t recommend it to someone who is getting into them. AoM was more colourful and unique, and AoE2 was more intense and challenging.
