I'd just like to open by saying I'm a huge Dark Souls fan, and that fundamentally, I enjoy this game.  It does a lot of things right, but given it's marketed directly to Dark Souls players, I feel a warning is due.
I'm gonna start with the good.
The game looks and sounds /fantastic/.  The VFX engine is absolutely gorgeous, even on lower graphics settings, and for a next gen game, it runs fairly well on aging hardware, with some small FPS hiccups.  On top of that, as an audiophile, the sound downright thrills me.  It's deep, punchy, and weighty - armour and chains rattle realistically, a weapon striking metal lets out an endlessly satisfying 'clang', and the soundtrack is excellent.  It's also got a massive variety of interesting weapons and armour - less variety than Dark Souls, but there's something here for most playstyles, and with items of varying rarity on top of random rune cards, the game has, functionally, a more complex loot system than Dark Souls.  Some may not like this, but I'm a sucker for random loot.  It also adds some interesting gameplay mechanics - the game rewards you for going long periods of time without saving by granting you a progressively increasing XP multiplier and improved loot drops for every enemy you kill without accessing a checkoint, but it also discourages checkpoint-scumming by making it so that checkpoints can only fill your health and replenish your health items a certain number of times before needing time to recharge.
But you can see the big red thumbs-down up there, so it's time to get to the bad.
This game is harder than Dark Souls.  Not more challenging, just harder, and this is due to a large number of lazy, shortsighted, and downright perplexing design decisions.  This is a game that wants to be like Dark Souls, but didn't study the source material carefully enough.  Boss arenas are littered with rubble you can get hung up on and plants that can obscure your view.  All enemies can spin on point to face you without any intervening animation, making maneuvering around them nearly impossible outside the designated 'attack windows' - this is a massive pain when it comes to fighting enemies with shields.  The lock-on system has far too short a range, making keeping larger boss enemies at a distance very difficult, because your lock will drop and your camera will snap to something else seemingly at random as you back off.  Some bosses have tiny crash boxes that make no sense - the ankles of the Beast boss are the worst offender.  Some enemy design makes absolutely no sense.  Slippery rogue enemies can sponge hits while tanky guys with tower shields go down in three.  Fat, bloated enemies that look about five hundred pounds can nimbly dodge and evade your attacks, while effortlessly breaking your block with a single floaty punch.  And that's not even going into the game's poor writing, story, and mediocre voice acting that inexplicably varies from louder than normal to barely audible.
To wrap things up, I personally enjoy this game, but I have a habit of liking bad games, and this one frustrates the /hell/ out of me.  In Dark Souls, I always kept playing because my death was my mistake, while I find myself frequently ragequitting from Lords of the Fallen because the game has done something stupid and it's gotten me killed.  Fundamentally, it's got some solid ideas, and it's outstanding in a few areas - I find myself genuinely enjoying the time between boss fights - but its poor enemy design and frequent mistakes in other areas make said boss fights an absolute chore.
TL;DR: Good in places, but blindingly frustrating in others, Lords of the Fallen can only be recommended to those with the patience to put up with the poor choices made by the developers.

Hacknet is a hacking simulation in the vein of Introversion's fantastic Uplink. It provides the player a virtual OS from which to interact with 'nodes' dotted around the map. Each node represents a computer system which can be approached using the software and hardware knowledge you accumulate throughout the game. Pretty simple stuff on the surface, but Hacknet is a fantastically well-designed story-driven experience, with considerable replay value which will only continue to grow as new content is invariably released.
This game deserves praise for it's graphics, in that they perfectly fit the tone of the game. In most other game genres we typically see a push toward more cutting-edge photo-realism, but here we have a clean, crisp environment that doesn't over-burden or confuse the player with menus and tedious repetitive interaction. Praise is also due to the sound design in this title. The music is, again, a perfect fit for the game's tone. Orchesteral strings move to thumping bass adding a sense of pressure and drive that has kept me going back just for the music.
There are some problems with this game however. Some people will say these aren't problems as such, more personal gripes, but take them however you wish.
1. It's short. Like really short. With no experience whatsoever, my first run was just under 3 hours from start to finish, completing every avaliable mission in the game aside from 'Junebug' which was bugged at the time. Hopefully, more content will be added soon, and the ability to open story creation to the community is an exciting prospect shound it be considered.
2. It's easy. The learning curve is pretty shallow, with a few basic commands covering every action you will be performing. Once you have got launching cracks using the TAB key down to a fine art, you can smash through any security in next to no time.
3. No Upgrade abilities. A key component of every computer interface is the hardware it's connected to, and in a game setting the ability to upgrade and customise that hardware is a given. There is no such system here. The only resource you have is RAM, which is set throughout the game and cannot be improved upon. This does give the game a streamlined feel, but I would still rather have an functioning economy and avenues to explore with my earnings.
Overall, I think Hacknet deserves your time if you enjoy the genre. If you do enjoy this quite esoteric game style, then you've no doubt played the alternatives. On balance, I would say that Onlink, the fan-made re-write of Uplink is the superior game in this category still. It is a longer, more challenging experience. That being said, with expansion and dedication, Hacknet will become the standard by which all other hacking simulation games will be judged. We should all help it get there, and enjoy the rewards when they come.

The spiritual successor to Uplink you've been waiting for.
This is a game that makes you feel like a real hacker. You type in a terminal to perform most functions, but don't let that alienate you, because you do it with only a dozen or so commands that are easy to remember. You'll pick it up as you go. But where it really shines is that it captures the same spirit of exploration and "Can I really do this...? YES I CAN!!" that made Uplink fantastic. There are some moments where the puzzles give you JUST enough information that you have to think - not by game logic, but real logic, about what to do - and it feels amazing when it pays off. It's not without flaws, being a new release at the time of writing, but save for one or two wallbanging moments it plays very smoothly. If you've played Uplink and want more (or felt that there was too much time/money management in that and would try a similar game with more story) Hacknet is for you. If you haven't played Uplink, play it first, because it has some shining moments but will feel extremely dated after the modern polish of Hacknet.

Yes, it will crash and freeze on occasion. Yes, it is difficult to master at first and will take time to figure out. Yes, you have to read the manual and instalation of addons can be a pain.
But still, there is absolutely NOTHING like it. It is hands down the best transport sim there is - most detailed, most realistic representation of driving a public transport vehicle, period. I own them all - and nothing else comes close.
The busses (the included ones and most 3rd party addons too) are infinitely detailed, with nearly all functions working and represented. Deep scripting allows for modders and 3rd party developers to represent nearly any of a bus' systems faithfully; and basic scripting it is not difficult to understand, so if you don't like something - you can put the time in and change it. The sounds are superb, best and most detailed of any sim. There is interaction with the passengers, they're not just props. There is an infinite ammount of freeware addons (I don't remember when I last played the default map or one of the default busses), some of which are not only as good as payware addons - many they surpass the payware addons. There are huge maps with 20 different routes and small maps with one or two routes. There are city maps and interurban maps. Busy maps and quiet, pastoral maps. And most of the maps coming out nowdays are detailed and pretty.
Of course, OMSI is also deeply flawed. You have to take that into account, especially if you're used to sims and games built by large companies with teams of developers. It has all the classic limitations of a game built in the living room by two passionate guys - a crappy engine (performance can suffer on large maps even on the best of systems), occasional crashes and errors, underdevelopment in many areas (the AI of cars can be infuriating, they are dumb as hell and never leave their paths, which can create gridlock sometimes). But the core of the simulation is so good that you get used to the flaws and learn to work around them. And yes, it is worth it.
Never had there been a sim on which I've logged so many hours. Big thumbs up.

Used to I thought it couldn't get any better than Star Craft in terms of RTS and certainly C&C made Time Travel look sluggish by comparison - This RTS game has Real-Time Multi-timeline travel. With Archon you can literally see the future or the past of the battlefield in real time and you can actually effect that battlefield in the past or future. Further just because you've been defeated doesn't mean the game is over - if you can travel back in time and alter it you can literally "undo" your defeat. There is a limit to the amount of time you can travel and the number of orders you can give, but overall the battlefields of RTS have never seen this scale of Time Travel. You don't even need a TTC. Lemme go over the Pros and Cons real fast:
Pros:
+Time Travel on the battlefield like nothing you've ever seen in RTS.
+Easy to pickup, Hard to master - You'll be on the first few levels of the campaign for hours, but you can play "skirismishes" or "multiplayer" in a cinche, most of the campaign's difficulty is in how to overcome the handicaps in the first couple of missions.
+Pause/Slow/Fast Forward The Current Time-line while you issue orders - but don't mistake this for turn-based because the time you can "pause" is limited (excludes full system pause, which cannot give orders) and the time-line continues on in the present.
+ Send your units backwards OR forwards in time using a "Chronoporter". BYOR (Bring your own Reinforcements)
Cons:
- The Campaign is a poor place to start in this game Your better off playing a few rounds against AIs in Mock-multiplayer rather than trying to start cold-turkey into the main story.
- The "level editor" is like trying to learn "blender" backwards (ie the 3d Studio Program)
- The Game isn't really upto modern Graphics Standards, but for RTS fans the graphics aren't as important as the gameplay.
- I can't really speak for the multi-player experience as I'm not much of a multiplayer kinda person but, if the AI is anything to judge by the time-line can get really warped with Humans going at it.
- There are a few bugs, mostly annoying - less critical more like "I wish that mission objective would stop replaying it's sound/text every 1/2 second" but I've only encountered that one on the second campaign mission.

Darkest Dungeon is an rpg with turn-based combat, exploration and horror elements.It's idea is the stress and metal challenge of exploring dark and sinister caverns, woods, ruins etc., with heroes that are not the valiant and fearless warriors of high-fantasy and facing terrifying and malicious monsters that will attempt to destroy your heroes bodies and minds.
The game's plot is that you're given a letter from your Ancestor telling that he requires your aid in purging the corruption from his land.You will find yourself managing your town, which serves as your base of operations, sending parties of four heroes to battle the creatures in the plagued land around the ancestral manor.
In terms of game mechanincs, I could say that it has a unique take on dungeon crawling and how your heroes react to the horrors of the dungeons.As said above, your heroes are as human as possible, meaning that they have their strenghts, weaknesses, fears and obsessions, affecting the way the behave in quests or town; these are called Quirks that can be positive and negative, and are treatable.Another mechanic is Stress.While exploring, fighting, interacting with objects in dungeons, your heroes can accumulate stress.Not everything gives stress though, so no worries on that.If the stress reaches to 100 two things could happen:They become Afflicted.Mad, eratic, unpredictable and will stress the other members of the party.In this case, the stress will keep rising until 200 and, if that happens, they will suffer a heart attack.On the other hand, the heroes can become Virtuos, resisting further stress, empowering themselves, bolstering and destressing the other members of the party.
The game features a permadeath system, meaning that if a hero dies(unless a certain event occurs) they stay dead for good, and constant autosaving, which makes every descision you important.
And now that I've covered the base of the game's mechanics, let me tell my impression of the game.
Despite the fact that the game can be frustrating and ruthless in most occasions("most" being a generous word), I had a lot of fun with the game.I've enjoyed the difficulty and the challenge that the game offered and the fact that it does not hold your hand at all, making you to take descisions more carefully and prioritise your targets in combat, think tactically and stratically.It's a game that it wants to think on your own and understand that you cannot just easily walk through dungeons like a badass and hoping to get out without a bruise.Real badassery comes from being able to learn from mistakes and preparing for anything.
So if you like base and character managment, dungeon crawling, horrific enviroments and monsters and challenge, get Darkest Dungeon.Just have some nerves of steel and don't get attached to your heroes, because that might stop your from playing.

You see: you ALWAYS have to be prepared to change plans, since circumstances can change drastically in the blink of an eye.
This, the general athmospere of the game, and the excellent storyteller make this game worth picking up, and coming back to it later (unless you are quite the masochist, you'll want to take a break from this every so now often).

Great Gameplay.
Inpired by the Dark Souls games, Lords of the Fallen is an atmospheric action rpg placing more emphasis on how you fight instead of how much you farm.
The Bad:
The story
The game is filled with insignificant permanent characters that you meet throughout the game.  Thier only purpose is to let the player know that they have gone the right direction.  On another note, the few non-plot characters you meet are actually quite brilliantly done, (the two murderers particulary).  If you look well enough most encounters are accompanied with an audio log about them and why they are there.
Voice Acting
pretty self explanitory.
The good:
Graphics
The minor detail ranging from the background, to furniture placement.  Particle effects are done nicely.  No clipping in thin materials eg. clothes and capes.

The GAMEPLAY
Here is a loaded subject as it is filled with both exeptional and poor decisions.  Firstly the rouge gameplay is beyond exceptional, much better done than the other classes, and not by a small margin either.  I find the rouge class has well over twice the dps and works much better with the game mechanics.
Warriors and Cleric classes on the other hand are well done but not exceptional.  The increaced poise damage on larger weapons is accurate but it seems like once you break an enemies poise (and thier recover animation finishes) it is back at its maximum when i believe it should have a longer recovery time. This brings me to greatshields and thier 'q'.  The purpose seems to be to deal significant poise damage, and after provide increased protection.  This is however made redundant then Harken's recover animation is longer than it takes for thier poise to recover.
On another note, a fast LATE GAME strength weapon appears to be missing (or i may not have found it).  kite shields and buckler provide exceptional versitility with only a slight reduction in protection.
Another great things is there doesn't appear to be any glass cannon weapons. I remember dark souls grabbing one of the black guards swords, casting magic weapon and litterally 4 shotting the moth queen miniboss.
The OK:
Music
Boss music is well phased in and sounds epic.  The consistent music was a bit bland (in my opinion).
Performance
Another thing to note is that it ran on an old pc of mine which was surprising. it had extremely long load times on that machine but a good average fps with dips when loading on demand.
Currently i am running this game on a new'ish system on max settings getting well above 60 fps.
here are the stats for people worried about thier expected performance.
Processor: i5-4590 3.30 Ghz
Ram 8 gigs (game did not use greater than 4 gigs)
64 bit Win 7
GTX 750 ti 2gig (150AUD)
running on a conventional hard drive, Not SSD
Seems to be a stable game, crashed 2 times on entry in the whole time i have played the game, and that was probably because i forgot to install my graphics driver on a recently formatted system *facepalm*.
To summarise:
Great game, the combat system whilst well done needs to be tuned for slower characters. (in NG+ i am easily killing bosses whilst my warrior struggles.)

I got this game as a part of humble bundle sale, so I don't really mind paying for this rubish. However, If you're going to pay for this game, I implore you to look elsewhere.
Ridge Racer Unbounded (RRU) is a sad case example of how a great publisher like NAMCO BANDAI games has lost its identity in the contemporary video gaming world. If I would like to play Need for Speed (NFS), then I'll play NFS games. If I would like to play Burnout, then I'll play Burnout games. RRU is the very definition of identity crisis. It borrows the "career" mode of most recent NFS, but the concept end up as very linear and boring with no story lines. It borrows the destructible environment from the Burnout series, however, it does not borrow enough to make it slightly fun. Unrealistic drifting was always fun factor and also the trademark of RR series, however it is undeniably toned down in an attempt make the game more realistic. As a result, RRU racing mechanics become something that is neither realistic nor unrealistic. In short, this game is just not good from any aspect it try to sell. The developer copied aspects from other games, yet failed to make it any good. Worse, they also droped many fun aspects which make the original series fun. This game is basically a fail reboot, akin to the fail reboot of the Fantastic Four (2015) film.
PS: NAMCO BANDAI games!!! If you, as a corporation, has allow any developer to bring your flagship RR series to fall this low, then how the mighty have fallen indeed.

Overall, Xcom 2 is basically more of Xcom. I remember when they first unveiled it, all sorts of hype about how this was going to be the Xcom game they always wanted (suggesting that was why it was going to be PC only-I know, I know, marketing hype, but still), with ideas that it'd take advantage of large memory found on PCs to make far more massive maps, etc, and that didn't really come to pass.
I'm not kidding when I say this is very much more of Xcom. There's been some slight changes, but if you played Xcom, you'll barely notice the changes and likely steamroll through Xcom 2.
Xcom 2 suffers from the same power issue of Xcom. The game is the most difficult when your toons are fresh/low level, but if they survive and increase in rank, the game gets increasingly easier. So, in general, the game is the most difficult in the beginning, and then gets easier as you spend more time in it. I'd far and away that work the other way around. Oh well.
And, once you have a handle on how Xcom 2 works (hint: pretty much the exact same way Xcom does), by the halfway point in the story, battles will largely be a farce due to how overpowered you are verse the enemies (assuming, again, you have any idea how to fight each mob type), and you're really just going through the motions for the second half of the game. The Xcom series is practically a meme in of itself in how the RNG works (missing shots at 94%, etc), but your characters-once they've managed to survive and progress a little and gear up-largely shrug off any hilariously bad RNG they face).
I haven't played any of the mods, but presumably community members will (or already have) address this type of thing via mod. They sort of did for Xcom, afterall.
The story is about as engrossing as it was in Xcom. Take that as you will.
Character customization was decent, but nowhere near as expansive as it could have been. But, again, people can make cosmetic mods, so that might have been on purpose.
So, why do I still recommend it? Poor power creep aside, Xcom 2 is still a lot of fun. And, making squad members as avatars of your friends, to purposefully get them killed, etc, while making gifs, makes for great entertainment.

This game is Ridge Racer in name only. Namco outsourced Unbounded to Bugbear, who are primarily known for their Flatout games. Flatout was basically the only legitimate contender to Burnout's throne. If you don't follow racing games, this big chain of game titles probably means nothing to you, but let's break it down:
Burnout is a game about crashing cars in to each other. Flatout is a game about crashing cars in to everything, including, but not limited to, other cars.
Ridge Racer is not typically a game about crashing cars in to anything. But, it's Bugbear, so, really, Ridge Racer Unbounded is basically just another Flatout game in disguise. Wearing the Ridge Racer mask does give Unbounded a bit more flair than you'd typically get from a Flatout game, of course. Streaking city lights, roaring supercars and electronic music separate it from Bugbear's typical "redneck demolition derby" aesthetic.
But it's still a game about crashing cars in to things. Given Bugbear's legacy, it does this pretty well. Not quite as well as Criterion did with Burnout, but better than most.
But, true to Bugbear and Flatout's legacy, Unbounded is about parsing through chaos. The old Flatout problem of your car getting hung up on random debris still holds true. I've lost races because I smashed through a wall and ended up being flipped in to the sky only to land facing the wrong direction. You never know when something like that's going to happen, nor can you really be sure what the end result will be -- you just have to roll with it and hope for the best. Losing races because of an unforeseen, unpredictable physics hiccup can be more than a little frustrating, but at least restarting events is quick and easy.
I'm sure people who are looking for a classic Ridge Racer game are going to be mad that this isn't one of those. And that's fine, because it isn't. But it's still kind of fun, if occasionally a bit annoying. The difficulty in general in later events gets to be quite high, too, especially in the Drift-focused events.
Shame that the online servers don't work anymore, though. The game constantly awards you parts for a level editor but you can't share your stages with anyone because the servers got turned off. Bad form, Namco.

First, let's get the obvious out of the way; yes, this game is hard. You will fail, inevitably, at some and several points. It will be a struggle, and you'll probably feel like you're just barely scraping by, which forces you to think long-term. This will be particularly true if you are not familiar with XCOM, or played the predecessors on lower difficulties. XCOM 2 is more difficult than XCOM: Enemy Unknown/Enemy Within. There are timers on most missions, forcing you to move forward rapidly in order to close in on the objective, meaning that by design you cannot scour the map eternally whilst the aliens don't know you're there in order to find your favorite ambush position. It's, frankly, there for balance and fits the setting marvelously. For those who hate timers, there are mods on the workshop that easily rid the game of them.
No beating around the bush. In my view, XCOM 2 compared to its predecessor is superior in virtually every way. For starters, and a major positive, the controls clearly no longer suffer under consolitis, and as such it's not only adviceable to use a mouse and keyboard, but clearly the superior input method; as it should be on a strategic PC game. The graphics has taken a giant leap up from XCOM: Enemy Unknown and Enemy Within, one that only really becomes apparent once you go back and play, or watch screenshots of the predecessors. The ambush/infiltration mechanic is an amazing function, and XCOM does itself much better as a ragtag group of rebels than a supposed international alien defense organisation that for some reason still can't afford more than one bloody ship to toss their redshirts at aliens with.
Customization has reached insane levels, wherein the purely cosmetic is simply through the roof (and continuously inflated by Workshop items, courtesy of an awesome community), and things that have gameplay impact includes stuff like weapon attachments, different kinds of grenades, Personal Combat Sims (small stat-boosters that are quite uncommon), most of which is either looted from aliens in the field, researched using alien bits you've looted, or traded on the dynamic black market that changes deals every month.
Maps are amazingly varied, and I'm only now (some 100 hours in) starting to recognise certain "pieces" of their generated content, only to enter mission upon mission to suddenly be slammed with something I've never seen before. Beautifully crafted, they offer both groans of dread, as you realize you have to traverse massive open space with only the occasional high cover, as well as elated chuckles as you get dropped into the mission on a rooftop and there's an alien pod right below you. Their randomly generated nature is, frankly, miles better than the hand-crafted ones in EU/EW.
Soldiers who gets killed, knocked unconscious or who lay bleeding out have to be carried off to the evac zone by another soldier in order to save their precious equipment, as uniquely researched grenades, weapon attachments etc will be lost if you just leave. Soldier skill trees are pretty darn amazing, and there is no longer just one viable way to build them like in EU/EW. I know people love snipers, but do not, and I cannot stress this enough, do not underestimate the gunslinger. It can save your bacon way more than you think. Also grenadiers synergize amazingly with most classes that have kill potential. Deny the alien its damn cover.
The geoscape is vastly improved where you plot out your realm of ragtag rebels, establishing contact with rebel cells and building makeshift radio towers to spread your influence; which also increased monthly income. Missions are frequent, varied and all come with some manner of consequences, and this time they're rather inuitive. The meta-game is actually fun this time around as opposed to a sterile globe that spins your head into borderline vertigo whilst occasionally forcing you to play a watered down arcade game about a jetplane trying to shoot down a UFO.
Now, the Doom Timer(TM) appears to be a common complaint from other reviewers, but I have so far only lost one game to the actual timer, and then simply due to faults of my own. As time progresses, the aliens are building on the so-called Avatar Project, which slowly fills bars at the top of your screen until you get to losing the game, akin to enough member nations leaving XCOM in EU/EW. The way to combat this is to destroy alien facilities that they build (and who individually slowly help accrue dots on the bar), setting back all the progress that individual facility has contributed, and then some. Story missions often results in setting the bar back as well, so as long as you're making slow progress, the aliens should be struggling. Whenever a facility pops up, simply plot out where you need to go and start working on it, and should the dots fully fill up you will still have a solid 2 weeks (unlike the instant lose state in Enemy Unknown/Within) to make a last ditch attempts to thwart the aliens should the entire alien progress bar fill.
The story is, frankly, miles better than EU and feels much less contrived. Characters are likeable, even if Bradford does get annoying as hell during retaliation missions. Thankfully, there's also a mod to shut him up.
Now, all this praise said, XCOM 2 has taken certain liberties with streamlining the experience. Weapons, once researched, promptly give every soldier that upgrade tier, meaning you won't see an unholy mixture of laser, projectile and plasma weaponry on a ragtag rookie crew because all your regular chums are wounded. Same goes for armors. A shame, as it was somewhat iconic in the predecessors.
Elephant in the room: performance can be a bit all over the place. I can have incredibly smooth transitions, and suddenly my game will freak out over a small fire. This has gotten vastly better with patching, and particularly with the most recent patch. Frames tend to drop particularly during loading transitions which, whilst understandable, can be a bit jarring and annoying.
Also, the final mission is brutal as all hell. Psychers are your friends.
Huge minus: still no Warhammer 40.000 total conversion mod.
Still deeply recommended.

UPDATED: 25 Oct 2017
Another year, another boat load of updates to my beloved FS. So what has changed? More ships, more crew, faster game pace, better visuals on EVERYTHING, and finally some semblence of a decent introductary experience.
For ages Fractured Space suffered from a steep learning curve and the only way to really "get in to" the game was through a stubborn refusal to stop playing it. Now there is actually a fleshed out tutorial and introduction experience for new players. Also a VERY handy player guide has appeard on
. Check it out.
Still, this isn't a LAN party game fresh out of the box. You will need to put in 2 to 4 hours to unlock enough features in order to play with your friends. After that, you are free to group with up to 4 other players and battle it out against bots or humans in glorious space ship battles!
Do I recommend Fractured Space? Unquestionably. It's worth those 2 - 4 introductary hours to get at the meaty heart of the game. Plus it's free! Unlike some other, namelss, free to play games nothing even resembles a "pay to win" mechanic here. Do you want to spend money on a fancy ship skin which speeds up the grind a bit? Cool, do that. Would you like to spend money on in-game items which give you an advantage over other players? I suggest you look elsewhere. I think there's a game with tanks like that. Tank Planet or something.
So give it a shot. Plus the explosions are SUPER pretty. Despite spending a lot of time in game, I still get to watch myself explode a lot, and have yet to tire of the pretty explosions.
UPDATED: 4 Oct 2016
Farewell Early Access, you were fun. Fractured Space is finally live! It's very exciting as the player base has increased dramatically. While the influx of new blood can be frustrating when new players are grouped with veterans, let us not forget we need a large player base for the game to survive.
For the live release the UI has seen significant improvements and the addition of Co-op play vs. AI bots will help to curb the learning curve. Fractured Space has always suffered from a steep learning curve, but that's the price you pay for a game with this level of tactical depth. This isn't "chess in space", it's more like "Axis and Allies in space". You can enjoy on a casual level, but if you wish to plumb the depths of optimal attack angles and diversionary tactics, that's all there too.
Be sure to check out the official Discord server for a community of active players and free voice chat channels. It's remarkable how well a coordinated team can perform over a random assortment of players.
Yup, still awesome. Check it out.

A lot of people give flak to this game with regards to the Avatar project (The Doom Timer) and timed missions (Oh no I have to rush and can't 'strategize' properly) I use 'strategize' with quotes because these are the people with myopic definition.
Using Dune 2 as the father of all RTS, most people even myself included would like to build up 50 tanks before we assault to have metaphorically speaking 100% victory chances. Unfortunately XCOM2 isn't like that. Resources and more importantly
is limited. Many times you have to make choices of the lesser of both evils.
XCOM deals with a lot of RNG (Random Number Generator) Yes you can miss your shots with 95% hit chance. Its part of the system. If you can't accept this, then this game isn't for you.
RNG can swing both in your favor and against you (more on the third section)
XCOM doesn't allow you to be 'fully prepared' before going on missions. Sometimes your A-Team can be wounded and you're left with B-Team or worst, rookies. Here you can decide to either go with rookies, or don't do the mission. Which is the lesser of both evils? You decide.
First playthrough was normal. It was difficult but do-able
Second playthrough was Commander difficulty. Still OK but there are frustrating moments
Third playthrough Commander + Ironman here I will elaborate a little
I had to restart 30 times. Yes
times because I had really bad RNG as bad as rookies dying on the first mission to crits. Other poor RNG was not getting any engineers at all thus delaying teching leading to poor weapons & armor on missions leading on to squad wipe.
More than one of my squad mates died to full criticals while in full cover. In the end I had 25 squad mate deaths.
In the end I finished Ironman + Commander (Nope won't do Legendary)
Does this game have room for improvement? Definitely as with all other games
XCOM allows mods to help in this section. There are many mods that improve your quality of life and balance the game.
Few examples are (just to name a few)
Gotcha
True Concealment
Overwatch All
Evac All
(There are more but I shall not list them)
Final words to those who 'want to relax with a game after a long days work', sure you can relax in XCOM. Its turn based. You can take 2 hours to ponder and think over your turn. Just because there is a mission timer doesn't mean you have to finish your turn in 30 seconds.
Think 1 step ahead and plan for contingecies like "What if this shot misses?" which happens
Scout the entire map while in concealment rather than engaging the first pod you see (Isn't this part of strategy?) (This is where True Concealment mod balances the game)
You will find that XCOM with timed events doesn't 'rush' you as much as you think!

First, there was 2D. Then 3D. We even have 2.5D (3D models in a 2D world). Could it get any better? Achron thinks so, and they have added a new dimension to gaming. The 4th Dimension.... Time.Achron - Adding the fourth dimension to real-time strategies
That’s right, Achron is the first game that allows you play in the past, present, and future.... simultaneously. Self-described as a "meta-time strategy", Achron is essentially a mix of a Real Time Strategy game and a Stephen Hawking book. Now I know that sounds complicated, but surprisingly you pick up on the gameplay and strategy rather quickly.
Let’s be honest. Nothing I say about this game will be understood, until you first understand the time travel mechanics in the game. Like most RTS games you have the same basic controls. Unlike other RTSs, the bottom of your screen is filled with a time line and an energy meter. The time line allows you to see when a skirmish is taking place. Any changes that you make to the time line in the past require Chrono-energy. The bigger the change, the more energy required. This keeps things balanced by keeping people from exercising God-like power, and encourages good strategizing in the present.
When changes are made in the past, a time ripple will pass by and you will see the battle shift on the timeline before your eyes. But be careful that you don’t move units into an occupied location in the past. The result is what the developer calls "chronofragging", where only the strong units survive (though with substantial damage)
The single player campaign tells the story of the human race. As they explore space, they are faced with an enemy that seems to be unstoppable. That is, until scientists stumble on technology that allows you to not only teleport units spatially, but also chronoport them through time. Equipped with this newfound technology, it is your job as an Achron (someone who can see the whole timeline and make changes to the past) to lead your Marines to victory against an enemy who seeks to destroy you.
When I started playing the SP campaign, I have to admit, gameplay felt incredibly slow. I am primarily an FPS gamer and the reduction in pace tested my patience. That said, I fully understand the reasoning for the initially slow gameplay. Hazardous Software is introducing an entirely new concept to games, and this slow introduction was necessary to prevent a steep learning curve.
All in all, the SP campaign was solid. At times, I had the feeling that I couldn’t lose because of my time manipulation abilities, but the developers compensated for this by making your allies self-centered and self-preserving.
I would venture to say that it is necessary for everyone who tries this game to play an hour or so in the SP campaign to familiarize yourself with time manipulation and tactics.
Achron requires careful thought and time line tracking
Starcraft, move over. You finally have some competition in the RTS genre. After familiarizing myself with the 4th dimension, it was time to play some multiplayer. Everyone knows that multiplayer is what makes or breaks an RTS game, and Hazardous Software has delivered a winner.
Starting out on a multiplayer map, the only learning curve that you start with is learning the new names of some traditional units you have in all RTS games (like the resource collecting unit, building to research new technologies, etc). Within 45 minutes, I had it nailed down.
When I felt like I had enough of an army built up, I proceeded to attack my opponents. Boy was I wrong. My enemy had massive forces built up and proceeded to destroy me. In most RTS games, the match would have been over quickly. But don’t forget, time is on our side. Before it was too late, I chronoported my forces back in time, and stopped them from attacking an enemy that was too powerful. Laughter ensued as I heard my friend on team speak shout "What the? Your guys are disappearing!?!"
The only logical response was for my opponent to go back in time as well. Which I responded to by moved into the future. The rest of the match was cat and mouse until squad by squad, my death became unavoidable.
Hanging on to my last 10 units, I ran for my life, back and forth through time. Upon going back in time, I noticed that I had about double the units. Excited, but seeing my inevitable demise, I pushed for one final assault. As I began to attack, I noticed different characters disappearing suddenly. Then it all became clear to me!!!! The units that I thought were extra were actually the same ones that I already had! They were disappearing because I moved them into the past. I had become a victim of a TIME PARADOX!
Achron is a game that will keep you begging for more. This is sure to become a LAN favorite across the globe. Plenty of thought, plenty of laughs, plenty of head scratching as players disappear and reappear before your eyes.
This game is a must buy for any fan of the RTS genre, anyone intrigued by time travel, and everyone with a keyboard.

Are you looking for a strategy game which involves intense tactical action across time? If you are, then you can keep looking, because this isn't it.
Interestingly enough, the main issue with Achron is the time travel mechanics themselves. In theory it sounds about right: Use future knowledge to plan your strategy, or fix past mistakes. It worked well enough for Prince of Persia. Where could it possibly go wrong?
Time waves. That's where it first starts going horribly wrong. In theory, you should be able to jump to the past, make a few fixes, and then jump back to the present and see the results, right? Wrong. You have to wait for the "time wave" to hit, and erase the incorrect present. And how long would that take? Well, as long as you've jumped back. The time waves only move at double speed compared to normal playing. During that time, you have to play in the past, at double speed, or at least re-watch it.
You can't keep playing in the present, because as soon as the time-wave hits, many of your orders will actually be wrong for the situation, if they remain valid at all. And that's assuming that the units to whichyou need to give orders even exist in the present. You can't just wait, either, because the present doesn't stop, and by the time the time wave reaches that "future event" to which you were reacting, it is already, itself, far in the past. So, even if you only make one change, and let everything else play out without interaction, you still have to play in the past just to continue from the same spot that was previously the present. It probably wouldn't be so bad if time waves moved at 5 or 10 times the speed of normal play.
Most of the time, it's best to just play in the present, or even a bit in the future. If you need to "undo past mistakes", save games work much better than time travel. Of course, this all goes flying out the window once you have an achronal enemy. The AI seems to thrive on playing in the past. And every time the enemy makes a change, you have to go back and re-watch the whole thing, because it's enough that one of your units moved 3 inches left for most of your future commands to not work. And there's nothing more annoying than taking out the last of your enemy units, only for a time-wave to hit and suddenly your whole army is gone and you don't know why. Be prepared to watch the timeline UI VERY closely, because it's not too obvious when major changes occur. And, of course, if you notice it only when it hits the present, then it is far too late to go back and fix things, since, as said before, time waves are VERY slow.
Once you get past the idea of having to replay or at least review the same section of time over and over, you're hit with chrono-energy. In a time when most RTS players pride themselves on their click-rate, you get a game that actually tells you that the number of clicks you have is limited, and horribly so. Forget micro-managed tactics, it'd be too easy for the enemy to screw them all up by changing one tiny thing, and it would cost too much chrono-energy to undo and redo them when that happens.
It probably wouldn't be so bad if you were just limited to not making too many CHANGES to the past. But, as noted above, you are often forced to play completely in the past, unable to jump back to the present, so you're actually being limited on the number of actual practical things you can do throughout play.
But the worst part isn't in how little control you're allowed, but rather how the game tries to compensate for it. It seems like decades of RTS evolution were thrown down the drain, and instead you get a control scheme that is worse than what Dune 2 had. Since group commands cost as much chrono-energy as individual commands, you're supposed to organize units into "hierarchies", where giving orders to "the leader" gives that order to the rest of the group. As tedious as it is to arrange these heirarchies, it becomes even worse to control them. Beside having to keep track of "whose the leader", be sure that a command asking them all to move to one place will send them all scattering in all directions.
And yeah, by the way, if going up against an achronal enemy, you can be sure your leader will be targetted back in time, rendering all of your commands invalid. Sure would have been easier to spot major time waves if the "advanced timeline UI" had an indicator for "given a command to a dead unit".
The units also have individual AIs so that you won't have to give them commands to do every little thing. Too bad the AI is horrible, forcing you to waste tons of chrono-energy trying to tell your units NOT to move. Too bad there's no "stop" command. There's an "idle" command, which basically means "stop doing what I say, and go commit suicide instead". I'm not asking for Supreme Commander level of unit AI and control here, I'd just settle for my units following orders.
And all that is AFTER you've the "undo" command - the command you are going to be using the most, as you repeatedly replay the same section of events.
Once you take away the utterly broken time mechanics, what you're left with is a rather poorly balanced strategy game, with really poor controls. There are a few units which are clearly more powerful than anything else, and they aren't significantly more expensive to create. In fact, some of them are actually cheaper than other units. A group of 5 octoligos or twin MARs can take out most anything. Except for an army of MCBs or black birds. Units with self-repair tend to have the most broken balance, as they are neigh-invincible, so long as you can convince them not to move too far from each other (See: Horrible controls). I guess that's the reason only the humans have them. I spent most of chapter 3 just making sure the one MCB I had was free to join the fight, since it was usually a game-breaker. Oddly enough, I got an achievement for it, even though it was the most obvious thing to do.
If you're thinking of creating mixed armies of aerial and ground units with anti-air and anti-ground, you can forget it. It would require too much micro-management to use these properly, and that, as noted before, gets screwed over fast, thanks to the time mechanics. You'd think the per-unit AI, given that it's probably intended to reduce the need for micro-management, would do something useful, like targetting aerial units with anti-air and ground units with anti-ground, but it seems to more often do the exact opposite. Fact is, it's better to just have a large enough all-purpose army, which can simply be told to go from point A to point B and destroy everything in its path. That tactic works WAY better than it should. Probably because, no matter how many times the enemy replays the battle with the overly large army, there is nothing it can do to prevent the resulting annihilation.
The main counter-measure the game offers to the "large enough army of all the same unit" is limited resources. And most maps sure do limit resources. Of course, there's nothing like using every last resource to build a huge army, destroying all of the enemy's units, and then getting a surprise mission to "build this and that" with resources you no longer have.
So, having covered how bad the game is all on its own, let's get started on the bugs. And this game sure is rife with them.
Let's start with the simplest one: Windowed mode does not work. I mean, it works, but the graphics are scaled based on the total window size, including the title. This makes the top of the screen be cut off. Too bad that's exactly where your resources are shown. The thing is, this should have been the first thing that should have shown up on even the simplest QA. It's like no one even tested if the game manages to go to windowed mode.
There's more I'd like to say, but it seems I'm out of room in this review (Why is this limited?). Suffice to say, there are worse bugs, but not enough space left. You have been warned.

Achron is a very interesting concept for a strategy game. If you like seeing entirely new mechanics for games, Achron is definitely something to pick up. However, obvious pitfalls make this game incredibly...tiresome.
The time mechanics in the game are interesting, and
intuitive. Travelling throughout a 7 minute time period (5-6 minutes behind, 1-2 minutes ahead), you can see things that have happened, and can
change the events that have happened. If you have problems with understanding, "What happened with that group?" you can just rewind to see why that occurred. The interface is also intuitive enough so you can understand when some things happen. Movement, orders, and normal actions doesn't deviate from the norm in top-down strategy games, so a player that plays other top-down strategy (Supreme Commander, Command & Conquer, etc.) will not see any kind of problems getting into this game.
The interface needs some serious tweaks to understand your actions, and what your actions in the timeline are affecting. Its also extremely hard to tell when your changes are getting propagated to the present when it has nothing to do with unit on unit combat. If you (or another time traveller) jumps back to the past, makes a change, and you (in the future), could see a change that doesn't exactly make sense (such as a building or unit not getting built). While you do have the ability to jump into the past and see the changes why, the user interface incredibly lacks when, why and how things are getting modified.
Pathing in this game is also a joke. Most games, you can just right-click the location and they will path around obstacles. However, in Achron, if you right click on the right side of the map, and in the center is a one-entrance gully, which they have to go to the North or South to avoid, they will enter the gully, and get stuck on the eastern edge of the gully and stop, without trying to repath. Also, groups have hard times keeping together, since formations do not exist. Friendly "nudging" to get out of the way of a building being built, or a tank trying to get through a line of friendly soldiers, does not exist. Even with this garbage pathing, one unit can only have five orders active at one time.
The unit creation queues are also a joke. You can manage it once its in the queue effectively, and the queue is hard to understand, with health bars on the queue for some odd reason. Its hard to tell if something is made for a purpose or not, and the creation of buildings with the wrong unit mentions "at a higher cost," but fails to tell you how much it costs. Also, if you place down one building, that area is not "reserved" for other friendly units to not build buildings on that spot, so you'll run into the issue that you might build where a building is going to go.
The fact that you can't stop Major characters from moving to repair/help build unless they are leagues away annoys me considerably. I can't count the times in which the main characters (that aren't supposed to die) broke formation to heal a front-line unit, and ended up getting killed, requiring me to go back in time to tell them run away.
Teleporters are also really terrible. Rather than teleporting units as close as possible to the specified point, they are teleported anywhere within a 20 block radius from the chosen point, creating problems that units end up on top of impassible terrain, or in the middle of canyons, unable to get out, even with a nearby teleporter.
The game also takes control too early for major objectives, using the simulated "future time" (1-2 minutes in the future) to determine when an objective is finished. Because of this, it causes major characters to die because the computer takes control of the characters and moves them out of formation, requiring you to go back in time to rectify it after the unskippable cutscene ends. Also, unskippable cutscenes (which doesn't pause the game while doing it) in game.
Its evident that they worked on the time-manipulation system for 90% of the time. Maps are built incorrectly; they have impassible 85 degree inclines with textures that resemble a rock formation rather than walls that are textured properly. The large walls, which are blended together with the floor patterns, make the inside of ships and buildings look like outside with just really steep walls.
Voice acting and story, I would say that its really dumb. Okay, that's being generous, the storyline is probably one of the weakest things in the game. Game introduces Tyr, an AI, but people talk to it like a person when it comes out, makes it confusing when Tyr is introduced as an AI later on. When you encounter another AI later on, everyone treats that same type of AI as the enemy, despite Tyr being that same type of AI. Events in the game occur in reasonable order, instead things happen that suit what the storyline needs at that point in time. Even when a chapter switches, which makes you go to another race and control it (ala Starcraft), is disjointed, problematic, anti-climactic and dumb. Character moods are inconsistent, and flat. Voice acting is lifeless, and I find myself skipping cutscenes just so I don't have to listen to characters that I don't care about drone on and on, making me more sleepy than when Ben Stein is talking.
Achron is a great and new game element into a game that would be great as a concept game, but fails to excite with lackluster AI, UI, Storyline and Voice Acting. 3/10.

Personally, I'm not a fan of zombie games and don't buy them unless they offer something special, and this is something special.
I understand that people still have the perception that this is "just another zombie game," but it would be a mistake to dismiss this game just because it has zombies in it.
In case you're unfamiliar with Telltale Games' adventure titles, they're fourth generation adventure games (1st: text adventures; 2nd; When LucasArts, Sierra and FMV dominated the adventure game; 3rd: The introduction of 3D graphics to adventure games). As opposed to the majority of adventure titles of the past, this one includes branching storylines and accomodates to your choices.
The nature of the choices you're expected to make in The Walking Dead are often difficult and tragic. This ISN'T the feel good title where you chew through hordes of zombies with reckless abandon. There are consequences for your words and actions. Other characters will remember whether you acted in their interests or not.
The characters themselves are all well written and voice acted. Interacting with them is one of the main draws of this game. You really feel for these characters and it makes some decisions harder and some seemingly easy, though you will have to live with the consequences.
The game is rendered in an art style that resembles a comic book in 3D. Here in lies my one problem with the game. The art style itself is not the problem, but sometimes you'll see lines that represent creases in the characters clothes levitating above their shoulders. It is detracting from the immersion, but it's an extremely minor problem.
This game is extremely replayable, especially if you're intreiged to see what happens if you chose your decisions differently.
If you've been avoiding this title because it has zombies in it then you may have missed the point. The situation this game puts you in is the point and the story couldn't be told in any other way. This is different than most zombie games where if you changed the assets from zombies to anything else it wouldn't make a difference.
If you're looking for something that is dark, tragic and challenges your ability to reason in tough situations then I think this is the game you're looking for.

This game is very addictive. I wont go on about the actual difficulty of the game, as I have yet to beat it and make it into the depths of my nightmares, so to speak, but I really dig the gameplay. It feels kind of like a RPG board game in that the dungeons are generated and usually you're going to be encountering the same types of objects through each map. Don't let that fool you, though - traps abound. Plan well, and you might survive. You might find yourself getting attached to your characters. Luckily, there's a graveyard for that.
This is a strategy game, largely revolving around small segments of resource management (during the dungeon delves) and little battles that harken to a number of other turn based strategy games we've seen throughout the years. There are unique aspects to the combat system, specifically relating to the mental well-being of your characters. I don't want to say much more, if you like dark themes, Lovecraft, and turn-based strategy, this game might just be for you.
Best of luck to you! I hope you get it, and enjoy it.

Complaints would be that the third chapter is a bit weaker than the others - the visual design of the area is much blander, there's a lot more open space, and you can miss solving a puzzle that is then all but needed to clear the final puzzle (I ended up having to use a walkthrough to clear the last puzzle as a result, but otherwise had no trouble clearing the game). But that's mostly nitpicks and yeah it's fine as a whole.
For a low price I can see this buying you a few hours of entertainment, I mostly only got this bundled with the sequel game and basically played it out of obligation but it's still enjoyable enough on its own.

TLDR: Don't buy this game, or at least wait for it to be finished first.  Now that the hype has died down, people are starting to see that this is just a suckier version of Terraria.
I wanted Terraria in space.  I needed Terraria in space.  I thought I was paying for Terraria in space...but no...
I like a lot of things about this game.  The art style, the music, the concept, the sense of adventure, but in its entirety, this game falls flat on its face.  When you start out, you'll have a few tutorial quests teaching you how to do things, and you'll cut down trees and make a fire, and then you'll be sent out into the world.  In my first few hours, I found military bases, ancient pyramids, sewer monsters, and all sorts of fun stuff like that.  The frustrating thing was that when I got to these places I usually got killed instantly by the enemies there.
Now, here's the devastating part.  To get armor and weapons, you need to get a bunch of metal bars and pixels.  Pixels are what everything is made of in Starbound, so you'll need them to make everything.  So even though you have a bunch of iron bars, and you want to make an iron chestpiece, you'll still need pixels to do it.  You get pixels by killing monsters, but when you die, you lose two thirds of your pixels.  So you'll need to be very careful, killing monsters one at a time and sleeping or bandaging if you get hurt between fights, which is just waiting and waiting.  And you will get hurt, because monsters in this game move at lightning speed, and they jump thirty feet into the air, so you can't hit them with your bow (Which wouldn't kill a monster at your level in just one full charge anyway), and then they kill you instantly when they get close.  And after a couple of hours of frustration, you finally have that iron chestpiece.  After that, to get the bow, sword, helmet, and pants, rinse and repeat.
And here's the best part:  Once you get fully geared up and the monsters aren't a challenge, you move out of the Alpha sector and move onto the Beta sector!  And you get insta-killed by the monsters again!  So start grinding to get that gear!  (If I wanted to grind in a video game, I'd play World of Warcraft, which is mind-numbing in a pleasant way instead of an agonizing one.)
Compared to Terraria, where it was really fun to to progress through the tiers of gear, and fight bosses, and make cool houses (In Starbound, time doesn't pass on a planet when you're not on it, so be prepared to have a farm and all of your chests on your ship), Starbound is too repititive and grindy.  I haven't gone through all of the game's tiers yet, but I've put over fourty hours into it, and I feel like that's enough to give it a fair judgement.  Of these fourty hours, perhaps half of them were spent in either frustration or the mind-numbing sensation of doing the same thing over and over to reach a goal.
I believe that Chuckfish have said they'll change the progression system in the future, but this game is in Beta.  I'm not giving this game a negative review because an ice planet I went to had a warm temperature, or a lava planet was freezing.  I'm not giving this game a negative review because it's a bit laggy for a 2D game with pixel graphics.  I'm not giving this game a negative review because they haven't added in a wide enough variety of food, or guns.  I'm giving this game a negative review because its mechanics seem to be utterly broken, and if it's that way in Beta, I doubt they'll ever be able to fix it.

I had extremely high hopes for "Lords of the Fallen" when I first discovered it. But the sad truth is that it is just not an enjoyable game, to any extent. It has many problems. Some are with the mechanics, while others are with performance. This game is absolutely terrible, not like a Sonic 06 disaster, but, like I said before, it is not fun.
My first complaint must be with the first few seconds after launching the game. I know this sounds ridiculous but when you first open up the game, you are greeted with a screen where you get to pick one of three different spell trees and one of three classes. First of all, I'm sure you all know that it is never good to lock people into options that they might not want to participate in later. A lot of people compare this game to the "Dark Souls" franchise, which I adore by the way. At the start of a "Dark Souls" game you do get to pick a class, but there is no spell tree to be locked into. Also, in "Dark Souls" your starting class could be "Sorcerer" but then you could eventually use ability points to level up into a warrior. I just don't see that happening with "Lords of the Fallen"
My next issue that is immediately apparent, is the horrid combat. I will admit it; the weapons feel great to use, and are very weighty. But something that comes with this is extremely heavy combat, most of which is just winding up for your next big swing, is that it feels extremely slow. The enemies move very quickly, and it is often just a waiting-game to see how long it takes to be able to hit them again. The combat is very clunky. I did try the faster class options, but that leads me to my next point. The rolling is disgusting. Rolling is critical in a game like "Dark Souls" because it is necessary to dodge attacks. And for faster classes (and sometimes in slower ones) rolling is critical. In the "Dark Souls" series, rolling feel snappy and responsive, but here it just feels like a big rotten mess. Also, they completely over-exaggerated the weight system. In "Dark Souls" all classes start off with weight that is much less than the capacity. Here, it starts you off with a bucket-load of weight, and the roll feels sloppy because of it. Even if you took off all your armor, the roll still feels unresponsive, and just generally off. I will talk more about the combat when we start to talk about bosses, but my last word on it is that it is great to swing the weapons, but getting there is an arrogance.
The bosses are boring and lackluster. They use the same moves over and over. Also, the second boss in the game in just horrendous. He keeps his shield up for half the fight! And I already learned his moveset by the time I was halfway down his health bar, so the rest of the fight was a breeze. You could argue that this is actually
game design, but the bosses could not have been more dull. The second boss that i mentioned earlier only had 3 moves of note! And one of those moves rendered him invincible until you killed some random throw-away enemies! Also, in different attack, he rained down little explosions from the sky that dealt about a fourth of your health. This is okay. But what is
okay  is that they are
. This means that no matter where you are, you could get a fourth of your precious health stolen away. In a game that is supposed to be challenging, but rewarding, you cannot make the challenge something that it random! If you do, then how do you expect the player to become better at beating the boss through trial and error? There is no way the player could know where those explosions are going to fall. With a bad combat system, the bosses
to be interesting, varied, and fair. But they aren't.
Now for the story. The story is unique, but certainly not in a good way. So many things are going on at once. You have a friend, and then you kill a boss, and then that friend is missing even though you saw him hit the wall and fall in the same room as you, then you find a woman and she's trying to kill someone,
do you save him? God, nobody
. Also, there's some weird stuff going on with these demons or something? And their excuse for these guys showing up is "They just came out of nowhere." A better excuse would've been "We needed the player to fight some stuff before the first few bosses." One of the first quests that you get is "Save your friend!" (the one that hit the wall earlier) I do not care about my friend. I, as a player, do not have a personal connection with this "friend" so I do not care whatsoever. This man is utterly pointless to me; I just met him! All I know is that the man I am playing likes this guy, I don't why, he just does. This could have been something so much more. Maybe the quest could've been something like "Meet up with survivors!" That would have been much more interesting. You could've met up with them and made a group. Then you could've gone to the hub area or whatever. That story is much more interesting than the one about this "friend". The story is very choppy and mixed up. I feel like it doesn't know what it wants to be. It is all over the place.
Now for the performance. This game runs like a fat man jogging on a treadmill for the first time in his life. When walking around a bit, you will often see black bars at the bottom of your screen for no apparent reason. Maybe it is loading the next section in the backround or whatever, but it is extremely noticeable. Also, the game will start to get very bad framerates for what seems like no reason! This is pretty much the same as my last complaint, but I feel it needs to be addressed anyway. The only good thing this game has going for it is that it doesn't freeze up too much in the boss fights. The performance is probably the least important of all the gripes I have with this game, but it is annoying and distracting.
On a final note, I will have to say that this game is bad. It had a lot of potential to be something amazing, but I don't think it really hit it this time. It needed to fix it's problems. A lot of people like a lot of different games, but if you come in to this game expecting an experience like "Dark Souls", but with a neat twist, I'm afraid you won't get one. Overall, this game is just not worth your time. Its combat is dull. And combat is what you will be doing most of the game. So, by extension, the game is dull.
Final Score:
6/10

You are the controller of a defense system and in order to defend yourself against waves of mutants, you must "activate the defense system"

Having played 8 hours of this game I think I have come to a solid conclusion. Don't waste 60 fraking bucks on it. Ubisoft has apparently determined that their customers are completely unimportant and released an utterly hideous game.
While yes, the gameplay remains loyal to the Assassin's creed style, which I appreciate, and the player customization does offer some interesting styles in which to play. The issues with the game simply outweigh the good...
Graphics: Normally I wouldn't be so judgemental on graphics, but even on Ultra High graphics, I felt like I was playing a 6+ year old game, the game does an utterly terrible job rendering anything more than a few (ingame) city blocks away...To a point a cathedral such as the notre dame looks like it was built in Minecraft, it has no detail at distance at all. Simply flat blurry walls. It's terrifying. There are numerous glitches, I've seen guards fall out of the sky, fall through the map, fly around. The framerate jobs are random and extremely game breaking, try playing a freerunning game at 60 fps then drop it down to 5 for a few seconds, you wind up facing the wrong direction, falling of stuff, and just generally dying. The graphics here, even on the highest setting, look like Call of Duty 4. And that may be insulting Call of Duty 4. I took some screenshots, If you want to see em they are on my profile.
Gameplay: It's still Assassin's creed, solid combat (not as fun as past ones combat wise), interesting customization options, ways to make your own gear unique to you and your style.
Story: I can't decide yet, aspects of it have clear plotholes, and really strange ones at that. Ones that I can assure you will never be addressed.
Honestly If i could ask for a refund, I would. Without hesitation. Maybe in a few weeks once (if) ubisoft starts rolling out patches for the games numerous issues it will be fun to play. But i doubt they will. Especially for us PC gamers. Even the console gamers have had issues...Which says how seriously FUBARed this game is.

A game even more punishing than Dark Souls!
If you're looking for a wickedly fun, though maddeningly hard game, look no further. Darkest Dungeon is certainly entertaining, with its stylish presentation, Lovecraftian story setting and delightfully grim tone. But it can be deeply frustrating! In over 100 hours of playtime, I have found myself rage quitting more than I care to admit after losing multiple top level heroes to the sadistic whims of the game... And when every hero death is permanent, potentially erasing hours of grinding, that rage can feel very justified.
While games like Dark Souls can be bested by improving your skills, grinding experience and learning the best ways to survive, Darkest Dungeon has a much greater emphasis on luck. True, you can improve your skills and learn from your experiences, but luck is always looming over everything - deciding if your top tier hero will miss that vital attack to kill a monster before it kills you, or deciding if your enemy will score a critical hit and severely injure your party. And with level caps to make sure your heroes never get too strong, there's very little you can do to buffer yourself against cruel fate and powerful enemies.
This is a very hard game. It even opens with a disclaimer, warning you how hard it is and how badly you are going to suffer. And still, I recommend it. For all the rage and frustration and creative swearing this game causes, when you overcome those soul crushingly hard challenges, the sense of achievement is enormous and you really feel like you've earned the victory.
Don't play this game if you want an easy ride. But if you enjoy a challenge, or are just a straight up masochist, give it a try. It's well worth your time.

Good game. Being so long, the most difficult part is probably remaining patient and invested in the game for the duration. Each lapse in conscetration and failure to mitigate for potential RNG scenarios is met with brutal party wipes that erase hours (sometimes days) of grinding a party out.
Personally, I enjoy when a game pisses me off and forces me to walk away and come back when I'm more clear-headed. Darkest Dungeon shines in that respect.
Art is good, combat is always challenging and keeps you re-working strategies, dungeons are good, with neat pathing choice and party management mechanics. But all of these aspects can become repetitive once the grind sets in, as it will.
Many people complain about the RNG-hell piece, but the game in designed to be punishing...that's it's entire schtick. Luck certaintly plays a role, but understanding of the mechanics, the classes and squad comp are just as important.
Surely not for everyone, but I would reccomend to those interested in a long-form, paitence-testing, well-crafted, rogue-like game.

The soundtrack will make you fond of the game, but it's nothing remarkable.
Controls aren't customizable. However, you can move with WASD or the arrows if you want.
Getting achievements has never been easier. Finishing a chapter gets you 8 achievements, and the achievement names are meaningless unless you're actually playing the game... seeing them unlocked while you play will make you chuckle more than once.
7/10 highly entertaining, but not for everyone

I had extremely high hopes for "Lords of the Fallen" when I first discovered it. But the sad truth is that it is just not an enjoyable game, to any extent. It has many problems. Some are with the mechanics, while others are with performance. This game is absolutely terrible, not like a Sonic 06 disaster, but, like I said before, it is not fun.
My first complaint must be with the first few seconds after launching the game. I know this sounds ridiculous but when you first open up the game, you are greeted with a screen where you get to pick one of three different spell trees and one of three classes. First of all, I'm sure you all know that it is never good to lock people into options that they might not want to participate in later. A lot of people compare this game to the "Dark Souls" franchise, which I adore by the way. At the start of a "Dark Souls" game you do get to pick a class, but there is no spell tree to be locked into. Also, in "Dark Souls" your starting class could be "Sorcerer" but then you could eventually use ability points to level up into a warrior. I just don't see that happening with "Lords of the Fallen"
My next issue that is immediately apparent, is the horrid combat. I will admit it; the weapons feel great to use, and are very weighty. But something that comes with this is extremely heavy combat, most of which is just winding up for your next big swing, is that it feels extremely slow. The enemies move very quickly, and it is often just a waiting-game to see how long it takes to be able to hit them again. The combat is very clunky. I did try the faster class options, but that leads me to my next point. The rolling is disgusting. Rolling is critical in a game like "Dark Souls" because it is necessary to dodge attacks. And for faster classes (and sometimes in slower ones) rolling is critical. In the "Dark Souls" series, rolling feel snappy and responsive, but here it just feels like a big rotten mess. Also, they completely over-exaggerated the weight system. In "Dark Souls" all classes start off with weight that is much less than the capacity. Here, it starts you off with a bucket-load of weight, and the roll feels sloppy because of it. Even if you took off all your armor, the roll still feels unresponsive, and just generally off. I will talk more about the combat when we start to talk about bosses, but my last word on it is that it is great to swing the weapons, but getting there is an arrogance.
The bosses are boring and lackluster. They use the same moves over and over. Also, the second boss in the game in just horrendous. He keeps his shield up for half the fight! And I already learned his moveset by the time I was halfway down his health bar, so the rest of the fight was a breeze. You could argue that this is actually
game design, but the bosses could not have been more dull. The second boss that i mentioned earlier only had 3 moves of note! And one of those moves rendered him invincible until you killed some random throw-away enemies! Also, in different attack, he rained down little explosions from the sky that dealt about a fourth of your health. This is okay. But what is
okay  is that they are
. This means that no matter where you are, you could get a fourth of your precious health stolen away. In a game that is supposed to be challenging, but rewarding, you cannot make the challenge something that it random! If you do, then how do you expect the player to become better at beating the boss through trial and error? There is no way the player could know where those explosions are going to fall. With a bad combat system, the bosses
to be interesting, varied, and fair. But they aren't.
Now for the story. The story is unique, but certainly not in a good way. So many things are going on at once. You have a friend, and then you kill a boss, and then that friend is missing even though you saw him hit the wall and fall in the same room as you, then you find a woman and she's trying to kill someone,
do you save him? God, nobody
. Also, there's some weird stuff going on with these demons or something? And their excuse for these guys showing up is "They just came out of nowhere." A better excuse would've been "We needed the player to fight some stuff before the first few bosses." One of the first quests that you get is "Save your friend!" (the one that hit the wall earlier) I do not care about my friend. I, as a player, do not have a personal connection with this "friend" so I do not care whatsoever. This man is utterly pointless to me; I just met him! All I know is that the man I am playing likes this guy, I don't why, he just does. This could have been something so much more. Maybe the quest could've been something like "Meet up with survivors!" That would have been much more interesting. You could've met up with them and made a group. Then you could've gone to the hub area or whatever. That story is much more interesting than the one about this "friend". The story is very choppy and mixed up. I feel like it doesn't know what it wants to be. It is all over the place.
Now for the performance. This game runs like a fat man jogging on a treadmill for the first time in his life. When walking around a bit, you will often see black bars at the bottom of your screen for no apparent reason. Maybe it is loading the next section in the backround or whatever, but it is extremely noticeable. Also, the game will start to get very bad framerates for what seems like no reason! This is pretty much the same as my last complaint, but I feel it needs to be addressed anyway. The only good thing this game has going for it is that it doesn't freeze up too much in the boss fights. The performance is probably the least important of all the gripes I have with this game, but it is annoying and distracting.
On a final note, I will have to say that this game is bad. It had a lot of potential to be something amazing, but I don't think it really hit it this time. It needed to fix it's problems. A lot of people like a lot of different games, but if you come in to this game expecting an experience like "Dark Souls", but with a neat twist, I'm afraid you won't get one. Overall, this game is just not worth your time. Its combat is dull. And combat is what you will be doing most of the game. So, by extension, the game is dull.
Final Score:
6/10
