The Walking Dead by Telltale Games is an episodic video game based on the popular Comic Book series of the same title which was made mainstream by an equally popular TV series, also of the same title. The game features 5 'Episodes' with a 6th Episode as DLC. It boasts an outstanding plot, great characters and immersive choice and consequence based storytelling.
You are Lee Everett, a professor on his way to prison for the murder of a US State Senator who was having an affair with Lee's wife. The game starts with Lee at the back of a police car when he met an accident that wounded him and killed his officer escort. All hell breaks loose when he discovers that the dead now walks and is hungry for human flesh but, in his desperate search for help, he stumbles across a young girl named Clementine. Follow their struggles as they try to survive a terrifying and deadly world in this post-apocalyptic suspense game where every choice you make directly impacts the lives of the people around you.
+ Great use of 3D cell-shaded art style
+ Excellent example of Consequence based choices and Story (The game's biggest selling point)
+ Great Story
+ Great voice acting
+ Memorable characters
+ True to the Comics source material
+ Good game time and nice replayability
+ Guilt inducing choices
+ Stress inducing choices
- Restrictive camera
- Very small maps with no room for exploration (I don't mean it should be sandbox, but it would have been nice if the players had more leg room)
- Gameplay is a bare minimum (not much to do)
- Some choices have no real impact to the overall plot
- Tendency to have some boring scenes and segements
GREAT GAME. RECOMMENDED for both fans of the comics and gamers who are into good stories and plots. The Walking Dead by Telltale Games is the best example of immersive consequence based storytelling I have ever had the pleasure of experiencing. The story is top notch with a well written and well round characters who were excellently voiced. The art style works in the game's favor as the cell-shaded world captures the look, feel and tone of the comics.
Gameplay, sad to say, is a bare minimum, nothing to do more than make decisions. Some of the action sequences are heart pounding, but in it's core, its just a regular Quick Time Event scenario. The game also suffers from a restrictive camera with some odd angles. Despite these though, the game is still WORTH IT whether it be full price or sale price. This is a MUST HAVE game even for just the experience.

You see, this game is an example of why I wish Steam's rating system allowed another option other than thumbs up/down.
On the plus side this game has beautiful visuals, great music, fantastic atmosphere and an ending guaranteed to get you right in the feels.
On the down side the puzzles can often be a touch on the unintuitive side. The game plonks you down in the world and gives you next to no prompting as to what your meant to do. There are points in this game that there is no shame at referring to a walkthrough (in chapter 2 there are two puzzles in the same area that will require you to do things that you have never done before without any form of clue). Also I did encounter a glitch in chapter 3 (the wall runes puzzle) which required me to have to repeatedly enter the solution many times as it would not register that the sequence had been added.
Negatives aside I did enjoy my time with this game. Would I recomend it?.. Errrrrrrrrr.......Well...
First, I would not pay the full price for it. Get it on a sale. If you are really into point & click adventures then I would say it is worth checking out. Unintuitive as it is it really does get easier as the game progresses and you get the hang of the logic (with a few notable exceptions that I have mentioned).
Second, if you are not a point & click adventure game fan or are new to the genre then this is not the game for you. There are points that are hair pullingly frustrating and it really does not throw you many bones as to what you should be doing.
All in all, yes. If its on sale and your a fan of the genre get it.

Telltale's The Walking Dead restored my faith in the adventure game genre. Rather than focusing on obtuse puzzles, TWD is a title that dives deep into decision-making and characterization. In fact, it's akin to the 1980s "Choose Your Own Adventure" books than games like Gabriel Knight.
The puzzles aren't particularly strong, but TWD emotionally connects you to characters in ways rarely seen in the video game medium. Lee, the player character, and Clementine, his ward, will go down in history as one of gaming's best duos. If you want a different take on the zombie apocalypse, this is your game.

Its optimization is comparable to that of the worst ports in PC gaming history. Seriously, I can run pretty much every game flawlessly with no FPS or net lag on the highest settings, but here there's massive performance drops in terms of framerate and latency.
I'm playing on the European server and I never get anything below 200ms ping, even though I live in the city next to the one in which the server is situated.
There's a crap ton of bugs, too.  Unless you appreciate invisible walls that shouldn't exist, crashing every time you start up the game or enter a map, objectives spawning out of boundaries, objective zones being limited to a tiny area that's far from the actual objective (in larger dungeons anyway),♥♥♥♥♥♥poor world-gen, etc. I don't think you'd be very happy with this game.
Even with those problems, I found the game worth playing, because you had so many things you could do and it was one of the few games that were truly free to play. You could essentially buy anything you wanted just by playing the game a little every day, except cosmetic items. Just the way an ideal MMO that's not P2W should be, right?
Well, they're changing that. They decided that they aren't making enough money and the only way to fix that is by making things that are necessary for game progression behind a pay wall. While you can technically grind for these things, it will be especially difficult for new players since, well... You technically need a certain degree of game progression before you have access to features of the game like gliding, challenges and shadow towers/arenas. Incidentally, the latter two are also your main way of making money. So have fun with that.
Honestly, though, I have most game content unlocked and this update doesn't affect me in the slightest, but I have enough of a conscience to turn new players away and boycott the game, because they're compromising fun and performance for nothing more than money, which I find to be completely deplorable of game developers and publishers to do.

A nice point-n'-click adventure. Not really a puzzle p-n'-c, but more of an atmospheric one. Gameplay takes around an hour, which isn't bad for the normal price of $7.
Storyline is pretty generic, little girl gets teddy bear stolen and gets transported to
a forest and proceeds to be helpful. That said, the art is very well done, and you can tell the developers packed a lot of love into the game. The animations are very smooth, and the little attentions to detail really take the cake.
My one complaint is that I feel like they must've ran out of time to complete the game. You unlock a musical alphabet throughout the game, and finishing the game really only requires half of the letters. I feel like it must've been planned for the player to unlock all the letters during the gameplay, but those sections of the game were either trimmed or never completed. Also supporting this train of thought is the fact you have 6 item slots, but will never have 6 items at once. The extra letters you're missing when you finish the game just get added to your codex when you spin up a New Game+ (which also feels a little out of place as nothing changes between the original and NG+ versions of the story.)
Overall, the experience was enjoyable for the price I paid ($1.79 on sale). You definitely don't have to play NG+ to get the whole game, that's only if you're an achievement hunter and want that juicy 100%.

Bayonetta is a spectacle fighter that originally released for consoles in 2009. The game has finally ported over to PC, and is still as good as I remember.
I'll start off by quickly saying that the PC Port is great. Textures look better than they used to, it runs at 60fps, you have mouse control in menus and can rebind keyboard controls.
Now that being said, I still prefer to play games of this genre on a controller, so that's what I did. Although, I did test the keyboard/mouse controls and it's definitely playable.
Onto the game itself. You play as Bayonetta. A witch that feels the need to fabulously pose in all sorts of over the top ways while you fight, and it is really a joy to watch. Combat feels so meaty in this game, with spells shooting out different colours, loot and gore flying everywhere while you string your combos together. It's really fluent and satisfying.
The combat mainly consists of combining your light and heavy attacks in different ways. Depending on the orders you press them, the directions you move in or how long of a break you take before pressing the next button, you will perform a variety of moves. Equipping different weapons also changes your attacks.
You can also freely incorporate your guns into combos whenever you want. Including your foot guns. Yes, she has guns on her shoes as well.
New enemies are constantly introduced throughout the game to keep it from getting stale. You will have to adapt to their moves, and can sometimes even pick up their weapons to temporarily use against their allies.
Obviously you'll need to make sure your health doesn't deplete, but you also have a magic gauge that will drain if you get hit. Upon filling it up, you can perform "torture" attacks that will inflict a huge amount of damage on enemies. They usually include stuff like kicking enemies into Iron maidens or guillotines. It feels awesome to watch, but each "torture machine" is unique to different enemy types. If you fight a few enemies of the same type, you might find yourself doing the same torture attack repeatedly, which can get tedious at times since it requires that you button mash or spin your mouse/analogue stick.
When you kill enemies, you gather their halos in order to spend them in the store. Here you can buy weapons, accessories that grant you powers like invincibility or cloning upon activation. As well as consumable items or costumes. Items are quite expensive, so it might take you a bit of time to gather enough money to really afford a lot of stuff.
Depending on how well you do in a chapter, you will earn a larger bonus of money. Every fight you partake in will be rated individually. The speed at which you complete the fight, your combo intricacy or number of hits taken all factor into your final score. This is great for replay value, and it's pretty satisfying when you score higher up.
Although, I feel like scoring very high in some areas on your first playthrough is really difficult, and will require revisiting that chapter once you've upgraded.
All the gameplay feels super rewarding and is just so much fun to play. Although the story isn't the selling factor behind the game, it had me gripped enough. Bayonetta is quite likable as a provocative, cheeky anti-hero, and the mystery behind her past is quite intriguing.
One relatively big gripe I have with the game is the inconsistency behind cutscenes. Some of them are animated great. Fluent, and look nice. While the other half are still images that shift back and forth as if you're looking at a slide-show. I'm not sure why they went with this. Obviously it was cheaper and easier to make, but that's not something you generally see in the base game. It's something developers typically do in DLCs. It's not a huge problem, because it gets the story across and they're still mildly interesting looking, but it would have been much nicer if everything was beautifully animated the whole time.
Although the music is decent, you won't be hearing it much over the combat sounds without turning it up, and it seems the me the same fight music is played over and over throughout the game. I didn't get tired of it though, which is surprising. Perhaps it's because I could barely hear it. It does successful set the mood for Bayonetta's personality though, which is nice.
Overall, I'm having a tonne of fun playing through the game a 2nd time after all these years, at 60fps. Boss fights feel epic, combat is satisfying and tight, the writing can be pretty funny at times, and it's just a cheesy fun experience to go through. Big props to the devs for reflecting the game's age in its price. I think for how cheap it is, if you are a fan of the genre, definitely do yourself a favor and pick the game up!

Fractured Space has evolved rapidly over the last year, and thanbkfully the developers have eliminated nearly all of the glitches and failed connection issues in the matchmakeing system. The game mechanics are well balanced and it runs great on most mid level PC platforms. The controlls and strategy have been made easy to grasp for beginners, but remain complicated ehough that hardcore guys can get invested in them.
PROS: Fractured space was a qnigue concept at the time of its early access launch. The orbital science fiction elemests and arcade phisics esssentally add a Z axis to what would otherwise be a naval combat game. The simplicity of naval combat simulators have incressed recent and Fractured Space's initial idea is appearing on other games like World of Warships. That said its still an uncommon idea that adds a waft of fresh air to the steam market.
The typical initial learning curve is about an hour, and the system matches you with bots in initial multiplayer matches so that you can practice, gradually introducing live players who match your skill untill you become compeditive.
The typical match is about twenty minutes, but there are no cutoff timers so two good teams can go at it for a ling time, with the longest match I have ever played lasting just over thirty minues.
CONS: There is no single player campign, plot, or story, to contectualize events in this game at all. Something it would greatly benifit from given that crew characters with names and faces have been thought of. Alongside a lor of concept are that is included in the interface that shows a lively world that we really dont see any of. This is clearly a world that could easily have these elements, but I have heard no mention of them anywhere.
The turd in the carpet for me has always been microtransaction systems because they are manipulative and nearly always result in games that require rediculus and protracted economics in order to unlock everything. These games almost always have random number slot machine dynamics that keep you from only buying the things you want, and these games are in a near constant fight between the non paying playerbase that demans balance, and the paying playerbase that demands a good reason to pay for extras.
Fractured Space shows signs of this fight in its game store in that you have two entirely different kinds of objects for sale, Skins and Modifiers. Skins are cosmetic changes to how a ship looks, and modifiers are crew, implants, or boosters which change how a ship performs in a given match. You get a starter crew, but no implants, which means that players who pay for implants early on have a performance advantage over players who dont. Crews and implants can be earned over time, but a long long long time. Having bought into this early I have about half of the crews needed. As I have played, new implementations of the game economy have gradually increased the amount of time between crew unlocks dramaticly.
The problem is that the effect crew and implants have is minor, to the point that an attentive free player could theoritically outmaneuver or out strategize a pay player. Which makes the varous packs they offer kind of mute, even when they have been on sale I struggle to find a reason to buy them because I cant controll what implants I get in the dedicated packs, and crew pods can give out the same crew over and over, in which case the crew gets autotraded for DNA, one of the three available in game currencies. Its designed to make it exponentally more difficult to unlock the last half of the available crew options.
I can recommend Fractured Space overall, but new players should understand that they are jumping onto a treadmeal that seems to get longer with ever update, one which has alienated me as an older 90's era gamer, and one which the younger generation seems all to eager to accept as "just the way it is". I still play and I still have fun playing, but I get irritated every time I finish a match and get awarderd what little earnings each match gives me as a vanguard player.
It takes over a month of frugal in game currency saving to afford the largest implant or crewpod pack in game for free. The thought of that, alongisde the constant reminders of how you could just buy platnum and get it now almost mocks me, because the economy is made so that you have to buy platnum in tiers that the random content packs all fall between, so you have to buy more platnum than you actually need in order to buy the packs themselves.
If developers what to have microtransactions fine, but please have an "unlock everything option" available so that people like me know exactly what the maximum possible spending amount is and can choose to skip all the randum number BS.
Also, just let me spend real money off my credit card for exactly what I want to get in the game. If I want to gamble, I'll drive an hour down to Las Vegas and hit the slots, at least then I have a chance, however reomte, to walk away with actual money.

Good game. Being so long, the most difficult part is probably remaining patient and invested in the game for the duration. Each lapse in conscetration and failure to mitigate for potential RNG scenarios is met with brutal party wipes that erase hours (sometimes days) of grinding a party out.
Personally, I enjoy when a game pisses me off and forces me to walk away and come back when I'm more clear-headed. Darkest Dungeon shines in that respect.
Art is good, combat is always challenging and keeps you re-working strategies, dungeons are good, with neat pathing choice and party management mechanics. But all of these aspects can become repetitive once the grind sets in, as it will.
Many people complain about the RNG-hell piece, but the game in designed to be punishing...that's it's entire schtick. Luck certaintly plays a role, but understanding of the mechanics, the classes and squad comp are just as important.
Surely not for everyone, but I would reccomend to those interested in a long-form, paitence-testing, well-crafted, rogue-like game.

There’s something oddly wonderful about a game trying to recreate niche, and bizarre parts of history. None more than OMSI, a game which sets out to lovingly recreate buses/routes in Berlin. Not just Berlin, but more specifically the Spandau district from 1980’s – 1990’s, a very peculiar, and to most of us obscure part of history. But does it succeed?
Let’s make one thing clear, this is not ETS2. It’s not lavished with game style game play mechanics about levelling up your character, running your company, and customizing your vehicles. Nor is it all that user friendly, or really all that approachable. This is a hardcore simulation, with hardcore simulation style lack of game play. The premise is as simple as coul  be, choose a bus. Choose a route. Drive..
Gameplay
The buses are very nicely recreated, with a full array of working features on the dashboard, from the usual wipers, lights, adjustable suspension (on the more modern buses) and fully functioning computers, and ticket machines. Although unless you speak German, good luck getting your head around those. Thankfully, you can set your bus up using the rather basic, but functional in game UI.
The game does have a rather steep learning curve, while it does have tutorials these are next to useless, so your pretty much on your own. Getting in to a position where you can pick up your first passengers, is rather more than just selecting a job, and pressing E to start your engine, and putting the bus in to gear and driving. Every button on the dashboard does something some of these things are more useful than others.
If your patience lasts long enough to get your head around the rather steep learning curve, you’ll quickly find the game is actually quite enjoyable in a mundane, driving a city bus kind of way. Driving your assigned route, you’ll of course be stopping at bus stops, picking up rather badly animated but very amusing robotic passengers, selling them tickets, and all the usual things expected from a bus driver. The simulation of this goes quite deep, even down to them complaining, if the bus is cold.
The actual driving of the bus feels very nice, and really the developers have managed to create the feeling of driving a very large, cumbersome heavy vehicle, turns will be taken slowly, and much care has to be taken when weaving in and out of parked cars, and other obstacles scattered around the lovingly created depiction of Berlin. Upon hitting something, the passengers, which by now you have become belligerent towards, will swear, and shout at you in German demanding to get off.
Sound:
The sound is absolutely spectacular, and a real master class in how the sound should be in these types of games, it’s incredibly atmospheric, and really transported me back to the 80s/90s as a kid travelling to school on those old double decker buses. From the whine of knackered old diesel engine, to the wind blowing in to the slightly open window, the bus rattling and banging as it chugs down the road. Its absolutely superb, and other developers of simulators should certainly take note.
Physics:
As said already, the basic driving physics are excellent, however the other world physics, are more hilarious than anything else. With vehicles catapulting about in an accident, or humping the ground, people being swallowed by the floor. It all makes for some highly amusing, if immersion breaking moments.
Control devices:
It’s a given that a game like this is best played with a wheel, rather than state the obvious, I think its best to discuss other control devices, not everyone owns a wheel.
Controller:
The mainstay of driving games, for those without a wheel at least. Unfortunately, using a controller is next to impossible. The over sensitivity of the Xbox 360 controller is not accounted for at all, no dead zones are added or able to be added. The stick simply functions as a wheel, which makes controlling the bus immensely sensitive, and next to impossible. Don’t even bother.
Keyboard:
While the keyboard is completely indispensable, with the massive array of functions, and systems, all of which you will need to control, driving with it is, really as to be expected. The game uses the numpad by default. 4 Turns left, 6 turns right, and 5 centres the steering. While its more than possible to drive using the keyboard, keyboards don’t feature any analogue devices, everything of course is either on or off, which can make for some pretty heavy accelerating and braking, which is usually met by lots of angry German swearing from the passengers.
Mouse:
This is my preferred method for controlling the game. Generally I hate mouse driving, its over sensitive, has very little feedback, or makes very little sense. But the developers of Omsi have definitely cracked it. Move the mouse up to accelerate, down to brake, and of course left and right steer. If you don’t have a wheel this is my recommended method of controlling it. The only drawback, is steering, and accelerating at the same time can be rather difficult, and tends to be a little haphazard.
The bad:
While I would like to say “The game is a triumph buy it immediately!”. That really isn’t the case. OMSI 2 is as awful as it is brilliant, an incredibly mixed bag. As already said, its not very approachable, a lot of the options, the controls list, and other things are not put together in a very user friendly or coherent way, at times it feels like it was designed by a madman! Even when trying to work out /change the controls The list seems to almost be randomly thrown together, without much regard for the poor player who has to find his/her way through it. In a game like this, which has an awful lot of controls, this really does make for frustration, and swearing.
In general the game is incredibly unpolished, mostly using simple OS ui windows to control various functions. More often than not, these windows can make little to no sense at first glance, and can take a quite some time to get used to.
Stability:
The games stability is atrocious, and really, unacceptable. The game quits to desktop on a regular basis, randomly fails to load, and throws up a lot of errors usually in German, leaving you with little idea as to what actually happened. Sounds will just stop working, and all manner strange things will happen. For a game that’s been out a year (longer if you count the original) these really are issues that should no longer be present.
Navigation:
This is done by a simple overlay with arrows pointing you in the direction and icons over the stops you need to stop at. While this sounds just basic but functional, at times, it can be incredibly confusing. You’ll get arrows pointing you off towards other routes, which have nothing to do with yours, at times it offers you absolutely no direction at all, and other times it just sends you off down side streets your not supposed to go down, or tries to send you down 1 way roads (of course the wrong way)
Content:
The base lacks a serious amount of content The map really isn’t that big, and you have a very small number of routes to drive. Simply put, I doubt it will have much lasting appeal.
Final thoughts:
This game is actually quite annoying. It’s very solid, and very well made in parts but has far too many glaring issues. While I did enjoy it, It’s certainly not something I can whole heartedly recommend. I actually find it quite annoying, the potential is vast. Should it be given ETS 2’s spit, polish, and level of content, I can’t help but feel it would actually be a superior game, capable of knocking ETS 2 off my favourite simulator spot. But in its current state, its incredibly rough around the edges, and falls very short. If you enjoy simulators, and are looking for something new, you might like this one. But don’t go in to it expecting a complete or approachable, product, it isn’t.

TL;DR
Lords of the Fallen is nice.
Not as great as Dark Souls, but good in it's own way.
Don't let your love of Dark Souls get in the way of seeing the game for it's own merits.
---Ok, rest of the Review is here---
It's definitely a slowed down process. More realistic fighting. Bosses are Dark Souls like, but aren't the unstoppable lightning blitz that most of Dark Souls bosses are. There's this one boss, the second one I faced, he has a tower shield he likes to hide behind a lot, it's a very slow-paced, watching animations and examining your opponent kind of boss. I managed to get that fight first try, not because the boss was easy, but because I watched him carefully from a distance and judged out all his distances, figured out all his patterns, and then danced in and walloped him.
I see a lot of people complaining that it gets most of Dark Souls wrong. It's like they expected it to be a straight up copy/paste of dark souls. On the one hand, yeah I see myself falling into a lot of Dark Souls habits. On the other, It's NOT DARK SOULS.
A lot of people complain about the combat being "clunky" or "sticky". It's not, It's just
. The characters don't move as quick as Dark Souls characters do. Once I got into a proper pace and rythym, all my tricks started working again.
A lot of people have been complaining about character customization. Because it's SO IMPORTANT that you be able to make a blueberry skinned, rictus-grinning lardball? (An extreme example I know.) I actually like that I actually have a character to play as, and not a mute, hyper-violent murderhobo. (Not that Harkyn isn't violent himself, but he actually reacts to things around him, instead of watching things with a blank stare on his face.) Maybe he is sort of a walking cliche storm of the grizzled old adventurer, I'm still enjoying the story.
To use a metaphor: You don't throw out Sausage because it's not Bacon, right? I mean, Sausage is still good, even if Bacon is better.
LotF is the Sausage to Dark Souls Meat Candy Baconness.

It's a good game. Cool concept and I love it. That being side, it's grindy and punishy. Here's what you do.
Mods:
raven (class)
anti grind + larger roster
stacking mod
assist class mod (for all healer types)
and a game speedup mod for animations
Level cap removing mod (so your level 5s and 6s can go whomp level one dungeons quickly and reward you.
After you get the mods in the workshop you go to play your save but before you click on your save file, to the right is a hammer you can click on to activate your mods.
Menu:
Go into advanced options or whatever and de-click all the annoying stuff like corpses stay after you kill a character, characters dont always escape, etc.
Gameplay:
When the Vvulf comes after you, you have two options. Send your level sixs with levelled gear and try to kill it so it doesn't show up again
or
Your guys are too weak so send four of your weakest guys even level 0 characters to go lose so he deosn't delevel your town.
Once you kill him you'll never need weak characters again, assuming you have the no level cap mod.
At this point you have a pretty balanced game. Start looking up team combinations and strategies if you need further help. There is still punishing against bad boss combos but The punishments aren't so severe to come back from.

A great hacking game with a story too linear. 8/10
People are saying Hacknet is Uplink but better. I'm saying Hacknet is a derivative work of Uplink.
Uplink can be seen as an "open world" game. The goal is simple; do contract work, get money, upgrade your stuff. There's a "story" involved but you can completely ignore it if you so wish.
Hacknet is more linear. There isn't much beside the story. There is contract work, but its point is to just advance in the story. You're locked out of some of the contract work after advancing through a certain point in the story. You cannot get money or upgrade your gear, you're limited to the same amount of RAM and power you have.
Based on what I said, Hacknet can be seen as a bad game, but it's everything but bad. The gameplay is amazing. The interface is well fit for what it's used for. The story is very appealing and really clutches on you to take you with it.
The game simulates a command line environment quite well, but is missing some really basic stuff you'd expect to find. The tab autocomplete is lacking. You cannot create files or folders, so you're locked to any files or folders the game gives you. There isn't a text editor, so your only way of editing files to use a
command. Then again, the game clearly isn't directed at experienced command line users, but rather to newcomers (or "skiddies", the game even calls you such at one point) who may have never used a command line.
Doing the hacking is not complicated at all. You don't have to memorise complicated command calls or signatures, you just run the right command at the right time. Most of the time you don't even need to use the command line, since usually there's a button to click or a scrollbar to drag.
I was expecting a tad more realistic simulation of a command line, but the game is really good nevertheless. It took me about 5 hours to beat, after of which there isn't anything sensible to do. There are small secrets scattered around to look for and discover, if you like easter egg hunting.

I'm not bombing this game because of crappy paid mods, or whatever the current whiny complaint of the week is that seems so prevalent amongst gamers these days. I'm giving it a negative because after about ten hours of play its become monumentally tedious.
Having purchased this about 6 months ago I thought I'd finally give it a shot, despite knowing full well that the Bethesda template is just as over used and underdeveloped as anything Ubisoft churns out.
I liked Morrowind, but after that its just the same bloated dull gameplay over and over again....Skyrim / Fallout  - the only difference is: in one game you stab things to death in a simplistic fashion, in the other you shoot them.
Same huge map with no actual proper gameplay in it - naff action, naff stealth, and unlike Skyrims mild saving graces - no puzzles or setpieces.
But hey! you get a ton of "content" and a 100 hours of play for your money....yayyy! Nevermind that it's consistently mediocre.....at least you get your moneys worth. Which in my case was £20, hence taking a chance on a game I pretty much knew would be dull as ditchwater.

Traipsing all over the map becomes tedious. Picking up one zillion items of useless junk, and constantly running out of inventory space, becomes tedious.
After 12 hours something broke inside of me. I didn't care about the quests anymore, and I decided the only thing of interest left is to murder every NPC in the game. I met a woman from the Covenant, who was against synthetic creatures that pass as human. She had a captive who she believed to be a synth.
I killed the woman from the Covenant.
Then I killed the hostage too.
Briefly I felt some enjoyment come back.
But then I did a hugely boring extended shootout in a power plant, that just seemed to be an endless amount of winding gantrys. And my enthusiasm for mass murder dried up - too much of a chore just to get some fun from the game.
This is a marmite title - you like Bethesda games? bully for you - tuck in. For me - it's marginally more intersting than watching paint dry, and a thumbs down.

Definitely a decent arcade-racer, but it gave me the same impression GRiD 2 did: It's not sure what it wants to be, and it just ends-up feeling mushy.
Drifting, as you'd imagine, is a central mechanic in games of this genre. And while they do require practice & nuance to do well in Unbounded, they just never feel good to pull off, and feel wildly inconsistent most of the time.
After I figured-out the drifting was something I didn't enjoy (even when I got decent with them), I tried to just race clean & fast, and take corners with an optimal driving-line instead. And surprisingly, it worked-out, and I actually got rewarded for finding ways to take tough corners at optimal speed (even just barely touching a wall can knock-off a lot of your momentum). Not something I expected from an arcade-racer, and I got some enjoyment out of that aspect.
And now, the issue of rubber-banding: Surprisingly, Unbounded does NOT have it. Or, at least, I couldn't tell if it was there. If I raced really well and maintained optimum speed on corners, I would usually be 2-or-3 seconds ahead of my opponents, and I'd stay that far ahead for the duration of the race - they'd only encroach if I messed something up. Although, courses with lots of straight-aways are another story: They usually inexplicably sped ahead of me during long stretches of track, even if I was way ahead of them on the last corner. Not a huge issue, but it can feel unfair when the AI magically speed past you if the finish-line is at the end of a long piece of track.
What I want out of a racer is either a) an authentic simulation that rewards good driving or b) a crazy arcade game that still has its nuances. Unbounded doesn't deliver either for me. Its drifting feels really bad, so that cuts-out the arcadey-but-naunced aspect for me. And the physics & handling are too arcadey to make optimal driving-lines feel good, so it's not in the authentic category either. It feels like a strange game that has no identity.
Unbounded's definitely not a bad game by any means, but there are many, many other better racers out there. Play them instead.

XCOM 2 does everything it can to fix the problems with the original game, and pretty much succeeds. There's randomly generated levels, more timed missions, a new stealth mechanic, and more sensible enemy movement to discourage the broken overwatching strategy, and a lovely helping of new skills, soldiers, items and enemies to play with. The problem is, it doesn't feel particularly new, instead acting like a big bandage on problems that existed in the previous game without bringing too many completely new things to the picture. As such, I can absolutely recommend it to people who haven't played the prequel (which should be nobody, because that game was incredible) but have to be more muted in recommending it to people who did play it. You likely won't invest as many hours in this one, unless you tinker with mods and higher difficulties. It's the difference between the nearly 20 years between X-Com and XCOM, and the four years between XCOM and XCOM 2.

Behold my attempt to review this game! TLDR? Fantastic game that wants you to react to the worst of situations.
Darkest Dungeon is a game about how you handle bad situations. Perfectly summed up after the opening cinematic. Quests will fail, heroes will die, and its up to you to make the most of bad situations. This personifies everything this game is about. Going in with the mindset that the game is fair and willing to meet you halfway in order to ensure your success is the viewpoint for most of the negative reviews. This game is not fair, will not hold your hand, and expects you make the best of what it throws at you. Its almost as if Darkest Dungeon says, “I bet you can’t beat me.” This choice of difficult and unfair gameplay blends masterfully well with its artistic choice of depressing hopelessness displayed in everything from the music, narrator, gameplay, and beautifully hand drawn gothic art style.
I believe that a game should be judged based on what it sets out to be, why hamper a game because of its difficulty if it wants to be difficult by design? This is how this review is going to structured: based off what it wants to be and where it succeeds and fails based of its mark.

Art Style
The first thing to notice about this 2D side scroll is the art style; hand drawn, gothic, and stylized. From the hopeless heroes being sent to slaughter, to the destroyed hamlet, the four different dungeon types, and the monsters and bosses that inhabit them, they all blend well as they should and strongly convey a grotesque dark style.
Sound/Music
The music is absolutely amazing on how it seeks to reinforce the themes that the art style sets out. The music uses the strings to display the games main theme that matches the hopelessness really reinforcing the motif. What music is there is done well and even changes to a match the more unsettling progression as light in the dungeons dim. However, the biggest problem for the music is how little of it there is. 80+ hours into the game and you have heard what this game has to offer over 80 times over. In an era where indie games lead the charge with breathtaking soundtracks, this one just offers to little for how long the game is intended to last to the point where you’ll probably just turn it off as you get bored with the repetition as you journey father into the dungeons.
Going along with the concept of sound, the narrator truly personifies the game with his excellence performance. His stinging insults and crestfallen mood never gets old. An absolute fantastic job done by Wayne June.

Gameplay (buckle down or skip this section :P)
The main hook (heh get it? Red hook? ... heh.) is the gameplay. Where the art and music build the atmosphere, the turn based combat side scroll, while simple on the surface is a little more complex than it might seem.  Combat is done in groups of 4 vs 4… or less and you have over 15 classes to assemble your rag tag band of adventures around to fit your own play style. Important to note: some compositions work better than others and not all classes work well in all of the four environments, and the placement of your four dudes in the four different ranks is key. This is also true for the enemy groups, which is important to keep in mind.  The procedural dungeon floors keep you on your toes as you try to navigate through encountering many things to interact with that can bring you the much-needed treasure to build your characters and enhance the hamlet, or total misfortune and ruin. And lets not forget the groups of enemies lurking as well. There are also plenty of bosses and they’re not spectacular or revolutionary but they aren’t too generic either… I’ll end there and let you make your decisions on the bosses :p
What makes the otherwise simple incredibly interesting.
The simplistic turn based combat is greatly affected by three great systems. Light, Insanity, and Quirks,
The Lighting system is unique and blends really well with the dungeon crawling. As you progress your light diminishes, and as light diminishes your chances to find sweet loots increases as well as your critical chance. But negative affects are abound with an increased chance of your party being surprised, increased monster damage, accuracy, critical chance, as well as increased stress being inflicted on your poor souls.
And what a great segue into the Stress system. This makes the combat pretty spicy as not only do you have to handle your party’s HP, now you have to worry about them having heart attack too. Various things will inflict stress on your heroes including certain enemies (those ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s) and managing it is key to coming out of the dungeon with all heroes alive. Stress is measured on a scale of 200, if you hit 100 stress on a hero they will either breakdown, or become your 11th hour hero. This is what really makes this game interesting, if stress builds up too high you may have a masochist who denies healing, a coward skipping turns, or a crestfallen sod that loves to inflict stress on other members. Ooorrr you’ll get valiant hero to (hopefully) save the day.
Quirks are the last system to affect gameplay and they do so passively. As you no doubt touch things in the dungeons, level up, or have a preexisting condition your heroes will attract quirks, both positive a negative which will affect gameplay in many different ways depending on the quirk. However, here lies a great fault of the game. Most quirks explain themselves such as increased scouting chance, or plus 20% stress. But some quirks don’t… such as kleptomania. What does that entail, yes we know it means they’re prone to steal, but what does that exactly mean? Other quirks face the same failure of explanation. And they can be very detrimental if you remain ignorant to them. This forced me on a trip the wiki to explain what some of these unexplained quirks do. Which absolutely shatters the immersion. I do NOT want to have to go to the wiki to explain something that should already be explained INSIDE the game.  The thing is, this could easily be fixed with a patch but nope… instead the game would favor kicking you to a spoiler abound wiki breaking the immersion and atmosphere, which they worked so hard to build.
All that being said, the game splits its dungeons in the three difficulty types an easy, medium and hard. As well as into three measures of length, short, medium, and long. I’ll leave you to decide how those descriptions match up. c:
The Answer to the games biggest problem.
Overall, Preparation is key to survival; your favorite heroes depend on your forethought and investment to guide them through the dungeon. But there are some things you simply can’t prepare for and that is RNG. This is the main gripe people have with this game and yes, a simple mob in the hard dungeons did crit my hero for 30 HP and sent that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to deaths door and the next mob booted him right into the after life. RNG will often not be on your side, and some people don’t see that as fair, you invested tons of gold in cultivating your hero from a stagecoach meat sack into a valiant hero pimped out with the best items and gear only to have a few spiders take him down. And yes, it is rage inducing which is why I will never play this game around other people. But slamming the game for this is only the fault of the player… first walking into a game built on RNG is a clear message that this can happen, and second there was a whole disclaimer telling you that this game is 100% NOT fair and NOT on your side. You precious cultivated heroes will die, its bound to happen. Needless to say, this sucks, everyone who plays this game feels the pain. But getting comfortable with Darkest Dungeon is the worst thing you can do, this game was not built for you not to get an easy win but instead is designed to see how you the player will make the most of a bad situation.

Darkest Dungeon has an excellent visual art style that's dark and filled with terrors. It's UI fits it so damn well. The sound and music design is top notch. The narration adds an excellent icing to the cake of the experience. The monster design is legitimately creepy. There's a making of a game of the decade here. Yet for all of its excellence, I have to say no. No to the RNG, no to the constant re-rolls, no to the constant waste of the player's time and the poor pacing that is rife throughout the entire experience.
I can handle being outplayed. But simply losing an hour-long run after building a band of characters for hours on end simply because the RNG decided "Nope, you die today" is one of the most discouraging aspects of playing this game. And then losing the next two follow parties for the same reason means you've basically started over at the beginning. Sure, you've got advanced buildings now but starting over again and again is a chore I'm just not interested in. It becomes less about skill, party management and just being damned lucky. And this game is ridiculously long. Even in the 37 hours I put in, I had only begun to see half of the supposed content in this game.
RNG is a tricky thing to balance but I simply think Darkest Dungeon goes too far towards RNG-hell and that's a game design I've become less and less tolerant of as time goes on. It's a great looker of a game, but it's core is one mean horrendous monster looking to kill you over and over while it whispers sweet things in your ears.

The game overall is not too bad since the graphic detail and animations are absolutely amazing--that being said if you plan to play this game on a PC you better meet Recommended (not minimum) System Requirements. If you do not have the recommended requirements, your frame rate will be tanking the entire time you're playing (around 15 to 40 fps MAX).
On another note, the campaign missions seem rather dull and no longer has me interested in finishing the rest of the game (the beginning missions before Arno became an Assassin were fine). The concepts behind the missions just aren't very appealing. The co-op mode, which was LONG overdue since the introduction of multiplayer in Assassin's Creed was finally delivered in Unity--but was not executed outstandingly. Although it is rather intriguing to see fellow Assassin's air-assassinate into the battle to assist you, the repetitiveness of the co-op missions gets overwhelming with the same formula of kill, investigate, steal, and other mindless objectives. Moving onto combat, I have no idea what happened but the combat in Unity just seems ridiculously difficult. You can slash all day but that enemy will NOT die unless you attack him at least 6-12 times. (Edit: I have finally figured out how to kill enemies faster, but that was only after upgrading the sword so you can actually do damage. Good luck getting enough money since the game is really stingy when providing means of income. The only way I got enough money was to grind the "It Belongs in a Museum" Heist which rewards you with $25,000-$70,000. You won't make enough money otherwise...) Meanwhile you have other enemies surrounding you to deal with, some which will shoot at you and most likely take 1/2 to 2/3 of your health away if the bullet hits you (maybe I missed a tutorial about meat shielding like the other games?? I don't know. As far as I know there's basically no effective way to not get shot and killed since you get stuck in kill animations). Furthermore, I personally do not approve of the new eagle vision that has a 10 or so second cooldown and only reveals targets for a FEW SECONDS (the minimap also doesn't tell you any information about enemies anymore unless they are revealed through eagle vision--this makes stealth much harder since you have to toggle eagle vision on and off constantly otherwise you have no clue where the enemies are on the minimap). On the plus side, the new eagle vision reveals EVERYONE within a certain radius from you, whether or not you directly look at them or they are hidden behind solid walls.
Overall, Assassin's Creed Unity seems to have lots of potential to keep the player entertained through the amazing graphics and partially enjoyable co-op mode (only when you play 4 man with some IRL friends), I would not recommend this game unless you have a really high-end computer. Anything below the recommended specifications and you will find a hard time "enjoying" the game. However, if the day comes that the game is substantially better in optimization (as in 50-60 fps for decent computer builds) Unity may restore its honor.
TL;DR Assassin's Creed Unity has great graphic detail, very poor optimization (consistently 15-40 fps), unforgiving combat system, a decent co-op mode that gets repetitive over time. Do not play on PC unless you have a top-tier graphics card and CPU.

I got the game in January 2015, after the initial disastrous launch with everyone having crashes at game launch etc.
The game actually played  nice for the first 30 mins , until after the first boss:
- I was running everything maxed out with Nvidia turbulence at 1080p, getting around 55-60 fps.
- my system specs are i7 4770k , 16 GB ram, 2x GTX770 evga  oc edition 2GB in SLi
After the bossfight and when the game transitions to the exterior, I started having huge random frame drops, going from 60 fps to 7-10 fps and the game became unplayable. This is unacceptable.
I had to disable nvidia turbulence, disable cromatic aberration (ugly and terrible decision to include this in the game) and disable most post processing options to get back to 50-80 fps.
Now my problem is that I get totally random crashes while playing (most of the time during boss fights, which is infuriating).
The game itself has decent story and good graphics but suffers from a problem: It wants to be a "Dark Souls Clone". And it fails.
If the devs would give the player the ability to save at any point, the game would probably last 3-4 hours max with all sidequests done, so this means the game is artificially lengthned by this gimmick saving point system.
Also the camera issues while fighting are real and most often than not responsible for ridiculous deaths of your char and more wasted time.
Fighting responsiveness is also close to none which on a fighting game really says it all. There will be plenty of times when your char will not respond accurately to the controls.
I would recommend this game ONLY if you get it on a sale around $10 (or lower) , it's not a AAA title in any way with this kind of technical issues.
At the current price point, in January 2015, please find something else to play as this game is somehow still in "beta testing".

Lords of the Fallen is the first "Souls game" I ever finished and I do not regret it one bit.
It’s a bit more forgiving than the Souls games and perhaps the balance is not as immaculate at different stages of the game, but it makes up for by the share amount of fun it brings to the table and by the much lighter atmosphere is has.

The bosses played out pretty much  similarly as well, just wait for the boss to pull off an attack with the longest cool down and strike him a few times and then retreat (repeat until dead). So little adjustments there would come a long way.
The story as such is pretty straight forward with a few alternative endings. I did like the ending but would have liked to see some more meaningful choices in the game and reflections of those choices in the end. But for an action RPG this is fine.

"It is possible to commit no mistakes and still lose. That is not a weakness; that is life."
~Captain Picard, Star Trek
~Also this game
Let me start off by saying that I feel this game has a lot of solid points. The art is great, the gothic atmosphere definitely sells dreary, if not spooky, and the narrator's voice is positively spine-tingling at first, and doesn't get old.
The premise, at least, is solid. Hire dudes, kill the evil dudes hanging out in the mansion, get better, don't get dead, win. You have two health bars - traditional health (you die at 0 hp, maybe) and stress (the bad guys can literally give you a heart attack.) And at first, the game is genuinely fun, atmospheric, and immersive, and if you're extroardinarily lucky, you won't see the game's fatal flaw until the best of your roster are about halfway up the ladder to greatness.
The fatal flaw, in case you didn't know, is the RNG. It is also why I cannot in good conscience recommend this game.
Which is extremely upsetting, because I -loved- Darkest Dungeon at first. It was everything I wanted out of a pseudo-roguelike, and it kills me to have to click the 'No' button. Unfortunately, this is a game that does not discriminate in its victims, and it can and will absolutely wreck your characters - and your mood - regardless of whether or not you make mistakes.
This game is not hard. Hard, in terms of difficulty, means (at least, to me) that the game will punish you more severely for making mistakes, but overall, if you are good - if your strategy is solid, your reflexes quick, or what have you - then you still have a reasonable chance of succeeding.
In this game, you can execute every move as flawlessly as possible, and the game will respond with a shrug and a coin flip as to whether or not you live or die, like some demented digital Two-Face.
I recall vividly sending my party out to clear out the ruins - they were all about 3 or 4, and it was a higher tier dungeon (my highest at that point,) so I was expecting the worst. Lo and behold, making my way (downtown) through a corridor, I am blind-sided by an enemy that I hadn't seen before, called the Collector. I felt a knot form in the pit of my stomach - this was it, this spooky skeleton ghost guy was gonna turn my party's faces into decorative ornaments to display to all of his skeleton friends at his skeleton tea parties... except he didn't. Seven turns later, my party emerges victorious with several gems worth their weight in gold, and nary a scratch on them. I was jubilant, nay, EXULTANT! Riding the high of my mighty conquest, I stormed into the next room, spirits burning bright and weapons ready.
Where I was surprised by a group of spiders, which rearranged my party order and melted half of them in 4 turns, and drove one of my two remaining idiots nuts.
I was gobsmacked. What the hell happened? Was it something I did? How could I have better prepared? I have no clue, and five minutes later I had abandoned the mission and closed the game, feeling extremely put out.
And therein lies the crux of the issue. If you've read this far, and you're looking for a summary, it is this: This game can and will brutalize you, regardless of whether or not you make mistakes. The RNG can turn a sure-fire victory into a ten minute slugfest, because everyone misses except that stupid pig with the stress bongos. Sure, it will, on occasion, turn certain death into a glimmer of hope - and that's dandy, but its a moot point, because that's like watching someone sucker punch someone else, then watch as they hand their victim an ice pack, and saying 'well golly gee, that's nice!'
Yes it is but YOU STILL PUNCHED HIM. He shouldn't need an ice pack because you shouldn't have punched him, and those 'Certain-death-into-one-in-a-million-victory' scenarios shouldn't happen because -THE RNG SHOULDN'T HAVE SCREWED YOU OVER LIKE THAT ANYWAY-.
You can do your best and still fail.
In real life, that sucks, but you bear with it because you have to.
In a video game, you stop playing, because -that's not fun.-
And there it is. Some people will argue that games are an art form - and I agree. If you enjoy art - if you don't necessarily play games to enjoy yourself, then sure, pick this up (on sale) and give it a whirl. If you want to experience literally any emotion other than fun/joy/happiness, then nab this game. It'll certainly make you feel something.
However, if you want to have fun, then spend your money somewhere else. You won't have fun here, you'll only have dead. And then also sad.

Stardew is a great game. It has a simple interface, easy controls, and is surpisingly addicting. There's something very alluring about making a quick mental list of things you need to do today, and then getting out there and doing them, only to create new items on your list as you go.
It takes a little while to get started, you have to clear out the rocks/sticks/trees on your farm, but then you start farming and making some money.
To occupy your time between farming, you can build up relationships with other villagers (and unlock special cutscene interactions with them), you can rebuild the community center, go fishing, go into the mines and fight monsters in a Zelda-lite format, or forage for goods.
This is the kind of game you intend to play just a little bit, and really sucks you in. Like civilization, you will be telling yourself "one more day" as you play into the evening. It will give you quite a few hours of entertainment (100+) before you can really say you've 'done it all'.
So in short, its a wonderful, peaceful, relaxing game that you may find playing far more than you intend. Check it out.

Very, very, very rarely do I come across a game that I end up playing a lot of hours on. The last ones were Warthunder, Dark Souls 3.......and then there's Fallout 4.
Graphics are gorgeous. But if, like me, you're still rocking an R9 270X 4GB or thereabouts, you'll probably slightly struggle on High (you definitely will on Ultra) settings as it's not a particularly well-optimised game.
Gameplay is amazing. You'll find yourself regularly using the massively improved VATS system. But normal gunplay is also excellent too.
Upgrade and crafting systems are good. Perk system is very good.
There's a tonne of brilliant and varied weapons. And shooting feels weighty, especially when you're blasting heads with your 50 calibre. There's even a gun that's literally a portable, handheld medieval cannon. And so much more.
The power armour is mint, and of course fully upgradeable. When you finally slap on your Jets you'll not be able to live without them.
As far as settlement building goes, I didn't bother really. I made the Rocket Shop my base of operations/home. I did make some simple colonies, though, and I did help settlements when they needed it etc. But I'm not bothered about building huge settlements with furniture and so on and so forth.
TIP: Get the Automotron DLC early on (or even at the start) to get the most out of it.
IMPORTANT TIP: I started on normal difficulty, but it makes the game WAY too easy and you'll end up essentially wasting the game and getting WAY less hours out of it than you should. So, I set it to hard difficulty and, though still not particularly difficult, it made it a lot better.
I wish Bethesda had put in adult options in, though. So, for example, you could bed beautiful female wenches etc.

Age of empires 3 is 10 years old already, so why am i writing a review now? Well, because it is one of a few games i have never really stopped playing.
Ill be honest, it probably is one of the best, if not the best RTS game ever made. Some may disagree with me, but before you do, listen to why i make such a bold claim.
Well, first off, being a success was a tall order for this game. Why? because of its prequil. Age of empires 2 was and still is amazing. I have yet to meet a single person who played that back in the day, even just once or twice, who have a bad word to say about it. because of this a lot was expected from Age of empires 3, and boy did they deliver!
They added a few things to the original recipe, and none of them bad might i add. First up, when it came out it was a graphical master piece, and even today it is not bad to look at, but graphics is almost not even worth mentioning compared to its features.
Probably the most notable feature they brought in is the Home City(the one thing that puts this at the top of RTS)
Basically what this is, is an off map support system that is decades ahead of any other off map support system even by todays standards. You have the ability to pick 20-25(depending on what version you are playing) shipment cards from 100-150 total available cards. These are age specific, with a limit on cards you can pick for each age, and they consist of unit, supply, building and upgrade bonuses you can send to the main map. You gain experience from building, destroying, killing things and collecting resources. This experience counts down on an experience bar until a shipment is ready to be sent. Through the home city you can refine and specialized your deck to your desired playstyle. you may also have more than one deck for each civilization, so there are lots of different ways to play each civilization. Almost anything can be viable in the right situation.
Secondly, aging. Most games have the first age figured out. It fucuses on aquiring resources in order to go to the next age. Age of empires 3 however has another aspect to it. You are actualy encouraged to explore the map with your starting explorer(a hero unit that can be knocked out and held for ransom, but not killed). In fact you are almost required to. There are treasures all over the map that are protected by treasure guardians. Once these are killed you can collect a treasure. Treasures can give you a unit, a worker, supplies and experience. Depending on which treasures you go for, you may further increase the effectiveness of your desired strategy along with shipment choices.
A third aspect to this game are trade posts. Trade posts are build either on a specified location on the trade route, or next to a native village. if placed on the trade route you may recieve extra experience or supplies everytime the trademan/coach/train comes by. If built on a native village, you gain access to training one or two types of native troops and some native research. Some of these are very powerful, indeed all of them can be powerful depending on what your strategy is.
So much strategical choices, and then the unit training and the fighting havent even started yet!
When it comes to fighting there is a very balanced counter system at play. everything can be hard countered by something else, and fighting styles change from age to age. In early ages you want to raid your opponents economy as much as you can to limit him from doing what he wants to do. At this stage it is a good idea to have a few cavalry around. Later on when cannons come to play battles start where players to for the kill. At this time cavalry is your answer again, only generally cannons are defended by Musketeers or pikeman, which hard counter cavalry. To kill these muskets and pikes you need bows or skirmishers, which in turn get countered by cavalry...so the aim is to catch your opponent out of position. Fights are decided by positioning and reinforcement ability just as much as unit composition.
And now i havent even started talking about the naval aspect! OOOOOH just check it out yourself lol. In short, this is a highly reccomended game. Its online population even after 10 years are still rarely lower than 1200. There are games to be found throughout the day, and they are relatively easy to find.

XCOM 2 does everything it can to fix the problems with the original game, and pretty much succeeds. There's randomly generated levels, more timed missions, a new stealth mechanic, and more sensible enemy movement to discourage the broken overwatching strategy, and a lovely helping of new skills, soldiers, items and enemies to play with. The problem is, it doesn't feel particularly new, instead acting like a big bandage on problems that existed in the previous game without bringing too many completely new things to the picture. As such, I can absolutely recommend it to people who haven't played the prequel (which should be nobody, because that game was incredible) but have to be more muted in recommending it to people who did play it. You likely won't invest as many hours in this one, unless you tinker with mods and higher difficulties. It's the difference between the nearly 20 years between X-Com and XCOM, and the four years between XCOM and XCOM 2.

The Walking Dead is an adventure videogame from the setting of the comic book series of the same name. The game tells the story of Lee, a man convicted for murder, who suddendly finds himself in a zombie apocalypse and in charge of Clementine, a little child who hopes to find her missing parents. The entire tale is divided in five episodes you have to play in sequence, plus a downloadable extra episode, 400 Days, which serves as a sequel hook to the second season.
Being an adventure game, The Walking Dead is mainly about exploration, interacting with several NPCs and using the items you come across to resolve the current issues of your crew. The actions sequences you may stumble across are dealt with with different QTEs. It's worth mentioning that while Lee, the protagonist, can indeed die to them, you will be just prompted to retry the scenario: the deaths of the NPCs are, however, final and can't be reverted. The navigation interface is pretty handy and choosing what to do is fairly easy most of the time.
The main beef of the Walking Dead game is about the choices you make along your journey: how you deal with the events and the people around Lee definetly changes how your crew members will threat you in return or how certain situations will develop. On top of having a great emotional depth to it, the way the story is told offers a great replay value. That said, prepare to meet some forced decisions along the way and the necessity to roll with them.
The whole title is rendered in a shaded graphic that greatly resembles the comic book from which the setting comes from. And, mark my word, the game isn't afraid to show some realistic design every once in a while.
The Walking Dead is a really great game, managing both being a title with deep storytelling and displaying a simple but handy gameplay everyone can grasp and enjoy

I am generally not a fan of the "zombie apocalypse" genre of fiction, with a few exceptions, but the buzz surrounding this game, along with my interest in Telltale's forthcoming
series helped to finally push me into playing this. My experience with
? In short: brutal. In every episode, there are moments that punctuate what a dark, unforgiving world this game is set in. Your choices have consequence and you feel like you are controlling the narrative in a meaningful way. I say "feel" because, ultimately, this is still a game that takes you from a predetermined point A to a predetermined point B over the course of its five episodes. That said, your choices impact the characters and you will be repeatedly reminded that there is no victory in this world; "victory" is merely surviving. Gameplay wise, this is primarily a point-and-click adventures, with some quick-time event style segments, and a few light shooter moments (I really wished for a lightgun peripheral at times). It's not overly difficult, but the gameplay is not meant to be the star of this series - rather, it serves to propel the story forward. Visually, the comic book style is a nice touch and nod to the fact that is based on the comic book series, as opposed to the AMC TV series (although, knowledge of either is not required).
All-in-all, I recommend this game to anyone looking for a mature, emotionally charged story. Adventure game fans will also likely enjoy this, too. Anyone looking for an action style game, or a more light-hearted or comedic zombie story should probably look elsewhere.

Finding Teddy has a lot going for it stylistically, but almost every other area of the game is a mess. Despite the obvious care that went into the audio/visuals, it faceplants as both a puzzle game and as a point-and-click.
Right off the bat and throughout the game, the controls are clunky and unresponsive.  Hitboxes of things that you need to click on range from bullseye exact to so wide that you'll activate them by clicking on them from out of state. Even those things pale in comparison to the awful music-note GUI. Arguably the key feature of the game is the ability to sing notes...that aren't visible to you from your note selection screen until you've solved some puzzle that they're involved in. The result is you're trying to solve puzzles with a palette comprised of some notes you can see and some you can't - until the very end of the game where you're essentially rewarded with a GUI that would have made the entire game more playable.
Keyword there is "more."
It's really not clear to me who this game is for. The cutesy but foreboding world seems to be reaching for a kind of LIMBO or more likely Dreaming Sarah vibe (both much better games worth exploring, FYI), but erring on the cutesy side. And yet this game is not for kids. Not because it will give them nightmares, but because they'll waste their precious young lives trying to figure out poorly-conceived puzzles.
The puzzles in this game jump from embarrassingly straightforward to face-scrunchingly obtuse, often with no transition between the two depending on what you have to do next. You'll lose even more time eliminating solutions you thought you'd tried only to find later the absurdly demanding hitboxes actually never picked up your earlier attempt.
The lack of widescreen support adds insult to injury since it hampers enjoyment of the one area the game excels in. On the other hand, it's probably a moot point: even huge pixel art fans should just leave Teddy for dead.

I'm not bombing this game because of crappy paid mods, or whatever the current whiny complaint of the week is that seems so prevalent amongst gamers these days. I'm giving it a negative because after about ten hours of play its become monumentally tedious.
Having purchased this about 6 months ago I thought I'd finally give it a shot, despite knowing full well that the Bethesda template is just as over used and underdeveloped as anything Ubisoft churns out.
I liked Morrowind, but after that its just the same bloated dull gameplay over and over again....Skyrim / Fallout  - the only difference is: in one game you stab things to death in a simplistic fashion, in the other you shoot them.
Same huge map with no actual proper gameplay in it - naff action, naff stealth, and unlike Skyrims mild saving graces - no puzzles or setpieces.
But hey! you get a ton of "content" and a 100 hours of play for your money....yayyy! Nevermind that it's consistently mediocre.....at least you get your moneys worth. Which in my case was £20, hence taking a chance on a game I pretty much knew would be dull as ditchwater.
First impressions were good - its funny, and the plot is intriguing. And that's it. Once the gory fun factor of the VATS system wears off, the shooting becomes tedious. Traipsing all over the map becomes tedious. Picking up one zillion items of useless junk, and constantly running out of inventory space, becomes tedious.
After 12 hours something broke inside of me. I didn't care about the quests anymore, and I decided the only thing of interest left is to murder every NPC in the game. I met a woman from the Covenant, who was against synthetic creatures that pass as human. She had a captive who she believed to be a synth.
I killed the woman from the Covenant.
Then I killed the hostage too.
Briefly I felt some enjoyment come back.
But then I did a hugely boring extended shootout in a power plant, that just seemed to be an endless amount of winding gantrys. And my enthusiasm for mass murder dried up - too much of a chore just to get some fun from the game.
This is a marmite title - you like Bethesda games? bully for you - tuck in. For me - it's marginally more intersting than watching paint dry, and a thumbs down.

Edit: After spending a few more hours playing, I started to remember the problems this game had years ago.
1. As the game progresses, Witch Time can no longer be triggered on certain enemies.
2. Static cutscene. Some may say this is an artistic choice, I say it's a lazy attempt at a cutscene.
3. Instant death QTE. I'm fine with QTE but this game's QTE are horrible. They came out of nowhere, have a small window of opportunity and the button prompts are different each time.
4. On rails segments. The part where you're riding a missile is my least favourite part of the game. It doesn't belong in this game and it went on way too long.
5. Bland characters. Everyone is uninteresting, even the MC.
6. Crotch/*ss shots. Back then, I was a horny teenager so I didn't mind it as much. Now? No, please. Every time it happens, I cringe with discomfort.
7. Most technique are overshadowed by other simpler and convenient combos. The only ones that are important are Stiletto and Air Dodge. Bat Within can be useful, if it can be triggered.
8. Worse of all, the story is garbage. I was too fixated with Bayonetta's crotch and *ss back then to notice the story but now I know without a doubt that the story is worthless.
I'm letting the thumbs up stay simply because I did enjoy playing it all those years ago but if I am to give it a score, I'd say it's a 3/5. It's not actually as good as people say it is.

Picked this up as part of the Namco Bandai Humble Bundle (which included all the DLC for the game), and I have to say, so far I've found it pretty dang enjoyable. After investing a large chunk of time into Split Second on my PS3, Ridge Racer: Unbounded felt immediately familiar, but different enough to make it stand out on its own. Split Second was super fun as racing games go, but I found the handling on the vehicles to be... not necessarily as advertised based on their stats. RR:U vehicles seem much more true to their description. Although a word of warning: A high drift score is, in my observation, not a sign that a car handles well under drift, even if it has a decent handling score. Rather, the drift score seems to indicate the willingness of the back end to swing out, so a car with max drift almost wants to drive in reverse after every single corner. These high drift cars require a delicate touch, and you'll end up facing the on coming field a lot until you get the subtleties down.
Continuing the Split Second/RR:U comparision:  While I loved the destruction in SS, merely placing in many SS tracks required that you hit every single destructible. And to win, you often needed to having the timing of using the destructibles down just so, rather than just relying on your skills as a driver. RR:U gives you the option to destroy, and it's definitely encouraged both by adding to your score and it's potential for shaving a little off your lap times. And of course, it's just fun to do. But in the end, placing and winning comes down to what you do behind the wheel. There will be moments of frustration, like when you're in the lead and some AI jerk three positions back starts a chain reaction accident, costing you your hard earned spot at the top, but even that feels fun and exhilirating, and makes you want to try again. Gotta say though, the SS soundtrack was better IMHO. RR:U has this very generic bassy electronica that I would rather have than be without any music, but it definitely doesn't evoke anywhere near the same kind of emotional pulse pounding rush that the SS tunes did.
Many will complain about the death of the online server, and I can understand that. But when I just wanna pick up and race, I don't really care. It'd be nice if they came back and fixed that, maybe rewrote things so that the player community could host servers so we could still play online. But meh.... it's a small thing in my book, and I'm not a ginormous fan of online gaming to begin with, especially when play is strictly competitive.
Havent' played with the editor yet so I can't speak to that, but I think it's a cool feature. Again, many will say it's nearly useless given the demise of online play, but I'll be interested to see what I can come up with anyway.
Overall, as long as you're not looking for multiplayer mayhem, I definitely recommend it, though you might be well advised to pick it up on the cheap, or as part of a bundle. Lots of single player fun to be had, as long as you don't go in expecting the world. Give the demo a shot.

So, this here is a decent racing game. Handling's pretty good, action-filled gameplay, excellent track editor. Sounds like a good game, so why's it a downvote?
: Unbounded (keyword: "Ridge Racer") is a spin-off, spun too far off track from the Ridge Racer project, as in not in the main series, and not made by the actual developers of Ridge Racer either mind you, but Bugbear. Yes, those people. Flatout. Wreckfest.
What is a spin-off? Probably depends who you ask, but to me it's a game that strays away from the main series, maybe experimenting a little bit by changing up the main gameplay formula. And hoo boy, let me tell you... it sure changed.
That's my main problem with Ridge Racer: Unbounded, it strayed WAY too far off from what Ridge Racer really is.
Ridge Racer is a high-speed, nitrous oxide filled drift-racing experience, and this game really just doesn't capture that timeless Ridge Racer feeling. The drifting is weird in comparison, it's definitely not as fast-paced and you're driving like a maniac.
Now don't get me wrong, many a person could probably describe the way you drive in Ridge Racer games as a way a maniac drives, but in Unbounded you take it to the n-th degree by pulverizing your opponents, literally just smashing them off the track. It really, really just feels like a Burnout game.
It'd probably do great as a Burnout spin-off. But then again, EA games would probably never allow this much creative freedom. So again, it's not a bad game, it's just that it really, really feels weird knowing it's named "Ridge Racer", because it's so much
Ridge Racer. Do I recommend it as Ridge Racer? Absolutely not! Do I recommend it as a game? Sure, it's alright.
I have to admit, it's a decent play once in a while, so play it if you're not expecting Ridge Racer.
