Great atmosphere, great art, great music, great narrator.
Hard, and a little unfair. RNG can mess you up, but part of the strategy is factoring in the risks. Is it worth healing your bleeding Leper, or should you take a risk with a plague grenade? When your heroes die, at least at medium levels, it's your fault. The RNG is just there to give you something to blame and to rub salt in the wound. At low level, however, you are going to die. I can not stress this enough: DO NOT GET ATTACHED TO LOW LEVEL HEROES! They are a recourse. Send a few low-levels in, then dismiss them. Do not underestimate how much supplies cost. Do not over-prepare for missions (excluding boss fights), and try to keep track of your net gold gain/loss per mission. Keep stress low: health comes back for free, stress sticks around. Do not use AOE unless it will kill one of the enemies, you're just spreading out damage otherwise.
Tl;dr, great game, worth every penny, can't wait for the DLC

As much as I recommend this game for being a quality product that works for what it does, Finding Teddy just isn't without its issues.
It's a point and click adventure game, but the movement is heavily restricted. You don't just click to walk somewhere, you only move when transitioning screens or picking up items, and you can't cancel these actions. So if you accidentally click on a transitional hitbox while clicking around for one of the game's many hidden collectibles, you're stuck moving.
The game also tells you nothing. I don't know what's with these types of games telling you nothing about their story and their mechanics but it works as well for this game as it did for Hyper Light Drifter (read: not very). Like that game, there's also a made-up language you have to learn. Mercifully it doesn't require a language course to master and is mostly based in regular alphebeticals, but it relies heavily on sound cues. So if you aren't good with sounds, you're not gonna have a fun time.
The game is also far too short. Not in the good way either, the only reason I barely scraped the two hour mark was because the game was so hard to figure out and I played it a second time in New Game+. I'd recommend the far longer (and far superior) sequel in comparison to this, but for what it's worth it's a great game if you really want it.

I love the heck out of this game. Sure, it's not the prettiest, and it's certainly very streamlined, but the tale it weaves is a true demonstration of how video games can tell an emotional story.
You play as Lee Everett, a history teacher who's being taken off to prison for murder, when the zombie apocalypse strikes. Fans of the television show "The Walking Dead" will be more than a little familiar with the southern twang to the setting, but this cast of characters is completely different. Be prepared for some crushing moments and some tough decisions as the plot moves forward. This game will claw out the feels from you as surely as the blood and guts of your fallen companions.
The game itself is divided up into 'episodes', multi-hour vignettes where Lee and his companions try to stay alive. Your decisions will play a key role in how the story develops, how your friendships blossom, and in some cases, who makes it out alive. The voice acting and the atmosphere all do a stunning job at establishing the tone, and the way a number of the cutscenes are shot weave into gameplay surprisingly well.
Those hoping for an action-packed survival game like State of Decay or Day Z, be warned. This is NOT a game about scavenging, it's about surviving. It draws out the philosophical questions about what you're willing to do, and leaves you hungry for the next season. Just trust me, get this game.

Before you buy this game, you need to know that it relies heavily on audio puzzles. Many of the puzzles require an English alphabet to music code. It can be extremely frustrating if you don't know that the sounds relate to the alphabet or if you can't tell many similarly sounding notes apart. I do not recommend this game to anyone with audial difficulties.
That said, this game is a cute, magical adventure full of death. It has the usual pitfalls of point and click adventure games - repetition, back-tracking, "why do I have this object?", use everything with everything, etc. - but it also has frustrating sound puzzles. Honestly, I almost gave up on this game because of the musical code puzzles. It does have this odd charm about it. Once I got past the frustrating bits, I ended up enjoying it. This is a game that takes a lot of time and thought. Unless you use one of the community guides.

Ultimately a bit of an unsatisfying game.  I gave up and started using a guide the moment the game expected me to match musical notes by ear against a note-to-alphabet cipher, and I did 8+ years of band in school + university.  I'm someone who is familiar with music, but tone matching is not something I'm good at doing without some effort and people without music experience are typically much worse.  Its a pain in the butt at first and becomes more obvious and easy as the game goes on but I just didn't want to deal with the hassle.  You have to use the music-to-note cipher to say simple phrases to creatures in the game, and then complex ones at the end very.  Its kind of weird because the game doesn't give you the whole alphabet cipher by the end and you ARE expected to use letters you dont know (you can sing them by clicking on their empty space on your cipher sheet).  I can see where from the developer side of things this makes sense, but from the player side its not so straightforward.  Its just not good game design and player confusion like this is something where point-and-click adventure games can suffer the most.
Lets assume I didnt find the music-alphabet cipher to be a problem, and look at the rest of the game.  Unfortunately, its just not that great.  There's more or less no dialogue until the very end of the game.  The creatures you encounter serve no purpose except to kill you King's Quest style unless you use the correct item on them.  They aren't really characters at all, they're just roadblocks.  The puzzles aren't that meaningful either, being both limited in number and scope, and they dont really feel like they contribute to a complete package.
The aesthetic is passable.  Graphics serve their purpose but dont amaze, and the music is a bit too light to be thematic or enjoyably ambient.  There's also a serious sound balance problem where the 'open inventory' sound is someting like 2 to 3 times as loud as the background music, causing some unfortunate earblasting.  Characters again, aren't characters.  Only the last encounter in the game has much depth or charm.  You also can't position yourself onscreen, only move to transitions, so a feature of the game where some onscreen invisible blobs have to be revealed by sonar mouseclicks gets more bothersome than needs be due to clicking on a transition and being unable to cancel moving to it.
With the Steam guide leading me after my initial foray, I finished the game in 75 minutes.  Given that there is no dialogue or cutscenes to skip this would only be padded by exploring / headbanging against some of the puzzles, some of which I am certain would have been unintuitive without the external assistance.  Normal for the genre in some ways, but as many recent amazing games by Wadjet Eye and Daedalic have shown point-and-clicks dont have to be that way.  Anyway, my additional listed hours in the game was merely to collect the trading cards before uninstalling.  The game has very minor replay value, in the form of an NG+ with a memetic alternate ending themed after nyancat.
The credits say that the game was completed in just 4 months, but perhaps some additional time spent on the game would have made it more worthwhile.
The game does contain failstates.  Most monsters in the game will kill the player while they are unsatisfied (colored grey), resulting in a reset to the moment immediately prior to the death and an unlocked achievement for dying in that way.  Deaths are not particularly gruesome aside from the one by the very first grey creature you encounter, but they don't really add much to the game as well and I would just as much prefer they not be there.

This game is the spiritual successor to the steam hit Terraria, promising a lot but fulfilling very little of its promises.
When I started playing this game, I loved it. It was like a 2D minecraft with a lot of possibilities, and an actual progressing "plot", that gave you boss monsters and better armor that gave you cool little bonuses.
You could modify your characters and while some parts were more boring than others, it was a fun game.
But this isn't a review for Terraria, so I'll stop there.
Starbound takes a lot of inspiration from Terraria, almost as directly as Terraria takes from Starbound.
However, it doesn't follow through on a lot of its concepts. It attempts to make a Skinner box of leveling progression, except there's no real "fulfillment". In Terraria, finding a chest early on was a cool thing, generally significant, and especially significant if you got an item worth using for a good amount of time.
Starbound relegates that strategy to one or two chests, and a "maybe". You're better off scouring the topside of the world and moving on to the next one directly after. You become less of a Starbound Traveler, and more of a Tourist, flicking through snapshots.
The worlds are lively enough, but there's no soul or character growth behind them.
The plot is piecemeal and unsatisfying, giant chunks of it are missing, and the chunks that are there are disconnected and uncooperative. In Terraria, the mystery served them well. You didn't know what the corruption was, and it was spreading. You could destroy parts of it, and parts of it would come after you. The eventual path to power gave you more and more interesting paths. It was a magical little experience that sent you from the ends of the world to hell and back.
Starbound splits up the worlds into randomly generated pieces, which end up feeling generic and lacking a lot of the charm as a result of the lack of a common 'goal'.
I would not recommend this game based upon its virtues, because it doesn't overcome its severe weaknesses as a game. As a sandbox simulator, it's fun enough. As a story, it's bad.
The promised features for the game are not in the game, and that's what honestly brings it down. It's a damn shame, and I think it's a symptom of the "Kickstarter Game".
5/10, was fun for a bit, then lost interest when the unfinished nature of the game revealed itself like the pretty tablecloth ripped off to reveal that the table only had one and a half legs, and no actual centerpiece. And used to be a chair.

Probably one of the best games I have ever played in my life.  It contains lots of drama throughout the entire game, and m gosh, the feels in this game, is too much.
You play as Lee Everett, a university professor convicted of murder.  As you are heading to prison, the outbreak begins.  Lee ends up meeting and befriending a little girl named Clementine, which is the best "kid" character in a game.  From there, you and Clementine now survive in the amidst of a zombie apocalypse.
There are five episodes; A New Day, Starved For Help, Long Road Ahead, Around Every Corner, and No Time Left.  Each episode has an amazing plot that will keep you playing for hours.
Episode 1: A New Day- Great startoff to the series, with lots of characters that come and go.
Episode 2: Starved For Help- Mmmmmm, huma-I mean, steak.
Episode 3: Long Road Ahead- Great first half of this episode, with a depressing, unfortunate scene toward the end.
Episode 4: Around Every Corner- The build-up to the finale.
Episode 5: No Time Left: You'll cry, is all I can say.
Overall, this has to have been one of the best games of 2012, and it is certainly one of the best games i've played.  The dialogue, plot, and emotion in each episode is great.  Pick this game up when you can.

What I thought I got: A more action-oriented edition of Dark souls, with somewhat thinner story, but with better graphics and more fast-paced, immersive combat. Easier, and more linear story-progression.
What I actually got: No story at all, uninteresting characters and flat voice-acting, run-of-the-mill "dark fantasy" world, with evil demonic tossers, invading a gothic world. Combat i more slow-paced than Dark Souls, at least to me, as there is barely ever an opening in your enemies guard, and it takes three years to raise your shield after finishing an attack. Also, half the time, you take damage or get stunned, even though you're rolling.
No enemy variety either, bosses: Tall guys with swords.
Normal minions: Guy with axe, guy with shield, guy with crossbow, idiotic  and blind abominations and then spiders.
It feels clunky and unpolished, even though you figured out the attack pattern of an enemy, you will rarely get a proper chance to attack without taking damage yourself, because after an attack, your character goes to an idle animation before being able to raise the shield or gtfo of the way.
Also, it took me 40 minutes to get the game running. And it still ran pretty bad, with severe FPS drops.
It does show a lot of potential, but perhaps this is just the extent of the developers capabilitites. Taken into account their other releases, that is very likely the reason.

Introduction
In the realm of racing games, competition is tough. However quality control in that said same category is lacking in my mind  There are too many racing game out there, and most of them suck or were great once, but then began to suck. Like it is with all the countless titles released under the banner of the NFS series, just to name one racing series.
For me NFS SE R&T Edition, NFS 2 (SE), NFS 3, NFS High Stakes, Underground 1+2, Most Wanted and Carbon were brilliant untill Undercover "happened".Then it just started to slip and fall down this downward spiral, resulting in one terrible release after the other.
Regardless, it can be difficult as a developer to keep your head above water. This is mostly because of consumers, demanding products to be better than before, while still urging developers to remain almost conservatively true and loyal to the previous released titles. I can understand that from the consumers and the devs POV, being a gamer myself, with a most of my free time spent from an early age to present day, in front of my PC (and consoles alike), playing computer games and will continue to do that as long as I can.
I have not played any of the previous Ridge Racer games, so I knew little about them. Nor did I play any of the Burnout games, before I tapped in to the vain of Burnout Paradise. Some say, to quote Jeremy Clarkson, that this game is NOTHING like the previous games, and I would not know, nor do I care.
So what about the game?
This game is quite good, very cliched, but good. Cliched because of the story. The setting is some random tech-noir-Sci-Fi near future city from what I understand, with some rebels racing to really stick it to "The Man" and fighting the power....by racing and destroying the city they want to change....Yeah okay. But nevermind the story. Nobody plays a racing game for the story. You play it for the racing dammit.
The story is Mirrors Edge meets P.O.D (and no not the band alright!!!) meets Watchdogs I guess.
As you might already know, this is an arcade racer. Keep in mind, that this is not a racing simulator.
One less great thing about the game is the sense of speed. I have to agree with Total Biscuit, in that the sense of speed is lacking and is quite poor. The speedometer might say 200+ kph, but it feels more like you are doing less than 150 kph at most times and some of the cars accellerate  very slowly.
This might be a minor thing for some, but I am a racing game fan and that matters to me. However, as you progress in the game, the cars become faster and this means that the sense of speed becomes better, but it will hardly take your breath away.
Aestically the game is graphically impressive, especially at levels that play in the night time in the city. The soundtrack is decent with your stereotypical cheap-bad taste-generic-mediocre-up tempo tween Dubstep techno ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t soundtrack like Skrillex. The soundtrack nevertheless fits the game quite well. The engine sounds are rather cheap though. They do not sound very authentic.
Gameplay is straight forward, no nonsense racing, where it is mostly about getting there first and in one piece. You can smash through certain areas of the map Michael Bay style, with loads of explosions and lighting effects
You also have stunt races, frag races (Yes, this game uses the term frag!!) and race where you race a semi-truck, with the objectives of destroying and crashing police cars, chasing you.
The cars feel very heavy and sometimes even clunky. No open world here. You pick a race from one of the unlocked locations and proceed until you have gained enough XP to let the game progress and unlock new cars, districts and levels.
The game is not easy, but it's far from being as difficult as some would have you to believe. Stop crying, there is NO BATHROOM, you little girlie men. If you have trouble progressing or win races, just keep on replaying the level you have trouble with and practice. It's that simple.
One tip I have is to save your boost. Not for fragging opponents, because that does little really. Save it for when the game prompts you for smashing through certain areas of the level you racing. This gives you the maximum amount of XP. These destructible set pieces act sometimes as shortcuts too, allowing for an easy overtaking and win.
There are better arcade racing games out there, like Burnout Paradise, Split/Second Velocity (hella good game btw...just awesome) or Flatout Ultimate Carnage (also a little arcade racer gem a la Destruction Derby meets NASCAR with more redneck destruction action) e.g. and all of the above surpass and overshadow Ridge Racer by several car lengths (pun intended).
I still recommend this game. It does the job well, but nothing more than that. Do not buy this game unless it is on sale. The current asking price is not worth it. No game on Steam is worth to buy at full price if you ask me.
I give it 7/10.

The Multi-player  is shut down so don't buy it for online play.
I have played many Ridge Racer games in the past and I loved R4 back in the day. Some may complain that this doesn't feel like a Ridge Racer game and they would be somewhat right. It's Ridge Racer to the extreme. The Ridge Racer game series needed to evolve with new gameplay and this game does that. It still has the Ridge Racer "vibe" with all the powersliding you can handle while listening to techno style music. But, it adds in destructible environments with alternate routes you open up by smashing through walls and buildings on each course. It also has opponent take downs like we have seen in games like burnout.
All of this destruction adds to your power/turbo meter. You can keep the meter filled up by causing destruction to the other racers and the environment. Keeping your meter maxed as often as possible is essential to winning races because the AI is not easy to beat. They drive well, boost often and will even "frag" you when you are ahead of them.  Even if you don't come in first you still get points so losing the race is not always a bad thing.
In additon to the main "domination" mode there are several other game modes to mix things up. There is a mode called "Shindo" that is a lot like recent RR games where you just get boost for powersliding and the envronment is less destructible. There's also drift attack, time attack and a "frag" mode where you try to destroy as many oponents as possible. All are fun in there own way and you can apply these modes to the tracks you create as well.
My biggest complaint with Ridge Racer unbounded is that there needs to be more options to change the graphics and control settings for the game. They are extremly limited and it's obvious this is a console port. The game still looks good but more settings for the PC version would have been appreciated. Other than that it's a solid arcade racer.
Overall, the game is just plain fun and that's what counts to me. I don't understand why people don't like it. Maybe they are struggling to win the races. Some races are very difficult and require multiple attempts to win. As with other racing games it takes some practice to get use to the handling of the cars. Also, there is a  button for drifting and you should use it instead of the brakes to start your drift.
Maybe the people who don't like it expect it to be like the older Ridge Racer games but I'm actually glad it's different than the previous games. Why make a new Ridge Racer game if it's doesn't add anything different ? Also, I don't care that the MP is dead. I don't play MP on many games anyway. So if your looking for a fun, challenging, over the top, arcade  racing experience give this game a try.

Ridge Racer Unbounded is completely unrelated to the original Ridge Racer arcade games. It managed to introduce a lot of new concepts, such as course construction set (with progressive unlock of building blocks), group racing, lots of cars, multiple modes, destructible scenes, and so on. However, with the shut down of the matchmaking servers in early 2015, buggy game (crash to desktop after several races), and odd handling (there is no tutorial on how drift works in this game) means the game, even at bargain basement prices, is not exactly a good investment.
As a new racer joining the scene in Shatter Bay, your task is to "take over" multiple neighborhoods by doing well or very well in the various races. Each neighborhood has about 7 races. Winning the races (or at least, get into top 3) will unlock higher races, while accumulating score will increase your rank and gain you access to better cars.
There are multiple race modes, but most races will be "domination race", where you race up to 11 other cars. Do the special moves like getting air, hit top speed, or drifting, will gain you boost. Once you fill the boost gauge, you can engage boost which allows you to smash through certain "targets", yielding shortcuts that gain you more boost (usually involve getting some big air) but since boost has limited duration, you have to time its use carefully. Smashing other cars will cause them to respawn, albeit several seconds behind.
So what's the problem? Very weird drifting mechanism. Some guides advocate holding down the handbrake button during the turn, others insist on releasing the handbrake as soon as drift had started. The problem is there is no "test track" for you to practice. It's always race, race, race.
The graphics are quite good, and as this is a Bugbear product (makers of Flatout series) the game has decent handling... except for the weird drifting. Sound is... okay, with a lot of decent soundtracks, again, just like Bugbear games like Flatout.
You were able to build your own race courses and as you conquer neighborhoods and raise your driver level you will unlock additional blocks to build the courses. However, with death of the matchmaking servers the courses are of little use now, as much of the fun is race others in MP games. In fact, the game is stuck for about a minute checking for nonexisting server when it starts up.
All in all, Ridge Racer Unbounded tried to do too much and lack of tutorial / test track made the game unenjoyable, and the shutdown of matchmaking server is the nail in the coffin. It's fast, it's furious, but it left an empty feeling.

Since the large amount of reviews are pertaining to performance, let me say that my AC unity runs perfectly fine using a GTX 760 (2gb vram) i7 4790 and 8gb of hyperx ram. By fine I mean High settings hovering around 50 fps, and at high settings the game is GORGEOUS.
Now that thats out of the way, let me start by saying gameplay wise this is the pinnicle of AC games, and there is very little they could improve on past this point. The parkour is seamless, a constant flow of movement ensures the player is never stuck performing tedious climbs and descents ever again. But more importantly, there is finally a combat aspect to Assassins Creed, no longer can you jump carelessly into an army and survive with no hiccups. At least to the point where I have reached the fights are difficult, and no longer can I cruise through a combat situation. There are minor clipping issues here and there with combat/movement however the amount is negligable. So much love has been put into the world, and finally you feel like you're actually part of a virtual city. Pedestrians are everywhere and much more unique than past games, and the city feels alive as promised by ubisoft. Coupled with masterful storytelling as always and incredible voice acting, this game plays just as delivered, and definetely exceeds my expectations. Do not let the other reviews fool you, the COOP is incredible, the gameplay is damn near perfect, this may well end up being my favorite game of the decade.
As for what I would like to see changed, optimization definetely needs to take place as far as graphics, although I am more than happy with high I would like to see how the game plays on ultra high.

If you can get past the unstable and buggy gameplay, and slightly questionalble graphics, OMSI is an absolutely brilliant simulator with a strong community making regular contend for both sides of the road.
OMSI comes with a total of 15 buses, all made by M.A.N and were used in Berlin in the 1980s/90s. This game also comes with 2 maps (Grundorf and Spandau, Berlin) and are pretty well detailed. This OMSI is cirtainly one of THE BEST bus simulators out there, even though it is very buggy. The DLCs are also highly detailed, and are at very competative prices when compared with DLC for Dovetail Games' RailWorks.
You may notice that (when you boot the game for the first time) no passengers will buy any tickets, this is not a glitch/bug, you need to change your settings by:
1. Press "p", this will pause the game. Esc. also works to pause the simulation, but the time still passes, press p first
2. Press Esc.
3. Find "Options"
4. This will open a new window, find "Ticket Selling"
5. Open the Drop-Down Menu.
6. Select "Easy" or "Advanced"
7. Click "ok"
8. Press Esc.
9. Press "p"
10. Continue driving :-)
I like this Simulator and I highly Recommend OMSI and it's DLC to anyone looking for a decent bus simulator, remember, it is very buggy and unstable.

This is not a game; it is a simulator in the purest sense. Unlike Euro Truck Simulator 2 and similar, there is no aspect of gameplay at all.
As such, if you don't really, really want to drive a bus, then I can't reccommend OMSI for you.
On the other hand, if, like me, buses are your thing, then this is the best - no two ways about it. The driving physics are excellent, the sounds are just superb, every individual switch in the cab works and attention to detail has been layered upon the vehicles you'll drive. The defualt maps are OK, and the default buses are excellent - but this simulator is all about the mods. There are dozens upon dozens of amazing freeware buses and maps out there, and a few excellent officially endorsed payware items (I highly reccomend the O305 and Three Generations bus packs).
In case none of the maps available meet your taste, the game includes a map editor which allows you absolute freedom to build your own maps, even if the controls take a little getting used to and the editor itself is really well hidden (google how to run it). With a little patience, you can learn to create assets for the game without too much difficulty in Blender and Sketchup, or, in my case, Gmax, via a very circuitous import route.
There are limitations - the game only really supports right-hand traffic, for instance. There are left-traffic routes and buses available, but there are issues with passengers walking through the bus. You'd also better get used to selling tickets in German.
There are flaws as well - you need a fast processor to run this game at all (multiple cores don't help), and an SSD, while not absolutely necessary, will significantly boost performance, as the game is constantly loading items as they come within range. Back when it was released, the game was not stable at all. This seems to be fixed for most people now, but you should be aware of it nonetheless. The physics can be jumpy occasionally, and I've had a few weird bugs like the back end of an articulated bus falling off. This kind of thing has been few and far between for me, though the game becomes less stable the more mods you have (clean up the ones you aren't using). Play with the settings until you get something that seems to be stable.
All in all, if you like buses, this is simply a must-have. Yes, there are bugs, but they're outweighed by the sounds, the driving physics, the wholly interactive dashboards and the endless customization.

Darkest Dungeon is NOT a nice game. It's a relentlessly grim and unforgiving turn-based dungeon crawler that stands firmly in the company of games designed for players who aren't expecting to have their hand held. The consequences of each choice, both in and out of combat, are permanent thanks to frequent autosaves. Depending on the player, this will:
(a) give each choice weight, meaning, and excitement, or
(b) cause frustration, a dismissal of the game as "broken" or unfair, and likely a refund request.
Thankfully, I was able to extract mostly feelings of the first type during my time with the game. It is of course not without its flaws, though.
Playing on Radiant, I was able to avoid many of the most common frustrations/criticisms of the game while still getting the full experience it seemed the developers were aiming to deliver. (Radiant Mode speeds up character and town upgrade progression, as well as a handful of other anti-tedium and quality-of-life adjustments, while keeping all combat difficulty untouched. Losing heroes still stings, but it becomes much less of a grind to get replacements trained up.)
Reading prior reviews, I notice a lot of exaggeration/misinformation when it comes to this game's difficulty; things like enemies taking more turns than the player (other than bosses) are just plain incorrect. It can feel brutal and unfair in those first few hours learning the basics of the combat system, but once lessons have been learned about class roles and enemy prioritization (hint: the back row almost always deals high stress damage and should be dealt with first!), the combat experience morphs into something more tactical, exciting, and satisfying. Trying out and refining new strategies and party compositions as they either succeeded or failed miserably was a huge part of the fun factor for me throughout most of the game.
This leads to one of those big bullet point thoughts from above: I think
Especially early on, I was often forced to retreat from combat and abandon missions altogether so that I could escape with what gold or upgrade points I was able to gather before falling dangerously close to death. If this sounds frustrating to you, you probably won't enjoy Darkest Dungeon.
When it comes to matching its aesthetics and mood to its gameplay, Darkest Dungeon delivers. The oppressive atmosphere conveyed by the gothic horror art style and music never really lets the player feel comfortable, even in town. The narration that accompanies your successes and failures during battle really adds to this (although hearing the same line about not getting overconfident for the hundreth time is as eye-rolling as it sounds). As your heroes become more stressed, the accompanying audio/visual cues instill the same feelings of dread in the player.
For all its novel ideas and fun twists, Darkest Dungeon also has its warts (literal and figurative!). Boss fights are strange departures from the rest of the game's combat ideas, often requiring knowledge of particular mechanics or team compositions that, frustratingly, can only really be figured out by either trial and error (and dead heroes) or looking online beforehand. I'm all for boss fights requiring different strategies and/or creativity, but there are better ways of indicating to the player that these things are necessary before they've already been annihilated by the boss' mechanics. Some of the fights suffer from this more than others, obviously, but it's still kind of a bummer.
Additionally, the game is pretty heavy on the RNG when it comes to hits, misses, crits, and damage in combat. This is an area where I feel people have some ground to stand on in their criticism of the game. It's just not fun when you're sure you've made the right choice in strategy, only to miss completely and be annihilated by the enemy's retort, all because of chance. While I still feel the game is very much a strategy-first, luck-second experience, the issue of RNG rears its ugly head more dramatically than any eldritch horror stalking its corridors.
All in all, I enjoyed my harrowing trek through Darkest Dungeon. It's a great example of ruthless, smart game design that knows what kind of experience it wants to deliver. It is far from perfect, but for the right player, it has elements in common with any great horror film: tension, uncertainty, and the thrill of the kill.

What I thought I got: A more action-oriented edition of Dark souls, with somewhat thinner story, but with better graphics and more fast-paced, immersive combat. Easier, and more linear story-progression.
What I actually got: No story at all, uninteresting characters and flat voice-acting, run-of-the-mill "dark fantasy" world, with evil demonic tossers, invading a gothic world. Combat i more slow-paced than Dark Souls, at least to me, as there is barely ever an opening in your enemies guard, and it takes three years to raise your shield after finishing an attack. Also, half the time, you take damage or get stunned, even though you're rolling.
No enemy variety either, bosses: Tall guys with swords.
Normal minions: Guy with axe, guy with shield, guy with crossbow, idiotic  and blind abominations and then spiders.
It feels clunky and unpolished, even though you figured out the attack pattern of an enemy, you will rarely get a proper chance to attack without taking damage yourself, because after an attack, your character goes to an idle animation before being able to raise the shield or gtfo of the way.
Also, it took me 40 minutes to get the game running. And it still ran pretty bad, with severe FPS drops.
It does show a lot of potential, but perhaps this is just the extent of the developers capabilitites. Taken into account their other releases, that is very likely the reason.

A rather neat and pretty decently-designed point-and-click adventure.  The solutions to puzzles are fairly straightforward, as are the achievements (which can be completed rather reasonably).
A relatively short game but this means that you should have time left over to explore the game's new-game-plus features -- including an easier way to find the collectibles and an alternative ending clued in by one of the NPCs.
The story is very atmospheric, with some horror elements, but challenges the usual association of antipathy with the grotesque -- just because something's ugly and scary-looking may not mean that it hates you and means you harm.  But you must figure out how to communicate with it, and what to say to it.
The game also has a distinctive way of "communicating" -- a "musicom" that lets you type out a message letter by letter using musical tones.  It's fun to use.
Apparently the musicom also features in this game's sequel, Finding Teddy 2.  And this game does have a scene at the end that ties into FT2.  FT2 is a metroidvania, though, and I'm even more excited about that game.
(Disclosure: I bought this game on the Humble Store, while it was discounted.)

This game is the spiritual successor to the steam hit Terraria, promising a lot but fulfilling very little of its promises.
When I started playing this game, I loved it. It was like a 2D minecraft with a lot of possibilities, and an actual progressing "plot", that gave you boss monsters and better armor that gave you cool little bonuses.
You could modify your characters and while some parts were more boring than others, it was a fun game.
But this isn't a review for Terraria, so I'll stop there.
Starbound takes a lot of inspiration from Terraria, almost as directly as Terraria takes from Starbound.
However, it doesn't follow through on a lot of its concepts. It attempts to make a Skinner box of leveling progression, except there's no real "fulfillment". In Terraria, finding a chest early on was a cool thing, generally significant, and especially significant if you got an item worth using for a good amount of time.
Starbound relegates that strategy to one or two chests, and a "maybe". You're better off scouring the topside of the world and moving on to the next one directly after. You become less of a Starbound Traveler, and more of a Tourist, flicking through snapshots.
The worlds are lively enough, but there's no soul or character growth behind them.
The plot is piecemeal and unsatisfying, giant chunks of it are missing, and the chunks that are there are disconnected and uncooperative. In Terraria, the mystery served them well. You didn't know what the corruption was, and it was spreading. You could destroy parts of it, and parts of it would come after you. The eventual path to power gave you more and more interesting paths. It was a magical little experience that sent you from the ends of the world to hell and back.
Starbound splits up the worlds into randomly generated pieces, which end up feeling generic and lacking a lot of the charm as a result of the lack of a common 'goal'.
I would not recommend this game based upon its virtues, because it doesn't overcome its severe weaknesses as a game. As a sandbox simulator, it's fun enough. As a story, it's bad.
The promised features for the game are not in the game, and that's what honestly brings it down. It's a damn shame, and I think it's a symptom of the "Kickstarter Game".

Telltale's The Walking Dead, is a fantastic point-and-click game set in The Walking Dead setting (hence the name). But it doesn't follow the story of the TV series, it is a parallel story and is completly different characters, other than a cameo in the first Episode.
The game follows a episodic lay-out and there are a total of 5 episodes in this first Season of this game series. The decisions you make throughout the 5 episodes effect the outcome so you might have a completely different experience in a situation than I have, depening on who lived and who died, which of your fellow survivors are your friends and who you sided with in previous situations.
And the game is dialogue-based, in fact I would say that most the game is dialogue and is very much about character development and making decision that you many times won't feel comfortable with. But if you make a decision and you feel like this: "No that didn't end well, I'll redo that." or something similar, then just keep playing and see what happens, if you feel like you did a mistake then do another playthrough and see what happens then.
The story follows former history teacher Lee Everett who just before the outbreak of the zombie apocalypse was conficted of the murder of a Senator who slept with his ex-wife. During the first day of the outbreak he finds a little girl named Clementine and decides to take care of her. I won't say anything else because I don't want to spoil what will happen but know that it will be heart-gripping, sad, horrifying and if you don't cry during the ending then you basically don't have any emotions.
Along the way you will meet many other survivors, each with their own personallity, backstory and priorities. Your relation to each one of them effect the outcome of the story, or at least part of the story.
Beware, you cannot save everyone!
There is a bit of a warning I have to give about the dialogue though and probably the one bad thing I can say about this game. You have a limited time to choose dialogue options, I do understand that they put it in (so that it wouldn't make the dialogue akward by having Lee standing there quiet for a minute and then continue like nothing had happened) but the time is just way too short, so short in fact that I several time didn't even have to read all the options. And since the game is so heavily dialogue based this is a problem, you should be aware of the problem. This is also true for when you have a decision to make (though you have a bit longer to think then), though not every single time. If you get into a situation and you need to think it over just press ESC and think it over, it doesn't break the game. Anyway now you're aware.
In summary The Walking Dead game is fantastic and the only thing done wrong the the limited time in dialogue but I still highly recommend this game to anyone, even if you don't like point-and-click games, I must say to you, play this game. The Story and characters are truly what makes this game as good as it is.
Score: Near Perfect
Finally I want to quickly talk about the 400 days DLC.
The DLC is good and I do recommend playing, but it was sad that it didn't impact Season 2 as much as it should have but that is nothing that we can change, but it was fun and the story for each of the characters was good and I don't regret playing it. And if you liked the original games 5 episodes you won't either.
And before I end this review there is only one more thing to say, to those who are still here that is, and that is: "Buy the game already!"

Amazing game. Definitely feels like a long-due spiritual successor to Uplink. Improves on it in a lot of ways, too; for example, by requiring the player to use a command-line interface rather than just clicking and dragging widgets around. It's also really fun and the soundtrack is pretty ♥♥♥♥♥in'.
Okay, now for the criticisms.
First, the game is way too easy and straightforward. Hacking every system can essentially be boiled down into three steps: take down firewall/proxy, open ports, run magical hacking tool. Missions are similarly straightforward: once you Hack into the Mainframe™ you dig around for clues, and if that fails, use your magical scan tool. Sometimes you're on a timer. And so on.
Second, missions are way too linear and the progression is kinda bugged. You are automatically assigned one mission at any given moment, and canceling it breaks the game by preventing you from proceeding to the next story-important mission. Some missions, e.g. the /el sidequest line, don't even trigger unless you meet some very specific criteria, and you can't backtrack to it later on. And even on the final set of missions, you can't even complete it unless you track down one very specific piece of software from a specific quest line which may or may not be available to you before the story-critical mission is forced upon you.
Third, a lot of hacking is just waiting for your damn magical programs to crack open ports and passwords for you after typing stuff into the command line. Which is boring, especially considering there usually isn't much of a challenge to begin with.
Anyway it's still a good game and I have zero regrets about throwing money at it.

I've never played this game before the PC release, so I'm not a old fan. Not a big fan of action hack and slash either. But Bayonetta I like. A lot.
Graphics may look a little dated, but the off-the-scale art direction more than makes up for that. Everything in this game looks refined, polished, excessivlely sophisticated (but never with bad taste). And that goes for everything, from the locations, to the character clothes and weapons.
Bayonetta herself is the eye-magnet for the entire game. Her looks scream of hours spent by talented artists on designs scratched over and over again,  until they got the one that clicked. This is how a modern adventure game should be. If you play games for their story, this is the right game for you. It is like watching a movie where your decisions make a difference.
Graphics are cell-shaded which looks like you are in a comic book. They make you feel like you are in a real world but also don't let you forget that this is a game. They really blend well with the story-telling. Game has a really touching tale with lots of twists in it. It is a zombie story but you deal with more realistic problems, like who to trust, how to use resources effectively etc. Your decisions changes the way story goes. I don't think they make a big difference in the main story but I played it for a second time with some different choices and it effects the way you look at things. About decision making, in some places, game forces you to make a decision so quick you panic and make one you didn't want, like in real life. This adds a depth to the game. Characters are created and used so effectively, you find yourself taking sides, feeling emphatic or simple hate for them. This is a great accomplishment I haven't seen in most of the games. You can really put yourself with the main character and the choices given you really shows your personality.
What about down sides? Most of the time gameplay is too easy (except speaking parts it is mainly quick time events) makes you feel like doing nothing at all. (But I told you this game is not for gameplay, it is for the story). Game is a little short (But they finish the story so well it takes some more time to recover yourself). And because of the story it is not a game to play a second or third time. (You can play a second time to see how your choices make a difference but main line is same so not as effecting as the first one.)
Btw you should know that this has nothing to do with tv series. I never watched it but really enjoyed this one.
As a result it is a really great story that everyone should see. Feeling inside a book or movie can't be done better.

is regarded as one of the best in the genre, and I can see why. The story is mostly nonsense and plot has terrible pacing but the game is carried by its rewarding fast combat. Executing a perfectly timed dodge gives you the opportunity to wreak havoc upon your enemies. The overall presentation is good, with awesome enemy and environment designs and a great soundtrack. If you like the genre then
is an easy recommendation, though it did little to change my opinions on the genre.
is set in a modern interpretation of Dante’s Divine Comedy. You play as Bayonetta, a powerful, arrogant and self-confident witch with magic hair who is part of a world where the natural balance between light and dark has been disrupted. I would like to tell you more about the plot but it’s just bizarre and I don’t want to spoil anything, overall it’s an insane roller coaster of events though the overarching narrative is fairly weak. Unfortunately the story has dreadful pacing, with the first half or so of the game having almost no purpose, luckily it really picks up in the second half.
The gameplay is the main appeal of
, though let me preface by saying that I don’t particularly enjoy this type of game.
is regarded as one of the best of the genre and I can see why. The combat has a decent amount of depth, though I found myself sticking to the same two or three combos. A unique aspect of
combat is the addition of guns, which you fortunately have strapped to your shoes. Though the guns are disappointing, and do such little damage that I found myself rarely using them. The best part of the combat in
is Witch Time which activates when you evade an attack at the last possible moment. When Witch Time activates all the enemies go into slow motion and you are free to bash away until the timer runs out. This mechanic makes evading attacks incredibly rewarding, though it is quite gamey especially toward the end.
For the most part the levels in
are fairly standard for the genre. Most levels have you progressing through a linear level fighting waves of enemies with the occasional secret. The best part of
is the boss battles, luckily there are many. The bosses in this game are massive and often have you jumping between platforms and climbing onto the boss. The difficulty of these bosses was good on normal with a nice balance between difficulty whilst not being too hard. There are a couple of unique levels that are incredibly different to the rest of the game such as one level where you control a motorbike which was actually really fun.
The story took me about 10 hours to complete on normal difficulty, the highest you can pick on your first playthrough. Once you complete the game you unlock hard mode, and whilst I did not try it I’m fairly sure you keep your upgrades and equipment from previous playthroughs. You unlock equipment by spending the halos you collect whilst playing the game, and you receive more halos for string long combos, being really good at QTE’s and generally badassery. There are a lot of things you can spend the halos on including weapons, techniques, potions, costumes and accessories.
was originally released in 2009/2010 so it’s hardly a new game. Though the PC version was recently released and features some graphical enhancements. The port ran really great for me and has fairly low system requirements though it is unfortunately locked at 60FPS. The graphics are fairly decent for a game of its age, texture quality is ok but the models, effects and anti-aliasing is really well done. The graphics are definitely enhanced by the unique and truly amazing art-style, it really can’t be compared to anything and features some great looking enemies. The soundtrack is also amazing and features a lot of incredibly catchy songs, which is fortunate considering there are not that many unique tracks.

I really loved this game. Hacknet provides a really legitimate-feeling hacking experience. It is satisfying when you solve a problem creatively. It is intriguing when you find new machines to hack. It is exhilarating when you just barely block a trace by the skin of your teeth. For that I commend this game.
However, there is a small but significant issue regarding the contracts system that I want everyone to be aware of. First, know that, in the game, you can only work on one contract at a time. I'm not sure why this is, but I believe the developers have said they are releasing a patch to allow for multiple contracts. Not sure when, though.
In the current version of the game, you can choose to abandon contracts of you want to try out a different one. That's all well and good, but here the thing: You cannot complete any contracts you abandon. At all. *POOF* They're gone! Here's the kicker: this includes story missions.
I got stuck on a story mission and thought that there would be some program I needed to get from a side mission. I abandoned the story mission to pursue other contracts, thinking, "They surely wouldn't lock me out of the story missions." They would. And they did. So now, I have to make a new game and start eight hours of work all over again.
Despite the whole novel of complaining I've thrown at you, I do really like this game. I do. Which makes it all the more frustrating when I encounter game-breaking and strangely arbitrary game design choices such as the abandon contract feature. Just take my warning before you play.

If it were advertised as an open world shooter, and left at that, this could've potentially been a 9/10 game. However, Bethesda has insisted that this game is indeed an RPG, so I must review it as one.
Fallout 4 lacks the weight of choice and consequence that games like Fallout: New Vegas thrives off of for integrating said mechanics so well.  However, the openworld design, Bethesda's bread and butter, is amazing. You could easily spend hours doing nothing but exploring the wastelands.
The gamplay and controls have been massively improved as well. I don't even have to rely on VATS to shoot things since the game actually handles like a modern fps and third person shooter.
Other things that have improved include: companions, quest narravtives, colors, POWER ARMOR, customization, and enemy types.
All that said, the game has taken some steps back. The brutally long loading screens are littered throughout the game. The very unstable and buggy ceration engine runs the game sadly (Besthesda needs to scrap it and start fresh). Also, the amount of available side quest following the completion of the main story is very small, but this can be somewhat overlooked since the quality of the quests has improved.
Honeslt, if you like open world shooters that you can easily burn 100+ hours of playtime (before DLC), then go for it. Just remeber that this is NOT an RPG. If you're dissapointed after those 100 hours because the promised RPG isn't actually very good at being an RPG, that's on you (given you've read this review).
It's a 7/10, but a fun one.

The OMSI Omnibus Simulator returns for another trip through the congested streets of Berlin. It’s one of the most realistic bus simulators you will ever have the chance of playing, unless you have driven an actual bus that is. Instead of taking place during the early 1980’s like the previous version, OMSI 2 takes place in Germany during the late 80’s, early 90’s around the time the Berlin wall fell. Since the gameplay is unscripted, you are given the freedom to choose your bus, the bus route and the weather conditions. There are no guidelines to follow; you are given the freedom to do as you wish. The feeling of freedom is present as you drive through Germany from one destination to another, dropping your customers off at their locations. For a change of pace, it felt good not having a story to follow or missions to complete.
OMSI 2‘s gameplay can overwhelm the player in the beginning, but as long as you use the provided tutorial system, you’ll be driving through Germany in no time. It’s possible to play the game if you decide to skip the tutorial but you will need prior knowledge of the previous game to do that. There are far too many instruments to use and procedures to remember, it’s very similar to piloting a plane in a flight simulator.
The in-game physics are incredibly realistic as you can almost ‘feel‘ every bump and turn you make.  Squeaks, squeals and rattles are heard from inside the bus every time you step on the break, hit a speed bump or even put on the parking brake. OMSI 2 is optimized for a steering wheel configuration, but this can be compromised with a keyboard/mouse combination.
OMSI 2 is an in-depth simulator that is not only complex, but entertaining to play, it may take the casual gamer a bit longer to grasp the game’s complexity, but with some patience it can be done.

Seed Generation
When balancing XCOM it was decided that that in order to LOCK players in to their choices and to help players repeat "lucky" events if for some reason they were forced to reload a save prior to those events they would store the SEED and INDEX inside the save file so they could resume the game exactly where the save left it. This game is like CS:GO with ADS (aim down sight). All weapon content is immediately availible to buy permanently, if you like the game and grind naturally you'll probably have all the guns you want in 1-2 weeks. There's even two free DLC packs with 15 day trial versions of (i assume) half of all the weapons in the game each, which I reccomend activating one at a time and stretching it out over a month. - That the battle mode in unintuitive and weird, two teams pelt eachother with ovwerpowered skills while trying to destroy the other teams boxes, luckily this is all optional.
- That ranked is linked to clans and is really quite stupid if you think about it, just doesn't work satisfyingly and doesn't give you a way to throw yourself into serious matchmaking without clan organization.
- I was going to complain about there being no female characters but one is coming on the 25th of October.

Darkest Dungeon is NOT a nice game. It's a relentlessly grim and unforgiving turn-based dungeon crawler that stands firmly in the company of games designed for players who aren't expecting to have their hand held. The consequences of each choice, both in and out of combat, are permanent thanks to frequent autosaves. Depending on the player, this will:
(a) give each choice weight, meaning, and excitement, or
(b) cause frustration, a dismissal of the game as "broken" or unfair, and likely a refund request.
Thankfully, I was able to extract mostly feelings of the first type during my time with the game. It is of course not without its flaws, though.
Playing on Radiant, I was able to avoid many of the most common frustrations/criticisms of the game while still getting the full experience it seemed the developers were aiming to deliver. (Radiant Mode speeds up character and town upgrade progression, as well as a handful of other anti-tedium and quality-of-life adjustments, while keeping all combat difficulty untouched. Losing heroes still stings, but it becomes much less of a grind to get replacements trained up.)
Reading prior reviews, I notice a lot of exaggeration/misinformation when it comes to this game's difficulty; things like enemies taking more turns than the player (other than bosses) are just plain incorrect. It can feel brutal and unfair in those first few hours learning the basics of the combat system, but once lessons have been learned about class roles and enemy prioritization (hint: the back row almost always deals high stress damage and should be dealt with first!), the combat experience morphs into something more tactical, exciting, and satisfying. Trying out and refining new strategies and party compositions as they either succeeded or failed miserably was a huge part of the fun factor for me throughout most of the game.
This leads to one of those big bullet point thoughts from above: I think
Especially early on, I was often forced to retreat from combat and abandon missions altogether so that I could escape with what gold or upgrade points I was able to gather before falling dangerously close to death. If this sounds frustrating to you, you probably won't enjoy Darkest Dungeon.
When it comes to matching its aesthetics and mood to its gameplay, Darkest Dungeon delivers. The oppressive atmosphere conveyed by the gothic horror art style and music never really lets the player feel comfortable, even in town. The narration that accompanies your successes and failures during battle really adds to this (although hearing the same line about not getting overconfident for the hundreth time is as eye-rolling as it sounds). As your heroes become more stressed, the accompanying audio/visual cues instill the same feelings of dread in the player.
For all its novel ideas and fun twists, Darkest Dungeon also has its warts (literal and figurative!). Boss fights are strange departures from the rest of the game's combat ideas, often requiring knowledge of particular mechanics or team compositions that, frustratingly, can only really be figured out by either trial and error (and dead heroes) or looking online beforehand. I'm all for boss fights requiring different strategies and/or creativity, but there are better ways of indicating to the player that these things are necessary before they've already been annihilated by the boss' mechanics. Some of the fights suffer from this more than others, obviously, but it's still kind of a bummer.
Additionally, the game is pretty heavy on the RNG when it comes to hits, misses, crits, and damage in combat. This is an area where I feel people have some ground to stand on in their criticism of the game. It's just not fun when you're sure you've made the right choice in strategy, only to miss completely and be annihilated by the enemy's retort, all because of chance. While I still feel the game is very much a strategy-first, luck-second experience, the issue of RNG rears its ugly head more dramatically than any eldritch horror stalking its corridors.
All in all, I enjoyed my harrowing trek through Darkest Dungeon. It's a great example of ruthless, smart game design that knows what kind of experience it wants to deliver. It is far from perfect, but for the right player, it has elements in common with any great horror film: tension, uncertainty, and the thrill of the kill.

, as the name subtly suggests, is extremely difficult, and that is because it often puts you at the mercy of horrible, horrible RNG. This is not for anyone who is easily stressed by games. You're going to have to put in some real work to conquer the challenges this game offers, and, even then, that might not be enough because some things are left to chance. However, I have found that, thanks to the community, there are many very useful mods out there that will lower the difficulty (and possibly your blood pressure) to a manageable level.
I have thoroughly enjoyed playing this game, both with and without mods, and I will continue to do so past completion and into the upcoming
expansion. I recommend it to anyone who enjoys a very punishing game.

Well, as I am coming close to completing this game I thought I would write a review for it.
First of all it's a great game, but you will only like it if you like to actually think when you play your games.
honestly this game has made me think about what strategies to use more than any other game I've played.
I've honestly enjoyed myself, and for that I thank you Red Hook.
But for the sake of this review let's break down the game into pros and cons, shall we?
let's start with the Pros:
#1-Great graphics, very dark artstyle that works great with the game's atmosphere.
#2-Good mechanics that give you ample choice in your tactics.
#3-A nice narrator whose voice is strangely soothing to listen to.
#4-Challenging gameplay that always pushes you to do your best.
Now let's look at the negative side of the game with the Cons:
#1-there aren't an incredible selection of quest types to choose from, its either: scout, eliminate,Touch 3 things, or a boss mission.
#2-speaking of variance, I personally think that the enemy variance(especially the bosses) is a tad too low, although others might disagree.
#3-The game tends to get a little "Grindy" during the middle and near the end.
#4-Sometimes it's easy to get frustrated with the game nearing the end due to the fact that all the enemies have a higher crit rate, E.g. you just started a mission but a melee character hits your character that doesn't have a lot of HP and gets a crit which puts them on deaths door at the very start of the mission, it can get really annoying to get crit hit.
Yes I recommend this game to anybody that thinks that they would enjoy it.

Is it a perfect game? no. is it a good game? yes.

This is the worlds most in depth and buggiest Bus simulator!
It's really a hit-and-miss game. From th e first purchase, there's not much content unless you buy quite a bit of DLC. The vanilla flavor of the game has only a whopping two maps to drive your Bus in, and only a handful of different buses to drive, many of them seem to be repeats. How ever, despite the two maps, one of them does have many different routes for you to take, so that's nice. From my experience, the other just has one.
This game does have a bit of a steep learning curve, and it did take me several attempts of picking it up and trying to go through the tutorials to figure out what was what, and then once I got that down, I had to try and set keys for my Logitech G27, which only added to the complexity, as you have more controls you need to be aware of for your bus then allowed on the Racing wheel's extra buttons. I'm not kidding, you literally control everything on the Bus. From doors to heating system, to interior lights to opening and closing your driver side window!
Beyond that, driving a bus, picking up and unloading passengers is actually kind of fun. If you find a route that you like, you can find yourself sinking some time into this game, if you like running around in circles, that is. Of course you have to make sure you are not late, punch tickets, print tickets, give change to passengers, etc etc.
The biggest thing that stops me from enjoying this game is that it crashes for no apparent reason with almost no indication of an update from the developers in the near future. The last update, according to steam, was in May. This really makes you wonder if the developers are doing something for this game or not, or if I've missed something.. Granted they are adding DLC but there has been reports of crashes happening still.
There are mods you can download and add into this game, but I haven't dabbled to much. It might help you out, maybe fix the game crashes, but you should proceed with caution.
Despite the game crashing bugs and the hard-to-learn controls, this game is .. Tolerable. Adequate. I would love to see where the developers take this game, but as far as I know, it's a hit-or-miss situation. Should you get it? Honestly, I wouldn't, at least not right now. The bugs in this game are to much to bare to really enjoy it. Believe me, I wanted to enjoy this game, but when it crashes in the middle of a route, I find that to be a little disappointing. You might have better luck then I do, and if you want to try your luck, go for it. Otherwise, I would stay away.

Playing without a shield, on the other hand, is unplayably annoying because the game loves enemies that block 95% of the time and you can't get past blocks without a shield (or at least I haven't figured out how, the kick is pathetic) - you have to wait until they charge, hit once, wait again, repeat. FPS is terrible on my pretty high-ish-end system (your mileage might wary) until I turned most of the graphical fanciness off, and it still dips at times. is regarded as one of the best in the genre, and I can see why. The story is mostly nonsense and plot has terrible pacing but the game is carried by its rewarding fast combat. Executing a perfectly timed dodge gives you the opportunity to wreak havoc upon your enemies. The overall presentation is good, with awesome enemy and environment designs and a great soundtrack. If you like the genre then
is an easy recommendation, though it did little to change my opinions on the genre.
is set in a modern interpretation of Dante’s Divine Comedy. You play as Bayonetta, a powerful, arrogant and self-confident witch with magic hair who is part of a world where the natural balance between light and dark has been disrupted. I would like to tell you more about the plot but it’s just bizarre and I don’t want to spoil anything, overall it’s an insane roller coaster of events though the overarching narrative is fairly weak. Unfortunately the story has dreadful pacing, with the first half or so of the game having almost no purpose, luckily it really picks up in the second half.
The gameplay is the main appeal of
, though let me preface by saying that I don’t particularly enjoy this type of game.
is regarded as one of the best of the genre and I can see why. The combat has a decent amount of depth, though I found myself sticking to the same two or three combos. A unique aspect of
combat is the addition of guns, which you fortunately have strapped to your shoes. Though the guns are disappointing, and do such little damage that I found myself rarely using them. The best part of the combat in
is Witch Time which activates when you evade an attack at the last possible moment. When Witch Time activates all the enemies go into slow motion and you are free to bash away until the timer runs out. This mechanic makes evading attacks incredibly rewarding, though it is quite gamey especially toward the end.
For the most part the levels in
are fairly standard for the genre. Most levels have you progressing through a linear level fighting waves of enemies with the occasional secret. The best part of
is the boss battles, luckily there are many. The bosses in this game are massive and often have you jumping between platforms and climbing onto the boss. The difficulty of these bosses was good on normal with a nice balance between difficulty whilst not being too hard. There are a couple of unique levels that are incredibly different to the rest of the game such as one level where you control a motorbike which was actually really fun.
The story took me about 10 hours to complete on normal difficulty, the highest you can pick on your first playthrough. Once you complete the game you unlock hard mode, and whilst I did not try it I’m fairly sure you keep your upgrades and equipment from previous playthroughs. You unlock equipment by spending the halos you collect whilst playing the game, and you receive more halos for string long combos, being really good at QTE’s and generally badassery. There are a lot of things you can spend the halos on including weapons, techniques, potions, costumes and accessories.
was originally released in 2009/2010 so it’s hardly a new game. Though the PC version was recently released and features some graphical enhancements. The port ran really great for me and has fairly low system requirements though it is unfortunately locked at 60FPS. The graphics are fairly decent for a game of its age, texture quality is ok but the models, effects and anti-aliasing is really well done. The graphics are definitely enhanced by the unique and truly amazing art-style, it really can’t be compared to anything and features some great looking enemies. The soundtrack is also amazing and features a lot of incredibly catchy songs, which is fortunate considering there are not that many unique tracks.

Telltale's The Walking Dead, is a fantastic point-and-click game set in The Walking Dead setting (hence the name). But it doesn't follow the story of the TV series, it is a parallel story and is completly different characters, other than a cameo in the first Episode.
The game follows a episodic lay-out and there are a total of 5 episodes in this first Season of this game series. The decisions you make throughout the 5 episodes effect the outcome so you might have a completely different experience in a situation than I have, depening on who lived and who died, which of your fellow survivors are your friends and who you sided with in previous situations.
And the game is dialogue-based, in fact I would say that most the game is dialogue and is very much about character development and making decision that you many times won't feel comfortable with. But if you make a decision and you feel like this: "No that didn't end well, I'll redo that." or something similar, then just keep playing and see what happens, if you feel like you did a mistake then do another playthrough and see what happens then.
The story follows former history teacher Lee Everett who just before the outbreak of the zombie apocalypse was conficted of the murder of a Senator who slept with his ex-wife. During the first day of the outbreak he finds a little girl named Clementine and decides to take care of her. I won't say anything else because I don't want to spoil what will happen but know that it will be heart-gripping, sad, horrifying and if you don't cry during the ending then you basically don't have any emotions.
Along the way you will meet many other survivors, each with their own personallity, backstory and priorities. Your relation to each one of them effect the outcome of the story, or at least part of the story.
Beware, you cannot save everyone!
There is a bit of a warning I have to give about the dialogue though and probably the one bad thing I can say about this game. You have a limited time to choose dialogue options, I do understand that they put it in (so that it wouldn't make the dialogue akward by having Lee standing there quiet for a minute and then continue like nothing had happened) but the time is just way too short, so short in fact that I several time didn't even have to read all the options. And since the game is so heavily dialogue based this is a problem, you should be aware of the problem. This is also true for when you have a decision to make (though you have a bit longer to think then), though not every single time. If you get into a situation and you need to think it over just press ESC and think it over, it doesn't break the game. Anyway now you're aware.
In summary The Walking Dead game is fantastic and the only thing done wrong the the limited time in dialogue but I still highly recommend this game to anyone, even if you don't like point-and-click games, I must say to you, play this game. The Story and characters are truly what makes this game as good as it is.
Score: Near Perfect
Finally I want to quickly talk about the 400 days DLC.
The DLC is good and I do recommend playing, but it was sad that it didn't impact Season 2 as much as it should have but that is nothing that we can change, but it was fun and the story for each of the characters was good and I don't regret playing it. And if you liked the original games 5 episodes you won't either.
And before I end this review there is only one more thing to say, to those who are still here that is, and that is: "Buy the game already!"

A technically inferior, but shinier Dark Souls.
I'll put it simply, the game's fun, and it looks great, but there's a few things that irritate me and not in the way that Dark Souls irritates you because it's difficult.
This game is difficult because of the choices made in some game mechanics, as well as small bugs that turn into big problems.
One such bug is enemies turning around to instantly face you if you manage to flank them, completely negating the tactic in the first place. I'm talking about the no-animation, teleport-y kind of turning around, allowing them to immediately attack you again without giving you an opening to attack them without being hit yourself.
It's also too easy to get stunlocked to death by groups of enemies. Sure, it's more "realistic" if one knock to the ground can immediately mean your death due to multiple enemies being able to still attack/hurt you when you're in a helpless position, but it's not at all fun, or indeed fair. If you die in Dark Souls, you know it's your fault, and you know what you can do to prevent it from happening next time. Further to the point, if you get swarmed by a group, your first instinct would be to retreat and take them on in a more tactical sense, right? In LotF it only takes a nudge for you to get stunlocked enough to suddenly get surrounded, and then you're done for, as there are no i-frames when rolling.
In LotF, you're forced to play tanky and take hits, as going the light route is simply a massive handicap, due to dodging not being as refined as in Dark Souls. So a lot of the time it's luck as to whether you're going to win a fight or not, or whether the enemy you're fighting is going to poise straight through your well-timed heavy and land you on your♥♥♥♥♥for a grizzly death. So a lot of the time you're relying on your health and defense in order to survive such things, and hopefully dole out more damage to them than they can to you.
Despite this, I would recommend LotF, just don't expect to be able to play like you can in Dark Souls, and don't expect the kind of well-crafted mechanics or indeed interesting lore/characters that Dark Souls is known for. Play tanky, get mad when faced with ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, have fun when not.

I bought
after some hesitation, due to reading a lot of reviews about stability issues causing crashes. However, after many hours of steadily working through the campaign, I experienced no issues whatsoever – no crashes, no lag, nothing; it would appear that the reported issues are not present since patch 1.4, at least in my case.
The game itself is clearly inspired by the
series, but has a character of its own. The story is nothing special but works, the world design is big and spread-out with a maze of ramparts and corridors, as well as routes up towers, down into dungeons, and even other dimensions, to explore. The character selection is quite small: three magic classes each offering three types of character. From there, the range of armour, weapons and trinkets is fairly large, allowing some good customisation and mixing of gear. I like how XP can be spent on magic or skills, and that using spells of a higher level requires skill prerequisites. Each magic class has four spells to invest XP in.
The graphics are excellent, sound effects are good. The voice-acting is okay but often lacks balance; Harkyn in particular sounds too monotonous and disinterested in everything he says, whereas Yetka's lines are a bit hammy and she is too corny to make her likable. The combat system can be awkward to pick-up but, much like
, it's a matter of perseverance, repeated combat, levelling and only entering areas when your character can handle the enemies there. Some of the bosses can be particularly tricky to deal with, especially early in the game.
Clearly the game has three possible endings, determined with a single choice rather than a number of choices made throughout the game, so the story is linear and pre-determined. I would like to see more of these hardcore action-RPG
-style games but with more variety, so that the story and outcome can change considerably depending on a number of player decisions. That way, no two playthroughs can ever be the same.
Overall I'd give this game 8/10 for being very enjoyable but lacking replay value, because the storyline will always be the same however it's played. Kudos to Deck13 for the effort put into
and here's hoping for similar quality in the future.

This is how a modern adventure game should be. If you play games for their story, this is the right game for you. It is like watching a movie where your decisions make a difference.
Graphics are cell-shaded which looks like you are in a comic book. They make you feel like you are in a real world but also don't let you forget that this is a game. They really blend well with the story-telling. Game has a really touching tale with lots of twists in it. It is a zombie story but you deal with more realistic problems, like who to trust, how to use resources effectively etc. Your decisions changes the way story goes. I don't think they make a big difference in the main story but I played it for a second time with some different choices and it effects the way you look at things. About decision making, in some places, game forces you to make a decision so quick you panic and make one you didn't want, like in real life. This adds a depth to the game. Characters are created and used so effectively, you find yourself taking sides, feeling emphatic or simple hate for them. This is a great accomplishment I haven't seen in most of the games. You can really put yourself with the main character and the choices given you really shows your personality.
What about down sides? Most of the time gameplay is too easy (except speaking parts it is mainly quick time events) makes you feel like doing nothing at all. (But I told you this game is not for gameplay, it is for the story). Game is a little short (But they finish the story so well it takes some more time to recover yourself). And because of the story it is not a game to play a second or third time. (You can play a second time to see how your choices make a difference but main line is same so not as effecting as the first one.)
Btw you should know that this has nothing to do with tv series. I never watched it but really enjoyed this one.
As a result it is a really great story that everyone should see. Feeling inside a book or movie can't be done better.
