Post DLC Review
For those who don't know, by way of pseduo apology, Ubisoft has offered its first DLC, Dead Kings, for free.  Of course, by downloading the DLC, you are giving up your rights to sue Ubisoft over Assassin's Creed: Unity, so there is that.
Anyway, I just finished Dead Kings on Xbox.  What I found there addressed some of the issues that I saw in the game, though if you are looking for a glitchless experience, you won't find it here.  What you will find is a more satisfying conclusion to Arno's story, which is one thing that truely disappointed me about Unity.  In addition, you'll get some more side quest goodness with some pretty decent rewards.  Its underground mazes add a new element to the game that is fun to explore as well.
It definitly does not fix things.  Bugs abound in the game, to include freezing you in place halfway through a mission, which I found to be the most common bug. Also, where as I found myself constantly relying on stealth in the main game, certain changes in enemy AI as well as the WMD known as the guillatine gun turned me into a melee fiend, kinda taking away from the whole 'assassin' thing.
But despite these lingering problems, Dead Kings is a step in the right direction.  If you have the game, the DLC is free, so there is no harm in playing through.  Dead Kings doesn't make up for all the problems that Unity STILL has... but it does at least put a period to the end of a painful paragraph in the Assassin's Creed Franchise.
-------
Game Completed Review:
So I played the game through on Xbox instead of PC.  I left the initial review comments below, for any interested parties, as I still cannot get it to work on my computer.
I am a huge fan of the series.  When AC: Victory comes out next year, I will buy the game before it is released, and I will have the season pass.  So when I say that if you are not a huge fan of the series, you should give this game a miss, that should let you know how I feel about the game.
Oh, it isn't that Unity is a bad game overall.  Paris is thus far my favorite AC world, and will give you hours of exploration to do, with dozens of activities.  I have been playing it almost straight for the last two weeks, and am still not complete with everything I can do.
But that said, it is certainly a far cry from what Assassin's Creed: Black Flag was.  Assassin's Creed Black Flag had a compelling setting, a very compelling protagonist, and the sidequesting was a dream come true - who wouldn't want to be a pirate?  It also ended on a high note, with one of the sweetest endings that I have seen in any game.
By comparison, AC:U had an interesting setting (the French Revolution), but interesting is not necessarily compelling.  Arno's initial introduction had me excited; it reminded me of Ezio, which is one of the all time fan favorite assassins.  But Arno wasn't nearly as well developed as he could have been.  Sure, you can go into the database and read Elise's letters, or see the database entry on Arno, but that is not the same as what they did with Ezio over the course of three games, or even Conner or Edward in one game each.  Sidequesting takes a lot of time, and provides a varied amount of activities for you to do, but at some point it got monotonous, and I did not have as much fun completing side missions as I could have.  And finally, the ending, while it brought everything to a nice resolution in one of the best boss fights of the series, left a lot to be desired.  I won't leave any spoilers, mostly because there is nothing to spoil.  In the other AC games, there was always a reason that you were still back in the Animus, finishing up whatever you didn't do; no such reason is given here.
If you are a diehard fan of the series, then check out the game when it goes on sale; aside from some major glitch issues (which UbiSoft is STILL working on), the game was alright, and the glitches don't render the game unplayable, just annoying.  But if you are just a casual fan, go get AC:BF or wait until the next AC release to check THAT out.  This game isn't worth the time (so heartbreaking to write that line...)
Also, in light of my continuing computer issues, make sure that you have a computer that can run this game well before you get it, if you get it.
**********
Initial Release Review:
Like so many other reviews of this game upon its initial release to PC, I must sadly give a downgrade to what I think would have been an awesome game.  I am biased of course; I love Assassin's Creed; I have been addicted to the series for years now, and have bought the last three games on pre-release.  On all three release days, I have been driven myself crazy trying to get the game to work.  Though I have enjoyed every game in the series (yes, even ACIII, I am THAT much of a fanboy), I have to say that Ubisoft is horrible when it comes to delivery, especially on launch day.
I see this game succeeding in spite of itself, as Ubisoft will possibly put out a patch that will make it easier for us all to play on PC, and eventually everyone will forget what a horrible launch day Assassin's Creed Unity had.
Until that time, I cannot in good consious recommend this game to anyone who is not a die hard fan.  When Ubisoft puts out that patch (or when I get a better computer in a few years), I will re-review the game at that time.

Following in the joyful wake of Black Flag, Unity's France is bleached, boring, and tiresome after a couple hours of playing.
Heres a couple things Ive decided so far:
- Combat is atrocious, many times amounting to two slashes traded followed by a body slumped on the floor... many times that of your own due to obnoxious bystanding assailants peppering you with shot as you awkwardly flail about. Sometimes you mysteriously fall dead at a nick. Firearms are also wielded with drunken repose. Clumsiest fighting system of the last several games...
- Crowds are much more dense, but also that much more painful to wade through. The engine is also quite happy to populate interesting places that really dont need 15 people to stand about gawking.
- The minimap and world is cluttered with crap that you really probably have no interest in anyways. Here, have some markers for newspapers on each block. Heres a glittery object that gives you stats on the fact that youve unlocked armors, despite the fact that you can do that by pressing tab. Heres a glittery object that tells how much of the game youve completed. Heres another glittery object that ambiguously ranks you against other people, because you care about that right? Heres a glittery object that lets you form a guild (Why?). Heres a mission where an endless parade of other players will pop into your mission and do nothing worthwhile, then die and disconnect.
- On that note, Ubisoft tries to shove multiplayer down your throat. Most people I know dont give two weeviled baguettes about multiplayer in a game like this. An immersive and thoughtful story and decent gameplay would be great. Try investing more effort in that.
- Arno is about as interesting as the sheet of cardboard I keep in my garage should I have to work under my car or lawnmower. The characters are so damned lame. Usually AC breathes stunning life into each era it works with, but this installment feels as dusty as a tomb. There have been several pretty cool segments so far, but theyre quite fleeting. I really have a hard time caring at all about the entire Revolution occuring during the game, frankly.
- Climbing is laughably bad this time around. You'll float up precipitous portions of vertical architecture like an ungodly ghost-ape, but have a great deal of trouble decending despite the hyped downward free action.
- The Ubisoft DLC money grab is shameless. I expected nothing less from them, but it really gets old...
Some of this stuff can be patched away, but theres some fundemental disappointments here. I really hope they work some magic on it, otherwise this might be the first AC I delete before I finish... And thats saying something considering how I always get pretty well completed with everything in the other games.

That being said you dont hit the adventure with the same party every time, since they need to rest.   Did I mention you can have a werwolf as a party member?  Every class has a benifit and a use.  Some are better in certain areas and against specific bosses, thats part of the learning experience.  This is a game where your experience and planning have a major impact on your success.  This game will not appeal to everyone and is not your typical dungeon-crawler. I highly recomend it.

The game is built around death. You are expected to die a lot. However, the developers took this too far and instead of expecting, they made every uneven and unfair move to make sure you die. If somehow you didn't, you'll likely leave your characters aside because their sanity level is too high.
I really love the idea of sanity and stress. However, the ways you lose your sanity is unacceptable. You lose your sanity when you fall in trap (unless a RNG happens and you see the trap, you can't avoid it). When you walk in dark. When enemies ambush you. When you don't camp etc. These are the acceptable consequences. However, you get stress even when you are walking in well lit room with your torches filled up. You get stressed when you get a HIT. Your entire team gets stressed when someone gets CRITICAL HIT. When someone gets a status debuff like bleed, you get 2 different stresses. Like 8 stress for the hit and 4 for the bleed. Every turn the bleed damages you, the stress meter fills up.
So what happens when stress get full? When it reaches 100, 90% of the time that character will get a ridiculously stupid debuffs. When it reaches 200 which is also the max limit, that character gets HEART ATTACK. This means regardless of the remaining HP, that characters goes down to 0 HP. So how do you get rid of stress? There are basic ways which is even more ridiculous. You either:
1) Get their stress relieved in TOWN which is AFTER the quest period.
2) Deal a CRITICAL HIT. This is even stupider because the enemy's critical hit will give you 18 or above stress while yours will relieve you 7-10. Either way, you get stress. Normal hits don't relieve stress.
3) Use a Jester to relieve stress from ONE team mate each turn via playing a music. However, unless you upgrade that skill, the stress that is going to be relieved is very little. In order to upgrade a skill beyond level 2, you have to upgrade the shop first, and then pay gold to upgrade the skill. Assuming your character lives that long.
The art style, the music and the brand new mechanics for a turn based game is absolutely great. I really liked the game for the first few hours. However, the game lacks one crucial point. RATIONALITY. This is a game and a game should be fun to play and relieve stress from the player. I am constantly trying to fight around ♥♥♥♥ing stress of characters instead of fighting the enemies.

Now I've had some fun with this game for sure. Maybe even $15 worth. But I'm going to not recommend it here because of some big issues that will probably stop others from having much with the game. Glitches and other early access issues are not really problems with this game anymore. Honestly, I'm not sure why it's still listed as early access.
First of all, you will discover very quickly that the game devolves into nothing more than repetition. Go to the new tier of worlds, get the new tier of resources, use new resources to go to the next tier. Rince, wash, repeat.
The exploration is admittedly exhilerating for a while. It didn't get boring to me until after I got to the 4th or 5th tiers when I realized that all 5 million planets are essentially the same exact thing. When I finally got to visit exotic biomes like the tentacle biome, I couldn't even tell the difference between it and the rest of the planets. The same boring algorithm randomly generates all planets using the same pieces. Once you seen the pieces, exploration is never thrilling again, so enjoy it while it lasts.
Lastly and most importantly, it's been half a year since I've seen a noticeable update to this game. I guess the devs got all the early access money they wanted and just stopped bothering.
This game is just one of the many successful early access games I've seen, and contributes to a larger problem I'm having with early access games. Once a game goes early access, it never seems to be anything but early access. This is the problem with a business model where the customer willingly pays a game company the full retail price for their game before the game is ready. The company no longer has any need to continue spending money and time on the product because they've already been paid. Unless some sort of contrat legally holds the company to a set of promises, the early access model will continue to be a flaw in the industry.

Its not a ridge racer game. Its burnout meets trackmania without a clear focus. The game is based around beautiful destruction physics but in order to destroy other cars, you need to drift, chase, or destroy items. Destroying items is worthless since you get a fraction of the boost needed, so you tend to be drifting a lot.
However the ai just gains boost at a steady pace, meaning they will just boost whenever their meter is full. The boost itself is odd, its designed around strategic use to either power through a corner, destroy a city target to get more speed/shortcuts, or take out a racer but instead the game requires you to be constantly boosting in order to keep up. As well, there are no mechanics to allow players to catch up. None of the short cuts drastically change the map and the leader can use his boost to open it up anyways so there is no way for someone behind him to catch up unless he messes up.
Given the nature boost is gained, the late game is also to the favor of the leader as there are less targets available and players are more spread out.
Combat is also weird. There are no rewards for damaging cars, and you don't get boost if you frag someone in a special way ala burnout. Also unlike later burnout entries, there is only one type of car per race. As a result, cars with good acceleration and speed trump all else since they can drift fine and use boost to make up for any lose of speed.
The game does have one very interesting part and thats the special events. These include some trackmania esque maps where you have to get to the finish line while hitting targets.
But what sells the game to me is the sense of destruction. The objects you destroy remain on the track making the track feel more and more wartorn and whenever you destroy a car you see an amazing slow motion view of it bouncing. It never got old for me.
As for the default levels, they are pretty generic and some end up being confusing since they reuse prefabs in an unusual way. The events aren't always balanced, either, some will prove to be a pain since you just don't have the right car for it or others are so easy because you can use a car that the level wasn't balanced for.
The star is the player-made levels, of which there are tons, which use the ingame editor and allow for a nice variety of fun and bizarre levels. The game to me seems like a case where there was a pre-existing game that was adapted with the ridge racer brand and then rushed into development.
I say get the game if you like arcade destruction racing , the 10 dollar price tag is appropiate but with games like carmageddon and NCG, there are more focused alternatives.

Would you like to know how it is to be a German Chancellor, British PM or PotUS? Then play this game but do not expect miracles.
Democracy 3 is turn-based meant-to-be politics-simulator where your goal is to lead your country to the status of a prosperous democratic state...or communist regime, green paradise or dictature of God, whatever you like. The mechanism is quite easy - your government generates you points which you later on spend on implementation/abrogation/adjustment of the tree of policies. Everything you do has, in some extent, its political/economic/diplomatic effect but sometimes you have to count with the side-effects which usually are not pleasant, e. g. some angry group of citizens or decrease in popularity. Your total-game goal is, as you may suppose, getting re-elected. That is sometimes easier, sometimes harder than you may expect.
Pros:
-variety of policies = variety of ways how to lead your country
-unexpected events+special questions (gay marriage, etc.) occur in the meantime between two turns
-experience of your government ministers are reflected e.g. in speed when implementing policies
-if you love statistical data, graphs and so on, you will spend your time in them when looking at the numbers or general development
-developers still publish new and new DLCs which actually enhance the game-experience
Cons:
-when playing one game longer it is increasingly boring
-player may sometimes get lost in the policy tree or, when the player wants to play the game properly and would like not -to get lost, needs a paper where he/she could write some notes
-difficulty really depends on the precision of the pre-game settings - if there is something wrong, the game may get unplayable
-some irrational events happen
-almost without a soundtrack (I know this is not obligatory for the game but some gamers like to listen to something)
To conclude this review, I recommend this game mainly to those who are interested in politics and generally like to think about the development of their country (moreover, this game may make you think about your country policies irl). In contrast, I think that this game is not for the players who like to experience new game environments and to enjoy graphical aspects (since this game looks pretty much the same all the time), even though this game provides replayability in its variety of settings. My final rating is: 77/100.

Overview:
Hacknet is at its heart a digital exploration game. Using a powerful suite of programs that you gain throughout the game, the player must gain access to systems and perform contracts. The game has a very similar feeling to the older game Uplink and hacking is done through speed, knowledge of your tools, and system resource management (RAM).
Plot:
The plot is pretty threadbare, but does a good job of pulling the overarching story together. The ending makes sense, but is a little lacklustre for the scope of what you supposedly accomplish. However, this is in character for hacking since public attention is bad for those at the fringe of legality. Overall, I enjoyed the plot, but the beginning intro and ending are really the only interesting points. It's difficult to do characterization when all you have is text, but I felt that more effort could have been put into letting the player get to know more of the other people in the story (naix, maybe some backstory on bit, etc.)

Gameplay:
The gameplay is separated into two parts: hacking and forensics. The actual hacking is rather easy since most trace timers last far more than long enough and some systems actually keep your admin after you disconnect. The main challenge in this format is simply knowing which order to run the port hacking programs in so that you can maximize efficiency and minimize time spent not logged in. These do get quite intense at times and a few conflict sequences definitely run the point home that you're not invulnerable. Progress through the game is blocked in a sort of metroid-vania way, in the sense that you need this power to unlock that type of port to enter. I enjoyed this, but wished that there were more early systems that you needed to backtrack to.
That backtracking is part of the second part of the gameplay, the forensics. By this I mean that you spend your time going through file systems trying to spot the file with the password, scanning computers to reach connected nodes, and searching for new IPs to check out. In fact, there is an entirely alternative gameplay path that is only reached with diligent use of your tools. I loved the exploring, but it did feel quite limited, or at the very least truncated to be more accessable for players who might not be used to the gameplay style.
Part of the joy of the exploration comes from the humor that you find in random files. From a script for "Titanic 2" that involves the icebergs running onto land and attacking people to
IRC logs, there is a decent amount of silliness and joy to discover. However, since the files in the systems you hack are procedurally generated, more content would have been nice. There's only so many times that you can see the same Bash log before you stop wanting
to check them out because you feel you've seen everything.
Pros:
*really fun
*sense of satisfaction from difficult hacks
*humor: From a mission where you need to write "d*cks" on the main webpage of "Nortron Security" to an homage to *chans (the secret /el/ image board), the game is very funny and self aware.
*exploration
*failure penalty fair
*short: Hacknet doesn't wear out its welcome, which it probably would have for some players by the end game.
Cons:
*repetitive
*short
*not enough content
*exploration feels like it was stunted for ease of access
Hopes:
*mods:
I feel that mods could make this from a good game to a great game. I'd love to try my hand at adding new features to the game.
*hardware changes
Uplink let the player purchase hardware upgrades to increase ram or processing power as well as giving access to more complicated systems. Hacknet's only customization for your computer is changing the display theme.
*more story
Getting to know the other hackers more personally would be very enjoyable.
*higher difficulty
clearing the logs on a system means that they won't track you down - but this presents a problem. You always leave a disconnect log, but the game doesn't notice that a disconnect log without a matching connect log implies
that the IP that disconnected was responsible for the attack. Having to selectively clear logs and/or bounce IP like Uplink might be a good idea. In addition, I would have enjoyed more difficult forensics and encrypted files
that you can't find the password for. I was a little miffed a few times when I spent some time looking through the files to find the next IP when all I had to do was type "scan". More threats to the player as well as uncertainty
in how well you performed the attack would be welcome.
*more challenges
Maybe adding in new network architecture requiring the player to do a different minigame than typing the first two letters of a program and tab completing.
*multiplayer
multiplayer is hinted at being in development in the files on the endgame server.
Bottom Line:
I love this game and want to spend so much more time on it, but sadly it seems that there's no more content. This type of game is sadly lacking in today's market and is quite unique. It pulls off what it does well and with much better guidance than Uplink. You should try it if you're interested in learning basic cmd/*nix commands and command line navigation/use while having fun, if you like tech and silly games, or if you're a fan of Uplink.

I just couldn't stand it anymore.
That's my short-review of Unbounded.
Is a long-review really necessary? *Sigh*
Well if nothing can be done about it, let's dive in.
I've been a Ridge Racer fan for quite a long time. Aside from Ridge Racer Vita, R: Racing Evolution, and maybe Rave Racer, I've played all the games. I'm extensively familiar with the series, but that's irrelevant. Unbounded is...I don't know what it is. Was it some game Namco bought and then had some RR music and cars included to tie everything together? I don't know. So yeah, if I compare this game to RR, or hell if I so much has even mention that game, then I've lost.

Unbounded takes place in Shatter Bay, where a mysterious group is involved in illegal street racing. Apparently they hate the city almost as much as they hate each other. This is one of those racing games where not only can you obliterate your rivals, but you can also bust through cafes, government buildings, and construction sites for a shortcut. The similarities to Burnout are pretty obvious, though in this game "checking" a rival is a bit more binary.
By catching air, drifting, and/or receiving various in-race awards, the player gets boost. Aside from a temporary increase in speed, anyone you run into during that brief period is going to get wrecked. This is about a 95% chance. If you're grinding next to someone (oh my) and you hit the boost, they're going to turn into flaming wreckage instantly. When not boosting you have a 5% chance of wrecking someone. This is a neat way to reverse all the dirty tricks that can happen in  a usual race. Say you're one of two racers making a turn. You're on the outside, and the inside guy is using you as a buffer to avoid hitting the wall. This is a great time to boost because they'll suffer dearly. Also whenever you wreck an opponent, the game auto-corrects your car, so you don't drive into a wall or anything. Exploiting this mechanic can be quite handy.
Your opponents can boost as well, and aside from the red trail there's no obvious indication that they've boosted. Something like a sound effect could have been really useful. As it stands you're better off handling the other racers with kid gloves (especially if they're cheating AI), because they could boost at potentially any moment and take you out. Boosting is also necessary for certain destructable objects. Their usefulness in the actual race varies, and they could just as easily glitch out and cause you to flip over or get turned around. To unlock more races you have to amass a lot of points, destroying stuff is how you get them.
There are no shortage of tracks in this game. That's because they're all created via a track-editor. It's a neat idea but not really fleshed out. Basically each track is divided into sections. Let's say there is a straight-away, a curve to the right, a squiggly line, a hard-angle right, a dip, a long-easy right, a hairpin right, and that's the track. A lot of time in arcade-racers is spent learning the track itself, but with this game it doesn't seem to matter much at all. Instead you familiarize yourself with particular turns (the 1 or 2 difficult ones to be precise). While the track-editor allows further customization by adding objects and other tools, it's not as deep as it could be. Let's call it a limitation of the game-design. It's difficult to create ornate tracks when it's expected that a handful of racers are trying to destroy each other. There are a lot of created tracks floating around, and some are really interesting. Consider spending some time checking things out online.
I don't like the handling. Normally I'd just tack this on to the end of a huge paragraph, but it's the #1 reason why I couldn't take anymore of this game. The main reason I don't like it is because it's inconsistent. With some games drifting has either A) a sizable learning curve, or B) can be picked up in the first few seconds. Both A & B work on their own. Daytona USA** is an A type, while Ridge Racer (I lose!) is a B type. Both games have appropriate learning curves, and mastering them is an exceptional feat despite the wildly different barriers of entry. Unbounded can't be an A type because the tracks aren't nearly as involved and well-designed. There's only so much you can do with such a base-selection of turns. Unbounded isn't a B type either because the cars have more weight, it takes more counter-steering not to lose control, and deciding between what type of brake to use to initiate the drift is more important. Essentially the system just doesn't gel for me, but I guess it doesn't matter.
This game apparently considers good drifting somewhere towards the bottom of "things you should actually be concerned about in a race". In the career mode there are very few time-attack races, and even then they have gimmicks like icons you pick up to freeze the clock. There are drifting events too, but you don't think about applying what you've picked up in an actual race. It's hard to appreciate a good drift in this game, when it's usually more effective to barrel through the opposition with a boost. Sometimes the winner is merely the racer that managed to get away from the chaos. More often than not, driving skill takes a backseat.
Altogether Unbounded just isn't satisfying. It never flicks the "Hell Yeah!" switch in my brain. Quad-kills, surviving a brutally difficult platforming section, or just executing the perfect drift through the hardest turn, these are just some of the many "Hell Yeah!" moments. Unbounded has never in my 7 hours* of play elicited that same response. I do all these supposedly awesome things but it's just not exciting at all.
*Yes I realize that by playing the game for a sizable amount of time, I've opened myself up to comments such as "If you didn't like the game, why'd you play it for that long?" I was ready to quit this game after 2 hours, but that wouldn't be fair would it? Although, I probably should have beat the game, but playing Unbounded for 10+ hours is just too much to ask of me.
Sorry.
**In Daytona USA it's called power-sliding. It's the same but different. DETAILS.

A racing game as directed by Michael Bay. I bought RRU cheaply while knowing some several bad critiques, so I came expecting nothing, and indeed nothing I got.
The drifting compared to previous iterations or other racing games is stupid to say the least. Using a controller take a turn, keep B pressed to increase the angle, release B to reduce the angle. You could rubber band the gas trigger, it would play the same.
There is some kind of boost which does not speed you up, but make you immune and able to oneshot and make other cars explode in thin pieces. Which can also happen to you btw. In front of the finish line. While you're first. With your car passing the finish line in a debris state, having several second delay cause of being FRAGGED and being respawned behind the line and finishing 3rd/4th at best if they don't frag you again.
"New game mechanics are fun", I thought to myself, "why did they complain?" Well, they complained because this game lacks to provide a minimum of enjoyment. RRU is basically a grind through a set of events to be completed more or less in order. You could pretty much ending up locked out of races because reasons. Also while you drive you are tasked to run through buildings destroying them, still for reasons. The game offers a lot of 90° turns with no basic control over the drift, and it's so bad that even AI fails to take those turns most of the time.
I was about to give it a "meh" review, if it wasn't that on my PC (which is far from being low spec'd) the game crashes while in full screen. And, while in windowed mode, the taskbar shows up. They didn't even get that part right.
Also there is no minimap ingame, so you cannot plan your turns strategically as per… like… any other racing game, ever. You also have health like your other opponents, but that information is also missing from your HUD.
In the 2-3h I played this game I chewed up a good portion of the so called campaign, not once I had some fun. I dare think there's none to be had here, unless you like to destroy buildings and cars and not caring about actual driving, in which case this game might be right up your alley. It totally isn't up my alley though.

This is it, the beginning of the legend, even though it is quite dated by today’s standards the game aged like a fine wine and gameplay feels solid. Here you get to know how to the amazing universe of Half Life and Portal started and the consequences of the chain of events Gordon got himself into.
A very bad aspect of the game is that many friendly human models and voices are the same throughout the game and said people will be torn to pieces and blasted full of holes and that somewhat gives a bizarre feeling and it makes a bit confusing to be able to tell who is the real Eli Vance and Kleiner but I guess technology was more limited back then.
The game itself tries to combine puzzles, shooting and a bit of sci-fi horror into a nice little mix. You might be trying to figure out how to turn on the water to some device but you know that when you go back to activate it you will to pass through those alien clawed tentacles of death or you will be having a flame throwing gargatuan on your tail and you have to see how to dispose of him while running like a mouse.
Small creatures will always be jumping on you and making you keep an eye out in every little hole and corner and the huge enemies will make you run and hide to safety giving that chasing sensation. In terms of enemy variety it’s a pretty nice selection going from generic army thugs and ninjas to energy shooting aliens, grunts that fire a barrage of homing “bees” to you and even vehicles and artillery strikes.
Every gun in here has its purpose, you want to explode a few barrels but not waste precious ammo? Use the normal gun. Want to see your enemies go up in pieces with some traps? Place some remote charges here and there and then cover the door ways in optic mines. A huge firefight got you trapped in a corner? Well thanks to a grenade barrel in your assault rifle you can noobtube your way out of trouble. But wait, massive ordinance is being deployed on poor little you? Well those huge aliens, tanks and helicopters won’t expect a guided missile on their face, or will they? In that case they should be no match for a charged radioactive shot or maybe your Gluon Hyper Beam that can rival the most legendary of Pokémon.
If all fails, nothing says DIE like a crowbar to the face.
There’s not much to say about the environments they are quite varied and include even ice parts and water parts where you will have to face the terrors of the deep with your “water usable” weapons only. Basically you go through offices, warehouses, factories, sewers a bit of desert canyon and at last the mysterious and bizarre Xen where everything came out of Gabe Newell’s fever dreams and rules of gravity allow you to be fabulous.
TL;DR: You should play this, see how old things are done right  and explode the microwave casserole.

Arrgh! I know I sound like an embittered cow who doesn't like change when I say this but I did actually used to like this game! In fact I even thought that the people complaining about RNG and corpses were just fools unwilling to adapt thier tactics to new situations. Heck I even liked a lot of the later changes to this game! The only major issue I had with this game was the heart attack mechanic which I was able to turn off. I was genuinely enjoying the experience!
Anyway I decided to go back to the game recently and found that for some reason the insanity meter kept increasing after 100. So I decided to go into the options to see if I had just forgotten turn off heart attacks in this save. Turns out they completely removed the option to do so! I had a look around the forums and found that red hook were for some reason dead set on having this as a feature in thier game to the point they just removed the option to turn it off after they had added it to keep people playing during early access!
It baffles me as the less objectionable easier to overcome mechanics such as corpses are still optional but the outright restrictive heart attacks are thrust upon you! I've had to pull out of otherwise challenging early game quests made impossible by this mechanic simply because my crusader, who's job would make you think he'd be physically fit, has the collesterol of a obese middle aged drunk.
Now granted there are tactics that account for this but the nature of the game is such that they can easily go wrong. I'm seriously surprised that red hook is so dead set on this frankly unnessiscary and unrealistic mechanic but they're quite happy to allow you turn off the all the artwork that went into the corpses that are at worst a nuissance. In the end I'm no longer enjoying this game so I can't say I recommend it. It's gone from a challenging tactical crawl to outright abusively difficult.

"Finding Teddy" is a simple-looking adventure game that builds on atmosphere, a retro-look and solving some puzzles.
In it you play a little girl who is stolen her beloved teddy bear. In order to get it back she enters a strange world through her closet.
First of all: It is quite a short game. Don't expect to be occupied or entertained for hours.
Also the amount of information you get is very limited (if any), you gotta figure out a lot by yourself (there's no text speech or something).
The variety of actions you can make is also limited: You can run from one end or object to another, collect a few relevant objects and solve puzzles mostly by singing "songs" of this strange world (I don't spoil but let's just say that the music notes look quite familiar). Personally I think the music idea is very original and sweet.
The story is as simple as it gets (I already told it). And as you progress the story won't really develope. So it's more about exploring places and enjoying the atmospheric environment.
The pixel graphic is very nice to look at, often very colourful and pretty.
The soundtrack does not contain sound effects, it only builds on music which gives the game a special touch.
Overall: I recommend the game because it was a nice short experience but I won't scream "Play it!" in your face. If you enjoy adventures where you get much more to do and don't like it otherwise, then "Finding Teddy" might not be something for you.
Right now, the normal price is 6,99 € but I recommend to wait for an opportunity to save money (like through a discount offer or something).
And when the announced sequel will be published, personally I'd like to check that out, too.

I got through about an hour of this game before deciding it wasn't worth my time.
As far as puzzles go, these were about as bad as they come.  Absolutely no logic behind them at all.  Use items randomly on other items.  Here's an example.  I get a saw.  Turns out I'm supposed to saw down a little green sprout?  Then I'm supposed to stick the sprout in a weird hole with symbols around it (as far as I can tell, nooo hints for this anywhere).  And then I get... a fly with a top hat.
Not only that, but in order to solve this I have to walk back and forth across at least 10 empty screens; much more if you include wandering, which you're going to do a lot of.  The game is ridiculously spread out, with 0 to 1 interactable things on each screen.  Lots of screens with nothing.
The main unique feature of this game is the musical alphabet.  The idea is cool.  But something about it's execution just wasn't working out.  The alphabet at first appears to be random, hard-to-remember symbols, but after you look at it for a while, you realize it is actually just the English alphabet in a misleading font (seriously, another one?  Why do people keep thinking this is a good idea?).  Once you realize this, a lot of things become much easier.  It feels a lot like cheating.  I'm still not sure if you're supposed to realize it or not.  If you don't realize it, the game is laborious and tedious.  If you do, it feels like you're skipping any gameplay that was there.
Other problems I had:
- The "companions" were basically items, but selected in a different way, and it was veeeery unclear when a companion was selected or not.
- Once you open your inventory and select an item, you have to actually deselect it before you can select something else.  If you don't do this, UI may stutter and flash.
- When you open your little keyboard to play on it (a crucial part of the game) clicking on the keyboard also clicks through to whatever is behind the keyboard, which means you can't play certain notes while on certain screens.
- Once you click on a door and your character starts walking over there, you can't make her stop or go somewhere else. And worse, you can still click on a bunch of UI things during this, but they are all broken and will stutter open and closed.
- Unlocking UI features was badly timed.  Over and over you catch a glimpse of a feature that you're pretty sure is there (like some new menu pops open and then closes before you can look at it); you can't figure out how to access it and fight with it for a few minutes; you give up and wander around; eventually you stumble onto an arbitrary screen and it finally gives you access to the UI.

I start off with the most important thing of the game, driving!
When you get in your bus for the first time, it could be a bit overwelding. The amount of buttons and switches are enormous. It isn't an easy to pick up game. If you want the full experience out of the game, you need to invest some time in it to learn how it works (the errors and the AI behaviour is a bit odd so in the beginning this can be quite frustrating but after some time you know how they respond so you can change your way of driving on it), and of course how to drive the damn thing ;-).
If you get the hang of it you will see that it's quite fun and challenging to drive a bus. You have 12 meters behind you to keep an eye on and a schedule. You also need to take care of your passengers that want to be comfortable and on time at their destination.
Omsi doesn't run on a fancy big graphic engine. Even the fastest PC can have some lag in this game. Omsi hasn't got a stable frame rate because the scenery is on any place different. But I can give you some predictions of what frame rate you will get:
Low-end PC: 10-18 FPS
Mid-end PC: 20-40 PFS

I really love the idea of sanity and stress. However, the ways you lose your sanity is unacceptable. You lose your sanity when you fall in trap (unless a RNG happens and you see the trap, you can't avoid it). When you walk in dark. When enemies ambush you. When you don't camp etc. These are the acceptable consequences. However, you get stress even when you are walking in well lit room with your torches filled up. You get stressed when you get a HIT. Your entire team gets stressed when someone gets CRITICAL HIT. When someone gets a status debuff like bleed, you get 2 different stresses. Like 8 stress for the hit and 4 for the bleed. Every turn the bleed damages you, the stress meter fills up.
So what happens when stress get full? When it reaches 100, 90% of the time that character will get a ridiculously stupid debuffs. This is still the best bus simulator.  It is a good improvement on OMSI 1.
MAPS/VEHICLES: The Spandau map is much extended with a new chronology function where you can see the routes/fares and most importantly the Berlin reunification/fall of the Berlin wall between 1986 and 1994.  Two maps are included the fictional test map Grundorf (one route, the 76) and Berlin Spandau (routes 92 (137), 5 (130) and also two night routes.  Two new buses come with this game the articulated (bendy) bus MAN NG272 (GN92) and the MAN NL202 (EN92).  The two double deckers from OMSI 1 are improved and the MAN SD202 has two new variants; the D90 and the D91.  There are new AI cars including ambulances with working sirens.  There is also much more trains in OMSI 2.
PERFORMANCE: As with OMSI 1, you will need a pretty good PC to run OMSI 2.  FPS is improved from OMSI 1 but lag can be experienced frequently in busy areas of maps.
I have an Intel Core i3, 6GB RAM and 2GB graphics card.  Here is my FPS on the Hamburg addon map.
Suburb areas: 30 - 60 FPS.
Inner City areas: 20 - 25 FPS.
City Centre areas: 12 - 20 FPS.
UI: The user interface is completely changed from OMSI 1.  The new UI looks much smoother and is easier to use.
BUGS: When this game was first released it was almost unplayable.  It had clearly been released too early, as there were very frequent bugs and crashes.  At this stage (version 2.1, the game is a lot better and crashes are rare.  I have played the Hamburg and Vienna maps for the past few days with no crashes.  Unfortunately crashes do occasionally still occur and there are still some minor bugs, although these do not normally affect gameplay experience.
ADDONS/COMPATIBILITY: Many freeware and payware addons exist for OMSI 2.  The OMSI 1 addons Vienna LU 200, Citybus O305 and Hamburg Day & Night have all been patched for OMSI 2.  Most OMSI 1 buses work in OMSI 2, but the majority of maps will not work in OMSI 2 without adjustments.  Many map creators have released new versions of their maps for OMSI 2.  A huge range of mods, repaints, vehicles and maps are available on the OMSI forum and other OMSI related websites.
DRIVING EXPERIENCE/FUNCTIONS: OMSI unlike most (if not all) other bus sims recreates the bus functions and driving physics as close as possible.  Over 90% of buttons are pressable and have a function.  For example you can set the destination using the IBIS computer, spray the windscreen, adjust the heating (involves many switches, not just one button!), lights and door controls.  The bus sounds are excellent.  All have been recorded off the real-life buses.  Particularly with the bendy bus, you can feel the weight of the bus you are driving.  This is enhanced with a steering wheel.
GAME CONTROLLERS: Buses can be controlled with the mouse or keyboard, but for a much more realistic experience a steering wheel is the best.  The best realism can be achieved in OMSI 2 with a 900 degree, force feedback steering wheel.  The one often preferred is the Logitech G27, but as this is very expensive other good wheels include the Logitech Driving Force GT.  TrackIR 6 can be used with this game for added realism of the camera views.
TUTORIALS/DOCUMENTATION: As well as a detailed manual, new to OMSI 2 are tutorials.  I strongly recommend users who have not played OMSI 1 previously to do these tutorials as learning how to operate the buses can be tricky at first.
Overall this is an excellent bus simulator (now that most bugs are gone anyway).  Remember if you purchased OMSI 1 you can get OMSI 2 at a discounted price at the publisher's website.

As a huge fan of Souls series, I've been waiting for some time to get my hands on this game. But due to some negative reviews stating the game's bugginess I have waited for a sale. And so I got this 40% off on Christmas Sale. Straight up I honestly think this game is not worth 50€, so I recommend waiting for a sale if you want to play it.
The pros: This game looks like a third-person Diablo (and I love that art style) with somewhat clumsy combat compared to Souls - but that is a fresh addition I welcome. Thanks to that there is some replay value (choose a different offensive, magic, etc.). When you get yourself over the bugs or FPS issues, the gameplay is like a breeze. The more you kill the more XP you get and this has kept me engaged. Finding new, imba weapons and armor that both look gorgeous always makes you happy.
The Meh: The boss encounters miss their "wow" factor (almost always a huge guy with a huge weapon) and they all can be straight up zerged - the only tactic is wait for them to be dazed after they swing their weapon and strike. The voice acting ranges from average to bad to poor along with lipsync. The story is bland and uninteresting. The crafting system could have used more love and invention. Oh and that backtracking sometimes gets on your nerves if you have poor spatial orientation combned with the maze-like design. NG+ is 0 challenge but at least you get the feeling of revenge on the poor sods that gave you hard times.
The cons: The few initial hours of gameplay were ridden with bugs, huge framerate drops (this game is very poorly optimized and I hope a patch will fix that soon) but since setting the details to medium-low with all facy stuff off I got it to run somewhat acceptable on my GTX660.
Final words: Enjoy the game for what it is - its combat and you looking badass, hurling enemies around with your huge weapon, and get it on sale for ~16 hours of gameplay.

This game shares a lot of obvious mechanical similarities with the souls series but really does stand out as its own title.  This is a relatively linear action rpg with some castlevania esque backtracking and a lot of hidden side quests and rewards for those of us that are itching to explore every nook and cranny ( like souls, but you know where to go nearly all the time to progress the story).  The story is played out through fmv cutscenese and for the most part  the game does a good job of letting you know what's going on and where to go next.  It's not all hand holding however as there are no quest markers or maps.  no, you'll have to get accustomed to the area and recall location names if you intend to follow the leads to that special magical item you're trying to discover.
Misc Pros:
Leveling and the whole purchasing stats to level thing works similar to dark souls here with its bonfire mechanic.  There are alternate hard mode challenges for each boss that rewards extra loot.  There are challenge portals that appear after a boss is defeated for those that remember to backtrack a little and get some more loot and items.  Mobs are varied enough and the bosses are distinctly unique.
Misc Cons:
You can't avoid damage in this game so much as mitigate it.  Sure you can avoid a lot of it but theres much you can't or just isn't worth trying.  Second, there are relatively straight forward, clear and linear upgrades for weapons and armor types.  Third; the movesets don't change much from weapon to weapon in each wepon class (ie: all greatswords handle pretty much the same.  Just go with the one with the biggest damage.)
That being said this game holds its own as a very good title.  Coming from someone with over 700 hours across the soul titles, i happily played through this game and immediately rolled into a second play through.

How mistaken I was to think this was some kind of zombie FPS!
.  With a title of "The Walking Dead" and a zillion screenshots of, well, zombies - I might sound like I'm off my rocker here, but no.  An unexplained disease outbreak has suddenly taken place (you never get to find out what, how or why in the game) which results in the dead returning to devour the flesh of anything they can grab (yep, sounds suspiciously zombie-like, doesn't it?) but this is really just the backdrop to the storyline.  The backdrop event could equally be about a nuclear holocaust, or some killer virus outbreak (kinda not far off this story actually).  It is the events caused by this cataclysmic, life-changing backdrop that you play through.  The game is a story-rich masterpiece about survival.  You will constantly be presented with moral choices and difficult dilemmas.  Do you trust fellow survivors or not?  Do you depend on them?  Do you let a threat live?  Do you let compassion rule over logic?  Do you be honest or withold the brutal truth from a child?  In truth, you might do a little of all these things because this is a game with very few rights versus wrongs.  There is little point flipping through walk-throughs in hope of pursuing the perfect game.  It simply doesn't work like that.  You will be presented with tear-jerking choices where neither is great, but you HAVE to choose.  Heartbreaking moments surface throughout - so all but the most hardened of players might appreciate a box of Kleenex by their side!  This game is very much the 8-person lifeboat scenario where you forever always seem to have 9 people.  Who goes?  YOU decide.  But not everyone can live happily ever after and life is not always fair...
I don't know how true to the comics the game happens to be, but I will say that the characters were very easy to care about (even the dislikeable ones had a story), the artwork is novel and effective (somehow 3D without losing the water-colour comic essence), and the haunting melodic music throughout sets the tone for the dark storyline perfectly.  The game plays well with both keyboard/mouse and gamepad and doesn't require a ninja PC to play it (which is always nice).  There are no pointless 'collectibles' missions to detract from the story and no quick-save options to dilute the pressure of the instant-decision process (though for busy people it is never-the-less possible to rewind back to an earlier point if part of the story is missed).
For anyone who enjoys a great story-driven adventure built strongly upon the choices you make throughout each episode, this game is the real deal.  If you want a game where what you do really seems to matter, and where a few shocks and anguishes won't be too distressing, then I highly recommend this game.

Before the Steam account integration, in the first half of 2011, I found this game through a web-banner on a site I can't recall. I joined up late in the craze of the Rose Regalia and caught myself a few cool sets. My interest started to wane in late 2011, after getting stuck in the early half of the third leg of the clockwork dungeons. I would always log in every so often after starting my hiatus, just to see what was going on and if anything changed; however, I wouldn't really stick around to do much besides look.
In 2012, they introduced the rank system; something that I still dislike. At first, it was kinda cool; you'd have more experienced players with higher ranks than those who didn't do missions. Unfortunately, in early 2013, they made what gear you can use and where you can go directly correlate to your rank. Having gear access and clockwork access tied to a rank system, that's based on character rather than account, was something to make me shy away from returning in general, despite being grandfathered in on my oldest character.
I feel the focus started to shift from gameplay additions to cosmetic ones over the years; a view most evident from my latest excursion into the game of Spiral Knights. What shocked me upon returning once again wasn't new combat actions, new animations, new dungeons. Instead, I found new costumes and effects that would cost hundreds of real-life dollars to collect. Accessories that would cost you more than Vanaduke carries? A falsehood! What an obscene claim... made reality.
I wish there was a neutral option for reviews. Spiral Knights is one of those games where, if you have a group of friends to play with and / or you're not easily drawn in by vanity, you will have some fun for a bit. I figure, if I hadn't been playing for a while, I'd get maybe ten to twenty hours out of the experience before it became dull.

How the game could be improved:
1. Add a leveling system with a cap of 100.
You gain experience from killing enemies, crafting gear, and pretty much doing any task. At level 30 you get a permanent weapon slot, at level 60 you get another permanent weapon slot, at level 75 you get a permanent trinket slot, and at level 100 you get the last permanent trinket slot. Other rewards are granted from 1-100, like orbs of alchemy or other crafting components.
This would allow you to have your full dream loadout without having to spend a crown on those temporary trinket or weapon slots.
2. A daily quest system
Npc's will ask you on a daily basis to complete special tasks, from hunting down a certain special enemy to defeating a boss. Rewards are granted based on difficulty and player rank. Completing quests also grants the player experience. The hardest quests will grant the best rewards and the largest amount of experience, this includes eternal orbs of alchemy and very rarely a unique weapon or resource.
This will encourage an active player base and would allow you to consistantly and reliably obtain crafting opponents you would otherwise have to spend hours grinding for.
3. More gear, obviously
The devs spend so much time on creating a bunch of cool armors that provide no statistical boosts AKA cosmetic armors and weapons/shields that are just reskins of other weapons. There are a few exceptions like the Mixmaster and the fire variant (I forgot what its called). The weapons themselves are powerful, but they are rare and expensive. I suggest the devs actually provide unique stats to the reskins and cosmetic armors they produce.
4. Improving battle sprites in general
Currently the Dragon sprite seems to be the most underwhelming of the 3, while the seraphynx (cat) seems to be the most vital. I get the whole Offense/Defense/Support role, but frankly it just seems flawed. The cat seems to provide almost an unlimited supply of hearts granting the player near immortality, The ghost pet allows the player to go invisible and deal double damage is used correctly, while the drakon just adds stat boosts and the most useful ability doesnt really benefit the player as much as the other pets in general. The fireball should deal double, maybe even triple damage to be even considered useful for its cooldown. The fireball does less damage than a single swipe from my Combustor for gods sake! The fire barrier should also deal increased damage and provide an increased defense bonus as well. The ultimate ability should actually do damage other than be a bootleg Ash of Agni bomb, The explosions dont even deal damage, they just set enemies on fire.
I think they should allow pets to passively attack enemies other than having to command them to do so. The dragon would be a powerful flamethrower, so it would fit its offense roll better, the cat would swipe its claws and knock enemies back, the ghost would cast an aoe spell that poisons enemies with a 30% chance to inflict curse debuff. I personally think this is the best idea on how to fix battle sprites. I am not saying to ditch all of the abilities, I think they should be kept. Im saying that the pets should provide SOME sort of usefullness while on ability cooldown.
I hope the devs see this if they even read reviews at all.

I was about to write this as a review:  "Utter trash of a game!  Why?  The camera does not center on your character and lags behind you, meaning you will have to go to the edge of the game world while moving around and can't see♥♥♥♥♥♥around you.  I uninstalled and will remove the game from my account."
BUT, it turn out this off-center camera is due to a bug when vsync is off.  Go into your the game's folder in steamapps and open alienshooter.cfg with notepad.  Change vsync=0 to vsync=1 in order to enable vsync and fix the camera bug.  After that, the game is a fun, but simple old-school arcade shooter with an upgrade system where you just clear levels and shoot aliens.  The devs should have fixed this before releasing on Steam.  I can't speak to all the differences in this game versus the original Alien Shooter, but this is the same game, so just get this one as it has somewhat updated graphics and all the same content.
I Recommend this game to those who enjoy battling an endless variaty of creatures and building with friends. If you love adventures this is the game for you!

This is it, the beginning of the legend, even though it is quite dated by today’s standards the game aged like a fine wine and gameplay feels solid. Here you get to know how to the amazing universe of Half Life and Portal started and the consequences of the chain of events Gordon got himself into.
A very bad aspect of the game is that many friendly human models and voices are the same throughout the game and said people will be torn to pieces and blasted full of holes and that somewhat gives a bizarre feeling and it makes a bit confusing to be able to tell who is the real Eli Vance and Kleiner but I guess technology was more limited back then.
The game itself tries to combine puzzles, shooting and a bit of sci-fi horror into a nice little mix. You might be trying to figure out how to turn on the water to some device but you know that when you go back to activate it you will to pass through those alien clawed tentacles of death or you will be having a flame throwing gargatuan on your tail and you have to see how to dispose of him while running like a mouse.
Small creatures will always be jumping on you and making you keep an eye out in every little hole and corner and the huge enemies will make you run and hide to safety giving that chasing sensation. In terms of enemy variety it’s a pretty nice selection going from generic army thugs and ninjas to energy shooting aliens, grunts that fire a barrage of homing “bees” to you and even vehicles and artillery strikes.
Every gun in here has its purpose, you want to explode a few barrels but not waste precious ammo? Use the normal gun. Want to see your enemies go up in pieces with some traps? Place some remote charges here and there and then cover the door ways in optic mines. A huge firefight got you trapped in a corner? Well thanks to a grenade barrel in your assault rifle you can noobtube your way out of trouble. But wait, massive ordinance is being deployed on poor little you? Well those huge aliens, tanks and helicopters won’t expect a guided missile on their face, or will they? In that case they should be no match for a charged radioactive shot or maybe your Gluon Hyper Beam that can rival the most legendary of Pokémon.
If all fails, nothing says DIE like a crowbar to the face.
There’s not much to say about the environments they are quite varied and include even ice parts and water parts where you will have to face the terrors of the deep with your “water usable” weapons only. Basically you go through offices, warehouses, factories, sewers a bit of desert canyon and at last the mysterious and bizarre Xen where everything came out of Gabe Newell’s fever dreams and rules of gravity allow you to be fabulous.
TL;DR: You should play this, see how old things are done right  and explode the microwave casserole.

Finding Teddy is a simple point-and-click game from a new developer. Featuring a 2D plane with rich pixelart and a musically inclined theme
. Your teddy bear has been stolen so you’re going through another world, trying to get him back. That’s pretty much it, there really isn’t much to the story and the other “characters” don’t do or say anything of significance. I know they intentionally wanted to craft a game without dialogue, but there’s a lack of narrative that I can’t ignore.
The main mechanic is a lot of simple inventory puzzles. Find an item, give it a creature/thing for another item and keep going until you reach the end of the level. All the while, you’re being sung to by creatures and walls. Which you’re supposed to figure out that the notes are actually letters from the english alphabet. But the game doesn’t really clue you in and the notes look so alien that I didn’t figure it out until a guide clued me in. Even if I was willing to let go of this complaint, it’s not that fun a mechanic. It’s more annoying as you try to match the notes in the right order to progress through the game but there’s a lack of feedback as to whether you’re doing it correctly.
Far too many of the puzzles are too obtuse to figure out, with clues too far and few between. There’s no real hint to what each item does and I had to use a guide to get through at least 50% of the game. I’m not the greatest puzzler on the earth but even for me that’s pretty bad. While I can’t fault a game for my incompetency, the obtuseness of the game with the rather meager puzzles and story can be faulted.
There is exactly one thing you can change in Finding Teddy: fullscreen on or off. Nothing else can be changed. There aren’t any .ini files that I could find either. It did run well during my playthrough but for such a short game, I do kinda expect that to be the case.
Soundtrack is simply ok, not all that interesting or engaging to listen to. There’s also the other issue that the sound effects are too quiet over the louder soundtrack. Which would be easily solved if audio sliders had been put in but well, that didn’t happen. Even more odd is that there’s a lack of audio feedback. When you click on objects or move around, there’s nothing to really back up that you did that. It bothered me the entire while during my playthrough.
For a scant couple of hours, Finding Teddy is merely ok, not all that special. The lack of audio-feedback, the obtuse UI and puzzle design can be far more aggravating than I think it’s worth. I’m sure for the devs it was a great starting point and it’s got lovely pixelart to look at. But I just didn’t really enjoy myself with it, not helped by the constant need to refer to a guide in order to finish the game. All that combined with a minimal story and I'm finding it difficult to recommend Finding Teddy.

The little I played is enough to realize that this game is not worth my time or patience.
In its blind quest to be "the revival of Point'n-Click," it takes only the worst and most frustrating aspects of that genre.
You'll spend most of the game not actually thinking about puzzles, but slowly backtracking through the same places, waiting for the damn walking animation from one endpoint of a screen to another to complete, over and over again.
It's neither fun, interesting, nor charming.
And when you get to a place, good luck with the obnoxious, no-feedback pixel hunting and poorly implemented item use controls.
If you're a fan of point and click, do yourself a favor and ignore this game.
Instead, grab something by Wadjet Eye Games, or a title from the Broken Sword series, or one of the various other, much more thoughtfully designed titles such as Machinarium, The Inner World and Broken Age, off the top of my head.
If you want a similarly pretentiously "arty" game, but without such egregious design flaws, check out Superbrothers: Sword & Sworcery EP.

The story of the game is that your past ancestors dug up underneath the riches of their mansion and luxery, only to find the uncomfortable truth, which is the horrorish monsters that are unleashed onto the land. The ancestors then, after dying from their numerous adventures with digging, send a letter to you to assemble your heros and mercinaries in attempt to kill the monsters, restore the evilness from Hamlet, and gain the riches of the
Now, for the pros and cons, I'm just going to make this simple~
Pros:
+Interesting Storyline
+Amazing artwork for graphics, including animation sprites
+Music is intense, heavy, and expected as you are fighting eldritch monsters
+Trinkets to help your hired mercinaries through the dungeons
+Controls are easy to navigate
+Attack, dodge, accuracy etc. quirks on your heros are easy to understand
+"Quirks" for your different heros, which are cool/interesting/funny sometimes
+Mods are easy to install. There are a few reskins, dungeon mods, and game changing mods that I love (but doesn't hinder my game experience to be non-enjoyable)
+An actual challenge (refer to cons section to inquire more information)
Cons:
-The "challenge", or RNG. Basically, your crew will die a LOT and you need to upgrade your stagecoach to find more expendable heros. The RNG is what you'll find the most annoying in this game; it's not particular to difficulty, because the game will constantly be hard and won't have an actual difficulty (I guess the "increased" difficulty is finding less stuff, including having to kill enemies by a specific round). There's not much to say besides that RNG is the main antagonist of the game, and not the actual enemies themselves.
-You can't escape from certain dungeons, despite the fact you waste a lot of money/time on your hero's skills and expensive trinkets.
-Not much other cons, but only because the RNG takes up a lot of the "cons" space. Seriously, you will get ♥♥♥♥ed over with this. Get ready to die.
-Some of the community (people who play DD: stop ♥♥♥♥ing comparing this game to Dark Souls. This game is nothing like dark souls in terms of graphics and gameplay.)
Unforgiving, cruel, but battle-inspiring, this game combines the classic dungeon crawl with the harsh, hindering enviornment leaving you with an unnerving experience afterwards. I'd give it an 8.7/10.
Ending statement:
"hey Ben, what did you do today?"
"I uppercutted an eldritch pig-god"

Eigentlich würde ich den OMSI gerne empfehlen aber leider kann man dass nicht grundsätzlich. Nur wer einen leistungsfähigen PC, mindestens bestückt mit einem Intel i5 Prozessor hat und das Spiel auf einer schnellen SSD installiert, kann den OMSI in vollem Umfang genießen.
Ich spiele auf einem PC mit AMD FX6300 und einer GTX560 Grafikkarte und habe das Spiel auf einer Intel Serie 520 SSD installiert und kann z.B. die Schatten im Spiel grundsätzlich nicht aktivieren, da die Performance dann in den Großstädten auch mal deutlich unter 20 FPS sinkt, was für einen Fahrsimulator dann doch zu wenig ist. Unabhängig davon kommt es beim Nachladen von Ressourcen, was regelmäßig alle paar Sekunden passiert, trotz der SSD zu heftigen Rucklern im Spiel. Die Grafikkarte wird hingegen nicht wirklich beansprucht. Es macht für die Performance keinen großen Unterschied ob ich z.B. Antialiasing deaktiviert habe oder ob ich 2fach oder sogar 4fach AA aktiviere, der Unterschied in der erzielten Bildwiederholrate im Spiel ist gering.
Andere Spieler die einen ähnlichen PC mindestens jedoch mit einem Intel i5 Prozessor haben, berichten sie können die Schatten aktivieren und erreichen dann z.B. in Berlin am Rathaus immer noch Bildwiederholraten von über 20 FPS.
Wer also einen modernen Intel PC (minimum i5) und eine Highend SSD besitzt und zumindest eine halbwegs aktuelle Grafikkarte sein eigen nennt, dem ist der OMSI zu empfehlen, alle anderen sollten sich bewußt sein, dass sie z.B. auf Schattendarstellung wahrscheinlich verzichten werden müssen.

How the game could be improved:
1. Add a leveling system with a cap of 100.
You gain experience from killing enemies, crafting gear, and pretty much doing any task. At level 30 you get a permanent weapon slot, at level 60 you get another permanent weapon slot, at level 75 you get a permanent trinket slot, and at level 100 you get the last permanent trinket slot. Other rewards are granted from 1-100, like orbs of alchemy or other crafting components.
This would allow you to have your full dream loadout without having to spend a crown on those temporary trinket or weapon slots.
2. A daily quest system
Npc's will ask you on a daily basis to complete special tasks, from hunting down a certain special enemy to defeating a boss. Rewards are granted based on difficulty and player rank. Completing quests also grants the player experience. The hardest quests will grant the best rewards and the largest amount of experience, this includes eternal orbs of alchemy and very rarely a unique weapon or resource.
This will encourage an active player base and would allow you to consistantly and reliably obtain crafting opponents you would otherwise have to spend hours grinding for.
3. More gear, obviously
The devs spend so much time on creating a bunch of cool armors that provide no statistical boosts AKA cosmetic armors and weapons/shields that are just reskins of other weapons. There are a few exceptions like the Mixmaster and the fire variant (I forgot what its called). The weapons themselves are powerful, but they are rare and expensive. I suggest the devs actually provide unique stats to the reskins and cosmetic armors they produce.
4. Improving battle sprites in general
Currently the Dragon sprite seems to be the most underwhelming of the 3, while the seraphynx (cat) seems to be the most vital. I get the whole Offense/Defense/Support role, but frankly it just seems flawed. The cat seems to provide almost an unlimited supply of hearts granting the player near immortality, The ghost pet allows the player to go invisible and deal double damage is used correctly, while the drakon just adds stat boosts and the most useful ability doesnt really benefit the player as much as the other pets in general. The fireball should deal double, maybe even triple damage to be even considered useful for its cooldown. The fireball does less damage than a single swipe from my Combustor for gods sake! The fire barrier should also deal increased damage and provide an increased defense bonus as well. The ultimate ability should actually do damage other than be a bootleg Ash of Agni bomb, The explosions dont even deal damage, they just set enemies on fire.
I think they should allow pets to passively attack enemies other than having to command them to do so. The dragon would be a powerful flamethrower, so it would fit its offense roll better, the cat would swipe its claws and knock enemies back, the ghost would cast an aoe spell that poisons enemies with a 30% chance to inflict curse debuff. I personally think this is the best idea on how to fix battle sprites. I am not saying to ditch all of the abilities, I think they should be kept. Im saying that the pets should provide SOME sort of usefullness while on ability cooldown.
I hope the devs see this if they even read reviews at all.

First, in just a couple of words, I recommend this, but you should know what you're getting into.
The developers clearly intended this as an homage to the Dark Souls franchise, and after playing through and beating the game once, that is being charitable.  Homage or "whole sale theft," you be the judge.  But for purposes of whether you should play it, it matters only insofar as you go in looking for an exact replica of Dark Souls' brutal challenge and unforgiving combat.  Despite many shared features/mechanics, Darks Souls this is not.  This is Guy Fieri to Dark Souls' Gordon Ramsay.  And you know what?  Sometimes you just want a Honky-Tonky Double Barrel Meat Loaded Blast (with extra Jack Daniels Sauce!) instead of caviar.  And that's OK.
If you can approach this game as the testosterone, Monster energy drink fueled Todd McFarlane 90's nightmare (knightmare, I think Todd would have gone with) that it is, you'll have a blast.  I swear they read every Spawn comic ever and just lifted art and designs from it.   It has much of the following: KNIFE ARMOR!, KNIFE HANDS!, KNIVES THAT HAVE/ SHOOT MORE KNIVES!, BIG ABSURD COMPLETELY UNFUNCTIONAL F*CKING WEAPONS!, BROODING!, GRRRRRR!
Combat mechanics are decent once you get the hang of them.  I used an agility Cleric build (WITH DOUBLE F*CKING KNIVES), so I was pretty much untouchable after I learned to time my rolls and figure out how to dance away from things then dart in to slice and dice.  Magic gets pretty broken across the board, I read.  I used the support path and "Shelter" immediately breaks the game if you focus on spamming it before, during, and after fights, as it can completely replentish your health bar.  I used it when I needed it, instead of as a security blanket, because the combat was pretty fun and not white-knuckle insane like DS (which can, again, be a good thing!)  I died a fair amount of times, usually through carelessness or camera issues, but I never felt totally SOL after getting killed after a decent amount of progress since the last checkpoint, again unlike DS.
Bosses are great looking (as is the entire game if GOTHIC HELLSCAPES RAAARGH! are your thing), and pretty straightforward.  I did not have to rely on cheesing/kiting any of them.  The first few boss fights, before you figure out how to dominate, can be intense.
As far as the story and character devel....HAHAHA just kidding.  Here, have some wicked knife armor and go kill some big f*cking monsters.
7/10 will probably check out NG+.

Lords of the Fallen is among the first entries of what I hope to be the beginning of the "souls-like" dark fantasy action RPG.  Like many early games in a new subgenre, it excels in some areas and falls flat on its face in others.  It ends up being a decent game that falls just short of expectations.
The graphics of Lords of the Fallen is gorgeous, with fantastic and consistent art style throughout the game.  Unfortunately, the game is not well optimized, and does not run well for many players.  Some are unable to play the game at all due to constant crashing.  The developer has been hard at work releasing stability patches, so this may not be a problem in the future.  Just keep in mind that you may not get a smooth experience if you don't have powerful setup.
The game offers some interesting lore, given to you mostly by audio logs found throughout the world, and a little more through dialogue.  Conversations have an awkward, jilted flow, leaving most characters dull and one-dimensional.
The meat and potatoes of games of this type is the gameplay, specifically combat.  Fighting in this game is broken in both senses of the word.  The biggest problem is the fact that you lose stamina at the beginning of your attack animation, instead of the end.  Weapons in this game have great, weighty attack animations that lose all momentum the moment you get hit, regardless of how close you were to completing the attack.  This makes fighting with slow, powerful weapons infuriating.  All too many times I've attacked with a long windup for an attack, only to get hit with a piddly 2 damage from a quick enemy swipe, losing the attack and the stamina invested.    Never spam the attack button, as you will most often get hit every time, losing all stamina leaving you unable to block or dodge, all the while dealing 0 damage to the enemy.  While there is a poise stat, I have never seen Harkyn tank a hit and strike through, even in the heaviest of armors against the lightest of enemy attacks.
The game gives you a variety of spells, most of which have very little use.  While a few spells offer utility, the casting animation of spells leaves you vulnerable for too long, making it difficult to justify casting spells in combat apart from a select few.  You are given a magic "attack" through the gauntlet item, but it is awkward to switch to mid-combat and  does little damage per point of magic usage unless you have invested heavily into it.  Because of this, combat is nearly always through melee combat.  Of note are ghosts and anything with a shield, which are difficult to manage without magic.
On the other hand, combat can be broken in your favor by the inexplicably strong effect stat scaling has.  You have no reason to put anything other than a Luck rune in your weapon, since the increase of damage outclasses anything else.  Because of this, any weapon without a rune slot or without any scaling (as in, most weapons) will be overlooked.
One thing the Lords excels in is boss combat.  Bosses are all unique and have segmented health bars.  With each segment you reach, the boss changes tactics or adds new attacks.  This leaves boss encounters fresh and interesting throughout the fight.  In addition, you pick up a weapon from each boss you kill.  By fulfilling certain criteria, such as taking no damage or ending the fight quickly, you will get an upgraded version of the boss weapon.  This is a welcome addition to add extra challenge if you are up to the task.
All in all, Lords of the Fallen is a bittersweet game.  It ends up being a mixed experience that may be worth it if you can work past its many flaws.  Expect around 15 to 20 hours of gameplay.  Consider giving it a look if it is on heavy discount, but you won't miss much by passing it by.
