Review on Lords of the Fallen:
After finishing Lords of The Fallen, it gave me a "Mass Effect 3" ending disappointment. The game is Overall Pretty Good, though the back-stab is rather iffy. but I swear the amount of bugs I went through really♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off which I will list down there later.
Positive points:
1. Just as current day gamers categorize Rogue-Like and Rogue-Lite, I agree with other reviewers out there that this is Dark-Souls-Lite. The game is very similiar to Dark Souls but the game was designed for you to take hits even if you choose the rogue agility class. Other classes will take damage from the beginning of the game until the end, but for the rouge, you have to take some damage at the start of the game to kill enemies and get experience to level up. After leveling up to a certain point and obtaining your final magic ability, that is where the fun begins and you can sneak almost every enemy, "Stab" and back-stab.
2. The weapon timing mechanic is very interesting especially when you dual wield. When you dual-wield, you cannot unleash your combo unless you successfully execute the perfect timing strike two times consecutively, any remaining stamina after that can be used to continue the multi-hit combo if you, once again, successfully execute the perfect timing strike.
3. I've played heavy-weapons as well, and it relies more on timing the strikes or tanking enemy hits to deal a heavy blow. Early on, the perfect timing strike allows you to attack 2 times and dodge roll before having your stamina deplete. Without perfect timing, you may only attack twice and have your stamina depleted, leaving you open to attacks. Also, with this stat called Poise, more Poise means you can take larger hits without getting staggered or falling down. It is a pretty nice way to portray the "Tanky-Feeling" of Heavy Armor.
4. The stamina/energy recovery is relatively fast compared to Dark Souls/ Dark Souls 2. In my opinion, this makes it a bit more enjoyable. Remember, this means the enemy has the relatively fast regeneration too.
5. The enemies in the game are quite normal and it was easy to figure out their pattern. Boss attack patterns are also easy to figure out cause every attack has a distinct preparation pose. This does not necessarily mean it is easy to beat them, you still have to figure out which attacks do they combo with. Depending which magic class and armor you chose to play with, you have to react accordingly. This makes it fun, it gives me a monster hunter feeling.
[The style reminds me of monster hunter, but why I did not use monster hunter as an example is because in MH, attacks do not consume stamina. In Monster Hunter, you can throw caution to the wind when fighting common mooks, and only fight seriously and learn the pattern of the boss monster. Whereas for Dark Souls and Lords, you have to fight every unit with the seriousness of a Monster Hunter Boss]
6. The Rune crafting is quite interesting, depending on what type of equipment you put the rune in, it provides different stats and different runes do different things too.
Negative Points:
1. Seems to me if you are a rogue and you meet an enemy with a shield, you must bring out your own shield which most likely won't work because you have low poise OR cheese'em with the magic gauntlet of pew pew. This kind of makes me feel like I'm forced to NOT play Rogue

2. Some bosses and units are too easy to cheese with the gauntlet, I experiment "the cheese" for a few shots and proceed to fight normally, when the boss changes style I experiment again to test if it can be "cheese-ed" and continue to fight as usual.
3. The walls will make your camera get screwed up. When you run into a wall, chances are that your camera will zoom into your face and you cannot see the enemy. Another possibility is that you get to look inside the wall and nothing else. Therefore, besides the enemies in front of you, you have to remember, walls are you enemies too. It would have been nice if they would make the walls transparent when you go too close to the walls and zoom out but hey, maybe it was intentional to make walls your enemies too.
4. The choices you make in game don't really matter which makes me feel like I should just do the main quest and nothing else if I ever play the game from start again. Just slight changes for the end, which gave me a "Mass Effect 3" ending disappointment, as said on the top.
5. Sometimes when you attack, you clip through the enemy and all you see are their undergarments (loin cloth) or armor. Screwing your camera up in the process, leaving you vulnerable. Also, when this happens, 50% of the time, your damage will not register.
6. The magical illusions are flawed. Not "Prayer", other skills like the Rogue's "Stab": occasionally the enemy will register that "Stabs" illusion is a target-able unit like all Magic Classes "Prayer" and proceed to attack that illusion. It is an advantage to the player but that is not suppose to happen.
7. I may have said that the Rune Crafting is interesting but there is too few variety of runes. Which make it quite dull at the same time.

1. Subtitle not disappearing if you change area when the subtitles are present;
2. Death but not death: black screen never fades back into game except when i pause, happens when you fall into a death pit but there are stones that block your way down to the bottom which make you take damage but so happens that part of the pit is also the death line;

It took me over 3 hours to get the game to load past the first cut scene. Turns out my problem was lack of virtual memory. Popped it up to 4Gigs and off I went with no crashes in sight. I've got 16 gigs of ram so I don't know WHY it NEEDED VM at all.
This game is wonderful. It's immersive, powerful and rage inducing at times. (Beside the stability issues)
Pros:
-Beautiful world and armor choices
-Heavy response based combat.  Each swing feels more realistic than Darksouls.
-Full fantastic voice acting
-Difficult but not too terribly mind numbingly painful.
-Powerful music
Cons:
-Crashing crashing crashing
-Lip synch during cut scene is just horrible. They didn't even try.
-First half of the bosses were so-so
-Lack of keybinding support. There's no way to set up a custom config for a controller.
-Lack of enemy variety.
-I got lost a lot... Level design is composed of a lot of tight hallways and caverns. No necessarily a con but was bloody annoying after getting lost in the same place 3 times.
When it comes down to it it was a great game, albeit short (13.4 hours first run through), fantastic combat that took forever to get the nuances to. Have a guy with a huge shield? You have to have a mace to knock it down. Low armor fast assassin type? Use a short sword or fists. You really have to adapt to who and what you are fighting through out the game or else you'll have to get creative or have a bad time. It took me about 6 hours to get the combat system down right.
I picked this up for $20 and it was $20 well spent. The standard $50 is a bit steep for the time spent though there are a lot of incentives to play NG+ more spells, armor, weapons, hidden items, side quests, multiple endings, etc.
I pray they make a second one with twice as much content and a wider variety of foes to sink my axe into. All in all I think I've enjoyed this more than Darksouls II and that's saying something. I just wish it was a bit more rounded out.

Bottom line: Its alright.  If you're expecting spine tingling adventure... yeah, this isn't for you.  If you like hacking games, go ahead and give it a try.

It is also immersive, so that you always feel like you are acutally running a virtualized hacking OS on your computer.
The game is a bit linear, and I have serious doubts about its replayability, but if you see it on sale, it won't hurt to pick up and play for a few hours.

Sigma Team has managed to sh*t out a real turkey this time.
Would not bother with this one because there are many better games in the series.
Here's why:
1: Useless starting weapon.
- Sure, it is has unlimited ammunition so it is okay for breaking crates but that's it.
- Becomes utterly useless half-way into the second level
(In first level you only break crates and blow up barrels).
- You will have great difficulty killing even the easiest enemies, let alone a larger group.
- In the original Alien Shooter you started with dual pistols that were actually useful.
1: Endlessly respawning enemies.
- Basically if you don't rush trough the levels you will run out of ammunition and the mission
will become uncompletable because the enemies will respawn faster than you can kill them to get even close to objective.
2: Small ammo pools.
- You rarely find enough ammunitionto complete a mission. The purchased ammunition is quickly used up,
making it very hard to manage it trough the levels unless you use the crappy starting weapon to tickle enemies to death.
3: Unusable shop interface,
- From what I have seen, in between the levels you are taken into a "shop" screen,
but you can not buy what you like. There are only a few options on what to buy,
and there is no way to upgrade the weapons you already got.
And when you buy a new weapon in a new slot,
they will not tell what it is beforehand.
You can sell it back to get a full refund but...
Want a different gun? Nope, you got no choice. That or nothing.
Also, you can not sell back the weapons you have bought or picked up earlier,
preventing any strategies on how to upgrade.
But why bother?
Usually the next weapon can be found somewhere behind a secret on the next level anyway.
4: About 90% of the art assets are recycled from the original Alien Shooter, released in 2003.
This game was released in 2010. Sigma Team seems to have gotten complacent and
seems to be content to just re-hash old content without any significant improvements.
Even the music is the same. In fact, they seem to have made it worse instead.
But it is not all bad. The game is more or less the same and gameplay on the levels has not been changed.
To sum it up, this is more of the same, and would not recommend buying it unless you are a hardcore fan.
I'd recommend buying one of the following instead:
- Alien Shooter (The original or with "The Experiment" add-on)
- Alien Shooter 2 (AKA Alien Shooter: Vengeance)
- Alien Shooter 2: Conscription
- Zombie Shooter
- Zombie Shooter 2

Despite the multitudes of crashes and errors I've had to deal with since first playing, the general performance seems to be gradually improving. Unity is a gorgeous game with an interesting and engaging storyline, and an abolute delight to play. Yes, many things have changed from Black Flag, and there are always those who will complain. I personally enjoy when major developers shift their style from game to game. It just makes players tweak their strategy, which is arguably the whole purpose of Assassin's Creed games, to actually think about combat in different ways. Because the hidden blade cannot be a main weapon, you can't tank your way through guards like in Black Flag. And I don't think that's necessarily a bad thing. Without minor changes there can be no progress, and minor changes in controls and weaponry don't even come close to ruining my game experience.
Yes, there are still errors present, but with the way things have been improving I believe it's only temporary. Bottom line is that Unity is a great game, and in my opinion, well worth the wince-inducing pricetag.

Okay, this game looks like an Alien shooter with reworked graphics, so i would compare them that way:
The gameplay itself is nearly identical to the 1st alien shooter - to complete the levels you have to kill every single mob on the map, you have plenty of secrets hidden in walls, you have exactly same enemies pool, and same weapons to kill them + same great OST. So what is different:
- money balance - you receive less money from levels, even with all the secrets found, you can feel how its harder to buy stuff.
- weapons reworked to more pleasurable in usage - instead of pistol you now have Uzi, semi-auto shotgun etc etc.
- multiple levels for drone upgrades
- more detailed statistics at the end of the levels AND it shows a number of secrets on the previous levels, so you can replay the level if you did not found all of them
- you can REPLAY any level that you beat before
- more difficulties up to IMPOSSIBLE which is unbeatable
- the level designs are close to the original levels, but they are different, bigger and contain WAY more secrets than an older one.
Graphics now darker, less colorful and more alienish, that fits the game good, because of aliens and their guts all around contrast that stuff very good.
Now about the problems of that game:
Both Original alien shooter is from 2003 and this one is from 2009 and yet, this game is less compatible with modern computers, if you have older machines it would run great, but if you have modern PC and win 7-8-10 x64 you may face various problems, like without Vsync, you can't move the camera, fps drops when enemy appear and so on.
If you have the camera glitch - turn on Force Vsync in your video card settings OR go the game directory find there .cfg file and edit it with notepad in that string with Vsync=0 to Vsync=1,
Maximum resolution is 1024x768 and no windowed mode -  If the low-res fullscreen is really a problem for you - as far as I remember *Dxwnd* (google it like Dxwnd window mode) should do the trick :)
As well as the original Alien shooter - this game would be awesome if someone would make HD remake
Overall this game is good if you lucky enough don't face the bugs (Not space bugs :) )

Anyone who remembers the old school RNG dependant RPG games of the past (Any D&D PC game, Might &Magic, Wizardry, etc) will appreciate the frustratingly difficult randomness of this game's design.
Frustrating-yes. Rewarding-yes.
Risk/reward. Always the simple formula for a sucessful turn-based RPG, however, this game also gives you something none in the past have...unlimited resources.
Your party members are RESOURCES. A means to an end, NOT beloved heroes drawn and thought out to be loved and remembered for generations. They are 100% expendable. They are fodder. Sheep led to the slaughter for one purpose...for YOU to succeed, not THEM. While I myself would be a liar if I said I never tried on numerous occasions to keep members alive by spending resources to remove bad traits and lock in good ones (game mechanic), and rage quit when they ultimately died...once I learned the aformentioned logic-I absolutely love this game.
Once players realize this mechanic, given the sheer amount of coach-brought potential sacricifical lambs, the more enjoyable this game becomes. Of course you will grind and toil thru areas and totally unbalanced RNG deaths, but this isn't a happy tale of sunshine and teddy bears...it's dark, bleak, depressing and crushing. Managing who you spend time making "better'" and who you use as simple fodder is entirely up to the player. I have learned after countless restarts...some that arrive on the coach just suck. They will NEVER be anything other than dead, so...why waste them? Why ♥♥♥♥♥ and moan they have trash stats and are riddled with bad traits...group them together, let them grab whatever resources they can, and then leave the area. Let the trash mobs be exactly that, and the ones with decent traits or seem able to be somewhat workable you dedicate some time into. Key word is SOME.
You have to play this game knowing they will die, parties will ultimately get wiped, and you'll lose time grinding....it's a given. The simple question remains...can you remove any self-induced emotional ties to any party member you come across, remember this ins't final fantasy or TES where you love a specific protagonist/hero/heroine, and instead you use them for what they ultimately are.....a resource like gold and bandages to satisfy the game's story-driven endgame?
IF you can, then Darkest Dungeon will reward you with a spectacular look at party-building RPG's.
IF you cannot, then the rage you self-induce is your own fault.
You have been warned...or anticipate to end up here....the graveyard....covered in the poisoned earth.
Now if you'll excuse me, I hear the coach coming..

Half-Life is, without a doubt, the most overrated game I have ever played. The story is virtually non-existant and what little can be found is generic beyond belief. The game's emphasis on minimalism also hurts it in this regard. While some games, like Journey and Shadow of the Colossus, use minimalism to emphasize the emotional impact of their stories, Half-Life simply uses it as an excuse to eschew storytelling altogether. The main character is an (essentially faceless) mute who basically serves as a blank slate for the player to project themselves onto. The supporting cast is composed entirely of lifeless, copypasted, automotons with hilariously bad pathfinding. The only character who is even mildly interesting is the guy in the blue suit (G-Man I think he's called?). While the story may suck it is told fairly well and the game's seamless area progression and lack of pre-rendered cutscenes does help to immerse the player. The graphics, while dated, were impressive for their time and hold up well despite their age. In terms of gameplay, compared to both its predecessors (Doom, Quake, Duke Nukem 3D), its successors (Halo, BioShock, Half-Life 2), and even it's contemporaries (Thief, Deus Ex, System Shock 2), Half-Life does not hold up very well. Freeman moves like he's on roller-skates and the game contains a ridiculous amount of platforming (which does NOT work in a first-person game without a physics engine). The gunplay is also significantly lacking. Weapon crosshairs are nigh invisible which makes aiming far more difficult than it needs to be. In addition, Freeman's health drops incredibly fast during combat, and while med packs and health stations are fairly common, armor is decidedly less so. A few of the enemies also feel a bit on the cheap side, namely the Marines (who attack in groups and can sponge damage like nobody's business), the Assassins (whose small frame and fast speed, coupled with the game's tiny crosshair, makes them annoyingly hard to hit), and the Vorts (whose charged lightning attack is difficult to dodge and decimates your armor). It is also worth mentioning that the game takes a noticable dip in quality around Chapter 11 ("Surface Tension") in which the game decides to eschew the action-adventure/survival-horror-y gameplay of the first ten chapters in favor of becoming a standard run-&-gun; needless to say, the latter half is incredibly frustrating (particularly the helicopter segment) and feels like an entirely different game.
In the end, Half-Life may be worth playing for historical study, but if you're looking for an enjoyable shooter with a good story just skip it and play the sequel.

I'm a fan of "hard" games, like Super Meat Boy, Dark Souls, Titan Souls, things like that. This is not that. Allow me to describe what "Hard but fair" means to the developers, because they don't seem to understand it. The idea is that every form of punishment comes from the player doing something wrong, and that there are zero situations in which the player is negatively effected for other reasons. In the examples above, Super Meat Boy is "Hard but fair" because its all platforming, if you're really good at platforming you will win first try. In Dark Souls, telegraphing is used hard so that players can determine when they need to do something, and deaths only come as a result of not responding right. In Titan Souls, it's largely trial and error, but because of the instantly repeatable nature the fact that the only thing you lose by dying is the time you spent on that try, and you actually gain knowledge of how to fight the boss with each death, it makes the game fair as there is no negative reprecussions for things that are out of the players control.
In Darkest Dungeon, it is entirely possible to do every correct move, absolutely everything correctly, and simply get beat because the game decided out of nowhere that you shouldn't have one of your best characters anymore. I see what their doing, with so much RNG applied to the difficulty, but its applied in all the wrong places. There is no telling if a battle is worth continuing or not, because the chance of being killed is high even if everything else has been going excellently. In games like XCOM that use a similar system of random enemies, random attack damage, and so on, it is made clear when things are going downhill, and the player is expected to and is able to recover, or at worst cut their losses. In Darkest Dungeon, there is no "going downhill", you're either winning or losing, and because of the heavy RNG it is hard to tell if you are on the losing side or the winning side.
This isn't the kind of game you can "git gud" at, people who don't enjoy hard games tend to call people who do masochists, but this is a true masochistic game. Built not for the fun of achieving difficult trials, but to randomly decide if it should punish you or let you continue. Worst part, the fun of Dark Souls is in achievement over seemingly impossible tasks, achieving things in this game holds no weight because you know you aren't getting better, it's just having lucky rolls. Maybe I'm not wording what I mean correctly in this and it comes across as just whiny or whatever, but regardless, I do not recommend this game to anyone.
EDIT: Gave it another shot, here's a specific incident that examplifies the above:
Walk in to a room with a team of four, Plague Doctor, Vestal, Highwayman, and Crusader (it was a new game). The room has four spiders in it, and my team was surprised so it got shuffled. On my turn I do what I normally do that had worked up untell that point, with some exceptions because of the mixed party, I had to spend some of my first few turns putting them back in order before I could actually do very much. One of the spiders shot my Highwayman dealing 10 damage and Blight. Then the second spider bites him dealing more damage. My turn again, but it's the Plague Doctors turn and she couldn't do anything because she was pushed to the front, whenever I could I dealt as much damage and healed as much as possible with the people who were in order. Then my Highwayman gets hit with more spit dealing more damage and reapplying Blight, this puts him at deaths door, then the last spider bites him and he dies. He came into the battle at full health. At no point in the entirity of this battle was I able to heal him, or even deal enough damage to kill one of them because all my attacks were either missing or dealt low damage. Mulling it over, I can't think of any possible way this could have been avoided. I was punished because I decided to walk into a room, which is what you do for almost the entire game.

A very high production value game featuring astounding art, fantastic music, excellent thematic design and very satisfying replayable combat.
The game however severely lacks in terms of content. It is entirely based around repetitiously raiding randomly generated dungeons in several different map types, however the dungeons themselves hold almost no real randomization. There are a limited amount of enemies, environments, and almost no depth to the dungeon progression itself. The gameplay is simply wandering around the dungeon by walking right, interacting with objects to get treasure and encountering fights. Essentially, a player only needs to play a dungeon once to experience ninety percent of the content to be found for that map type. Any successive raids of that map type is literally the same assets just rearranged. The game has maybe two hours worth of unique content, which is recycled into dozens of hours worth of required grinding in order to defeat every boss.
This is only made tolerable by how immersive the combat system is, which makes fighting the exact same fights with the exact same enemies moderately enjoyable even after multiple times.
The game does decently well to try to balance strategy, customization and the like. However the primary unique feature of the system is the stress mechanic. It is not a unique mechanic. It is simply a secondary health bar which certain enemies and certain actions can deplete, which few characters are able to heal and thus players can mostly only heal stress in the hub. If stress reaches half, the character becomes panicked and they stop responding to the players commands. If stress reaches full, they instantly die. It is about as fun as it sounds. Your characters can instantly die because of a statistic you can barely manage when actually raiding. And random chance massively impacts how bad stress hits your characters. Even worse, is when stress is at half your character will start to mentally fall apart and misbehave. They will forcibly pass their turns, deny the ability to be healed, forcibly use certain abilities on their turn, they can even force a retreat and take you out of the current fight and make you lose all your progress in it; and if it's a special fight then you won't even be able to return back to it. Basically, it is a mechanic which removes the players controls and makes them randomized. Which can completely, and utterly, destroy a party and the fun of the experience in general. And it is all tied to a secondary health bar players have very little control over on the fly. It is horrible, and obnoxious.
In the same vein, another system the game claims it has which is unique is the quirks system. Basically, characters random contract good and bad passive alterations to their statistics and functions. It is random, and often cannot be avoided. If your character gets a bad quirk, some of which cause them to take treasure from you or forcibly interact with objects so you can't, you must spend money and temporarily put them out of commission to remove it. The same applies to them contracting a disease, or getting too stressed, you must disable your ability to use them for awhile and spend coin to make them playable again. Once more, the highlighted elements of the game are random chores and hindrances that only serve to make the experience more obnoxious.
This is much akin to the levels of random chance that this entails, which can lead to ridiculous strings of good luck and poor luck simply because the game leaves so much room for random number generation. It is almost card game levels of chance, which makes the significance of even playing subjective when the experience can be so highly influenced by arbitrary and obligatory failures. The gameplay itself entails very little strategy, and is mostly just the player hitting enemies and enemies hitting back. Leaving massive amounts of room for random chance that can make the players constantly miss, the enemies constantly land criticals, the game constantly spawning high level mobs that are supposed to be rare. The game claims you are meant to become attached to your characters, which is laughable when the game will take them from you at the drop of a hat because of chance. Sunk a couple hours into leveling up a character, you can lose them in one dungeon from complete chance and have to get a new character and level them all up again. Making the grind that much longer and more boring.
The sacrifice of high production value for little content would be acceptable if it were not for the fact the game is sold for nearly half the price of a full production game. This game has roughly two hours worth of unique content, recycled into dozens of hours, and they sell it for the cost of two rogue-like games which would provide more content and replayability each then this. The price bracket this game puts itself into, makes it not worth buying at all in terms of actual value.
This game fails completely at providing a stable, logical system of success and failure. The combat system while enjoyable involves almost no strategy and is mostly just pressing buttons; and the game lacks content, randomization and even basic depth to the dungeon crawling. Most of the primary strengths of this game are from an artists standpoint instead of a players, and there is essentially no reason to even play it because it is almost exclusively controlled by random chance and not the players choices.
Everything is up to chance. The game can spawn bosses as regular ambush fights, the game can spawn all the stronger mobs over and over and over as your enemies, the game can spawn mini-bosses with no restriction as well. Enemies can choose to use their more overpowered attacks over and over if they want, enemies can randomly land critical hits over and over if they want. Everything, everything, about the difficulty is entirely controlled by what the game chooses to throw at the player; and the player is just along for the ride.
Have your party get wiped because you got the boss to one hit left from death, and every character started missing their hits while the boss kept healing and eventually killed them all because anytime they hit it wasn't enough to kill the boss because it just out healed the damage and anytime they got it to low health they started missing again.
Have a character reach half stress and become inoperable in one turn because the game spawned a party of stress damaging enemies which all attack first and all targetted the same character.
Have a raid fall apart because the enemies spammed stuns on your healer and made it impossible to support your damage dealers so the healer died because they could not even heal themself and then the rest of the party had to run.
Have your game become unplayable because everytime you level your characters up, the healer gets killed and so you cannot use those characters to raid since you need a healer in the group. But everytime you get a healer that high level they die, so your roster becomes flooded with trained damage dealers that can't raid and low level healers you are trying to level up who cannot fight on their own.
This game is an unenjoyable, amatuerish chore of an experience that does not deserve to be sold for cash. And honestly, it is so potentially frustrating and arbitrary that the developers should be paying people to afflict themselves with it.

She is just "aware of her sexuality and presenting it in a self-confident way" if this statement makes sense. I really like her a lot.
Overall this game is "weird meets beat-'em-up perfection". The only weird thing I dislike is the flow of the story. The other thing is a big selection of instant death quick time events. I absolutely hate them. But you can get used to them in this game.

Pros:
+ Some death scenes are funny
+ I somewhat found the music charming
Cons:
- Forced jokes
- Short (it will take you an hour max. to complete) and you need to idle the game for several hours to get cards after completion.
- Bad gfx, ui and animation (it looks uglier and uglier on higher res, this looks like a ported game but as the developer warned me, it is not.)

Its a pity on developers part, if they invested more time to develop it, and get some help on gfx/animation part, it could have been a much much better and enjoyable game. Idea was cool. In this state, its more like a free game... If you are still curious try it on sale (-75% min) or get it from a bundle.

I'm not much of a low tech gamer but this game seems to hit a spot for me. I could loose myself in this game for hours exploring planets for their resources to keep my ship full of fuel for the next planetary trip across the stars those resources also help you advance in the story to biuld more advanced stuff. you could aimlessly wander the randomly generated planets in search of villages and towns or even cities, under ground dungeons and all the varied life civilized or not. or use your imagination and biuld anything you want! the possabilities are 100% open.
There isnt much of a tutorial for this game, you just find your self stranded in orbit of a random planet with no fuel to go anywhere so you are tasked with beaming down to the planet surface to gather resources. biulding a shelter becomes first priority or just use your ship as a base of operations. just note that when you beam down from your ship it will only beam you down to one spacific area of that planet and no where else. this games level system is based on biulding your boss or biulding something that will bring on a boss battle battling it and once defeating it obtaining the schematics and starmaps to biuld more advanced stuff and travel to higher level star systems. failure to defeat a boss you created or lured results in exploring for those often times hard to find resources and rebiulding them all over again so make sure you have the perfect stragety for the type of boss you will be battling wether is biulding a trap for it to fall in, protective wall or biulding a spacific arena and always make sure you make or obtain a powerful weapon one ranged and one close range for any situation.
This game has a very minecraft feel to it on the exception that its a side scroller only. biulding anything requires resources certain items can be created using one type of resource some items or biulding materials require a combonation of multiple resources and some even more advanced items require multiple items biult from many resources seperately than added together to make the disired item. experimentation is key to biulding some elaborate items available on the current version.
Coal is a primary resource used in alot of different stuff. torches for lights, repairing tools "yes coal can be used to fix any tool" discovered by accident select coal bring it to the tool selected and right click the mouse to repair as well as fuel for your ship until you find uranium which is a very hard resource to find. tools are a great item to have to dig faster or harvest faster.
you could never have the best armor, never assume your armor is top of the line and expect to breeze through a planet untouched. some enemies can come out of no where and defeat you without as much as a blink so always be prepared. same goes with weapons. weapons and armor both have their unique levels of rarity which also determins its effectiveness simular to borderlands weapons and armor have a color code white or no color code is very common all the way to purple being very rare and they are not limited to level so your first mission could net you a purple weapon or armor which can go A-Long way to your survival.
Survival is not limited to just enemies you are fighting but also involves the elements wether its to stay warm on an ice planet or finding shelter from a meteor shower and hunting for food and cooking it for eating is also essential for survival or avoiding chemical pools and lava pools.
I highly recommend this game for those who like these type of games and have alot of time to burn.

Disclaimer: In 30 hours of inflated gametime, I have experienced two crashes. My sympathy goes out to all who were not as lucky as I was. At the time of writing, I have completed the game as a cleric and I'm wrapping up my NG+1 mode as a Warrior. I had to cut a lot of content for this review because of the word limitation Steam puts on it's user reviews.
++Let's start with the good stuff first. While graphics aren't important anymore in this day and age, because every single game looks gorgeous these days, it must be noted that Lords looks absolutely stellar. Even though my system can barely run it, you can clearly see that there is a lot of hard work that went in almost every single area of the game. The game doesn't look as magnificent like in the screenshots though, but don't let that dissuade you: this game looks superb.
++I liked the compactness of the game world. While every single RPG of the last 8 years is trying to be the next World of WarCraft or Skyrim, Lords keeps it neat and tidy. Lords doesn't have many locations, and, logically, every location in the game looks gorgeous and lavish with detail. They all look like real, believable places. There is no silly padding, no unnecessary: "Harkyn! Please kill ten demon hounds and then return here!" questing. There is one main quest, about ten side quests and a neatly compacted game world consisting of a handful of locations for you to do them in. If you're great at the game, you'll just blast past all the content in a matter of a dozen hours and have seen all the locations. But I really like this style of RPG and it's a system I definitely I want to see more of.
 
++Honorable mentions: Awesome looking armor and weapons. They're a real treat to behold and there's a huge amount of armor and weapons lying around if you look hard enough. The XP system is also a real treat. It allows the unskilled player to grind himself XP, plainly making him more powerful versus other enemies, but since it costs so much to gain a level, I think it maintains a very nice balance, not allowing the player to become overpowered. Above-average soundtrack, very appropriate tunes that don't get boring or samey.
--And now for the bad stuff. My problems with Lords (and the Souls games for that matter) are actually very simple and yet difficult to explain in few sentences. Souls, but especially Lords feel difficult for no good reason. For me, the very core of a game, the single most important aspect, the goal of any video game developer should be the endless quest of making sure your players are having a good time with the it: that they are having FUN. I would truly like to discuss both these games with a mature Dark Souls player and ask him or her to explain to me why he or she loves these kinds of games. I think I'm the only one who doesn't enjoy these games because everybody who hasn't slept under a rock seems to be enjoying this huge 'Souls'-fix. The argument I always hear is that in game worlds this depressing and bleak 'fun' is not something you should be experiencing and I find that to be such bullsh*t. You CAN have bleak virtual worlds and the concept of fun mashed together, guys. Ever played Deus Ex before? Or Bioshock? Or Wolfenstein: The New Order? Or hundreds of other games I'm sure exist with this combination. I do not find dying in a game fun. There are only very few and very specific games that get away with 'dying a lot' for me. Super Meat Boy comes to mind, and that game was magnificently designed. When said game is not created perfectly, dying over and over and over again should never, EVER be the goal of a developer. And yet, both these games have had developers behind them wanted, WISHING you to die over and over again.
 
--The reason why I claim that Lords and Souls feel difficult for no good reason is because when you look at these games they just seem like regular third-person hack 'n slashers where your character feels like he weighs a billion tons and moves ridiculously slow. Your adversaries can move much faster than you do and when they hit you it eats 75% (figuratively of course) of your lifebar away. The enemies themselves, however, take many, MANY hits to go down. Most have a shield that can block any attack coming from you, and the weaknesses they show go away in an instant, only giving you time to get in one attack if you're lucky. Surviving some encounters often feel like strokes of luck rather than skill. Both games often feel like the developers made these games and just tweaked the sliders for health bars and damage outputs. I've had enemies in the early hours of both games stunlock me to death over and over again, resulting in screaming frustration, something I haven't experienced in over a decade in a video game and yet, it's only games like these that bring so much depressing anger for a product that should be designed as fun.
--Even when you get used to the combat, there are moments where you feel the game itself is actually taunting you. There are fat demons who are hunters in Lords who usually have a wild dog with them. When you try to hit the dog, it understandably usually dodges your very slow attacks. The hunter demon simply jumps backwards like a nimble ballerina and attacks you again. It defies all logic that so many enemies in Lords can dodge attacks that should not be dodged, predictably leaving you with more loss of health and an even bigger loss of stamina, until you finally push him in a corner and finally kill him.
--When I say that the combat is slow, so is the magic. It would be quicker to educate me in magic in real-life than Harkyn doing his spell in the game, I'm not kidding. Magic, which usually plays a supportive role in Lords, is often essential for certain situations, providing you with a protective shield for especially hard-hitting enemies or a spell that stuns lighter, simpler enemies when they attack you. And when you are in dire need of a spell in the game, then you can kiss you sweet experience goodbye because you are going to LOSE. Not because of the mana requirement, not because of the decades of game time it needs to be cast, but because it's the kind of magic that cannot be interrupted. One hit, and it's canceled out, often leading to your demise, as usual. You almost have to know the placement of the enemies in advance BEFORE you cast your spell.
--The 'bankable XP system' that people seem to be praising so much isn't that amazing or exceptional. Considering the amount of crashing this game does for most people, and how ridiculously easy it is to die in this game, I actually see no point to hold on to the XP you are carrying. The interests of the multiplier aren't that huge, and when you are early in the game you desperately need all the XP you can get. When the time comes you can hold your own in this game to let that multiplier go up, you already have all the tools you need to win the game anyway so the bankable XP system is rendered completely null and void in the end.
--Extremely long loading times and frequent FPS drops.
Closing thoughts on Lords of the Fallen: Lords of the Fallen is a game that is too hard for its own good, and would've been a million times better if it focused more on story aspects rather than trying the be Dark Souls: Viking Edition. I have completed it almost twice, but I know after uninstalling it, I'll probably never play it again. The reason I completed it twice was because for what little good the game did, it does it exceptionally well: I was nuts about the aesthetics of the game, the very idea of a Space Marineish character battling hordes of demonic creatures sent by God to annihilate the world in a snow-buried castle, and you are all that's standing in their way. I will be interested in seeing a sequel for the game that fixes my issues with it. Only buy it when it'is very cheap in a sale.

I have a casual interest in politics and having enjoyed watching some gameplay I decided to splash out the couple of quid to buy it in a recent 75% off sale.
PROS:  It's a very well put together game that goes into a lot of depth and really emphasises how complex politics is and how difficult it is to please everyone. It's a simple game to play with a lot of very complicated ideas and I don't know where I'd even start making a game like this. It's also very cheap, especially on sale so if you aren't sure, wait until there's a discount and then I'd be very surprised if you felt you weren't getting your moneys worth.
CONS: The main issue is that debt doesn't actually matter despite being constantly made out to be a crisis. You're never penalised for overspending outside of a small red bubble. Also the game was clearly designed by people leaning more to the left so it's not entirely unbiased as basically anything liberal is seen as good and anything conservative is seen as bad. Although I do enjoy the pretty accurate graph of different groups of people's feelings, the game itself will generally swing your way if you stick left. Additionally, there aren't a lot of new policies to implement so your government isn't as customisable as it's made out to be, although you can cancel all policies. Finally my biggest gripe is that one game can become dull if you manage to cruise along quite nicely. After maybe 4 hours I had a fanatical cabinet and the vast majority of support and votes so outside of trying to fix a few issues there really isn't anything left to do at this stage other than start again or experiment with the policies.
Overall I do enjoy the game but it's not without its issues. I recommend it to those with an interest in politics but I'd definitely wait till a sale as there's no guarantee you'll enjoy the format.

I bought this game as part of a package many years ago, but only now decided to finally give this game a shot. Is it worth buying? Not really in my opinion.
1. I manage to complete the game on medium within three hours. Now granted, the game can be quite difficult even on medium difficulty, which means if you really want to gain hours from the game, play it on impossible difficulty. It is quite an annoying difficulty to play on, but to each their own I suppose.
2. The game doesn't really offer anything else other than, walk into level, blow MASSES of aliens up and complete the level. Of course after each very short level you make a ton of cash that you spend on permanent stats upgrades and a couple of things like weapons (which are essential in some levels) and of course lives to survive a bit longer. Yes, there are many games that follow the same principle of only blowing♥♥♥♥♥♥up that I am a massive fan of, but this one is just not one of them.
3. Yes, the game is fun to some extent... but again it didn't last very long until things just became too tedious and ridiculous. Some times, the level is so alien infested that you need a specific weapon just to get past their numbers, which if you didn't buy before the level started, you'll have to restart the level and make sure you spend money on that weapon. On the same note, once you get the last and most powerful weapon, there is literally nothing, and no amount of their numbers that can stop you, unless you make silly mistakes.
Finally, this is suppose to be a remastered version of the original. I couldn't play the original because of problems with Windows 10, but this game probably offered a bit more visuals than the original.
Again, it was fun while it lasted, but I don't recommend any paying money for this game.

Yea, some way to start a review huh. Anyways, at this point I still just started the game but overall a few things are already pretty apparent.
The game became faster, enemies (at least generally speaking) telegraph a tad less and overall the flow of combat is faster. This is pretty good in a way. At least I like it.
On the other hand the game suffers from similar issues akin to Dark Souls 2, basically having the worst parts of DS 1 all around the place. And that is inconsistency. The game has rules that may or may not work the same way in a situation. Parrying is a fine example - apart from obviously not being able to parry extremely heavy attacks... you sometimes can parry some of those. Except when... but then...  and normal attacks sometimes get parried, sometimes don't. Yea, timing, I get it. But when my shieldswing HITS the blade coming at me but it does not register as a parry I get annoyed. You can tell me all you want about game mechanics and stuff but then change the animation. If it looks like I hit the blade with my shield, it clangs then it was a parry.
Yes, that's just a rant but this is what you have to prepare yourself for. Things may appear to be perfectly logical, line up nicely, happen as you planned and for some reason still do nothing or even get yourself killed. Sometimes they might even work without any reason you can think of, no apparent sign or cause for an effect.
DS2 had ridiculous hitboxes, so far I don't seem to get hit be a forward thrust while standing BEHIND the enemy like in that game but I'm still early in. Will see.
Anyways, if you are oogling the game during a sale like I did, think about what you want from the game. Tactical combat? Hack'n'slash chaos, swinging like there is no tomorrow? This is not the game for you then. If you want to suffer and in case of success feel like a bada** that you actually figured it out just to get your a** handed to you the next time you try the same thing and realize it was just luck, then this game is for you.
Perhaps I should go for sorceries...
All that get good nonsense sounds annoying and really funny - but if like me you do not necessarily have the time to do something over and over without any real result to show after all that suffering... you might want to reconsider and allocate your time for some other game that might be even fun.

Half-Life - One of the most iconic, revolutionary and groundbreaking games of all time, then and now.
The original Half-Life and it's expansions are by far some of my all time favourite games, I'd even venture to say that they are in fact my favourite FPS games even to this day, Half-Life defeats any modern FPS game (and Halo games) no competition.
I don't know where to begin when it comes to listing my favourite things about this game, there are hardly any faults with it at all. Sure, the graphics may be questionable to some by todays standards, but for it's time they were groundbreaking. A vast selection of weapons, areas, an amazing storyline and puzzles make this one really brilliant single-player experience. The Hazard course by extension is also the most well implemented tutorial I've seen in a game.
This is a game that I could play for many more years to come and still enjoy it by setting myself challenges. The only thing that would improve upon Half-Life (and Opposing Force, even Blue Shift) would be to create a list of acheivements just so there is some extra singleplayer playability, but other than that, there is nothing out there in the FPS world that even comes close to matching Half-Life, and I doubt that there ever will be.
Valve are amazing story tellers, this is evident in essentially every title that they release with the exception of one or two more silly games and I (like everybody else) eagerly await the upcoming Half-Life titles. It is torture to make somebody wait so long for something so promising.
To cut a review short, this game is amazing and it always will be. It is well worth the full retail price and so are it's expansions (even though Blue Shift is extremely short), so pick it up and you won't regret it. Period.

In the third game of the AoE series the battlefield moves from the great mainland of Europe, Northern Africa etc. to the frontiers of the Early Americas, where colonies fight each other to gain control of the New Lands.
Compared to the second of the series, it feels like a lot of things are simplified. For example, gathered recources must no longer be carried to specialized buildings by settlers, but are automatically added to your stockpile, ranged units always hit their target, no friendly fire,....
However, this game introduces Experience generation and Shipments. Shipments are bonusses that are send from the Home City (in Europe) to your colony on the Americas to give you a boost in the battle. These can be recources (in the form of recource crates), soldiers, or even special buildings (like a fort). Shipments are earned by gaining experience, which is awarded when killing enemy units, construction, training,...
Another fun feature is exploration. Every colony has an Explorer that can scout the various areas your colonies might be. He can also construct trade posts, which can connect your colony to the local trade route (and receive some of its profits) or establish relations with the local natives (who can provide you with warriors and interesting bonusses). Each map has different features, so exploration is (as always) an important thing to do.
And last but not least: gunpowder. In the second game it was something only available at the very last, now it is available at the very beginning, in the form of riflemen, musketeers, and many different types of cannon. Because, let's be honest, it is a lot of fun to see a regiment of enemy infantry getting blown to pieces by a handfull of your heavy artillery pieces.
It is a very fun successor of the second AoE. Put it on your wishlist and get it once it is on sale

The Walking Dead Season 1 weaves poignant story-telling and beautiful art to create a game that I can only describe as a masterpiece. This point-and-click adventure game features excellent character development and a well-paced plot which serves to maximize immersion. Even if you are not familiar with the Walking Dead in other mediums (i.e. the TV show or comics), you will find yourself attached to the characters in this game. Every heart-wrenching decision you make has consequences, some large, some small, and you will often find yourself wondering if you made the right choice.
Keep in mind, however, that this is not an action game. Don't look to this game for any sort of combat or survival mechanics. The purpose of the game is to tell a story, and it is an amazing narrative about love, loss and morality. If this is what you are looking for, then I would HIGHLY recommend the Walking Dead Season 1.

The word "bad port" is thrown around a lot in PC gaming these days, and while I don't think this game is necessarily the best port, it's not a bad one either. It's pretty par for the course as far as that goes.
I'm seeing a lot of bad reviews for this game, and I feel like some of these people are simply new to PC gaming.
There has never, and will never be an issue-free PC game launch (or any system, for that matter). A few weeks ago, Ubisoft released minimum specs for this game that seemed steep, to say the least, but they aren't without merit. This game is very demanding. However, you can go on youtube and fine plenty of examples of people running the game on older GTX 660s, and having a great time. Granted, these people won't be maxing it out, but what do you expect? I think that's a lot of the issue with PC gamers these days, they expect mid-low range hardware to run everything at 60fps, but the issue is, these same people will be the ones accusing consoles of holding back PC gaming tomorrow.
Now, on to my experience, and firstly, my specs:
CPU: Intel Core i7 3770k @ 4.9GHz
GPU: EVGA GTX 980 4GB
RAM: 16GB G.SKILL 2133MHz
Soundcard: Creative Soundblaster Zx
OS: Windows 8.1 64 Bit
My experience has been great. Granted I do surpass the recommended requirements, but by definition, in PC gaming, there's nothing wrong with that. If you meet the minimum, you should be able to have a playable experience (and sometimes expecting 60fps running minimum or less specs is unreasonable). If you meet the recommended, your experience should be pretty good (assuming you don't have crashing issues, which could be attributed to a million different things that may not be the fault of the game).
Anyway, as I said, my experience has been great. I have everything maxed out, except anti aliasing (for obvious reasons) and I have my shadows turned down to High instead of PCAA or whatever that option is, and honestly there's no real difference between the two. Everything else maxed out, textures, occlusion, vsync on etc. I'm getting a very stable 60fps, with some drops down to 55-56 or so when the game is saving, but it's not something I notice.  So it's definitely a great experience.
There are two issues I see, though. Texture streaming/pop in is one of them. I assume this is something that will be fixed relatively soon, and it's not game breaking. It's more model pop in than anything, and it's not like it's right in front of you, but it is in the realm of 20 feet away which I think isn't really good. There's also the FPS drop in cutscenes, but at the same time, they're cutscenes, so it doesn't really cause a fuss.
I recommend this game, but I don't guarantee a good experience for you if you just meet, or are under the minimum spec. I don't guarantee it won't crash for you, because that could be attributed to many different things with PC's, and it's hard to pinpoint because every PC config is different, which is something that comes with the territory of being a PC gamer.
I implore you to take the reviews with a grain of salt (Mine included)- it's launch day, and a lot of people tend to, like it or not, expect everything to be perfect immediately, which is literally not possible on PC. You'll find a lot of people just let their anger and frustration get the best of them, and sometimes that hurts ones ability to take logic into consideration.

Finding Teddy is a mercifully short, deeply mediocre game with no idea what it is doing, backed by a very strong aesthetic that makes its numerous faults more or less tolerable for the scant one and a half hour it takes to play through it as long as you don't kid yourself and get a walkthrough immediately.
The game begins with the titular Teddy being taken away by some manner of monster in the unnamed girl's closet. Thus begins the quest to retrieve the stuffed toy and immediately problems with both the narrative and gameplay present themselves.
From the moment controls are handed over to the player, nothing whatsoever is explained. Some random clicking around the screen will likely reveal the basic controls, and soon thereafter the deeply uninspired, vapid point-and-click gameplay becomes apparent. The rest of the game consists of finding the single thing in a screen which matters to the rest of the game and using the correct item collected from a previous screen to interact with it. Intermittently, sound puzzles present themselves and do as such things usually do, cause progress to grind to an absolute halt.
Now in and of itself, the point-and-click gameplay isn't horrid, however it has several major flaws that pushes it from mildly obnoxious to outright annoying. It has no comprehension of "quality of life" improvements to gameplay, such as minimizing backtracking, the puzzles are more or less all either blindingly obvious or painfully obtuse, and the controls are minimal and surprisingly annoying.
Even this could have been but a stumbling block, older games have certainly had all these problems and worse besides. However to compound all this, the story - such as it is - is frankly not even remotely as clever as it seemingly likes to think it is.
It consists of essentially five segments, of which only three are actually relevant to the "story", and of those, one is the introduction, and the other is the very final scene. Of the meat of the game, two of three "chapters" are essentially completely pointless. They add nothing, not even contributing in any real sense to an "Alice in Wonderland" atmosphere, because the insipid puzzles and the half-random, incoherent design ruin any such attempts. The attempt at purely environmental storytelling is in a sense admirable, but that still requires there to be an actual story! You cannot simply string together elements and pretend it makes sense!
Additionally, the finale completely breaks with its own thematics and mood. The aesthetics and the progression through the environments had a steady darkening of tone, and the brutal deaths the unnamed protagonist might suffer during the game imply that the otherworld she travels through is a fundamentally hostile and dangerous place inhabited by enigmatic and unnatural creatures that make no attempts to communicate. Yet the final puzzle has more in common with a quaint children's picturebook than what the game was seemingly trying to be.
The only verdict I can give is that the developers had no idea what they were actually trying to do, with their complete failure to understand how narrative structure and adventure game mechanics should actually work.
Still. While incredibly flawed, it is not a bad purchase if the price is hanging around a single euro. If nothing else, the art itself is rather well done.

Lords of the Fallen is a third person action-role-playing game with heavy emphasis on melee combat mechanics and tactics.
The Great:
- Melee combat is exceptional and some of the best in the industry
- Significant weapon variety that leads to numerous differing yet satisfying playstyles
- Each weapon's unique playstyle feels great and is fun to experiment with
- Combat is timing and pattern based making each encounter important and fulfilling to complete
- Game is gorgeous to look at even with details turned down
The Good:
- Environments are beautiful and intricately crafted (if a little small)
- Enemy and boss designs are interesting and show creativity
The Bad:
- The story is forgettable, confusing at times and makes little sense given the scope of the game
- The side characters feel tacked on, tropish, and overall of little value or consequence
- The main character is meant to be a jerk, and there are few options to choose not to be a jerk
- I experienced several game-crashing bugs over 25+ hours
Conclusion:
The game is buggy, and the writing of the characters and story leaves much to be desired, but the combat in both its precision and variety is able to save this game from the trash pile and ultimately make it one of the best RPGs of the year.

I have a casual interest in politics and having enjoyed watching some gameplay I decided to splash out the couple of quid to buy it in a recent 75% off sale.
PROS:  It's a very well put together game that goes into a lot of depth and really emphasises how complex politics is and how difficult it is to please everyone. It's a simple game to play with a lot of very complicated ideas and I don't know where I'd even start making a game like this. It's also very cheap, especially on sale so if you aren't sure, wait until there's a discount and then I'd be very surprised if you felt you weren't getting your moneys worth.
CONS: The main issue is that debt doesn't actually matter despite being constantly made out to be a crisis. You're never penalised for overspending outside of a small red bubble. Also the game was clearly designed by people leaning more to the left so it's not entirely unbiased as basically anything liberal is seen as good and anything conservative is seen as bad. Although I do enjoy the pretty accurate graph of different groups of people's feelings, the game itself will generally swing your way if you stick left. Additionally, there aren't a lot of new policies to implement so your government isn't as customisable as it's made out to be, although you can cancel all policies. Finally my biggest gripe is that one game can become dull if you manage to cruise along quite nicely. After maybe 4 hours I had a fanatical cabinet and the vast majority of support and votes so outside of trying to fix a few issues there really isn't anything left to do at this stage other than start again or experiment with the policies.
Overall I do enjoy the game but it's not without its issues. I recommend it to those with an interest in politics but I'd definitely wait till a sale as there's no guarantee you'll enjoy the format.

Don't let your decision wether to buy this game be influenced by the "Mixed" status of the user reviews. Most of the bad reviews are not actually about the game, they are rage reviews by people who experienced crashes and technical issues that have for the most part been solved in recent patches and will be addressed further in patches to come. I and many others can play this game without any problems. It's just that customers who are content with a product are much less likely to write a review about it than discontent ones. I just wanted to bring a little balance to that.
The game is often accused of being a Dark Souls ripoff. That's not entirely false, but it doesn't really cover what this game is. Lords of the Fallens approach to combat is basically copied from Dark Souls with a few subtle differences you will only notice after playing for a while ... and why not? Hardly any game did combat as good as Dark Souls did. And that's where the similarities end. The level design, the approach to character progression and a few other things, like UI and so forth, all that is new in Lords of the Fallen. It's still inspired by other games, like Darksiders, but most games we love build on concepts other games have introduced in the past, don't they?
Another famous argument against this game: "It is too slow". In fact, it's not that much slower than Dark Souls. People just tend to start the game in the heavy tanking warrior kind of starting gear, which is full plate armor, and they think that's the pace of the game. As a rogue you can roll and sprint and jump all over the place in absolutely sufficient speed, believe me.
The most important thing to me is that Lords of the Fallen is fun to play! It's modern in all the parts, where being old school doesn't bring any benefit: presentation, controls, interface ... but it's old school wherever it's important: the challenge, telling you only the basics and letting you figure out the rest, lots of secrets! Yes, it has a few design flaws: there's one particular move in the shield + one-handed moveset that allows for exploitation so that most enemies can be beaten effortlessly. That's Something the developers definitely have to nerf in a future patch. Boss fights are not as varied as in Darksiders or Dark Souls, though still fun an challenging they feel somewhat repetitive. Also there are neither the dramatic dialogues Darksiders had nor the intriguing lore of Lordran (Dark Souls), but what people tend to forget to mention in reviews is how much fun they had playing: I had tons of it.
Objectively I have to admit that this is inferior to both Dark Souls and Darksiders, but in fact I feel much more like playing Lords of the Fallen most of the time, than I feel like playing Dark Souls. Lords gives the same challenges and emotional rewards for beating them without being as overwhelming. This game is pretty good at tying you to the computer: "Gotta get back my experience points after dying", "gotta beat this boss", "gotta hunt loot Diablo-style", "gotta find the secret way to this area over there", "gotta find the key to this door/chest", "gotta grind me a new level up", "oh I heard I get a unique armor/weapon when I do this while fighting that enemy", and so forth. It does this no worse that Dark Souls or Darksiders and I got to say it looks better while doing it.
Important info: Although the combat works much better with mouse and keyboard than in any Dark Souls game, you're still much better off with a gamepad. In fact you can add an XBox 360 controller to the requirement list.
So TL;DR, this is my thumbs up for a great, challenging Action-RPG that is best described as a blend of Dark Souls and Darksiders, with minor flaws but lots of fun to be had.

I've pre-ordered the Deluxe Edition of the game on GMG with the TRUST I had to the FIRAXIS name and I was sorely let down. I've yet to play this game. I've waited MONTHS before writing a review, hoping for optimization but I almost forgot that the game even existed at this point. The 3 hours of playtime I have with this game is launching the game with tweaks here and there to fix the issue, and checking to see whether it's playable after every patch for 2 months.
XCOM 2 is one of the most demanding games out there performance-wise and it's made by a dev team that almost only makes PC games. The unoptimized nature of the game renders it impossible to play on lower end machines, not to mention miserably low FPS on high settings on the newest PCs (with 48 FPS on ultra for GeForce GTX 1080). This is a turn-based game folks, meaning that there are a lot of downtimes where nothing is happenning. And on my laptop the game runs at a solid 20 FPS with NOTHING happening on the screen (other than idle animation of course). Comperatively, another company that almost always makes PC games, Overwatch from Blizzard runs at a smooth 37 FPS on low settings on my crummy old laptop, and that's a high paced FPS game.
TL;DR: Avoid this game like the plague if you have anything lower than GTX 960M and you'd be okay with playing it on medium settings with 30 FPS.
UPDATE: I've reinstalled the game since I wrote this review and it seems it's a bit more stable than release. It runs at 25 FPS in missions and 15 FPS in the base. Had I not loved XCOM franchise to death, I wouldn't have continued to play it with these terrible conditions. It's an amazing game through and through, but I'll never forget the dissapointment I had, dissapointment I have for Firaxis for ruining my experience with this game.

Let me start off by saying this is not a bad game. Instead of "yes" or "no" I'd like to vote "meh". But what tips it toward "no" for me is I find the premise flawed. A simulation of a political and economic system will necessarily reflect the opinions of the simulation's creator. Trying to construct a Randian paradise in this game will only lead to failure, whereas a socialist paradise can be quite successful. That doesn't prove that Randian economics is a bad system; it only proves that the creator thinks it is. By tweaking a few numbers and formulae, you could make the reverse true. I say this as a person whose political opinions match the game's fairly well; I'm just aware that the simulation agreeing with me means little other than that the designer agrees with me.

Ridge Racer Unbounded is a bit different from the PlayStation Ridge Racer games most of us know.
The whole setting is less "party racing" and more "dark fight for domination", you're out to take the city - a bit like in NFS titles where you want to climb up the ranks to become the leader of the street gangs, just better ;-)
Also, unlike in PS Ridge Racers, you can crash and there is a (very simple, though) damage model (cars have a certain "health level"), this adds fragging your oponents, or be fragged by them, like known from BurnOut and the likes.
You also can destroy (and earn bounus points by) certain parts of the city along the track you're racing.
Yet, with all those differences to the PS versions, Ridge Racer Unbounded is a great game and a lot of fun!
The different setting is interesting and an OK change from usualy more "party" like arcade action of the other RR titles.
The damage model and intentional destruction of the city adds well to the gameplay and makes things more interesting and fun.
Also worth mentioning are the "frag cams", where your frags, crashes and destructions are shown in from a cinematic perspective.
Last but not least does the game feature a couple different game/race modes like normal races, drift attacks and the such.
The graphics are absolutely amazing and eye candy, the music fits well to the overall experience.
If you enjoy arcade racers, you will likely have a lot of fun with this one.
This is kind of a mix of PS Ridge Racer + NFS + BurnOut and the result is a very fun and solid arcade experience.
If you're still unsure wait till you can grab it at a deal, definitaly worth it's money, esp. with a few % off :-)

I got this game through a humble bundle package first of all. So bare that in mind before reading the review.
However, Democracy 3 has maybe 4 hours or longer of actual depth. And then it falls flat.
Basically the game can be summed up as "get rid of the red bubbles while trying to fullfill the people's demands."
The problem with this model is that you reach a point where you've gotten rid of the red bubbles and debt magically doesn't matter in this game. And you're like "well now what?" And you instantly become bored out of your skull because you've effectively fixed the country's problems, are winning the election and have stopped caring about the game entirely.
One of the biggest problems is the policy tree. Effectively, there are not enough policies to go around. After one full term, you will have exhausted all possible policies. Because again, all the red bubbles have been popped and there's nothing left to do.
The other biggest flaw is realism. Rather then having to pass a bill or tax change through congress and praying that it gets accepted, you simply do it because you're the president with magical wizard powers that bypass basic political laws. This again leads to a dull system with a lack of depth or any level of meaningful enjoyment.
Instead of having realism, you have assassinations. How many United States presidents have been assassinated you ask? According to a quick google search, four presidents. Of course this game could've just used my idea in the above paragraph that would've made for a funner game where you have to bribe politcans to pass your bills and the like. But instead, we have assassinations which aren't really fun but the developer couldn't think of a better game over screen like I don't know, "empeachment."
At a price tag of a whooping 25 dollars, I can't recommand it. Not because it's an awful game but because there are other games at the same price tag that offer a ton of extra content that this simulator doesn't meet. If however, you recieve the game for free or on a massive sale, then I can recommand trying it out and having a good solid 4 hours of gameplay.

This is one of the most underrated games i have ever played. I have been a fan of the Ridge racer series since Rage racer hit the ps1 in 1997, I’ve loved the way cars can drift around corners at impossible angles and speeds...and how its all about the skill of drifting. Half-Life - One of the most iconic, revolutionary and groundbreaking games of all time, then and now.
The original Half-Life and it's expansions are by far some of my all time favourite games, I'd even venture to say that they are in fact my favourite FPS games even to this day, Half-Life defeats any modern FPS game (and Halo games) no competition.
I don't know where to begin when it comes to listing my favourite things about this game, there are hardly any faults with it at all. Sure, the graphics may be questionable to some by todays standards, but for it's time they were groundbreaking. A vast selection of weapons, areas, an amazing storyline and puzzles make this one really brilliant single-player experience. The Hazard course by extension is also the most well implemented tutorial I've seen in a game.
This is a game that I could play for many more years to come and still enjoy it by setting myself challenges. The only thing that would improve upon Half-Life (and Opposing Force, even Blue Shift) would be to create a list of acheivements just so there is some extra singleplayer playability, but other than that, there is nothing out there in the FPS world that even comes close to matching Half-Life, and I doubt that there ever will be.
Valve are amazing story tellers, this is evident in essentially every title that they release with the exception of one or two more silly games and I (like everybody else) eagerly await the upcoming Half-Life titles. It is torture to make somebody wait so long for something so promising.
To cut a review short, this game is amazing and it always will be. It is well worth the full retail price and so are it's expansions (even though Blue Shift is extremely short), so pick it up and you won't regret it. Period.

Alien Shooter: Revisted is an updated version of Alien Shooter. It has been ported to an engine that looks very similar to Alien Shooter 2, and comes with all the improvements you might expect from that process. Some of the flaws that haunt the original game still appear in this one, however.
Like you would expect, Alien Shooter: Revisted involves shooting lots of aliens, and that may be an understatement. On some levels your kill count will be up in the thousands. You control with WASD and shoot with the mouse, holding down the left button to shoot and using the cursor to aim.
The style of this game is an isometric top down shooter. I found that the isometric view could actually be a hindrance at times, with many enemies being hidden along the wall. You will find yourself being injured by aliens that you could not possibly see, and I have a slight problem with that.
The graphics have been drastically improved from the last version, and some light RPG elements have been added. You can purchase upgrades to your skills or weaponry, however a lot of weaponry can be found in the open throughout the levels. The enemies and characters have some additional detail over the original, and the environments have been give a new coat of paint. This looks more like a commercial title and less like a free flash game that the original did.

This is a game that is almost worth your patience, and if you somehow make it through you'll find that it has a great ending to accompany its neat art style and solid sound direction.
However, the game falls apart in the gameplay department.
There is absolutely zero handholding in this game, which some might think to be a good thing. I do not think that myself.
You click to move the unnamed protagonist to various points of interest on the screen and to navigate between screens, the core loop is simple. Find a place you can't get through yet, find the correct thing to open that passage and then go through that passage. The required items aren't even that much of a stretch, you get past the web of a giant spider by releasing ants into it to distract it, for example.
However, there are two exceptions, one is small, the other gigantic.
The smaller one is that you gain several companions over the course of your journey and they can help you with certain puzzles. The first time this happens you actually get a helpful arrow that explains this, but later times you're just left guessing whether you're missing the item or need to select your companions to help. There are about four times where this is needed over the course of the game though, so it's not that critical.
What really slows down the progress in the game though, is the music note system.
Now, I love the concept behind this, picking up clues from characters you meet to slowly learn a musical alphabet that you then use to convey messages to others. A great example of a moment where this works well is that you encounter a mole about halfway through the game, minding its own business but singing the notes D, I and G (spelling 'dig') as it's digging. Then, a few screens further, you find a sleeping mole. Reciting the DIG notes wakes up the mole, and causes it to dig a new passage for you to explore.
Unfortunately many of the messages you encounter are audio-only, leaving you to match and then memorize the correct notes without necessarily knowing yet which letters they correspond to or what you might need the message for. At the start of the game when the music system is introduced it isn't even clear that they correspond to letters yet...
I can imagine that some players love piecing this system together, but to me it felt clunky and detracting from the fun.
If you feel like piecing together a challenge, sometimes not a very logical one, then this little adventure game might be a good fit for you. Don't say I didn't warn you though.
