This is a great game, no doubt about it. It's one of those games in which you have two different gameplays: the tactical part, in which you manage a group of four heros navigating a 2d dungeon, and an administrative phase in which you upgrade buildings and pay for your heroes recovery. But before entering the gameplay, let me tell you: the artstyle looks gorgeous, at least to me. The characters, the background, it all catches your eye. The music is also effective, as well as the sound. The ring you hear when you receive a critic will make you tremble, I guarantee it. But what I like the most is the narrator. Because your ancestor, the one that gave you his manor in legacy for you to recover it from the hands of evil, will be commenting your every step, and besides the great voice actor they picked up, the lines are superb. As the game itself, they sound like a Lovecraft tale, with sentences full of ominous adjectives and strange comparisons that will stick in your memory ("As life ebbs, terrible vistas of emptiness reveal themselves").
But now let's dicuss the gameplay itself. It is difficult, no questions about that. It surely is not a casual game. Your erros will be punished, but even when you think you are doing everything by the book, you will fail. Once and again. The first levels are easy, but as your heroes gain experience and refuse to go to the low level dungeons, you will enter a kingdom of pain and failure. Heroes will die, your favorite squad of four will be beaten to the pulp in what seemed an easy fight and you will find ridiculously difficult combats in a stupid aisle where nothing should be (I'm looking at you, Collector). I've played a lot and I still feel I barely scratched the surface.
I recommend it, but you have to be patient and allow yourself to fail. Or be beaten even when you didn't fail.

(Interestingly, my review's been up for less than 6 hours and I already have 1 upvote and 10 downvotes. I'm no professional, but I'd consider it a pretty balanced review. I understand things can get weird in Steam's reviews section, but this seems extra peculiar to me. Also added some tips on the bottom for new/struggling players.)
Wow! Some people have some very strong opinions on this game, and for good reason! I finally just finished the game after a few breaks away from it, and most things everyone says are true. It's super grindy. Like REALLY grindy. It's also incredibly deep, and there are a multitude of twiddly knobs and tweaks to manage. While the gameplay is very much RPG influenced, I think one thing that's not mentioned is that this is equally an "Unfortunately-Fated-Hero-Management-Simulator". It's really quite a unique experience. The closest comparison I can come up with is X-COM with a heavier emphasis on risk/reward. So if you found yourself truly frustrated with the permadeath system in that game, you're either going to want to adjust your expectations for Darkest Dungeon, or find something else to play.
If you've read a few reviews and are thinking "Yeah, this could be my thing", I STRONGLY recommend you play on the games shortened 'Radiant Mode' campaign. This is NOT an easy mode. It wasn't initially available, and so I didn't have the luxury of playing through it this way, but as I understand you will not be missing any content. This simply removes what was, for me, an unnecessarily long, gruelling, drudge through the games unfortunately repetitive content.
The first 20 hours or so were a lot of fun for me, and the next 20 hours were still solid, but I began to notice the repetition mounting. Finishing the final "Darkest Dungeon" quests is one of the hardest bloody endeavours I've had in my gaming 'career', but finally getting to the point where it felt surmountable reinvigorated my love for the game, and completing these final quests was supremely satisfying.
I feel like I understand what the developers were going for and I'd like to debunk the two big misconceptions I see in the reviews section. Firstly, that the game is unfair. As the opening warns, the game asks a lot of you, but majority of the content is very well balanced. This game is unlike any other RPG I've played, and so requires a different approach than most. Don't get attached to your heroes. Don't expect to succeed on every quest. Sooner or later, the game will turn on you, and you'll be forced to effectively cut your losses, or otherwise be punished. Don't go into the final stages of the game without having characters so pimped out Xzibit would be like "Daaaamn".
For some, I would even say: don't expect to finish the game, just enjoy the ride for as long as you actually enjoy it. I can easily justify purchasing this game with the first 20 hours of content alone.
Secondly, this game isn't for everybody. The complaints levelled at the game are very valid, and anybody saying "you don't like it cuz u need to git gud" are tools. I feel like I can reasonably say that this game is too popular for it's own good. While I adore a lot on display here, this is a very niche game, and its popularity is a little boggling to me.
Anyways bullet points for those who don't like to read:
+Very original take on traditional RPG mechanics
+A truly challenging game with lots of ways to play and strategies to put to the test
+A deep and nuanced party management system with lots to tweak and play with
+Well crafted world with beautifully horrendous visuals and satisfyingly sinister audio
-Repetitive content, through rehashed enemies, bosses, and the same four dungeons
-The game can quickly and unexpectedly take much from you, which may be frustrating
-Steep learning curve, demanding you either learn the mechanics or struggle against them
-The higher "difficulty" settings basically just drag out the game. Extreme masochists only
So that's it. Play it... or don't. I'm sure you'll figure out what's best for you.
PS: If you want some less obvious tips on how to adjust to the games difficulty, read on:
-While I expect not everyone is so fortunate, I played it safe and didn't actually experience my first party wipeout until the games final boss. You can retreat from almost any battle, including bosses, and there are many times that you should.
-Early in the game you want to upgrade the stagecoach and keep rotating out your characters with garbage quirks/skillsets and fractured minds. Darkest Dungeon doesn't take kindly to your feel-good socialist worldviews. Besides, the poor souls will probably be too traumatized to care.
-On the trinket selection menu, there's a little button up top that allows you to remove all trinkets from your heroes. It's more time consuming, but if you redistribute your best trinkets every mission, you'll have a much easier time than dedicating trinkets to each hero individually.
-Enemies have effective parties, just like you. Learn to dismantle the most important threats one at a time. If you can eliminate the biggest threat on the first turn, you're going to have a much easier time. This also leads to the next point...
-Learn to single out weak enemies at the end of battles and keep them stunned so you can recover health and stress before your next fights. You'll be punished if you take too long, and it won't always be viable, but this is a fundamental strategy; especially for beginners who don't have access to more specialized party builds

While there are still bugs and occasional crashes (the developers are working as hard as they can!), and it is still badly optimised when compared to other games; you must also remember that this was made by two people, who were at college at the time they started making Omsi 1. It was never designed to be the best, most optimised game ever with the best graphics; but merely to be a slice of nostalgia for the two Germans who grew up riding these buses. If you like buses, or are into painstakingly re-created simulation, and don't mind the occasional glitch or crash, then this simulator is for you. If you like high framerates and next-gen graphics, then you try making your own bus simulator from scratch with a friend!
There's also lots of additional user content available, mostly for free, that includes real and fictional maps, buses and cars; and also objects to make and detail your own maps that you can make in the built-in editor.

Hi! This is a review! If you want an objective, detailed, and considerate review, you've come to the right place! Let's Begin!
Want to skip straight to the truth? Here's the scores: 3/10 Storyline, 7.5/10 Graphics, 6.5/10 Gameplay
Spiral Knights is an action-adventure game which is packed full of monster-slaying and boss battling. There are different areas and terrains that enemies spawn in, and there are great varieties of monsters.
The storyline of Spiral Knights isn't particularly noticable or moving. It's fairly typical, cliche, and boring. It seems that most of the explanations and description within the game are simply excuses to include the crazy enemies in the game. It's pretty irrelevant in terms of gameplay, and is simply unnecessary. Honestly, the game would be better if there was not storyline at all! This pitiful excuse for a storyline only takes up space and wastes time. Don't bother with the story whatsoever. Actually, you can even skip all of the text. The dialogue adds no tension or suspense. It's just an ordeal to wait for it to got by. Honestly, just skip through all the dialogue if you want the most out of the game.
3/10 For Storyline
We all know that graphics aren't everything. Take a look at Minecraft. An instant BLOCKbuster. Heh. However, it'\s graphics are terrible by today's standards. Luckily, Minecraft's great gameplay saved it completely. Spiral Knights tells a similar story. The Knights are not particularly detailed or sculpted amazingly, but the animation is smooth and somewhat realistic. The graphics are definitely average, but depending on the person likeability can fluctuate. Aside from the characters, the armors, skins, and weapons you can get are modelled well and textured in a great fashion. In other words, they look pretty darn good. If you combine decent character design and sculpting ALONG with great texturing of weapons and armor, your character will look great!
7.5/10 For Graphics
The 'Meat' of a game is the gameplay. No kidding. That's exactly why gameplay should be great! That's the whole point of a game! So, what about Spiral Knights? Well, as I mentioned before, Spiral Knights is action-packed. It has different types and varieties of enemies, and it's fairly challenging. As you advance, more enemies appear, and soon enough, there are tons of enemies EVERYWHERE, and the game becomes difficult. While the gameplay is so full of action, variety, and difficulty, there is ONE fatal flaw. There is a catch for the game being free. There are in-game purchases, and, unless you're a dedicated gamer who's willing to spend hours on this game to progress, it's pretty much garraunteed that you'll have to buy them. The game expects you to find tons of rare items which can only be found in a specific area. This takes a while. Just look at how much time I've played this game! I think it's around 200 hours. Yeah. Takes a while.
6.5/10 For Gameplay
Here's a short Recap before we move on: The storyline is bland and boring, but the graphics and visuals are pretty good. Ultimately, while the gameplay is very interesting, as well as challenging and full of variety, it's likely you'll have to pay to progress far in the game. The difficulty of gameplay may cause rage, but everything is beatable with a bit of luck and skill.
6/10 For Overall

I do recommend this game. As of 1/2/2015, game is "playable." I do understand that the devs recommend 4gb of vram and specify that double gfx cards with 2 Gb of vram do not equate to 4 Gb (SLI). However, my gtx 680s in sli have handled everything thrown at them thus far including some games that require a higher VRAM. That said, when I switched to CPU controlled physx, the game handled better (I realized after this game that Black Flag runs infinitely greater with this option as well). That said, this game is still choppy at some points. I haven't experienced the crash to desktop others have attested to but I do feel as though these stutters occur at inopportune moments. I have read that the DRM is a resource hog. I have never hacked a game but others have said that the hacked version is better because it doesn't hog resources. This is a major problem for me because I feel penalized for paying for the game. I am going to continue playing the game and I want to beat the game because I like the look, the lore, and the gameplay. I have heard people compare this game to the Dark Souls franchise. I just purchased DS2 and have yet to download. I'll download it after I am finished with this. I did play the DS1 port for PC and only played for 30 minutes. I simply found the graphics insurmountable. I've heard there are mods for it increase texture res and I can't recall if I installed them or not, I think I did before I even played the game, but I just could not get passed how horrific the game looked when I played it. Maybe in the future I'll revisit it.
As far as this game is concerned, I like the combat. I have run into some glitches with bosses that can be exploited (I cut a bosses life in half and almost defeated him but got slaughtered before potion consumption) but they provide a decent challenge. I've died a ton of times but I do not feel useless or hopeless. Another thing I've noticed is that if you save at a certain point you have to fight all of the people you've encountered until that point. This is meant to increase difficulty but fortunately you gain XP for it. I like this aspect because if you face a boss that seems too difficult you can go backwards, gain XP, and increase your attributes.
One thing I strongly advise against, that I also noticed on PC Gamer's review, is using the rogue. Agility in a cramped corridor is useless and much of this game takes place in said environment. I found it discouraging initially so I deleted my save, and restarted as the warrior class. I've been much more successful with this class. One thing that definitely could use some patching, aside from the horsecrap DRM, is the target selection. When using the right joystick, you have to quickly tap the direction you want to change to. In the heat of battle this is very annoying and it does not have a wide FOV, while on paper this sounds good and challenging, when playing with a warrior class character this is annoying as your character is already clunky enough. There should be an option or the devs should just retroacctively change the setting completely.
Pros: Beautiful graphics when running smoothly. I consider myself a graphics freak. Though I haven't played LOR: Shadows of Mordor, this game is one of the best looking games in the genre as far as its use of nVidia Turbulence and other graphics features. I like the setting and the shine on your character. The character looks completely B.A. in my opinion.
Other than the target selection the combat is very fun and challenging in this game. There is a pattern to every boss and every boss requires some thought prior to engagement.
The music is very fitting for an epic game with bagpipes and a choir.
The attribute system is very plain and simple but each decision is evident in combat thus far.
A major plus is that you are not forced to discard inventory. Some people like Dragon Age style inventory, I can't stand inventory management. I understand the realism of it, but I hate the time that it takes to manage it. There is nothing worse than having an objective in a game but travelling back to your home base/chest to dump off inventory.
Cons: The resource hogging DRM. I know my GPUs aren't the latest and greatest but some of the newer high end cards are only 10-15% stronger than my GPU (GTX 680). There is no reason why I can run other games that require more resources but this game I get fps dips because of DRM. I've read that the DRM even taxes the GPUs. I haven't read the technical aspects of this but it's annoying. I'm hoping the devs patch it so I can play the game again with a different class/build with better graphics.
The target selection/acquisition is extremly clunky and definitely needs some patching this gets annoying when fighting a boss and its minions converge on you and you can't quick change your target.
Lip syncing. The lip syncing in the game is horrific. This is probably the worst lip syncing I've witnissed in a long time. I know games aren't as good as live action films but when you play this, you'll notice what I speak of.
Conclusion: This game definitely has some glaring flaws. However, at its core it's a great game with solid gameplay. I know it's received bad reviews on some popular review sites but I recommend this game. If the devs can polish the game it can become ven better; I hope they continue working on this game.

I recommend the game with caveats. In general, it's a pretty interesting simulation. And the relations and trade offs between the various policies, social classes, interests groups etc. is quite good, despite what radical "libertarians" seem to think.
But the game has also some serious problems. First, in time realism. Everything is way too fast. I've managed to improve health, education and technology by huge ammounts in one single term of government. Got elected with 57% of the votes and 73 of approval only to than be assassinated by a capitalist plot, despite having my intelligence agency at maximum levels. My point here is not to promote myself, but to give an example of how extremely fast improvements could be achieved.
Unfortunatelly, not realistic at all. The kind of policies I was choosing may very well have the impact the game, and I, were expecting in reality, but certainly not within a short time period. And in real life, the dichotomy of good long term policies and short term pressures and needs, that often go directly against the long term goals, is a major difficulty of government and development that I'd have expected a good political simulation to exploit more.
Another point of critique is the extremely limited choice of countries to run, ALL of them developed western ones. That was very disappointing. I was at least expecting to have some developing countries, say a middle income one and a very poor one, to run. And it'd have been interesting to have at least some geographical and cultural variety. IF you had to run a fully developed capitalist country, at least put Japan or Korea in there, instead of the whole anglo-saxon club.
And there is my third major crititcism. The countries that are presented seem quite weird when compared with their real life counterparts. I played as Germany and the country started with a lot of very un-German problems and choices. Like, an uncompetitive economy and high crime rates? Creationism x evolution, community policing, private schools and health care, a lot of possibilities of patriotic policies etc. that simply are transpositions of American policy issues that simply don't exist in that form in Germany.
Still, it's fun and interesting nevertheless and it's the only game like that in the market, afaik, so I recommend it on that basis alone. But there certainly is room for improvement. And I don't like to rely on mods for that, as they inevitably reflect the modders point of view about a lot of political questions.

I've pre-ordered the Deluxe Edition of the game on GMG with the TRUST I had to the FIRAXIS name and I was sorely let down. I've yet to play this game. I've waited MONTHS before writing a review, hoping for optimization but I almost forgot that the game even existed at this point. The 3 hours of playtime I have with this game is launching the game with tweaks here and there to fix the issue, and checking to see whether it's playable after every patch for 2 months.
XCOM 2 is one of the most demanding games out there performance-wise and it's made by a dev team that almost only makes PC games. The unoptimized nature of the game renders it impossible to play on lower end machines, not to mention miserably low FPS on high settings on the newest PCs (with 48 FPS on ultra for GeForce GTX 1080). This is a turn-based game folks, meaning that there are a lot of downtimes where nothing is happenning. And on my laptop the game runs at a solid 20 FPS with NOTHING happening on the screen (other than idle animation of course). Comperatively, another company that almost always makes PC games, Overwatch from Blizzard runs at a smooth 37 FPS on low settings on my crummy old laptop, and that's a high paced FPS game.
TL;DR: Avoid this game like the plague if you have anything lower than GTX 960M and you'd be okay with playing it on medium settings with 30 FPS.
UPDATE: I've reinstalled the game since I wrote this review and it seems it's a bit more stable than release. It runs at 25 FPS in missions and 15 FPS in the base. Had I not loved XCOM franchise to death, I wouldn't have continued to play it with these terrible conditions. It's an amazing game through and through, but I'll never forget the dissapointment I had, dissapointment I have for Firaxis for ruining my experience with this game.

Right, where to begin?
The game itself bring nothing new or exiting, even when first released. Still, being a huge fan of the "Fallout universe", i of course just had to get it. So, i bought the game and added the season pass, in order to make certain i got all the following add-ons that was promised. Boy... was this ever a hype...
The main storyline can be done easily in about 5 hours of gametime, and that is if you take your time doing it, so that is not what makes this game good in any way. However, if you're a fan of speed runs, this Fallout game is equally easy to beat as the first ones. No, the big part of the game being decent, is the large amount of small things. Te many minor quests, the easter eggs that are very numerous, and a few recurring characters from previous games.
So why isn't this game good then? It became painfully obvious when Bethesda dropped new content, which you had to pay for unless you got the season pass, that the company had no intentions to really make this a good game to begin with. The added material (add-ons) were poorly made most of the time, with only two real add-ons given, two that could only be deemed to be a semi add-on, and a few extra creation kits for the settlements. The game could have a HUGE potential, but in my honest opinion, it was botched at the planning stage. From everything like the voice acting, to the inability to play a truly "evil" character, this game is more of a streamlined story, than an actual open world game. It's truly sad to see that the original games (1&2) was less of a main story quest chain, than this one, some 20 years later...
The final nail in the coffin of this game is when Bethesda introduced the Creation Kit (i think it's called that, most likely because of the ancient G.E.C.K.), which is essentially hijacking 2 gigs of hardrive space, in order for the player/customer to be able to purchase in-game "stuff". This is basically paid modding in lack of a better term. They haven't removed the ability to mod the game (yet), but in the way of how this game is going, and how Bethesda is acting at this point, i see no problem with them actually shutting down non-Bethesda mods entirely in the near future.
If not looking through rose-tinted glasses, this game started as a 6/10, after the regular add-ons it was about 4/10 due to the lack of good content provided by them... Now, i could not even give it 2/10... i logged in once to the game after the installation (forced update i might add) of this last, sad, patch. I can't even force myself to even bother to do so again, not until Bethesda offers an apology to the gaming community, to the modding community, and at the very least give the harddrive space back, or let the season pass work as "in game currency". There is very little else they can do to save face, or this game at this point.

Is it easy to make a utopian paradise where the people who like your reforms love you and the people who don't still tolerate you because you've somehow managed to eliminate your country's debt whilst simulatenously providing free houses to the homeless?
Sure.
Does it feel a little cheap to just steamroll the nuance of politics and governance in favor of an idealized view of the world as a whole?
Yeah, kinda.
Point is, sometimes that's exactly what you want from a game. You want a simpler version, where the happy ending you want in the real world is something your judgement and experience can make happen.
Sometimes, you don't want a gritty, challenging politics sim, you want a simple game with pretty graphics and cute little statistics to keep that number-glutton in your head happy.
If I wanted a perfect simulation of how dangerous and hectic it is to run a government, I'd run for office.

When I purchased this game, I expected a Ridge Racer experience: alien vehicles drifting at impossible angles and blinding speed in every curve with a very passionate commentator. Ridge Racer™ Unbounded is none of those things.
This game differs from the rest of the series. A lot. You can actually drift off into wall and crash your car, or bump into your opponents in an attempt to take them out. There's a handful of game types you can play, from your typical race to the finish where drifting fills up your boost meter (Shindo racing), to causing as much damage to the city as you pass through it, including your opponents (Domination race).
Each car has a unique feel to it, although most of them just slide all over the place, or can barely turn at all. The lower the "Drift", and the higher the "Handling", the easier to drive!
The graphics are simply beautiful. The attention to detail is remarkable, from the different shops in the city to the spot-on reflections on the cars. The weather changes the look and feel of the track in an immersive way, although there is no precipitation. My only complaint is that lighting effects are sometimes blindingly intense, especially at night, to the point where wearing sunglasses would almost make sense.
The music is upbeat and powerful, unfortunately we do not get a set of original tracks this time around. Ridge Racer™ Unbounded borrows a few tracks from previous games in the series, as well as songs from other artists.
The game features a fairly simple track editor, which reminds me of Accolade's Grand Prix Unlimited (DOS). Published tracks are uploaded online, where everyone has access to them. That's an infinity of maps to play on! I must admit, however, that most people are very uncreative when it comes to making custom tracks, but there's always a few gems in there. You just gotta find them!
Unfortunately, I can't say much about the multiplayer experience. You can invite people from your Steam friends to play with you, but don't expect anyone else to join your game.
I've encountered a few bugs here and there (glitching graphics, flipping cameras when boosting during a collision, and one area where you can drive off the map), but nothing major or game breaking.
What I'd love to see in this game would be a better controller support (for non-Xbox 360 controllers), rural-themed tracks, and maybe a multiplayer lobby where all players can actually see who's online and play together!
Overall, Ridge Racer™ Unbounded's title can be misleading, but it's still tons of fun, and has a high replayability value for a modest price. I recommend it to anyone who'd love a neat little pick-up-and-play urban-racing game.

A game can be free, but that doesn't mean it isn't a "pay to play". Plenty of games are free but require in-game purchases to do certain things that greatly affect the gameplay. For example, Trove's class coins. Players used to be able to obtain class coins for an in-game currency that you could achieve just by playing the game. Now, you get two class coins by leveling up and then you're done. Oh, but of course, you can buy credits and get your class coins.
The only way to get credits (besides buying them) is by, "Credits can also be rewarded for players submitting game content like user-made items, decorations, lairs, and dungeons. Each item that is submitted and accepted has its own reward amount (highly dependent on necessity). Rarely, players can report a valid dupe bug (or other game-breaking bug) and receive a plethora of Credits from Trion" -Trove Wiki.
Sure you can get credits like I did, by playing for 86 hours. Even then, you barely have enough for a single class coin. And what would be the fun in that?
Would you like to know how many credits you need for a class now? 1050 credits(Thanks to TheGoldenYoshi and my other friends) It cost $4.99 to get 750 credits. You need to buy two of those to get a class. So, you need to pay $9.98 for ONE CLASS! There are around 14 classes in Trove. You can play 3 for free, that leaves 11 left. Multiply the Eleven classes by the cost of one class, $9.98 and get $109.78 for the whole Trove experience.
Now I understand that Trove is "free to play", you guys have to get profit off of your game somehow. But this isn't the way to do it. If Trove cost money, and it didn't have in-game purchases, I would still buy Trove. If Trove still had in game purchases it would still be ok with me, just not if it cost over one hundred dollars. Trove was and still is a great game, but for over $100 no one is going to want to keep playing Trove.
So yes, for the true and whole Trove experience, it is a pay to play. And an overpriced pay to play at that. If you play Trove, skimming over all of the fun parts and spending hours farming like I did, it is a free to play.

This is a great game, no doubt about it. It's one of those games in which you have two different gameplays: the tactical part, in which you manage a group of four heros navigating a 2d dungeon, and an administrative phase in which you upgrade buildings and pay for your heroes recovery. But before entering the gameplay, let me tell you: the artstyle looks gorgeous, at least to me. The characters, the background, it all catches your eye. The music is also effective, as well as the sound. The ring you hear when you receive a critic will make you tremble, I guarantee it. But what I like the most is the narrator. Because your ancestor, the one that gave you his manor in legacy for you to recover it from the hands of evil, will be commenting your every step, and besides the great voice actor they picked up, the lines are superb. As the game itself, they sound like a Lovecraft tale, with sentences full of ominous adjectives and strange comparisons that will stick in your memory ("As life ebbs, terrible vistas of emptiness reveal themselves").
But now let's dicuss the gameplay itself. It is difficult, no questions about that. It surely is not a casual game. Your erros will be punished, but even when you think you are doing everything by the book, you will fail. Once and again. The first levels are easy, but as your heroes gain experience and refuse to go to the low level dungeons, you will enter a kingdom of pain and failure. Heroes will die, your favorite squad of four will be beaten to the pulp in what seemed an easy fight and you will find ridiculously difficult combats in a stupid aisle where nothing should be (I'm looking at you, Collector). I've played a lot and I still feel I barely scratched the surface.
I recommend it, but you have to be patient and allow yourself to fail. Or be beaten even when you didn't fail.

(Interestingly, my review's been up for less than 6 hours and I already have 1 upvote and 10 downvotes. I'm no professional, but I'd consider it a pretty balanced review. I understand things can get weird in Steam's reviews section, but this seems extra peculiar to me. Also added some tips on the bottom for new/struggling players.)
Wow! Some people have some very strong opinions on this game, and for good reason! I finally just finished the game after a few breaks away from it, and most things everyone says are true. It's super grindy. Like REALLY grindy. It's also incredibly deep, and there are a multitude of twiddly knobs and tweaks to manage. While the gameplay is very much RPG influenced, I think one thing that's not mentioned is that this is equally an "Unfortunately-Fated-Hero-Management-Simulator". It's really quite a unique experience. The closest comparison I can come up with is X-COM with a heavier emphasis on risk/reward. So if you found yourself truly frustrated with the permadeath system in that game, you're either going to want to adjust your expectations for Darkest Dungeon, or find something else to play.
If you've read a few reviews and are thinking "Yeah, this could be my thing", I STRONGLY recommend you play on the games shortened 'Radiant Mode' campaign. This is NOT an easy mode. It wasn't initially available, and so I didn't have the luxury of playing through it this way, but as I understand you will not be missing any content. This simply removes what was, for me, an unnecessarily long, gruelling, drudge through the games unfortunately repetitive content.
The first 20 hours or so were a lot of fun for me, and the next 20 hours were still solid, but I began to notice the repetition mounting. Finishing the final "Darkest Dungeon" quests is one of the hardest bloody endeavours I've had in my gaming 'career', but finally getting to the point where it felt surmountable reinvigorated my love for the game, and completing these final quests was supremely satisfying.
I feel like I understand what the developers were going for and I'd like to debunk the two big misconceptions I see in the reviews section. Firstly, that the game is unfair. As the opening warns, the game asks a lot of you, but majority of the content is very well balanced. This game is unlike any other RPG I've played, and so requires a different approach than most. Don't get attached to your heroes. Don't expect to succeed on every quest. Sooner or later, the game will turn on you, and you'll be forced to effectively cut your losses, or otherwise be punished. Don't go into the final stages of the game without having characters so pimped out Xzibit would be like "Daaaamn".
For some, I would even say: don't expect to finish the game, just enjoy the ride for as long as you actually enjoy it. I can easily justify purchasing this game with the first 20 hours of content alone.
Secondly, this game isn't for everybody. The complaints levelled at the game are very valid, and anybody saying "you don't like it cuz u need to git gud" are tools. I feel like I can reasonably say that this game is too popular for it's own good. While I adore a lot on display here, this is a very niche game, and its popularity is a little boggling to me.
Anyways bullet points for those who don't like to read:
+Very original take on traditional RPG mechanics
+A truly challenging game with lots of ways to play and strategies to put to the test
+A deep and nuanced party management system with lots to tweak and play with
+Well crafted world with beautifully horrendous visuals and satisfyingly sinister audio
-Repetitive content, through rehashed enemies, bosses, and the same four dungeons
-The game can quickly and unexpectedly take much from you, which may be frustrating
-Steep learning curve, demanding you either learn the mechanics or struggle against them
-The higher "difficulty" settings basically just drag out the game. Extreme masochists only
So that's it. Play it... or don't. I'm sure you'll figure out what's best for you.
PS: If you want some less obvious tips on how to adjust to the games difficulty, read on:
-While I expect not everyone is so fortunate, I played it safe and didn't actually experience my first party wipeout until the games final boss. You can retreat from almost any battle, including bosses, and there are many times that you should.
-Early in the game you want to upgrade the stagecoach and keep rotating out your characters with garbage quirks/skillsets and fractured minds. Darkest Dungeon doesn't take kindly to your feel-good socialist worldviews. Besides, the poor souls will probably be too traumatized to care.
-On the trinket selection menu, there's a little button up top that allows you to remove all trinkets from your heroes. It's more time consuming, but if you redistribute your best trinkets every mission, you'll have a much easier time than dedicating trinkets to each hero individually.
-Enemies have effective parties, just like you. Learn to dismantle the most important threats one at a time. If you can eliminate the biggest threat on the first turn, you're going to have a much easier time. This also leads to the next point...
-Learn to single out weak enemies at the end of battles and keep them stunned so you can recover health and stress before your next fights. You'll be punished if you take too long, and it won't always be viable, but this is a fundamental strategy; especially for beginners who don't have access to more specialized party builds

Do you think your monitor would look better with a hole in it? Do you think your newly built computer can handle every game on the market? Are you on anti-psychotic meds that make life seem dull but yearn to have something spice up your life? Well, there is good news! You can have all these things if you buy Assassin's Creed Unity! Be in awe as you mysteriously travel underground into the magnificent underground white dome to which you will fall into oblivion, never to return to the hustle and bustle of Paris. This game will bring you into the story of a young lad who's hair will mysteriously change colors, or will run in one direction then simultaneously into another direction making you fail your missions in haste! Much like the guillotines of the French Revolution, you will lose your mind as you attempt to make your way through the spontaneous NPCs that will block your path with no remorse.
Unlike many Assassin's Creed releases of the past, Unity offers many heart-racing, brain-blending moments in which you will begin to question your view on life itself. Unity will push you into bringing every aspect of your life into philosophical conundrums, hoping that you could perhaps one day witness a multi-million dollar gaming empire release a game with more optimization than a government's forceful placement of mandatory health insurance.
In all seriousness, this game could have been a great step forward in the right direction for Ubisoft and Assassin's Creed. However, due to poor optimization amongst other reasons, Unity has failed to impress on multiple levels. Hopefully a patch (or likely a series of patches) will solve the issue(s) that many are experiencing, but for now, Unity is a bust.
EDIT 11/27 - Even after the third patch, the game will still not run correctly with overclocked recommended hardware.

It seems when you set out to make a point and click game, there are several characteristics your game must have. It must have visual and audio effects that reflect a relaxing atmosphere. It must have a simple interface that makes you feel like a complete dullard when you inevitably fail to understand what you're supposed to do. Each solution must incorporate a logic that is completely unique to the creator and makes everyone else say, "Umm okay... I guess that makes sense..." when/if they find the correct solution. And finally, it must have gameplay that encourages the player to rub every item in their inventory against every interactive surface in the game, in hopes they'll get lucky and stumble onto the creator's train of logic.
So with that in mind, let's go down Fondling Teddy's checklist.
-Calming visuals? Check.
-Soothing ambient music and sound effects? Check.
-Ridiculously simple interface? Check.
-Puzzles who's train of logic just pulled in from the twilight zone? Double check.
-Gameplay and level design that makes the player wander aimlessly back and forth throughout the game, mashing random objects together like a confused, alcoholic alzheimer's patient that just pulled themself from a car crash? Ultra check.
In fact, backtracking is such a huge part of Finding Tiddy that it should be one of it's big selling points. "Now with 75% more backtracking!", the store page would say. "Do you enjoy seeing the same 8 screens over and over? Too bad!", the store page would exclaim.
But all the backtracking pales in comparison to the absurd "solutions". The breaking point for me occurred when I eventually got sick of the usual, "mash item X against surface Y in a vain attempt to understand what I'm supposed to do" technique and committed the ultimate and most dishonorable sin of all: looking up a walkthrough. As it turns out, I was supposed to play a series of notes from my newly acquired sheet music notepad thing to make a rock happy. Which would make sense, but here's the catch, over half of the music notes were missing from the sheet music notepad thing and I had no donkey punching idea how I was supposed to get the rest of music notes. Or what order I was supposed to play them in. Or even if I was supposed to play music at all. None of this is explained. Even after I copy-pasted the solution from the walkthrough, nothing is explained. There wasn't any sort of message saying something like "hey you figured out the right music notes by giving a sensual massage to the tree of pounding" or "it's a good thing you booty bumped the stone of throbbing cause he had right idea" or anything at all to show what planet the developer was on when they made that puzzle. All I can assume is that I was
to look up a walkthrough. As far as I can tell, that was the developer's
solution.
In short, Fondling Tiddy is your typical, mundane, nothing special, point and click game. Much like a stripper, it's fun to look at but once you get down to business, you'll see why looks aren't everything.
If you want a good point and click game, then check out Machinarium and Return to Mysterious Island. Those games do point and click right.

Finding Teddy is a point and click game that uses words as one of its central mechanics.
The main character will not move unless walking towards another screen, or an interactive object, and often when using the inventory system, it felt clunky as I'd select an item which might lead the character to walk to another screen. The game looks nice, simple, but nice. The different areas and creatures look unique and interesting, with the exception of the third area, which mostly looks the same, but I feel that it helps improve the overall effect of the area.
You might need an online guide if you don't immediately understand the game.

He's the same physical person, but he likes different things, has a different sense of humor, and he is a sore loser at games and often cheats. That's how XCOM 2 feels compared to XCOM. It's not more of the same, but instead it throws out the well balanced strategy layer I and others found fun, and it replaces it with a chaotic mess with a timer that can randomly tick up faster certain months. The resource restrictions feel more annoying than enjoyable, and much of the game feels scripted, the opposite of what any XCOM game should feel like.
In all honesty, I take this personally. I love XCOM and have bought it on PC for myself and others, on XBox, and even on iPhone. This was a day one purchase, but I've put off playing it because it feels like the game is upset with me playing it. The game is no longer well balanced for Iron Man mode and seems to encourage save scumming instead.
To be honest, because I want to beat it and see the ending, I've been playing on Beginner difficulty (with Iron Man selected because I enjoy the perma death aspect still). I've almost beaten it in my sixth game. I've lost five games on normal difficulty and had to resort to beginner just to have a chance, and it's still hard.
XCOM 2 feels like playing a game with a child who cheats and changes the rules. What hurts my feelings is that my favorite game is XCOM, so this feels like an old friend who has changed who he is for no reason and has become a sore loser to boot.

The Walking Dead Season 1 weaves poignant story-telling and beautiful art to create a game that I can only describe as a masterpiece. This point-and-click adventure game features excellent character development and a well-paced plot which serves to maximize immersion. Even if you are not familiar with the Walking Dead in other mediums (i.e. the TV show or comics), you will find yourself attached to the characters in this game. Every heart-wrenching decision you make has consequences, some large, some small, and you will often find yourself wondering if you made the right choice.
Keep in mind, however, that this is not an action game. Don't look to this game for any sort of combat or survival mechanics. The purpose of the game is to tell a story, and it is an amazing narrative about love, loss and morality. If this is what you are looking for, then I would HIGHLY recommend the Walking Dead Season 1.

I have finished this game on a debatably medium PC. It has not crashed once on me. The 1.4 patch did wonders, I guess. Otherwise, I found the game to be quite entertaining. It has a small world, yes, but it's filled to the tip, and you'll be backtracking a lot, since some areas open only later in the game. The design is kind of power fantasy, you look like a spiky tank most of the time, and the enemies are grotesque. The combat is clunky, albeit realistic. It focuses on tactical blocking, evading and timing of your hits, and the heavy weapons WILL feel heavy (some of them need two hands to be used, regardless of your strength). It kinda forces you to use all the tools at your disposal, which is a good thing, since it varies the gameplay and forces you to think up strategies on the go. The main story is meh, but you are a criminal and you can totally mess up humanity if you chose one of the three possible endings, so in the end it's fine by my standards.

X2 is a more polished base to build from. The gameplay puts you as the invading force making tactics and on the fly decisions and reactions more important as the timer runs down and pressures you to evolve. Overall it feels like a sturdier base but with less content as of now. The last DLC will be very critical in seeing how this game stacks up to EW especially with the existence of Long War. As of now X2 even with mods can not match the experience of Long War and the last DLC will be a big factor in giving modders enough base tools to be able to deliver as rich an experience as EW.
If you never played Long War or didn't like it or looking for something different then X2 is a beautiful game that provides more XCOM. However if you are looking for a replacement to Long War the game is not yet able to provide it.

So, i'm enjoying Beyonetta, and having fun, but it's not perfect. I've never played this in the past, and will finish it, but it's not perfect. Here's my run down....
Right now i'm on Chapter 6....
So it seems. I kind of feel like I got far into the plot at a neck snap.  So far, it's been fun, but at the same time, i'm not very impressed. Level design is actually really nice and they do a good job changing it up from time to time from running on walls, to a little "run away" setup. I bought Unturned back when the game was still new on steam. I still remember long nights with friends playing in our own little zombie apocalypse and absolutely loving it. Sadly, there was little content at the time so once we'd built our base and had all of the best equipment for our characters we drifted from the game and it feel into obscurity.
Earlier this year I decided to reinstall the game and was shocked at how badly the last few updates had affected the game. Gone was the fair challenge. Gone was the sense of fun. Instead of a challenging and enjoyable experience I found myself unable to progress at all in the game. When before a single zombie might pose a problem if you were unarmed it was still reasonable to be able to pummel at least one at a time until you could properly level up and find decent equipment. Instead we get unshakeable nearly unstoppable enemies that will persue you indefinitely and outrun you with ease.
When every enemy is capable of taking you down in seconds while you hopelessly flail at an opponent that has more life, hits harder, doesn't relent and is able to make you bleed to death with a strike or two it quickly becomes evident that there is little enjoyment to be had. Even my experience with difficult games was no preperation for a game meant to force you into a slow and plodding playstyle while offering little in the way of reward. This was enough to encourage me to write this review.
This is a shame since this game had such tremendous potential. Now it's a frustrating mess of a title that quite frankly isn't worth my time, and if you're a working adult such as myself, not worth yours either.

I beat this game just now, and am thinking of writing a reveiw. Overall, I would give a 6.5 out of 10 for this game.
If you have never played a similar genre before (like Dark Souls) , I recommend you pick this game up, as the first time  into such this game genre is definitely mindblowing; besides this game theoretically is 'lighter' than dark souls hence should be more 'friendly' to new player. This is generally true from my own experience.
However if you are a veteran from the Souls series, don't expect too much from it. The reasons are listed below:
0. combat-mechanics: the combat mechanics in this game genre is always entertaining. The credit however should go to the original Souls series.
1. Story-wise:  the plot of lords of the fallen is really lousy. Actually I prefer to say there is no story at all. The hero is a rather stale character. The final cutscene is lousy as well.
2. Mobs: only a handful type of mobs exist int the game . Some of the mobs has disgusting mechanics that makes  fighting with them feels more like chore than fun. Besides, most of the mobs are humanoids (Roghars) that lacks the disctinct feel as the enemies in dark souls. Another thing is, I think the designers have overly exploited some of the game mechanics, such as defense with a shield. In this game, there are simply too many mobs bearing shield playing turtle with you from start to the end.
3. Boss fight:  The difficulty of Boss fight is not much challenging for a venteran. but may prove a bit challenging for a newbie. Genreally the design of the bosses is ok, but but Some bosses have really ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ mechanics, including: many bosses bears shield, and too many of them summon minions during the fight, including the final boss. As said before, when these things are overly exploited by the developers, the boss fight does not feel distinct and some times feels annoying.
4. Map and level design: All the stages feels similar and everywhere looks the same color. And you really can get lost in those convoluted tunnels, especially in the 3rd scene. Yes you can argue that throughout the game Harkyn actually fight with a rather limited area,  but it doesn't justify the lack of creativily in level design of this game. This level of similarity makes the player extremely hard to find his/her way and sometimes get frustrated, it is good that the developers everntually release the maps online for free. But then it lost the whole point of the distinctive feature of this game genre: gaming without a map.  As it for the treasure chests, the mechanics is not that attractive as well: many chests are locked and requires a key to open when you initially find them, and sometimes the key has to be dropped randomly from the mobs you kill. Most of the time, by the time you got the key, you either already forgot where the orignal chest was or you are too annoyed to bother going back fighting through all the respawning mobs for a chest that may yield some crap.
5. Graphics: the engine they pick make the graphic looks good, but you have to have a relatively high-spec PC I'm afraid. In my case, I am playing on a middle-end gaming laptop I picked up mid-year 2013, which has 8G RAM and nVidia GT650M (2G graphic mem).  I can hardly play this game on 1600x900 resolution with a reasonable framerate. And We all know a good game is not always about graphics.
6. Bugs:  there are a lot of bugs ever since this game is released. Many of those are game-breaking. It's good that the developers tried to fix some of these by releasing patches, however, it is really unfortunate that up until now,  which is literally the start of a new year (Jan 2nd 2015), some of the game-breaking glitches are still left hanging around. For example, a glitched trinket may cause your mana become a negative value and never regenerate.
Generally speaking, Lords of the fallen a moderate piece of work, not too shabby, and not that fascinating. You can kill 30 hrs with it.

Bayonetta on Steam is a must-own game for anyone who has not had the opportunity to experience the game previously. My first experience with the game was on Xbox 360, where I've put well over 100 hours into it. It is one of, if not the finest, character action game ever made and certainly the best on PC. DCM3 and 4 are simply outdated in  their mechanics, the rebooted DMC lacks the depth and complixity of either DMC3 or 4, and Platinum's other PC offerings like Korra, Transformers and Turtles all pale in comparison to the masterpiece that is Bayonetta. With Bayonetta 3 just teased today, there has been no better time to become a fan of the series.
I'll leave the in-depth reviews to other people, but here are the highlights of Bayonetta.
Exceptional combat that is simple to learn, but deep enough to rival Street Fighter
Exceptional music, particularly the combat tracks, that really fit the game and get you excited
Exceptional replay value between striving to obtain Platinum ranks, or Jubilius forbid, Pure Platinum ranks on eacho f the nearly 20 stages, an extremely challenging optional boss fight to unlock, a half-dozen costumes and two unlockable extra characters.
Exceptional performance on even less powerful software--I could get a solid 60fps at 720p on 960M laptop and have flawless 1080 60fps on my 1060.
Exceptional value for the insane asking price of $20. You'll get your moneys worth at full price, but you should absolutely not miss this when it eventually goes on sale.
My biggest complaints with the game are as follows
No easy way to skip cutscenes on repeat playthroughs, though I suspect a mod will soon faciltate their removal entirely
No easy way to restart a stage or from a checkpoint to allow faster, easier attempts at the stupidly hard Pure Platium ranks. No idea if a mod could assist with this.
The motorcycle and missle stages are pretty much trash if you care at all about rank
In the end though, the pros far outweigh the cons. Buy this now.

This game... I really just... The game has potential. It does. When the game works well it's pretty fun, and there are some neat mechanics in the game. But it just isn't put together all that well. After one play through nothing really changes and I found myself speeding through content just because I didn't want to listen to it again.
Then there's the added problems of glitches, leveling, and really odd difficulty spikes.
The glitches are said to be improved from where they were originally. I played that game in patch 1.4 and it's still buggy as all get out. At one point the final boss walked through a wall, got stuck. I hit him a couple of times, he telleported, moonwalked for a little bit, and then insta-killed me with lord knows what. That's just one glitch there's plenty more to choose from.
The leveling system in this game is completely broken past the first play through. Once I got to about level 80 I stopped really being able to level through gathering experience. I had to go through all the secrets I already found to pick up attribute shards in order to level up because the experience needed was so high. By the end of my third play through to get one level I would have needed 1.5 million experience off of enemies that give about 2 throusand experience with a full multiplier. That's pretty crazy. I wouldn't mind if it weren't for the last problem.
Difficulty in this game makes no sense. It isn't a hard game, not even close. It's that some enemies are much much stronger than others and it doesn't always make sense. In NG+ and NG++ some of the most annoying enemies for my agility build were the zombies. The trash mobs that are everywhere. Nasty looking guy with a giant shield, no problem. Stupid puss zombie that can't even swing a sword well. Ya that thing will take three times as many hits to take down. Granted it has to do with my using the agility staff with three runes for most of the game and it being mostly poison damage, but even when I switched weapons those things were damage sponges. Then there's the bosses. In NG++ I was to the point where the second to last boss couldn't take off more than 5% of my health bar in an attack. I easily tanked through that fight and all the others. Then I got to the last boss and he damn near one shotted me. It didn't matter what armor I put on he still did it. And by then I couldn't do things like change my build to try different tactics. I was stuck trying to beat this guy when he would kill me that easily. It just felt unfair. Not even challenging, just unfair.
There are positives though. The game is pretty. Well not pretty so much as the graphics are nice on higher settings. And the combat, when it works correctly, is pretty fun. The positives just aren't that great though.
It's tempting to compare the game to Dark Souls, but it's really nothing like that game. This one is more like a game that started out that way and some one just get saying to extreme it up. There's armor in the game? Give him huge pointy shoulder pads with a fist on his chest! There's daggers in the game? Make some that have extra pointy bits and detailing all over the place. Put skulls on shields, put tatoos on the guy's face, put a giant hand in the background! EXTREME!
My first playthrough was fun, and if that's all you want go for it when it's on sale. If you're like me and you want to get all the stuff you might want to look else where. With the above mentioned stuff the experience is frustrating. Not difficult, not at all, just frustrating.

There are a lot of things I love about this game... For one, it's very similar to Terraria in a lot of ways, but you don't have that closed off feeling that comes with the singular world in Terraria. I mean, sure, you can visit your friend's map (with a good hamachi connection) in Terraria, but when you've mined and mapped out a whole world in Starbound, you can simply just head to the next one and continue your cartography/mining ad infinitum.
Another thing I'm keen on is that the planets you're landing on are completely random as to their contents... Will you find a USCM Penal Colony? Maybe a hidden Glitch town? Maybe an Apex science lab? It's really wonderful when you land on a friendly planet and you are welcomed in by the NPCs, the personalities can actually be pretty endearing. On the otherhand, it's pretty terrifying to land in a world populated by nothing but dudes who want to kill you and make soup from your spine. C'est la vie~
As for the overall play, it's fairly easy to adapt to and figure out... My only real complaint is that the actual "questing" halts at the low levels, acting more as a short tutorial. I'd love to see the quest lines extend onward up until the final tier of equipment, and perhaps onward into some postgame story bits. Starbound lacks a bit of narrative which they've tried (meritably) to make up for with an expanded in-game lore which you can access by books, but they'd do better with an active quest line. Needs more Space Adventure, IMO.
Sure, Starbound isn't complete.... Sure, they might be a bit late with their delivery.... But hey, it's a diamond in the rough with some real promise of sparkle. I, for one, am not at all mad at the wait for final release. It's a beautiful game and I enjoy every minute of it. Thank you for the good ride.
-Ben

Having been a fan of Harvest Moon since Back to Nature was released, Stardew Valley was almost exactly what I've been looking for. Almost.
For a farming game it's got everything you'd want and more; I was actually surprised by the number and variety of animals there are. There's plenty of crops to grow and sell, turn into pickles or jams or wines, and if you get bored of watering them all then you can eventually just set up a sprinkler system and you'll never have to water another plant again.
The NPCs have more distinct personalities and hobbies than those from Back to Nature, and a handful of them are eligible to be your romantic interest. As of this review there are six men and women to choose from, plus same sex marriage is a thing in this game so you don't need to worry about choosing to be a man or a woman to get the one you like the most.
And then there's the combat system. Yes, that's right, a combat system. In a game primarily about farming. I must admit that for the longest time I'd been waiting for a Harvest Moon game to introduce monsters to slay, but Stardew Valley beat it to it. Okay, it's not the most engaging of combat systems, but it's something. At the very least it gives you something to do once you've run out of chores to do on your farm, and there's a lot to be gained from the mines where the hostile creatures lurk.
I could do a short list of things that I found slightly dissapointing but I really only saw them as such because I'd been comparing with Back to Nature... Alright, festivals and cooking, that's all I'll say. Other than that, this game is great. There's so much to do: building your farm up, selling crops and produce, fishing, mining, mob slaying, helping out villagers with small quests, and there's even some adventuring and hidden places to find. There's no doubt more that I've neglected to mention as well. So if this genre is something new to you and you'd quite like to try it out, or even if you're an experienced Harvest Moon player and aren't sure how good this is, I'd highly recommend it. You won't be sorry.

I can see this game being a fun free to play MMO at the start but I couldn't bring myself to actually like this game as I went through it.
Keywords = "at the start"
Let me explain. This game is just a literal grindfest. You will do nothing but grinding the same dungeons over and over again in a portal to get different levels and get higher tiers of gear. Once you have done all of that, you will proceed to the next portal and do the exact same thing and then after that,you go to the next portal to do the same thing which makes the game really repetitive as well.
To counter the amount of grinding in the game (mostly by a few hours), you will need to pay the developers/publishers real life money which can come in amounts of £7,£15 and to even go as far as £80. Yes, £80 (Which is the highest amount I have seen so far but it probably goes higher than that). So if you want to save a few hours of grinding to get another class or healing item, be prepared to pay quite an amount of money.
There is no endgame. Once you have gotten to the uber 5/6 tier (Whatever the highest is) with the best tier of gear, there is literally nothing else to do after that. Well, there is Shadow Tower which is kinda like raid bosses but you will need to get keys to be able to get into the place which will takes hours/days to get or you can pay them money to get the keys faster. If you do manage to a get key for it, you will probably get killed in like 1 minute if unprepared and then since your key gets consumed, you will have to pay even more money or grind for another day just to get another one.
Customisation. Although this game has tons of weapon skins, hats and masks which make up for the actual lack of character customisation - There is literally nothing but hair, eye colour and skin type. That's it. No gender, no race, nothing.
The community. The community is what you would expect in an MMO like this; rubbish. In some cases of this, I have seen people calling other people anti-homosexual slurs, racial slurs or just general insults just because they don't like a certain part of the game or they don't like another game such as League of Legends and say that Dota 2 is better than it when it's just their opinion. I have also seen people trying to fish but then you have people come in the areas with massive boats to block the other player's sight so they can't tell whether a fish is hooked or not and then the players in boats keep shooting the cannons so the player's fishing can't hear the sound cue for the fish bite either. There are also tons of scammers in this game too which include fishy trades and then being kick straight after, people overpricing items which are probably worth nothing and even getting people to type in referal codes saying it will help them but it will only help the scammer get a mount.
Finally, there are no quests or NPCs... well, there are mobs in this game which don't really count as NPCs. There are no NPCs such as wandering travellers/merchants, no quest givers, nothing but mobs. There is no quest system either so no saving a village or shadowing or anything. Instead they put challenges in the game which can takes hours to complete (depending on what it is) which will earn you a currency called "Cubits" which allow you to buy things in the ingame store such as classes or healing flasks because literally everything else in the store such as mounts, wings, chests and all that other stuff costs real money.
Although this game has a lot of negatives, there are a few positives too. Biomes. Biomes in this game are different areas you can explore which are different environments like snow, dragon peaks, isles with pirates, forest and even medieval highlands. All of these biomes have certain items in them that you can't get anywhere else such as gear, pets and crafting materials, and certain ores.
Another positive to this game (And probably the only other one) is the building/crafting mechanic. You have the complete freedom to build whatever you want in this game (providing it's in your cornerstone which is your buildable home, of course) so you can build a house, massive towers, massive male genitalia and whatnot. You can also get different colours such as green, black, blue... Screw it, the whole colour spectrum is at your disposal. You can also craft decorations such as "gumball machines" (or whatever they're called over here in England), pool tables or you can even hang the heads of your enemies on the wall too. You will also be able to craft helpful items such as portals to get into different tier grindfests, different tools such as a forge to help improve your gear and other basic things in an MMO.
That's about it. If you're looking for an MMO which is nothing but a timewaster with the amount of building and grinding or if you are literally made out of money, this is the MMO for you. But if you are looking for and MMO with quests or an interesting story and whatnot, then there are plently of better MMOs out there and you should skip this one.

Alien Shooter Revisited takes you back to the campaign of the original Alien Shooter but with many of the new features introduced in Alien Shooter 2.
Alien Shooter Revisited is a isometric shooter where you run through a a secret laboratory while fighting off what seems like unending hordes of aliens hellbent on your gory demise.
As you progress through the levels you gain access to better and stronger weapons and the games level of gore reaches rather insane levels towards the end where entire maps will be painted red with alien intestines. You also have access to two separate last stand horde modes where you fend off a truly never ending mass of aliens as either a person or a static gun turret until you are overcome for the sake of high scores.
This time around, you get to pick from a number of different characters each with slightly different stats and in between missions you get access to the shop menu from Alien Shooter 2. The graphics have also been improved to match the later games.
This is all however, not nearly enough. Alien Shooter wasn't a great game and neither was it's sequel. Simply adding a few features on top of the same old missions does make this worthy of a replay or even a new purchase for newcomers to the series.
There is nothing really worthy of note in this repackaged version and the updates made are easily forgettable. If you honestly want to play one of the Alien/Zombie Shooter games then you should pick one of the sequels as they are slightly less lacking than the old versions, even "revisited" ones.

This game is good. If you have already played some Wargaming game ("World Of" series), Space Conflict or WarThunder, the UI and control is quite similar. Gameplay are fun and require teamwork and strategy more than reflex and mindless actions. Having high ping or lagging didn't really affect what you could do to contribute to victory, since some ships have autotargeting weapon and ability and ship movement is not that fast so you could still play fine. I have only played the Conquest Gamemode, the map is divided (or instanced) by sector rather than one big open map. You could still see what happened to other sector and see what your teammate could see though. Moving from and to sectors is done by "Jumping" ability to forward base in each sector or to your home base. This makes up for the generally slow paced gameplay inside the sector, making it faster to reinforce pushed friendly sector and helping pushes faster.

As a fan of city transport, trains and simulation games, I can recommend this game.But,there are some problems that are slightly ruining experience from this simulator. I mean crashes. They are everywhere. When the tile (part of map) next to you is loading,when you´re placing a spline in editor - error pops up. I've seen a crash in editor - "program OMSI2.exe has stopped working" out of nowhere. The bad thing is, MOST of errors are written in German language.
I shouldn't just hate this game.So,there are many good things i like. For example,better optimization. The game uses 2 cores of CPU (which is not the best, but for single-player only game it´s good). And the articulated bus.The joint of the bus is very realistic and works almost like in real life.
And the main point of simulations - mods. Since OMSI 1, the game is very highly moddable and comes with its own map editor and downloadable development kit.
You can make your own busses from your city, make your own city or make fictional city. Or - just download them, choose a map, spawn a bus and go.
Default busses works as in real life, most of controls works as they works on real busses. Sounds have very high quality.

-Upgraded performance in comparsion with OMSI 1
-Compatibility with lots of mods from OMSI 1
-AI cars has their own engine sound
And more that i can´t remember....
Cons:
-Crashes and errors
-Errors are written in German, so I can´t understand that
-Stupid AI (they don´t stop and crash into your bus on intersection without traffic lights)
I recommend, 75%.

For £1.49 I got much more than I expected in this charming little point and click adventure.

:
First of all I absolutely adore both the music and the art style. I think it is a very pretty game and considering you get the soundtrack free with the game I would say £1.49 is worth that alone.
When it comes to the game itself you play as a little girl who is adventuring through this magical land in search of her teddy. Do not be fooled though, this is not a game about sunshine and rainbows, in fact the game I would liken this to the most would be LIMBO, and for those of you that have played that you know what kind of deaths await you.
Throughout the game you travel through different areas in order to help the creatures in your way. You do this in most cases by singing to them. It's a very interesting mechanic and I like it a lot.
While the game is rather short the odds are that you will not see 100% of it on your first play through. I personally only saw 60% of the game on my first playthrough and because of that I will be playing it again to get 100%. Past that however there isn't much replayability here other than achievements and hidden artwork you can unlock and look at in the game, however for such a low price I wasn't really expecting something I would be playing for weeks to come.
As much as I love this game I did however have one problem with the final puzzle in the game. Without spoiling anything I'd like to say that I found this specific puzzle to be pretty poor. This is because in order to complete it you need to have completed it pretty much 100% on your first try, otherwise you will have to google the answer. While this wouldn't be a bad thing if you could back track and look for clues, you are instead stuck on the final screen until you solve the final puzzle. Personally I did not get 100% on my first run through and instead had to google the answer after a while and I'm sad to say that even if I had really thought about it for a long time I would never have gotten past this screen because I missed a couple of parts. This could reasily have been solved by only making the mandatory sections part of this puzzle. However they didn't and therefore it ended on less of a "Yay I beat  the game!" and more of a "How was I supposed to ever get that?".
Overall I would still very much recomend this game to anyone, especially for the price it is currently at. Plus it has steam trading cards which is nice too.

Dive to the Titanic is ridiculously boring yet at the same time deeply frustrating. The controls and physics feel very accurate to piloting a real submarine, but there's just nothing interesting or fun to actually do in the game.
-Every single level is a fetch quest; go through the ship until you find two items to grab or photograph
-Both subs move RIDICULOUSLY slowly, so it takes forever and a half to get anywhere.
-The game's scripting breaks if you don't follow one EXACT path to each objective, causing key objective markers to disappear and leave you totally lost or photos of key objects to not be counted.
-Objective markers are vague and confusing, often leading you to wrong floors or down completely wrong paths.
-The game world is built with a ton of dead ends, so each mission inevitably results in a ton of back-tracking to figure out where you're supposed to go in a sub that crawls at an unbearably slow pace.
-Your mission control chimes in about every 20 seconds (not joking) reminding you to "go up!" "you need to go upwards!" "now move upwards!" You will do yourself a huge favor just muting the game.
-The game is now 7 years old and not optimized AT ALL. It takes a LOT of work and tedium to get the game to not only run but run with few enough bugs to be playable.
-The interior of the ship is so featureless it doesn't even feel like you're exploring the Titanic. You're exploring a series of empty rooms laid out in a Titanic-like shape.
-What I can only assume is a recurring glitch prevented me from being able to access the game's ending. The minigame at the end is horribly explained and takes a ton of trial and error just to figure out how to play it.
-The default key bindings are utter garbage and if you change the bindings the tutorial button prompts don't change- it keeps telling you to press the default buttons, which are now wrong.
It's just a lot of wandering down featureless corridors with the slowest movement speed ever recorded. It has nothing to offer flight or submarine sim fans and it has nothing to offer Titanic enthusiasts or history buffs curious on the topic. Completely useless.

Lords of the Fallen is very similar to Dark Souls.
I like all of the differences to Dark Souls and Lords of the Fallen is what I hoped Dark Souls 2 to be.
The combat favors blocking more than dodging, though if you're wearing the heaviest armor, fighting with 2 handed weapons and without a shield is quite viable.
The character classes and stats are a manageable amount. You can pick between Warrior, Rogue and Cleric twice, once for the spells and once for the starting equipment and the combination of both determines the starting attribute points.
The graphics are top notch, but it also sometimes drops down to 30fps (which max for Dark Souls btw).
The art style has similarities to Darksiders, though it looks less clunky and more refined. The Warrior's heavy armor sets look bamf. The animations are very fluid.
If you kill enemies and don't bank your souls, you get an XP and loot chance multiplier (capped at 2.00x).
The levels are well designed so that while you traverse them the first time, you're doing loops and unlocking shortcuts and when you're done, going through a zone is very quick, so that there's no need for quicktravel. Half of the levels are very clear, but the other can be somewhat confusing, especially Catacombs etc.
