I've sunk a bit too much time so I might as well make a review, I'll include what went wrong too.
Yes, this game is fun, but as others have mentioned the grinding gets pretty tedious and intense, especially later on. It took me a full year to get 5* gear because I played pretty casually.
The first 400~ hours will simply blow your mind if you initially enjoy it, but after those sweet moments there isn't much. There just simply isn't enough content or motivation to keep you going. I only stayed around because I made some fantastic friends, whom I still talk to after quite a few years. But after some pretty bad financial decisions by Three Rings,(who also destroyed whirled, another fantastic creation by them) the game started to go down hill quickly. They sold Spiral Knights to sega who turned it into a cash grab immediately, and started to release less and less actual content and updates. The developers started thinning out for all of their projects, including their lead supervisor. Kudos to him for leaving, he's moved on to greater things (I think he's in charge of Slime Rancher now) but once he left is when things really started to get bad.
The constant "updates" became simply reskins in loot boxes, similar to CS:GO, Overwatch, ect. The lack of updates and bug fixes along with poor advertising started to thin out Spiral Knight's fanbase. When more and more vets started leaving, their friends started following, including me. What's the point of this game when you have all your items and your friends start leaving? Well the answer, quite simply, is for you to decide. You can still have fun, but it's all mental, you have to choose whether it's worth still playing the same bland levels over and over again while less and less of your friends are there to play with you. There are still plenty of dedicated players but they are few and far between, and more and more people leave on a daily basis.
Now the game is pretty much a skeleton of it's former self. Sega resold Spiral Knights to Grey Havens, which i'm almost 99% sure is a group of Three Rings employees desperate to keep their creation alive, which I give huge props to them. They certainly did care a GREAT deal about all of their projects, and it's sad to see them get screwed over like this. All great things do come to an end.
The good:
-Great soundtrack
-Art is extremely vibrant, approaching acid trip levels of bright. Color literally everywhere, and the cutesy design fits perfectly
-Extremely creative
-Very very very friendly community, for the most part (not pvp)
-Enemies are really creative (even if they do start to get boring after 1000 hours)
-Weapons are pretty diverse and fun, even if some are outclassed by others completely
-Outstanding controller support and configuration, I play this game with an NES controller occasionally. If it fits in your usb slot, you can play on it.
-PvP is very fun
The mediocre:
-PvP might be fun but it's also very heavily based on your gear. If you don't have great gear you WILL get stomped, the dedicated players do not show any hint of mercy to anyone. Even if you do have good stuff, it ends up being like sports and steroids: there will always be someone on more♥♥♥♥♥♥than you and outdo you.
-Levels get old and fast, but they are creative and well thought out
-After a while, personally, the walking just feels sooooo slow.
-pets are kind of useless and niche
-somewhat pay2win but you can get everything free if you spend time on it.
-really weird and unusually long tutorial, like a few hours worth of tutorial.
The bad:
-Dear lord some enemies are SO
- Expensive if you're looking for shortcuts.
-Ranking up to get to more difficult levels takes forever
-Not a lot of people playing anymore
-LOTS of lag, mostly server sided so you can't do anything to fix it.
The ugly:
-no updates anymore, last one took a full year to come out lmao
-reskins everywhere, like MS paint kindergardener levels of reskinning.
-Dear
-♥♥♥♥ing
-LORD
-The grinding is so intensive and boring it will ABSOLUTELY be a turnoff for you, if you want to just pay for everything and not waste hundreds of hours of your life, it's exorbitantly priced.
-After 200-400 hours you have seen everything and there's no more motivation
-Greaver enemies are so annoying you might actually tie a noose
-frequent unfixable Lag every 30 seconds to 2 minutes, if you're lucky
All in all a great game that you will most likely enjoy if you get into it, even if the playerbase is thinning out. Play it while you still can, it might not be around for much longer.

This game is not Ridge Racer, it is a generic Burnout clone with the Ridge Racer name on it.
Ridge Racer games are bright, colourful, with happy techno music and wide open streets where you drift round corners.  The drifting mechanic is extremely simple to learn and is very well designed and implemented.  It is Ridge Racer's trademark gameplay.
In this game we have only dark, tight streets, mostly annoying music (there are a tiny number of tunes from other RR games, 2 or 3 from memory) and worst of all, the drifting is terrible in this game.  It is badly designed and you have to smash into objects in order to earn boost.  It is the most ill-conceived and unintuitive game design I can remember.  Some objects are breakable and give you boost, others will make you crash.  The difference between these objects in appearance is not obvious so you have to either learn from trial and error, or hope for the best.  Other larger objects can be smashed through when you have full boost, but not at other times.  The game will take control of your car during this time, and often hand you back control when a crash is unavoidable.  So the game basically forces you into crashing.
The game varies between easy and maddeningly difficult.  Make no mistake this can be a very frustrating game indeed.  I don't think there is any catch-up or rubberbanding, because typically if you let the AI get a lead and crash on the harder levels you might as well restart as you have next to no chance of winning.  On the other hand, I have found myself with huge leads and I've even found myself stopping and waiting 20 seconds for the other cars to catch up, so I can try and score more points in order to unlock the next stage.
I have completed the career mode but in the end it was more for my own personal satisfaction than because I was really enjoying myself.  I've recently been playing Ridge Racer 6 on the 360 and Ridge Racer 2 on the PSP, both of which are PROPER Ridge Racer games and are miles more fun than this game is.  Loads of fantastic tunes, open roads, addictive drifting, colourful happy environments.  Real feel good games.  We still wait for such a game on the PC - this isn't it.
Oh yeah and it likes to crash to the desktop a lot (I'm using Windows 7) seemingly randomly.

It is a shame that newer players that are used to the styles of more modern games and expecting just a lower-graphics version of Half-Life 2 have trouble getting in to this one. In my opinion, this is the best of the series, and is one of the greatest games available for the PC. The latter is nearly a given. Scores for this game across the board are at least in the 90% range, but people often cite the second game as being better than the first. That alone is enough for recommendation, but why does this phenomena happen? I think most of it comes down to the way that the story is told, and Half-Life 2 is a masterpiece of direct storytelling in games. The characters you meet feel real- and the engine does a very good job at animating them. You want to see them succeed, and the process of the game is helping them through various challenges that are faced. Half-Life 1 is very different though. In the first, your protagonist is silent because he has no reason to speak, and doing so would reduce immersion. Half-Life truly is a 1st-person game; YOU have to figure your way through the problems because the character is YOU. The method of telling the story is for the player to figure out- throughout the game you figure out piece by piece what the whole picture is. In many ways the game feels real, despite extreme environments and unrealistic situations. You feel that you are a smaller part of a larger story, and you feel that every action you take directly advances the story. This is the main difference between the two. Nuances in gameplay also are a factor, but this is the primary reason why I think that Half-Life is better than Half-Life 2.

One of my favorite games of all time. This is a game with no perfect strategy. A perfect team can be sent into a death spiral by an enemy crit at the wrong time. It's not uncommon to be think "Huh, this expidition is going rather well, things are looking up!" and later in the same mission "OOHH GOD EVERYTHING IS GOING WROOONNNG". The game gives no clemency and no mercy. Circumstances completely beyond your control can result in a complete party wipe as you just sit there and watch, completely unable to do anything about it. But if you play it right, this game which mercilessly slaughters your heroes who have the audacity to miss a single blow provides an excellent experience and an immersive atmosphere. You will go most quests without losing a single hero, but then an afflicted hero does something stupid and messes it all up for the other poor souls with them. The mental stress mechanic really makes this game. It provides such a huge variable that is almost impossible to plan for. I once had a Leper become masochistic on Death's Door (0 HP, next damage might kill them), and on his next turn decide to harm himself for pleasure (one of the possible effects of masochism) and literally kill himself. I had another Leper fighting an eldrich god on Deaths Door, watch the other three members of his team die in front of him, then became couragous and survive three consecutive strikes from the final boss and two rounds of bleed and STILL manage to land the final strike that won the game. The game does a fantastic job of making the biggest variable in the game the fragility of the heroes themselves. Words cannot express how much I love this game.

The Walking Dead Season 1 weaves poignant story-telling and beautiful art to create a game that I can only describe as a masterpiece. This point-and-click adventure game features excellent character development and a well-paced plot which serves to maximize immersion. Even if you are not familiar with the Walking Dead in other mediums (i.e. the TV show or comics), you will find yourself attached to the characters in this game. Every heart-wrenching decision you make has consequences, some large, some small, and you will often find yourself wondering if you made the right choice.
Keep in mind, however, that this is not an action game. Don't look to this game for any sort of combat or survival mechanics. The purpose of the game is to tell a story, and it is an amazing narrative about love, loss and morality. If this is what you are looking for, then I would HIGHLY recommend the Walking Dead Season 1.

TLDR; Game is hard at first. If you like a challenge and are willing to learn the game it's very fun.
As someone who has spent over 200 hours on this game I can certainly say that I enjoy the game, however it should be made clear what you are getting yourself into and how to approach the game if you plan on purchasing it.
Most, whether they enjoy the game or not, commend it for the well crafted character design, atmosphere, unique mechanics1, and art style. However most who dislike the game will do so on the basis that the game is too RNG dependent, too unforgiving, too "grindy", or too difficult. Its likely that your first campaign will make you feel like the game is all of those things. I myself complained of these points at the start. The first few hours will kick you in the teeth, bang your wife, and eat your leftovers.
For many beginners the unforgiving nature of the game and its steep challenges can be very overwhelming, leaving a bad taste in their mouth from the start, but if you can embrace is impossibly tough nature and you over come its challenges, which you will eventually do, it makes it all the more rewarding. If you are just starting and you are someone who gets mad at games easily I would recommend spending some time in the options and do what you can to lessen the punishment of failure until you can learn the game. You will learn the game and its mechanics with experience, such as what skills to prioritize, which party combinations work, when to use what skills, where to use which supply items. If you're reading this before playing the game at all I would NOT recommend look up anything in the wiki unless necessary. It can help maintain that sense of acomplishment and retains a sense of mystery, wonder, and terror as to what will be in the next passage, room, or what will happen when a torch is placed in the alters of darkness. But if you don't understand a mechanic or enemy to the point of frustration you may want to look to the wiki, don't ruin the game for yourself.
However after awhile, once you learn how the game operates and how to tip the odds in your favor, you can begin to appreciate some of these other claimed "dislikes" of the game. Take for example the RNG dependency. Even with the perfectly talored party with all the right heroes, skills, and stats (usually in the form of "Quirks" or items in this game), there's still a sense of real danger. All it takes is one or two crits and a hero is on the verge of dying, and I think that that threat of real danger, paired with the atmosphere and art, makes the game truly terrifying.
That threat of danger is also what also helps keep the grind from feeling "grindy". There's always a sense that you can lose all your progress you've worked towards, making it all the more precious. Instead of a grind the game becomes and uphill battle towards your goal. Another way of overcoming the sense of the game being "grindy" is experementing, though be warned what does and doesn't work will be apparent very quickly. Theres alot of strange party combinations and item builds that can be very fun. Take for example, some of my favorites, the 4 crusader party or the 4 vestal party. The constant need learning and adaptation keeps me guessing even as of past hour 200. I will say though for those who feel like they've been punished even with perfect execution I can understand how the game can become less fun, even "grindy", in which case I would say that unfortunatly the game is not for you.
I also appreciate Red Hook for working so hard on their game, regularly working on updates and DLC even past its official "full release". They've spent a lot of time on their work and it shows, and I couldn't be more happy to see the money I spent on this game being put towards a company that truly cares about their game. In all this game with it's brutal difficulty, unforgiving nature, and commitment to the idea of a world working against you creates one of the most challenging and rewarding games I've played.

Finding Teddy is a surprisingly challenging point & click adventure game based on a simple fairy tail scenario.  A giant spider from another world kidnaps a little girl's teddy bear as she sleeps.  Your mission is to help her get Teddy back.
The game doesn't have any verbs or action icons for interacting with the world, thus making the interface pretty simple.  You can collect items and then use those items from your inventory with the environment.  There is no need to combine items  with each other via the inventory system.
The characters that you speak to don't have any english dialogue, but they instead communicate through melodic sounds.  There are many puzzles that can be solved through brute force trial & error, but it's definitely worth the effort to discover the cypher to the creatures' musical language.
The graphics are the old-school pixel graphics reminiscent of the point & click adventures published  back in the 90s.  The animations are fluid and beautiful to watch.  The music and sound only serve as ambient noise while you explore the world.  Unfortunately, you won't find any catchy theme music in this title.
I highly recommend Finding Teddy and hope that the developer produces a sequel!

OMSI 2 is a great follow up to the first OMSI.  OMSI 2 includes new buses, new routes, and a huge addition to the default map.  The Berlin-Spandau map has been extended to include Falkensee, previously only available through addons.  The new single-decker NL202 and articulated NG272, both highly detailed, are now also included as defaults in the game.  There are also audio files played whenever the player clicks the IBIS button to load the next stop.  There are, however, a few issues.  The increase in detail and size of the map has added a considerable lag factor.  Also (this may be a result of the lag), there are lots and lots of traffic glitches.  Vehicles will stop at traffic lights inside each other, and if you're driving the NG272, vehicles will run into the back of your bus.  Other than the few glitches currently in the game, OMSI 2 is a great follow up game that any OMSI fan should get.

Right, where to begin?
The game itself bring nothing new or exiting, even when first released. Still, being a huge fan of the "Fallout universe", i of course just had to get it. So, i bought the game and added the season pass, in order to make certain i got all the following add-ons that was promised. Boy... was this ever a hype...
The main storyline can be done easily in about 5 hours of gametime, and that is if you take your time doing it, so that is not what makes this game good in any way. However, if you're a fan of speed runs, this Fallout game is equally easy to beat as the first ones. No, the big part of the game being decent, is the large amount of small things. Te many minor quests, the easter eggs that are very numerous, and a few recurring characters from previous games.
So why isn't this game good then? It became painfully obvious when Bethesda dropped new content, which you had to pay for unless you got the season pass, that the company had no intentions to really make this a good game to begin with. The added material (add-ons) were poorly made most of the time, with only two real add-ons given, two that could only be deemed to be a semi add-on, and a few extra creation kits for the settlements. The game could have a HUGE potential, but in my honest opinion, it was botched at the planning stage. From everything like the voice acting, to the inability to play a truly "evil" character, this game is more of a streamlined story, than an actual open world game. It's truly sad to see that the original games (1&2) was less of a main story quest chain, than this one, some 20 years later...
The final nail in the coffin of this game is when Bethesda introduced the Creation Kit (i think it's called that, most likely because of the ancient G.E.C.K.), which is essentially hijacking 2 gigs of hardrive space, in order for the player/customer to be able to purchase in-game "stuff". This is basically paid modding in lack of a better term. They haven't removed the ability to mod the game (yet), but in the way of how this game is going, and how Bethesda is acting at this point, i see no problem with them actually shutting down non-Bethesda mods entirely in the near future.
If not looking through rose-tinted glasses, this game started as a 6/10, after the regular add-ons it was about 4/10 due to the lack of good content provided by them... Now, i could not even give it 2/10... i logged in once to the game after the installation (forced update i might add) of this last, sad, patch. I can't even force myself to even bother to do so again, not until Bethesda offers an apology to the gaming community, to the modding community, and at the very least give the harddrive space back, or let the season pass work as "in game currency". There is very little else they can do to save face, or this game at this point.

This is a deeply flawed game that anyone who's interested in political science or simultation games in general should really enjoy. It's just important to acknolwedge the shortcomings beforehand.
Democracy 3 works by allowing you to have a certain amount of quantified "political capital" which you can spend each month. The longer you're in power, the less power you gain per month (unless you shake up your cabinet)-- you have to deal with crises that pop up as a result of your actions (or as a result of the country you've been elected to take over). And as you're fixing the issues, you have to fight elections too.
The game itself is heavily biased in favor of running a socialist state to fix problems-- it's by far the easiest way to gain credibility with the electorate and allows you to quickly have non-competitive elections. It's not an issue from my side of the real political spectrum, but it makes gameplay kind of boring as you use the same solutions for every problem. The base game does not have many country choices or variety to them (I haven't tried the DLC) and the simulation becomes very, very predictable. Every time at the end of the month, you're given a political choice pop-up event. Every time you start to go too heavily in one direction, a terrorist group will try and assasinate you.
It can get kind of mundane, but somehow, someway, this game perseveres. It becomes strangely addicting and fun to try and balance out the different policies. Do you create a carbon tax to manage your budget? Do you create a security state that rivals the NSA in its breadth?
This is not a frills and image-filled experience, but it's a solid game that's worth your time if you're interested in this kind of thing.

It's a fun racer, but there is more than one hair in this soup:
The technical issues are rather minor: No cloud support and literally zero settings to adjust the graphics beyond their resolution. But the art direction of the title is mostly quite elegant and it looks and runs well, so these are more representative of a lack of effort than any serious problems.
One of the problems is the drifting: It's a game all about drifting, it's the core mechanic and what the series is known for, so it's the one thing they had to absolutely get right. But I'm not sure they did, at least not entirely - it ended up both unrealisitc and surprisingly hard to control.
Unrealistic drifting in an arcade racer isn't a problem, sacrificing realism for speed, control and fun is what you expect.
In RRU it requires some skill to learn and master its magic-physics based drifting mechanic - and you stand zero chance in the game until you have wrapped your brain around it. And the game certainly doesn't help you with that at all.
However, this will eventually happen and once it clicks, the game mechanic works reasonably well.
There is neither a difficulty curve nor any difficulty settings. The AI knows only one mode and it's merciless. Screw up once and you can restart the race in many of the (not even that short) events and its easy to screw up: in good old Bugbear fashion you can drift out of 80% of all curves without losing any speed and the remaining 20% (often placed right enar the finish line) will kill you and effectively end any chance of winning a race - there is no rewind mechanic either. There's a fine line between satisfyingly difficult and unfairly punishing and this game walks this line like Barney Gumble.
I found it shockingly hard to advance in the beginning - now that I unlocked almost all of the tracks and cars and learned the mechanics I'm dominating many of the later events left and right. But returning to some of the earliest races, with better cars and much improved skills and I'm still unable to properly pass them. That's what I meant when I said something went terribly wrong in playtesting.
The AI is weird. There doesn't seem to be any rubber banding (although it feels like they somehow speed up near the finish line, almost like the opposite of rubber banding) and they aren't overly aggressive (it may frag you once per race so you can get points for fragging your "rival") but they are also completely inhuman: They never create any shortcuts (the other core mechanic of this game) but readily take them if available, basically make zero mistakes, take some corners faster than they should be able to and are generally very fast.
It just feels unnatural and at times just punishingly unfair.
There are other little details, for example the displayed speed. While RRU certainly conveys a good sense, the speed of your car bears almost no resemblance to the speed actually displayed on the screen.
The tracks look nice and are fun to drive, but since they are all made from the same building blocks and all have the same setting the "infinite possibilities" end up feeling a lot more samey and repetitive than those of other racers.
This all sounds a lot harsher than it should be: The more I play the more I'm enjoying this game and there are many times when I'm having a blast. And it keeps drawing me back in. Much like "The Binding of Isaac" I disliked it at first but it constantly made me come back for more.
I certainly got my money's worth and then some out of this game, so I guess at this point I should fully recommend it. I'm not disappointed by what I got, but more by some this game's wasted potential: With a bit more polish, some extra playtesting and some better decision making during the development process this could have been a classic - as it stands it's fun but flawed.

Cons:-Graphics do not hold up today. Compared to the amazing looks of Half-Life 2 (and new games like Titanfall) it's graphics suck. It looks like original Playstation. Yes, I know it came out in 1998.
-Gameplay is weird! You run WAY too fast. The only way to slow your♥♥♥♥♥down is to press Shift to walk or crouch down. It is really hard to walk on narrow paths. Jumping onto ladders is weird too. If you keep pressing SPACE you don't grab on. That can be a problem.
-Headcrabs are too F**KING STRONG! It takes 2 pistol shots to kill them. That's not bad. Then it takes like 4 or 5 hits with the crowbar to kill them. Um.. isn't the crowbar a headcrab's weakness? The tiny knife from Opposing Force insa-kills them! WTF?!

“Dive to the Titanic” Review, 1 May 2015
To make Steam/TML Studio’s “Dive to the Titanic” more enjoyable, I’ve assembled notes from the forum, reviews, game files and my experiences at the (not very) “Easy” level. A fairly difficult game, it becomes more so with each dive. You will become familiar with the parts of the wreck in play and how to pick your way around debris. The game resembles a real dive: long periods of boredom punctuated by moments of terror and triumph. There’s more (or less) to see than you might expect; graphics, while dated, are effective. You must install DirectX 9.0c even if you have newer versions; later DirectX versions do not replace earlier ones. Some report needing to replace their version of Quick Time; an installed is provided. There are no add-ons, patches or updates. I use a modest older laptop with good results. Game specifications are at the end.
Expect to re-map the keyboard; key assignments are often wrong . Don’t immediately change the navigating, camera or claw operating keys or the tutorials in the first two dives will not sense the correct keys. Do any initial key re-mapping such as the number keys from ‘Settings’ in the main menu and fine-tune them later in the game after the tutorial by pressing ‘ESC’ for the menu; you can also use this menu to save a dive in progress. Check all the keys (use the ‘DOWN’ arrow to get to the later pages; click on the key’s assigned value and press the one you want instead. The left mouse button (button 0) does what you expect: in the sub and ROV outside views, click the right mouse button (button 1) then move the mouse to change the view.
There are five dives leading to a free-roam exploration scenario, and three levels of play:
o	Easy: for familiarization with the game. A grey visual cue shows the direction and distance in meters to the objectives, in order. There is extra time to look around. Use TAB to pause the game when needed.
o	Normal: no visual cues, the battery charge and your range are reduced, so time is more limited. You will need to know where you’re going, how to get there, and what you’re looking for.
o	Difficult: for experienced players. Operational parameters (battery, range etc.) are more critical; you have little time to spare.
At the Easy level, just follow the cues. Except on the last dive, you have some extra time to use to explore as you go. At the advanced levels you must plan your dives with increasing care so you know what you’re looking for, where it is, and how to get there. The map will help, but not everything is shown. Deck plans from the Internet help, but some game locations, especially cabins, don’t match the real thing. At the Difficult level you probably stand no chance without having a few practice runs behind you.

As a huge fan of XCOM: Enemy Unknown, I was really excited to get a chance to play the next evolution of the genre. Many improvements have been made which add a lot to the depth. Many other elements stand in the way of making it truly enjoyable.
Good: Depth of strategy; Modular weapon design allowing you to better customize; Psionics as a unit type with many more abilities; Turn limits on many missions which force actions in a reasonable time; Hacking things for bonuses
Bad: The unit loadout screen should make it more clear what is and isn't available for use; The general interface makes it somewhat difficult to see what's going on; UFOs searching for my ship- sometimes they fly literally over the top of me without seeing me other times they're very far away when they do; The black market is significantly harder to use and uses up time to travel there just to see if there's anything of interest. Turn limits on too many missions; The engineering interface could also be much more intuitive with more information available; Overwatch shots miss with an alarming frequency.
Ugly: Concealment is completely unrealistic at times and it's really difficult to tell if an enemy will walk over, flank and thereby discover a unit, then blast them into oblivion before you have the chance to do anything; Faceless aliens (which suddenly turn from a human into an alien) and Chrysalids, which then also move and kill you before you have the chance to react. On top of that, they seem to usually go after the most vulnerable troop; Not being able to see how far an enemy can move so that you can stay out of their attack range.

First (and probably last) review I've ever written for a game, and I'm writing after uninstalling the game in question.
Bayonetta is a schizophrenic, glorious, unplayable mess.
The game's enemies are lovinly designed, with lots of cunning details revealed as they take damage and go from menacing but angelic baddies to revolting, chthonic monsters. When you're fighting regular groups of bad guys, the gameplay feels like 90% of a perfect game - Bayonetta's dizzying array of combo moves lets you easily slip into your own playstyles, and the game clearly delights in disrupting your favorite tactics with a vast menagerie of enemies whose special abilities, armor, attacks, and teamwork will challenge you to find new strategies to beat them.
The camera is occasionally spastic, fibrillating unpredictably when you're near a wall or corner at times while at other times holding steady. Annoying, but you want to forgive it due to the game's age and the immersion of regular combat.
The story is almost always a campy, overly generic send-up of too-serious action games where The Fate of The Universe rests on your shoulders, as The Promised Child who was born of Forbidden Love between Light and Dark. Nearly every cutscene is a great mix of story progression and clever, wink-at-the-audience snipes, bawdy jokes, and anime-style doubletakes. Certain characters are relentlessly serious, however (Jeanne in particular), and you're unpredictably yanked out of the fun MST3k-style atmosphere and slapped around by a story bit that clearly wants to be serious, but you can't take it seriously because you're still chuckling over Bayonetta's last one-liner.
But the game falls apart completely during the boss fights.
Each boss fight (and some viciously hard encounters like Gracious and Glorious) shatter your enjoyment. The camera swings wildly when you're leaping and dodging, or zooms out ludicrously far when you're fighting gigantic enemies. The boss fights are a mix of repetitive dodge-and-dash challenges and stupidly difficult straight-on brawls with enemies that are faster and far tougher than you.
In particular, recurring buzzkill Jeanne is a nightmare to fight in later chapters. She is smaller than any other boss, every bit as fast as Bayonetta, capable of chaining together brutal combos you can't break out of as they devour great chunks of your health, and blasts out super-attacks (wicked weaves) with only a split-second of warning. I stopped playing at chapter 14 after two days of being completely unable to beat her in a tortuously long, multi-section fight that takes at least half an hour.
Gigantic bosses have fast, devastating melee attacks you cannot accurately dodge because the game's 3d structure and bad camera angles don't let you get a good guage of how close to let them get before dodging in order to get a 3-second window of super-speed called 'witch time' which is critical to building your long, devastating combos.
Some enemies have stupidly powerful laser attacks which do great damage and stun Bayonetta, which they tend to fire in overlapping salvos to maximize chances of hitting you - always followed up with swarms of attacks to catch you at your weakest.
Overall, it feels like I'm playing 3 games at once. A dumb, dull, repetitive dodging sim has been mashed together with a fun and gleefully funny action game that wants you to smash baddies and tropes in equal measure, and both of these were chained to a sadistic, Gaiden-Razor's-Edge-hard melee game which demands bleeding-eye attention to detail and hair-trigger reaction times in order to scrape past.
Finally, the game is chock-full of super-items (accessories) which, when equipped, give you special abilities to make the game easier. But each one is behind an extremely high paywall which will force you to grind through each level multiple times with careful attention to your save files in order to chain together enough high-ranking performances to afford even one.
So yeah, the game is too hard. It's one of those sad fighters that wanted to find the Dark Souls edge between vicious difficulty and addictively fun gameplay, and shot way past the mark.
Someone really dedicated and obsessed could beat this game, and probably enjoy it too. But it's simply not worth the hours of being smeared across the floor again, and again, and again, and again, to do it.

Finding Teddy is a textless point ‘n’ click adventure game with astonishing pixel art, simplistic plot, somewhat clunky controls, and an unnecessary musical puzzle aspect.
Finding Teddy is a cute and beautiful little point ‘n’ click that was made with love, but it set its goals too high by trying to be an art-only adventure game.
Sure, the plot is so simple it hardly needs any dialogue: you play as a little girl whose teddy bear gets stolen, so she enters a magical land where she encounters some unfriendly beasts she needs to tame with certain items or code phrases.
The problem comes from acquiring these. The items are not too problematic– if you are patient enough, brute force will eventually let you pass. But the code phrases…
They use a musical alphabet where you only receive the letters
you solved the puzzle tied to them. So in order to beat the game you either need to be an experienced musician or have an exceptional hearing. Also, if you play with laptop speakers, don’t even bother.
Still, if you don’t mind relying on a walkthrough, the game is adorable enough to spend a few hours with it.

It might be a bad game. I've been playing it through again and again. I'll say this before hand though, despite having sunk several hundred hours into XCOM:EU the main thing XCOM2 does right is being a totally different game from XCOM:EU. The game's major changes are obvious. A need to actually build up your supply base. A need to expand in the face of Advent's already massive infrastructure and global presence. This creates a massively new strategic experience. A lot of squad missions have a timer now.
Note: I've read an interview with the project designer where he admits that maybe a month before releasing XCOM2 the design team ramped up the difficulty in response to game testers repeated comments that it was easy. I expect the largest difficulty is the low numbers of missions with a timer. The timer forces youtp pursue a rapid pace in almost every mission, however that pace will cause Total Squad Death. Almost a year after release the game still has an inconsistent LOS. These errors in LOS can be somewhat reduced by the use of a few mods.
The strategic layer is well done in it's design but was implimented to restrict your progress. The restrictions come in several forms. A limitation of starting income supply instead of a large starting supply income reduced by success you have to expand your supply base by increasing the number of rebel bases in different countries you seek out contact with. For each new country you contact you get more supplies and you can get additional supplies from building additional radio towers. The advantages of this changed approach to supply income is that perfection in the missions isn't what reduces your income. Dark events or failing to respond to retaliation missions (terror attacks) are. Note: The once great Long War team from XCOM:EU made a mess of imbalanced weapons and bad changes to strategic layer. They instead made it too difficult to keep track of all the objectives you have to juggle. Even most of the options they thought made squad missions better make them more chaotic.
Let me talk about retaliation missions a little bit. Retaliation missions are a take on terror missions where the Advent/Alien forces strike a rebel base. Your goal is still to rescue civilians, in that these rebels are not fighters just persons who do not believe Advent is legit. In a retaliation mission your goal is to rescue an arbitrarilly decided 6 civilians. I say arbitrarilly decided in reference to the designers. However. A few random civilians whom you have to rescue are also alien shapeshifters.
Shapeshifters who have large health pools and a substantial melee attack. There is no research or facility you can create which will ever remove these from rebel camps or alert you ahead of time to their presence. One of the nicer changes is the ability to build a facility which will list the types of enemies your squad will face on missions and even with that built you're not alerted to their presence.
Enemies do come in a range of types. The classic enemies return. There are some new enemies. Enemies have all the advantages. Advent forces can call in air strikes. Select alien units can call in air strikes. Enemies call for reinforcements. Enemies occasionally set up ambushes. Players can expect any mission labeled supply run is actually the aliens drawing you out to a remote location and assasinating you with an overwhelming diversity of Alien+Advent abilities and weapon types.
There is at a glance a surprisingly deft effort from the design team to create a game where guerilla troops / forces struggle against the embedded infrastructure of an enemy. You really do rise up to fight the aliens almost at the last moment. In just twenty years they're ready to start work on the Avatar project. But between the inconsistent LOS and the already victorious alien HOST I felt less like I was steering the squads of Stargate to victory, and more like I was struggling to rationalize every decision or opinion as if I was in the Earth: Final Contact setting. Maybe it's all the science fiction I've read. Maybe it's the extremely dull video that plays when you lose. Maybe it's the very dull video that plays whe you finish the game. But on the whole the only reason I wanted to keep replaying XCOM2 was in the hopes that I'd change my mind.
For me the largest frustration is still the tactical squad based missions in the game. There are mods available to let you adjust or change this part of the game but I kind of hate it. What may work best for you is to combine smaller tweaks that are available which may let you customize the combat into something less incoherent. Even with a host of mods I remain unimpressed. My take away from playing the game again is still that the squad based combat isn't honest or predictable - I'm not talking about missing a 98% shot. When I say predictable I mean that things happen in the missions I was regularly blindsided by. Sometimes I'd lose an entire squad without knowing quite why. Once in a retaliation mission I had a unit aside some obviously discarded barrels and tanks of some sort. These were, unknown to me, explosive, and I lost a high level squad because I wasn't informed about that fact. One squad member died and the rest paniked badly. There wasn't a voice line, icon, or, alert, that my squad member was next to an explosive threat.
I also have concerns now about the story. When I replayed this recently I found myself disliking the XCOM forces. I'm still struck by the plain facts. In this game the XCOM "alliance" or "forces" made everything worse. The aliens do want to consume a lot of human's and yes after they find a cure they will probably absorb our now limited cultural uniqueness to their own but through our intervention against the Avatar project we forced them to escalate and threaten our species with genocide. In this regard it's an almost nuanced nod to complex plots and a footnote that the Elder's are desperate and will regret annihilating our species. Indeed by the end of the game the Elders strongly imply that they can't actually be killed and all we've done is hasted our inevitable destruction. What strove to destroy them still pursues them.
Now if the final video had included a change in the alien's behaviors. If indeed, the aliens once enslaved or enveloped by the Elders showed independce afterward... then the player would know that the Elders have indeed been defeated. In the videos what we're shown is civilians and rebels retaking city centers. But without any additional information in the form of an epilogue clip or narrative notes at the end, it seems clear the aliens remain a threat and indeed, so too will the Elders. While I can accept the practical limitations for story telling in a video game for this one to make such an effort to expand the story but not resolve plot threads is, vexing to say the least.
I'm marginally more impressed with the strategy layer than I was last year, and, with a few LOS & Additional UI Information mods (los fix, gotcha, and, a peek mod) I found the game to be less an increasingly frustrating experience. I enjoyed the railroading of the science less but appreciated it more because the strategy layer already has a vastly different feel. But I still never got into it. I enjoyed the SPECTRUM GREEN mod - and the collection of mod's he recommends to use with it - for it's effort to diversify and complicate both the economy and the science while presenting much more coherent enemy mobs.
I was overall still struck with a persisting feeling of distrust which I do not recommend.
Distrust in the UI. Distrust of what is a flanking angle. Distrust of partial cover. Distrust in my squad's equipment. Distrust in the protagonists. Distrust of the black market. Distrust in my squad's abilities working as described. I also distrust that guy who's always backlit now. I worry that he wasn't telling me the whole story. Maybe you shouldn't trust this review...

First off, most of the reviews complaining about the optimization problems are no longer valid. That being said, there is no excuse for games these days especially non-indie titles, to be released as beta feeling as this game was. Unforunately that seems to be just par for the course these days in the industry and I won't let my personal feelings on that matter apply here.
This game is a third person action rpg that uses a similar control set-up to the dark souls games and leveling system, but that is where the similarities really end. You do gain and lose your experience by killing/dying and must go to where you died to retrieve your exp. This exp does start to disappear overtime though, and you're not likely to retrieve most of your exp if you're very far from a checkpoint.
The game's difficulty is not high, and most of the struggles you'll face are at the beginning, and very end of the game. The mid-game seems unbalanced and you will be mowing through most enemies.
The combat is much faster paced than the Souls games and I'd say it's about a mid-ground between that and Darksiders 2's combat. They did an excellent job of making each weapon type feel differently and I feel the physics here surpass the Souls series by far. The staff weapons were incredibly overpowered during the time I played the game due to it's fast attack speed and good scaling damage. This could always be fixed in balance patches or mods however.
The bosses were fairly underwhelming, but there are a good variety of enemy types which take different tactics in order to combat as opposed to the souls series (lock on and circle) method of killing just about everything which detracts from my enjoyment of that particular franchise. There were multiple ways to defeat a few of the bosses, and this allowed you to receieve special equipment upon killing them which I thought was a rather neat addition. Some of the weaker and early bosses become elite enemies that you will fight throughout the game as well, forcing you to adapt your combat style when fighting them as well as a group of lesser enemies at the same time.
There are many collectibles in the game, and while the lore is pretty generic, it's still interesting enough to warrant collecting all the scrolls and finding the secret equipment (which there is a good number of).
The games length was decent, and it could probably be played through 2-3 times in order to play different styles, and colelct the new game + gear, however, new game+ difficulty does not scale nearly fast enough in order for it to be a challenge.
As a final note, I do recommend the game, and while it's not anywhere near perfect, there are some innovative ideas here, and I'd like to see a sequel one day improve on what worked, and change what didn't. This is definitely the best game this particular studio has made to date, and I think they should be supported for adding some creativity to this genre which is pretty much dominated by a single franchise at this point.

Dark souls 3, out of all of the ones I've played, is my least favorite. It's not a bad game. There are a lot of gameplay issues that just made this game harder for me to get motivated to play the game.
For starters let me talk about what I like
The bosses are fantastic. This game has some of the coolest bosses out of any of the souls games I've played. They aren't necessarily all challenging, Some of them are harder than others.
Honestly, my favorite part of this game is how you can really tell that this is the same world as DS1. Some of the places are definitely the same and are just reworked for a different age, the return of a few iconic areas from the first souls game as well as some completely new areas.
Now, for my least favorite parts
, its very linear. There are hidden areas, and some of them are really cool and host quite a few bosses, optional areas where if you walk off the path a ways you'll find a hidden set of stairs that Drags you into hell itself.
Not only is it linear, there are bonfires so close to eachother at some points. it makes the world look super small and adds to the linearity, instead of searching around for a shortcut and exploring just run to the next bonfire, you could probably just run right to it anyway. Some areas are an exception to this, but especially the later parts there are so many bonfires
the world was bland. It was not fun to look at and explore for me. Eventually I got to the point in the game where I mostly just wanted to beat it so I didn't have to play anymore. Still working on the DLC.
Huge saving grace is that this game is probably the easiest game in the series to play Co Op. Im glad that FromSoftware sees that as a viable option and made it even easier to accomplish.
DS3 isn't bad, its my least favorite. Still totally pick this one up especially on sale.

Right, where to begin?
The game itself bring nothing new or exiting, even when first released. Still, being a huge fan of the "Fallout universe", i of course just had to get it. So, i bought the game and added the season pass, in order to make certain i got all the following add-ons that was promised. Boy... was this ever a hype...
The main storyline can be done easily in about 5 hours of gametime, and that is if you take your time doing it, so that is not what makes this game good in any way. However, if you're a fan of speed runs, this Fallout game is equally easy to beat as the first ones. No, the big part of the game being decent, is the large amount of small things. Te many minor quests, the easter eggs that are very numerous, and a few recurring characters from previous games.
So why isn't this game good then? It became painfully obvious when Bethesda dropped new content, which you had to pay for unless you got the season pass, that the company had no intentions to really make this a good game to begin with. The added material (add-ons) were poorly made most of the time, with only two real add-ons given, two that could only be deemed to be a semi add-on, and a few extra creation kits for the settlements. The game could have a HUGE potential, but in my honest opinion, it was botched at the planning stage. From everything like the voice acting, to the inability to play a truly "evil" character, this game is more of a streamlined story, than an actual open world game. It's truly sad to see that the original games (1&2) was less of a main story quest chain, than this one, some 20 years later...
The final nail in the coffin of this game is when Bethesda introduced the Creation Kit (i think it's called that, most likely because of the ancient G.E.C.K.), which is essentially hijacking 2 gigs of hardrive space, in order for the player/customer to be able to purchase in-game "stuff". This is basically paid modding in lack of a better term. They haven't removed the ability to mod the game (yet), but in the way of how this game is going, and how Bethesda is acting at this point, i see no problem with them actually shutting down non-Bethesda mods entirely in the near future.
If not looking through rose-tinted glasses, this game started as a 6/10, after the regular add-ons it was about 4/10 due to the lack of good content provided by them... Now, i could not even give it 2/10... i logged in once to the game after the installation (forced update i might add) of this last, sad, patch. I can't even force myself to even bother to do so again, not until Bethesda offers an apology to the gaming community, to the modding community, and at the very least give the harddrive space back, or let the season pass work as "in game currency". There is very little else they can do to save face, or this game at this point.

I've just finished Hacknet, and as you can tell by my total playtime (which also includes a profile I didn't quite complete), it's not a very long game. However, I'm quite sure that you will love every minute of it.
I'm not entirely sure how this game stacks up if you just want another Uplink (I haven't played that particular game), but there are other reviews that focus on that. What I can tell you is that this game is a stylish, sleek, and very impressive hacking simulator. The plot is woven very well into the game, and there are easter eggs and hidden things aplenty. I made it a point to look at every IRC archive on every computer I hacked, because I'd be laughing even while they traced my IP address.
The game's solution to everything is elegant and new; nothing feels like a tired concept. The game is just long enough to be as impressive as possible with all of its assets.
On the negative side, the slightly buggy nature of the game is where the indie nature really shows. My first playthrough went well enough until I was hit with a progression-ending bug that I didn't realize until I had actually made progress into a hidden sidequest. From then on, I was a little bit afraid to explore and screw around in case I got hit with another glitch. An option to load from saves wouldn't be amiss, but I'm sure people would use it to save-scum (and unfortunately miss one of Hacknet's coolest features:
, which adds to the game's tension).
Some objectives and game aspects are a little unclear, especially when worded in the game's cool cyber-security lingo (which actually adds to the charm to some extent). For instance, there's only a small sliver of documentation about a considerably-important yet optional feature: setting up proxies as "traps" to be sprung if a trace is about to reach you, which overloads your computer but stops the trace from doing any lasting damage. Experimenting is rendered difficult due to the fear of bugs as above - again, some sort of feature to load a session might help.
However, above all, you will find that Hacknet is well worth your time and $10 (or $8 if you buy during this Steam sale), because - be honest with yourself - you're looking into Hacknet to feel like a Hollywood Hacker, and that's exactly what this game makes you feel like.

One of my favorite games of all time. This is a game with no perfect strategy. A perfect team can be sent into a death spiral by an enemy crit at the wrong time. It's not uncommon to be think "Huh, this expidition is going rather well, things are looking up!" and later in the same mission "OOHH GOD EVERYTHING IS GOING WROOONNNG". You will go most quests without losing a single hero, but then an afflicted hero does something stupid and messes it all up for the other poor souls with them. The mental stress mechanic really makes this game. It provides such a huge variable that is almost impossible to plan for. I once had a Leper become masochistic on Death's Door (0 HP, next damage might kill them), and on his next turn decide to harm himself for pleasure (one of the possible effects of masochism) and literally kill himself. I had another Leper fighting an eldrich god on Deaths Door, watch the other three members of his team die in front of him, then became couragous and survive three consecutive strikes from the final boss and two rounds of bleed and STILL manage to land the final strike that won the game. The game does a fantastic job of making the biggest variable in the game the fragility of the heroes themselves. Words cannot express how much I love this game.

Absolutely love this game. Probably in my top 5 favourite games of all time. A lot of people resentAoE III because it's such a radical departure from AoE II, but once you give it some time, you realize that this game has way more depth than AoE II could ever have hoped for.
Some contrasts with AoE II:
-Less Civs that are more unique: AoE II has dozens of civs, but ultimately all of them have the same characteristics, whether it be the graphical style, units, similar sampling of techs, etc. There is a good deal of difference between the Euro civs alone in AoE 3, each one plays really differently. Dutch for example has villagers created from coin and bank buildings that generate free coin. Russia generates masses of troops that are weak in strength. Ottoman vils cannot be trained and are generated automatically. When you add the native civs and Asian civs, the difference is even more pronounced. They age up differently, have different classes of units (Sioux for example are mainly cavalry only and Indians have various elephants), have different ways of aging up, have different ways of collecting resources (japan cant kill hunts, but they can build shrines), different ways of generating units (asian civs can ally with a european civ not ingame that gives them euro troops and aztecs can generate infantry from a dance pit). The civs take time to master. You can be an export Iroquois player, but you can fail miserably with the Portugese in the very next game. In AoE II, it was not so hard to transition between civs.
-Streamlined economy. While micromanaging economy can be fun to an extent, handling all those idle villagers has always been a ♥♥♥♥♥. building a mining camp in the middle of nowhere only to get slaughtered by a light cavalry always sucked. Villagers now no longer have to walk back to a resource depot. There are also many new ways of automatically generating resources like shrines, infinite farms/plantations (coin), whales and factories. This allows you to focus more on the battle than on your 5 villagers in the middle of nowhere.
-Homecity: The card system looks simple at first, but ultimately the difference between a noob and an expert are the card shipments. The cards allow each civ to be even more differentiated. The same civ can become a rushing civ, a naval civ, a mercenery civ, a boom civ, all based on your card deck. You can choose to have early shipments of villagers or resource gathering boosts, or troops, based on whether you want to rush or boom. India gets free villagers with each shipment, but you can ship a card that makes them send rifleman instead.
-Units: gunpowder units are immensely satisfying. It's arguably a lot easier to micro them than mobs of AoE II. It's fun to watch all your cannons and mortars blow ships, infantry and building to smithereens. You can get a hot air balloon or an invisible spy. You can have surgeons set up field hospitals. You can have a flamethrower or an arsonist. You can set up a gatling gun to mow down villagers. You can get a dog or an orangutan, You can old school if you want and have two handed swordsman as the german (doppels, one of the best units in the game). There's a lot more variety in the battle.
-All the small things: trading posts, native villages, treasures, merceneraies, revolutions, explorer/monk/warchiefs, special wonder, treaty, dance pits, consulates, pets, etc.
Some of the downsides are as others mentioned: weak AI (strong early game, but become downright stupid in the late game), lag issues, small community (but it's been growing recently. There are tournaments with prizes of 2000$-3000$) and lack of support/patches, though the civs are fairly balanced (with the exception of ottomans).
Full Price is a bit too much imo, but wishlist the game and nab it while it's on sale. Give it some time and you won't regret it.

TLDR; Game is hard at first. If you like a challenge and are willing to learn the game it's very fun.
As someone who has spent over 200 hours on this game I can certainly say that I enjoy the game, however it should be made clear what you are getting yourself into and how to approach the game if you plan on purchasing it.
Most, whether they enjoy the game or not, commend it for the well crafted character design, atmosphere, unique mechanics1, and art style. However most who dislike the game will do so on the basis that the game is too RNG dependent, too unforgiving, too "grindy", or too difficult. Its likely that your first campaign will make you feel like the game is all of those things. I myself complained of these points at the start. The first few hours will kick you in the teeth, bang your wife, and eat your leftovers.
For many beginners the unforgiving nature of the game and its steep challenges can be very overwhelming, leaving a bad taste in their mouth from the start, but if you can embrace is impossibly tough nature and you over come its challenges, which you will eventually do, it makes it all the more rewarding. If you are just starting and you are someone who gets mad at games easily I would recommend spending some time in the options and do what you can to lessen the punishment of failure until you can learn the game. You will learn the game and its mechanics with experience, such as what skills to prioritize, which party combinations work, when to use what skills, where to use which supply items. If you're reading this before playing the game at all I would NOT recommend look up anything in the wiki unless necessary. It can help maintain that sense of acomplishment and retains a sense of mystery, wonder, and terror as to what will be in the next passage, room, or what will happen when a torch is placed in the alters of darkness. But if you don't understand a mechanic or enemy to the point of frustration you may want to look to the wiki, don't ruin the game for yourself.
However after awhile, once you learn how the game operates and how to tip the odds in your favor, you can begin to appreciate some of these other claimed "dislikes" of the game. Take for example the RNG dependency. Even with the perfectly talored party with all the right heroes, skills, and stats (usually in the form of "Quirks" or items in this game), there's still a sense of real danger. All it takes is one or two crits and a hero is on the verge of dying, and I think that that threat of real danger, paired with the atmosphere and art, makes the game truly terrifying.
That threat of danger is also what also helps keep the grind from feeling "grindy". There's always a sense that you can lose all your progress you've worked towards, making it all the more precious. Instead of a grind the game becomes and uphill battle towards your goal. Another way of overcoming the sense of the game being "grindy" is experementing, though be warned what does and doesn't work will be apparent very quickly. Theres alot of strange party combinations and item builds that can be very fun. Take for example, some of my favorites, the 4 crusader party or the 4 vestal party. The constant need learning and adaptation keeps me guessing even as of past hour 200. I will say though for those who feel like they've been punished even with perfect execution I can understand how the game can become less fun, even "grindy", in which case I would say that unfortunatly the game is not for you.
I also appreciate Red Hook for working so hard on their game, regularly working on updates and DLC even past its official "full release". They've spent a lot of time on their work and it shows, and I couldn't be more happy to see the money I spent on this game being put towards a company that truly cares about their game. In all this game with it's brutal difficulty, unforgiving nature, and commitment to the idea of a world working against you creates one of the most challenging and rewarding games I've played.

First (and probably last) review I've ever written for a game, and I'm writing after uninstalling the game in question.
Bayonetta is a schizophrenic, glorious, unplayable mess.
The game's enemies are lovinly designed, with lots of cunning details revealed as they take damage and go from menacing but angelic baddies to revolting, chthonic monsters. When you're fighting regular groups of bad guys, the gameplay feels like 90% of a perfect game - Bayonetta's dizzying array of combo moves lets you easily slip into your own playstyles, and the game clearly delights in disrupting your favorite tactics with a vast menagerie of enemies whose special abilities, armor, attacks, and teamwork will challenge you to find new strategies to beat them.
The camera is occasionally spastic, fibrillating unpredictably when you're near a wall or corner at times while at other times holding steady. Annoying, but you want to forgive it due to the game's age and the immersion of regular combat.
The story is almost always a campy, overly generic send-up of too-serious action games where The Fate of The Universe rests on your shoulders, as The Promised Child who was born of Forbidden Love between Light and Dark. Nearly every cutscene is a great mix of story progression and clever, wink-at-the-audience snipes, bawdy jokes, and anime-style doubletakes. Certain characters are relentlessly serious, however (Jeanne in particular), and you're unpredictably yanked out of the fun MST3k-style atmosphere and slapped around by a story bit that clearly wants to be serious, but you can't take it seriously because you're still chuckling over Bayonetta's last one-liner.
But the game falls apart completely during the boss fights.
Each boss fight (and some viciously hard encounters like Gracious and Glorious) shatter your enjoyment. The camera swings wildly when you're leaping and dodging, or zooms out ludicrously far when you're fighting gigantic enemies. The boss fights are a mix of repetitive dodge-and-dash challenges and stupidly difficult straight-on brawls with enemies that are faster and far tougher than you.
In particular, recurring buzzkill Jeanne is a nightmare to fight in later chapters. She is smaller than any other boss, every bit as fast as Bayonetta, capable of chaining together brutal combos you can't break out of as they devour great chunks of your health, and blasts out super-attacks (wicked weaves) with only a split-second of warning. I stopped playing at chapter 14 after two days of being completely unable to beat her in a tortuously long, multi-section fight that takes at least half an hour.
Gigantic bosses have fast, devastating melee attacks you cannot accurately dodge because the game's 3d structure and bad camera angles don't let you get a good guage of how close to let them get before dodging in order to get a 3-second window of super-speed called 'witch time' which is critical to building your long, devastating combos.
Some enemies have stupidly powerful laser attacks which do great damage and stun Bayonetta, which they tend to fire in overlapping salvos to maximize chances of hitting you - always followed up with swarms of attacks to catch you at your weakest.
Overall, it feels like I'm playing 3 games at once. A dumb, dull, repetitive dodging sim has been mashed together with a fun and gleefully funny action game that wants you to smash baddies and tropes in equal measure, and both of these were chained to a sadistic, Gaiden-Razor's-Edge-hard melee game which demands bleeding-eye attention to detail and hair-trigger reaction times in order to scrape past.
Finally, the game is chock-full of super-items (accessories) which, when equipped, give you special abilities to make the game easier. But each one is behind an extremely high paywall which will force you to grind through each level multiple times with careful attention to your save files in order to chain together enough high-ranking performances to afford even one.
So yeah, the game is too hard. It's one of those sad fighters that wanted to find the Dark Souls edge between vicious difficulty and addictively fun gameplay, and shot way past the mark.
Someone really dedicated and obsessed could beat this game, and probably enjoy it too. But it's simply not worth the hours of being smeared across the floor again, and again, and again, and again, to do it.

Third person action game with mechanics similar to Dark Souls 2.
Graphics:
High end graphics with a lot of indoor areas, however the cut scenes and NPCs are not that great. Also, if you get to close to a wall during a fight you will probably disappear from the screen and take damage from your enemy.
Grade: 8/10
Sound:
SImple ambient music and sounds. Lots of sound reuse and similar sounds that trick you. You think there are more enemies, yet you just killed the last one. You open a chest and the sound tricks you into thinking a enemy is behind you.
Grade: 6/10
Controls:
Copied directly from Dark Souls 2, which is not a bad thing. Right button to lock camera on enemy, L1 to defend, R1 to attack, B for magic, X for items...
Grade: 9/10
Game Story:
Simple story and very straightforward, get ready to do a lot of backtracking and get lost forever indoors at areas that look all alike. Did I mention that I hate games like these not providing us a map? I do hate it.
Grade: 7/10 (yes you lost points for not having a fu... map)
Difficulty:
There are enemies that are harder to beat than bosses, as some require you to find his heart before being able to kill it, others defend like hell and some explode after dying, killing you instantly if you do not retreat. The first boss fights are harder as you are a low level player. After you get to higher levels, the boss fights become a pacience game taking a longer time but easier in the end.
Grade: 8/10
General Grade: 7,5 - 8/10.

I haven't played a lot, and sadly I don't think I ever will. I've given all classes a try and killed a few bosses with the rouge, which ended up being my favourite.
Mostly, this game kinda feels like the original Dark Souls. However, there's a few things that makes LOTF a bit less enjoyable.
First off, I don't feel the same motivation to try again when I die as I do when playing the Souls games. This is a huge flaw since the game is trying to be the same kind of punishing RPG that the Souls games are. I chalk this up to the fact that when I die, I don't feel like it's my own fault for playing badly but rather that I died because the game feels unfinished.
The combat feels clunky and unpolished, the lock-on seems to be almost required to perform well. The enemies also uses lock-on, meaing that they'll move to face you mid-swing as if you're a magnet.
The big spell investment of the rouge, stealth, is completely broken. Enemies usually ignore that you're stealthed and attack you anyway. The bonus damage from breaking stealth, while good, is impossible to land if you're not locked-on.
The game doesn't feel like it's hard in order to challenge you and keep you ever vigilant, it feels like it's hard only to ♥♥♥♥ you over. In that regard, LOTF is more a rage game than a challenging RPG like Dark Souls.
The story is standard "save the world" stuff and the voice acting and dialouge is lackluster.
It's not without positives though. I like the aesthetic of everything, it's a breathtakingly beautiful game. The gear/loot and customization feels fun and interesting. Sadly, it's not enough to redeem the negatives.
I want to like LOTF, I really do, but I can't in good concience recommend it. There's lots of potential to be found, but the game feels rushed and unfinished, making it all go to waste. A weak 4/10.

Playing this for the first time, it's easy to get sucked in. It's sort of a Minecraft Lite in MMO form, where the main worlds are generated at random but seeded with prefab dungeons with bosses and loot. Deconstructing a piece of equipment lets you add its style to a permanent list, so when your awesome-looking trident is outclassed by a wet fish you can still keep using that trident's skin. You also get a "cornerstone" of limited horizontal but impressive vertical dimensions in which to build a base/home that you can slap down anywhere an empty lot is present.
Probably the biggest draw of the game is the variety of classes available, all of which have playful spins on existing class tropes and most of which are significantly differentiated and fun to play as. This is important because the core gameplay is really just the trickle-feed of watching your classes gain levels and get shiny new equipment drops as you plunder the same set of dungeons you've been through 30 times apiece already. Unfortunately, on top of the already somewhat ridiculous cash shop prices there's been an announcement that Trion are going to be jacking things up even more and locking the classes behind a paywall (unless you're willing to grind yourself into a fine dust to get class tokens from the player market). It was fun while it lasted, but being told that this is not only going to happen but is also going to be FOR THE BETTER is pretty much EA levels of dickery. Don't give these people your money or your time.

Yes bus driving does seem a bit tedious. Yes, setting it in late eighties to early nineties Berlin doesn't increase its sex appeal any more than announcing that Anne Widdicombe finally got a Brazilian either.
However, there's something special about OMSI2 - Der Omnibussimulator 2, or simply put: The Bus Simulator 2 in English. It's truly magnificent if you want Germans to swear at you or if you want to waste half an hour on figuring out what "Ernerungsterif" or"Betriebsfahrt" means. It'll leave you frantically skimming though the manual as you try and figure out why the bus all of a sudden seized to move (curse you, auto kneeling mechanism), however all is forgotten the moment you roll out of the depot on a dark Sunday night as you make your way to your first stop though the calm Berlin streets. There's nothing quite like driving a night bus in BS2, your passengers, albeit few and far in between, really gives you a sense of satisfaction. Sure the passengers has about as much excitement and enthusiasm as the performers in a strip club has during their 9AM Monday morning performances but they still sit there in your bus, quietly waiting for their destination, they leave you thinking about who they really are. Is the younger chap five rows down making his way across town at his lovers behest.
The technical aspect of BS2 is less so, it crashes as frequently as Lindsey Lohan runs out of cocaine. The graphics is about as exciting as a carton of milk is to look at, you're lucky to find a tree with at least one polygon and god forbid you leave the carefully designated routes as you will encounter the sky dome with no warning whatsoever if you do.
BS2 shouldn't be good, it shouldn't make me want to play it for hours on end, but something about is just so appealing. Maybe it's because the two people (really, two people made this) made this game purely based on the fond memories they had when they rode on the buses operating on the Berlin Municipal bus lines 25 odd years ago.
It's pure nostalgia and passion, the audio side of the game is nothing short of perfect and the game itself is nothing short of amazing. It doesn't take more than a minute or so behind the wheel of my bus of choice before I'm sitting feeling quite content with life.
The review submission page asks whether or not I recommend this game. Yes, BS2 is as polished as Battlefield 4 is and still are. Yes, it really is about driving a bus.
It's not for everyone, but I do recommend this in a heartbeat if you have even a vague desire to play this.
I do, however, feel that I need to add more requirements to the list provided by the publisher:
You need a gamepad, preferably a wheel in order to drive in a way that doesn't look like you've had 6 racks of beer and 7 bottles of vodka.
It's also based in Germany so there's quite a bit of German language involved. They do have transcripts of what type of ticket the passenger wants in English as well as a manual and quick reference guide. But every single switch, knob and control interface on the buses are in German, good luck figuring out what a "Regler Heizlüfter vorne" or a"Nebelschlussleuchte" is.
The quick reference guide will save your life when you're in a bus full of people at FreudStrasse that won't move an inch.
Still loving it.

TLDR; Game is hard at first. If you like a challenge and are willing to learn the game it's very fun.
As someone who has spent over 200 hours on this game I can certainly say that I enjoy the game, however it should be made clear what you are getting yourself into and how to approach the game if you plan on purchasing it.
Most, whether they enjoy the game or not, commend it for the well crafted character design, atmosphere, unique mechanics1, and art style. However most who dislike the game will do so on the basis that the game is too RNG dependent, too unforgiving, too "grindy", or too difficult. Its likely that your first campaign will make you feel like the game is all of those things. I myself complained of these points at the start. The first few hours will kick you in the teeth, bang your wife, and eat your leftovers.
For many beginners the unforgiving nature of the game and its steep challenges can be very overwhelming, leaving a bad taste in their mouth from the start, but if you can embrace is impossibly tough nature and you over come its challenges, which you will eventually do, it makes it all the more rewarding. If you are just starting and you are someone who gets mad at games easily I would recommend spending some time in the options and do what you can to lessen the punishment of failure until you can learn the game. You will learn the game and its mechanics with experience, such as what skills to prioritize, which party combinations work, when to use what skills, where to use which supply items. If you're reading this before playing the game at all I would NOT recommend look up anything in the wiki unless necessary. It can help maintain that sense of acomplishment and retains a sense of mystery, wonder, and terror as to what will be in the next passage, room, or what will happen when a torch is placed in the alters of darkness. But if you don't understand a mechanic or enemy to the point of frustration you may want to look to the wiki, don't ruin the game for yourself.
However after awhile, once you learn how the game operates and how to tip the odds in your favor, you can begin to appreciate some of these other claimed "dislikes" of the game. Take for example the RNG dependency. Even with the perfectly talored party with all the right heroes, skills, and stats (usually in the form of "Quirks" or items in this game), there's still a sense of real danger. All it takes is one or two crits and a hero is on the verge of dying, and I think that that threat of real danger, paired with the atmosphere and art, makes the game truly terrifying.
That threat of danger is also what also helps keep the grind from feeling "grindy". There's always a sense that you can lose all your progress you've worked towards, making it all the more precious. Instead of a grind the game becomes and uphill battle towards your goal. Another way of overcoming the sense of the game being "grindy" is experementing, though be warned what does and doesn't work will be apparent very quickly. Theres alot of strange party combinations and item builds that can be very fun. Take for example, some of my favorites, the 4 crusader party or the 4 vestal party. The constant need learning and adaptation keeps me guessing even as of past hour 200. I will say though for those who feel like they've been punished even with perfect execution I can understand how the game can become less fun, even "grindy", in which case I would say that unfortunatly the game is not for you.
I also appreciate Red Hook for working so hard on their game, regularly working on updates and DLC even past its official "full release". They've spent a lot of time on their work and it shows, and I couldn't be more happy to see the money I spent on this game being put towards a company that truly cares about their game. In all this game with it's brutal difficulty, unforgiving nature, and commitment to the idea of a world working against you creates one of the most challenging and rewarding games I've played.
