I did not enjoy this game much at all. You play as a girl entering into a dream-like nature world of animals with puzzles to solve in order to find your teddy bear. This is fine, but the puzzles are very hit and miss. Sometimes they're intuitive and sometimes 'stuff happens', such as using a fly to lift a cat to extract a root in the background you didn't you could touch which contained a cooked chicken underground to take somewhere else. It sounds quirky, but puzzles need some kind of logical progression, otherwise it becomes mindlessly clicking things in hopes of triggering some bizarre game logic. Finding Teddy doesn't always include those. Contrasting, some puzzles are very simplistic and clever. There's just no even ground between the two.
Graphically, this game is wonderful. It uses a simple palette to give it a cutesy appeal, and while you might not always understand what object you picked up is, the animals/monsters are pleasant to look at it.
Lastly, there's a weird theme with using alphabetic music notes to do some of the puzzles and damn if the font isn't incredibly hard to read. It's already masked, but the lettering is small and the letter characters look similar to one another. Many times I had to squint with glasses on to make sense of what something was supposed to be.
Also, fair warning, this game isn't for kids despite the graphical style. It's probably too nonsensical in terms of what is supposed to be done (the game doesn't explain anything, be it gameplay or controls) and there's almost fetish-like running theme of gory deaths for the little girl at the hands of the monsters and animals who all have to be placated or they kill you. Some younger players might find it disturbing.

This game is awesome. I got it as part of a bundle, and almost gave away my key before I watched a let's play, and that convinced me to hang onto it.
I've played through the game three times tonight. There's a learning curve the first time through as you figure out all of the puzzles. The second time through I didn't load my old game, so didn't end up with a new game+ (hint: load your game before you second play through.) Finished up my achievements, and then went back through the final time to get the alternate ending and the few achievements you have to get through a new game+. Three and a half hours total, with most of that going to the first play through.
Don't think that just because it's short means that it's not worthwhile though. The art style is polished, even if it's pixel art. It doesn't look cheap like many indie games do. It looks intentional and professional. And it's dark in almost every way, which I appreciate in a game.
The story is almost hilariously over the top. Or maybe it's completely and hilariously over the top. A giant tarantula steals a teddy bear from a little girl? Who then hunts down said tarantula because she don't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥ Honey badger got nothing on her, son.
If that kind of thing tickles your fancy, then this one is for you.
There are some mechanics which I've never seen elsewhere, which did trip me up on my first play through, but which are totally what makes the game what it is. Namely, how it utilizes music/sound. If you're tone deaf like me, it can make certain parts of the game more challenging than necessary. There are some places in the game where there are audio cues and I was in desperate need of visual cues as well. A little glow on the fireflies when you get close would be nice, instead of just the volume of the ping. And showing the letters associated with each sound during all the puzzles would help out the tone deaf like me.
Still, those minor quips fail to detract in any meaningful way from an otherwise enjoyable game. I definitely recommend it.

This makes finding your objectives frustrating, given the time limits involved.  The jerk won't even give you distances.
If you do play, save regularly, so you can restart a day that goes badly or so you can recover from an occasional crash.
No manual.  Shame.

As a huge fan of XCOM: Enemy Unknown, I was really excited to get a chance to play the next evolution of the genre. Many improvements have been made which add a lot to the depth. Many other elements stand in the way of making it truly enjoyable.
Good: Depth of strategy; Modular weapon design allowing you to better customize; Psionics as a unit type with many more abilities; Turn limits on many missions which force actions in a reasonable time; Hacking things for bonuses
Bad: The unit loadout screen should make it more clear what is and isn't available for use; The general interface makes it somewhat difficult to see what's going on; UFOs searching for my ship- sometimes they fly literally over the top of me without seeing me other times they're very far away when they do; The black market is significantly harder to use and uses up time to travel there just to see if there's anything of interest. Turn limits on too many missions; The engineering interface could also be much more intuitive with more information available; Overwatch shots miss with an alarming frequency.
Ugly: Concealment is completely unrealistic at times and it's really difficult to tell if an enemy will walk over, flank and thereby discover a unit, then blast them into oblivion before you have the chance to do anything; Faceless aliens (which suddenly turn from a human into an alien) and Chrysalids, which then also move and kill you before you have the chance to react. On top of that, they seem to usually go after the most vulnerable troop; Not being able to see how far an enemy can move so that you can stay out of their attack range.
Horrible: Lines of sight- This one element has largely broken this game for me. You can never tell when the enemy will have a line of sight to you (or vice versa). Units see and shoot through walls, doors, ceilings- anything. Except sometimes they can't see you after all (and vice versa). Grenades have been made much more important, but often your high cover (or even low cover sometimes) element restricts you from throwing your grenade in the needed direction.
The real tragedy is that most sessions end with getting blown out of the water due to a reason other than strategy. To do well too often means getting really lucky. I want to love this game but too often I walk away angry. If it weren't for the line of sight flaw, I would be recommending it.

Another minimalistic puzzle game that I was able to pick up on sale awhile ago... I was able to pick this up for 40% which is a bit worse than what the holiday sale gives but for such a low price the game is well worth it no matter what price you get it at. The game is similar to a sudoku game with a little bit more simplicity, and while I was playing I was stuck between having the simplicity as a pro or a con, and I eventually decided that it was more of a pro than it was a con. Anyways, here's a list of pros and cons about the game.
Pros:
- Simplicity
Many games like this might have tools that help you make the game easier (for example, when you lock in a number remove others of the same number from other squares) and while playing this game I wasn't sure if this was good or bad for the game. In the end I decided that I enjoyed it because it kept the game more difficult and made you think that extra bit.
- Good soundtrack
The soundtrack was nice background music and helped to preserve that "zen feeling" that you got when you were playing this game.
- Achievements
The achievements along the way were nice and popped at the precise moment that they were needed. It was nice finishing a level and reading "Level 5 unlocked" and then a few seconds later seeing the achievement pop up on the bottom right.
Cons:
- Tedious
While this isn't a huge con I felt like the game was a tad bit repetitious at times. You'd go from a difficult level (4th one in the pack) to an easy level and wouldn't get back up to the difficulty until the 7th or 8th pack... for all of the level packs. It would have been nice to introduce something (I don't know what) that made the game mechanic feel a little bit different.
Overall however, I really enjoyed the game for the price I got it at, and I think this one would be worth the full price even on sale! The 3 dollar price tag for ~4-5 hours of entertainment is definitely a big thumbs up for this game. I'd give this one a 9/10 and it definitely earns my thumbs up!

It might be a bad game. I've been playing it through again and again. I'll say this before hand though, despite having sunk several hundred hours into XCOM:EU the main thing XCOM2 does right is being a totally different game from XCOM:EU. The game's major changes are obvious. A need to actually build up your supply base. A need to expand in the face of Advent's already massive infrastructure and global presence. This creates a massively new strategic experience. A lot of squad missions have a timer now.
Note: I've read an interview with the project designer where he admits that maybe a month before releasing XCOM2 the design team ramped up the difficulty in response to game testers repeated comments that it was easy. I expect the largest difficulty is the low numbers of missions with a timer. The timer forces youtp pursue a rapid pace in almost every mission, however that pace will cause Total Squad Death. Almost a year after release the game still has an inconsistent LOS. These errors in LOS can be somewhat reduced by the use of a few mods.
The strategic layer is well done in it's design but was implimented to restrict your progress. The restrictions come in several forms. A limitation of starting income supply instead of a large starting supply income reduced by success you have to expand your supply base by increasing the number of rebel bases in different countries you seek out contact with. For each new country you contact you get more supplies and you can get additional supplies from building additional radio towers. The advantages of this changed approach to supply income is that perfection in the missions isn't what reduces your income. Dark events or failing to respond to retaliation missions (terror attacks) are. Note: The once great Long War team from XCOM:EU made a mess of imbalanced weapons and bad changes to strategic layer. They instead made it too difficult to keep track of all the objectives you have to juggle. Even most of the options they thought made squad missions better make them more chaotic.
Let me talk about retaliation missions a little bit. Retaliation missions are a take on terror missions where the Advent/Alien forces strike a rebel base. Your goal is still to rescue civilians, in that these rebels are not fighters just persons who do not believe Advent is legit. In a retaliation mission your goal is to rescue an arbitrarilly decided 6 civilians. I say arbitrarilly decided in reference to the designers. However. A few random civilians whom you have to rescue are also alien shapeshifters.
Shapeshifters who have large health pools and a substantial melee attack. There is no research or facility you can create which will ever remove these from rebel camps or alert you ahead of time to their presence. One of the nicer changes is the ability to build a facility which will list the types of enemies your squad will face on missions and even with that built you're not alerted to their presence.
Enemies do come in a range of types. The classic enemies return. There are some new enemies. Enemies have all the advantages. Advent forces can call in air strikes. Select alien units can call in air strikes. Enemies call for reinforcements. Enemies occasionally set up ambushes. Players can expect any mission labeled supply run is actually the aliens drawing you out to a remote location and assasinating you with an overwhelming diversity of Alien+Advent abilities and weapon types.
There is at a glance a surprisingly deft effort from the design team to create a game where guerilla troops / forces struggle against the embedded infrastructure of an enemy. You really do rise up to fight the aliens almost at the last moment. In just twenty years they're ready to start work on the Avatar project. But between the inconsistent LOS and the already victorious alien HOST I felt less like I was steering the squads of Stargate to victory, and more like I was struggling to rationalize every decision or opinion as if I was in the Earth: Final Contact setting. Maybe it's all the science fiction I've read. Maybe it's the extremely dull video that plays when you lose. Maybe it's the very dull video that plays whe you finish the game. But on the whole the only reason I wanted to keep replaying XCOM2 was in the hopes that I'd change my mind.
For me the largest frustration is still the tactical squad based missions in the game. There are mods available to let you adjust or change this part of the game but I kind of hate it. What may work best for you is to combine smaller tweaks that are available which may let you customize the combat into something less incoherent. Even with a host of mods I remain unimpressed. My take away from playing the game again is still that the squad based combat isn't honest or predictable - I'm not talking about missing a 98% shot. When I say predictable I mean that things happen in the missions I was regularly blindsided by. Sometimes I'd lose an entire squad without knowing quite why. Once in a retaliation mission I had a unit aside some obviously discarded barrels and tanks of some sort. These were, unknown to me, explosive, and I lost a high level squad because I wasn't informed about that fact. One squad member died and the rest paniked badly. There wasn't a voice line, icon, or, alert, that my squad member was next to an explosive threat.
I also have concerns now about the story. When I replayed this recently I found myself disliking the XCOM forces. I'm still struck by the plain facts. In this game the XCOM "alliance" or "forces" made everything worse. The aliens do want to consume a lot of human's and yes after they find a cure they will probably absorb our now limited cultural uniqueness to their own but through our intervention against the Avatar project we forced them to escalate and threaten our species with genocide. In this regard it's an almost nuanced nod to complex plots and a footnote that the Elder's are desperate and will regret annihilating our species. Indeed by the end of the game the Elders strongly imply that they can't actually be killed and all we've done is hasted our inevitable destruction. What strove to destroy them still pursues them.
Now if the final video had included a change in the alien's behaviors. If indeed, the aliens once enslaved or enveloped by the Elders showed independce afterward... then the player would know that the Elders have indeed been defeated. In the videos what we're shown is civilians and rebels retaking city centers. But without any additional information in the form of an epilogue clip or narrative notes at the end, it seems clear the aliens remain a threat and indeed, so too will the Elders. While I can accept the practical limitations for story telling in a video game for this one to make such an effort to expand the story but not resolve plot threads is, vexing to say the least.
I'm marginally more impressed with the strategy layer than I was last year, and, with a few LOS & Additional UI Information mods (los fix, gotcha, and, a peek mod) I found the game to be less an increasingly frustrating experience. I enjoyed the railroading of the science less but appreciated it more because the strategy layer already has a vastly different feel. But I still never got into it. I enjoyed the SPECTRUM GREEN mod - and the collection of mod's he recommends to use with it - for it's effort to diversify and complicate both the economy and the science while presenting much more coherent enemy mobs.
I was overall still struck with a persisting feeling of distrust which I do not recommend.
Distrust in the UI. Distrust of what is a flanking angle. Distrust of partial cover. Distrust in my squad's equipment. Distrust in the protagonists. Distrust of the black market. Distrust in my squad's abilities working as described. I also distrust that guy who's always backlit now. I worry that he wasn't telling me the whole story. Maybe you shouldn't trust this review...

There's a decent story full of lore and interesting characters, monsters, and set-pieces. I love it, and this is from someone who could never really get into the Souls series.

A decent puzzle game that is similar in style to Sudoku, in that you are given a set of numbers and must ensure each row and column contain one of each number. The puzzles vary in size, up to 9x9, but are not as complicated as Sudoku puzzles (those which also require you to complete nine individual boxes of 1-9, in addition to rows and columns).
As a simplified Sudoku game, each level is generally quick to solve. With a total of 64 puzzles, it likely won't take more than a few hours to complete the game. But the replay value is the same as any Sudoku or similarly-styled number game.
The game allows you to lock in numbers that you're certain are correct, but locking-in numbers isn't required to complete the puzzles. This game could be improved with a couple small QOL features such as the ability to save your progress on a partially-completed level, and the ability to strike-out numbers on individual tiles that you've deemed to be incorrect... but overall I'd say this game is worth the $3 price tag, and very much worth a buy if on sale.
Pros:
- entertaining puzzle game
- works as it is intended with no bugs encountered.
- small price tag, and does go on sale (currently 45% Off, as of writing this review
- I felt the colors worked well. They are neutral and calming yet still colorful; a good combination for a puzzle game.
I wouldn't classify these as cons, but.. as far as puzzle games go, it's not riveting or groundbreaking and there's no wow-factor.
All in all, I'd say a solid 8/10.

Lords Of The Fallen excels at what it wants to be. Not for the easily discouraged, Lords Of The Fallen is a difficult, rewarding action RPG. The combat is fluid and feels rewarding; swinging a heavy hammer feels slow and makes a big impact while wielding daggers makes you feel swift and agile.  The combat is truly the best part of Lords Of The Fallen. The story falls a bit short, though. Much like similar games in this new genre of RPG's, the gameplay is the primary reason you'll continue playing.  Fans of Dark Souls will certainly enjoy this title as they share many similarities, but the biggest difference being Lords Of The Fallen isn't quite as punishing. There is also no physical character customization, however Harkyn, the protagonist, can wear a variety of different armors and wield various different weapons ranging from daggers to a gauntlet that fires projectiles. As you kill enemies you gain xp that can be cashed in at save points to level up and assign attributes to your character or can be gambled on runes to empower your equipment. Lords Of The Fallen's voice acting is phenomenal, however the character animations don't quite match their words. The dialogue itself is a bit boring, but the voice actors definitely make it bearable. All-in-all, Lords Of The Fallen is an excellent game if you're looking for challenging, rewarding combat but aren't too interested in story.

Season 1 of Telltale's The Walking Dead is a work of art.
Let's just get the bad out of the way up front- the game is jittery- due to the engine Telltale uses or whatever, and the gameplay itself is pretty average. But these two things aren't honestly that important for what this "game" tries to accomplish.
Over the course of five episodes, you play as Lee durring the first months of the zombie apocolypse. At the very start, he meets a girl named Clementine, and takes her in.
You will meet tons of other survivors, all of which are genuinely interesting, and you'll care about in some way. Outside of the average point and click gameplay, the majority of your time will be spent talking to these characters, figuring out their back stories and why they are who they are. I can't say I've ever played a game where I've cared so much about so many characters, and it's also due to the amazing writing and voice acting.
If you've read anything about this game though, you'd know about the choice system it uses. Durring conversation, you can choose what Lee will say or do, which effects how everyone around you percieves you. This may lead to certain characters liking you or disliking you- varrying from playthrough to playthrough. Sure, in the end the story ends the same way, but it's all about shaping relationships and forming your own version of Lee.
The 10 hours I have on steam here represents my 4th playthrough of this season (twice on xbox once on iPad). Pick this game up- it's an emotional rollercoaster with fantastic writing. Right, where to begin?
The game itself bring nothing new or exiting, even when first released. Still, being a huge fan of the "Fallout universe", i of course just had to get it. So, i bought the game and added the season pass, in order to make certain i got all the following add-ons that was promised. Boy... was this ever a hype...
The main storyline can be done easily in about 5 hours of gametime, and that is if you take your time doing it, so that is not what makes this game good in any way. However, if you're a fan of speed runs, this Fallout game is equally easy to beat as the first ones. No, the big part of the game being decent, is the large amount of small things. Te many minor quests, the easter eggs that are very numerous, and a few recurring characters from previous games.
So why isn't this game good then? It became painfully obvious when Bethesda dropped new content, which you had to pay for unless you got the season pass, that the company had no intentions to really make this a good game to begin with. The added material (add-ons) were poorly made most of the time, with only two real add-ons given, two that could only be deemed to be a semi add-on, and a few extra creation kits for the settlements. The game could have a HUGE potential, but in my honest opinion, it was botched at the planning stage. From everything like the voice acting, to the inability to play a truly "evil" character, this game is more of a streamlined story, than an actual open world game. It's truly sad to see that the original games (1&2) was less of a main story quest chain, than this one, some 20 years later...
The final nail in the coffin of this game is when Bethesda introduced the Creation Kit (i think it's called that, most likely because of the ancient G.E.C.K.), which is essentially hijacking 2 gigs of hardrive space, in order for the player/customer to be able to purchase in-game "stuff". This is basically paid modding in lack of a better term. They haven't removed the ability to mod the game (yet), but in the way of how this game is going, and how Bethesda is acting at this point, i see no problem with them actually shutting down non-Bethesda mods entirely in the near future.
If not looking through rose-tinted glasses, this game started as a 6/10, after the regular add-ons it was about 4/10 due to the lack of good content provided by them... Now, i could not even give it 2/10... i logged in once to the game after the installation (forced update i might add) of this last, sad, patch. I can't even force myself to even bother to do so again, not until Bethesda offers an apology to the gaming community, to the modding community, and at the very least give the harddrive space back, or let the season pass work as "in game currency". There is very little else they can do to save face, or this game at this point.

This game is kind of fun if you're a satist like me.
However, even a satist like me notices when a game goes from niche to cash-grab, and Trove is about to take that dive. Locking new classes behind either a premium currency paywall or the rediculously expensive Class Coins is making players pay to play the game at a competent level or spend way too much time doing the basic, boring grind, strangling the new players of all their enjoyment. This ignores whatever content they're gonna lock behind Patron, which they have refused to release as of now.
Developers making money is not evil by nature. Games can't run for free, and anyone who thinks otherwise is insane. However, there are ways to do it right and ways to do it wrong, and Trion is doing it all wrong with Trove. Locking the full gameplay content behind a paywall is terrible, whereas paying for cosmetics and (potentially) a quicker way to upgrade is a great way to let people skip what they want to without shutting down the players and severely reducing the size of the player base.
If you had started playing Trove a few months ago, you saw what I believe to be the top of the game. However, at this point, I believe Trove to be a dying game, and therefore not worth your time.

Performance: For me it is improvement. Please mind, that game is using only one core of processor and is 32bit so doesn't matter if you have big memory. Overclocked CPU and graphic card with at least 1GB memory will do magic. When you set antialiasing and so on graphics to override and fiddle with settings in the game, you can make it work easily.
Bugs after release: I have experienced some weird behaviour. Game crashing and so on, but after verification through Steam it downloaded some missing files so I think this is more Steam error that of Omsi developers. After that the game is not crashing anymore.
Contenet from Omsi 1: I had some problems, but it was pointed to me, that I was missing some files. After installing missing files, I managed to run all 5 of my favourite addons without any issues.
Graphics: Yes, it is not state of the art, it is not very well optimized, but for me it is enough. I can create my own sceneries and other content.
Physics and realism: There is no real simulator, FSX, Trainz, or this Omsi. But Omsi is trying to get to deep details in siimulation. What you don't get on performance or graphics, you will be repaid when feeling the drive. In other games you don't feel connected, physics are off. In Omsi it feels spot on even no game has real world physics.
Details: You have button and gauge for everything like in real bus... And I mean every little button that is in the game is functional. You have realistic smoke coming out from exhaust, sounds of transimission, axles, doors, rattling of loose parts in interior. This is what you don't get in "fun" games. You may think you are getting very little for the price, but if you grasp the amount of detail in this game you will get it.
PS: I am a big fan of Omsi1, even bigger of Omsi2. Developers of this game never lied. When something was not possible or they disliked it, they announced "forget it". If they are saying that they are gonna fix it, wait for fix and read new reviews.

Cross Set is a sudoku-like puzzle where the objective is to make sure digits appear only once horizontally and vertically in the grid. The tweak is that the available digits for each cell are limited and displayed. Your job is thus to cycle through the digits in the cells, use logic and right-click the cells you're sure you've solved until you've completed the level.
If you're a sudoku or a puzzle game addict, Cross Set will probably be worth your while, especially on sale. But do stare at a screenshot long enough to make sure it will not be as visually uncomfortable for you as it was for me.

Ingredients
4 cloves garlic, crushed
2 tablespoons butter
2 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil
1 loaf crusty bread, split
3 tablespoons grated cheese, Parmigiano or Romano, optional
Chopped fresh parsley
Directions
Combine garlic, butter, and oil in a microwave safe dish or in a small saucepan. Heat garlic and butter and oil in microwave for 1 minute or in a small pot over moderate-low heat for 3 minutes.
Toast split bread under broiler. Remove bread when it is toasted golden brown in color. Brush bread liberally with garlic oil. Sprinkle with cheese, if using, and parsley. If you added cheese, return to broiler and brown 30 seconds. Cut into chunks and serve.

Okay, I'm leaving the original for transperency sake. My issues with scanning below stand, it was poorly designed. HOWEVER, I am changing this review because of the support for mods. The mods are amazing and fix most of my issues below. Modders have made new classes, new weapons, skins, and things that are irritating. (Central talking too much in civilian rescue missions for example). Also, the black market is fixed with the use of a reddit list of what you can sell and what you shouldn't that fixes my issue with its new design.
Original review:
This is a tough one. The game is fun, but it feels like XCOM 1.75 rather than a 2. You spend an inordinate amount of time bouncing between engineering, clearing debris, and the research facility while "scanning" different locations around the world and getting interupted the whole time. It is fustrating, and the characters are nearly exact replicas of the first with minor changes. If you bought "Enemy Within" than the first XCOM has more content.
Aggravetiatingly the "stealth" component that they have introduced in this game basically only impacts up until your first shot, you can set up well I grant you, but if you used scanners in the first game its basically the same
.The game is stream lined items and gear which is great. Now you "upgrade" your entire squad's armour, or weapons, you don't build individual ones anymore. But, you can still build scanners, med kits and new nifty items. The item system is superior to the first.
CQC (Rangers) class sword is immensely satisfying
The council is gone. Thank god. But replaced with a more annoying "avatar project" that builds up and is difficult to stay on top of and requires you to drop what you are doing often to deal with it which just results in you going back, scanning mroe, and getting interupted again.
The black market has changed too. Since you upgrade all units at once with different weapons and armour it no longer tells you what is not useful anymore. This is a decent change, but the problem is the "black market" is a place now...and you have to fly there...and you can be interupted en route.
I really want to like this game more, but it feels like it needs an expansion and by accounts the DLC that currently exists does not do the trick. The vanilla game is inferior to that of XCOM: Enemy Within. Some welcomed improvements but lacks the true feeling of a squel with new mechanics that simply not flushed out enough while maintaining the existing class structure.
If a full expansion comes out I will revisit this review.

I have had much, MUCH more fun playing this than I expected.
A combination of a clever plot, interesting puzzles, atmospheric music and a well managed difficulty curve makes it very easy to lose yourself entirely to being the hacker that we all saw in films in the early 2000's.  Only actualy capable of using a computer.
The game starts you off with a straight-forward set of tools, which rapidly expands to meet the various challenges you meet.  By the end, I was utterly enthralled by and immersed in the game.
It's more story based than the obvious comparison, Uplink, so you do less in the way of freelance hacking.  It would have been nice to have the option to be slightly more mercenary, but the story blossoms as you approach the climax of the game - motivating you emotionaly as well as intellectualy to see the game through.
What's more, there are lots of little easter eggs you can find, people's activities you can track and secret activies to uncover - if you know your way around the computer languages the game is built around I have no doubt that there are even more possibilities.  I haven't, but I didn't feel that I was missing anything.
I would seriously reccomend givng this game a go, its been a while since I've played a game that made me feel genuinely clever - neither led-by-the-hand nor over-faced by its challenges.

I'm just going to be open right here - I LOVE this game.
I've just beaten it for the first time and I'm going to beat it agaIn and then again in NG+ and NG++.
So what's so good about it?
Well, a lot of people compare it to Dark Souls. And in some ways it's similar. It does have the same weighty combat system, where you have to commit to each and every one of your attacks, that have lengthy animations and can not be interrupted mid-swing by the player; hits received, however, will stop your attack. You need to know the attack patterns of all enemies you encounter to survive in the first half of the game, looking for opportunities to strike without losing precious HP.
HP in this game can be restored in 3 ways - by a trinket called Life Leech that I personally only got in the later part of the game, that gives you HP for every monster you kill; by casting a Prayer spell, that acts as a decoy for your enemies and also regenerates a little bit of your health; and, most efficiently, by drinking health potions. Your supply of potions is limited and can only be restored by using a Shard - a checkpoint, essentially - or by dying.
This works really well with another system in place - the XP modifier. The more monsters you kill without using a checkpoint or dying, the more XP you get for each consequent kill, up to 2.0 times more XP for kill. This is very handy, but forces you to refrain from healing and restocking at checkpoints for longer and longer. The game's progress still can be saved at a checkpoint without losing the modifier, but that will not restock your potions and health. It is also said that the more XP you have "banked" - kept unspent with a risk of losing it - the better loot you can get.
This all makes for a thrilling experience, where your stakes are high, and combat feels important, as every monster you meet has a good chance of killing you.
That said, the feeling only lasts throughtout the first half of the game.
Unfortunately, as you grow stronger, especially if you min-max the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of your character the way I did it, the fights get easier and easier. In the beginning bossfights took tries and tries to win, and even ordinary monsters had me respawning time after time. By the time I entered the Rhogar Realm for the first time, after, apparently before my time, killing the Rhogar Lord the Champion (I've killed him 4th, later discovering that he should've been the 5th boss to die), I felt immensely powerful. I still could be killed, don't get me wrong, and I died quite a few times when I goofed up, but most of the fights came to "Bash-Leap-Dodge-Repeat", with some enemies often dying from one heavy attack after being bashed in the face with a Tower Shield.
Boss fights, while each having their own mechanics and even bonus difficulty conditions rewarded with special loot, got easier. 5th and 6th bosses I've met I've killed in 2 minutes and 50 seconds respectively. Last two bosses took me two tries each, in contrast with the 3rd boss that took 6.
The game also feels short. It took me 14 hours to beat it for the first time, and the ending certainly feels a bit abrupt, and not much is explained to you, definitely setting the players up for a sequel.
Overall, Lords of the Fallen has very solid mechanics, absolitely GORGEOUS look to it, wonderful aesthetic and atmosphere, but feels like the developers ran out of steam in the second half of the game, quickly wrapping it up with whatever good ideas they still had. It's a great experience, yet short, and it definitely could use some more difficulty in the end.

Cons:
- The interface is not great, requiring excessive clicks. Some information is missing (not for a gameplay reason), or displayed in awkward or unintuitive ways.
- The terrorism mechanic:♥♥♥♥♥♥off a faction too much (almost unavoidable) and your avatar may get shot. This is RNG ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that straight up ends your playthrough, and it's at odds with how realistic the game otherwise is (very few IRL first-world leaders are assassinated).
- The game unrealistically forces you to do MUCH better than status quo if you want to be in the running for a second term, since your popularity starts at 0. It's a mystery how you got elected in the first place.
Pros:
- Challenging, yet fair.
- Gives a unique insight in the real-life struggles of politicians. The game give you an unrealistic amount of power and clear data, and yet within one playthrough I found myself compromising on my egalitarian and ecological ideals for the sake of just keeping the economy on a vaguely upwards trend. Often you'll have to choose between effective policies and popular-but-actually-terrible ones, or sacrifice long-term benefits for short-term boosts. Spending more money to make things better (and to make everyone love you) is very easy, but FINDING money to spend is so much harder (and pisses everyone off).
This is honestly my #1 reason for recommending this game. It's all things that I knew on an intellectual level, but being actually put in the politician's shoes was eye-opening.
- Similarly, the way your decisions trickle down in deep and sometimes unexpected way is instructive (and fun).
Fire some useless government employees, and now your unemployed population is larger, which feeds into crime and housing issues. Raise the tax on tobbacco, and the poor addicts that won't quit will be even poorer, which affects the amount of money they can spend on other things. Lower employee benefits too much to try and revitalize your economy, and you might have a strike on your hands, which will make your economy tank, which will worsen your worker conditions even more, which will make THE GODDAMN IDIOTS EVEN MORE WILLING TO GO ON STRIKE until you bitterly admit defeat and spend a ton on a stimulus package, which causes deficit, which worries the financial institutions into raising your interest rate, which you pay for by raising taxes, which creates a black market, which raises crime... On and on it goes.
Some things, like crime and GDP, are insanely important yet impossible to affect directly. You have to rely on 2nd-, 3rd-, or even or 4th-order effects. Realistic and insightful. (Even where the simulation is unrealistic, the insight that every policy has countless indirect consequences is valid.)

I'd like to say that DS3 is probably the most approachable of all the souls games, as it's a bit more streamlined and easier than the previous ones in my opinion. That also makes it all the more enjoyable when invaders show you the courtesy of letting you clear out the mobs around you first, even heal yourself and make it a duel.
All in all this is a great single player game, a great multiplayer game and certainly a challenge for new players.

After spending hours in Terraria, I saw like a lot of other players in Starbound a dream coming to life. Seriously, Terraria in space, countless worlds to explore, different races to choose from, NPCs, quests, tons of items... That's some heavy stuff !
After launching the game, the style is nice, and being in command of your own starship is exciting. The first quests acting as a mini tutorial are nice.
And that's all, saddly the fun ends as you need to craft the antena. At the point, the game reveal it's true self, and the false sens of freedom is crushed by the Bosses acting as marks for you to go to the next tier. Ok, Terraria had Wall of Flesh you need to kill to go to the "second" part of the game, but it felt more like a fun thing to do than an obligation.
Here, you HAVE to kill the boss to move to the next tier, and as soon as you do that, everything done previously become totally useless.
Speaking of doing things, gathering ressources to craft or build is incredibly slow, and borring. What should have been one of the most important and fun part of the game quickly transform in a sad necessity. You have to craft, but you don't do it just for fun, you do it because the game tells ou to do it. Same goes for building : you may be tempted to make houses, or even towns, but it's useless, as your ship will quickly become your only house, as going back and forth between planets is useless, ressources and time consuming, and boring. So you end with a nice storage ship, leaving a planet to never set foot back again.
Speaking of towns, it's fun to find random NPC villages and structures, but in the end, you just storm in, grab the loots and leave. No point to settle in, vendors most of the time only sell junk, it's like the whole "random generated buildings" purpose is for you to open some chests, and leave as fast as you came.
But hey, we still have fighting ! I can still remember those super fast paced hard Terraria fights with crazy weapons, flying all around the mobs and proudly getting victorious of that damn boss/wave. In Starbound, it's the same, without fast paced action, weapons, and abilities. Yep, fights are you smashing the mouse against mobs jumping randomly around. And forget those guns, not only they are uber rare drops, but when you finally get one, it's most of the time weak, and consume ammos so fast it's not worth it at all. The bosses add a bit of a challenge, meaing they kill you faster, not they are actually fun to fight.
Ok, so gathering sucks, fights are boring, and crafting is a pain... what's left ? hunting and farming ? sure, hunting gears stop being upgradable at some point, so you either come back to lower tiers just for that, or struggle to get some materials with a totally underpowered weapon... farming could have been a fun idea, but as nothing happens when you're out of a planet, it's pointless, and end in your spaceship, like the rest.
Last point : quests and story ! I got bored of the game before I could see any real quests, past the tutorial-like ones. Not even some hidden stuff to do to have that NPC join your crew... Story-wise, you grab some lore here and there, and you can read them later in your ship...
I won't speak about the public relations of the dev team, seeing the reactions of most of the people, I stopped myself from going to CF website, I'm disapointed enough with Starbound to add more.
In conclusion, Starbound is a game that could have been a real killer, it had so much potential... Instead, we end with promises, and a sad game reminding us all that time what it could have been with a devoted team.
If you haven't played Terraria, go for it, it's worth every penny. If like me, you played Terraria so much you have chests filled with every possible item, and would like to play a game like it.... send me a PM when you find one ;_;

Making The Decision to put down your beloved Half-Life
Perhaps the kindest thing you can do for Half-Life that is so sick or so severely injured that he or she will never recover normal health is to have your veterinarian induce its death quietly and humanely through euthanasia. Your decision to have your Half-Life euthanatized is a serious one and seldom easy to make.
How will I know when?
If Half-Life can no longer do with you and your family the things he or she once enjoyed, if your Half-Life cannot respond to you in the usual ways, or if there is more pain than pleasure in his or her life, you may need to consider euthanasia. Likewise, if Half-Life is terminally ill or critically injured, or if the financial or emotional cost of treatment is beyond your means, euthanasia may be a valid option.
Your veterinarian understands attachment to Half-Life, and can examine and evaluate your Half-Lifes condition, estimate your Half-Lifes chances for recovery, and discuss potential disabilities and long-term problems. He or she can explain the medical options and possible outcomes. Because your veterinarian cannot make the euthanasia decision for you, it is important that you fully understand your Half-Lifes condition. If there is any part of the diagnosis or the implications for your Half-Lifes future that you don't understand, ask to have it explained again. Rarely will the situation require an immediate decision. Usually, you will have time to review the facts before making your decision.
As you make your decision, you may wish to discuss the care of the remains of your Half-Lifes body with your family and veterinarian. You have several options, and your veterinarian can provide information about burial, cremation, or other alternatives.
What should I do?
Your relationship with your Half-Life is special, and you are responsible for its care and welfare. Eventually, many owners are faced with making life or death decisions for their Half-Lifes. Such a decision may become necessary for the welfare of the game and for you and your family.
A decision concerning euthanasia may be one of the most difficult decisions you will ever make regarding your Half-Life. Your decision is a personal one, but it need not be a solitary one. Your veterinarian and your family and friends can assist and support you. Consider not only what is best for your Half-Life, but also what is best for you and your family. Quality of life is important for Half-Lifes and people alike.
What if the game is healthy?
Euthanasia might be necessary if a Half-Life has become vicious, dangerous, or unmanageable. However, some undesirable and abnormal behavior can be changed. Economic, emotional, and space limitations or changes in lifestyle also may force an owner to consider euthanasia of a game, but it is better to find another solution or an alternative home for these Half-Lifes. Euthanasia should be considered only when another alternative is not available.
How do I tell my family?
Family members usually are already aware of a Half-Lifes problems. However, you should review with them the information you have received from your veterinarian. Long-term medical care can be a burden that you and your family may be unable to bear emotionally or financially, and this should be discussed openly and honestly. Encourage family members to express their thoughts and feelings. Even if you have reached a decision, it is important that family members, especially children, have their feelings considered.

The mod workshop is also good for a laugh, as people with non-viable ideologies essentially create cheats to alleviate their distress that their people don't love their governmental system.
I'm not sure if you can lose. Apparently my specific brand of socialism is too viable?
Really, my biggest critique is the lack of a handful of policies (A UBI would be nice, rather than having to simulate it with unemployment benefits, for example), and a lack of "two-state" status effects - unemployment and high automation can't displease your Socialist base when inequity is high, and please them greatly when no-one has to work, and Equality is through the roof.
But otherwise, decent fun with enough complexity to warrant a few playthroughs.

Alright, well first of all here are my PC specs;
MSI GT72 Dominator Pro Gaming Laptop, Intel Core i7 4710HQ (2.50GHz) 32GB RAM, 512GB SSD, and an NVIDIA GeForce GTX 880M 8 GB GDDR5
I'm running on a top of the line gaming laptop so I'm not running into what seems to be the 99% of problems others are having. Also, I'm not a big Assassins Creed fan, I haven't played any of the previous games aside from the first Assassins Creed, so I'm going into this game completely unbiased and not expecting anything except to be entertained.
That being said, I'm having a lot of fun with this game so far, the story is interesting and I really enjoy the flow from the cut scenes into the gameplay. It really immerses you into the world, and I love when games focus on story telling done like this.
The gameplay is a bit awkward for me at first using the keyboard, I'm not familiar with the AC games so it feels a bit clunky. Sometimes though, it is a bit frustrating when the character does not climb or jump to where I intended, and sometimes he will get stuck in a corner or on a ledge and wont do what I want him to do, but these kinds of issues will work themselves out once I get more practice with game mechanics.
The graphics are amazing, it seamlessly transitions from story cutscenes into gameplay. I run it on ultra settings but keep the anti aliasing down. I do run into minor skips and hops which kind of pull me out the atmosphere of the story, but these are only a minor nuisance.
My first impressions on this game are positive. I'm going to continue exploring this game and trying out to the different features. For me it was well worth the price and I recommend anyone who has the rig for it to pick this one up, you won't be dissatisfied.

I was interested in this game since release and finally picked it up during christmas sale of 2014. Dark Souls is one of my all time favorites, so I was ready to ignore negative steam reviews and form my own opinion. The game is highly recommended to every Souls games fan. It is also a nice introduction to these types of games, so if you really wanted to try Souls but wasn't sure it's for you, I'd recommend this game. It's somewhat easier and more friendly, so beginners will have good time playing it.
First of all, it is a sure clon of Souls series games and I can't escape comparing it to them. Combat mechanics is absolutely the same, leveling up and saving is almost the same, the spirit of the Souls is here. But with a nice twists here and there. It is surely more a western game, then japanese for starters. The art and graphics are absolutely gorgeous, UI is fantastic and easy to use (which cannot be said about Souls), every mechanic is nicely explained and you don't need to read dozens of guides just to be able to do basic things. But it doesn't mean the game has no secrets, no. Like every Souls game you will miss a lot on your first playthrough, but that's okay.
The things I would've liked to be improved in Lords Of The Fallen:
- Content and length of the game. I finished it in 16 hours and that's counting some grinding. Locations lack variety, there are disappointing number of bosses and there's no "wow" effect like it was in Dark Souls. I hope next installment brings more epic fights in a bizzare locations
- More class variety and leveling up options
- More interesting and engaging NPCs. There were some, but nothing to write home about. The only interesting one I think was some dude you had to bring human skulls to
- No multiplayer options. May be it was too difficult to achieve, but it would've been nice to at least place some clues for other people.
And that's basicly it. Technical side wise the game run nice for me. It crashed only one time and there were couple wierd sound glitches, but nothing too bad or gamebreaking. Developers did nice job patching and I didn't encounter too much problems. Of course they should've shiped more polished game, but they didn't abandoned it, so it's all good.
What I did like about Lords Of The Fallen:
- Magic is more of an addition to the main combat then focus of it. I liked how easy it was to use and how uncomplicated the system was. It's more of a support style magic and I thought it worked great with this type of game
- Design of the world, design of the weapons and armors. Absolutely fantastic. Every time I've put new set on myself, I couldn't believe it can look more bad♥♥♥♥♥ but then I've picked another one and once again was amazed. Just stellar job for designers. Great weapons, ugly enemies, great UI and overall vision. A+++
- Sound design. Music is awesome and right on the money, great ambient sound. Enemies make terrifying sounds. Great!
- Although it's a secret, but you can completely respec into a differenet class during a game. Liked that a lot
- Story is good. Not super great, but decent. And little pieces of it in form of audio logs were interesting
- Different endings depending on what you did during a game, nice little addition
- New game + of course
- Challenges during boss fights were super nice addition
- Level design with shortcuts that wraps around itself
In the end, I would say that I enjoyed this game very much. In current state it has no technical problems any more and it's very fun. It's not as hard as Souls game, so a lot more people can enjoy it. I would purchase any future projects from this studio.

Sincerely,

A grudging recommend. The audacity to go after this scope and actually achieve some of it is admirable.
Story: You are a space traveler and you go around the universe to whatever end you please. So the story is up to you.
Tone: There are bits here and there that would give you some idea of a narrative thread here, flavor text, lore books, faction style, etc. However I personally ignored all of that to travel and mine.
Visual Style: A very, very, very rich 2-d world. The amount of assets and care put into the design of worlds and objects keeps you exploring. Visuals are strong and dovetail nicely with the narrative element, I know the lore just based on looking at the worlds rather than doing any reading.
Fun to play: Hmm while it is fun to explore new worlds and collect treasure, the nuts and bolts of the game (digging like crazy all the time) is mind numbingly tedious.
Gripe: Buggy game. I know it is a beta, but losing 60 hrs of gameplay twice hurts a little. Seriously, back up often, serious.
Special hint: Play this game with a spreadsheet, eventually (to help keep track of planets visited, make notes.) There should be this type of interface in the game, but there isn't yet. Then again I think making my own spreadsheet is fairly fun. Also there is some semblance of a communal repository for planet information, and you can be apart of that if you wish.

Hacknet takes cues from a mix of places, primarily Hacker Evolution and Uplink, creating a blend that can safely be summed up as a hacking puzzle sim. Your job is to utilise the tools you acquire to probe and gain access to a selection of progressively trickier systems and networks, and unravel the story of a hacker who recently deceased in a supposed accident. Initially you're given control of HackNet, a revolutionary OS that makes you essentially invincible from traditional tracing methods, and a few basic tools, from there your job is to gather the resources you'll need to piece together the mystery of what happened.
Hacknet hews a lot closer to the real nature of exploiting individual ports (even if the programs are automated and require little work to figure out the relevant exploits), and you'll be picking apart servers step by step, usually using command line textual input which makes the game "feel" an awful lot more real than say, Uplink (though uplink succeeded much more from a neuromancer perspective). You'll be learning the concept of using shells to overwhelm proxies, cyclical analysis and syndication to deal with firewalls, and the use of various tools to pry open specific ports to eventually use your swiss army knife tool "PortHack" which will then turn over Admin control of a system to you. Then you get to explore, and use various commands to remove evidence of your tomfoolery.
The game is LOADED with internet culture references, the devs made liberal use of
for IRC logs which litter the servers, taking a "best of" the IRC culture and invariably having some real funnies tucked away on the servers for you to discover, along with various text files with references to games and other internet geekery. There's a lot that's relevant and interesting, and you'll no doubt enjoy what you find as you explore the various servers. There's also hidden paths, servers lying out of the way, and secret side dishes for those willing to investigate and probe various elements of the games rather cavernous depths.
The game is presented in a very slick x-term package, anyone who's used X11 interfaces in Linux will be very much at home here, and more entertainingly, there's the ability to replace your xterm with ones you find, changing up your wallpaper and colour scheme as you progress through the game. The music too, is very well thought out, and very appropriate, with music that's contextual to various events kicking in and ensuring that you get pumped up at just the right times. Even the HackNet OS boot sequence is pleasingly authentic, right down to little details such as memory allocations and devices and the like.
The one big criticism is that this game is hand crafted, this is both a strength AND a weakness, because unlike Uplink, once you've finished the game and plumbed out all the secrets, there isn't much more to come back to. However, what there IS that's here, and there's a good 6-8 hours, is stylish, well written, and very nicely presented. Not to mention a great callback to -good- hacking games, which is something that's been sorely missing as of late.

First off I want to preface that my review is based on "what you pay for, and what you get in return." Secondly, I realize I'm going to get flak for this so if you are a die hard fan of Firaxis or the XCOM series you can stop reading now because I doubt this review is for you. This review is for people who want to know if the money they spend is going to be returned.
That being said, I flat out cannot recommend XCOM2 right now. I know a lot of people have mentioned bugs and poor optimization. I personally run the game on ultra, haven't seen anything exceptionally bad except for frame rate issues when a mission is loading. So my gripe isn't because of it being poorly optimized. My problem with XCOM2 is game play, or lack there of.
First, it is the real lack of character customization with the base game, sure you could pay $5 for the anarchy's children pack which adds a little more to the game but even then it's not really worth it. Secondly, where you do have some armor choices, the tactical advantage conferred by those armors is either overlapped by other armors in various ways or not something worth utilizing a lot of the time. Third, the missions very quickly begin to feel repetitious, the environments all feel the same, the goals very often are the same and the enemy variations and tactics don't really call for major squad changes for most missions. In fact my third gripe is the one that really killed the game for me because XCOM2 got so repetitious so quickly I very quickly lost interest after feeling I had seen all the game had to offer.
Now it's not all negatives, between XCOM and XCOM2 the tactical turn based strategy hasn't changed all that much. There are a variety of powers and weapons you can bring onto the battlefield to help give you an advantage, along with class specification getting some nice new additions (like the gremlin which I really enjoyed). During XCOM2 there is this AVATAR project timer that is supposed to give added pressure and force you into making decisions at times rather than waiting for when your squad is optimally prepared for the mission. However, this isn't a problem,  and I find this change acceptable given the story.
In conclusion, I really wanted to love XCOM2, I really enjoyed Enemy Unknown and was so hyped to see a sequel to a game I enjoyed so much. So in some ways this is my disappointment talking, XCOM2 feels very unimaginative and doesn't bring anything new and necessary to the series. So for this reason I suggest if you love the series either wait for a sale, or wait and see if there is a DLC release that really opens the game play up (not just a rehash of the previous game please).

Completely rewrighting the review, as I felt like the last one had a few lies in it.
So, right off the bat I'm going to say that this is definetly not as bad as people are saying it to be. It has everything most people want in a game, like combat, a good story, stealth, historical timeline, multiplayer, and the ability to customize your character, the list goes on and on. However it lacks some things too, like having a stable framerate, or a good civilian A.I. Throughout this review, I am going to go over all the key concepts you have to know.
You play as Arno Dorian, a brand new Assassin introduced to the series. Arno at first is portrayed as a very innocent, curious, and daring young boy. After the death of his father he was then adopted and raised by François de la Serre, the grand master of the Templar Order. Many years later François is killed and Arno feels like what happened was completely his fault and fights for revenge, along with Élise, François' daughter, who is fighting for avengence. There's only one catch, Arno is following his original father's footsteps and becomes an Assassin, where as Élise is following her father and becomes a Templar.
Arno is almost like all the past Assassin's combined. He is charming like Edward, can be funny like Ezio,  brutal like Connor, and respects the Assassin order like Altaïr. The result comes out great in my opinion.
Most of the game takes place during the French Revolution. You will be able to see many real events, like the Reign of Terror, the Rise of Napoleon, and just plain out riots. One of my most favorite things is just to explore, and if you already have the game I  encourage  you to do it too. I have no goal at all, I just run. You will be able to see so many cool landmarks and events, Like crowds protesting infront of Notre Dame, or a crowd just sraight up flipping over a carriage. It's moments like these that can really make you just stop and stare at what a work of art this game is. (that is of coarse if your game isn't lagging like crazy)
Speaking of lag, the game is definetly not the best PC port ever. I can still play it at a pretty steady framerate in most areas, but when I get infront of a very detailed building, I'm seeing like 20 fps. I don't like to base reviews around how the game is on pc, and mainly just focus or the game itself, but this really effects the flow of the game. However, I am glad to see that Ubisoft is paying attention to us. A day before releasing this review a patch was released that fixed many bugs, and they said they are working on a more patches.
Now onto the gameplay. Assassin's Creed is known for there Parkour system. The last major improvement was shown in Assassin's Creed 3, which really only changed the climbing, not the basic flow. But this feels like a entirely new game. Unlike past games, Assassin's Creed Unity allows you to have more control over where you are going, and even adds the ability to climb down faster, which no matter what looks bad♥♥♥♥♥♥ Parkour is not the only thing changed though, unlike what Assassin's Creed has been doing by making combat easier, they made it extremely difficult this time around. There's no counter attacks, no human shields, and no more wiping out a entire army with a pistol. This makes the game even better, you have to actually think about your next attack, instead of just mashing mouse 1. And I'm not done yet. They also added the long awaited ability to crouch and hide behind cover. The cover system rarely works though, I will find myself mashing the space bar infront of a wall, just for Arno to hide against a chair or table. It didn't kill me to much, just really irritates me. Also, they got rid of the ability to pick up bodies, it would be great if I could be able to slide a body while crouched, and to pick it up while standing. I was expecting this but sadly did not get it.
Onto what Ubisoft made the biggest deal about, the co-op. Co-op with friends is one of my most favorite things in games, and now it's in one of my most favorite games. But does it work good is the question. Well, yeah, I guess. We all know by now that the game is VERY buggy, and Co-op is even buggier. Sometimes you will be teaming up on one guy, then every one will preform a finishing move all at once, and freeze in place for a second. However, the co-op has high replay value, and when everything does go smoothly, it's one of the coolest things.

Well now, after 4.4 hours I finished this minimalistic but nevertheless challenging logic puzzle game.
I don't think it should be neccessary, but I will write it anyway: You should like numbers and maybe you should have done at least SOME Sudokus. Otherwise it might be either very frustrating or a fun but strange guessing game.
Actually it is like the normal Sudoku but only with the rows and columns, so no boxes here. Plus, the "candidates" (which doesn't always even make sense) are always already written down.
It starts very easy, actually you can do the first 1 or 2 sets without even using the "fix" function (right mouse click). But then the difficulty raises constantly until the level 5-8 (set 5, level 8), which was definately the hardest one for me.
The music is totally ok, except of one track, which is really wonderful.
After you have finished all the levels you will have earned all achievements available and there might also be another surprise :)
Conclusion: If you like numbers and especially puzzles which are similar to Sudoku, then you should give Cross Set a shot.

I love the concept of Starbound.  The promised features, the visuals, the music, even many of the functioning mechanics.
I've been cautiously optimistic despite all the setbacks and drama and, frankly, horrible decisions on Chucklefish's part.  I've been hoping that deep down they want to see Starbound completed as much as any of the players who jumped in early.  Even if jumping in early was supposedly going to speed up the 2013 release of the game that was going to happen no matter what, which not only didn't happen but that particular FAQ item was removed from the site and Chucklefish seems to think no one noticed or remembers its wording.
Still, I've held onto hope.  Then I read this.
"I feel 1.0 is an arbitrary release number and it’s down to us to decide what 1.0 means in the context of our game."
That's Tiy, in a recent post to Starbound's website.  Stating his philosophy of what "1.0" means to a game release.  First they redefine what qualifies as a beta, which is apparently the state Starbound is in right now (it's alpha, very early alpha even).  Now they're redefining what qualifies as a 1.0 release.  Because it's down to them to decide these standards, since they've earned that privilege.
This is exactly what everyone in my situation has been fearing.  That with Starbound being declared a beta when it was clearly not in any way close, it would be declared released when it was finally in a beta state, if even that far (it is still not in any way close).  And now Tiy has basically announced that Chucklefish will do just that.
I can no longer in good faith recommend Starbound.  I recommended the game it was supposed to be, despite it being unfinished, because I had some faith that it would be completed.  And maybe if you cram it full of mods it can approximate that.  But Chucklefish may go down as the worst developer ever, if they keep this nonsense up.  They've redefined the industry standards for what qualifies as "alpha" and "beta," and now they're doing it again with "1.0."
Tiy mentioned all the good reviews Starbound has received.  It shouldn't be receiving any reviews.  It's not done.  Early access impressions, maybe, but any critic who reviews Starbound as if its complete should stop writing reviews because they've failed pretty hard (especially if they won't acknowledge how that incompleteness hurts the game).  And any critic who writes an early access impression that doesn't factor in Starbound's rough history is still failing pretty hard.
They've made over $20 million on this game (over $4 million just through preorders on their site), and they couldn't be bothered to put that money towards a development team that could help them fulfill their promises, or at least make up for those they've broken.  This has to be a record for poor financial management by a game developer.  They not only didn't expand their team, they defended that decision by claiming it would actually make things harder.  And in some contexts that might be true, it's probably possible to have too large of a development team, but Chucklefish wasn't and isn't close to having that kind of problem.
That money is also why I don't feel bad about giving a thumbs down.  They've probably made more money on this game pre-release than most indie devs can hope for after they release their games.  They've made EA-level money, and really don't need more of it.  They don't deserve more of it.  They need to start properly using what they've already made as they explicitely promised they would (before removing that promise, anyway).
I am legitimately depressed by this development.  The reason Starbound brought in this kind of money is because so many people want what was promised, and those people hyped it to other people who also want that.  This is a game people want, it's very appealing, and they paid for it in an incomplete state because that's how much they wanted it.  But they also paid for it in that state because Chucklefish promised so hard that it was going to be completed last year no matter what.  It was so going to happen, just trust them.
I want the game that was supposed to be released in 2013.  Any claims that we got what we paid for because this is early access, or because it's beta (it's not), are ridiculous.  And with this talk about what 1.0 means for Starbound, it's not clear if we'll ever get what we paid for.
I'll write a more positive impression or review if and when I get it.
Which I really hope happens.  It's just really, really hard to believe it will.

The Walking Dead: The game is a really unique take on Zombie/Apocalypse type of games. Rather than making it a typical "shoot the heck out of everyone" game, Telltale went with a different approach. They simply do what they do best; telling their story in the best way imaginable.
The Walking Dead puts the player in the shoes of a man named Lee Everet. As the Zombie Outbreak occurs, he needs to entirely adapt to his new envoirment; a whole new world. As the story progresses, you come across several other survivors who try to make it. The game does a good job at introducing the characters at the right time and letting you know about their personalities and intentions. But The Walking Dead wouldn't live up to it's name if they wouldn't on occasion throw you right in the deep; put your life on the line, and at times, wrench your heart to tiny little bits. I'm not going to spoil anything story wise, but be prepared; whoever decides to play this game is in for an emotional Roller Coaster Ride.
Packed with a beautiful comic book style and a touching story, The Walking Dead succesfully drags the player into a world that might as well have been just like ours. Follow main character Lee Everet in journey through a new apocalyptic world.  How well he fares is entirely up to you. During the course of the game, the player will be confronted with several quick time events. You only got a few seconds to decide, but your decisions will have consequenses in the long run; choose quick, but very carefully!
As far as gameplay goes, The Walking Dead is kind of a free roamer. Certain actions or conversations will trigger certain events, but aside from that, there's plenty of room for the player to explore. Be sure to look around whenever time is given; you might come across something interesting!
As much as I love the game, there's one thing I would like to point out. The lack of personality in our main character is something I found to be rather bothersome. I've played through this game two times, and I've seen several playthroughs. I would have liked more your decisions have effect on how Lee acts as well, not just the characters around him. Other than that, I have little to no complains. This game is among my favorites, for sure!
The Walking Dead is an interesting, refreshing take on Interactive Stories. It has everything you could ever ask for; Action, Comedy, Thrilling experiences and Heartbreak. The graphics have a certain charm to them, and I really adore Telltale's approach of using Chapters for their games rather than just putting the game together as a whole. Waiting for chapters was like waiting for your favorite comic book to come out; an original way to present a game to the audience. It keeps players on the edge of their seats, eagerly waiting for another chapter to come.
The game as a whole scores a solid 09/10 in my book. Would definitely reccomend to anyone who's looking for something refreshing, that's easy to play, and doesn't take much to get into. If you ever have the time, and a stable mentality, give this game a shot!

Wanted to give this game a positive review, alas it was not to be. I played through the main campaign without too many issues. Yes, there were some glitches, mostly graphics related, but no game breaking bugs, no quests being uncompletable, etc. However, in the Dragon Storm campaign I cannot progress past the 2nd mission to Sevenkeeps, because the game keeps crashing (error during platform switch -> access violation). I have tried all sorts of fixes, but to be honest there's not even a lot of sources to find any solutions. I have verified the game files, downloaded a new graphics driver, etc. Doesn't matter. I simply can't progress past this point. Now, this may be because of a script but, maybe the whole save file is corrupted, I don't know, I don't care anymore. If you're releasing an "Anniversary Edition" you'd better make sure it actually works on modern systems as well (I did also have lots of micro stuttering issues). It's not worth the effort, because:
While the game is definitely a lot better, more accessible and more streamlined than its predecessor it still struggles to combine RTS with RPG elements. The RTS part is completely dumbed down. You basically have three resources: Stone, Silver and Lenya. Every faction has access to the same ones, which is not inherently bad. There are no building deviations though. Every faction plays exactly the same in terms of buildings. You have your production facilities for each of the three "subraces" and a tech building for them as well. And a defensive structure that can be upgraded three times, but actually doesn't do anything vs. an actual army, even if you build 10 of them. There are also NO upgrades for units, no variations. And some of the subraces are just plain better than others and don't complement each other. For example, is there a reason there are crossbow men AND elven archers in the same faction? Why wouldn't I build healers for anything else? Or why build axemen instead of orc archers? It's just that many of the faction units serve the same purpose, instead of being real options that would make for an interesting army composition.
This was somewhat fixed in Dragon Storm, at least as far as I could play, since the "new" Shaikan faction has mutually exclusive upgrades for its units, which is really interesting.
Unfortunately the RPG aspect of the game is also not very good. There's barely any customization and the game stubbornly refuses at times to let you assign skill points to your companions manually, even if you have disabled the auto feature...but does it really matter? There aren't many skills to choose from anyway and for some reason you need to invest for example into light combat arts before you can progress further down the heavy combat arts tree. Why?! Why would I invest single points into skills I will NEVER use? I'm using a Two hander, I don't need skill points to use daggers? Pointless and wasteful. There is also no possibility I think to get spent skill points back.
On the other hand the campaign has been streamlined quite a bit, which is good, because, frankly, it's long enough already without having to teleport all over the world for the 5 million fetch quests of Spellforce 1 (which by the way was also broken for me and even on easy had impossible creature spawns that were not defeatable even with full armies...I got obliterated in fact, and that in almost every level). No longer do you need to gather new runes for better workers, soldiers or companions, no longer will you have to run from A to B to C to B then to D then to E and back to B and finally A again. Only Sevenkeeps retains a little bit of that and that's ok, because it's a hub city and you're only gonna be there 2 or 3 times. You even get to build up your very own fiefdom with its own little quest chain.
The equipment system, however, is a total mess. Still. After a few levels you will be drowning in pointless items, which you can of course vendor, but that takes ages, since there's no easy one-click way to sell an item...comparing items and finding good ones is also a chore...and to this day I have no idea why my main character with a Twohander can take a lot more punishment than a dedicated tank in heavy armor with a shield.
