OMSI is an excellent bus simulator, but not in the same respect as Euro Truck Simulator 2 - buses are a very niche subject, a lot of people can relate to wanting to be a truck driver, a pilot, or even a train driver. But a bus driver? What?
Most people's first impression of OMSI is that it's just another broken, unfinished simulator that isn't worth your time. You're not exactly wrong. If you're not a bus enthusiast and you think OMSI looks like a piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥ I'm not going to try and convince you otherwise. This game is not for you. Don't buy it. Why are you still reading this?
Now, OMSI mainly caters to those of us who grew up on buses, and developed a liking for how they work and all the sounds that the various parts made. It does that by offering astounding levels of detail and realism in the sounds and models. As a result OMSI is a proper, full-on SIMULATOR. If you picked up ETS2 in a sale, enjoyed it, and thought "hey, these simulators are actually pretty fun, and people are raving about how OMSI is one of those good simulators, I should try it" then I fear that you MAY be sorely disappointed by OMSI.
Don't get me wrong, both OMSI and ETS2 are fantastic simulators but in very different ways. With ETS2 there are simple controls and tutorials to make it easy for people that are new to driving simulators, or just want to finish the objective without a care for how realistic it is - and on the other hand for the enthusiasts there are options to enable things like realistic air brakes, set up a steering wheel and so on.
As for OMSI, there are a few tutorials and arrows to guide you through the routes but apart from that there is no hand-holding. (almost) everything on the dashboard works, and you have to do everything yourself. I mean, anyone can play it, don't get me wrong. The physics are clearly optimized for a steering wheel controller but it still works very well with the mouse too. It's just that when you go into OMSI you need to understand that it is a simulator for enthusiasts, and have the patience to forgive its little flaws, figure everything out and play it properly.
Yes, you COULD take a wrong turn and crash your bus into an invisible wall that launches your bus into space. The solution? Don't do that! If you go into OMSI with the right mindset, and especially if you are a bus enthusiast, I can assure you that you will have a great time. Sure, the graphics for the environment look a bit dated, the pedestrian animations are hilarious and the AI can be a bit weird at times. And, of course, it being a niche simulator on Steam means it will recieve endless hate from idiots who have bought it without doing any research beforehand, and then complain about finding it boring. But you have to remember it was only made by two students, and the level of detail that has gone into the things that really matter is truly incredible.
Some may find the price unreasonable, but the bottom line is anyone who can truly enjoy this simulator will find that it is worth the money to them. Otherwise, wait for a sale.
In conclusion, OMSI is a fantastic simulator but is more akin to Flight Simulator than Euro Truck Simulator, and as a result is not for everyone.

Where do I start... Oh well, what I like about Germany? Beer, maybe sausages? No. It's MAN bus manufacturer, and OMSI. It's been almost 3 years since OMSI 1 came out, and a long journey from 2012 announcement has ended. It's finally here, but does it stand up to the name of great simulation like the last one? Is it worth the asking price? Let's find out.
After starting the game, pretty simple menu greets you. It has everything including tutorial, options, starting new game. Everything is self explanatory. Options may be confusing for people who aren't really into computers and configurations, but I'd say, set overall settings to PC 2006 or 2011 (options names) and you're good to go. Controls could be confusing too, but driving on keyboard (even is game is designed STRICTLY for steering wheels) is pretty well done, and is fun. I've had no problems setting up two steering wheels in it. After short configuration, I've finally started the game up. After pretty long loading, game had no bus whatsoever. So I've pressed ALT, and then a simple menu came out of nowhere. That little thing is handyas from here you can get new bus from there, fix it, choose timetable or change the Bus display. There is a lot to have fun with. So I've choosen Advertised MAN NG272 and then the fun began. First of all, this game is not for casuals. You need to know what exatly you need to do in order to start the electricity, engine, and then finnaly move your bus. You need a basic knowledge of how buses work in order to find OMSI 2 fun. So after some clicking with mouse on virtual cockpit of my NG272, I've finally heard this bearutifull beast. WOW the sound design is AMAZING. Everything is in place, even creeking of the joint of the Bus. Sound quality is TOP NOTCH. It's better than most games out there.
Graphics however aren't that great. 2D trees crossed to make a 3D like impression, 2D bushes, and blocky buildings with pretty low-res textures and berlinians who walk pretty badly... but who the hell looks at graphics in simulation? Bus Models are top notch. Well detailed, well textured. However the deal breaker could be optimisation. It lacks a bit, but it's certainly better than the first one. After configurations you can get most out of it, that's why everything is so complicated in options menu. I'd recommend setting Texture Max Memory to max of your graphic card. Lags in game could be a little annoying while loading next map tiles, but you'll get used to it. Ai can also be pretty jerky, and pretty tough to cooperate with, but hey, when you get used to it, it doesn't really matter. We all need to give credit to Marcel Kuhnt and Rudeger Hulsmann (yes, those two guys created this game) for even doing such a great job on other aspects of the game.
Physics are top notch. Every bump has it's feeling. You feel the mass of the bus, and also how well in handles (when of course you know HOW to drive a bus). You will feel significant difference driving on snow, and or dry asphalt. It's incredibly well made. What shines in this game is it's flexibility. You can do everything you want in bus. Open windows, manually open doors, press all buttons on cockpit and see what they do. It's like, literally, you can do EVERYTHING you always dreamed of with a bus, including even manipulating Roll-Band displays.
Another great thing is it's modability. You can install user created buses, maps, scenery objects, sounds, Ai etc into this game. What's even more awesome, is that OMSI 2 is backwards compatible with all user created content for OMSI 1. Yay!
For what it is, and for what it provides, yes, OMSI 2 is worth the money. Your childhood dreams of being bus driver finnaly came true, and what's more important, they are on steam, available to everyone. Aswell as Euro Truck Simulator 2, HEED THE MOCKERS. Don't listen to anybody who say that simulation games suck, because you will miss the pinnacle of simulation games on PC. However you look at this game, it's maybe not perfect, but it's excusable, due to low human resources of MR Software. I mean, come on. I've never saw two people creating such good game with such attention to detail. After starting up OMSI 1 and OMSI 2, I felt like they were both passionate about busses. Bus driving seems boring to some people, but believe me - it's a hard job. Those two guys captured the true feeling of that job. Game itself shows how much they loved what they did in this game. It shows how dedicated both Marcel and Rudiger are to simulation and re-creation of real-life feeling of such universal job. Yes, animations are lacking,  graphics too, and optimisation a bit aswell, but we cannot deny the fact, that nothing beats the OMSI 2 in terms of physics, sound and design. Other companies (Including TML Studios) cannot even think of being close to what OMSI 2 did. I won't spoil how many new things are in game. Certainly MAN NG272, thus argiculated bus support is there, which is a very nice touch. There have been improvements, and they certainly add even more depth to already impressive and deep simulation.
It's a good game, for a good price. Pick it up if you're not affraid of it's downs.

The visuals are nice - particularly the level of detail on the ships - and the sound design is excellent, but ultimately all you've got is multiplayer CTF that encourages you to spend money upgrading your ship to better the other guy who maybe hasn't got quite as much cash in his wallet.
That may seem harsh given the obviously high production values and effort that has gone into producing this, but without a single player story arc to work through, it's all just... pointless. The "Proving Ground" training missions are too easy and are really just there to familiarise you with the excessive number of hotkeys required for combat. There's no backstory to pull you in, no story arc to make you care about the limited number of crew "characters" (there's no interaction with them anyway), and nothing beyond the absurdly simple maps that lock you in perpetual battle to get into the other team's base.
Fractured Space has high production values, but they forgot to include one critical thing; a compelling game. This is really just a marketing team's wet dream. There are plenty of other Free To Play titles out there that, while they may not have such impressive graphics and sound, offer far more in terms of a rewarding playing experience. To my mind, Star Trek Online is the gold standard of those as they've invested in building story arcs through multiple Seasons not only to suck you into becoming something of a tactical math genius while working out your ideal starship build to beat the Bad Guys du jour, but happy to hand over the cash to get the latest gear. That's what FTP needs to aspire to. Fractured Space just doesn't have any of that. On the plus side, there's no resource grinding as in Battlestar Galatica, so the points are picked up through actual combat. But once again, it's all too dependent on having better weapons than your opponent.
I know this is early access, and maybe in future they'll offer a single player campaign, a story, and some more interesting maps, but in my opinion they should have launched with all of those as part of a traditional game build.
Possibly one to watch out for, but in the meantime keep your cash in your pocket, or spend it on a more mature MMO.

Finding Teddy is a very charming indie point and click adventure game developed by Storybirds (a French start-up developer) and published by Lookatmygame.
Graphics:
- Wonderful, imaginative, colourful and vibrant colour palette
- Art style is unique
Sound:
- Very unique in its implementation as it's a major component when it comes to the puzzles
Story:
- Fairy tale in its imaginations. You play an anonymous young girl whose teddy is stolen in the middle of the night, by a monster that comes out of her wardrobe. It's her mission to locate the source of these troubles and to get her teddy back!
Gameplay:
- Unique both in terms of art design and in the fact it features no dialogue
- Combines traditional point and click elements
- Has musically-inspired puzzles using actual notations
- Not too difficult
- Companions may join you adventure
- There's an interesting side-quest for players to unravel once they overwrite their previous save game
- Has some nice achievements and artwork to collect
- Very short (though from my point of view this is not detrimental)
Conclusion:
- Use of music as the basis of its puzzles is interesting
- Very short
- Charming art direction
Indie rating 8.5/10

Right, where do I begin?
Hacknet is a game with a lot of potential. I enjoyed it thoroughly, found the story to be very engaging, and the "think fast" moments were executed well enough for some noticeable pressure to kick in. The music and visuals work *really* well together to deliver a captivating experience.
However, Hacknet is not quite at a stage where I'd call it a full release. Right now, it looks more like a competent early access preview. The game is riddled with game-breaking bugs (What's that? You're a completionist and decided to do all quests for one faction before moving on to the next? I'm afraid you just got the storyline out of sync and will find yourself stuck shortly!) and a bit too short to make a strong case for the price tag. The severity of the bugs is somewhat mitigated by the simplicity of the save file format, so if you end up screwing yourself over, you can cheat your way around it.
All in all, Hacknet is a less advanced but still oh-so-enjoyable Uplink. If you already know Uplink and are looking for more of the same, you'll enjoy Hacknet despite its flaws. Since the game is still being actively patched by the dev, it will hopefully become even better over time.

First off I want to preface that my review is based on "what you pay for, and what you get in return." Secondly, I realize I'm going to get flak for this so if you are a die hard fan of Firaxis or the XCOM series you can stop reading now because I doubt this review is for you. This review is for people who want to know if the money they spend is going to be returned.
That being said, I flat out cannot recommend XCOM2 right now. I know a lot of people have mentioned bugs and poor optimization. I personally run the game on ultra, haven't seen anything exceptionally bad except for frame rate issues when a mission is loading. So my gripe isn't because of it being poorly optimized. My problem with XCOM2 is game play, or lack there of.
First, it is the real lack of character customization with the base game, sure you could pay $5 for the anarchy's children pack which adds a little more to the game but even then it's not really worth it. Secondly, where you do have some armor choices, the tactical advantage conferred by those armors is either overlapped by other armors in various ways or not something worth utilizing a lot of the time. Third, the missions very quickly begin to feel repetitious, the environments all feel the same, the goals very often are the same and the enemy variations and tactics don't really call for major squad changes for most missions. In fact my third gripe is the one that really killed the game for me because XCOM2 got so repetitious so quickly I very quickly lost interest after feeling I had seen all the game had to offer.
Now it's not all negatives, between XCOM and XCOM2 the tactical turn based strategy hasn't changed all that much. There are a variety of powers and weapons you can bring onto the battlefield to help give you an advantage, along with class specification getting some nice new additions (like the gremlin which I really enjoyed). During XCOM2 there is this AVATAR project timer that is supposed to give added pressure and force you into making decisions at times rather than waiting for when your squad is optimally prepared for the mission. However, this isn't a problem,  and I find this change acceptable given the story.
In conclusion, I really wanted to love XCOM2, I really enjoyed Enemy Unknown and was so hyped to see a sequel to a game I enjoyed so much. So in some ways this is my disappointment talking, XCOM2 feels very unimaginative and doesn't bring anything new and necessary to the series. So for this reason I suggest if you love the series either wait for a sale, or wait and see if there is a DLC release that really opens the game play up (not just a rehash of the previous game please).

TL;DR: Puzzle game with mechanics similar to
.
is a simple puzzle game that has been compared to
a number of times. Basically it presents a square grid of boxes, each containing a set of digits. Your task is to choose a single digit for each box so that no digit is repeated on a given column or row. Just like in a
.
Unlike in
, the grid size is variable up to 9x9 and it is not divided into separately managed squares. Instead, the puzzle is constrained by the digits allowed in each box.
Many of the same techniques as in
work in
. You can (almost) always systematically go through the whole grid to find the solution or at least lock in a couple of digits.
Difficulty goes from simple (early levels) to challenging and time consuming (later levels) to nigh impossible (optional bonus levels). There are seven main sets (each with eight puzzles), one ultimate set with just one puzzle (set number 8) and two bonus sets each with eight puzzles.
Curiously the difficulty is jumpy in each set because of the varying size of the grid. A set of eight puzzles always begins with a small grid but the puzzles get bigger until the halfway point of the set (puzzle number 5) where they start small again. I found it convenient to play through four puzzles of increasing size in a row and then take a break after the last, more difficult one.
Interface looks clear and works splendidly. Left-clicking on a box will switch through the chosen digits and right-clicking will lock a digit to its place (or alternatively unlock it). Only three things I would have liked as improvements:
First, I would have liked a way to mark a box with a different colour for testing a certain digit (e.g. to find a contradiction elsewhere). Second, sometimes a digit eliminates another in the grid and I would have liked a way to mark these numbers as eliminated so I wouldn't accidentally choose them. This would also aid in finding correct digits.
The worst oversight is the lack of saving feature within a puzzle. One can get around it by screenshotting before quitting but it's still cumbersome compared to proper save files. Good thing that all but the most challenging puzzles are short and can be done in half an hour at most.
Completing all the main puzzles (and therefore 100% achievements) was a task of almost 10 hours for me. Some of the puzzles were very challenging but none were unfair.
I also tried a couple of the bonus levels. Admittedly they are meant to offer extra challenge after beating the rest of the game. However, for these puzzles the simple systematic approach doesn't lend many freebies and one would probably need a lot of the so-called advanced techniques to solve them.
Regrettably I finally gave up after beating just a couple of the plus puzzles and none of the double-plus superhuman problems. They will probably always remain there mocking me and my inferior intellect.
The present price (3 € here) would be good even for half the content. I'd recommend
especially for fans of casual puzzle games or alternatively as a light snack to play between more hardcore games.

Do you like Sudoku crosswords? If your answer is yes, this game will interest you for sure!
The basic principle in Cross Set is similar to Sudoku - all numbers in each row and column must be distinct. But you can't select the right number from all (that would be pretty easy to fill 1,2,3,4,... to grid), there's always a limited selection of numbers for every rectangle. If you are afraid of getting lost in which numbers are set correctly and which not, don't worry because you'll be able to lock the rectangles which are (hopefully) right.
And that's all! Combine that with great minimalistic design and good sounds, and get into eight level sets full of number grids. As I usually like to lay on the bed and do crosswords, this is a nice alternative for 3 euros that isn't even much challenging - it just mostly require patience and attention, as you'll be able to make mistakes pretty easily.
Also, the game has Steam achievements for beating all levels, so this game may also be a magnet for 100% achievement hunters - expect few hours of playtime, depending on your speed and amount of mistakes you make (because mistakes usually lead towards restarting the whole level).

The Walking Dead: The game is a really unique take on Zombie/Apocalypse type of games. Rather than making it a typical "shoot the heck out of everyone" game, Telltale went with a different approach. They simply do what they do best; telling their story in the best way imaginable.
The Walking Dead puts the player in the shoes of a man named Lee Everet. As the Zombie Outbreak occurs, he needs to entirely adapt to his new envoirment; a whole new world. As the story progresses, you come across several other survivors who try to make it. The game does a good job at introducing the characters at the right time and letting you know about their personalities and intentions. But The Walking Dead wouldn't live up to it's name if they wouldn't on occasion throw you right in the deep; put your life on the line, and at times, wrench your heart to tiny little bits. I'm not going to spoil anything story wise, but be prepared; whoever decides to play this game is in for an emotional Roller Coaster Ride.
Packed with a beautiful comic book style and a touching story, The Walking Dead succesfully drags the player into a world that might as well have been just like ours. Follow main character Lee Everet in journey through a new apocalyptic world.  How well he fares is entirely up to you. During the course of the game, the player will be confronted with several quick time events. You only got a few seconds to decide, but your decisions will have consequenses in the long run; choose quick, but very carefully!
As far as gameplay goes, The Walking Dead is kind of a free roamer. Certain actions or conversations will trigger certain events, but aside from that, there's plenty of room for the player to explore. Be sure to look around whenever time is given; you might come across something interesting!
As much as I love the game, there's one thing I would like to point out. The lack of personality in our main character is something I found to be rather bothersome. I've played through this game two times, and I've seen several playthroughs. I would have liked more your decisions have effect on how Lee acts as well, not just the characters around him. Other than that, I have little to no complains. This game is among my favorites, for sure!
The Walking Dead is an interesting, refreshing take on Interactive Stories. It has everything you could ever ask for; Action, Comedy, Thrilling experiences and Heartbreak. The graphics have a certain charm to them, and I really adore Telltale's approach of using Chapters for their games rather than just putting the game together as a whole. Waiting for chapters was like waiting for your favorite comic book to come out; an original way to present a game to the audience. It keeps players on the edge of their seats, eagerly waiting for another chapter to come.
The game as a whole scores a solid 09/10 in my book. Would definitely reccomend to anyone who's looking for something refreshing, that's easy to play, and doesn't take much to get into. If you ever have the time, and a stable mentality, give this game a shot!
Strongly recommend

La desesperación de Day-Z y un estilo visual retro que recuerda a Minecraft, Unturned es un juego de supervivencia entre zombis para los que prefieren un apocalipsis algo más suave.
El ataque de los bloques
Si bien el estilo geométrico lleva a pensar inmediatamente en el tan clásico juego de construcciones, Unturned le debe mucho más a Day-Z. Te encuentras en la poco apetecible situación de ser un superviviente tras una invasión zombi. Tendrás que moverte por el mundo buscando provisiones, transportes y armas.
Aunque el modo multijugador te llevará a encontrarte con otros jugadores en los dos mapas disponibles, lo primero con lo que te cruzarás son los no muertos. Así, deberás usar la fuerza y la precaución para aguantar hasta estar bien armado para la lucha que llegará más adelante.
Dale fuerte a esos bloques
Unturned usa los controles típicos de los FPS. Las teclas WASD sirven para moverse, mientras que las de correr, agacharse o gatear están situadas cerca. Para disparar, podrás usar el ratón, que apunta de un modo natural pese lo abstracto del mundo del juego.
Al empezar no tendrás nada en tu inventario, con lo que está en tus manos explorar y conseguir llenar tu mochila para la batalla. Éste es uno de los aspectos más flagrantes del juego: cuando un zombi te haya visto, te perseguirá sin cesar, incluso si estás dentro de un coche (incluso si el zombi solo puede arrastrarse). Acabarás pues corriendo por el mundo buscando artilugios que te ayuden a pelear, lo que resulta bastante complicado.
Como resultado, te verás en situaciones desesperadas donde aunque estés jugando bien, no encontrar la pistola o la munición que necesitas te frenará sobremanera.
Los escollos
Pese al estilo visual simplista tipo Minecraft, Unturned ofrece numerosas opciones de escalado para disfrutar la acción de su mundo abierto con equipos de distintas potencias. Podrás escalar la distancia, añadir efectos de agua, sombras, iluminación y foco, con lo que se consigue dar un aspecto realmente atractivo a su mundo geométrico. Eso sí, elijas los ajustes que elijas, de noche no verás prácticamente nada.
Acaba con sus bloques
Unturned ofrece una divertida experiencia, es gratis y tiene un buen equilibrio entre la desesperación de su mundo y un estilo y aspecto alegres. Si bien hay pequeños problemas con la interfaz, no hay motivos para dejar de probarlo e intentar sobrevivir a la invasión de sus zombis cuadriculados.

Updating my review, now that I've completed the game.
For those who have played the Souls games, you may find LOTF to be somewhat slower, less responsive in that your movements are sluggish, be it evasion, recovering from attacks or casting spells. Plus side though, is that it's a smaller world IMHO, so it's a little bit faster to finish it.
Control wise, I can only comment that you are better off using a controller, as with the Souls games. With it, it's quite okay.
However, you will need to take note of your own handling of the control when it comes to running and evasion. Running here uses the L3 button, so that has a tendency to sometimes work or not work in the heat of battle. So happens one of the key attacks in this game is a running jump attack, allowing you to close the distance and whack during an opening, and openings are a tad hard to come by in this game.
As for Evasion, it uses the A button (Xbox 360 for PC controller) and the button also doubles up as the sprint jump button. Hence, you need to make sure you are not running in order to pull off a proper roll.
Weapon setup wise, I don't find LOTF to be very balanced. Unlike Souls, you practically need a shield, both for breaking down walls to hidden areas as well as to stagger shield-bearing opponents (Rhogar Bulwarks). The kick in this game doesn't help with breaking shield guards, thereby rendering your two-handed moveset pointless in such a fight. For dual-wielders, you can't really out-circle strafe the shielders. Hence, the game creates much frustration if you do not wield a shield.
And for those who fancy using Magic only, look elsewhere.
Spells here are only to support melee and they are terribly slow to cast, often preventing you from pulling one off successfully in the heat of battle.
Range damage comes in the form of The Gauntlet, which is a magic arm cannon.
Doesn't do much damage but does provide some effects with the use of different runes.
Hence, you WILL need to rely on Melee.
Bad points aside, the game does have good graphics and some of the elements it has are pretty good ideas:
1. The Combo-Timing System
2. The EXP Modifier Streak / EXP banking System
3. The non-respawning of enemies when using the recovery crystal/savepoint.
4. The ability to save without resetting your XP Modifier.
Story wise, it feels a bit weak, especially since you have no idea about Harkyn's (the main character) background.
Overall though, I guess it's not too bad a game, but ultimately I suggest to get this while it's on a good  discount.

Maybe I'm the only one that think this game isn't too bad after all? A few thoughts on the game though:
- You definitely need high specs to run this game and really enjoy it. I'm rocking a dual crossfire 290x OC system and an i7 at 3.8ghz and I'm running all of the graphics on ultra high. Things seem to be quite smooth for me and I haven't come across lag so far. I still need to look into the game some more and put more hours in for sure.
- The story is interesting and I am impressed by the choice of time era this time around. Really digging the French revolution. Helps that I know French as well as I can understand most of the citizens.
- The citizens are really lively. You don't see the same face too often and each one is unique and doing their own thing. The render times for each map impress me based on how many building textures and clothing textures it has to render for the whole city.
- I'm not too impressed with the hair mechanism, don't get me wrong, the textures are amazing in this game and hair is difficult, but it just keeps bugging me as I play more and more.
- The new physics are very creative and help to put a more realistic full to the game. Although I've already ran into 2 glitch where i'll be free running down a building and I jump off to the street and seem to fall through into an endless abyss. I think it more funny than annoying.
- This game has some of the most impressive in-game graphics that I've encountered throughout my gaming venture. Keeping the cut scenes close if not the same as the in-game graphics helps out as well.
- Sound seems to cut out at times and can be a little annoying, but doesn't happen so often as to annoy me too much.
- Not too sure how well the multiplayer mechanism is going to work, i'll have to test it out in the near future.
- Looking forward to play this game some more and considering all sides, I'd have to say that I recommend this game. Hoping there will be some updates to the game soon though.

I've tried really hard to beat this game but I just cannot do it, as the biggest problem with this game is how actively it plays against you. I am very a much of fan of these tough-as-nails perma-death ironman games, XCOM is even my favorite game series, but this game just does not handle that formula properly. One of the first things you'll see the game tell you is that you have to "make the best of a bad situation", but that's a complete joke. Every now and then you'll come up against a challenging fight and sure you can salvage a tough fight but when the game starts throwing the dice against your favor you just can't win. Most of my squad wipes have come from purely random crits decimating my team without me being able to do anything to fight back.
Honestly, this wouldn't really be a problem if the game actually provided you with the the ability to come back from squad wipes. Sure, early on a few deaths here and there don't impact you that much, but if you have your four best heroes equipped with your best trinkets and get a squad wipe you will lose all of those trinkets and essentially have to start from scratch, making all future missions harder without the bonuses provided by those trinkets. When you're a decent way into the game you can get completely crippled by squad wipes rather than just set back like in other perma-death games.

The combat is pretty solid and will keep you entertained for a while, but once you've assembled a good army and know which squads synergize best it just becomes a rather bland repetitive experience of cycling through attacks that only ever gets spiced up if your squad randomly gets surprised which causes them to shuffle positions. It's really unfortunate that so many of the enemies are just identical and far too easy to exploit weaknesses on, which is then made extremely frustrating when your entire strategy falls apart due to the aforementioned random dice rolls that ruin everything.
This game is just so beautiful though, the art is fantastic and sets a devilishly good tone for the grim and daunting environments you are put in. The narrator adds some much appreciated flair to the events you'll come across and the many Lovecraft-esque monsters will make you just as stressed and terrified as your heroes fighting them. If I could recommend the game for this alone I absolutely would, but there are just too many debilitating pitfalls all over the game that simply ruin the whole experience.

Finding Teddy is one of those games in which I walked in not expecting anything at all, and came out completely awed by what the developers were able to accomplish with this little adventure title. There's a saying that simplicity is the key to brilliance, and that completely applies here.  Everything from the story and gameplay to graphics and music is very minimal, but all come together to create something more magical than flashier games are able to achieve.
Our story is fairly basic, a little girl sleeps soundly in her room when a monstrous spider sneaks in through the wardrobe and steals her teddy bear.  Venturing into the wardrobe to a dream-like world full of dangerous creatures and beautiful landscapes, she must find the spider and rescue teddy.  That's all we are given to lead us through the game, and despite the very simple premise, it works.
The mechanics is your basic adventure puzzle fair of finding items and using them on objects and creatures to further your progression through the game world. There is no written dialogue or item descriptions, so a bit of trial and error willl be needed for some puzzles.  Despite not having anything spelled out for you, there is a logic at play in specifically the music puzzles; as you slowly figure out the method, everything begins to make sense and the dream world in which you're lost doesn't seem quite as enigmatic as before. This unveiling is accomplished so deftly, it's difficult to explain without destroying the sense of discovery in figuring it out yourself, so I will just leave the point here.
Musically, the soundscape is atmospherically ambient with subdued melodies that resonate an ethereal, dream-like quality. This complements the strange and mysterious game world and creates a base for the melodies in the music puzzles.
Hand-made pixel graphics make up the world you explore.  Knowing that the artists designed every image pixel by pixel is awe inspiring.  The colorful palette and gorgeous visual style incorporates impressionistic geometrical elements that give off an otherworldly feel. Everything from the landscapes to character and creature designs are imaginatively conceived, with the final world featuring some of the most creative imagery I've seen from pixel graphics. And to think this game was developed in only 4 months time...
I have very little to complain about as I feel the design is perfect for what it accomplishes.  Some may find the lack of instruction or direction to be frustrating, but I believe this was a design choice meant to enhance gameplay and impress upon the player a sense of being lost in a strange world. I came across a few bugs in which the game froze or crashed, but didn't seem to be able to recreate those situations after coming back to it later.  Outside of those few bugs, there's not much I consider at fault with the game.
All said, I feel every element of Finding Teddy comes together so perfectly that it elevates the game to a digital work of art. $6.99 for 3+ hours of immense enjoyment seems very fair to me, although it has been featured in numerous bundles for a fraction of that cost and sees frequent sales.  Either way, if you are looking for a beautiful game with a simple yet unique take on the adventure genre, I highly recommend picking this one up.

I recently wrote a scathing review for this game. I absolutely loved the artistic style and grim gothic tone, but the game was very difficult. After restarting the game three different times, and countless rage quits, I decided I was done for good. But it felt so wrong to abandon a game like this due to difficulty. So I decided to start over ONE more time, naming my campaign the "One last try" house. Since then I have been completely obsessed and addicted to this game.
It appears as a simple cartoony RPG game with little depth or variety. But in reality it has so much to offer. There is a lot of layers of gameplay mechanics which work behind the scenes in combat. The RNG system which I originally cursed and hated, turned into one of my favorite aspects. It adds an unpredictable and wild feeling to the game, with crit hits able to  turn a battle completely upside down for better or worse. There are many classes, and all of them are incredibly unique and play completely differently. The lore of the game reminds me of Dark Souls. There is no strong narrative but the mythos of the game permeates from every facet and line spoken by the prolific narrator.
This is by far my favorite game I have played this year, and I would rate it:
9.7/10
Pro tip for people struggling with difficulty: save scum. The game autosaves constantly so if someone dies, its for good. This was the main instigator that was making it hard for me to get into the game. So I decided to make and backup manual saves from the file directory in steam, so I could play the game without constant fear and anger if things went south. This provided comfort and security, and I started being able to play the game the way I wanted, unrestrained. In truth, I never ended up even needing to reload a save, despite dilligently backing up my save before every dungeon run. This would be considered shameful behavior in the DD community, but I disagree as it was the sole reason I was ever able to get into this game. If the difficulty is too much to bear dont give up, there are also mods to help. Three essential mods that assisted me were: iventory stack increase, trinket overhaul, and no hero level restrictions. I am so glad I didnt quit, missing out on this would have been a sin.

Really unique game, thats definitly not for everyone. As its heart its a simple dungeon crawler, with an gothic style. Where it stands it out is that perma death, heroes suffer stress, and you have to manage supplies and decide what to interact within the dugeons. The downside is that this game turns into a grindfest as if you lose one of your high-level heroes your just going to have a train another by grinding more dugeons.
Gameplay wise the game its a party based rpg dugeon crawler. Compared to many JRPGs you have to arrange your heroes in a certain order (putting your arbalest in the back, your crusader in the front) and there a variety of skils that can shuffle around this order. Charecters also have a stress bar, where if it reaches 100, they will role a willpower test determining if they become afflicted with a postive or negative effect (more likely). When your charecters break they might pass their turn in combat, or refuse healing. Light also play an important role as your party is more likely to be suprised, but you will recieve more gold.
In town you teach your heroes skills, buy and sell trinkets and equipment, and use one of the stress reduction buildings, and cure any ailments. Buildings are upgraded through artifacts found within dungeons.
The biggest problem with DD is that god damn end game grind. Their are no manuel saves, and the game is saved on real time, so theres no save scumming like in XCOM. This is a problem, because to beat the game you need high level charecters to progress through the endgame dugeon. So if you♥♥♥♥♥♥hits the fan, congratulations on having to spend another hour trying to get a replacement.

THIS IS A VERY HESITANT THUMBS UP, THE PRIMARY REASON IT IS A YES AND NOT A NO IS DUE TO THE HARD WORK AND NUMEROUS UPDATES PROVIDED BY DEVELOPERS, THAT TELLS ME THEY ARE WORKING HARD WITH THE COMMUNITY TO SOLVE ISSUES AND MAKE THIS A BETTER AND MORE COMPETITVE GAME
Like its PCGAMER first look, i believe that this is a great game that offers a nice ammount of fun, while boasting some pretty serious issues.
First I am a DotA vet been playing since the first release of allstars, so i am no noob to the MOBA genre, this game provides a unique but familiar experiance, 5v5 objectivebased gaming, however Fractured Space isnt about skill, or farming ability like DotA, you dont need to sink 1000 hrs to understand all the systems, income is in the form of mines you capture, the primary mode plays out like a game of domination, the more mines you own the higher level you obtain, levels are automatic, you recieve them once enough ore is obtained and you stop in at your home base or a forward base. every three levels you choose between more dmg, more defence, or utility (cds etc.) the level system is probably the weakest part of the game, and it is BY FAR the most bare bones of any moba i have ever played, you can not level up skills individually, the customization of ships is restricted to premium skins and a couple weapon altercations, like upgrading your base cannon that deals 40 dmg on a 5 second cd to a light cannon, that deals 20 dmg on a 2.5 second cooldown, its essentialy the same dmg but different attack speed, not much thought has gone into customization, hopefully they will bring more to the table as the game progresses. While it isnt as strategy or skill based, knowledge of the genre will still come in handy. I have played 7 rounds, and have yet to lose, even though my clunky starting ship is a heap of junk compared to most other ships in the game.
THE GOOD: while the game is not skill oriented, good accuracy is required, not in the twich shooting style of a game like CS:GO rather in a calm strategical sense, you aim where the enemy is, or lay in wait striking only when they enter the killzone of your ships primary weapons, and when your strategy works, it truly feels like you are a captain.  While leveling and custimization are pretty much as bad as they could be (what would usually be a deal breaker for me) they are overshadowed by the great diversity in the ships. Like in DotA, every ship(hero) has its own skill set, but not 4 skills, instead each ship has 8 weapons/tools at its disposal, and each ship has different armor values based around each of its sides. There is one, for instance, that can only fire its primary cannons from its sides, these sides are where its unusually thick armor is at its weakest, however in order to shoot upon its weaker armor you must put yourself in its killzone, so bringing one of these behemoths down requires great coordination and strategy, do you get beneath it with fast attack fighters while your HEAVY pulls its aggro? or do you line up with it hoping your allies manage to make the most out of your sacrafice?  The best part of the game is the joy of strategy that bore fruit, and (surprisingly) the very friendly community, something pretty much every moba falls short on. Game starts on usually led by people saying "CAPTAIN ON DECK" or "ALL HANDS ON DECK" its a playfull roleplay that really does go a long way to immersing you in the experiance.
THE BAD: So while this is a Thumbs Up review, i have to touch base on some pretty game breaking flaws that will be turn offs for a lot of people. First, and probably most imporant, the que system is♥♥♥♥♥♥right now, there is no penalty for denying it or leaving a match, other than you have to wait for the match to end to start a new one. My first game, the system put only 2 players on the enemy team, and two of my allies dropped out before hitting "R" your way of saying you are ready for the game to start...after you are in the game flying around...it seems like a REALLY REALLY REALLY redundant (see my irony) system, and to make matters worse the countdown couldnt start because one of the players left without hitting ready, so all 5 of us left in the game are sitting there waiting for a game that cant start, if we leave it tells us we have to wait or rejoin...about 1/4 of my play time is represented in sitting there trying to get a match to go, finally i inscructed everyone to leave, hoping that would fix the problem, and it did. I have not had the issue since
As i touched on in the first section, the leveling is awful, easily the worst being boasted by any moba on the market, automatic leveling is a systen that HAS to change if this game wants to grow, and this game does want to grow (the devs are constantly working on new stuff, and it is still in alpha) the level 9 cap needs to skyrocket for longer more competitve games, there needs to be more diverse maps of much larger size, and the environment looks awful, asteroids are more pixelated than pixel piracy, and ofcourse the choice every three levels needs to be updated to a system catering to diversifying your individual ship. And the last, but maybe worst system is the purchasing of new ships. I mentioned before the diversity of the ships, unfortunately it takes so damn long to unlock a new ship (unless you are using real money...) that literally everyone you see in every game will be using one of the three starting ships. I saw someone write in a review that this game isnt pay to win, but that at its current stage is false. This is very much pay to win, at least, pay if you want to fly a ship that isnt garbage without sinking 100 hrs in first. While this game was given away for the weekend for free, it is still a game you must purchase, you can tlel the devs are new to this, they know how to make a game, but are confused on how to make money form their game. You want us to pay to purchase the game, then you hound us with innumerable pay walls and force "Boosters" in our face after every game...you have to choose, is this f2p microtransactional paywalls, or is it a pay to play game, you can not do both you will lose fan respresct and your game will dissapate. I mean, you wouldnt be needing to give the game away for free if you hadnt royally ♥♥♥♥ed up the pay structure in the first place. Either get rid of the special credits or make it free to play, there is no inbetween.

Combat is the best part of the game. I started slashers with Devil May Cry 3, and that game ruined most slashers for me because after it they mostly seem trivial, their combat braindead and the abilities unimaginative. Bayonetta actually offers very good combat, and even some new clever ideas like weapon slots on both hands and legs, each opening a new set of combos. You can also unlock new techniques and movements apart from regular kicks and punches, you can combine melee attacks with shots (and in case of some weapons even more interesting technique which all can be literally woven into combos), and all in all you get a pretty deep and complex combat system. My only problem with the combat is that, while there are many moves with various effects, when it comes to basic combos which should just deal damage and nothing else, there are too many of them. The problem isn't that it's hard to learn them, the problem is that there's no reason to: when you already have a good attack window and just need to dish out some damage, it really doesn't matter much whether you go YYYYY, YYBBB, YY*BBY or something else similar — you'll still just get a basic damaging combo. But then again, you can just forget about it and enjoy all other opportunities you have.
The rest is where the problems begin for me.
* Bosses. While fights are pretty cool, bosses aren't anything interesting. They're mostly just big enemies. Yes, they're different from regular enemies, but not different enough. And you rarely have to do anything different to fight them, mostly you fight them the same way you fight regular monsters. In fact, after a few hours of the game I'm not even sure how many bosses I fought because I don't know which ones were bosses and which ones were just rare big enemies, that's how bad it is. Not memorable, not impressive, just okay.
* Items and healing. Like in DMC you can use items and like in DMC they'll reduce your rating. But while in DMC they were optional helpers and I beat the game on all difficulties without using a single one, Bayonetta basically offers no other ways to heal apart from those items (which you also need to buy or craft). And I mean, no other ways outside of combat, because healing items are a very rare drop. It's great when a game is hard, and I'm all for being unable to heal during a fight, but not letting us heal at all between fights or, say, before a boss fight? That's just bad design.
* Instant deaths. Deaths reduce rating, and that's great. However, there are plenty episodes in the game when things go sour and there's some sort of a QTE event or something similar, and if you mess up, you die immediately. In addition to that, those QTEs are very badly directed, and it's often hard to understand there's going to be one instead of a regular cutscene. A slasher game is about learning how to fight well, it shouldn't have instant death opportunities which are OUTSIDE of the main gameplay. Resident Evil 4 had better-directed QTE events (you could immediately tell something was going on) and deaths in those felt right, but in Bayonetta they just don't really work.
* Cutscenes. I love cutscenes. Hell, DMC3 had tons of cutscenes. And I'm the one to always watch cutscenes, that's why this part annoys me. I like the game's design and everything, but you just don't care about this story and these one-dimensional characters. What's worse, most of the cutscenes aren't cool fights or even cool dialogue. Most of them are BORING dialogue about nothing and they AREN'T EVEN ANIMATED. That's right, they're static. Also, there are just too many of these, and IMO they really break the gameplay.
* Menus. It's not a huge problem, but still. I like the craft menu, but...
- To find the combo list you need to go through various other books you don't need
- Pressing B doesn't close the in-game menu but instead highlights the Exit button which you need to activate by pressing A — seriously?
- Practice mode which shows up during load times (which honestly makes no sense on PC considering how short they are) isn't easily accessible (you need to activate it during one of the load times, you can't access it through a menu)
- Picking up every mildly special item gives a full-screen notification which pauses the game. You know, I get it for new items, but hell, I already know what those butterflies or red tears do, why stop and tell me again? It sounds minor but it really starts to get to you after a while.
All in all, a pretty good game especially for its time, but it has way too many annoying gamedesign decisions for me to enjoy it.

Really impressed! Having played Uplink and the like, I've fallen in love with this game which is much more realistic and somehow less cumbersome at the same time. A lot of old cliches are simplified down, you get a 99sec timer instead of repetitively bouncing connections around a map. You can remove all log files with a single command instead of running through each one with a log deleter and worrying about leaving suspicious deletions.
So what replaces all this? The game puts much more emphasis on discovery and exploration, chasing through IRC logs and network maps to find other computers to break into. Missions are scripted, story-based, and much more interesting than Uplink's procedural "delete this, copy that, forge this" procedural mission list.
There's still breaking past firewalls and proxies, and it's handled the same way as Uplink. UNIX shell knowledge is advised although this would be a great introduction for someone wanting to learn. The command list isn't too big or complex, but it doesn't try to cater to the average bloke-on-the-street either as shown by it's five-minute barebones tutorial.

Gameplay core is mostly good, turn timers force players to think ahead but can sometimes be frustrating due to unforeseen twists. Campaign pacing leaves a lot to be desired, you spend a lot of time repeating the same types of missions and hunting avatar facilities. Enemy design is also a lot more generic with more humanoids and less memorable designs all around comapred to the first game. There is procedural generation which makes each map unique but they're all governed by the same five themes making it boring.
There is a great deal of potential missed in terms of delivering a compelling narrative and aesthetic. They've gone and retconned the events of the first game and made playing it completely pointless from a narrative perspective. The mobile base is somehow able to evade detection for months without the aliens that only twenty years ago took over earth, detecting them, no explanation is ever given for this. One would think that given twenty years time they'd be even more advanced than when they initially took over earth, not only that, earth and humanity are the key to the survival of the ethereals. One would expect them to have the place completely on lockdown. Why even go through all the effort of simulating a safe society filled with luxury and comfort when they're clearly advanced enough to just farm us anyway.
Art direction doesn't work with the revolutionary / seperatist theme, a weak and disorganized splinter cell of old XCOM somehow has the ability to produce factory fresh equipment just as good as the old. The music has the same heroic tone as it had in the previous game but it doesn't really work well outside of the idealistic context of a united global effort. Another small pet peeve of mine is that Central looks nothing like he did in the first game, and wears mascara.
From launch this game was a technical mess, now after several patches it still manages to run poorly on setups clearly meating recommended system specs.
Mod support is very nice, many good mods are available, some that add basic features and tweaks that should've been in the game from release, as such while yes, the mods are good, the game itself should be judged without those taken into account since we pay the company, not the modders.
Perhaps in a while after all DLC's have been released and some more tweaks have been applied this will be worth getting on sale, right now i'd recommend getting XCOM:EW instead.

I enjoyed the game for the most part, it's not a bad game, only voting negative to emphasise certain problems.
There are hard limits on how high or low you can get every stat. It's kind of lame to be unable to be that extra bit of productivity or technology, but it's even more lame when your private healthcare is capped out (or just plain not supplying enough) because you took away public healthcare. This is also part of an overall trend you will find in this game.
Smaller government simply isn't a viable strategy. The game is designed so that more government policies is the solution to everything. The benefits to lowering taxes are negligable, and no one really cares that much if you increase it. There is a bit of a laffer curve, but it's evidently too far to the right. Putting money in the hands of rich people, or really any class of people just doesn't seem to do all that much either.
Increasing the size of the police and research teams is pretty much always a good choice. Things like govenment corruption in research doesn't exist, and I feel should be a much, much bigger problem for big government. Also having all these government beaurocrats doesn't create any "burdensome regulations" affecting buisness, which is very unrealistic. There's also no inflation.
I'll be a bit less critical for this next point, as meeting this one would be above and beyond what I'd have expected, but this game is a bit too materialistic. I think it missed an opportunity to focus on other things than just money, happiness and votes. Things like religiousity, beauty, and national pride. Now they do actually have things like religious voter happiness, tourism, and patriotism, which do technically suggest these things, but I feel they could have taken it a step further and make it more of an end in it of itself instead of just a means to more happiness, money and votes. I recognise that politics does tend to have a bit of cynicism associated with it, but that doesn't mean you shouldn't be able to have higher pursuits.
Another thing is that you're essentailly competing against yourself. It isn't terrible, it's just that it'd be cool if say you were competing with france for tourists, or china for manufactoring jobs, ya know?
There's also no growth rate, and therefore no policies that affect growth rate, which would have been nice touch.
Immigration is too hard to curb once you're doing amazing, which is silly because it's very possible to defend a boarder from most immigration, just take a look at the effectiveness of isreal's boarder barrier.
I'd say overall this game does have a bit of a normie bias (center/left, big government), and doesn't really allow or work for any of the more interesting experimental governments that have/haven't been tried yet like republicanism, snekonomics or anarchy. You can be socialist, and have a big military, so I guess that's close enough to nazism, although you can't make it into a dictatorship, though there is survelance state which I guess is close enough. Appearantly you can actually achieve "real communism" because communist policies actually work in this game, which realistically they really shouldn't, (although I'd say still allow it too for the fun of it... even though I hate communism). Really I just feel they needed to explore more different types of governments and make right wing / anarchist playstyles more viable, and especially, big government and liberal policies need to have more intrinsic consequences other than♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off conservatives.

There is NO WAY to mark that you have eliminated a number as a possibility in a given square. You can only mark that a square is 'locked' to a particular number. This means that you end up having to reexamine the same numbers in the same squares over and over to eliminate possibilites that you already eliminated. It mostly just made me want to play a real Sudoku game where you can do whatever you want with the pencil marks.

Sudoku-like puzzle game with ranging difficulties and challenging end-game puzzles.
I've seen a lot of reviews complaining that the game is too easy, but there'd be even more complaints if the game was any harder than it already is. If you're familiar with Sudoku, Cross Set may be a little easy for you, but surely that's expected..?
My only complaint is that the level set-up is a little confusing. The start of set 1 is an easy puzzle and then it gets progressively more difficult as you get through the set but the start of set 2 is, again, another easy puzzle. I think it'd make more sense to have all of the easy puzzles in set 1, then get progressively more difficult throughout sets 2 > x.
It'd also be nice to have a way to change the colour of the background or have customization of some sort, but I think it's a very clever little game and I'd love to see more levels in the future.

It seems to be taboo for any Souls fan to slate this game. Apparently you have to adapt to the different style of play and accept it.
The problem is this game was an obvious attempt at capitalizing on the Souls' games success, yet at the same time, the game doesn't really know what it wants to be.
The combat is a threeway mess of Souls type meleeing, Generic action RPG button bashing with overpowered and clumsy spells, and terrible RPG stat mechanics.
Gameplay is intentionally clunky and slow, which isn't a problem in of itself. It's just poorly executed. if you want to create a realistic, reactionary melee style, everything has to be fair and on an even playing field (ala Monster Hunter). Instead all enemies possess far greater poise, stamina and speed, making general combat a case of hope swinging and damage sponging with heavy armor. All enemies seem capable of shield-upping after swinging far too quickly. Same applies from recovering from poise breaks. The enemy just outruns even the swiftest of sword playstyles in your arsenal. So you are just left to cheesing the game with the overpowered spells and a rather amusing tactic of using the run-strong attack, which few enemies seem to wise up to. As for why the run-strong attack strikes 3x the speed of a normal standing attack, I don't know. It's one of the many technical flaws in this game.
Also, enemies can change attack aim in mid execution. That's a rule 101 breaker right there.
In summary, slow, clunky, tedious.

Played between 3 and 4 hours as of writing, spent about an hour in the rhogar realm.
Seems to me to be a relatively poor b-movie equivalent of dark souls. If I'm not fighting hordes of enemies that never lower their shields, I'm fighting the poor, corridor-based level design, the abysmal inventory system, the confusing item switching system, the laughable dialogue or the non-existant story.
It's quite a clunky game. Often you'll fight enemies with shields. Shield bash them, or kick their shield, and they'll lower their shield. For about a second. There is no time, even with some of the faster weapons, to follow up with an attack. It's as if Lords took the Dark Souls combat system but forgot to tune it based on their enemies.
As for story, there are quite a few side characters about, that all seem to care greatly what's going on. Even the playable character, Harkyn, seems to care what is going on. But I can't for the life of me give a single solitary damn, becuase I have no idea where, who, what I am, why I'm doing it, who I'm doing it with... You're just not given any of that information, so it's rather hard to empathise with any of the 2-dimensional characters.
The animations are stiff, in dialogue especially. Dialogue sounds like it was recorded somewhere that wasn't a recording studio, and that the VAs weren't really fully immersed.
And after my good 3-4 hour excursion, I've met cumutavely a total of between 5 and 7 different enemy types. There's undead hollow thing, smaller undead thing with sword and shield, bigger undead thing with sword and shield, bigger undead thing 2handing, fat undead thing with a crossbow... It's not the most creative game. Sure, the skyboxes can be pretty if you can make it out behind all that lens flare, but I'm a bit tired of snowy castles and towers.
It can be quite entertaining. quite. I've found myself thinking it's like dark souls but with the darksiders aesthetic and lack of fun.
In no way could I recommend this for it's RRP. I grabbed this on sale for roughly £12, and to be perfectly honest, at the moment that's about the maximum I'd tell someone to buy it for.

There's a reason this game has such mixed reviews. In fact, I've never felt more ambivalent about a game before. I'll try to break this down into the good and bad, with an expanded version down below.
For those who don't want to read a long review, I'll say this:
I'll expand on this later.
Good:
- Great looking game - armor/weapons/scenery/weapons
- Fun different styles of play/different class combos
- Fun spells (caveat here, sometimes there is no way to use your spells which is annoying and makes a spellcaster class of any sort somewhat impossible, more on this later.)
- Overall fun/challenging game.
Bad:
- Still somewhat buggy/optimization issues for PC - IE binding to a certain key caused my game to freeze up and crash, had issues playing in Fullscreen mode (couldn't click on things, was gamebreaking issue).
- Very poor pacing/storyline. In fact, the "choices" you are given which affect the story mean absolutely nothing to you because the story is so poorly developed. But, not to worry, all you get is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ narrated cutscene at the end that has no real weight to it anyways.
- Irritating camera angles when fighting in close quarters (which is a lot). Also, a lot of times you're put in a narrow hallway with a heavily armored enemy with a giant shield and strafing around them is impossible.
- My biggest issue with the game was the poor direction.
on accident because I took a "secret" path which caused me to miss talking to a guy who sent you into another dimension and progressed the storyline. I spent about 2-3 hours trying to beat an area that was scaled way too high and even made it to the boss before I found a guide online and realized what had happened. BAD game design in my opinion.
EXPANDED VERSION:
Overall, I enjoyed the game, but damn it has it's problems. I read the reviews here and didn't think much of the gripes. But they're justified and frustrating, and at one point I'd wished I hadn't bought the game at all.
Due to the bugs with the keybinds/fullscreen mode, I ended up having to replay several areas over entirely.
Due to the horrible story design, I missed an entire area and had to play the entire thing over after I had figured out I wasn't even supposed to be there yet. (Although it was MUCH easier the second time around.) But trust me when I say the story the entire game feels unfinished and just plain bad. For a game that looks as good LotF, the story really seems like it was written hurriedly by a 5th grader or something. Half the time hearing the dialogue I found myself saying "what..? why?...alright...I guess." It was just very poorly developed, and the dialogue choices sometimes didn't even match, I recall someone saying "The [thing] isn't a threat" and my character said "All the more reason to destroy it"....like, what?
Some of the scaling seems off. I went from being able to demolish any enemy in way to getting stomped by mobs toward the end - I suppose it's possible I didn't do enough of the side-questing, however, the side-quests are very unclear and cumbersome. From what I could find, I didn't see anywhere to read about where I was supposed to actually go to complete a lot of my sidequests. I did some of them, but never found an opportunity to turn them in. I attribute this problem to the poor story direction/design that I already mentioned.
The game did have it's fun points though. I enjoyed the combat - I went light armor and dual wield weapons/staff, so I did a lot of rolling around and dodging more than blocking. A big complaint I have, though, was upon meeting the larger, armored "elite" enemies, their huge swinging near-one-shotting attacks didn't leave much of a window for counter-attacks, which I thought was stupid. You're more or less required/forced to use your spells/gauntlet to take down some enemies, which I also didn't care for. Why would I weave and dodge around an enemy when it's easier just to spam the gauntlet and chunk his HP down? Only limit to doing it is your Magic bar.
Now seems like a good time to point out, this game tried really hard to be like Dark/Demon's Souls, however, then it tries NOT to be. Like mentioned above, it basically forces you to use your spells/gauntlet to be effective, even if you're not really specialized in them. So, I found myself dumping points into Faith because I had to, not really because I wanted to. But I will say, the game got *stupidly* easier once I used some of my Cleric spells - one had a damage shield/reflect that also healed, the other stunned any enemy that attacked me and damaged them. Much much easier.
Casting these spells however, is nothing but a chore. They have long cast times, and if you don't cast them before entering a fight, good luck. You're going to HAVE to dodge around a corner and hope you can get the spell off, and the AI seems programmed to attack you when you start casting. If my spells weren't centered around shielding/healing a lot of the times I'm pretty certain I would have died just trying to cast them - I definitely got hit *A LOT* before the animation finished, but the spell still went off.
However, once I got around the idea of trying to play Dark Souls style and embraced that stupid gauntlet and my death-trap-cast spells, the game became a lot easier and a lot more enjoyable (when I wasn't skipping entire chunks of it inadvertently). Most the time is spent fighting so I tended to just kind of ignore the story - maybe next go around I'll pay more attention to the side-quests and "storylines".
Ultimately, my advice is this:
- Only buy this game if it's on sale. Seriously, it's not worth more than 20 bucks.
- USE A GUIDE. Just do it. The game is far too ambiguous and counter-intuitive. If you're lost or stuck or having trouble, I'd recommend looking up a guide and just sticking with it. The game just doesn't do a good job of explaining much anything.
- Try to use every tool at your disposal at all times. A guide here on combat mechanics might help, I spent a lot of time kind of figuring it out.
- Remember the game is crappy and if you find yourself playing in a way that seems cheap or ridiculous that you're on the right track.
This is a fun game that you can enjoy playing for a little while. However, the entire game takes about 10 hours to beat. Given the very short and shallow story, the bugs, and the overall lack of polish, I can't recommend this game ESPECIALLY as listed at full price for 50 dollars. I would have had SEVERE buyer's remorse.
If you can snag it for 20 like I did, or 25, I'd say it might be worth it, especially if you really enjoy this genre.

There are a lot of reviews that call the game downright unfair. At this time of writing I've only sunk a few hours in.
Darkest Dungeons is a turnbased crawler where a group of 'righteous' albeit flawed heros are generated periodically in the game. This is worth mentioning, because you'll be lucky to have anybody that survives past the inital resolve levels which are used to grow your characters abilities and equipment. So naturally, you have to keep filling up your roster with what you can get.
Yes, the game is unfair sometimes. But it goes both ways. I've had what are supposed to be challenging 'boss' fights and I've crit them almost every turn and wiped the flaw with them. On the other hand I've hand dungeons where I get slaughtered after two rooms. It does go both ways. Its the RNG.
I've had a blast with it so far, but you have to realise what you are getting into. Rimworld comes to mind, you build up all your assets and then old Randy Random comes along and kicks your behind back to space. But people love it, me included. Darkest Dungeon is similar in that regard but I think due to the more tedious and repetitive gameplay compared to something like Rimworld, the brutality is not as highly welcomed.
It is frustrating, it is unfair, it is repetitive. But it is FUN.
I got it on sale for a cool £7-£8. People are rightly skeptical of paying for something they may hate. If you're keen I'd either wait for sale or keep an eye on your playtime, so you can refund it if under two hours you realise you are not interested in this kind of RNG masochism.
P.S. Art and visuals are top notch.

All in all, I found myself disappointed at all turns. Can't recommend picking this up.

Finding Teddy is a colorfully pixelated point and click game that places the player in control of a girl whose teddy bear has been stolen by a monster from out of her wardrobe—because, for the little girl in Finding Teddy, her teddy bear means everything! When she follows after the teddy bear, she is transported to a fantastical world filled with musically-inspired puzzles and several animal companions that can be used to solve riddles and unlock secrets.
The majority of Finding Teddy's puzzles can either be solved by gathering and using the correct objects from within the level or by playing a specific melody on an alphabetical musical scale that the player slowly fills out throughout the game. The puzzles are thought-provoking without being aggravating. Often your goal is to find a particular item that will cause a creature that is blocking your path to move out of your way. As you progress further into the game, the little girl will be joined by two helpful sidekicks that will allow the player to reach otherwise inaccessible objects and areas.
One of Finding Teddy's most charming features is its naivety; the game never presents you with a problem that must be solved via an act of mean-spirited trickery, but instead offers you sad creatures whose problems you must solve in order to continue. In Finding Teddy, you'll find missing baby spiders, sing "Hello!" to a group of frogs, and retrieve food for globular monsters with gigantic tongues. Finding Teddy is very much a game that embraces the perspective of the little girl that you play.
Finding Teddy's high points can be found in its disarmingly childish storyline, its lush and detailed pixelized backgrounds and characters, and its attractively dialogue-free, music-centered gameplay. Perhaps the only downside to this casual point and click game is its short gameplay time and low replay value—most players will finish their first playthrough in under two hours and completionists with quick minds will find themselves completing all of Finding Teddy's achievements in that same time frame.
Despite its short gameplay time, Finding Teddy is a brilliant example of quirky point and click games. This game presents you with sympathetic characters, unique puzzles, and a wonderfully vibrant atmosphere, giving it more than enough reason to earn a recommendation as a casual, light-hearted point and click game to play between some of your more intense adventures as a gamer.

Like Sudoku, but worse.
The idea behind this game is pretty much ok: imagine you're doing a Sudoku, you've narrowed it down a bit and marked the cells with the numbers they can have, and that's where this puzzle comes in. Since the range of numbers in each cell is limited, you can draw some conclusions about which numbers go where and eventually "fix"the grid.
In fact,
: because every square can only be part of 2 number sets, not 3 as in actual Sudoko, the logical deductions never get very deep. You can solve every one of the 57 regular levels by checking each row and column for a) digits that appear only once; b) squares that have only one possible digit left; c) consider cycles (if you have two 2-5 squares, they must have the 2 and 5, so they can't appear elsewhere in that row). Cycles can extend to 3, but that's rarely needed; you can also check for cross-row and -columns, but that is also more rarely needed than in Sudoku. The last regular level is 8-1, andit took me 20 minutes. (My overall time includes lots of idling.)
The problem is in the game's interface, and it only starts that you can either have no sound or you're forced to listen to someone incessantly hammering on the same two keys on their piano. The problem is that a lot of the puzzle solving involves checking which numbers are where, and as you can see from the screenshots, not only are there no visual cues (like, I don't know, colors or shapes with the numbers), the numbers switch places each time you click on a square, so you have to exert a lot of brainpower reading and parsing the numbers on the buttons. Unlike a pencil-and-paper Sudoku, you can't erase any numbers, either. Fix a 4 on the grid, and you'd erase all 4s in the same row and column, but you can't. They don't even dim. If you could, then a control that would e.g. "highlight all 6s that aren't dim" would be really helpful in doing the actual thinking and deducing. As it is, there's a lot of pedestrian checking and very little thinking involved in solving these puzzles. Then you have to repeatedly click a square to select a digit, as if we only had a touch-thumb and no mouse available. Good thing the puzzles aren't that difficult because you can't save your progress. The final straw is that there's no "undo" button either.
Recommended if you enjoy Sudoku of medium difficulty. Personally, I like the hard ones.

A follow-up on XCOM that preserves the spirit of the franchise. It is more of XCOM, but with enough novelty to make it worthwhile.
I have completed one playthrough in more than 100 hours, and found only a few glitches. Worst was that, in two circumstances, my squad member and the enemy saw each other through a solid roof, which of course should not have happened.
Missions where the squad starts concealed add a twist, and having a counter (it is not a timer!) that limits the number of available turns to complete the mission rebalances things nicely. There are also plenty of missions without a counter anyway.
Like the previous XCOM, it has a reverse difficulty curve, where survival is more difficult early in the game, before obtaining various upgrades, trainings, etc.. However, the enemy keeps getting more dangerous, and improving the ship and the crew is fundamental.
I can only heartily recommend it, if you enjoyed XCOM EU/EW. If you have not played those, then I would recommend starting with them... why miss-out? And meanwhile, the price of XCOM 2 can go down.

I did see the a performance issue when I first started the game.  But after I adjusted the video options it played 100% better.  I tried running the game in ultra settings but was sadly stuck at 10 fps.  I changed it down to high and now getting about 25-30 fps stable (even with the MASSIVE amount of npcs on the maps, I'm talking more than you can fit in a football field at times).
Game is running at 2560x1600 resolution and  the hardware setup is  i7 3770k 16gig ram with 1 680 GTX.  This game is hardware intensive and for the resolution I'm using, I honestly believe that a GTX 690 or 970 SLI'd would allow me to run Ultra.  Keep in mind the devs did mention that this game would require an above normal hardware setup.
It also would be better if the player was forced to adjust video settings before starting the game.  I think this is the main reason for all the low performance reviews.  For example, when you start the game for the first time you hit the title screen and all you get is "press any key to continue".  You get thrown right into the intro, which to be honest, is pretty engaging and done well in my opinion.  Problem is if your settings are not optimal, you get a lot of frame loss and tearing.  I think the work around so far is "quit to desktop" at a save point so that the next time you start, the menu appears asking what you would like to do.
Accessing the menu is a bit rough and confusing at first but not hard to understand.  For example, when you access the menu and click on "options", you go to "Game Options" with 3 sub selections below it.  Since there is no scroll indicator, you would not know that there are more options until you spin the mouse wheel.
In addition, "Game Options" is also clickable which gives you more options.  I mean if it did not look like heading text then it would be less confusing.  Also there is so much screen real estate that the options could have just been listed in columns.  But I assume this was primary designed with console in mind.
As far as story goes and the potential of co-op and side missions, the game is pretty engaging and I am enjoying the story.  Of course it's only been 2.5 hours but I guess a little more time will tell.  Hope this helps you guys.
