If you're looking for a review you're at the wrong place, but heres a receipe for spaghetti!
Step 1: Get Your Supplies
Before you can start making your spaghetti you will need to first get the proper supplies and materials. To make this spaghetti you will need:
a box of spaghetti
a jar of marinara sauce
1-2 pounds of ground beef or Italian sausage
two large pots, one for boiling the pasta and the other for making the sauce
serving untensils
salt
water
You can use as much meat as you want, really - but anywhere from 1-2 pounds per large jar of sauce should work out best. I tend to use 1 pound of meat nearly every time.
Step 2: Cooking the Meat + Get the Water Boiling
Before you start, fill up a large pot with water and add a handful of salt. Put it on the stove and turn it to high so it'll start boiling!
Next you will need to cook the of meat. Take all of the meat out of its container and set it all in a large pan, then put the pan on the stove and set the stove to medium.
After that you will need to break the meat into smaller pieces. When the meat is in small pieces you will then need to start flipping the meat and make sure it gets brown all-around and cooked thoroughly. The cooking should take approximately 10-15 minutes. When all of the meat is brown and cooked you can add in the sauce.
Step 3: Mixing in the Sauce
Next you will need to mix your marinara sauce with your cooked meat. Take your jar of marinara sauce and pour all of it on the cooked meat and then stir it all around until it is all blended together. Then turn the heat down to low and let it simmer while you cook the pasta.
Step 4: Cooking the Spaghetti
Once the water has come up to a boil, you can throw the spaghetti in. Typically it should cook within 7-11 minutes - just follow the time on the box!
Make sure to stir every couple minutes to keep it from sticking.
Depending on your timing, you can either strain the spaghetti and set it aside, or you can put it right into the sauce.
Step 5: Serving Your Spaghetti
You can do this in a lot of ways but I prefer mixing the noodles in the pan with the sauce. I use tongs to drain the noodles and place them in the sauce, and then put in a couple spoons of pasta water. Stir it all together really well - the pasta water coats all the noodles and lets the sauce stick more.
You can also put plain spaghetti on individual plates and spoon the sauce over top. Whatever works for you.
Top with cheese and enjoy!

With Darkest Dungeon, during the 1st hours of play, you fight against the game, not within the game, in a degree I had never met with other games.
The rules aren't well explained, are often counter-intuitive or just plain weird.
For example, you can use your healing spells during the fight, but can't anymore outside of fight. Why that ? It's not a world logic, it's only a game balance logic.
At 1st, you'll also need to get acquainted with DD world : you have a village with several buildings which are unlocked 1 by 1 after every quest you do. A quest is only crawling in an extremely basic dungeon with a team of 4 heroes. There's no real exploration as you only have something like 5, 10 or 15 rooms (depending of the quest length) connected by vertical or horizontal corridors on a 2D map. Once in a room, you select the next room you want to go, but it doesn't have any real consequence. You just want to select the rooms in the best order to avoid backtracking. The goal of the "quests" is usually to explore 90% or 100% of the rooms, or kill the Boss, or destroy a couple of altars.
And for this crawling, you constantly need to light up torches, as fighting in the dark gives handicaps to your team. You'll also need a few items to maximize the looting of the different curios (eg: you need a key to open locked chest ; holy water to purify an altar, etc.), and food to eat at random intervals. At 1st, you don't know how much torches or food you'll need, and they are a bit expensive and you can't keep them from 1 quest to another. Why, oh why ? Oh, it's just to waste your money so you'll have trouble upgrading your heroes at 1st, as everything is money based.
But after these few hours of adjustment, the game becomes actually quite simple. There's no gear for your heroes except 2 trinkets. There's no leveling choice either, nor anything that would look like a real RPG game. Your heroes starts at level 0 and their max level is 6. They get a random positive or negative perk at each level up. There you'll be able to upgrade their skills, weapon and armor in the Guild & Blacksmith buildings of the village. There's no choice in this. Your only choice is in a what order you'll unlock the additional upgrade level in each building. Spoiler alert : usually, you need Armor -> Skill -> Weapon.
Although your heroes can permanently die, it's really easy to avoid this by playing conservatively and carefully. There are dungeons of Level 1, 3, 5 and the final one of level 6. So as long as your heroes aren't fully upgraded to Level 3 or 4 skills, armors & weapons, just stick to the Level 1 Dungeons. Simple. Also, don't go to fight the Level 1 Bosses before your heroes are entirely upgraded to Level 2 or 3. Your heroes also don't die when reaching 0 HP, they still need to be hit once more and there they still have a chance to survive. And you can run away from a fight and abandon a quest at any time.
Moreover, there's no special event, no randomness that can lead to different outcome, so this game is not a Roguelike. There's nothing that looks more like your current dungeon run than the previous run and the next one.
So, it's not a Roguelike, it's not an RPG, and you keep on doing the same thing over and over again. Yup, it shouldn't have been called Darkest Dungeon but rather the Grindest Grindy Grind.
Let me explain. So your heroes constantly get stressed by crawling in the dungeon and often they'll end the quest with high stress. So you have to put them to rest in the Tavern or the Church to lower their stress. Meanwhile, you are forced to send another team for the next quest.
It doesn't stop there as your heroes can get very annoying negative perks that will also require 1-quest off to be removed. If unlucky, they can even get 1 negative perk from leveling and 1 from checking items in the dungeon, so you may need 2-quest off to remove both. And it doesn't stop there either because there's also diseases that you'll need 1-quest off to remove. So all in all, you need between 2 and 4 teams to roll.
Another very annoying thing is that your inventory is very limited, with very small stacking ability, thus if you do a medium or long quest, you'll be constantly juggling about what to keep or not. Personally, I installed these 2 Mods that extend stacks
&
, but it's still very painful : you feel like you're totally wasting your time, as you can't even keep the little loot you're finding.
And it takes many runs to get the necessary items to unlock the upgrades of your weapons, armors & skills and thus you're often stuck with leveled but not fully upgraded heroes. And it can get badder, as Level 5 Heroes refuse to go to Level 1 Dungeon, so if you didn't manage correctly your team roster, it can lead to additional headaches.
I have been playing the game with latest Radiant mode, which halves the time needed to finish the game. I can't imagine the horrible grind & repetitive feeling it must have been to play with the normal mode. Or I can : only 1.4% of the players finished the game with it 14 months after release. On Radiant, we're at 0.6% 2 months after its release, not exactly great either.
One note of the curios : to find the item to optimize their use and their result, you'll have to spend countless of time & tries to figure out everything, or you can head there :
.
So almost all the interest of the game relies on its combat system. It is in itself really not bad and quite interesting for 4 or 5 hours. But unfortunately, it's not deep nor varied enough to justify chaining the quests, as you're mostly walking straight in corridors, opening containers, and fighting, fighting & fighting.
Most fights are only 2-3 rounds long, which doesn't allow any evolved tactic building, so you just repeat ad nauseam the same skills over and over again.
Quickly, you'll figure out you need an healer in your team and a stress reliever ; as pointed above, you can't use these spells outside of combat, so you'll use & abuse of the stun to make the fights longer, to heal & lower the stress of your heroes ; after 4, 5 or 6 rounds your heroes will start to stress out, because the Devs limited that abuse.
And unfortunately, the Boss fights don't bring much on the table. They are straightforward enough and won't require your brains : your team is ever strong enough to kill them or it's not.
There are 16 classes, I tried 11 of them and didn't feel enough gameplay differences from one to another. Mastering a class requires not much more than the 2 minutes needed to read its different ability descriptions.
DD is a game that hides its relative simplicity by not clearly explaining its rules, and is based on way too much grinding and on its interesting but not deep enough combat system.
- Unique enticing visuals
- Interesting combat system, although ultimately lacking of depth and surprises
- Village with buildings to upgrade
- Way too grindy
- No real challenge
- After a few hours, gameplay gets ultra repetitive
- No exploration
- Enemy mechanisms strongly lack of variety
- Bosses fight are a stats check and not tactically challenging
- Most trinkets comes with strong handicaps, making them nearly useless
- All the negative things in the game have actually very little influence on the gameplay ; ie: they don't lead to choices for the player
- Dull quest system without accomplishment feeling

This game is about hacking as the name implies, starting you off with a bare few programs and growing your arsenal as you progress its storyline. This game stands as a spiritual successor to Uplink bar a few features that keep it from reaching Uplink's cult following, but still make the game interesting and make me wish the two games had merged into one supergame with the visuals of Hacknet and the in-depth sandbox nature of Uplink.
Starting with a bootup sequence, an automated message box by the "Bit" character and a tutorial program with a cool digital background soundtrack sets the tone for the game immediately. Given basic instructions to hack your first terminal can take time to figure out even with the tutorials. Learning these commands will be the bread and butter of this game, and so with every successful command you'll be rewarded with a visual representation of the program functioning to unlock ports or simply find a password.
This game doesn't rely on money for upgrades, and in turn missions do not give money but instead increases your rank. Increasing your rank will allow you bigger missions, and will grant you access to servers to download more powerful programs which will allow you to crack more secure servers and reveal that the missions lead a linear path with admittedly little room to shift the way the story goes.
Like Uplink, this can be a very short and very easy game to get through if you know what you're doing. This is made easier with the ability to save and the Trace Aversion game, should you lag behind or stay on a server while being traced and run out of time. The Trace Aversion sequence isn't anything special in terms of gameplay, but you will be given a timelimit to hack a server and type in your IP address to avert a game over, requiring a few midgame tools at the least.
I've yet to finish the game, and I've recently gotten stuck at a point where I require a program from another mission before I can finish my current mission. I'd advise doing everything you can before starting the endgame, because there's some programs hidden behind locked missions waiting for you to reach the top rank before allowing you to take them, these missions hold programs that are required for the end game. There's also a few guides available for the little confusing things, in which they are in abundance.
Overall I do like what I've seen, and there's definitely a charming nature that comes from these hacking games with Hacknet being no different. I'd recommend it for anyone interested in simulations, puzzles, and anyone who just likes to solve things on their own. This is Hollywood hacking at its core though, and it doesn't represent real techniques used by actual hackers.

THE PUZZLE:
Cross Set is, as advertised, a game of logical elimination similar to sudoku. Each square has a list of candidate numbers from which you can pick, and the objective is to force each row and each column to contain exactly one of each number.
Unlike sudoku, this puzzle format allows for more interesting thinking right from the beginning, because Cross Set does not necessarily need any of the squares to be fixed (though they can be). This shaves off some of the early "fill in the obvious" steps common to many sudoku puzzles. Unfortunately, limiting the choices by square appears to make the later "finish filling stuff in" phase come earlier. I find the puzzle format fresh enough to hold my interest.
THE SOFTWARE:
The software is very basic. Window size (and Windowed/Fullscreen) are options before the game boots, but there is no volume slider (only a mute button). Oddly, the fixed puzzle squares do not begin locked, even though all of the advertising shows them as locked. Hopefully this is some kind of oversight, as manually locking them just wastes about 10-15 seconds per puzzle.
OVERALL:
It's an interesting new puzzle format with 64 puzzles included for $3. I've spent about as much per puzzle for Kakuro and Sudoku books, so I'd say the game is more than worth the price if you're at all interested in logic puzzles.

Bayonetta is a game that just nails everything from presentation to music to (most importantly) tight and satisfying controls. You'll often see Bayonetta being compared to DMC or even being slandered as a rehash but I think that's a pretty unfair assessment. Both games play extremely differently especially regarding the pace. DMC is far more slow and combo based while Bayonetta is fast and centers a lot around timing your dodges. Combos still exist here and they remain important but there is a bit of a focus shift in terms of how to score well in Bayo compared to DMC. Because dodging is a big part of the game, your score suffers immensely if you take a lot of hits. Pulling off flawless verses to earn Pure Platinum medals is immensely satisfying and for me personally the scoring system is one of the biggest strengths of the game overall. Suffice it to say I'm a huge fan of both games and I just wanted to highlight some of the things that make Bayo stand out despite having a less complex combo system.  It is more than made up for with other gameplay elements that balance it out and produce a game that is just as good as (if not better than, depending on your prefrences) the Devil May Cry series.
It's also worth highlighting that in the modern age of cut content, and relentless dlc/microtransaction hell Bayo is a game that actually just rewards you for playing instead of paying. As you play you can unlock things such as new difficulties, hidden upgrades within levels, secret weapons, characters, outfits, etc. To use a modern example, Zelda Breath of the Wild just charged extra for its "Master Mode" difficulty, where Bayonetta simply lets you unlock Infinite Climax for free. On the same topic of BotW, there is gear that can only be unlocked through buying and using Amiibos instead of, you know, exploring the giant world they made and feeling rewarded when you find it. Bayonetta is made by a team of people who have real passion for videogames, and aren't trying to rip you off. Support companies like Platinum every step of the way to encourage these consumer friendly game design choices.
Bayonetta alongside Devil May Cry 3/4 are easily some of the finest action games ever made, so it's fantastic to finally see this on Steam. If you are an action game fan you absolutely owe it to yourself to pick this game up if you haven't yet.

The game is a competent and typical of its genre. It runs fine, and it's essentially exactly what you'd expect.
I finished the first two dozen boards, which is the first three levels. I reviewed it so early because there were no other reviews; its window of new release exposure was closing, and it didn't deserve to miss sales on account of consumer uncertainty.
The "tutorial" consisted solely of a box of text; it was still sufficient, even having heard and read nothing about the game except the store description before playing.
The difficulty is fine so far; the first 6 boards averaged under 2 minutes each, and the next 18 took a bit over 4 minutes each.
The presentation is simple and functional. The art style is essentially all displayed in the marketing screenshots accurately.
The achievements look to be quite doable, so this game would probably be good for 100%ers. All of them are for simple completion; none can be missed, are timed, or even require perfect input.
There are no hidden in-game purchases.
The game never has time pressure. The interface requires enough precision to hit boxes of the size in the marketing screenshots without hitting the adjacent ones; it does not require dragging. The interface is fully mouse-driven. (It may support touch screens, but I don't have one.) There are no vital sounds. There is no dialogue written or spoken.
Locked tiles are distinguished from unlocked tiles purely by color; that mechanic is optional, though helpful for remembering which numbers you're confident in. Some tiles are locked in the marketing screenshots, so you can check before purchasing if there's an issue for you.
As a non-expert, I see no other problems.

Gameplay core is mostly good, turn timers force players to think ahead but can sometimes be frustrating due to unforeseen twists. Campaign pacing leaves a lot to be desired, you spend a lot of time repeating the same types of missions and hunting avatar facilities. Enemy design is also a lot more generic with more humanoids and less memorable designs all around comapred to the first game. There is procedural generation which makes each map unique but they're all governed by the same five themes making it boring.
There is a great deal of potential missed in terms of delivering a compelling narrative and aesthetic. They've gone and retconned the events of the first game and made playing it completely pointless from a narrative perspective. The mobile base is somehow able to evade detection for months without the aliens that only twenty years ago took over earth, detecting them, no explanation is ever given for this. One would think that given twenty years time they'd be even more advanced than when they initially took over earth, not only that, earth and humanity are the key to the survival of the ethereals. One would expect them to have the place completely on lockdown. Why even go through all the effort of simulating a safe society filled with luxury and comfort when they're clearly advanced enough to just farm us anyway.
Art direction doesn't work with the revolutionary / seperatist theme, a weak and disorganized splinter cell of old XCOM somehow has the ability to produce factory fresh equipment just as good as the old. The music has the same heroic tone as it had in the previous game but it doesn't really work well outside of the idealistic context of a united global effort. Another small pet peeve of mine is that Central looks nothing like he did in the first game, and wears mascara.
From launch this game was a technical mess, now after several patches it still manages to run poorly on setups clearly meating recommended system specs.
Mod support is very nice, many good mods are available, some that add basic features and tweaks that should've been in the game from release, as such while yes, the mods are good, the game itself should be judged without those taken into account since we pay the company, not the modders.
Perhaps in a while after all DLC's have been released and some more tweaks have been applied this will be worth getting on sale, right now i'd recommend getting XCOM:EW instead.

Bayonetta is a third person “character action” game in the vein of Devil May Cry. Focusing on spectacle and style akin to an anime, you are constantly subjected to ADHD shifts in gameplay, jump cuts, and over the top escalations of stakes. The bombast and variety keep things from getting boring, but there is so much cringe here it makes me want to puke.
 
  I can't help but feel this is the third or forth game in a series that is past it's prime, run out of ideas, and is simultaneously paying heavy fan service to a fanbase that doesn't (didn't...) exist and trying way too hard in every other conceivable way. There's a focus on Bayonetta and the cast of rejected cartoon characters that surround her, and they're all terrible. Bayonetta herself is leggy witch of some kind who conjures powers from her hair, which causes her to lose her clothes (also made out of her hair.) She's part posh British librarian, part hyper sexualized dominatrix. If that sounds cool (or hot)... nah. Any “adult” aspect suggested by her is so juvenile and superliminal you can't take it seriously. The innuendo comes down to, “Let's ♥♥♥♥.” and the answer is “No thanks.”. It doesn't help that the supporting cast she's surrounded by; “cool” Blaxpoiltation dude, fat loudmouth Italian guy, metrosexual goofy ladies' man, and annoying little girl should all be D list background characters in another game. Here they're slapstick archetypes, or rejected action figures from the '90s.
 
  The nonsensical/poorly translated story about angels and demons, alternate dimensions, time travel, left and right magical eyes, and familial betrayal that ends up in outer space is utterly incomprehensible. I could take the anime stupidity in stride if it was presented well, but the numerous cutscenes seem like they weren't even finished. Randomly switching from traditional CG to motion comic with voice over and a half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥movie reel filter is jarring. It's a poor trick to try to hide a lack of a budget with “style”.
 
  The saving grace of Bayonetta is the core brawling mechanics. When you are on foot kicking, shooting, and juggling the crap out of various angelic monsters the game is solid. Dodging attacks at the last second activates a slow motion Witch Time, which when combined with your unlockable combos and several weapon/gun combinations can produce an enjoyable combat flow and is visually appeasing. Chaining attacks while avoiding damage builds up a magic meter which can be spent on special moves or bloody finishers that award you with more currency depending on how quickly you can mash buttons during mini-QTEs. While there are some cheap hits and camera issues, it's an entirely competent fighting system.
 
  Unfortunately, those bright spots are few and far between. Not only does the game break up the combat into super small arenas where you fight a dozen enemies at a time if you're lucky, but the majority of Bayonetta is spent doing other activities. From bad motorcycle levels to finicky platforming to light gun bonus stages to a Space Harrier clone, if you don't like what you're doing in Bayonetta just wait a few minutes. Then you'll be doing something much worse. Half of the time you won't know what the ♥♥♥♥ is going on to begin with. Variety can be a great asset; random garbage is just random garbage.
 
  The game also has a tendency to want to stop you from playing at any given chance. Aside from the ever looming threat of cinemas, pick up an item for the first time and the game will stop, giving you a description of what it is. That's fine... but there are A LOT of items, and to use them you have to enter a poorly designed submenu and concoct other items in a confusing minigame for some reason. Other collectibles are scattered around the levels as well, but I've never lost interest in collecting them so fast as I did here. Books are available to read up on the history of the witch versus sage battle, but the text is full of typos and doesn't make sense, so it just adds to the confusion.
 
  Technically Bayonetta on PC is a very good port of an almost decade old game; it runs smoothly at 4K resolution with almost zero load time, and there's plenty of graphical and HUD options to mess around with. I wouldn't say the problem here is the game has aged poorly; it was never good even when it originally released.

Reading about it, it seemed like a good game on paper (that I would love), a mix of RPG and RTS, medieval fantasy genre. a combination of Warcraft, Neverwinter Nights/Dragon Age, and Diablo, games that I played a lot. It is also regarded as being loosely similar in concept to Mount and Blade, another favorite of mine.
I refrained myself from watching let's play videos not to ruin the fun and straight just bought it. but sadly when I finally played it, I was kind of disappointed. I wished I checked the gameplay videos first.
I haven't played it that much(0.6 hrs) but I think it's not for me. First, I love good graphics but I do make exceptions to really great games with great gameplay, but this doesn't quite cut it. The game still looks decent though, and still playable. not sure if the devs have patched it throughout the years to look better, or if it looked like this in 2004. if it was like this back then though, i'm sure it looked good in it's time. but it's more than a decade old already, and I'm used to today's graphics, UI, and gameplay now. clearly my fault for not discovering the game way earlier.
The world also looks sad and bland, I'm more of a sandbox type guy, so the story didn't quite interest me, and I wanted to try the free play game mode. characters were just standing around in the city, and the city was quite empty, with no life to it. The quest are also non-interesting and there's no interesting things to do in free play game mode. Base building and combat indeed feels similar to Warcraft and Dragon Age/Diablo, but the mix up didn't work well for me in this game. The scaling/proportion of the models in this game is very inconsistent and off putting for me. Base buildings looks pretty small and the characters looks so big in proportion to it, like an RTS. and then you get to a place and some structures will be big, like an RPG, so it definitely switches back and forth between RTS and RPG, but in a bad way (for me).
The messed up scaling kinda worked in Warcraft because it was purely an RTS and it was consistent, and the fact that I've played it way earlier. I haven't got into most of the game obviously, so maybe I am not in a good position to recommend it, but I'm still putting it out here. I was thinking of refunding, but I thought maybe I'll give this a second chance and change my review in the future. so this not my final recommendation.
If you can stand playing old school graphics/UIs, with old school unit scalings like in old RTSs, and are more inclined towards RTS gameplay more than immersive RPG gameplay(surprisingly enough, the RPG content is much more deeper than the RTS content, but the overall feel of the game is kinda RTS-ish), and if you are interested in playing a story campaign and not just playing sandbox then maybe you'll like it instead.

I've jumped on and off this game over the past few years. As it currently stands I would like to recommend it, But I just can't for any newcomers.
The game itself is fine, The control setup is easy enough for anyone to grasp and you can easily get a few hours out of this game. The main problem that has persisted over the past five years is the immense grind required to advance through the game. The old energy system was far from perfect, But I would take it over the god awful Fire Crystal system.
Originally on top of the massive quantity of crowns needed to buy a recipe for gear/Create said-gear, You would need up to 800 energy per item. (You did have 100 base energy, But energy was needed for practically everything including actually playing the game, So I'm not counting it towards this.) As of the current day writing this review, Energy on the market costs about 9,000 crowns/100 units. For a bare minimum set that translates to a staggering 315,000 crowns. Factoring in the cost for materials/recipes, You needed a little under half a million crowns to advance from Tier 4 to Tier 5. Stacked with the aforementioned energy need to actually play the game, It was extremely tedious to grind this many crowns.
I eventually ended up stepping away from the game for a few months near the end of 2012, When I decided to come back in Late 2013 the first thing I had noticed was that the energy system seemed to have disappeared almost entirely. Energy was still being used, But it wasn't nearly as much of a priority as before. Instead of requiring hundreds of energy per item, You instead need three Orbs of Alchemy to craft an item. You can still technically pay for orbs with same amount of energy needed as the old system, But they have a rare chance to drop and I've never found it to be a problem amassing them while grinding. I still think this decision was a good one, The orbs drastically lowered the cost needed to craft items. As much as the orbs helped however, The Fire Crystals dragged the system back to where it was.
To clarify what Fire Crystals do, When you craft a new piece of equipment it starts at Level 1. As you complete missions you're awarded Heat which is basically just an EXP system for gear. The stats will continue to rise up until Level 10 when they reach their peak. The only original requirement for levelling up gear was just that, Collecting enough heat. Unfortunately it was decided this was far too easy, And thus Fire Crystals were added. Now when you reach the next level on a piece of gear rather than just levelling up you need to forge the piece. In order to forge the piece, Fire crystals... And you better have a crapton of them.
Rather than just having a set cost, You need to pay more crystals for each level, And pay ADDITIONAL crystals to increase the probability of the forge being successful. (300% of the starting cost to guarentee the result). It starts out cheap enough for the first couple levels, But that hardly lasts. Around the time you've forged your gear to Level 5/10, You're strapped for fire crystals. By context, Sure the orbs are a rare drop but you only need three of them to make a piece of gear. To actually level up said-gear after creating it, You need hundreds if not thousands of these damn things.
Ultimately the end result is the same with both systems, The ridiculous amount of grinding needed to even progress turns everyone away. It really is a shame because this is one of my favourite games on steam from a gameplay standpoint.

So it seems that the folks at CF have [finally] did a bit of necessary tweaking to the game and -- since my curiosity was peaked -- I decided to revise my review.

They worked on a bit more variety on this end, which is good.

Still has yet to be implemented in the game.

Probably the only selling point. Because does this game sure need it. Still does, however the vanilla version is far less reliant on that end.

Basically PC/Mac/Linux multi-platform.

The Darkest Dungeon is an intially fresh RPG with a rich gothic aesthetic, but it slowly turns into a deeply unenjoyable soul-crushing experience. Calling the Darkest Dungeon a "strategy" game or "difficult" is deceptive. Both these terms imply navigating and problem solving within some matrix of information you are given, and rather in the Darkest Dungeon pretty much all valuable information you need is only given to you after post-hoc trial-and-error. This might be fine given the games self-described morbidity, but unfortunately each "mistake" creates such a setback that the real pain doesn't come from a character that you lost, but from the thought of how many hours you were just set back.
The most succint way I can describe the Darkest Dungeon is to picure a game of chess where you perpetually only know 3/4ths of the rules, random spaces on the board are booby trapped, and your prospects of either winning (or losing) appear to approach infinity.
While I certainly enjoyed the first 20+ hours of the game (and hence technically I got my money's worth) the next 20 were so egregious that like matter meeting anti-matter, anything nice I would have to say about this game was cancelled out by the real horror that lies inside the Darkest Dungeon: its game design.

Bayonetta is a third person “character action” game in the vein of Devil May Cry. Focusing on spectacle and style akin to an anime, you are constantly subjected to ADHD shifts in gameplay, jump cuts, and over the top escalations of stakes. The bombast and variety keep things from getting boring, but there is so much cringe here it makes me want to puke.
 
  I can't help but feel this is the third or forth game in a series that is past it's prime, run out of ideas, and is simultaneously paying heavy fan service to a fanbase that doesn't (didn't...) exist and trying way too hard in every other conceivable way. There's a focus on Bayonetta and the cast of rejected cartoon characters that surround her, and they're all terrible. Bayonetta herself is leggy witch of some kind who conjures powers from her hair, which causes her to lose her clothes (also made out of her hair.) She's part posh British librarian, part hyper sexualized dominatrix. If that sounds cool (or hot)... nah. Any “adult” aspect suggested by her is so juvenile and superliminal you can't take it seriously. The innuendo comes down to, “Let's ♥♥♥♥.” and the answer is “No thanks.”. It doesn't help that the supporting cast she's surrounded by; “cool” Blaxpoiltation dude, fat loudmouth Italian guy, metrosexual goofy ladies' man, and annoying little girl should all be D list background characters in another game. Here they're slapstick archetypes, or rejected action figures from the '90s.
 
  The nonsensical/poorly translated story about angels and demons, alternate dimensions, time travel, left and right magical eyes, and familial betrayal that ends up in outer space is utterly incomprehensible. I could take the anime stupidity in stride if it was presented well, but the numerous cutscenes seem like they weren't even finished. Randomly switching from traditional CG to motion comic with voice over and a half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥movie reel filter is jarring. It's a poor trick to try to hide a lack of a budget with “style”.
 
  The saving grace of Bayonetta is the core brawling mechanics. When you are on foot kicking, shooting, and juggling the crap out of various angelic monsters the game is solid. Dodging attacks at the last second activates a slow motion Witch Time, which when combined with your unlockable combos and several weapon/gun combinations can produce an enjoyable combat flow and is visually appeasing. Chaining attacks while avoiding damage builds up a magic meter which can be spent on special moves or bloody finishers that award you with more currency depending on how quickly you can mash buttons during mini-QTEs. While there are some cheap hits and camera issues, it's an entirely competent fighting system.
 
  Unfortunately, those bright spots are few and far between. Not only does the game break up the combat into super small arenas where you fight a dozen enemies at a time if you're lucky, but the majority of Bayonetta is spent doing other activities. From bad motorcycle levels to finicky platforming to light gun bonus stages to a Space Harrier clone, if you don't like what you're doing in Bayonetta just wait a few minutes. Then you'll be doing something much worse. Half of the time you won't know what the ♥♥♥♥ is going on to begin with. Variety can be a great asset; random garbage is just random garbage.
 
  The game also has a tendency to want to stop you from playing at any given chance. Aside from the ever looming threat of cinemas, pick up an item for the first time and the game will stop, giving you a description of what it is. That's fine... but there are A LOT of items, and to use them you have to enter a poorly designed submenu and concoct other items in a confusing minigame for some reason. Other collectibles are scattered around the levels as well, but I've never lost interest in collecting them so fast as I did here. Books are available to read up on the history of the witch versus sage battle, but the text is full of typos and doesn't make sense, so it just adds to the confusion.
 
  Technically Bayonetta on PC is a very good port of an almost decade old game; it runs smoothly at 4K resolution with almost zero load time, and there's plenty of graphical and HUD options to mess around with. I wouldn't say the problem here is the game has aged poorly; it was never good even when it originally released.

So I've waited for the DLC to come out to see if Firaxis would release an update to fix this game. After realizing that almost nothing is fixed, I've just about had it with waiting for this game to be good. Instead of having a list of every single problem with the game, (for example, how health is displayed, the imbalanced difficulty, how detection tiles are incosistant, enemies are just given buffs later in the game instead of new enemies being designed, etc.)  I'll just list and explain the 4 fatal flaws with this game:
1. PERFORMANCE: If you look at other revieews, other people are having a hard time getting this game to run well. For me its not too bad now, as I noticed that general stability is improved to a good range of 20-40 frames. But that's far from optimal. It's also far from the only thing wrong with the game.
2. CHEATING AI/BAD AI: You can test this out on the first mission with the statue if there is one enemy left and you have a soldier (with no other soldiers nearby to possibly flank the enemy) near a statue. If both of you are in the high cover of the statue, and you move out of sight into the low cover base of the statue, the ai will abandon high cover and go into the low cover base to flank you, even though he couldn't see where you moved before. This makes fighting the AI holy unsatisfying. In addition, the AI in general is easy to predict (when it's not glitching out). Psionic enemies in particular always use their special abilties first before shooting, even if they go out of their way to flank you. Enemy soldiers have no sense of preservation, so overwatching in front of them will never keep them in place.
3. BAD PACING: The biggest problem to the actual gameplay (in both combat and base management) is that the game always forces you in a rush. Got to capture a VIP? Hurry up and get him in 12 turns even though the enemy doesn't even know that you're there yet. Capture this cargo in 8 turns otherwise it blows up for no reason. Did you actually win a combat mission? Tough♥♥♥♥♥♥ the doomtracker's clicking down. It's always rush, rush, rush. There's never a time that the game (and by extension the player) can have a breather to calm down and get his bearings. In the prior game, base management was the way the game calmed down. You didn't have to worry about moving your base constantly that takes 4+ hours to land and take off in each area.
4. LINE OF SIGHT BUGS: The thing that kills this game is the constant line of sight bugs. Literally anytime urban warfare is involved, you can expect to have shootouts through solid walls and ceilings with no visibility. Sometimes cover just doesn't work and you'll get flanked by an enemy who is clearly right infront of your cover. You might move a soldier behind a wall so an enemy won't have a shot on him, only to realize that the enemy can still see him and he will get shot like he wasn't in cover at all. The worst that has happened to me is when I was rescuing a VIP from a truck, and when I came into visual range, the walls of the truck didn't work so I saw the VIP. When the VIP was revealed, the enemies saw the VIP, and since the VIP isn't in concealment, then everyone of my soldiers lost concealment, no less after i made all of my moves. The game is frustratingly unfinished.
There are positive additions to the game, which is what kept me for playing this long. But the more I played it in general, the more I was frustrated at its bad design and terrible stability. This game is unsalvageable.

Pros:
-There are many gameplay improvements over Enemy Unknown, such as a stealth system. The stealth system finally teaches your soldiers to not scream like a baby when they see an enemy until AFTER they fire their weapon.
-Your Scientist isn't a psychopath.
-You aren't juggling plates to appease a board of shady people who apparently think countering an alien invasion is like swatting a fly.
-The workshop allows you to remove most of the Cons below.
Cons:
-The DLC (Two as of this review) are at best lackluster and at worst completely gamebreaking.
-More than half the missions are on a timer, encouraging risk-taking in a game where even the slightest risk
will result in a failed mission.
-Juggling plates is replaced with two missions that are extremely difficult (One of which is timed) either when you're unlucky or at set intervals.
-Personal experience: One Crash to Desktop and one endless loading screen. (However, I did mod the game with the Workshop)
If this will be your first XCOM game:
-XCOM has a reputation for being hard and this game is no exception. If you REALLY don't like RNG, I wouldn't recommend this game to you.
-Also, play on Rookie (Easy). Veteran (Normal) is XCOM/Strategy player/Masochist. Commander (Hard) is for masochists that also don't like winning... or Sectoids. Legend (RNG be with you) is for people who want 100% completion... or people with psionic abilities.
Overall I would say the Workshop really saves this game from a negative review. Removing the timers really made this game fun, so I recommend XCOM 2 with a handful of mods.

New to spellforce game series, saw SF3 and thought it looked alright and SF2 anniversary edition (no other dlc) for $2, why not. (update : Was pleased with SF2, I decided to buy the $11 bundle including spellforce Plat and other DLC)
My overall impression was it was a great game, few minor hiccups but for 2006 game i enjoyed it. Runs smoothly, quite a few graphical options.. not as many game ones as i'd like. One with "show health bars always" would be nice, can be hard to find out which units are getting hurt in a big fight.
Firstly it takes a bit to get into the game, the UI isn't top notch. I found the "level point" button hard to see/notice sometimes when i've leveled, with it being all the way to the top right. There are no quick hotkeys on the skills, and no quick control grouping (ctrl+1) for units/heroes but you can still group them by clicking a down-arrow button. Using this method you can control+Click infantry units and then archer units if want in different groups (1,2) to use tactics/strategies better, or you know.. archers aren't the facetankers.
Although there are no hotkeys on the skills, it isn't too bad cause when you click on a enemy it shows all the heroes abilities that can be used, so can use 3 strong abilities by 3 heroes to quickly nuke a certain enemy down, or quick clickin to stun a specific enemy, or simply double stun in a row on a stronger monster. I like it.
What made me decide to write this review was the movement of the units AND the voice acting which i felt did immerse me into the gameplay and the story it was unfolding... the movement of artilery units like "dwarven catapult" was great, speedy and had a good fire rate.. not this sloww sluggish this, and it stood out with the dmg it does to buildings.
There is also a 3rd person view, which is cool but i don't use. Can go in and out of it quickly and even move around with wasd the main "avatar"/character.
When i got to the part where you get into the base building and creating units, I was dissapointed there didn't seem to be a control group option for the buildings to my knowledge, i even tried the drop-down button to. The resource collection was nice and simple, i liked watching the animations and graphics of the workers.
I really liked the feeling of amassing quite an army and the movement of them, they don't just run into this specialized combat position. That made it feel more immersive to me, I am impressed by that..a human-like feeling with the units, not robotic created infantry and the movement is smooth and can micro injured ones back and forth nicely. Revolutionary feel with it being that RTS/RPG atmosphere,  look forward to SF3 for sure. I Have to also mention i find the guards looking like mortal kombat guards (helm appearance) hilarious.
The combat is amazing, like stated before, an RPG/RTS blend. Each unit really feels like it counts, and you can level your heroes up , give them abilties and gear to which they feel like... heroes! they definitely stand out. I've only played on normal difficulty so far, feels like a nice balance of difficulty. And the mechanic with damage and armor is great. For example if have a level 3 soldier (dmg 10-75) vs lvl 9 stone golem (armor 84), soldiers petty blade wouldnt be able to hurt the golem, see a nice armor dink effect to.
There are also skirmish modes and free mode. I did a 1v1 vs a computer RealmVsRealm , while i did early harass with 2 soldiers, ai had 10. I was try get a eco advantage. Was able to hold off ai attack. I went way ahead in eco and army but fighting with ai is a bit imba, cause it can execute heroe skills perfectly. Took 3 full waves of my army against essentially one of his to overwhelm, was fun and everything is at max level in this mode - I would of liked the system to be able to level the soldiers up to 18, not start there.
Free mode was a bunch of other non-goal orientated campaign like missions. Can be RTS or RPG. The first lowish level one i played (lvl 1-3) was broken, the enemies didn't seem to die, not sure why.. can level up a main avatar in that mode and save him to re-do or play missions that are in the level range.
Some minor problems ive dealt were : - Cinematic camera was way off in scenes, when showing a dialogue of your avatar/champion.
- When trying to micro too fast, splitting my army up for the fun of it more than anything else (like marine split vs banelings in sc2), if you go to fast the game just scrolls on you.
- AND my biggest problem so far was i failed a mission on timer, but there was a merchant there, so i thought i will sell/buy some stuff..got time right?.. but fail, and re-load last checkpoint is apparently at the very start of this mission. But i am having fun and intrigued by the combat and what the campaign will unfold for me.. so i aint even mad... yet. Note to self.. save often.
- (update) Hit a major bug on a mission to kill hagards summoned minions, they wont die unfortunately. Something to do with version of game or patch? : (update) after a patch they die now.
I got it for $2 sale and has been definitely worth it.

Very good and fun game, provided you enjoy "Nintendo Hard" games that is. For those who played the first game be warned because they upped the difficulty a notch, which means the 'Normal' difficulty of this game is equivalent to the 'Classic' of the previous game.
Pros:
- Improved soldier abilities, almost all soldier abilities are now useful and you are no longer locked to one path like the previous game. It does give you new dilemma in picking abilities however.
- New mechanics, giving you new ways to complete a mission, like concealment and armor exclusive weapons and abilities.
- Interesting story
- Unique enemies and each with different abilities, you need to get familiar with them.
- Soldier customizations, even without the DLC you can already pimp them out.
Cons
- Even after months of endless patches, it is still buggy and sometimes crashes. I doubt most of you still don't want to do an ironman run on this game just for this reason.
- Performance issues, sometimes the game freezes a bit during some actions.
Pros or cons?
- Nintendo Hard even in the lowest difficulty, not for the faint hearted. If you are expecting a treat like some easy flash games, then it is going to be hell.
- Timed missions, timed missions, timed missions, love it or hate it. You can't turtle here and need to play more aggressively.

People still play multiplayer, and MP is very fun, as it has modded modes, to just normal gameplay, so the community is not dead.

Surprised to see the complaints. This is a phenomenal continuation of the anthology of Fallout.
As per usual in this series, you recieve a partial story line where you as the main character fill in the remainders that are missing. Fallout has its' mechanics based in the same universe as Elder Scrolls where in true D&D fashion you imagine and complete the stories within any time frame and order that you like.
The main plotline is the only guarantee, however, based on when and in what order you discover and complete side missions, in-game context is always a moving target; both in the ways that you feel and interpret interactions to the game and in the ways that the game relates to you.
With this context in mind, a true D&D adventure is never complete, never the same twice, and will always leave you wondering "What if"
Completionists will be frustrated with this game. It has no "high score" or  absolute finish. It is a saga and journey that theoretically can never end.
The crafting engine is immense and the options almost overwhelming. This game has many options and opportunities for you to configure modifications, machines, weapons, armor and even building structures. One could theoretically spend an entire month creating the perfect settlement by way of one example.
The fact that it is a risk taking leap for Bethesda is what makes it both so very good and so very frustrating at the same time. For those still considering a purchase here are a few facts to consider as of 9/1/2017 on why you should buy this game:
The game at release cost $60 (more if you bought the season pass)
The game has released 8 DLCs, which in most cases are equal to full standalone games
The game has only improved since release, as it should, which in itself is interesting to me as many games that I have bought in the last 2 years have ceased improving or developing their games within 8 mo of release.
The game is a true drop and pick up where you left off game. For those who have a busy life but want the release, relaxation and escape of an espisodic fantasy adventure, this is your game. Your wife, mom, BF, or grandma can literally walk into the room and start shouting about the backedup toilet, dog ate the couch, we were supposed to leave an hour ago, why in the hell havent you finished _______, or what ever and you can simply save the game and placate the situation immediately without the stress of loss.
Finally, it really is an eye candy experience. Few games have made good on their promise to deliver a visual experience second to none with great value and consistency. I run this game at 4k with Dual 980Ti's and I have yet to peak. It only makes me wish I could go without my wife, as I'm sure she'd leave me if I dumped the cash on a couple of Vega's or 1080's.
Now the draw backs.
You get what you pay for in a game like this. Hardware is key to meeting the extreme on visuals. There should not be an apology to anyone who cannot get this experience- life isnt fair and if its' what you want in life you must plan, create a strategy, and then execute until you reach your goal- budget, save and discipline.
The UI is burdened by aged slide trees rather than inuitive pop ups or curtain drop downs. (Of note, this game is a take on an imagined future that was made aware to the public in the 1950's, NOT the future we began to see in the 1970s- so Im not sure these UIs would have appeared)
Occasionally a person will start talking to you while you are getting it handed to you by something.
NPCs die in this game for no reason, or reasons beyond you- And somettimes this ruins the story.
There is a content store. incremental revenue is not something we are accustomed to seeing in any of the Bethesda games- this is something you would see in a money-whoring Ubisoft game.
At times, the side quest or journey is so vague that if you are restrained and do not look it up in a walkthrough, you can be scouring for hours (which incidently is where most of my most funny, insane and memorable side incidents have come from....something to think about)
It isnt co-op. What all of the Elder Scrolls and Fallout games really need is the opportunity to make a close friend one of your side-kicks in the adventure. A big gripe of mine is that you dont actually share any of the pleasure in this game with anyone unless you are recording, and even then it's no different than a real life "guess what happened" story- no matter how funny something is, it will always be a minimum of 15% less funny than when it actually happend.
Fallout 3 vs Fallout 4 isnt really a storyline departure. It's more of a "while Fallout 3 was happening, this was happening over here." Now for those who are really reading this review, and know the story, I know you are going to call me out for this not being factually correct. I wont say why because it would contain a spoiler, HOWEVER, no matter how the story arcs align in this universe, the "FEELING" is that this is a different perspective of the same thing- not something new, which is what I would expect.
Is this game worth buying?
Yes, but only if you like to use your creativity and imagination. If you like ribbons, trophies, achievements and tidy completeness- nope, not for you. Find another game.
Keying on my last comment as I wrap this up, this game is not tidy. It's far from it as is the Bethesda tradition on these games. The source of value always comes from the community and it's always the team of fans who move these games to an artistic completion.
I've played about 400 hours on the PS4 and 130+ here on Steam, maybe 100 hours on the XBOX One (I like the PS4 due to my ability to stretch out and play on the couch in front of a 60" HD TV - even though the graphics and audio experiences are sub par compared to my PC experiences).
Haters are going to mostly fall into the misunderstanding or envy bucket when it comes to this game. Either they are envious of the people who have the hardware to play this game at full tilt or they just dont understand the genre of story telling in this series' culture.

So it seems that the folks at CF have [finally] did a bit of necessary tweaking to the game and -- since my curiosity was peaked -- I decided to revise my review.
Like last time, let's go over the key features:
•6 playable races
We were promised 7 at the beginning of the fundraiser, they have finally touched up on that. Racial traits like they discussed still seem to be absent.
•A procedurally generated universe with unlimited procedurally generated planets
After a while, it feels as if it's a copy/paste of the last planet you were on. This also makes building bases/houses totally useless. Good thing there are upgradeable ships and a few missions here and there to make it somewhat easier.
•All content available in online drop in/drop out co-op
To an extent, yes this is true. But if you build a base in single player and want your internet friends to see it on a public server, not gonna happen. Which means you gotta fire up Hamachi (or the Starbound Server feature that's available via the launcher) and start up your own server.

•Generated dungeons full of unique enemies
They worked on a bit more variety on this end, which is good.
•Randomly generated monsters
With terrible AI and are repetitive to no end. This part still is true
•Thousands of items
Finally reached up to that point. I suppose building materials still count as "items"

•A deep crafting system
...Which runs on a mostly currency system, which you lose 50% of when you die. Oh, did I mention there's no means of a bank system? Still haven't fixed this bit since my last review.

•PVP gameplay
PvP in this game is a joke. 90% of the multiplayer community have more or less modded their equipment via Starcheat to one-hit kill everything. <-- You guessed it. Still a problem in multiplayer.

•Own and decorate your own Starship
Which they gave more space via upgrades, a huge problem that should have been solved on day one.
•Develop your own home planet
Still has yet to be implemented in the game.

•Menacing boss battles
Which now take place on maps you cannot edit, so there is a bit of a challenge with this bit now.

•Procedurally generated guns and melee weapons
Which, again, can easily be cuztomized to be stupid OP thanks to Starcheat. I have yet to understand why the devs added playerkill.projectile into their code.
•Farming, hunting and survival mechanics
Now it's time for hunting 101!
1. Keep walking left.
2. Click on the monsters
3. Obtain meat!
•Built from the ground up to support modding
Probably the only selling point. Because does this game sure need it. Still does, however the vanilla version is far less reliant on that end.
•Ongoing free updates
Which are actually frequent! Yaaaaaaaay!
•Multi-platform multiplayer
Basically PC/Mac/Linux multi-platform.
Final note: This game has still been in Early Access since the last time I wrote this review (So basically...I wanna say since 2013-2014?) and the multiplayer community is still as toxic as I remember, which is unfortunate to say. And I really hate to say this, since the game has lots of potential, but it's going to be -VERY- repetitive after a while. My recommendation? Grab a few friends, fire up Hamachi or the starbound server, get a Skype call going, and just enjoy the vanilla version of the game. By no means am I saying this is a bad game, but it could be SO much better. Save your money, folks.

With the recent 'Radiant mode' update and now Steam Workshop integration there's never been a better time to get stuck into Darkest Dungeon. This new mode reduces the grind, allowing you to build a bit faster towards that final assault on the Darkest Dungeon itself, without reducing the actual 'difficulty' of the game. I had actually started a normal game at some point last year, but gave up after around 13 in-game weeks as it began to feel a bit grindy. Started up Radiant mode a couple of weeks ago and had a great campaign all the way to the end, enjoyed every minute of it. Even considering starting NG+ now
The game is still very punishing, and you either have to learn fast from costly mistakes, or do a bit of research on the side. I feel a lot of people put off by the punishing nature of the game could benefit from looking up a guide or two. Personally I had a curio guide open at all times (curios are objects in dungeons you can interact with, but if you use the wrong item on them it can have dire consequences), and did some research on the final unique dungeons so I could know what to prepare for, as at that point I didn't feel like party-wiping with top level heroes just to learn a few things for next time. This way of playing may not be to everyone's taste, but it can alleviate some of the harsh punishment that gets doled out. It's perfectly possible to do a bit of reading up on the different areas and curios etc without spoiling that feeling of discovery and 'clean' progression, it's all about finding a balance that you're comfortable with.
Also, as is well established, the narrator, sound, and art work are all absolutely fantastic. Even the journal pieces you find are worth collecting - each set of six tells it's own short story, with typical literary flair, which you can piece together and read at your leisure back in town. I would advise waiting until you've completed each set before reading through to get the whole story.
All in all I think it's a great game. I can understand the complaints, but Radiant mode addresses a lot of those, and a bit of light reading can help too. I also think the difficulty aspect has been overstated slightly by some. The RNG gods do definitely come out to play, but if you embrace and prepare for that, you'll do just fine...

A great game, but don't expect to actually ever finish it.
Pros:
- A rich, tactically rewarding set of classes with tons of tactics and synergy to discover and explore
- Tactical and deep, yet fast paced turn based gameplay
- Stylish presentation reminiscient of Warhammer Fantasy and H.P. Lovecraft that even low end systems will have no trouble with

- The stress mechanic adds an extra layer of tension and strategy to the gameplay
- Dozens of hours of gameplay
Cons:
- The amount of grinding needed to progress in the later stages of the game is simply ridiculous
- The difficulty ramps up to an insane degree once you get to the highest level dungeons, and tactics that worked before cease to do so
- Managing the equipment of all your heroes, even though they only have 2 slots each, is a chore
- The RNG will very commonly screw you over, with parties being wiped out or wrecked by stress for no other reason than a roll of the dice
- The bosses can either be alright or frustrating bordering on unfair. One, for example, has both the ability to incapacitate one of your party members AND heal itself. Either on their own would be fine, but together they only serve to ramp up the blood pressure.
Overall the game is well worth its full price, but it's not for everyone.

While this game is being sold as a "hacking simulator", a debate will likely rage about what exactly it simulates. In either case, it comes suspiciously close to being a realistic simulation of hacking. So close, in fact, I'm left wondering why the dev didn't go the extra yards to make it inarguably so (maybe something he can shoot for in the future). Realism nit-picking aside, this game is full of very realistic nods to hacker and IRC culture, and in broad strokes, represents some of what goes on in actual exploits. While the experience of compromising systems is streamlined for the sake of keeping it an actual game (again, is it a puzzle game or a simulator?), in that "push a button, get bacon" sort of way you see in "hacker" movies, there was still much in the game that reminded me of taking the OSCP (for those who know my pain, you will find much in each mission to make you smile in that corpse-like rictus you had while laughing at emails and files during enumeration pratice in the Offsec lab).
After a while, I realized I was playing not so much because of the faux-hacking experience, but because there was a rather compelling story unfolding. Can't pick that apart without spoiling it, so I'll critique the gameplay instead (positives first):
This game is hilarious in a sick, twisted way. References to chan and IRC culture litter the storyline. While the majority of gameplay involves limited exploit combinations, there are moments where you don't know what the f**k is going on, and you have to think fast to avert a crisis. If you're into security culture, you'll find your intuition meshes well with the challenges, and you can improv what to do most of the time. It's like a Drunk History version of real hacking, so it's probably an ideal game to play while you're drunk.
People with zero knowledge of hacker culture or basic unix commands and quad notation will walk away familiar with all of the above.
The game is cheap, so whether you enjoy the simplistic, repetitive nature of the "hacking" it simulates, you won't regret the purchase, because it will entertain you regardless. The story itself is worth the price, and the way the story is told using the genre is clever.
If you liked TIS-100 (and I'm a recovering TIS-addict) you'll appreciate this for some of the same reasons, but the games aren't identical by a long shot. In fact, that would be the one constructive criticism I'd like both devs of these two games to hear: if TIS-100 had the narrative of Hacknet, and Hacknet had the coding fatures and complexity of TIS-100, you'd have a seriously ground breaking game on your hands, guys.
Pushing buttons to get bacon gets fairly boring after a while, and the game loses some of its puzzle quality attributes as a result of the limited attack combinations, and the lack of customization or tweaking of exploits and tactics that is the real joy of hacking. If this was never going to be a hacking game, and more of a puzzle game, I wanted to see a complexity progression throughout, instead of a chaotic difficulty plataeu.
Each mission certainly could have involved more manual hacks to achieve both realism and puzzle difficulty, but this would require adding more OS commands to the game, or a limited scripting engine of some sort. It couldn't have been that hard to add a mission where the solution was to exploit weak service permissions, tampering with programs launched by the OS at boot. Perhaps telling the print spooler to reset the system's admin password by re-writing it to launch a file with a "passwd" command in it, or to add a user account with "admin" privileges, something along these lines. A phishing mission, or getting a target to open an email and trigger a malicious trojan embedded in a PDF file would have been fun. These kinds of scenarios would require no "hacking tools", and might actually require the player to struggle. I'd rather struggle than push "exploit" over and over, my only real enemy being the trace timer.
To do this would require more system commands like "touch", privileges to edit, the ability to create files, maybe a basic word processor and the ability to write emails (instead of just reply... to some of them). All we had to work with were pre-existing files, a "replace" command that replaces lines and is too cumbersome, and no manner of scripting available. No complex chains of commands, no writing or editing code beyond some HTML (so I can change "chicken" to "c**ks", but that's not really hacking as much as being a d**k).
Once you get to that long slog of a valley mid-game, it stops feeling like hacking AND puzzle solving, and starts to feel more like grinding mobs in an MMO to get to the next bit of storyline. Each player will have more or less patience for that experience. Exploit tactics become routine too quickly, and the difficulty drops off.

So I've waited for the DLC to come out to see if Firaxis would release an update to fix this game. After realizing that almost nothing is fixed, I've just about had it with waiting for this game to be good. Instead of having a list of every single problem with the game, (for example, how health is displayed, the imbalanced difficulty, how detection tiles are incosistant, enemies are just given buffs later in the game instead of new enemies being designed, etc.)  I'll just list and explain the 4 fatal flaws with this game:
1. PERFORMANCE: If you look at other revieews, other people are having a hard time getting this game to run well. For me its not too bad now, as I noticed that general stability is improved to a good range of 20-40 frames. But that's far from optimal. It's also far from the only thing wrong with the game.
2. CHEATING AI/BAD AI: You can test this out on the first mission with the statue if there is one enemy left and you have a soldier (with no other soldiers nearby to possibly flank the enemy) near a statue. If both of you are in the high cover of the statue, and you move out of sight into the low cover base of the statue, the ai will abandon high cover and go into the low cover base to flank you, even though he couldn't see where you moved before. This makes fighting the AI holy unsatisfying. In addition, the AI in general is easy to predict (when it's not glitching out). Psionic enemies in particular always use their special abilties first before shooting, even if they go out of their way to flank you. Enemy soldiers have no sense of preservation, so overwatching in front of them will never keep them in place.
3. BAD PACING: The biggest problem to the actual gameplay (in both combat and base management) is that the game always forces you in a rush. Got to capture a VIP? Hurry up and get him in 12 turns even though the enemy doesn't even know that you're there yet. Capture this cargo in 8 turns otherwise it blows up for no reason. Did you actually win a combat mission? Tough♥♥♥♥♥♥ the doomtracker's clicking down. It's always rush, rush, rush. There's never a time that the game (and by extension the player) can have a breather to calm down and get his bearings. In the prior game, base management was the way the game calmed down. You didn't have to worry about moving your base constantly that takes 4+ hours to land and take off in each area.
4. LINE OF SIGHT BUGS: The thing that kills this game is the constant line of sight bugs. Literally anytime urban warfare is involved, you can expect to have shootouts through solid walls and ceilings with no visibility. Sometimes cover just doesn't work and you'll get flanked by an enemy who is clearly right infront of your cover. You might move a soldier behind a wall so an enemy won't have a shot on him, only to realize that the enemy can still see him and he will get shot like he wasn't in cover at all. The worst that has happened to me is when I was rescuing a VIP from a truck, and when I came into visual range, the walls of the truck didn't work so I saw the VIP. When the VIP was revealed, the enemies saw the VIP, and since the VIP isn't in concealment, then everyone of my soldiers lost concealment, no less after i made all of my moves. The game is frustratingly unfinished.
There are positive additions to the game, which is what kept me for playing this long. But the more I played it in general, the more I was frustrated at its bad design and terrible stability. This game is unsalvageable.

Pros:
-There are many gameplay improvements over Enemy Unknown, such as a stealth system. The stealth system finally teaches your soldiers to not scream like a baby when they see an enemy until AFTER they fire their weapon.
-Your Scientist isn't a psychopath.
-You aren't juggling plates to appease a board of shady people who apparently think countering an alien invasion is like swatting a fly.
-The workshop allows you to remove most of the Cons below.
Cons:
-The DLC (Two as of this review) are at best lackluster and at worst completely gamebreaking.
-More than half the missions are on a timer, encouraging risk-taking in a game where even the slightest risk
will result in a failed mission.
-Juggling plates is replaced with two missions that are extremely difficult (One of which is timed) either when you're unlucky or at set intervals.
-Personal experience: One Crash to Desktop and one endless loading screen. (However, I did mod the game with the Workshop)
If this will be your first XCOM game:
-XCOM has a reputation for being hard and this game is no exception. If you REALLY don't like RNG, I wouldn't recommend this game to you.
-Also, play on Rookie (Easy). Veteran (Normal) is XCOM/Strategy player/Masochist. Commander (Hard) is for masochists that also don't like winning... or Sectoids. Legend (RNG be with you) is for people who want 100% completion... or people with psionic abilities.
Overall I would say the Workshop really saves this game from a negative review. Removing the timers really made this game fun, so I recommend XCOM 2 with a handful of mods.

By far one of my favourite games of all time. If you're going to buy this, the one piece of advice I can give you is to be patient. This game is brutally difficult, but in a fair way, and overcoming a challenge that you were stuck on is a great feeling. When you fail, it isn't an unfair glitch or broken mechanic that gets you killed, and there's always something to improve on, so that when you finally succeed it doesn't feel like you just wasted your time, there's a sense of fulfillment to it. Dying is just part of the game, and once you accept that, it becomes less of a rage-inducing nightmare and more of an exhilarating challenge.
I'm not gonna lie, I've always been one to choose the easiest difficulty settings in games, but after playing this I realize how much fun a good challenge can be. The combat is exceptional, the world and atmosphere is great and the lore behind it all is masterfully woven together to create a world that is still being avidly debated about to this day, nearly two years after its release and almost a year after its final DLC.
The multiplayer system, despite receiving hate from the community for its differences to the past two games, is still in my opinion very entertaining and innovative. Sure, lag does happen, but no game is without its flaws, and even with occasional lag the multiplayer can still be very fun, especially if you have a friend to play with you.
In short, this game is definitely worth buying, even at full price, because even if you don't enjoy it at first, it will grow on you soon enough, I can vouch for that. My only suggestion other than being patient is to choose a light set of equipment,  as the enemies and bosses in Dark Souls 3 are considerably faster than the ones in the first two games.
Well, I hope I managed to convince you, at least a bit. If you end up buying this game, good luck and have fun!

Sure, the voice acting is terrible, the graphics are a bit sketchy, but dang this game is fun. I mostly play in "Free Mode". What you do is, you create a character, and start out in a quest hub area with some merchants. You can also recruit followers there; additional heroes that you can level up and equip with gear. From the main town, you can leave through a portal, which gives you a list of scenarios or maps you can jump to. These maps are sorted by level, so you may end up doing some of them more than once, but that's part of the fun. As you level and get gear, lower maps become easier, so you get a sense of progression that way.
The game has three main factions you can play as. They're not very well described in the interface, but one of them is sort of human/elf/dwarf, and the other two are different types of monsters. There aren't really tech trees exactly.... like, you don't research things. You purchase up to three masteries from your town hall, which unlock different types of buildings and units. Certain units require certain types of buildings, and then you can upgrade those buildings to unlock additional units. So it's not exactly a tech tree, but kind of.
Combat is interesting. You form groups with ctrl-number keys. You can click on enemy units in the battlefield or use Tab to target. Once an enemy is targeted, you can direct one or more of your groups to attack it (the groups show up along the top, and when you have something targeted, you'll get sword icons for attack). Your heroes have portraits up in the upper left, and their abilities are underneath their portraits. If you have an enemy targeted, attacks and debuffs come up for you to click on. If you have a friendly or one of your heroes selected, heals or buffs come up, or PBAOE abilities if you have them. You can also right-click for context-sensitive actions like attack, move, repair, etc. Finally, you can select a hero, click one of their abilities on the bottom bar, then select a target for that ability. It's way easier to select a target first, though. It takes a bit of getting used to, but once you get the hang of it, it's not bad.
There are three main resources; plants (lyra), silver, and stone. Most military units require a combination of silver and lyra, while most buildings and upgrades require stone. You create peasants to gather resources and build or repair structures, and farms to increase your army size. I don't know if there's a cap to army size, but most maps I've played I ended up with 80 or so and that seemed to be enough. Peasants don't count towards population cap, they just get more expensive the more you build. Towers can be customized to one of your faction's three main subfactions. An elf upgraded tower will heal units, dwarf towers are tougher, human towers have better damage and range, that sort of thing.
Around the maps are chests and special monsters which, when killed, grant quest credit or drop loot. Heroes don't level up just by killing things, you get XP strictly for completing quests or objectives. If you wipe out one of the enemies off the map, you get a decent chunk of XP. Some missions require you to defend one or more towns, others require you to destroy enemies or rescue NPC's.
It took me a while to get the hang of this game. At first it seemed very difficult, espcially in some of the earlier maps (on free mode) which required you two defend two different towns at the same time. You pretty much have to split your armies up, use lots of towers and patrol routes, and keep your economy going. Resources come in clusters, and only one gatherer can be on one node at a time, so you have to pay attention to how many peasants you have gathering resources. Like most RTS's, when resources run out, you have to roam around and set up new outposts.
As you level up you spend points on either combat, magic, or you can mix it up. I don't know how viable a hybrid build is. The gear you find requires points in one of the two main schools, and there's quite a bit of variety. Even two items with the same name can have different stats.
If you click the middle button, you can zoom in to third person view of your main hero. Then you can use WASD to move around. You can select your army and have them follow your main character as well. I find it's kind of fun to run around like that, but if you get into a large battle you'll probably do better zoomed out like a normal RTS. The game has been patched to support widescreen, and they fixed multiplayer. There are a few weird glitches still, like flashing textures in third person view, or a bit of lag in the inventory or merchant screen. Don't click and drag items, just click to pick up and click again to drop.
Quirks aside, this is a pretty fun game. Whether you like RTS's or RPG's, if you spend a bit of time getting the feel for this game you'll probably end up liking it.
