It took a very small team a very short time to make this very small game, and it shows. It might hide behind being retro styled, but it still feels a bit sloppy. I don't mind the retro graphics at all, I have been gaming since 1984, so the retro hits my nostalgic heart. What doesn't though, is the sloppy animations, controls and lack of creativity. Some of you might find this "musical" aspect new and refreshing, but it has been done before, and IMO it has been done a lot better. "Loom" is a game that comes to mind when playing this, and even though it is a very long time since I've played that I remember how much more fun I had in that game than here.
The game itself is a point & click like style adventure game where nobody holds your hand at all (not that it is needed). There is very little explanation of what is going on and how to play the game. It is mostly hidden in some vague clues here and there. For the game itself that doesn't matter much. Most will find out how it works quite easily, and the puzzles you need to solve is also quite easy. Well, at least if you have played a fair share of similar games or point & click adventures in general. It shouldn't take much more than an hour or two on the first playthrough, but if you collect achievements you need to play through it at least twice. I encourage you to use an achievement guide though as some of them are very hard to figure out without any guidance.
There is very little going on in this game, and even less to do. This whole game has less content than most first chapters in any other adventure game I've played. That being said, this game has a "to be continued" in the end, so I guess this is a first chapter too. I just wish that they just made the whole game in one, then maybe it would have a little more meat.
Even though the game in itself is not THAT bad and is built on a good idea (just not done well) I don't feel it is worth its asking price of $6.99 (at the moment of this review). Many might enjoy it and find it original (especially if you haven't played "Loom" or similar games) and many won't mind it being short, so don't base your decision on this review alone. I got it dirt cheap in a bundle and would recommend to look for a deal for this one if you are deciding on getting it.

Wow. So many people complaining about game difficulty and RNGesus.
Yup, this is darkest dungeon. It is hard, it is brutal, and at times utterly unfair. And I just had to write this to defend what I felt was one of the best games that came out in 2016.
You can't prevent yourself from getting critted by mobs and unluckily losing a party member when a run goes south.
What you can mostly control though (with the exception of the darkest dungeons!), is leaving the dungeon and forfeiting the run. Over time, you will progress towards the end goal.
A good tip for beginners: You do *not* have to push your luck if your party is already half insane and dying. There is not that much of a penalty in leaving the dungeon - survive to live another day.
DD is probably not for everybody, and it has already been toned down some to be less grindy than in earlier versions. And champion dungeons now in the latest patch have some really nasty new mobs, so you can't just say there is no variation.
My guess is that lots of players never even got that far into the late game as they were frustrated by the game. DD is brutal, and RNGesus is capricious, but it is never unfair. You can crit the mobs as hard as they can crit you. You can decide when to leave the dungeon and when to push on.
If you hate to lose people (sometimes to an unlucky  dice roll, e.g. like XCOM on certain difficulties), you will absolutely absolutely hate this game, and DD is not for you.
However, if you like hard, fairly grindy (yes this is legitimate) tactic-based games, then you are going to love DD. This is the type of game that you sink ridiculous number of hours in (about 200hours for me so far) because the tactical layer is just so good, and ever so once in a while I keep coming back.
You might curse and rage, but you will eventually succeed at the Darkest Dungeon.

All the puzzles are pretty straightforward, although the music puzzles are slighty more challenging. There is no spoken dialog, and essentially no text either. I came to Half Life with no idea of what it was about.  Just that it was a momentous release in gaming history that I felt compelled to play.  I'm not a huge FPS player, but if a game has a good story then I'm interested.
Because of its reputation I had high hopes for Half Life, but I was a little disappointed.  The game looked better than I expected, but the story didn't really engross me and I found myself frustrated with the game as much as I enjoyed it.  For this reason, because my memories of playing this game are tinted more with frustration and annoyance than any other emotions, I cannot recommend this game.
Firts of all:
Serious technical issues!!  This game and my computer were not best friends.  I had to do a lot of research just to get this game to run.  First of all I had to change DEP and then change launch options in Steam.  I had to remap some controls to get them to work (long jump), and framerate always dropped dramatically whenever I turned on the torch. On top of that the game was constantly crashing.  At loading screens, in large arenas, when there were flashing lights, when a sound effect played.  All sorts of reasons, but constantly.  Like at least 100 times on my playthrough.  Now I could re-open and play the game immediately, but can you imagine the number of save games I had because of the fear I would instantly lose it all?
My other major problem with the game was the control of the character.  Now I suppose this is a 1998 game and the Source version might be better for this, but I found it very frustrating to carefully control the character and unfortunately there is a lot of that needed - so many ledges to hop on to.  Frustrating and tedious.
So did the story and gameplay make up for this?
The gameplay, maybe. Running around and shooting♥♥♥♥♥♥is fun, solving puzzles is satisfying, and I like not having regenerating health.  Though I could have done with a little more guidance at the start. There are no instructions for secondary weapon use, didn't know how to turn on torch - didn't realise there was one! - didn't realise that powering up the suit was equal to armour.  These things aren't obvious if you're new to the game, and you shouldn't have to go online to find this stuff out.
But I suppose that drip feeding you of selected info is part of the Half Life story telling experience.  Which I was unfortunately completely underwhelmed by.  Maybe because there's not actually that much of a story, it's just go here and do this, without any reason behind motives.  Maybe because the sound effects are too loud and the voices too quiet (and unable to turn up volume) so that you can't hear what the characters you meet are actually saying.  Maybe because, I didn't really care about my character - this random scientist who is far too happy to pickup a weapon and run off shooting things rather than use his voice to ask some questions about what the hell is going on.  What would a scientist be more likely to do?
I did finish the game, but more through the feeling that once I'd invested a few hours in it I had to keep going, and the hope that maybe it would all just get better. Maybe the Source version or Black Mesa reboot would be more enjoyable, but I am not invested enough to want to try. I haven't played Half Life 2 yet and maybe that will vindicate this playthrough, though I doubt it as there's not that much of a background story provided in Half Life. You see, I really want to say that this game is worth playing, I can see why it was highly lauded, I just can't add my voice to the praise.
And final little gripe: Female characters anyone?  I can deal with an all-male army, but no female scentists, seriously?

While this game is being sold as a "hacking simulator", a debate will likely rage about what exactly it simulates. In either case, it comes suspiciously close to being a realistic simulation of hacking. So close, in fact, I'm left wondering why the dev didn't go the extra yards to make it inarguably so (maybe something he can shoot for in the future). Realism nit-picking aside, this game is full of very realistic nods to hacker and IRC culture, and in broad strokes, represents some of what goes on in actual exploits. While the experience of compromising systems is streamlined for the sake of keeping it an actual game (again, is it a puzzle game or a simulator?), in that "push a button, get bacon" sort of way you see in "hacker" movies, there was still much in the game that reminded me of taking the OSCP (for those who know my pain, you will find much in each mission to make you smile in that corpse-like rictus you had while laughing at emails and files during enumeration pratice in the Offsec lab).
After a while, I realized I was playing not so much because of the faux-hacking experience, but because there was a rather compelling story unfolding. Can't pick that apart without spoiling it, so I'll critique the gameplay instead (positives first):
This game is hilarious in a sick, twisted way. References to chan and IRC culture litter the storyline. While the majority of gameplay involves limited exploit combinations, there are moments where you don't know what the f**k is going on, and you have to think fast to avert a crisis. If you're into security culture, you'll find your intuition meshes well with the challenges, and you can improv what to do most of the time. It's like a Drunk History version of real hacking, so it's probably an ideal game to play while you're drunk.
People with zero knowledge of hacker culture or basic unix commands and quad notation will walk away familiar with all of the above.
The game is cheap, so whether you enjoy the simplistic, repetitive nature of the "hacking" it simulates, you won't regret the purchase, because it will entertain you regardless. The story itself is worth the price, and the way the story is told using the genre is clever.
If you liked TIS-100 (and I'm a recovering TIS-addict) you'll appreciate this for some of the same reasons, but the games aren't identical by a long shot. In fact, that would be the one constructive criticism I'd like both devs of these two games to hear: if TIS-100 had the narrative of Hacknet, and Hacknet had the coding fatures and complexity of TIS-100, you'd have a seriously ground breaking game on your hands, guys.
Pushing buttons to get bacon gets fairly boring after a while, and the game loses some of its puzzle quality attributes as a result of the limited attack combinations, and the lack of customization or tweaking of exploits and tactics that is the real joy of hacking. If this was never going to be a hacking game, and more of a puzzle game, I wanted to see a complexity progression throughout, instead of a chaotic difficulty plataeu.
Each mission certainly could have involved more manual hacks to achieve both realism and puzzle difficulty, but this would require adding more OS commands to the game, or a limited scripting engine of some sort. It couldn't have been that hard to add a mission where the solution was to exploit weak service permissions, tampering with programs launched by the OS at boot. Perhaps telling the print spooler to reset the system's admin password by re-writing it to launch a file with a "passwd" command in it, or to add a user account with "admin" privileges, something along these lines. A phishing mission, or getting a target to open an email and trigger a malicious trojan embedded in a PDF file would have been fun. These kinds of scenarios would require no "hacking tools", and might actually require the player to struggle. I'd rather struggle than push "exploit" over and over, my only real enemy being the trace timer.
To do this would require more system commands like "touch", privileges to edit, the ability to create files, maybe a basic word processor and the ability to write emails (instead of just reply... to some of them). All we had to work with were pre-existing files, a "replace" command that replaces lines and is too cumbersome, and no manner of scripting available. No complex chains of commands, no writing or editing code beyond some HTML (so I can change "chicken" to "c**ks", but that's not really hacking as much as being a d**k).
Once you get to that long slog of a valley mid-game, it stops feeling like hacking AND puzzle solving, and starts to feel more like grinding mobs in an MMO to get to the next bit of storyline. Each player will have more or less patience for that experience. Exploit tactics become routine too quickly, and the difficulty drops off.

More like an interactive novel for hackers than a puzzle game or simulator, but with elements of both; you will feel haunted putting together what your *actual* role in the missions might have been, and to what extent the Ayy Lmaos were involved.

After spending 180ish hours beating Spellforce+expansions on hard, I was excited to jump into SF2.  This edition contains the core Spellforce 2 and the first expansion (Dragon Wars).  Overall, I really like the updates they had made to the game.  They worked out a bunch of the issues from the first game (ie. Avatar not attacking, losing units when switching maps, etc.) and made a polished sequel that rivals the first in terms of being enjoyable.
GRAPHICS:  9/10 - The game is from 2006 so again, cannot expect much here.  I was pleasantly surprised with the world design and the characters themselves.  For those using a newer system, the FOV console command will be your best friend!  At the start of each level, you'll find your FOV pretty limited.  Do this:  Ctrl + ] to access the console.  Type "UI:SetCameraFOV(1.060)" to back the camera out a bit.  The higher the number, the further out you go.
STORY: 10/10 - The Spellforce storyline has really come along since the first game.  You could see them hitting their stride as you went through the expansions of the first game and it continues here.  Really enjoy the story!
GAMEPLAY: 9/10 - I personally like the new leveling system as it allows more customization between all characters (not just your avatar).  I wish they would allow full customization for all characters but your fellow party members all follow a certain path with only a few skill points allowed to be distributed by the player (ie. Whisper will go Dual Swords, no matter what).  I understand the need to direct the player towards a healer, tank, etc... but maybe allow for a mode where experienced players can completely customize the skills. Part of me would just like to let this game go unreviewed, but, apparently, that part has been stifled and gagged by the other part writing this review. And I guess that's a proper diagram for how this game makes me feel: Split down the middle.
Having just recently (re)played Loom, I could draw the obvious parallel there. But Loom A) didn't have an inventory system and B) only used 8 notes in a way that forced you to learn the spells along with Bobbin. Yes, it may be nitpicky for me to slam the inventory system and (mostly unused) music notes in this game, but a majority of it was unnecessary.
Finding Teddy gives the player an alphabet with which to "communicate" with the world and get real feedback from it sometimes. You've already given the player a voice and immersed them into the experience. Why cluttler it up with items and allies? If the inventory was simplified or even removed (and absolutely scrap the cat and the fly. They're cute, but only perform two or three tasks the whole game), leaving only the alphabet, the game would have been so much more intuitive. Instead of hopelessly using every item in your inventory on every seemingly interactive thing in the game (in ADDITION to typing musical messages at them, or maybe using the cat or maybe using the fly), the player would have nothing but their words. It's a welcome limitation.
Actually, let's expand on that: The whole experience feels like a game that could be strictly text interactions, but has inventory items and allies shoe horned in. Instead of giving the text-based genre new life, it just causes a loss in momentum when you have to open your inventory on every screen. It causes the game to fall flat by having too many options.
Don't get me wrong, I did enjoy this game. But I feel like text based games and point and click adventures are most rewarding when you hit on those "Ah Ha!" moments, of which this game has very few *because* of its varied mechanics. I do ultimately recommend it, however simply because of the graphics and ambient music.
It's too bad that it's an insult to your visual and music talents when the core mechanics are convoluted and sometimes frustrating. No spoilers, but I wanted the whole game to be just like the ending. Hell, the ending itself could have gone on a lot longer. Adventure games are all about using your key mechanics to keep the player forgetting that they're actually playing a game. And it felt like the ending put me in that immersive stranglehold only to let me go after a short time.
Final word: Never leave your player wanting to be strangled more. Let's hope the sequel brings out more of the positive aspects of this game and reduces the detritus.

Well, well, well, what do I  say about this game.  Currently I am only level 13 so keep that in mind.
Positives
I will start off with the positives. It is a lot of fun, when it works ( more about that later).  The classes all seem to have something fairly unique about them in the form of their "2" ability.  The graphics are great if you are a fan of this style and I personally am.  The game offers a great deal of variety in the different zones and mobs.  The loot is also very varied and has seems to have a cool aspect to it already.  The game is clearly meant to be played with friends and it is a great deal of fun when playing with them. Dungeons are very cool structures that match the zones that they are in.  The dungeons thenselves are pretty easy though ( so far at least).
Negatives
With all that being said this games have a lot of negatives.  The biggest one being the servers.  I have fine internet, I play other games such as League of Legends, Black ops 3 and so on with little to no lag.  This game on the other hand...  This game has some of the worst rubberbanding ( when your character appears to be doing something, but then magically appears somewhere differnet and you never did that thing at all).  I was clearing a dungeon with my friend and I was fighting the boss then all of a sudden I somehow was outside the room and my friend said I never even hit the boss.  On my screen I hit him multiple times and almost killed him.  Also there is a houe building aspect to the game, but with the rubberbanding i was completely unable to use it.  I would place blocks and they would dissapear from my inventory only to reappear about 2 seconds later and the block would be gone.  The game is already getting grindy (which MMO isn't though...) and I am only level 13.  It is essentially doing dungeons over and over to get resources to make something. The dungeons are failry cool though so it is not that bad. the bosses of the dungeons though are very easy and seem to have no mechanics.  I am not sure if this is true because once again, rubberbanding.
Overall
This game is fun to play for a little while, but only if it works.  My two friends have no problemwith lag and they love the game.  It will eventually get very grindy twards the end. Wish their was a "sort of reccommend" button, but overall I had a decent amount of fun playing the game. I am not sure what the end game is but it appears to be a raid style dungeon.  Now granted it will probably never have an endgame as good as World of Warcraft, but it isn't anywhere near that level.
Final verdict
It is a solid game, but has some of the worst servers I have ever played on.

I am extremely disappointed in this game. I went into this game with hope from Fallout 3 & New Vegas. I wanted to enjoy this game. My opinion comes from a couple of different areas, from small nitpicks to things that ruined my experience I had to turn to the Nexus to fix most of my issues.
Negatives:
- Terrible perks - In previous Fallout games the perks provided much more interesting choices where as in this game they generally just provide your character with better values in damage or taking it.
- Side Quests - Most quests just make you go to a location and kill everyone there. Little depth in choices if at all. Fetch quests are dull and repetitive.
- Main quest - Considerably worse compared to previous games. Only 4 possible endings in Fallout 4 and considerably more in previous games.
- Factions - Factions feel overwhelmingly trusting of you as well as a most of the quests being just bad. Only 4 factions in the primary game, this is just... atrocious. Fallout NV had 12+ which had unique quests and interfered with the main quest and ending.
- Dialogue - Charisma normally just tries to persuade others to give over more caps. No option to ask for more details when questing, even if you say no you still get the quest. Most side characters have no dialogue, no back story, nothing interesting.
- DLC - Too expensive for the quality and quantity right now it would cost me £100 to buy all of the DLC, that's just appalling.
- Paid Mods/Creation Club -  Just a joke. Offers mediocre overpriced content when better mods are available on the Nexus for free. 2GB update and likely to require more space. Genuinely feel disgusted that Bethesda do this.
- Difficulty - Lazy aspects to survival mode, had to add mods to make it playable in my opinion. My immersion broke to often.
- Companions - Some interesting ideas but feels very formulaic.
- Enemies - Little variation. Most harder enemies feel like bullet sponges.
Positives:
- Nexus Mods - Fantastic range and some incredible detail went into some of them.
- Survival - When I added a few mods it made the game quite good in its survival aspects.
- Random encounters - a few were quite unique and provided some interesting gameplay.
- Combat - Smooth and solid.
Overall it's an okay game and I have had some good moments. However it is the worst Fallout game in my opinion and is considerably anti-consumer. Ones money is better spent on a game like the Witcher 3, Skyrim (not special edition) & Fallout New Vegas.

This isn't a point and click adventure nor is it a puzzle game. This is just some weird handicapped version of both genres.
The controls are just bad - you never know where you can click and where you can't because almost everytime just nothing happens. Sometimes it's because you're clicking slighty off an invisible boundaries of a screen exits and other times you're just clicking on a background non-playable object. And also you don't move like you would expect from a point and click adventure. No, in this game your character just stays on one place until you click on one from maximum three clickable objects or exits (there really are max three clickable objects per screen including exits). Most of the time the controls are just confusing and not responsive (for example your inventory just pops out when you are trying to select one of your companions). So that's enough for the point and click part.
The puzzle part is even worse. There are just two types of puzzles - one is a primitive combination of one item from your inventory with some environment object (most of the times in a pretty random manner). Second type is this "original" playing with horrible sounds (which represents alphabet) when you have to speak with beeps to the others and make them do something. This is not only boring but also very tedious and the climax is a final boss which is just a totally random use of this game element.
Throughout really short gameplay (about 2 hours max) you are accompanied by a horrible music which consists of short loop of polyphonic beeps. This in combination with an ear-tearing beeps from objects interaction in the game (even the inventory pop up sound is annoying) makes you want to turn the speakers off.
PROS:

CONS:

-Bad controls

Even though this game has, compared to most newer games, pretty bad graphics, this game is still one of the best FPS's out there.
Half-Life's story goes like this: You play as Gordon Freeman, your average every-day scientist, working in the Black Mesa Facility. Your co-workers have been studying mysterious creatures and resources from another world, known as Xen. One day, Gordon is tasked with pushing a sample crystal from Xen into an Anti-Mass Spectrometer. Upon doing this, the whole facility ends up going to hell, and Gordon eventually ends up having to travel to the other end of the facility, fighting creatures from Xen, and eventually soldiers along the way.
Upon reaching the other end of the facility, the Lambda Complex, Gordon must travel to Xen, where he is tasked with killing the powerful being, known as Nihilanth, who is holding a portal open from Xen to Earth. After Gordon fights his way through various other Xen creatures and the Gonarch (A giant head-crab) Gordon eventually gets to the Nihilanth's chamber, where he kills the Nihilanth and is then greeted by the G-Man, a mysterious being who has been watching over Gordon throughout the game. He offers Gordon a 'job' which Gordon can accept or decline. Accepting will put Gordon into stasis, where he would later wake up during Half-Life 2, and declining will have Gordon face an almost-endless army of Alien Grunts, without any weapons, and would certainly die.
Despite being extremely old, Half-Life is definitely still one of the best games ever created. 9.5/10. Definitely play it, and all the expansions/sequels. You won't regret it.

If you plan on buying this game, or have any interest in playing at all, PLEASE HOLD OFF.
(Note that this is a review for the current state the game is in)
When I originally heard news of Starbound, my hype boner extended into the stars above and could not be held down. It was basically Terraria. In Space. With promises of being much more. Hell, the game was developed by ex-Terraria developers. That lead me to thinking: How could developers of Terraria mess up their game by simply putting the damn game in space? At that point it didn't matter to me. Numerous friends already bought the game and bombarded me with "WHY DONT YOU HAVE THIS GAME YET????", and, "PLAY WITH ME!!!!!" They never seemed to run out of things to rave about the game. So I bit the bullet. I bought the game, immediately installed, and dove into the universe of Space Terraria. What could possibly go wrong?
Now, onto the gameplay.
Diving head-first into singleplayer, the game introduces you to the quest system by having you retrieve your first item in the game from a storage compartment on your spaceship. Simple enough. The controls seemed nothing out-of-the-ordinary. WASD to move around, spacebar to jump (even if jumping momentum seemed clunky), clicking to interact with various "blocks" and items, yadda yadda. Already the game seemed like SpaceTerraria. After beeming down to my starting planet's surface and completing the remaining "tutorial" quests, I had a cozy little camp with a fire and a crafting bench. I made myself a pickaxe and mined some of the obviously low-quality starting ores (copper, iron, and some coal). Using coal to power my spaceship, I had already travelled to a few planets, and scavenged enough resources to create a distress beacon: the item required to summon the game's first boss. A penguin piloting a giant UFO dropped from the sky, and my first boss battle had begun. It ended just as quick. As it turns out, the boss was extremely easy to "cheese," as a trapped myself in a small dirt box with a one-block opening to swing a weapon out from. The battle was done and over with as quickly as it started. I climbed through the various tiers of armor and weaponry with extreme ease, and had "beaten" the game faster than I imagined.
The controls, as I stated were nothing bizzare: WASD movement, click on things to interact. No complaints in the controls department aside from extremely wonky jumping mechanics. The gravity on a planet's surface varied with different planets, but none of that seemed to matter. Jumping sends you in the same, awkward arc that is extremely hard to control. Getting the right trajectory and angle of a jump is tedious and waaaay harder than it needs to be.
Combat is simple. VERY simple. Like, boringly unsatisfying. Swords, spears, axes, it doesn't matter. You click when a monster is within the weapons reach, and repeat. No RNG (besides criticals) to spice things up, you click. Click, click, click. Guns are no better. All the guns seem identical. Oh, and did i mention you click? Click to win!
Being a Terraria-esque game, being able to build a house or base is to be expected. This is where the game shines, in my eyes. Having thousands of different planets to explore means having a diverse selection of landscapes and atmospheres to contruct an ideal spaceport or cozy cottage. Along with diverse landscapes comes diverse building blocks. Want to build a tropical-themed, thatched-roof hut on a frozen, desolate moon? Knock yourself out! A intimidating and looming stone castle on a world of cotton candy trees and talking birdmen? I dont see why not! Even after I "beat the game" and reached the highest tiers of tools and armor, building a giant fishbowl for my geisha fish girl and defending it from sphincter-headed dinosaurs was a gaming experience like no other. Make sure to bring your creativity and roleplaying mindsets with you if you venture into Starbound.
Multiplayer was a different story entirely. The game was oodles more entertaining and replayable with a crew of friends to join up and plunder the universe together with. I could write an entire book of the crazy-fun times I had with my buds in Starbound, but that almost feels like another game entirely, and I'm here to focus on Starbound.
Unfortunately, I'm starting to run out of good things to say about poor Starbound.
Being an early-access game, paying for and playing an unfinished game is to be expected. However, even for an early access game, the whole thing seemed rather...underwhelming. While it might just be the dying-down of my hype, the game was not what I expected it to be at all. It seemed very unfinished and empty. Even a group of good friends couldn't fix the empty gameplay. But the advantage of an early-access game is seeing the addition of new, exciting content before your very eyes, right?
Starbound didn't get that memo.
Call me cynical, or whatever you will, but I feel lied to. Cheated. Scammed. The developers over at Chucklefish were on an incredible streak of fixing and patching the game tailored to the findings of the community and playerbase. This streak continued for months. Then♥♥♥♥♥♥hit the fan.
Developers started leaving, including one of the big-men-on-top. The developers took their patches and fixes with them. Progress on the game seemed to come to a standstill. However, the development website promised and displayed what content was being worked on and would "soon" (my definition of soon =/= Chucklefish's definition) be added to the game. Every day, the website showcased new features being worked on. Features that never seem to see the light of day. The website is a catalog of broken promises and wasted potential. The last "update" posted to the site is a collection of GIFs of monsters with promises of "...updates soon!" These no longer mean anything to me, and are just the developers' way of waving my money in my face.
In summary...
Starbound is a sandbox, Terraria-esque game that takes place in outer space. Immersive exploration is plagued with lackluster gameplay backed with broken promises of updates and constant new content. Playing with friends makes things a bit more bearable, but feels like you're bringing an umbrella to protect yourself against a rain of flaming dookie.
As much of a♥♥♥♥♥♥I've taken on this game, I sure had a hell of a time eploring and building. Who knows? Maybe the developers will but away their hashpipes for a bit and work on the game. It might have a brighter future ahead of it, but for now, spend your money elsewhere. I truly await better times for this game :(

Love it, hate Alien Hunters DLC.
Positive:
In my opinion many aspects of the global managment portion of the game have been improved. There is still a sense of urgency in getting things done, but no more <insert nation here> whining and leaving the global defense effort because you were a month late sending them a satellite.  Many of the unit upgrades do cool things and give you interesting ways to position yourself and approach a battlefield. Largely the research and development cycle of the game hasn't changed, which is good because it was solid in XCOM enemy unknown. Plus points for 'squad upgrade' on buying certain basic weapons and armors. In enemy unkown this was a little more tedious with having to acquire said items per soldier using them.
The regular combat loop I believe has also improved over enemy unknown. The covert segments at the start of most missions allows you to map out the field and the locations of some enemies before you engage. More opportunites for set-up and field control. Also the pre-combat enemy teleportation that was present in enemy unknown is gone. Though this was hilarious in enemy unkown, it was also very annoying, I am sincerely glad this has been fixed. Enemies now actually patrol the map before first contact has been made. The addition of a scout class, which can remain in this stealth mode is also very welcome, especially for those who like to utilize long range snipers.
Negative 'Alien Hunter DLC':
My gripe with this DLC, the cause of much rage and disappointment, is the addition of "Ruler" units. This is an enemy unit with the capability of being your best friend over the course of several missions, and by best friend, I mean mop the floor with your guts. While the concept of having a recurring enemy or nemisis is interesting, I find the implementation here unappealing and very irritating. I believe what I mean will be clear, with a short description. While "Ruler" units come in many shapes and sizes, they share the annoying trait of "Ruler Reaction". This allows them to make a FULL action for every HALF action one of the player units makes. For instance, if you move a unit, the "Ruler" unit will then be able to move and attack, and it will do so immediately. This is the same for overwatch, hunker down, fire, or any other action made available to the player. So, for a standard squad of 4, if you really wanted to, you could give the "Ruler" unit 8 moves on the your turn, and then it would still get to move on its own turn. I percieve this as an attempt at creativity, but it comes off as formula breaking and leaves a sour taste in the mouth.

It keeps the same frustrations from XCom and adds to them. Unfortunately, everything comes down to a dice roll, which is not good for a strategy game.

The randomly generated maps means you often end up with a map which makes the objective nearly impossible unless you bee-line to it and pop every pod of enemies on the way.
Not to mention you sometimes simply don't have any cover when the enemies have plenty of full cover - then again you can't rush to it without risking popping another pod. This wouldn't be a negative if it was intentional map design, but its not, its randomness which screws the player.
There's a lot of positives, the new classes are pretty good and fit the Guerilla style very well but the game has fatal flaws at its core which feel like a much bigger drag on enjoyment than with Xcom EU/EW. I've put hours in, finished it on veteran/ironman and tried a second playthrough but it's hard to try and enjoy honestly.
Not to mention the DLC so far has been atrocious.
The mod community is pretty good though.

Graphics are fairly simple but detailed and well done. The music, though, is quite short with repetitive loops that get tiring/annoying after a while. Would be nice to load your own tunes..Devs!
It's fun for a few relaxing minutes or perhaps hours. Not much brainwork. The multiplayer levels are usually half-players/half-bots (randomly selected, you cannot choose a team) so keep that in mind.
Lastly, it could do with a bit of network optimization as I get packet losses frequently or low ping even though the computer connection is fairly idle.
Maybe not at full 4€ price but on sale I'd get it..

Honestly, I ORIGINALLY downloaded the game to get the free TF2 hat but as I kept playing I realized it was really fun! Read other reviews and I'm REALLY not sure why so many people downvoted with the complaint "P2P" Because I see 0 elements of P2P. I believe what constitutes a p2p game is a game in which you are UNABLE to progress or effectively play through it without submitting to microtransactions and me and my girlfriend have been playing together a LOT, and it's very balanced. I did notice SOME features require you to pay a fee but those are completely optional and don't effect it's core gameplay at all, if you manage to beat the quests it rewards pretty handsomely whilst remaining a decent and enjoyable challenge, and it reminds me a lot of Zelda mixed with a hint of dota, a dash of WoW, all packaged in a cute and charming chibi type art style. I've only picked it back up for the last few days so who knows I might run into a bullcrap p2p feature the further I get but so far it's all 100% fair, provides fluent and interesting gameplay with no overcomplication whatsoever, and rewards you for strategy, focus, and quick thinking in the battle system and keeps your brain moving with decent and simple puzzle mechanics. I highly reccomend this game, especially if you're looking for some good old fashioned monster slashing, dungeon crawling, puzzle solving action. Now I haven't tried PVP yet and I actually don't intend to unless it's with someone I'm positive didn't lazily and stupidly go blow 100$ on really powerful♥♥♥♥♥♥(can't understand why someone would do such a stupid thing but I don't try to be judgy honestly you do you) But even then I doubt I'd be into it, the experience and impression this game left on me didn't leave me wanting to fight other people, don't get me wrong, love PVP centric games but to me this isn't that kind of game, this is a game thats fun to play with friends where you work together to fight monsters both big and small. Some people complain it's grindy but I like it like that in this case because it's so much more rewarding to craft or virtually purchase the item I want knowing I worked for it (when I say purchase I mean it's in-game currency, havent spent a PENNY on this game) Note to new players, once you reach soldier rank I reccomend purchasing recipes from the hall of heroes, the merchants in the bazaar will COMPLETELY rip you off, most of the good items are 3,000 sometimes in upwards of 7,000+ crowns for an item you can make yourself or earn in a quest. The only thing the merchants are good for is for you to dump all of the garbage items for some free crowns and MAYBE a decent recipe or necessary crafting material that you might have trouble getting monsters to drop in arcade mode. Anyways, I sincerely reccomend you play this game, the whole thing is such a great tribute to classic video games, even the music, there is legimate 8-bit elements in the orchestra of some sound track pieces. Hope you enjoy and keep those shields up :)

Though many people say AOE2 is the best in the franchise, I actually think AOE3, with the abundance of exotic civs from 2 expansions and unofficial mods, has surpassed that timeless classic.
Graphics: AOE3 looks great at distance, even up to today's standards. That's mainly due to the excellent using of lighting effects (shades and HDR), the textures and animation on a closer look however, are on the same level as Age of Mythology (kinda obvious they used the same engine), which is a little bit dated. But it doesn't hurt at all, for some of the best RTS games like SupCom and COH aren't beautiful up close either.
Sound: Soundtracks are awesome, definitely the best in the franchise and probably one of the best in the whole genre. I especially love the track of revolution event, it pumps me up so much that I want to punch a freaking baby in the face. Sound effects are even more impressive, more so the sound of canons. God how I love the sound of canon fire in this game, every shot is like the mixture of bass solo and Morgan Freeman monologue coming out of a subwoofer. Pure heaven.
Gameplay: Quite different from the previous games. The tempo has been speeded up a bit. Range attack becomes the mainstream and melee the sidekick. Resources are down to 3, which I think is acceptable. Civs feel very distinct from each other especially those from different continents. Balance is marginally okay, with 3 pretty OP civs and same amount of trench tier ones. Many new features like homecity and card deck building are actually great fun and add a lot to the strategic depth. Online games are quite stable and smooth, and usually end in stomping.
Mods: I love the mod Napoleonic Era to death. This along with another mod called The War of the Triple Alliance make me rate this game among top 3 RTS on my list. Holy crap the additional civs and features are mindblowing. I really wish for 2 things, that we will one day get Steam Workshop for AOE3 and one day the devs of these two mods be contracted by Microsoft to combine the mods into an official expansion, just like The Forgotten to AOE2.
Community: Friendly, steady, small in size but alive. That's all I can say.
Conclusion: Don't let nostalgia get the best of you. AOE3 is different from AOE2, but in a good way.

I will start off with the positives. It is a lot of fun, when it works ( more about that later).  The classes all seem to have something fairly unique about them in the form of their "2" ability.  The graphics are great if you are a fan of this style and I personally am.  The game offers a great deal of variety in the different zones and mobs.  The loot is also very varied and has seems to have a cool aspect to it already.  The game is clearly meant to be played with friends and it is a great deal of fun when playing with them. Dungeons are very cool structures that match the zones that they are in.  The dungeons thenselves are pretty easy though ( so far at least).
Negatives
With all that being said this games have a lot of negatives.  The biggest one being the servers.  I have fine internet, I play other games such as League of Legends, Black ops 3 and so on with little to no lag.  This game on the other hand...  This game has some of the worst rubberbanding ( when your character appears to be doing something, but then magically appears somewhere differnet and you never did that thing at all).  I was clearing a dungeon with my friend and I was fighting the boss then all of a sudden I somehow was outside the room and my friend said I never even hit the boss.  On my screen I hit him multiple times and almost killed him.  Also there is a houe building aspect to the game, but with the rubberbanding i was completely unable to use it.  I would place blocks and they would dissapear from my inventory only to reappear about 2 seconds later and the block would be gone.  The game is already getting grindy (which MMO isn't though...) and I am only level 13.  It is essentially doing dungeons over and over to get resources to make something. The dungeons are failry cool though so it is not that bad. the bosses of the dungeons though are very easy and seem to have no mechanics.  I am not sure if this is true because once again, rubberbanding.
Overall
This game is fun to play for a little while, but only if it works.  My two friends have no problemwith lag and they love the game.  It will eventually get very grindy twards the end. Wish their was a "sort of reccommend" button, but overall I had a decent amount of fun playing the game. I am not sure what the end game is but it appears to be a raid style dungeon.  Now granted it will probably never have an endgame as good as World of Warcraft, but it isn't anywhere near that level.
Final verdict
It is a solid game, but has some of the worst servers I have ever played on.

This is a good game for a good price. In a lot of ways it's similar to a scaled down version of the recent X-COM games. Essentialy it's a mixture of base and roster management with some exploration (mostly linear) and tactical RPG battles. It also shares with X-COM the notion that your roster is mostly expendable and mitigates the fact that the gameplay is heavily RNG dependant by having new recruits show up every week (which are free to recruit).
From the few negative reviews, I see that this is where most people's complaints come from. Personally I don't understand this complaint because on the default difficulty it's impossible to lose the game no matter how many heroes you go through, so even if you are terrible at the game, I would hope that eventually you'll figure out how to come out on top.
In addition to this there is a highly detailed wiki that gives plenty of information about the enemies in the game and how to avoid most of the negative effects from the curios that you will discover, so really, there's no excuse to suck so badly at this game that you have to post a negative review about it being "too hard".
I honestly don't have much serious criticism about this game. It does exactly what it says on the tin and it does it well. In my 22 hours of playing I haven't encountered a single bug. The only thing I would say is that how much you like this game is going to come down to if you enjoy the battle system or not - If you do, then it's a definite "must by" if you don't, then stay away, because that's the core interactive mechanic of the game.
In fact, my only criticism is an odd one - If you are good at this game and find yourself managing your stress well and keeping your heroes alive, you'll find that your heroes quickly out level the facilities they need in order to keep par with the enemies (blacksmith, guild). I often have to start 2-3 extra teams just to collect more treasure in order to upgrade so that I can progress. This is kind of annoying as even with just focusing on those upgrades, I can quickly get several heroes up to level 4 or 5 before I have even gotten the 4th blacksmith upgrade. The net result of this is that you end up stalling on veteran missions to do apprentice missions because medium apprentice missions will give nearly as many resources as medium veteran missions, even though the facility cost goes up dramatically.
Oh well, it's a minor problem in an excellent game, and hey, if I do eventually lose some people at least I have lots to replace them with.
TL;DR - If you enjoy the game combat (watch a stream) and can imagine yourself doing that for hours on end, then buy this game.

is a package of three Hacker Evolution games: the original one, Untold and Duality. All of those three also come with source code, written in C++.
If this review is too long for you, I suggest you to only read the first paragraph about the game's content and the final verdict at the end.
you have to crack servers, bounce, steal info, solve puzzles, "fight" other hackers and avoid getting traced. Hacker Evolution series consist of pretty standard hacking games like Uplink or soon-to-be-released Hacknet. As a big fan of this kind of games, I enjoyed HE as well.
of course, if you wanted to play hacking games, you wouldn't buy this. The main feature about this pack is the source code. It is written in C++ and it can be opened with Visual Studio (as well as the Community Edition, if you don't want to pay for the full version). This pack is intented for programmers or maybe people who want to learn programming and (like me) prefer learning by looking at something that is already made and figuring out why stuff works the way it does.
If you are a programmer or just somebody who wants to know how to code, I really recommend this to you. You can't get a chance to look at some game's cource code very often. It includes three games so you should be occupied for more than enough time with the code.
If you're in for the games, I only recommend you to buy this if you want to support the developer as you can get the games much cheaper and the DLCs aren't included.
Also, I sincerely apologize that this review is not as lenghty as my other reviews are, it is exceptionally harder to review a source code than a game. Thank you for understanding and I hope you liked my review.

Space combat a la Star Conflict but with capital-scale vessels, slower and more methodical. Ships have a variety of tactical abilities to use. Full range of ship movement, but handles more like a submarine then a spacecraft: your ship autocorrects its pitch, and can move forward/back, strafe left/right, rotate, and up/down. Maps are divided into "lanes" that must be jumped between using a warp drive ability. Progression is exactly like Star Conflict or War Thunder, there are three ship manufacturers and using a given ship earns you XP which is then spent on higher level craft of that manufacturer. A thinking person's shooter, with a far more forgiving damage model then Star Conflict.

This is Bayonetta.  I'm going to assume you're familiar with the game, or have read other reviews of the gameplay itself.  It's a seven year old game, it plays the same as I remember from the XB360, both the good and the bad.  We'll leave it at that.
As for the port, my experience so far is positive.  I haven't seen a ton of bugginess/laginess that some have reported.  I did have some mild issues running it on my Alienware Alpha (i3/860M).  Vsync caused huge jumps/slowdowns, rendering it unplayable while turning off Vsync led to the (predictable) tearing.  Really bad tearing.  Was able to get "Fast" Vsync enabled through the Nvidia Control Panel, and at that point it was good to go at 720p, medium quality, 60fps.  Could probably turn it up, but I'm fine there.  It's basically a "laptop," don't expect more out of it, and for a game like this smooth is more important than pretty.
Also runs at 1080p, max quality, perfect 60fps on my i5/1060-6GB.  Expected, since again it's a port of a seven year old game.  But no tearing, no slowdowns, no glitches, nothing.  Just runs fine.  I was worried.
It's $20 as of this writing.  For a newly released port it's a fair price.  It's as fun as I remember.  The plot is as ridiculous as I remember.  Recommend.

Gameplay/Levels: This is an old-school arcade style game in the vein of Donkey Kong & Donkey Kong Jr. You need to get from the bottom left corner to the top left corner to beat the "boss" character on each screen. For variety, the exact level layouts are randomized, and there are 4 different "boss" types, each of which has its own attack modes. The thing that confused me at first is that each "Level" of the game actually consists of 4 screens (so, it will say "Level 1" for 4 screens in a row; you can think of it as Level 1-1, Level 1-2, etc.). The true "boss battles" shown in the trailer/screenshots are fairly far into the game (20 screens or so).
Controls: The controls/movement felt a bit stiff at first, but have become much more comfortable after playing for a bit. It's important to note that when you hold down the run button, you don't jump as high. You often need to jump first and then hold "run" to move faster in the air. Also, when you collect three blobs of the same color in a row, you can use the "boost-jump" button, which allows you to get to slightly higher ledges. I think it would be more rewarding if the boost took you a bit higher, as some of the needed boost-jumps are very tight. (I should note that there is also a "secret" move that I had overlooked at first, as it's not explained in the instructions. Once I discovered it, I was able to navigate through the maps much more quickly,)
Other notes: There are unlockable characters and super-powers in the "Store." You need to amass quite a lot of points to unlock the super-powers, though.

Though many people say AOE2 is the best in the franchise, I actually think AOE3, with the abundance of exotic civs from 2 expansions and unofficial mods, has surpassed that timeless classic.
Graphics: AOE3 looks great at distance, even up to today's standards. That's mainly due to the excellent using of lighting effects (shades and HDR), the textures and animation on a closer look however, are on the same level as Age of Mythology (kinda obvious they used the same engine), which is a little bit dated. But it doesn't hurt at all, for some of the best RTS games like SupCom and COH aren't beautiful up close either.
Sound: Soundtracks are awesome, definitely the best in the franchise and probably one of the best in the whole genre. I especially love the track of revolution event, it pumps me up so much that I want to punch a freaking baby in the face. Sound effects are even more impressive, more so the sound of canons. God how I love the sound of canon fire in this game, every shot is like the mixture of bass solo and Morgan Freeman monologue coming out of a subwoofer. Pure heaven.
Gameplay: Quite different from the previous games. The tempo has been speeded up a bit. Range attack becomes the mainstream and melee the sidekick. Resources are down to 3, which I think is acceptable. Civs feel very distinct from each other especially those from different continents. Balance is marginally okay, with 3 pretty OP civs and same amount of trench tier ones. Many new features like homecity and card deck building are actually great fun and add a lot to the strategic depth. Online games are quite stable and smooth, and usually end in stomping.
Mods: I love the mod Napoleonic Era to death. This along with another mod called The War of the Triple Alliance make me rate this game among top 3 RTS on my list. Holy crap the additional civs and features are mindblowing. I really wish for 2 things, that we will one day get Steam Workshop for AOE3 and one day the devs of these two mods be contracted by Microsoft to combine the mods into an official expansion, just like The Forgotten to AOE2.
Community: Friendly, steady, small in size but alive. That's all I can say.
Conclusion: Don't let nostalgia get the best of you. AOE3 is different from AOE2, but in a good way.

EDIT:: I have neglected to edit this review since I was able to play, and finish AC Unity. Still rage-filled so here we go.
This game is terrible. I'm saying this as an AC fanboy, but this game is terrible. Ubisoft should be held to a very high standard, especially with AC games; however, AC Unity does nothing but disappoint and confuse me. My dislike of AC3 and Black Flag were because of the weak protagonists, but Unity takes it to another level.
Arno (who's name I couldn't even remember 3/4 of the way through the campaign) is an utterly flat, boring and blatantly trasparent attempt to recreate the magic of Ezio Auditore. Arno is brash, unlikeable, and maintains an immense level of stupidty to further the 'plot' of this game. The sad thing is, most of the characters in this game are about the same, or worse.
Elise, your on and off companion throughout the campaign, is an equally flat, idiotic character. She is a plot pusher that comes along whenever the storyline stalls out to the point of it being laughable. Aside from that, she offers precisely nothing to the game whatsoever apart from decent voice-acting.
Overall the story is boring, drawn out, and confusing. I never knew who I was killing and why I was killing them, also, whenever you complete a contract your victim does not speak to you (like in previous AC games 'requiescat in pace') but Arno somehow absorbs information from their brain into his. This leads to weird out-of-body experiences that are never explained. Or maybe they were, I was half-asleep from boredom while playing through the story mode.
I would say that this game's redeeming quality would be the world, and don't get me wrong, Paris is beautiful, but even with a GTX 970 I can barely manage 24 fps on this poorly optimized insult to AC fans everywhere. Ubisoft should be ashamed of this title, and I truly hope that the next AC game actually works. Try harder next time or you may just kill the franchise.

The game in short: You have to send groups of four heros into randomly generated dungeons and archieve certain goals in these dungeons, e.g. explore 90% of rooms or clear 100% of rooms or find certain items or kill the dungeon-boss.
You can have a total of 30 heroes on your roaster who can be of 15 different classes. The game treats your heroes  as replacable / disposable assets. Most of their specific stats profile is class based and thus not unique, carefull picking of skills to level up is not part of the game, unlike most RPG games. Instead the true individualisation of the heros is not done by the player but occurs randomly when they gain certain treats or "quirks", e.g. the ability to fight better v.s. certain types of enemies or the fear of a certain type of dungeon.
This lack of intentional customization is actually a clever design choice: The heroes being pretty random it does not hurt so much to lose a certain hero in combat, there is little investment in them. On the other hand the random quirks are to be considered carefully, when chosing the right team for an expedition.
There are 5 different locations of the quests / dungeons, four of them are basic ("warrens", "weald", "cove", "ruins") and one is a "darkest" ultra-hard offering the final quests to complete the game. The dungeons of these different locations differ in map-layout and the types of monsters and interactions encountered.
Each of these basic locations will typically provide several quests per in-game week of different length and difficulty to choose from - picking the right quest is part of money and hero management as quests will need equipment that comes at a cost and they will exhaust ("stress") your heros.
Typical things you will consider when picking a quest:
- Are the heroes you will need for a certain quest well-rested or still stressed from their last expedition?
- Do you own the right trinkets to equip for a certain quest?
- Is the trinket you will gain as a quest reward worth the investment and the risk?
Combat in darkest dungeos is turn based, your four heroes agains at most four foes.
Each of the four heros you send on a quest will be at one of four positions / ranks in your "battle order". Certain skills can only be used in certain positions. Some classes of heroes fill differnt roles depending on their position. Also, during the combat heroes can be moved from their position by the player or by an opponent's skills which will change their available skills.
I could go on and on about the details but I hope to have given you an impression of the complexity of this game that requires lots of strategic and tactic considerations.
If you like strategy / puzzle games (and dark humor) this is likely on for you.
One word of warning at the end though: This game is hard. I only play it on easiest difficulty as a casual enjoyment and it is still more challenging than other games on their harder setting.
My verdict: Both thumbs up, ingame time >100h and counting.
Update: I now own both expansions and I am still very happy. The new content fits in well with the base game and I can recommend to get the "whole package".

I found this game on kickstarter about 3 years ago and when I saw it I was just overwhelmed by it's art and by the idea and the atmosphere, unfortunately at the time I didn't have any money to contribute to the team.
When the game finally got released on Steam, I got it right then. The day it got released, I bought it and after finishing the campaign for the first time now, I just want another reason to play this game. I never want this game to die and I want more games done by the studio about this world. I want there to be a connections, as loose and silly as they may be, I want it.
Why did it take me almost 130 hours to finish the game once? Because I kept starting over and over and over. Whenever a new update hit the game, I started anew. The Cove got released? start a new game. New characters? start a new game. Town events? start a new game. I don't regret doing so, because I enjoy the lore, the narrator and the gameplay so freaking much. I took some time between updates or because the game got stale at times, but I always came back. The memory of the darkest dungeon was etched into my mind and soul and I will play this game again, anew. In a few days, maybe weeks, maybe months, when the new update, the crimson court, comes out. But the time WILL come when the darkest dungeons calls out to me. And I will heed its call.
About the game:
Storytelling:
The first thing you hear in the opening is the amazing narrator, the voice of Wayne June and he will be your best friend through the game. Whether you ace through a dungeon or lose all heroes to madness, he will be there to guide you and remember you of your goal and ambitions. He will tell you about the lore, town events, bosses and everything else. His voice is the thing breathing life into this game and which elevates this game from being "pretty good" to "absolutely amazing".
The Art Style or graphic:
Somewhat edgy, dark and gruesome and yet incredibly beautiful and intriguing. I've played a lot of games throughout my life but this is still my favorite graphic. It just fits, it doesn't require much power from your computer and still does everything right. It helps deliver the atmosphere of the game and it does an incredible job at it. It's fitting and makes this game as special as it is.
Last but not least, the gameplay:
The game is somewhat Rogue-like, but only to a minimum extend. Every dungeon is a new gamble but I always had the feeling that experience, preparation, the knowledge of skills and the use of trinkets paid off immensely. When I first started this game, I didn't know how a good party would look like, in the end I didn't even have to think about it anymore. At the start of the game I only took as much provisions with me as I needed to survive, meaning food and torches. At the end of the game I took multiple items with me to interact with curios, because they can make the difference between life and death.
Knowing which classes interact well with others was another point that I had to learn, but is extremely rewarding if you have it memorized. For example, the cultist has the ability to Mark certain enemies (which is especially helpful against tanky foes and bosses) and there are a few other classes that deal additional damage if a target is marked, best example is the Bounty Hunter or the Arbalest. Figuring out what class excels in which area will reward you in the long run and that is exactly how it should be.
Many people claim that some dungeons can be lost based on a coin flip or a roll of the dice, that is true..to an extent. I seldom had the feeling that the game was "unfair" by any means. Every death I had, I had because I was careless, not well enough prepared or just screwed up my whole team compilation for that particular dungeon that I was heading in. You get punished for not thinking your turns through, if you choose to deal damage to all enemies instead of outright killing one, then you have only yourself to blame. Kill one enemy at a time and don't try to kill all at once. Don't be greedy, be careful and mind the enemies and their attacks.
After this long review, all I have to say is: One of the best games that I have played in all my life. I will continue to play it and I enjoy the game. Thank you, Red hook, for this great of a game. Blessings to you. I'll give the game a 11/10.

Dark Souls III just does NOT live up to the hype of the previous "Soulsborne" installments.  If I were to rate every game of the series from best to worst, it would go Dark Souls > Dark Souls 2 SOTFS > Demons Souls > Bloodeborne >  Dark Souls 2 Vanilla > Dark Souls 3.  Yes, that's right, in my opinion Dark Souls 3 is the absolute worst of the series.  You may ask, "why?" and so I shall tell you why.  Dark Souls 3 comes after "Bloodeborne" but is a different type of game.  It is a SOULS game, but yet it attempts to be something it is not.  It attempts to be fast paced like Bloodeborne, but suffers because now only fast paced weapons are viable in PvP.  PvP has now devolved to battles of who can roll through the most attacks.  It is not uncommon for me to have to roll through 6 consecutive attacks at a time just to land one on an opponent.  There is also less variety in viable, useful builds for PvP.  The equipment from the "Ringed City" DLC greatly outperforms all the other weapons and armors in the game.  However, there is little reason to play through the "Ringed City", because the level design is boring and unimaginative.  In Dark Souls 2, the DLC was phenomenal, and probably, if counted on its own, the best content in the entire Souls series.  The Dark Souls 2 DLC had such amazing levels such as Brume Tower, where you would walk miles in the sky on a dangling chain tightrope from tower to tower, and gradually make your way down into the dungeons with very challenging bosses such as "Blue Smelter Demon", "Fume Knight", and "Sir Alonne", widely regarded to be among the best boss battles in gaming history.  Dark Souls 3 cannot compare to these fights at all.  The vanilla game is largely rehashes of boss battles from previous games, but contrary to other games, VERY little is NEW.  Wheras the reimagined Ornstein fight in Dark Souls 2 was purely optional, in Dark Souls 3 the reimagined Ornstein fight is part of the MAIN story, and one of the final bosses at that!  It just sucks the ingenuity and sense of wonder out of the game when you make your way through a level only to find out you are fighting the same boss you fought in the last 2 games!
I would not recommend picking up Dark Souls III unless you are absolutely in love with the Souls games.  A fair warning however: I was in love with the Souls games until I played through Dark Souls 3, and dare I say it, it ruined the series for me.  I have no intention of buying a new title from FROMsoft unless they get back to their roots.  Dark Souls 3 feels more like a very long demo instead of a full game.

Finding Teddy is a rather average 2-D pixel adventure game.  The most notable gameplay feature of it is it's primary puzzle-solving gimmick, which may take you a while to catch onto, and discussing it much is a spoiler since this is a short game at around 2-3 hours long.
The most interesting part of Finding Teddy for me are the character deaths.  There are various points where a failed puzzle solving attempt will result in an NPC killing the main character and they are effectively unsettling.  It's a good use of the disparity between the game's visuals and your expectations of what a failed puzzle will bring.  I recommend anyone playing through the game to try to trigger them, especially since dying has little negative impact on progression.
As for the rest of the game, it just didn't pull me in.  The puzzles, locations, characters, and so on kind of washed over me and weren't particularly memorable or brought me much enjoyment.  Not a bad game, but I only finished it because I though the deaths scenes were interesting and  I wanted to see how the game wrapped up.  I don't think I would've completed it if were much longer since it had a tenuous grip on my attention.  A thumbs-down, but not a wholly negative review and if you're interested in puzzle games and can grab this in a bundle or on the cheap, it's probably worth an install.

Well, Finding Teddy was a cute little game that was included in a bundle I bought a while back and finally got around to trying out. The story itself is cute/quaint, and the sort of tale you could expect to come from the mind of somebody's little daughter (or having been written for somebody's little daughter). That said, the strength of this game was definitely the puzzles, which incorporate music into riddle form fairly brilliantly. Once you realize what is happening, you wont have any real issues solving them, but learning them initially will take most people a bit of time, and you will need to pay attention in order for the final puzzle to become obvious. Outside of that, there are also objects you find that you will need to progress, much like every point and click game, which this is (albeit, done in a refreshingly different fashion).
All told, this game probably took me about an hour and a half to finish, and there is replay value for the completonist. In fact, I get the sense that other things are unlocked in NG+ (unconfirmed by me personally).
Anyway, I found this game to be a pleasant surprise and can easily recommend it.

So, just a quick warning, this is a ramble. An unorganized, opinionated rant. If you want the tl;dr, it's that XCOM 2 is highly moddable, so if there's something you don't like in vanilla, I can gurantee you'll find a mod that fixes it for you. And while the arguement that "you shouldn't have to mod it to make it better" is definetely valid, I feel like a lot of the complaints are those of personal preference, as opposed to inherent flaws.
________________________________________________________________________________
There's something I really do have to adress here, and it's that a lot of the negative reviews seem to stem from the idea that this game isn't like the Long War mod from Enemy Unknown/Within, and that the mission timers are too restrictive. Aside from being personal preference, they're valid reasons to dislike XCOM 2, but at the same time, both of those problems can easily be changed with the plethora of mods out their. Hell, the True Concealment mod fixes the timer issue, and I've used it nearly since launch.
It seems like a lot of people were really hoping for this to turn out like Long War, which, for the unfamiliar, was a mod that expanded upon the original game so much that it could've been compared to the Enemy Within expansion. Multiple base assaults and defenses, new UFOs, weapons, classes, skills, missions, enemy types in the form of "bosses", alien research systems, all contributed to, well, a longer war. Overall, it just added so much to an already great game.
XCOM 2, however, is not Long War. It's not Enemy Unknown or Enemy Within. That might seem like an odd thing to say, but that includes the mindset and strategies you'll be using. You're a guerilla force now. The aliens kicked your♥♥♥♥♥in the first war. ADVENT is their puppet government, controlling the populaces of several large, advanced cities, with the rest of humanity scattered about in small rural towns and the wilderness. As XCOM, your job is to now get as many resources as you can scrounge up, break down the Elders' plans, and free humanity from these ADVENT-burger-advertising ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s.
You don't have the resources of dozens of first world countries to back you up. You don't have highly trained military veterans. What you're working with are scrips and scraps, the bottom of the barrel. You're a resistance, a bunch of rag tag, xenophobic individuals, who really hate those ADVENT burgers. You don't have the luxury of time on missions or on the geoscape. You have the turn timers, and you have the Avatar Project, basically you're doomsday clock. Once that thing is full, you have anywhere from 10 - 20 days to make a dent in their research before you get a classic game over.
XCOM 2 is a game about guerilla warfare. You have to beat the time. Obviously, this won't sit well with some people, and again, I encourage you to take a gander at the modding scene. Aside from the expected gameplay changes, there are some really great quality of life mods, such as Numeric Health Displays and Show Soldier Icons. And don't even get me started on all the soldier customization options. Seriously. In my current campaign, I'm rolling with Cole Train and Mr. Torgue, in addition to various Halo and Titanfall armor pieces. The mods are the established meta of this game, and it's a meta that you can choose.
So, overall, yes. I recommend XCOM 2. It's a fun game, highly customizable, with a lot to do. There are some mods that I'd encourage you to download before even playing the game, or at least to look at them. Grimy's Loot Mod, ADVENT Ascension, Capnbubs Accessories Pack, Free Camera Rotation, any map pack, Free the Hood, Numeric Health Display, Quiet Bradford, and True Concealment are all mods that I use in my current campaign, in addition to a large number of other mods. I'd recommend that you check out the XCOM subreddit and ask some questions if you need any help. Great community.

As an IT person, this game is redooooooooonk!
Sorry, but I can't help getting white-girl excited about Hacknet and its command-line hackerism shenanigans that are so engrossing and believable you'll start looking over your shoulder.
The game is structured around a command-line interface using Unix commands, a sort of Baby-*nix if you will.
Now, regular *nix users may criticize it simply because it's a reduction of the standard command set(switches and variables aren't implemented), but to newbies and occasional users like myself, the illusion is complete. I also appreciate the fact that it builds automatisms (like using cat for reading text) that I never really acquired - we're just missing grep and we'd have a party here,
The connections are easily made by clicking on a node in the network "map", although more hardcore players can also choose to type in "connect" followed by the IP address of the machine they wish to access.
From what I have seen so far, the writing is fascinating, the design supports the immersion experience very well, and I almost feel like I'm using my regular work tools - in a really badass way!
I feel that there's almost an educational value to this game. Suppose there was a system administration course built within this interface... wouldn't that be stupendous?

There seems to be a lot of complaints about aspects of this game, which I personally haven't experienced. The common performance issue seems to be random to an extent, with my build using the FX-8350 (overclocked to 4.7), and a GTX 960. The issues may be related to higher resolutions, since I run mine at 1080p with drops below 60 fps happening only on loading screens.
The common complaint of a "countdown" timer on everything is a bit misconceived, as it's not really an issue. The avatar project hitting it's countdown gives an enormous amount of time to complete a mission to delay the project before a game over actually happens. Timers within missions result in a mission loss, which is 99% of cases is pretty much meaningless. Timers within missions were put in place to increase the pace of the game, rather than people slow playing. I played XCom enemy unknown, and slow playing was 99% of the game; it was boring.
The ongoing complaints over the timer on the Avatar project are more of less focused around having a "limited amount of gameplay", this is again false; as you can play the game non-stop and never have the Avatar project complete. In fact my first play through included me unlocking everything possible in the game, and yet upon completion had 1 bar on the avatar project.
Personally I find this game far less challenging than Xcom Enemy Unknown, and at a faster pace. There's far more variety in this game than EU, especially among the classes.
It's impossible to make everyone happy with this game, but I feel there's far more improvement in this game. You have FAR more variety among both soldier classes, and enemies. EU only included a handful of enemies you encountered on every mission, while XCOM 2 there's a wide variety. There's just more to this game than previous generations.

More importantly, the game doesn't have nearly enough players at the moment. I have never seen more than a few people playing each arena and this is simply not enough for enjoyable gameplay. The game does feature bot players too, but they are extremely stupid and provide pretty much zero challenge.

After beating the game, I feel like I can write an accurate review finally.
Combat(6/10): Combat is more difficult than previous installments. However, for all the wrong reasons. It's more difficult because the camera angle makes it impossible to see who is about to attack you half the time. Also, when someone is pointing a gun at you, it let's you know when they are about to shoot (sometimes). I say sometimes because half the time, it doesn't even show that someone is pointing a gun at you. Also, unless you are in combat, you cannot dodge bullets from snipers. This is a massive flaw because they have the most accurate 1800's rifle you will ever see.
Story(1/10): Absolutely and utterly disappointing. As a huge fan of the AC storyline, beating this game and watching the credits roll made my jaw drop, again, for all the wrong reasons. Your character outside the animus basically no longer exists and doesn't really tell you why you're searching for this "antagonist" in the first place. Then, it hardly touches any of the Eden story and explains nothing about how the pieces got into the hands of the "antagonist". The story is basically about how Arno is trying to avenge the death of someone important to him. No twists. A five year old could have written the story to this game.
Mechanics(8/10): The mechanics are much better than other AC games, but still have some flaws. Going through a window is harder than it should be. Going into cover is generally worthless because you can't go around a corner in cover, which defeats the purpose most of the time. If you are seen by someone you can literally just run away without any sort of trouble. Just keep running and you eventually lose them. No need for fancy tricks when you can just outrun the guards.
Unlockables (2/10): One of my biggest pet peeves with this game. About 80% of the best armor is locked with absolutely no way to unlock it besides playing Club Competition, which ISN"T EVEN OUT YET. God knows when they will release it and when they do, it'll probably be bugged to hell. Extremely infuriating because I have about 500,000 in game currency and nothing to spend it on. To give you an idea of how fast you can get the best gear, my friend had a corrupt file and had to restart. Doing a few heists and missions, which took about 2 hours max, he was almost the max "level".
Co-op (3/10): Co-op has so much potential, but there are about 11 co-op missions and 7 heists. These aren't exact numbers, but you get the point. For a game that focused so heavily on co-op, they skimped heavily on the co-op missions. Honestly, the only heists you should be doing are the most difficult ones. The only thing that changes is the level of the guards. So if you do a level 1 heist, there will be 40 guards. Do a level 5 heist, and there will be 40 guards. Since you have to sneak around anyway, it's basically the same thing except your reward is about 10000% greater.
Classic.
