I want to love this game!!! I really do!!!
This game is so amaizing!!! It features little cute and chibi knights in armor that goes in dungeons, defeats cute monsters , get money and materials and then return to town to socialize with other cute knights or buy stuff from various shops.
It all sounds great, it really does and I really would wish to continue in this format but I can`t unfortunatelly!
You see, Spiral Knights is a MMORPG puzzle dungeon crawler, main focus being not on the classic leveling up with XP but with Armor Type of leveling (simillar to DCUO end-game, if you played DCUO) where you gather blueprints, craft armor and weapons at Alchemy ATMs and complete your remaining ranked quests. It also features a free-form dungeon system where you have no specific objective other than farming for Crowns (in-game currency) and/or materials.
And since it`s a MMORPG of course that relies heavy on grinding for F2P players and on microtransactions for so called "whales" (rich players who can afford anything in the game and who doesn`t bother with grinding too much).
You will feel this grinding wall around Rank 2 to 3 where you will need to farm Alchemy Orbs inside Elite Dungeons (and even this difficulty doesn`t guarantee Alchemy Orbs, like it should) or farm Crowns in Normal and Medium difficulty dungeons (or even on Elite) so you can convert those said Crowns to Energy, at an Energy Depot.
I stopped playing and caring about this game at Rank 6 to 7, where I was supposed to farm Elite Alchemy Orbs to craft my gear. I considered that is simply not worth this much farming.
Let me explain why:
You see, each piece of your gear, to be able to craft it, it requires 3 Alchemy Orbs (these Alchemy Orbs are of different rarity, depending on the Rank you are and what you want to craft) that costs 400 Energy.
At Energy Depot, 100 Energy values around 8,600 Crowns. For rank 7 you would need 400 Energy so, 4x8,600 = 34,400 Crowns. Remember that you need to farm these Crowns only for 1 piece of gear and there`s 5 pieces in total: Helmet, Chest, Sword, Shield and Pistol.
5x34,400 = 172,000 Crowns.
You`re supposed to farm your @ss for a total of 172,000 Crowns to be able to obtain a total ammount of 2000 energy!!!
And that`s only to rank for Rank 7 which precedes Rank 8 which is the last one.
Also, did I forgot to mention that armor has different types of strengts and weaknesses for different types of enemies?
So if you want to craft a different set of armor for a different type of enemy, and you`re rank 7, guess what?
Another 172,000 Crowns to farm!!!
Isn`t life just great???
Yeah, this is the reason, I simply cannot recommend this game!
Grinding is over-excessive in this game, when it should be somewhat moderate.
Not too easy but not to hard either.
For any other Spiral Knights fans and active players that sees my review and don`t agree with me, I am deeply sorry!
But the game it is how it is, at the moment. There`s nothing I can do about it!
I`m just a single voice that may or not be heard!

Here is my review of this game that I've played for so long during the years, and no, this won't be a "The game is dead fug OOO/GH" (has +4000 hours in the game, yes I do have a hell ton of play time, but I'm not here to complain, I'm here to review) so sit down and enjoy this small (large) text of mine :)
The early game of this game is extremely fast to go through, and is quite okay in terms of balance until around the last parts of early game, but at this point, you'll have an upgrade to the next tier, which won't even let you notice the difference, its a fun introduction to the game, everything's new, and there is a lot to explore, from doing your rank missions that give you a slight introduction to the game's mechanics, and other elements, although, like most MMORPGs or RPGs in general, there will be alot more lacking in these tutorials that you're better off finding yourself or other higher ranked players.
Usually regarded as a very balanced stage in the game, you deal decent amounts of damage, and it doesn't takes long to kill anything, your T2 equipment is good all along the tier, but here is where the tedious grind begins, getting those
orbs to make your progress into the late game (Tier 3) its really a headache, but its possible, even easier with the help of friends, and if you're a solo player, its not impossible, don't give up, it'll be worth it :) the bosses in the Tier might be a bit challenging for a new coming player in this tier of armour, but again, nothing's impossible, there's also friends and higher ranked players that can help.
Usually people say this is very broken, either its too easy or too hard, there's different opinions, skill matters more in this tier than the others, you now have the amazing feeling of power of getting your first 4 star weapons and armour, seeing how the difference in stats between Tier 2 and 3 is so noticeable, but as you might be packing a punch now, so do your enemies, a non careful player can get killed within a matter of seconds (mostly in the vey last depths, first depths its okay) and another very tedious grind appears here, the very last "Hall of Heroes" people seem to quit the most when in this stage, but its not so extremely complaicated as people say, Eternals are the most common kind of orb drops, so much that you might even find one or two while doing the grind for your upgrade from Tier 2to Tier 3, lol, but there is a nother very tedious grind, which is that of Radiant Fire Crystals, whih are only obtainable in the very last depths of the game, that is in my believe, the biggest issue with the leveling system, but with friends, its not as difficult, and the last normal challenge
Lord Vanaduke, the last normal boss of Spiral Knights, and arguably the best money maker, arguably as Operation Crimson Hammer is also a graet money maker if you have alot of eternals. And so many more things to do and learn, up to ou to find out :)

So if you are having trouble hearing nodes, you might have a hard time finishing this game
All in all I quite enjoyed this game, it took me about 3 hours to 100%, and then an extra hour for a last playthrough, it ran very smooth and lived up to my expectations, I give this an 8/10

After hearing a lot of positive stuff about Bayonetta I was eager to see it on the PC, since I've never owned a console.
First of all, the game doesn't have any problems for me on Windows 8.1, a core i5 4460, 16GB RAM and a Radeon Rx480. I've experienced no frame drops/bugs/glitches or other things, people are reporting. It always ran with 60 FPS at max settings in 1080p. Though this shouldn't really impress anyone, since this game is over 7 years old. Still, I have to say that for such an old game, it looks decent (aside from some Video sequences which are only in 720p and pixelated when using a higher resolution). The character models are quite detailed and the environments look also nice to this day. However some of the effects (fire and smoke) look pretty dated and ugly. Another small downside, is that even the ingame cutscens are in 30 FPS. And while this isn't a big deal, I hope it'll get patched in the future. Using Keyboard and Mouse as your input devices works also quite well. I actually preffered K&M over an Xbox 360 Pad. Overall I experienced a decent PC port.
Now let's talk about the gameplay. I've heard a lot of praise about this game. Some people even called it the best spectacle fighter in existence and what not. I admit, that the only other game I've played in this genre was Metal Gear Rising: Revengenace and just from the gameplay aspect I found it to be just as good if not better. I would describe Bayonetta as competent, though there are a lot of things which muted my enjoyment. The first and most severe thing being the awful quicktime events. It is really frustrating, having to repeat entire sections of a bossfight, because you missed a split second QTE, because you didn't know which button you were supposed to press. Sometimes the QTEs appeared out of nowhere, during a supposed cutscene and I missed them, since I simply weren't prepared. Another thing are some "rooms" where you have to fight the enemies. Sometimes you just have a narrow hallway, with two intermediate bosses, that frantically try to hit you. The fact that the camera controls aren't very cooperative doesn't really help. There is also some ridiculous platforming, which isn't some much defficult as it is tedious. Sometimes the angle of the camera is so awkward, that you don't see where you're jumping and fall into your death. One other thing is, that there are no loading times (even from a nomral hard drive), which is good of course. The problem is, that there is no trainig room where you can see all the different combo moves while practicing them. You only have a training room during the non exisitng loading screens. You can of course look up each combo individually in the menu, however this is a really clumsy way of doing it. I wish, they have included the loading sequence as a normal training room.
Segments, which could have been completely scrapped, are the aouto scrolling sequences, they neither require a lot of skill nor are they particularly fun. They are just flimsily disguised turret sections. I also don't understand the games save system. Fractured Space can be thought of as a moba-esque, action oriented, team based space shooter. I had the chance to play it this weekend as it was both on sale for half off while also being free to play for the weekend. Overall I would say it is a good game and has potential. I'm still sick of early access in general, but am willing to try it out when free. I am going cover the good and the bad so make sure not to make assumptions until reading it all.
The match making functionality is buggy, unreliable and only allows you to play with a single friend at a given time. Some of the game systems feel shallow and unexplored, such as the crew system which I think is a great basis for a system though I would like to see more management or customization within the crew members, slightly more in-depth RPG elements. I would also like to see more maps or game modes as there are currently only two in game, one of which has been disabled.
The controls feel well thought out and intuitive. Movement as well as combat feel authentic and not blown out of proportion, even though it is science fiction some level of perceived realism is nice and it works well in this case.  The User Interface feels crisp and I like the look and feel of everything overall, it seems polished.
As you progress in level you earn experience with a given ship manufacture as well as credits to spend on upgrades and ships. I have only unlocked the cheapest ship for a single manufacturer so I cannot speak to the pacing of the progression and how long it takes to unlock new ships. Though if you want to progress to higher tier ships you may be sticking with a single manufacturer for a while, unless you fork out some cash.
I still need to play a few more games to get an idea for the balance of ships, mostly up until this point I have seen the standard entry level ships as most of the players I've encountered have been newer players who started during the same free weekend.

XCOM2. What can I say? It's a good game that I'll play every now and then but it does have its own set of annoying quirks. Overall I would recommend this game to anyone that enjoyed XCOM: Enemy Unknown.
The Cons first:
- Frame rate that bogs the game down. The game ran fine when you start out but it will eventually slow down until the characters are moving and speaking in slow motion. I thought it was my old PC initially until I heard that others are facing similar issues. It's annoying but I've learnt to live with it.
- Long load times in the Skyranger. When your squad is heading to its mission or coming home from one, expect the journey to take some time.
The Pros:
- Great story. XCOM lost the first war and now they are fighting as guerillas. The twist and the role reversal explains most of the mechanic changes in gameply such as the mobile base and the time it takes to do anything from picking up supplies to contacting resistance camps. It also explains the intense demand on the scarce resources that you have. Every decision you make now truly have palpable consequences. Ignore a research item too long and your squad just might pay the price because they don't have the needed upgrade.
- Concealment. I like this new addition to the squad. It's always nice to see an ambush plan come together nicely and don't for one single moment that you can stay in concealment throughout the mission. It's just illogical. Do you really think that alien species that came across galaxies to invade your planet will be dense enough to not notice you are out to sabotage them on missions? Concealment is just an added perk for you to get the jump on the enemies once per mission and to give you that very little leg up at the start of a mission. Think of it like a single use weapon or ability. Then you will learn to appreciate it more.
- The new classes. They are pretty much balanced and I often have a hard time deciding who to bring. I usually bring 2 snipers when playing XCOM:EU but now having 2 snipers seemed to be crippling the squad. Snipers were a little overpowered in XCOM:EU and with 2 I could pretty much cover my squad all the way but in XCOM 2 the changes made snipers clunky to use for short range combat. I had to pick another ranger or specialist to even things out depending on the mission. In XCOM:EU grenadiers were too often missing their shots to be very helpful but in XCOM 2 they could mean the difference between a successful or failed mission. Their grenade range and demolition ability really helps your squad to get kills.
- The ramped up difficulty. This is the very reason you are playing the game now, is it not? Sometimes it's frustrating but it is always rewarding to have a mission go according to plan. Even if a mission starts going south, it's almost always possible to salvage it. Love it.

If you were a hardcore Long War player, you can kinda get closeish to it with enough mods but the game probably won't be for you. If you weren't a hardcore Long War player, occasional bugs aside XCOM 2 is a complete and total improvement over EUEW in my opinion. Something as simple as your squad taking overwatch shots one at a time makes it almost impossible to go back to EUEW after playing XCOM 2 without getting frustrated.
Mission timers can sometimes feel a little cheesy but are pretty much never short enough to make you feel like you have no option but to over-rush, mostly the classes are conceptual improvements over the vanilla EUEW classes (though as fun as swords are with the right balance tweaks I do miss the original Assaults sometimes) and, blasphemous though it may be to some, the removal of the air game is frankly good riddance. it that you realise how actually-kinda-dull the air game really is.
With that said, there are plenty of minor gripes. Shotguns are a little too strong in relation to assault rifles, I used to play a lot of riflesaults in EUEW and expected I'd want to do the same with blademaster rangers but it's just suboptimal to do so. Swords are stupid weak in comparison to concealment rangers. There are other problems too, but I can't really bring myself to complain too much about them purely because every single problem I've had with the game so far has been fixable through mods, .ini tweaks or a combination thereof.
Thoroughly and wholeheartedly reccomended whether you played/liked EUEW or not, but do be forewarned that it's got a bit of Skyrim syndrome. The vanilla game only feels fun until you've played the game absolutely plastered with mods, at which point going back to vanilla feels empty and weird.

If  you are looking for a single-player RTS/RPG hybrid with way more emphasis on the RPG elements, then you might find this game appealing. I bought it because I had been led to believe it is similiar to Warcraft 3, which is more or less true: There are heroes, and there are different races. I have not played the game for a considerable amount of time so I will not comment on the story.
What I will comment on is what is probably the laziest programming I have ever seen in a game. The game has 3 modes:
Campaign, where you play through the main story and can save at any time.
Free mode, where you can play through other campaign-ish maps and custom campaigns at your leisure.
And Skirmish mode, which is just straight-up RTS against bots or on Lan.
Having gotten over an hour and a half into the main campaign with barely any RTS whatsoever, I decided to try out skirmish mode. The insane thing is, after doing some digging, I found out that you CAN in fact save, but only through using the case-sensitive console built into the game. So the game is perfectly capable of saving, but apparently it was too much work to add a friggin save button. This is seriously the laziest thing I have EVER seen in a game from a major developer/publisher, especially since they've had years and years to patch it in.
As for the RTS part itself, it's rather simplistic, you build buildings to unlock units and you can make heroes. You can't upgrade any units and the hero skills seem horribly unbalanced. You're better off sticking to Age of Empires 2, Warcraft 3, or any of the other RTS/Strategy games if that's what you are looking for.

I liked it at first but after playing for a while and seeing what it's all about, I have to say I'm very disappointed.
Let's put aside the terrible RNG system for the moment (worst I've seen by far) and focus on the gameplay.
The "First" XCOM game (The first by Firaxis anyway) was alright. It couldn't touch the real first X-com game in terms of atmosphere and gameplay, but it was alright.
At first glance, XCOM2 has some improvements, namely in the graphics and customisation of soldiers to some extent (Though they have put more voices in the game, there are still only voice actors for British English, American English, Australian English, German, French, Italian and Spanish soldiers. Nothing for Japanese, Chinese, Russian, African or any others. Still, it's better than the "first" game in that regard.
XCOM2 takes place some time after the story of the 2012 game. The aliens have taken over the world and run it in an EU/Communist sort of way, rife with propaganda and harsh punishments for non-conformity. Funny, since I finished XCOM and seem to remember kicking the aliens' heads in. A bit of disparity there which is not explained.
The part where XCOM2 really falls apart is in the gameplay. Gone is the hidden, underground XCOM base. Gone are the fighters and thus, the UFO interceptions.  Now you have the "Avenger" which, quite amusingly, looks a lot like the flying aircraft carrier in the Avengers movie. The idea is to liberate humanity in this game utilising guerilla tactics and working with resistance cells and black markets to secure victory. To this end, missions will appear on the map and you will fly to them in your mobile base when they are offered, avoiding any UFOs that are tracking you down and unable to shoot them down yourself. The joy of storming a downed UFO to secure tecnology and corpses is notably abscent and replaced with more of the pop up "some stuff is going on, click this botton to do a random mission and be punished if you ignore it" chores. It just doesn't feel like XCOM. Whether this is a conscious effort to leave the old behind and embrace the new, is unknown, but it certainly feels like it.
I find myself modding it a lot and I'd thank god if I believed in one for putting steam workshop into the game. I just had to get rid of the "Avatar" timer... a timer which will continually tick down, pushing you to complete the game as fast as possible.
Overall, there is just nothing really new to this game, despite the obvious (slight) graphical updates. It's a lackluster title which has me pining for the good old days of XCOM where you could sneak up on aliens properly and they didn't get a free turn to go and take cover after YOU spotted them. We had cover back in the oldest days of XCOM too you know... it was called "standing behind a wall". Oh and the cover system? Even worse than the first reboot game - now soldiers will shoot through floors, trees, walls and over solid objects, with no attempt at all to ever disguise that fact.
This game is just so lazy in my opinion. It could have been so much more, but after the relatively good reboot of 2012, it's just a resounding "meh" in terms of scope and direction - more of the same: out with the good, in with random pointless stuff that they will insist is an improvement.
I bought this game on sale and still feel a bit ripped off. While there is some fun to be had, there is far more in terms of frustration. And modding. Lots and lots of modding to "patch" this game's glaring, chore-like gameplay.

I thought this was the perfect sequal to Enemy Unknownl; they added all the soldier customization, map randomization, bug fixes (mostly), and mission type variation everyone wanted. The ability to choose soldier classes is great (through some minor training) as well as the ability to save soldiers you make to a character pool. The loading times are rather long- I have all settings at the lowest and there are still pretty intense frame rate drops at the begining of mission cut scenes. The central command map is atrocious. Every time you need to travel farther than a contintent you have to finagle the whole thing jumping around far too quickly and putting you at the bottom or top of the globe. That part really handles poorly.
With all that said I would still put this game in my top three and highly recommend it to any fan of strategy games. If you are new to the genre I'd highly recommend XCOM: Enemy Uknown first. The apocalypse (of any short) has become one of videogames favorite landscapes to draw their stories, which would be awesome if so many times the writers and creators didn´t seem to show a very sheltered way of looking at life by avoiding all the real horror that will come in such worlds. Dead Synchronicity is not one of those games.
The game starts slowly, you don´t remember who you are and it would seem things aren´t that bad. Until a few minutes in the world starts showing it´s true color. Sex as a transaction, predatory people taking advantage of the weak, death on every corner, a shady governemnt in panic... The game holds no bars and even the protagonist is change by this world, or perhaps he was always like this and he doesn´t know yet, you´re not a hero, you´re a victim of circumstances that doesn´t understand who he is and how the world ended up like this and is willing to do anything to find out, and things for him get tripy and weird ASF pretty quick. The only true negative I have for the game is that is just Part 1 of a story and that came out of nowhere, it has a great cliffhanger, but if you don´t know this is part 1 it will boil your blood to get to the end just to stop when finally we are getting some answers, something I wouldn´t have feel if the game had Part 1 on the title or something alone those lines.
Overall this adventure is amzing, it creates a very bleak but realistic view of an apocalypse and it doesn´t even rely on the old troopes like war, environmental problems, corrupt governemnts and such to create this new world; but rather a new perspective related to time itself which.
Creative, intriguing and extremely well writen this is in my honest oppinion another beggining for a great series from Daedalic Entertainment, which is becoming in later years in one of the greatest adventure games companies out there with very innovative and powerful narratives. Don´t miss this game if you enjoy the genre or the devs previous games, you won´t be disappointed.

Xcom EU/EW is easily one of my favorite games of all time.  If you don't have that one, skip this and get that.  If you do, keep reading.
Summary:
As a lot of people here have said, this is one of those games that I really wish I could give a middle recommendation for.  The underlying mechanics are mostly solid, but as people have said, the graphic problems are surprisingly bad.
Specific Areas:
Performance:
Dominions 3 is one of my favorite games...I do not generally care about graphics.  But if I could go back in time and not buy this game, I would because of how bad the graphics issues are.  I don't care enough to type up a bunch of specs, suffice to say that xcom runs worse that possibly any other game I own.  Frankly I wish they had just left them alone, because EU/EW ran at least.  While the game technically runs on the max settings, I can't see anything that is happening.  Even on the lowests settings, I'm probably getting about 20 fps and the game is extremely jumpy.  Its distracting to the point of being stressful.  The cutscenes are great, and I would be happy if the rest of the game looked half as good.  Be prepared to be constantly taken out of the moment.
Difficulty:  I don't mind the timed missions, though they can be "unfairly difficult".  But xcom has always been this way. War is not fair, and xcom has never been a game of chess.  It is more about recovering from impossible situations...or even just failing spectacularly.  Xcom 2 just ebraced the dark side.
That said, this creates a new issue that EU/EW didn't have.  Xcom2 isn't more unforgiving, because that implies that if you didn't make any mistakes you would be okay.  While I appreciate impossible situations...here they feel a little arbitrary.  This might be an odd comparison, but Dragon's Dogma handled this extremely well.  From the beginning, you could run into dragons that you had no chance of beating, but you could also just look at them and being like "yeah no way is that happening".  In xcom, there is giant pressure to do a million things at once, and any one of them may be just completely impossible given your tech level, current team, etc. You have very little insight into what you will run up against, which given how much "recon" is talked about, seems like a missed opportunity.  From what I have played so far, half the time I am collecting or securing some kind of recon, but at most it is always "hey there is a mission here".  Why isn't it ever actual recon, such as "there are 3-8 vipers in the area".  Instead I go on what seems like a story mission, and hey its a Viper King and he kills my entire team in two turns because he follows different rules than anything else and has a billion health.  Which would even be kind of okay because then the game is about how do I recover from losing an entire team, BUT NO hey one of those guys was critical to the story so I lose.  If you want to reload saves a lot that's fine I guess, but I'm only really interested in Ironman.
Long story short, Xcom2 is often not great at giving you leeway to think on your toes.
Everything else:
Its xcom, there is just more and its different.  If you can get past the stuff above, you'll like it.  I'll probably try to finish it.  Someday.  But the performance sucks enough that I might wait til I have a better computer. 5 years from now.  Maybe they'll fix it somehow and I'll change the review and get to enjoy the game.

Technical:
Updating my graphics driver definitely helped, but I still have to play on medium graphics with a core i7 nvidia 860 graphics card and 16gigs of ram... which is sad... definitely not a very well optomized game. Other than that there is the occasional bug - I've fallen out of the world once, been trapped between objects (unable to move), and experienced a series of crashes upon loading the game so far.
Gameplay:
Combat is really hard, much harder than in black flag and honestly a bit more exciting despite being much harder. Stealth combat seems to be the best way to kill early on in this game, as a group of guards will kill you if engaged upon.
The map is pretty incredible, their are lots of people on the streets and the city feels really alive. Rooftops are much easier to navigate than in Black Flag (at least so far) due to the lack of guards on them, often the easiest way to lose a group of guards is to go on the roof (so I've found). The lack of haybales is slightly disheartening, but it fits with France in this time period.
I'm not sure how much I like the co-op missions, unless you are playing with friends I haven't found a good way to communicate with your partners and that makes it really confusing. That being said it seems to work pretty flawlessly from what I've played.
Now the story is interesting but so far hasn't been incredibly exciting. From what I've found so far the storyline is a lot harder then previous Assassins Creed games due to the difficulty of the combat AI, but that could very well be because I'm terrible at fighting with the new combat system.
All in all I will keep this review negative until most of the bugs are patched and the game runs smoother on higher end PCs, but it does look like it will be a decent game once technical problems are sorted out.

Review Summary: 4 out of 5
Great so far, 3.2 hours into the game. Fans of the series will thoroughly enjoy the gameplay, and the overhauled control scheme has a learning curve, but fits right in. The "Present Day" sequences feel shoehorned in and tiresome, but I understand the need to continue the trend.
-----------------------------------------------------------------
To jump right in to the system issues other reviewers are mentioning, I am running 1080P and 45-60 FPS on full settings with the following set up:
GeForce GTX 760
AMD 6350 Six-Core
8.00 GB RAM
Windows 7 (If you game on windows 8, you're gonna have a bad time.)
I have had ZERO issues playing this game, so dont let the naysayers sour your view on purchase. The Visuals are stunning. Its very easy to see the new engine desinged for the game, and the facial expressions on the character models are beautiful. I watched the trailer many times after pre-ordering, and they simply do not do the game justice. There are a few things in the game that remind me of other Ubisoft franchises (Farcry 3's Cave mushroom sequence) and I hope there aren't many more.
The story could be so much stronger if the Modern Day sequences or cutscenes were omitted completely. They really break up the story tension and not in a good way. Just after your first kill youll be dragged right out of the setting and pace, and forced to take part in an absurd sequence that does nothing to further the story.
I also have become momentarily stuck due to interesting camera functions and strange angles. The combat is unforgiving, and unlike Assassin's creed 4, the camera does not zoom out to give you a sense of your enemies position. The game can and will punish you severely for not properly analyzing any situation you enter.
The combat is unforgiving and rewarding; the character customization is unparralelled. Just after the story is set up, you are thrust right into a rich world where you almost feel you can smell the streets of Paris and feel the environment around you. While the Combat, graphics and past story line are everything I had hoped they would be and more, the modern day sequences, though much less obtrusive that those in black flag, detract from the story flow, and could have been implemented effortlessly alongside the sequences as Arno. Im excited to see how the game takes shape as I continue the adventure.

Surprised to see the complaints. This is a phenomenal continuation of the anthology of Fallout.
As per usual in this series, you recieve a partial story line where you as the main character fill in the remainders that are missing. Fallout has its' mechanics based in the same universe as Elder Scrolls where in true D&D fashion you imagine and complete the stories within any time frame and order that you like.
The main plotline is the only guarantee, however, based on when and in what order you discover and complete side missions, in-game context is always a moving target; both in the ways that you feel and interpret interactions to the game and in the ways that the game relates to you.
With this context in mind, a true D&D adventure is never complete, never the same twice, and will always leave you wondering "What if"
Completionists will be frustrated with this game. It has no "high score" or  absolute finish. It is a saga and journey that theoretically can never end.
The crafting engine is immense and the options almost overwhelming. This game has many options and opportunities for you to configure modifications, machines, weapons, armor and even building structures. One could theoretically spend an entire month creating the perfect settlement by way of one example.
The fact that it is a risk taking leap for Bethesda is what makes it both so very good and so very frustrating at the same time. For those still considering a purchase here are a few facts to consider as of 9/1/2017 on why you should buy this game:
The game at release cost $60 (more if you bought the season pass)
The game has released 8 DLCs, which in most cases are equal to full standalone games
The game has only improved since release, as it should, which in itself is interesting to me as many games that I have bought in the last 2 years have ceased improving or developing their games within 8 mo of release.
The game is a true drop and pick up where you left off game. For those who have a busy life but want the release, relaxation and escape of an espisodic fantasy adventure, this is your game. Your wife, mom, BF, or grandma can literally walk into the room and start shouting about the backedup toilet, dog ate the couch, we were supposed to leave an hour ago, why in the hell havent you finished _______, or what ever and you can simply save the game and placate the situation immediately without the stress of loss.
Finally, it really is an eye candy experience. Few games have made good on their promise to deliver a visual experience second to none with great value and consistency. I run this game at 4k with Dual 980Ti's and I have yet to peak. It only makes me wish I could go without my wife, as I'm sure she'd leave me if I dumped the cash on a couple of Vega's or 1080's.
Now the draw backs.
You get what you pay for in a game like this. Hardware is key to meeting the extreme on visuals. There should not be an apology to anyone who cannot get this experience- life isnt fair and if its' what you want in life you must plan, create a strategy, and then execute until you reach your goal- budget, save and discipline.
The UI is burdened by aged slide trees rather than inuitive pop ups or curtain drop downs. (Of note, this game is a take on an imagined future that was made aware to the public in the 1950's, NOT the future we began to see in the 1970s- so Im not sure these UIs would have appeared)
Occasionally a person will start talking to you while you are getting it handed to you by something.
NPCs die in this game for no reason, or reasons beyond you- And somettimes this ruins the story.
There is a content store. incremental revenue is not something we are accustomed to seeing in any of the Bethesda games- this is something you would see in a money-whoring Ubisoft game.
At times, the side quest or journey is so vague that if you are restrained and do not look it up in a walkthrough, you can be scouring for hours (which incidently is where most of my most funny, insane and memorable side incidents have come from....something to think about)
It isnt co-op. What all of the Elder Scrolls and Fallout games really need is the opportunity to make a close friend one of your side-kicks in the adventure. A big gripe of mine is that you dont actually share any of the pleasure in this game with anyone unless you are recording, and even then it's no different than a real life "guess what happened" story- no matter how funny something is, it will always be a minimum of 15% less funny than when it actually happend.
Fallout 3 vs Fallout 4 isnt really a storyline departure. It's more of a "while Fallout 3 was happening, this was happening over here." Now for those who are really reading this review, and know the story, I know you are going to call me out for this not being factually correct. I wont say why because it would contain a spoiler, HOWEVER, no matter how the story arcs align in this universe, the "FEELING" is that this is a different perspective of the same thing- not something new, which is what I would expect.
Is this game worth buying?
Yes, but only if you like to use your creativity and imagination. If you like ribbons, trophies, achievements and tidy completeness- nope, not for you. Find another game.
Keying on my last comment as I wrap this up, this game is not tidy. It's far from it as is the Bethesda tradition on these games. The source of value always comes from the community and it's always the team of fans who move these games to an artistic completion.
I've played about 400 hours on the PS4 and 130+ here on Steam, maybe 100 hours on the XBOX One (I like the PS4 due to my ability to stretch out and play on the couch in front of a 60" HD TV - even though the graphics and audio experiences are sub par compared to my PC experiences).
Haters are going to mostly fall into the misunderstanding or envy bucket when it comes to this game. Either they are envious of the people who have the hardware to play this game at full tilt or they just dont understand the genre of story telling in this series' culture.

I personally do not like point and clicks and this didn't change my mind. The game is super slow paced and it has a lot of tedious backtracking in order to complete really simple and obvious grab-the-new-item-you-got-and-give-it-to-the-enemy-you-just-saw" "puzzles". The game has a musical note representation of the alphabet that you use to talk to the characters you find. But the problem is that when characters talk you can only hear the notes played, and you cannot see the actual notes. And so you have to use your music note book and try to match the notes they are playing by using trial and error. You can spend about 5 minutes trying to figure out which of the 26 notes he is playing. And that is just to figure out what letter he is saying. Often times he is saying a 4-6 letter word. And so you can spend up to 20 minutes trying to figure out just what the hell the character is trying to say. And then, after all that work you find out the "puzzle" is that he is saying "Happy". HMMM maybe I'll go play that "happy" song to the guy I found crying. So then you spend a good minute or so slowly walking ALL the way back to the guy you previous found, and you play him the notes that spell "Happy". Wow, what a top notch puzzle that was. Definitely worth that 15-20min I spend trying to figure that out.
Point is, these puzzles are barely puzzles and they are so obvious it does not feel satisfying to figure out. Majority of the game is padded out with sequences like that in which you have to figure out what the noises that characters make mean, and with the tedious backtracking. Overall there was barely a story, the puzzles were so straightforward they felt pointless, and the tedious backtracking will surely make you want to uninstall the game.
To its credit the game does have really nice ambient music and a really great pixel art style, but the gameplay just didn't do it for me. I was ready to quit when I noticed that it said I was 70% done, after about 1 hour of gameplay...and so I proceeded to finish this really tedious yet short game.
FINAL THOUGHTS:
PROS:
- Art and Style.
- Ambient music
CONS:
-Pointless puzzles
-Tedious backtracking
-Forgettable characters and story
-Very obnoxious music note alphabet puzzle mechanic.
OVERALL: 5/10

Great game, but too many game breaking bugs. I recommend the game because I'm looking at the intended finished product, but right now, I found several bugs that break the game or make it too easy.
If you are being traced and you finished all the hacks, and begin your PortHack.exe, you can disconnect, wait for it to finish, and it will automatically reconnect you as an admin. This can go around the servers with automatic proxy closing, or just be used to have infinite time on a server.
If you decide to investigate a little more on Naix's proxy after getting your x-server.sys back, you can scan and find his actual computer. You can find your own x-server.sys labeled as [YourName]x-server.sys under /home, and if you delete the x-server.sys under /sys then you can become friends with Naix and you will continue a short "side quest" of sorts. However, if you want to reply to the email that told you to hack Naix, it will say mission incomplete, even if you have done what it asks. No way to fix it as far as I can tell, meaning you can't advance beyond that point. This can be avoided by ignoring Naix's computer and just doing what you are told.
And on to the biggest, worst, most game breaking glitch of all. *Drumroll please*.
Once you get to the CSEC mission when Vapor wants you to look for Bit, you will find a file on his repo station that is decs encoded. If you have finished all the contracts you know how to trace the encoding to find the password for Decypher.exe, but it's unhackable. This is because it does not tell you how many ports must be open to get through, and if you open them all you will still be unable to use your PortHack.exe. This is not the glitch, settle down people. The glitch is that you are unable to reply to Vapor with the IP, meaning you can not progress from this point. There is no way to avoid it, there is no way to fix it. That's the end of the game, wait for a patch.
Please Surprise Attack, fix these glitches. Although if I may be a bit rude, you should have tested this game a bit more or released it on early access instead of making it the official release. You have some work to do, so get to it!
The gameplay itself is fun, I love it, but I just can't play more than a one hour session without being unable to progress. So this is going to be unnoticed in my Steam Library for quite some time, but I will check it occasionally to see if I can finish the rest of the game.

If you were a hardcore Long War player, you can kinda get closeish to it with enough mods but the game probably won't be for you. If you weren't a hardcore Long War player, occasional bugs aside XCOM 2 is a complete and total improvement over EUEW in my opinion. Something as simple as your squad taking overwatch shots one at a time makes it almost impossible to go back to EUEW after playing XCOM 2 without getting frustrated.
Mission timers can sometimes feel a little cheesy but are pretty much never short enough to make you feel like you have no option but to over-rush, mostly the classes are conceptual improvements over the vanilla EUEW classes (though as fun as swords are with the right balance tweaks I do miss the original Assaults sometimes) and, blasphemous though it may be to some, the removal of the air game is frankly good riddance. It's not until you play XCOM
it that you realise how actually-kinda-dull the air game really is.
With that said, there are plenty of minor gripes. Shotguns are a little too strong in relation to assault rifles, I used to play a lot of riflesaults in EUEW and expected I'd want to do the same with blademaster rangers but it's just suboptimal to do so. Swords are stupid weak in comparison to concealment rangers. There are other problems too, but I can't really bring myself to complain too much about them purely because every single problem I've had with the game so far has been fixable through mods, .ini tweaks or a combination thereof.
Thoroughly and wholeheartedly reccomended whether you played/liked EUEW or not, but do be forewarned that it's got a bit of Skyrim syndrome. The vanilla game only feels fun until you've played the game absolutely plastered with mods, at which point going back to vanilla feels empty and weird.

Edited review, still keeping 'no' vote. And I have more than two hours in this because I'm a semi-completionist for those who are curious:
TL;DR: Great concept of strategy rpg, but very buggy, very simple strategy, very basic rpg and some of the most obvious padding and Macguffins I've ever seen.
There is a game-breaking camera glitch. This glitch happens when certain cutscenes/dialogues end; your camera is forced to an awkward location, set looking at the sky or something. You cannot see the world and cannot therefore order units effectively or interact with quest objects. There is a patch that 'seems' to fix most instances, except the dwarven camp where I needed it to fix it. You can mash the space bar/escape button to rush through/skip dialogue. That seems to avoid the camera bug, but NPC behavior can get wonky, since sometimes (at least once) NPCs might need to spawn or despawn during cutscenes.
Another bug where you sacrifice 'light worshippers' and one of them doesn't walk properly. Going into 3rd person and bumping her seems to fix. But readers can see the game is buggy. This is all apparently because of the way they mashed two games together to make the 'Gold Edition'. Reminds me of what I've heard of the Homeworld re-releases: apparently not-breaking code during a copy-paste marathon is harder than it sounds... But I'll go onto the game itself now.
The story involves you getting reinforcements to stop an army and save your village/city. So you convince a count to give a letter of recommendation (LoR) to a baron, after saving the count from annihilation. You escort the count's son and some supplies to the baron, who you save from annihilation in return for a letter of recommendation to the king. The count's son escorts you to the king, who says 'no'. But there are others who might rally to the cause, you have to convince them to join and bash through the enemy's fortress from behind, because that is
There's a part where you have to wake a passed-out drunk dwarf. That involves a four-part quest with at least four NPCs. The word that describes this is tedious. Much of the plot is 'we need to go to X' but the only way to X happens to be through Y and Z levels. So out of 20 or so regions, 10 of them are padding and 5 or so more hold MacGuffins. Great.
You have armies, including semi-unique 'titan' units, which are as ROFL stomping-forgot your bubblegum-s**t just got real-as you'd expect. But I'd rather have the player become that way, well, eventually. For a little bit. Well, anyhow... The strategy element is kiiinda okay, except the difficulty is very arbitrary and base-building is very formulaic. Example: one mission you need to free captured orcs by beating a human base. Except, for no good reason there are giant spiders attacking your base constantly. And when you beat the humans you get surprised dialogue about 'the spiders are coming', suggesting the spiders should have only started spawning at this point. The game also feels like is was made with the Warcraft 3 map editor, with some voiceovers added.
You also get access to different cool races! But how this happens is the previous race that you can finally use with all their units, the race whose territories you just saved from annihilation or lead to impossible victory, they give you the finger and for no good reason your defeated foes now trust you to lead their forces. It's just a little better than "Message from the developers: you're going to play the next part of the game with this new race, starting from the ground up again. Have fun!"
There are other gripes, but this is my second REwrite of this review, so I'll leave the smaller things to others.

Alright, I'll concede it's a game now. The new hotbar is absolutely TERRIBLE, the reworked character sprites are slightly worse, and you have to go through a LOT of crap at the mercy of a completely random low-level loot system before you're even permitted off of your starter planet and out of your starter system. Digging implements besides your matter manipulator are entirely an afterthought now, which is kind of sad because the old progression from pickaxes to drills was really fun.
But they actually made the combat decent. Subterranean exploration isn't nearly as awful and tedious as it used to be. The old summon-on-demand bosses are gone and replaced with much more challenging and interesting instances. As long as you can manage to get the game working, it SEEMS to be much more stable and optimized than it ever was.
It's not the game I was hoping for. A lot of fun stuff from the older builds (particularly mobility techs) are sadly gone for good, and there are a lot of features that ended up underdeveloped or abandoned. (Space combat and mechs, anyone?) But it is a pretty fun experience in its own right.

I liked it at first but after playing for a while and seeing what it's all about, I have to say I'm very disappointed.
Let's put aside the terrible RNG system for the moment (worst I've seen by far) and focus on the gameplay.
The "First" XCOM game (The first by Firaxis anyway) was alright. It couldn't touch the real first X-com game in terms of atmosphere and gameplay, but it was alright.
At first glance, XCOM2 has some improvements, namely in the graphics and customisation of soldiers to some extent (Though they have put more voices in the game, there are still only voice actors for British English, American English, Australian English, German, French, Italian and Spanish soldiers. Nothing for Japanese, Chinese, Russian, African or any others. Still, it's better than the "first" game in that regard.
XCOM2 takes place some time after the story of the 2012 game. The aliens have taken over the world and run it in an EU/Communist sort of way, rife with propaganda and harsh punishments for non-conformity. Funny, since I finished XCOM and seem to remember kicking the aliens' heads in. A bit of disparity there which is not explained.
The part where XCOM2 really falls apart is in the gameplay. Gone is the hidden, underground XCOM base. Gone are the fighters and thus, the UFO interceptions.  Now you have the "Avenger" which, quite amusingly, looks a lot like the flying aircraft carrier in the Avengers movie. The idea is to liberate humanity in this game utilising guerilla tactics and working with resistance cells and black markets to secure victory. To this end, missions will appear on the map and you will fly to them in your mobile base when they are offered, avoiding any UFOs that are tracking you down and unable to shoot them down yourself. The joy of storming a downed UFO to secure tecnology and corpses is notably abscent and replaced with more of the pop up "some stuff is going on, click this botton to do a random mission and be punished if you ignore it" chores. It just doesn't feel like XCOM. Whether this is a conscious effort to leave the old behind and embrace the new, is unknown, but it certainly feels like it.
I find myself modding it a lot and I'd thank god if I believed in one for putting steam workshop into the game. I just had to get rid of the "Avatar" timer... a timer which will continually tick down, pushing you to complete the game as fast as possible.
Overall, there is just nothing really new to this game, despite the obvious (slight) graphical updates. It's a lackluster title which has me pining for the good old days of XCOM where you could sneak up on aliens properly and they didn't get a free turn to go and take cover after YOU spotted them. We had cover back in the oldest days of XCOM too you know... it was called "standing behind a wall". Oh and the cover system? Even worse than the first reboot game - now soldiers will shoot through floors, trees, walls and over solid objects, with no attempt at all to ever disguise that fact.
This game is just so lazy in my opinion. It could have been so much more, but after the relatively good reboot of 2012, it's just a resounding "meh" in terms of scope and direction - more of the same: out with the good, in with random pointless stuff that they will insist is an improvement.
I bought this game on sale and still feel a bit ripped off. While there is some fun to be had, there is far more in terms of frustration. And modding. Lots and lots of modding to "patch" this game's glaring, chore-like gameplay.

Note: I received SQUAKE for free from the developer and chose to review it.
SQUAKE (all caps) is a multiplayer arena battle game based on the classic 'Snake' game.
Rather than a snake, in SQUAKE you control a weird snake-train thingy that gets longer as you pick up extra carriages from the floor of the arena, but if you're familiar with Snake, you'll pick up SQUAKE pretty quickly.
SQUAKE's graphics are great! The little snake-train thingies speed around, blowing smoke from their engines, exploding, and leaving nice, smokey trails behind them. Arena graphics include large blades and attractive little large-particle fire pits.
I did find the arenas a bit confusing at first -- particularly the bunkers -- as they look quite busy, but once I worked out which parts I could enter, and which lines on the background were just part of the background and which ones represented walls that would kill me, I got the hang of it pretty quickly.
Graphics options seem to be non-existent: I couldn't find any settings whatsoever. The game starts in full screen mode ran well on a new gaming laptop.
There's no music, which I found a bit odd, except for a little ditty at the end of each level. The title/lobby screen could really do with some music, and background music for the levels wouldn't go astray either.
Sound effects are acceptable. There's nothing special about them, but nothing cringe worthy either.
SQUAKE plays like Snake. It's that simple.
There are additions to the classic game, of course, and I don't just mean the pretty graphics. It's multiplayer, for a start, with each arena populated with a host of other snake trains for you to avoid or destroy as you desire. It also has a few different game modes, including carting dynamite to your opponent team's base, and trying to hold the title of longest snake train for a set period of time. And there are collectibles -- buffs and debuffs -- and upgrades and levels and all that sort of goodness. But it's still basically Snake, and that's not a bad thing, because anyone can pick it up and play it, and even with no instructions or tutorials it should only take you a few minutes to grasp what you have to do in each arena.
The developers have added tasks to try to keep you interested and increase the replayability, too. The game includes up to three seemingly random challenges available at once, which include things like creating a train of only one colour of a certain length, finishing in the top three of a designated game mode, or dynamiting a base a certain number of times. These provide you with credits, which you can then spend on upgrades, which either increase buff times or decrease debuff times, giving you a slight edge against other players. There are also pretty smoke effects that can be purchased with credits, but these may only be active for a limited time -- I'm not sure.
The real let down for SQUAKE is that it's online only -- even when only playing against bots -- and the ping is terrible. When I first started playing I thought the controls were very weird, with significant lag between when I pressed a key and the movement on screen of my snake. I also noticed that I'd crash into other snakes that weren't there anymore, and collision detection just seemed a bit off. Then I noticed the ping reported in the bottom left. I don't know where the servers are located, but playing from Australia I had a pretty constant 375 ms -- more than double what I get with
to a USA server, but just about right to Western Europe, so I can only assume there's only one server farm, and it's somewhere there. From reading the Steam Community Discussions for the game it looks like I'm not the only one, either, as a number of people have posted that their ping times make it unplayable. This really needs to be addressed in an online-only game like SQUAKE, where a third of a second makes a huge difference in whether you manage to keep building up your 100-odd carriage snake train or you're just another explosion trailing smoke in your wake.
I can see why the developers have gone with an online-only approach, and it does make for a seamless transition when new players join or leave a game, but it does mean that the ping issue becomes important for bot games as well. And in a bit over an hour of play so far, I've only managed to play a game with one other person, even though there are apparenty "11 Online" in one of the game modes right now.
Other than the very high ping, which is definitely a problem, but not really a bug as such, I found two issues that I would call bugs, although these were both in an earlier version of the game and may have been fixed now. The first was a crash to desktop in the middle of dropping off dynamite in the bunker arena. My 'snake' was long and made up of both colours of dynamite, and a blade cut through the middle part way through the drop off, so I'm guessing that was what caused the crash. The other was seemingly random rebounds off of nothing, where my snake would change direction suddenly for no reason in the middle of an arena. I suspect this latter issue was somehow due to the high ping.
Pros:
+ Easy to pick up and play
+ Very addictive
+ Pretty graphics
+ In-game challenges and Steam Achievements to keep you playing
+ Trading cards
Cons:
- High ping makes playing more frustrating than it should be
- Only limited game modes and arenas
- Not enough information on server populations, locations, pings, etc.
- No way to customise your in-game name or 'snake head' appearance
SQUAKE is actually a lot of fun, it's just a shame that the high ping makes it so much harder to play than it should be, even in single-player mode, since the developers have opted for online only. If it weren't for this I'd be happy to recommend SQUAKE as a fun casual game that anybody can play. Instead, I'm much more hesitant. Recommended, but only if you can be sure you'll have a good ping.

Disappointingly unfinished. That's the main issue, and if you ignore everything else, at least be forewarned that if you buy this game currently (as of October 2017), you are buying half a narrative. There are, of course, plans for a sequel to be released. But in a world where even the biggest name studios can't seem to finish their narrative arcs, I find it hard to trust any promises to complete a story until I have the full thing in hand.
Aside from that, this game is a flawed gem at best. What it does well is create an interesting, if grim world. The most intriguing concepts are, sadly, only hinted at and left as hooks for the sequel.
On the negative side, the game seems to be trying way too hard to be dark. We get it, the world sucks and everyone is dying. But it's so overdone that it's like painting in black on a black canvas. It doesn't bring out the darkness even more, it just makes it veer beyond tragedy and into farce. And of course the traditional adventure game cliches of the protagonist being an amnesiac who steals everything not nailed down, in order to solve sometimes nonsensical puzzles, just highlights the absurdity even more. Beware of eye-rolling. This also isn't helped by the voice acting, which ranges from awkward to stilted.
All that said, I would probably still recommend this game if the sequel existed. It's worth playing through for the things that it does do right, even if it has issues. But since it currently only exists as half a story, that's a hard no from me.

This game is great! If you are a fan of the XCOM series I highly reccomend it. If you are a new fan there is a tutorial but it might be a little frustrating at first.
I thought this was the perfect sequal to Enemy Unknownl; they added all the soldier customization, map randomization, bug fixes (mostly), and mission type variation everyone wanted. The ability to choose soldier classes is great (through some minor training) as well as the ability to save soldiers you make to a character pool. That way you don't have to remake soldiers in every game if you have very specific characters and it makes it fun to run into them randomly. The autosave is lovely and absolutly life saving though it does feel like you end up with an overwhelming amount of saves in a very short amount of time. It's very fun, addictive, frusterating (in a good way), and it very quickly became my absolute favorite strategy game.
There are a small handful of draw backs to the game but some of these may have to do with my setup. The loading times are rather long- I have all settings at the lowest and there are still pretty intense frame rate drops at the begining of mission cut scenes. The central command map is atrocious. Every time you need to travel farther than a contintent you have to finagle the whole thing jumping around far too quickly and putting you at the bottom or top of the globe. That part really handles poorly.
With all that said I would still put this game in my top three and highly recommend it to any fan of strategy games. If you are new to the genre I'd highly recommend XCOM: Enemy Uknown first. (Though some people may disagree and say go for the originals I believe that this is the most 'user friendly' title in the XCOM series).

1 Disappointing Thing: The story wraps up REALLY quickly at the end, and the creators basically just explain how all of the mysterious things are connected, most of which the player could have almost pieced together on their own. More disappointing than this is that you are given the impression that you'll have some further missions to complete, and very little is given to indicate that your current condition would prevent you from being able to do this, but then the game just ends with things unresolved. I'm not one to insist on closure in narratives, but as a player, this was really unsatisfying for me. I'm not sure if the creators had a series (or at least sequel) in mind from the start, but this game is definitely not a standalone narrative.

The game itself is great, with the new features succeeding in freshening up the core XCOM gameplay. The only problem is that you need a pretty decent machine in order to run it well. But, if you got the power, you'll find it is quite worth the cash.

Xcom EU/EW is easily one of my favorite games of all time.  If you don't have that one, skip this and get that.  If you do, keep reading.
Summary:
As a lot of people here have said, this is one of those games that I really wish I could give a middle recommendation for.  The underlying mechanics are mostly solid, but as people have said, the graphic problems are surprisingly bad.
Specific Areas:
Performance:
Dominions 3 is one of my favorite games...I do not generally care about graphics.  But if I could go back in time and not buy this game, I would because of how bad the graphics issues are.  I don't care enough to type up a bunch of specs, suffice to say that xcom runs worse that possibly any other game I own.  Frankly I wish they had just left them alone, because EU/EW ran at least.  While the game technically runs on the max settings, I can't see anything that is happening.  Even on the lowests settings, I'm probably getting about 20 fps and the game is extremely jumpy.  Its distracting to the point of being stressful.  The cutscenes are great, and I would be happy if the rest of the game looked half as good.  Be prepared to be constantly taken out of the moment.
Difficulty:  I don't mind the timed missions, though they can be "unfairly difficult".  But xcom has always been this way. War is not fair, and xcom has never been a game of chess.  It is more about recovering from impossible situations...or even just failing spectacularly.  Xcom 2 just ebraced the dark side.
That said, this creates a new issue that EU/EW didn't have.  Xcom2 isn't more unforgiving, because that implies that if you didn't make any mistakes you would be okay.  While I appreciate impossible situations...here they feel a little arbitrary.  This might be an odd comparison, but Dragon's Dogma handled this extremely well.  From the beginning, you could run into dragons that you had no chance of beating, but you could also just look at them and being like "yeah no way is that happening".  In xcom, there is giant pressure to do a million things at once, and any one of them may be just completely impossible given your tech level, current team, etc. You have very little insight into what you will run up against, which given how much "recon" is talked about, seems like a missed opportunity.  From what I have played so far, half the time I am collecting or securing some kind of recon, but at most it is always "hey there is a mission here".  Why isn't it ever actual recon, such as "there are 3-8 vipers in the area".  Instead I go on what seems like a story mission, and hey its a Viper King and he kills my entire team in two turns because he follows different rules than anything else and has a billion health.  Which would even be kind of okay because then the game is about how do I recover from losing an entire team, BUT NO hey one of those guys was critical to the story so I lose.  If you want to reload saves a lot that's fine I guess, but I'm only really interested in Ironman.
Long story short, Xcom2 is often not great at giving you leeway to think on your toes.
Everything else:
Its xcom, there is just more and its different.  If you can get past the stuff above, you'll like it.  I'll probably try to finish it.  Someday.  But the performance sucks enough that I might wait til I have a better computer. 5 years from now.  Maybe they'll fix it somehow and I'll change the review and get to enjoy the game.

I really wanted to give this game a positive review and until today I was pretty sure it's going to happen. Let's start by saying, that I've played both main Spell Force games when I was much younger and it was great to remind myself why I enjoyed these games. It's very good combination of rpg and strategy. So why the negative review?
Well... First of all, this game is better than the first one. I find it hard to believe that someone without sentiment towards first Spell Force would have a different opinion. Plot is solid, in both games, but Spell Force 2 has better graphic, better music and most importantly, better controls. It's also much better paced. You finally don't feel like you wasting eternity just going from one point on the map to another. It has aged much better that the first game, it's still very enjoyable, you don't get the feeling like the camera or characters movements are clunky. Strategic elements of the game were also improved. The only thing that I've enjoyed better in the first Spell Force was the fact, that it has definitely more freedom in terms of creating your own character.
As for Spell Force 2 itself...
Pros:
+ interesting plot
+ original and well done mix between strategy and rpg
+ game is truly challenging
+ great music
+ interesting and useful spells/special abilities that unlocks when you level up
Cons:
- low resolution
- lack of truly interesting quests
- gaining another level doesn't really feel that rewarding
- pretty limited character creation
- dialogue scenes are essentially broken - characters not always shows up or does not shows up properly
- BUGS.
Yeah, I'm sorry, but how can you recommend a game that basically make you feel like you've wasted 16 hours of your life playing it? I am really understanding, I'm not the type of person who gets over frustrated and never wants to play a game after encountering a less or more serious bug. Sure, it's pretty annoying, but if it can be fixed somehow, if I can replay some sequences or just restart the whole mission, I'm still going to do this. So I've encountered few serious, game breaking bugs. Two times restarting missions worked. In other instance, skipping the dialogue was an only way to avoid being literally stuck in the void. And now... Well, now I actually can't finish my quest, because even though I've done everything that was needed to be done, even get a note in journal to go back to the person that is crucial for moving the plot forward... Well, this person does not want to talk to me. At all. There's no scene. No dialogue. Nothing. Replaying the sequence and the whole mission didn't work.
Maybe this game works better on older systems (I don't remember having this sort of problems in the past), but with this amount of serious bugs it's not really worth a recommendation. Buy it only if you want to replay it or just remind yourself the whole series.

Pros:
+ A free platformer with truly challenging gameplay that feels fresh.
+ Includes variety of unique levels (from everyday kitchen to dark underground sewers) that get increasingly difficult.
+ Beautiful hand-drawn animation and visuals. Each level comes with its own unique visual theme, with amazing effects like lighting and particle.
+ Simple yet adorable playable character. You play as a water drop navigating variety of obstacles to reach each level's end zone.
+ Thanks to science, you are granted with the ability to change from one state to another (depending on your environment). For example, in order to reach high places, you can touch a steaming hot pipe to convert yourself from liquid to a puff of steam that float upwards. But your journey will end soon if you go on forever without any replenishment.
+ If the previous point is somewhat complicated, just remember you have a very cute personality.
+ Inspiring soundtrack reminded me of World of Goo.
+ It can be one of those games that feel rewarding (if you manage to overcome its difficulty and shortcomings). Or it can be a very rage-inducing experience.
Cons:
- Framerates tend to drop during certain levels. For a game like Drop Alive, this is quite odd. I suspect lack of optimization in different places.
- Some levels exhibit questionable level design. These often lead to frustrating moments that require you to try the same obstacles over and over again.
- Sluggish controls. Combined with unpredictability in framerates, some questionable level design and checkpoint system, you will be getting a game that is both challenging and ridiculous.
- Settings menu does not work. For example, I could not change the resolution. There's not a lot to customize in the settings menu either.

(Edited slightly just in case the 0% helpful rating is because the tone of my review seemed condescending. If it's just 'cause my suggesitons don't work for you... YMMV!)
So far I've played several hours so far over a few sittings and LOVE this game. To be fair, I like games that can, at times, vex me with their difficulty. Darkest Dungeon is meant to challenge your ability to manage your characters' health (including diseases), stress, money, supplies, equipment, traits and skills while balancing risk vs reward.
Folks complaining about RNG and difficulty level: It's possible this just isn't your kind of game. You've already heard the "cry moar, game is supposed to be hard" line from other reviewers, though, so here's some helpful advice if you ever want to give this game another try:
1. Don't start each quest with the mindset that you will absolutely win. You can run from battles and leave dungeons prematurely, and you should do these things whenever you think things are getting bleak.
2. Make sure you train up at least TWO full parties (4x2 = 8 characters) so you can trade off when the first party needs a rest. If you can avoid it, don't let any character go questing with more than 50 stress.
3. If you lose a higher level character, be willing to train the new one in lower level quests. Train multiple low level characters together if you're replacing multiples. This will also have the added bonus of earning you a surplus of gold.
4. Skip exploring whenever you can to maximize your chance of finishing a quest. This means:
- If you do a 90% scouting mission, remember you can skip one room guaranteed in a short quest, possibly more in longer quests. Choose wisely to skip rooms at a dead end to preserve health, resources and stress levels.
- If you do a 100% room battles mission, try to bring characters that have high scouting chance (pretty sure there are character/class specific traits that can ensure this). That way you can check whether particular hallways or rooms have battles and potentially bypass the ones that do not.
- If doing a quest that has a boss battle, skip as many unnecessary random chance events or battles as possible, and save your strength for the boss.
5. When provisioning, always buy a surplus of torches (the game says 4, but I bring a min of 10). Generally you want to keep radiant light level as much as possible because luck is generally better for you (particularly when it comes to surprise chance. Getting the jump on monsters is a huge plus.) Also don't ever leave without shovels (at least 3). As for food, 12 units at a minimum works for me (they can double as low-grade healing in a pinch).
6. Try to always have some sort of healer in your party. Vestal is generally the best right off the bat for this as they have access to both a group heal and a single target heal. Arbalest has a very handy healing skill, good in a pinch since they're also generally fast. Occultist's Wyrd Reconstruction has a large range and bleeds the target but is the best single target heal in the game. Crusader can heal both health and stress (and doubles as frontliner). Jester has one of the best stress heals, good to keep your party from going over the brink.
7. Ideally bring at least a couple of characters with group damage skills (hit more than one enemy at once). Some of my faves for this are Highwayman, Grave Robber and Arbalest.
8. Take advantage of status effects. Stun is great--keeps targets locked down until you can deal with them. Use party buffs that increase dodge chance. Use Mark to increase damage dealt on enemies or to make your tank a target.
9. To take out single threatening targets, make copious use of Bleed and Blight (for undead particularly) effects. I've noticed they stack from different sources, which can add up to incredible damage over time.
10. Besides treating your party's stress levels, keep up with treating their diseases and negative quirks at the Sanitarium. These give some annoying (and in the case of disease, HUGE) penalties that will make your characters easier to kill. There's also a whole bunch of negative quirks that can force your party members to interact with dungeon features, which is extremely inconvenient when you're trying to minimize stress in order to complete a quest.
11. This is a bit of a repeat of #1, but if you ever feel any sort of doubt your party can survive its current quest, retreat from combat. If you're absolutely desperate, abandon the quest. Yes, you won't get the quest reward, but you'll live to fight another day, and hopefully you've collected enough treasure and curios by then that abandoning isn't an total wash.
12. If the game is getting too frustrating despite your best efforts to be careful, e.g. you just lost a character you spent hours training in a cheap shot, or you've retreated from the fourth dungeon in a row and you're low on money, go play something else for a while. If after some time, you still feel revulsion and no urge to return to the game, then go ahead and leave that negative review.
I would still argue the game has done exactly what the devs set out to do, which is make a game where you're always stuck making the best of a terrible situation, but doing so doesn't necessarily translate to a game fun enough to be worth buying. So even if I disagree, I get it.
