Welcome to the game. This game is not hard. This game
challenging. It tests both perserverance, and your abilities. You'll need to make yourself forget a couple of things. Firstly, forget that you will come into this game with experience from other games and use it to your advantage. The combat in this game is something you have never seen before, but i'll explain more later. The second thing to forget, is your rage. You will die. A lot. And, other than having your anger filled screams being quite annoying, they will do nothing but slow down your progress, make it harder to learn from your mistakes, and generally make your game a ♥♥♥♥♥how. Suspend your frustrations, and you will find these challenges less annoying. Now, lets get into it.
The presentation of the story is a great aspect of this game. A lot of games like to put the story down your throat, which is not necessarily bad, it's just how most games work. They have to flesh out a world, a story. If i'm playing D&D, there is an expectation of story to be told. If I watch a movie, I expect a certain amount of narration just to set my view of the world up. Its the same in games. But, Dark Souls is different, for a couple reasons.
First of all, the story is fragmented. Its no Skyrim, with hundreds of books to weave together into a full fleshed game as the storyline is far from complete, and leaves much to personal interpretation. That's not to say the story is made lazily, or without effort. Whether the developers specifically made it like this, or it was just a side effect of creating holes to fill in in another sequel, it can't be denied that these leave some pretty convenient holes. Regardless, the story is set up in a way that if the player has (atleast) brainpower of a small fruit, they will slowly build theories based on the lore to fill in said holes. It's why you can see a lot of debate over the history of the lore itself amonst fans (though we'll talk about the
later). It's pretty neat having to piece together a lost story, rather than being a scholar and hitting those books to learn the lore.
One of the other things about the story that makes it unique, is that
Off the top of my head, I am pretty sure there are only 3 cutscenes that have anything to do with the story; Two of those are the intro and the outro, and all cutscenes are skippable. As for the rest of the lore, it's all delivered in item descriptions and vaguely in dialogue from characters. An interesting way to deliver lore, but effective at that.
Dark Souls has good AI. Most of the time. Most of the time, these NPC's will also be able to kick your♥♥♥♥♥ You'll need to learn spacing, timing, poise, parry timing, toxic resistance, dodging, blocking, and 40 other things.
This is far from impossible. In fact, most of the things listed (Timing, dodging, blocking, etc.), you will grasp pretty easily. But mastery will take a long while. And these are how you master the enviroment, and by extension the game. Be cautious, be alert, practice, and have fun.
The general enemy populace is, well, interesting. Whether you're level 3 or level 300, these guys can still kill you if you aren't careful, or if you have a stroke of bad luck. That is one of the most interesting things about this game in my opinion. Grinding is often tedious and boring, so often people tend to let their minds wander, and are inattentive. You cannot do this in Dark Souls III unless you master the things listed on the last paragraph, which most, well, just can't. (Neither can I, so I say that in the least narcissistic manner.) As for the bosses, they are mostly hit and misses. Don't get me wrong, when they hit, they do it well (Insane Dragon man with Invisible Baby being eaten halfway through the fight? One of the coolest boss fights i've ever finished!) however, some of the bosses are a 'meh,' and some are even worse. You almost forget about them. (Champion Gundyr? That fight was a 'meh' for me. It was just the same boss tweaked a bit. And I couldn't even remember Vordt on my second character.)
PvP in DS3 looked promising at first. I had a lot of fun dueling with friends and trying out different builds and setups, and coming up with fun ways to create weird and wacky builds. (Try the winged knight armor with the lothric knight greatsword and Yorm's greatshield. Being a juggernaut is fun to try and play.) However, here's the thing. The 'meta' right now is poise builds. Now, you don't need to know what it is, and you're free to go look, but just know that its terribly hard to counter with anything but another poise build, or a player that is really skilled in spacing and skirmishing. So yeah, it may be fun playing with your friends, but there is rarely a deviation from the normal meta build in actual PvP with strangers, which often just makes it a game of 'how can a squeeze a few more poise points into this character?' It quickly loses flavour once you experience that three or four times.
This game is suprisingly beautiful, and well optimized. I've never dropped below 30 FPS, except in the loading menus, which are, of course, usually a frozen frame anyways. Some of the views are breathtaking, but to be honest, I missed a lot of them due to the constant threat of enemies. Loading times are short, and there are a lot of graphics options if you need to turn some down. Overall, its suprisingly scenic routes might be overlooked, but it is certainly not lacking in it's beauty.
The fanbase, although it has gotten better about it, still likes to flaunt its 'This game is not for anybody but the most hardcore' flag around, which more oft than not turns people off to the game. I do not play games in a 'hardcore' fashion. I probably played DS3 three times a week. I still made it to soul level 231 and to the third new game. (New game +++) I played PvP as a Blade of the Darkmoon for more than 40 hours. Most of all, I had a fun time playing it. So take your 'only hardcore players can be good at Dark Souls' and kindly shove it.
A lot of people (including a couple of my friends) like to preach this game like the new age of video games, like its so good other games just aren't enjoyable or challenging enough to compare. I'm not going to. I think it certainly has some features that make it a great game in all respects. But I don't consider it 'hard.' Its combat is different and has a learning curve, and its strategy in swordplay is certainly dizzying if you spend too much time on it. Don't take it the wrong way, this is one of the best games i've played in a while. But I won't make it out as some revolution in game design that it isn't. I think people far too often fall into a confirmation bias with the game, where they point out parts of the game that were supposedly designed in a perfect way (Sometimes despite how little or accidental the feature may seem) And that all badly or otherwise shoddy designing was simply an accident or oversight, and couldn't possibly have been an idea gone wrong or a stupid design that someone approved.
I dunno. That's my review with a little rant stapled on, free of charge (minus your electricity and internet bills :S)

During your adventure, you have to find items to help you get past obstacles, and there are a few hidden treats for achievements, but overall, I enjoyed my time with Finding Teddy and would recommend it.

Bayonetta is a masterpiece in the hack and slash action genre, and to have it release on steam with a fantastic PC port allows this game to shine again. Gameplay is fluid and just feels so right. This has to be one of the best controlling hack and slash games to date. But it's not for the faint hearted. You will be punished for even the slightest mistake. The soundtrack needs to be spoken of, because its stellar. The way it melds with gameplay to create tone and atmosphere pumps you up for every moment. The story is your usual over the top action from platinum games but Bayonetta's character really shines. She's sassy and extremely likeable for an anti-hero. It's refreshing to see instead of the moody sterotype these characters tend to end up as.
There's also a wealth of replay-value. You will only see the very basics on your first playthough and on subsequent sessions you can unlock new characters, abilities and some pretty neat cosmetics. You're constantly rewarded for the time you put in, which a lot of modern games find diffcult to do. The only negative I can truly push onto this game is the small amounts of platforming might take away from the fast paced combat. But regardless; Bayonetta is outstanding. Simply a must have.

I don't need to exalt the virtue of Bayonetta as a title - Its one of the best, if not THE best Spectacle fighter on the market. Excellent art, design, combat mechanics and gameplay pacing combine this into a near perfect game.
And now it's on PC for a reasonable price? Hell yeah.
Video:
Text:
Ok, so it's a game from 2010, and while it's showing its age graphically in places. Especially in terms of ground textures, tessellation, foliage and AA / color depth. In terms of its animations it feels like a release of today. Fluid animations that flow and choreograph the combat and gameplay flawlessly and it's exactly that flawless gameplay that makes this game very much NOT an outdated title. Obviously, the unique artstyle and worldbuilding don't harm the title either.
That said, this isn't new - and the PC Version doesn't add anything to that excellent mix. But what it does add is a nice mix of resolution support up to 4k (no ultra-wide though) and a solid performance at 60FPS (locked to 60). Adding to that is support for keyboard / mouse with rebindable keys, that while not fully recommended for this type of game, works surprisingly well.
While the graphical options leave something to be desired they are not a major point of complaint overall, outside the fact that the AA settings don't appear to have any effect and there is some serious screen tearing with Vsync disabled.
That said ... at the end of the day its a $20 dollar release for an still excellent title on a stable PC Port. I'd be insane not to scream my recommendations for this one from the rooftops. Bayonetta is excellence, wrapped in a bow of awesome.

XCOM 2 is definitely a game with a few issues, mainly in the performance department. That said Firaxis have been supporting the game and patching it to solve issues many have had. I can run the game fairly decently, and enjoy my time with it.
It's also a turn based game, and while that's no excuse, a lower FPS than 60 is still playable here. The gameplay itself is a step up from it's predecessor, with you taking on the role of Guerillas rather than Soldiers. It's an interesting take on the franchise as you'll be the one making the decisions on when to attack and ambush rather than the other way around.
In the first game you'd overwatch crawl your way to victory, trying to avoid activating pods in unfortunate scenarios. With Enemy Within, meld was an incentive to do more than just crawl across the map, and it worked fairly well. XCOM 2 expanded on that idea with a good chunk of missions having a timer where you'll fail the mission if you don't complete it in time. It's a bit contrived but gets the job done, however to make up for this you start most of these timed missions in concealment allowing you to pick when to engage and blow your cover.
It's not a stealth game, I still have yet to complete a single mission without 'alerting' the aliens, however the stealth system does allow you to do something you had a harder time doing in the first game, ambush the enemy and pick when to engage.
The gameplay itself has a lot of mods in the works, and is much easier to mod than the first game. Already there are plenty of mods that add new enemies, soldier customizations, voice lines, and map parcels (Maps in XCOM 2 are randomly generated so they get less static than the ones in the first game). There's nothing on the level of Long War for Xcom 1 yet, but the possibility is there and if the community makes the effort to create something like that, I'm sure it can be done.
Is XCOM 2 a worthy successor to the first game? I'd say so. Is it a replacement for the first game? Well, the first game with no expansions I'd definitely say so. However is it a replacement for Enemy Within? No, I'd suggest anyone who's yet to try XCOM try out Enemy Within first, however I do think XCOM 2 is simply better than Enemy Within (Optimization aside).
I'd put it like this, Long War for XCOM 1 has more depth than XCOM 2, however XCOM 2 is far superior to Enemy Within and Enemy Unknown. I'd also argue that XCOM 2 is an easier game on the harder difficulties, however mods already exist that can tweak the game to be harder or easier to whiatever suits you.
Whether it's worth the price of admission is up to you, but with Steam refunds being a thing I'd certainly suggest trying it and giving it a shot, especially if you're a fan of the first game. If strategy games with a bit of chance are your thing, then XCOM 2 and it's tense engagements will certainly be for you.
Edit: I've read a few negative reviews and most focus on the timed missions and Strategic side of the game. Here's the thing, the timers prevent you from simply crawling up the map without taking many calculated risks. If you dislike the timers you can edit them in LTX files or download mods from the workshop that elongate or remove them.
As for the Strategy side, many were complaining that they didn't have enough time to do everything available there before getting into a mission. That's the point, with Advent controlling the world you'll have to make decisions about where you dedicate your resources. You'll usually be able to get one of the 'resource blips' before a mission, but not all of them. It's about choosing which one you think is more important to you, going for it, and then doing the mission.
What's nice about XCOM 2 is that failing a mission or skipping a mission isn't a death sentence like it was in the first game. Yes on higher difficulties missing early missions can be terrible, however there are ways to get around this. Missions simply aren't as impactful, they're still important...But you have ways of getting around the cost of failure.
You may have failed a mission and lost a Veteran soldier, but you now have ways of acquiring new soldiers for resources you have. Managing your resources is an important part of the strategic side as I mentioned, and they're much more important in XCOM 2 than the first game. Not only can you get new soldiers but you can get Scientists and Engineers as well, though it's important to remember you'd miss out on other things such as making new contacts, or getting some weapon upgrades. You can even spend resources to rush some research or building if that's what you'd like to try doing.
The types of strategies you can emply thanks to these extra systems are just another bit of depth outside the Tactical game. So yes you won't be able to get everything available on the world map, you'll have to pick and choose. The thing is, you have much more to do resource wise, and many more decisions to make that add depth to the game.
Also important not to forget, thanks to how easy it is to modify the game and how open the devs have been with this, you can change things such as timers or how long collecting resources takes yourself or by looking around on the workshop. Hope this helps clear a few things up and spread some light on a few issues I've seen people have.

Let me start off by saying that yes, this game has some graphical problems.
I have an i7-3770, 16gb RAM, and an EVGA 670 FTW Edition with 2GB of RAM.
I have not toyed around too much with the graphical options but I can run at high settings with 30 to 40 frames.  It rarely ever drops below 30 unless it is a cutscene which drops it into the teens sometimes.
I have noticed that every few seconds the average gamer will be able to notice a millisecond long stutter, which is gets to be annoying but I have looked past it and it's whatever.
There are some problems with distant textures looking like textures from an N64 but I have not yet tested to see if a higher texture setting will fix that.
I also had a problem on the last Versailles mission where I crashed in the same spot 4 times in a row.  I restarted my computer and I made it thorugh the sequence just fine.
(And please be aware 30 fps is MORE than fine to play this game with.  Anyone who says differently only seeks to hate Ubisoft because that is the cool thing to do these days)
Through all of these things though, this game is BEAUTIFUL.  Everything is so pretty.  Go inside Notre Dame, the work found there is jaw-dropping (especially if you are like me and love everything about the real Paris).
Gameplay-wise: So far- the story is solid, I have been hooked, I am engaged, and it's better than Black Flag's so far.
The parkour is the best the series has to offer, after you get used to jumping into windows that is.  Never before has it felt so easy and so smooth.  They have really outdone themselves here.
The combat is WAY better than previous series.  They did NOT lie when they said they made it harder.  The fights are much much longer in this than before.  In Black Flag I would just fight loads of guards because I could.  In this one, I find myself running from large groups more often than I engage them.  That is definitely a plus for the series.
Overall, I find this game a spectacular addition to the series.  Paris is a marvelous setting and it is really done well, from what I have seen.  I have by no means been everywhere.  Yes, Ubisoft have not optimized this game like they need to.  It does run very ineffeciently, but if you have a machine that can even run this game at medium, I would REALLY recommend you think about buying.  If you are, however, intent on smearing Ubisoft just because you can, or you don't realize that games can and do have bugs, please just stay off the internet.
I would give it, from what I have seen so far, an 8.5/10.  The 8.5 mainly due to the inefficient performace and texture pop-ins.  Gameplay is a solid 9.

Spiral Knights is a chibi-style MMO dungeon crawler that encourages build building and gear engineering as the two things that will save your life against the monsters found in the Clockworks. The game was previously available as a standalone title but became Steam integrated, and has become one of the most popular free to play games to pioneer the genre.
The graphics are designed to be simple, stylistic, cute, and attractive. You'll find even the most monstrous of enemies to be some of the most adorable creatures in gaming, and the world itself to be heavily influenced by both steampunk and dungeon aesthetics. The game runs well due to its simplistic nature.
The balance of this game is based on a tier system, going from zero to five stars. In general, you can assume all weapons that fit into a single star level, ie one star, will be equal. There are some exceptions, most notably the bombs, but the situational effectiveness of these weapons outweighs their lack of general usefulness. You are encouraged to switch weapons at the start of every new level, to use your statuses and damage types to your advantage after learning the design of each level of the Clockworks.
The items system is based on a helmet and armor for defense, whilst offense includes two-four weapons depending on your buffs. The weapons can be swords (or hammers, maces, shovels, and machetes,) guns, or bombs. These items focus on one or two damage types, which will be more or less effective against enemies depending on their resistances. Some weapons also feature status effects, which in addition to doing extra damage, add even a second layer to effectiveness against only certain enemies. An additional tertiary type - trinkets - exists. These trinkets give small, varying bonuses such as defense, resistances, or health.
Most items in this game blend together in sets, giving you bonuses for combining certain items. This encourages owning multiple different sets, to properly fight everything the game has to offer. In addition, the four player coop allows you to fight with your friends where each person fills a specific niche role, combining to allow you to fight everything a level can offer.
The general 'idea' of this game is to make your way to a boss at your current tier. The world is split up into three tiers, and multiple different progressions down each tier. At the end of each progression through a tier, you fight a boss, which gives you exclusive loot and crowns (the game's currency.) Alternatively, you can use the relatively new missions feature to take a more story-based approach to the world, and fight everything the game has to offer at a good pace. After the fighting has cooled, you are brought to Haven, a public ground where you can do just about anything you expect from an MMO. Guild halls, an auction house, a training ground, and most importantly; vendors and crafting. Vendors sell items, sometimes exclusive for tokens or crowns. The crafting stations allow you to make items with a mixture of materials you find throughout the world, energy which you can purchase with crowns, and a recipe which you either earn from missions or purchase from the marketplace.
The progression of this game is wonderful, allowing you to slowly rank up and even engage in player versus player modes. You will slowly go from a weak, no star recruit to a five star knight of whatever specialization you choose to create. This truly engrosses you with your character, creating an attachment that can be tangible and real. You will truly come to love that cute little knight running around slaying cubes of grape jelly.
Servers are all official servers, as per usual with an MMO. The connection is good but unstable, where server disconnects are known to the playerbase but are relatively rare.
The story of this game is rather simple. You are a young knight in a seemingly desolate area who must help the army around you both rebuild and conquer the Clockworks. A simple premise, for sure, but an intriguing one. The missions system, which has not been a constant feature of the game, has added to this story and allowed it to blend seemlessly with progression.
The business model of this game is weak. A free to play game at its core, you can hop in and technically play the entire game in its entirety for free. Originally, to play more than ten levels a day you had to pay money to unlock more energy to keep going. This feature was removed, but with it, many prices were raised outside of that cost. This means that the game allows more grinding per day, but will take longer for that grind to be worth something. I would say this is a good thing as it encourages playing more per day than just playing for an hour a day. The prices are still definitely affordable.
Overall, this game can be fun for everyone; veterans of MMOs, young kids who enjoy the art and simplicity, or casual gamers looking for a cooperative experience. Stay for the cute art, the grinding and character building, or the engaging combat.

First off I'd like to say that I knew what I was getting into when I dropped the 60$ on this game. I knew Ubisoft's previously release of Watch_Dogs was sub par, I had also pre ordered that game as well. I also knew that my specs were borderline minimum when it came to the horsepower required to run the game.
BUGS
I didn't expect to run the games top notch graphics settings, and thats not even where my gripe is. There were obvious bugs right from the start that weren't caused by my hardware. If you have a mid-range computer I would definitely find this game a tough sell.
*Some cut scenes would just skip part of the scene and place me ahead of the story line. It would also do this if I died during a cut scene instance. It just didn't seem like it was very streamlined.
*The shadow flickering was horrendous and almost stopped me from playing altogether. I played around with some graphics settings (which are sparse) and finally got it to stop.
*Constant stuttering. While I understand this could be hardware related, I went ahead and tested it in various parts of the maps. My character continues to stutter even in areas with very low clutter.
*I'm sure you've heard about the hair glitch, floating hair that seems to drift at odd times.
*The "Initiate" program doesn't seem to work for me when I attempt to do anything with it. (more on this later)
*Ai just acting straight up odd. Glitching through roofs, floors, running in odd areas. (kinda like all the previous games including watch_dogs)
*A few CTD's (could be hardware)
STORY/ GAMEPLAY (**NO SPOILERS**)
Outside of the bugs I enjoyed myself quite a bit, with a few hiccups along the way.
*The main missions are a ton of fun and you have quite a few choices to make when tackling these.
*The parkour is better than the last few installments and is probably the best part about the game as a whole. Trekking the city and just looking at every detail that goes into each inch of the world. Unfortunately the movement is plagued by many of the same issues such as, you're still frequently getting stopped in your tracks from either bad pathing, or odd obstacles. The downward parkour (new) is nice for sure but doesn't act how i expected either. Sometimes Arno jumps impossible heights without taking damage or suffers from the same issues as the upward parkour and goes a path you didn't wish him too. Some paths that seem like they should be, are not.
*The combat is much slower imo and rugged, it's fun but there isn't really anything revolutionary about it. In the beginning the enemies seem to be tougher but there are only a few enemy models so their patterns are easy to learn over time.
*It seems to be that they tried to make this game much tougher without certain upgrades from either your equipment or weapons. While I'm a veteran gamer I enjoy the challenge this brings. I can imagine a more casual gamer getting frustrated over how the parkour, combat, and AI work together. Maybe even frustrated enough to buy some "hack" points? (**We'll talk about this later**"
*The side quests are mostly one dimensional requiring you to fetch something or kill this, some of them have arcs that keep going. The eventual feel of these quests is grinding though.
*They mix in a combination of 5 or so random crowd events (pickpocket, criminal, police vs revolutionaries, templar vs whomever.) these happen often and you get rewards for doing them. They are redundant to say the least.
*None of the characters are really that intriguing. They seems to be cookie cutter Templar vs Assassin attitude.
*The crowds themselves are quite massive but, but for the most part they stick to a particular spots. Theres obviously roaming people from street to street, but there doesn't seem to a concious of the AI. Once again there are only so many models and some many outfits/colors. They don't react to you directly or your deeds you've accomplished. I kinda expected the city to be more "alive," at the time period it was a very turbulent and the city was of the edge. This is not the feeling the game gives off at all.
*Customization is better than the previous installments but once again nothing revolutionary. There are plenty of outfits and you can individually pick head, chest, pants, gloves, and belt. You CAN NOT choose your own colors but from the pallets given which include three colors per pallet.
*Menu's are a step up from the last couple games but seem to be super laggy. Map loads laggy, and there is like a billion icons on it ( you can choose which ones show up but there are still things that pop up that you can even access like Red and Gold chests)
*I managed to do one Co-op mission without friends, either people disconnect, or leave. Some just troll. I did not try again because it was annoying. It sucks that i'm driven away by this type of feature.
MONEY STUFF
This is where we get to the money game, which they seem to have put an awful lot of time. There are several currencies:
Franks are used to buy consumables, outfits, weapons, and property.
AC points(whatever that symbol is) which is a "abstergo" increment of money used to upgrade weapons and buy colors for the outfits.
Hack points are the microtransaction increment. You can buy everything in the game with these points if you have the real life dolla bills to throw down. This is where I get a little irritated. What it feels like they're doing is slowing down progression in various ways.. getting to places feels slower (possibly because our character runs slower on a 1:1 ratio of paris? Idk), combat is slower. Leveling seems to take forever, which also means I don't get to use all of the abilities throughout the entirety of the story.
In combination with the Initiate program... which you have to sign up for.. to unlock certain items.. so that you can eventually buy them. There is also mobile apps i've yet to download that unlock other in game♥♥♥♥♥♥ This also allows you to open up certain Red and Gold chests. So basically theres stuff in the game that you can do because you haven't downloaded all the crap yet on all your devices.
So what this feels like to me is a they've added a grind to the game so you either
*dump tons of time into if you want to complete everything, and buy everything.
*OR buy upwards of 100$ worth Hack points so can buy better equipment earlier, or buy boosts to level up or w/e.

I came extremely close to refunding this game, but I chose to write a review instead. Maybe I'll change my mind in the future, because I really did want to like the game. Art's nice. Atmosphere has a good dark gothic tone, and the gameplay tries to reflect that, but fails in my opinion.
This game is a pseudo-Lovecraftian horror dungeon crawler where sanity/stress plays a part in your dungeon delving. My first experience with the game was relatively enjoyable, but game mechanics which at first seem interesting very quickly turn into obnoxiously tedious obstacles to actually enjoying the game. You gain a new affliction EVERY time you go into a dungeon because it's impossible to not get up to 100 stress for at least one party member and there's a good 90% chance you get an affliction from that. Only dodged it twice in three hours of play. And once that happens, your heroes start to think that skipping all their turns is a good idea and the entire game just becomes infuriating. Stress can only be removed by engaging in town activities, but OOPS, there's only one ♥♥♥♥ing slot per unless you spend 3 dungeons worth of heirlooms to upgrade it, and each activity costs 1000+ gold, so to de-stress all your heroes it takes all the gold you made on your last run as well. And you need to go on an expedition for those activities to take effect which means running with a second group, which is probably also already stressed, and collecting new afflictions for them as well. Gotta catch em all. Stress accrues at a rate far beyond the rate at which you can remove it, if you can at all. Most classes don't have an ability that removes stress, and the ones that do remove 6, and when you're already gaining stress every turn, and all your heroes are♥♥♥♥♥♥talking each other because that's a great mechanic, adding more stress, it's like♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥in the ocean trying to abate the stress buildup, and all the while wasting turns on top of it. Saying that the stress system is more unbalanced than a one-legged elephant on stilts would be to put it lightly. You can't carry nearly enough torches to keep the light up for longer dungeons, and camping feels pitifully useless, especially when you've already gotten stressed AND YOUR CHARACTERS DENY HEALING ABILITIES. Stress is an interesting idea for a game mechanic. I like the idea, but not the implementation. Certainly not when it's completely unmanageable.
This game does rogue-like wrong. There's no way to prepare for the things you'll face, or manage the problems your heroes rapidly accrue, and it all just snowballs downhill starting from the very first ♥♥♥♥ing mission. It's not challenging or complex, it's a slap in the ♥♥♥♥ing face for all your efforts, and then the game tries to tell you that you like it that way.
♥♥♥♥ off. Don't buy this game. Especially not for the full price tag.

I don't need to exalt the virtue of Bayonetta as a title - Its one of the best, if not THE best Spectacle fighter on the market. Excellent art, design, combat mechanics and gameplay pacing combine this into a near perfect game.
And now it's on PC for a reasonable price? Hell yeah.
Video:
Text:
Ok, so it's a game from 2010, and while it's showing its age graphically in places. Especially in terms of ground textures, tessellation, foliage and AA / color depth. In terms of its animations it feels like a release of today. Fluid animations that flow and choreograph the combat and gameplay flawlessly and it's exactly that flawless gameplay that makes this game very much NOT an outdated title. Obviously, the unique artstyle and worldbuilding don't harm the title either.
That said, this isn't new - and the PC Version doesn't add anything to that excellent mix. But what it does add is a nice mix of resolution support up to 4k (no ultra-wide though) and a solid performance at 60FPS (locked to 60). Adding to that is support for keyboard / mouse with rebindable keys, that while not fully recommended for this type of game, works surprisingly well.

Well, first and foremost I am a dark souls fan so my review will be both biased towards Dark souls gameplay, and a little critical of the other aspects most may ignore, namely the world and atmosphere of the game.
Dark souls III continues the in the same spirit of the souls series. In case you don't know, that means this game is quite difficult, both in the combat, and your initial level of control. New players will find this game rather unforgiving as enemies do high damage (about the same as you) and are very aggressive. Your controls are going to be a bit sluggish at first, but trust me when I say that veterans of this series can get through the entire game without ever dying if they try. You will get used to it. The game is difficult, but it leaves nothing to chance, meaning that while you are as frail as every other enemy attacking you, you can conceivably block or evade every incoming attack if you are good enough. And the fact that most enemies are as fragile as you means the game is tough, but also fair, as it is very possible to get through the game without ever dying. Though be warned, if you are new YOU WILL DIE. This is part of the game.
Compared to the previous games, the gameplay is faster than both DSI and DSII, and a bit more fluid and responsive. This is the first Dark Souls game I have played where taking on three low level enemies is entirely possible if you are moderately experienced simply because of the surprisingly long range of most weapon's hit arcs, and the quickness of some smaller more reliable weapons (longsword ftw). The enemies have been ramped up to balance this as well. Also, for miracle users and sorcerers, the scroll system where you would have a limited number of uses per spell, has now been replaced with a mana-pool like from demon's souls. The mana pool usually starts out small, giving you a limited number of uses compared to the scroll system, however, ashen estus flasks have been introduced, allowing you to replenish mana via these flasks. Overall this makes magic/miracle builds more viable than previous games.
The gameplay is good no doubt, and don't get me wrong, I love this game, but if you love something you sometimes have to show it tough love. That being said, I really feel this game lacks its own identity unlike the previous two games. Too many aspects of the game, such as the fact that Anor Londo still exists, and the 'hub area' is called firelink shrine, and all the constant references to the first game, all make this game feel like its reveling in the shadow of the first game and very poorly establishes its own plot, its own continuation of the souls series. I like references every once in a while in any game, but with this game it feels continuous. Not to mention almost all the references feel like they are from the first game, which i dislike. I really loved Dark Souls II despite people's constant complaining that it was different from the first game (yes lords forbid we make a new game that does things somehow not exactly like the first, otherwise it would just be DLC). This game feels like it's trying to distance itself from the established plot to some degree. Overall, storywise, this game just feels lacking compared to the previous two titles, and I am a little disappointed.
Another minor criticism is that this game is ambush-happy. Seriously, nearly every room in the beginning of the game has something trying to hide around a corner, or pop out trying to give you a big sloppy kiss. This isn't a huge complaint, because you can easily spot most of these ambushes if you are reasonably cautious and paying attention to your surroundings. Being paranoid also helps. This doesn't ruin the game though and it kind of mellows out in the late game.
Overall, I would give this game an 8/10. Its good, its fun, I'm still going to play the heck out of it, but its just not quite as good as the other two games in my opinion, besides the basic gameplay upgrade (which should be a given if this is the third game in the series). The ending were particularly disappointing, just due to the lack of atmosphere that the previous games had in their endings. Though to be fair, I have definetly seen worse, although you will probably be confused the first time around.
Oh, also the pvp is just as broken as the first two games, so no change there. Play in offline mode if you want to avoid getting griefed by hacking invaders.

Homemade Tortilla (for 8 servings)
Prep : 30 mins
Cook : 25 mins
Ingredients :
- 1 3/4 cups all-purpose flour
- 3/4 teaspoon salt
- 1/4 teaspoon baking powder
- 1/4 cup vegetable shortening
- 1/2 cup hot water
Directions :
1. Whisk flour, salt, and baking powder together in a large bowl. Add vegetable shortening and work into flour mixture using a pastry cutter until it resembles coarse crumbs.
2. Form a well in the middle of flour mixture and mix in hot water. Work flour and water mixture together with a fork and transfer to a cutting board.
3. Knead until a smooth, soft dough is formed, about 3 minutes. Add more flour if dough is too sticky.
4. Place more flour on cutting board, cover dough with bowl, and let rest for 15 minutes.
5. Cut ball of dough into eight equal parts and cover until needed.
6. Roll out balls of dough either by hand or with a tortilla press.
7. Heat a large skillet over medium-high heat. Place flattened tortilla in skillet and cook until it begins to bubble, about 1 minute. Flip tortilla over and cook for an additional minute. Flip again and cook for 1 more minute. Repeat with remaining dough.

You also cannot upgrade your hardware, bounce your signal all over the world before hitting your target (goes to trace time), and there is no passive search (that I have noticed) going on on the background, which means that either I'm really carefull in removing my tracers or the police will never actually go looking for you.
It is however, very true to the feel of the game. So if you like your hacking games with old-school typing and none (okay, a little) of that sissy-pants clicking with mice this is definately a recommended title for your library.
Interesting side-note; You get to hack into someone's pacemaker to fullfill his wish of being euthenized. It's stuff like that that bring this game a new moral level.

-Insultingly easy, you need to go to a planet thats not recommened for your character just to have a slight amount of challnege
-No mods worth talking about
-Guns are basiclly airsoft
-No depth in the combat (whack whack whack)
-Unlike what the devs said prerelease, robots can eat human food, monkies can eat bird food, etc etc. Your character is essentially just a reskin. Do you want to be the bird one, the chimp, the human, or the robot (glitch master race)
-Decent music but a real ear sore after several hours of play
-Ships are clostrophobic, and you cannot edit their size without a buggy mod
-NPC ai is so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that it will kill itself trying to reach you (jump off cliffs, fall into lava/poison)
The only good things i see in this game are
-Character animations (only for movement, everything else is generic swatting)
-World design (although like i said earlier, it looses its charm after you find out its just a reskin)
-Space travel (as dull and lifeless as it may be, its fun for a bit to explore in your space ship while playing Space oddity
-Soundtrack, but as stated, it gets on your nerves after a bit due to the lack of variety for each world type. Lots of tracks in general, but not enough for each area
Decent concept, executed poorly. Very poorly
This game goes on sale fairly often, buy if its onsale if you reeeeeeally wanna spend 10 dollars on a terraria rip off with some half decent (half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ space travel
Just keep in mind, for that 10 dollars, you could buy a couple gallons of gas and drive somewhere and see new things. Rather than sitting on your♥♥♥♥♥playing with computer toys
